lectures.title: Innate immunity
lectures.covers: Where immune cells come from, the cells and receptors of innate immunity, and its three effector mechanisms: phagocytosis, inflammation and NK-cell killing.

items.p: The immune system keeps the organism intact. It protects against pathogens and danger signals, and it takes part in cancer prevention and defense.
Innate immunity is the first line of defense. It acts within hours, before the adaptive response (days) is ready.

ul: Recognizes common patterns, not specific antigens
Rapid: present before exposure or reacts immediately
No clonal expansion and no memory
Not transferable
Stimulates and shapes adaptive immunity

items.p: Most immune cells are made in the bone marrow. T cells are made there too, but mature in the thymus.
Some tissue-resident macrophages, such as microglia in the CNS, come from the yolk sac or fetal liver during embryonic life.

ul: Primary lymphoid organs: bone marrow and thymus
Secondary lymphoid organs (where cells do their work): lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils, mucosal tissue
Myeloid progenitor: megakaryocyte/erythrocyte and granulocyte/macrophage lines, mast cells, dendritic cells
Lymphoid progenitor: T cells, B cells, NK cells
Avoidance: barriers, physical and chemical (antimicrobial proteins)
Resistance: effector mechanisms that attack the pathogen
Tolerance: the tissue becomes better at resisting damage, without lowering pathogen fitness

items.p: Disease tolerance is not the same thing as immunological tolerance.

table: Lives in tissues; main phagocyte there; orchestrates the response with inflammatory mediators
Circulates; short-lived; most numerous innate cell; main phagocyte; dies after entering tissue
Third phagocyte; main job is antigen presentation (best APC) and activating other cells
Parasites too large to ingest; allergic inflammation
Matures in skin, gut and airway mucosa; histamine granules; worms and type I allergy
Innate lymphoid cell (group I); kills tumor and virus-infected cells; early antiviral defense

items.p: Small proteins (about 25 kDa) released after a stimulus. They act through specific receptors.

ul: Autocrine: same cell. Paracrine: neighbors. Endocrine: distant cells through blood.
Families: IL-1, interferons, TNF, hematopoietin
Hematopoietin receptors signal through JAK kinases, which activate STAT transcription factors

items.p: Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) detect PAMPs from pathogens and DAMPs from damaged tissue.

Injured tissue releases metalloproteinases and hyaluronidases. They cut the extracellular matrix, and the fragments trigger inflammation. Necrosis releases many DAMPs; apoptosis releases few and is cleared silently.

ul: TLRs: on the plasma membrane or in endocytic vesicles; sense extracellular microbial products; activate NFκB and IRF, giving inflammatory cytokines and type I interferons
Humans have 10 TLRs. TLR-4 senses LPS of Gram-negative bacteria.
NLRs: cytoplasmic sensors; some activate NFκB, others form an inflammasome (NLRP3) with cell death and pro-inflammatory cytokines

items.note: The slide lists lipoteichoic acid as sensed by TLR-1:TLR-2 and TLR-4. Standard texts give TLR-2 heterodimers for lipoteichoic acid and keep TLR-4 for LPS. Answer the exam from the slide.

items.p: Receptors that trigger uptake: complement, Fc, scavenger and C-type lectin receptors. G-protein coupled receptors drive cytokine production.

ul: Bind, engulf (membrane zips up), phagosome, fusion with lysosome, phagolysosome
Killing: lysosomal enzymes, reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide (iNOS: arginine to citrulline)
NADPH oxidase: O2 to superoxide. Deficiency causes chronic granulomatous disease.
Superoxide dismutase: superoxide to H2O2. Myeloperoxidase: H2O2 plus chloride to HOCl.
NADPH comes from G6PD (HMP shunt)

items.p: NK cells kill without priming. The decision is a balance between two kinds of receptor.

ul: Inhibitory receptors recognize MHC I on healthy cells: no killing
Infected or tumor cells often lose MHC I: the brake is gone
Activating receptors recognize stress molecules on infected or tumor cells; a strong signal can override inhibition
Killing: perforin and granzymes from cytotoxic granules
NK cells also secrete IFNγ and TNFα, which boost macrophages and dendritic cells

cards.q: Which lymphoid organs are primary, and which are secondary?
cards.a: Primary: bone marrow and thymus. Secondary: lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils, mucosal lymphoid tissue.
Yolk sac or fetal liver, during embryonic development (not from bone marrow monocytes).
Pattern recognition, rapid, no clonal expansion, no memory, not transferable (and it shapes adaptive immunity).

cards.q: Avoidance, resistance, tolerance: what does each mean?
cards.a: Avoidance = barriers. Resistance = effector mechanisms against the pathogen. Tolerance = tissue resists damage better, pathogen fitness unchanged.

cards.q: Which cell is the most numerous innate cell and a short-lived main phagocyte?
cards.a: Neutrophil
Antigen presentation (best APC) and mediators that activate other immune cells; not clearance of microbes.

cards.q: Cells for parasites too large to phagocytose
cards.a: Eosinophils and basophils (mast cells protect surfaces against worms)

cards.q: Where do mast cells mature, and what do their granules hold?
cards.a: In peripheral tissues (skin, intestine, airway mucosa); histamine.

cards.q: What makes innate lymphoid cells different from lymphocytes?
cards.a: They lack antigen-specific receptors. NK cells are group I ILCs.
JAK tyrosine kinases, which activate STAT transcription factors.
PAMPs (pathogen) and DAMPs (damaged host tissue)

cards.q: Which enzymes generate DAMPs from extracellular matrix?
cards.a: Metalloproteinases (MMPs) and hyaluronidases (HYALs)

cards.q: TLRs: location, and transcription factors activated
cards.a: Plasma membrane or endocytic vesicles; NFκB and IRF (inflammatory cytokines, type I interferons)
TLR-4

cards.q: NLRs: location and the named inflammasome
cards.a: Cytoplasmic; NLRP3 inflammasome (cell death and pro-inflammatory cytokines)
Chronic granulomatous disease (no superoxide in the respiratory burst)

cards.q: Which enzyme makes hypochlorous acid in the phagolysosome?
cards.a: Myeloperoxidase (from H2O2 and chloride)

cards.q: How do phagocytes make nitric oxide?
cards.a: iNOS converts arginine to citrulline, releasing NO.

cards.q: What switches an NK cell off?
cards.a: Inhibitory receptors recognizing MHC I on a healthy cell.

cards.q: Why are virus-infected and tumor cells vulnerable to NK cells?
cards.a: They often lose MHC I (no inhibitory signal) and show ligands for activating receptors.

cards.q: How do NK cells kill, and which cytokines do they secrete?
cards.a: Perforin and granzymes; IFNγ and TNFα.

cards.q: NK cells versus cytotoxic T cells: priming
cards.a: NK cells kill without priming; cytotoxic T cells need priming by antigen-presenting cells.

questions.stem: Where do microglia, the resident macrophages of the brain, originate?
questions.explanation: Most immune cells arise from bone marrow (T cells mature in the thymus); tissue-resident macrophages such as microglia originate from the yolk sac or fetal liver during embryonic development. A: Other macrophages can come from monocytes, not microglia. B: T cells mature in the thymus. C: Not immune. D: Most immune cells, but not microglia.

questions.stem: The immune system is described as responsible for maintaining the integrity of an organism. Besides protection against pathogens and danger signals, which role is named?

options.C: Storage of iron in peripheral tissues
options.D: Control of body temperature set point

questions.explanation: The slides give two roles: protection against pathogens and danger signals, and involvement in cancer prevention, development and defense. B: Not listed as a role of the immune system in this lecture. C: Not a role given for the immune system. D: Not listed among the roles of the immune system. E: Clotting factors are not mentioned as an immune role.

questions.stem: Once mature, where do immune cells reside according to the lecture, and which organs are classed as primary lymphoid organs?

options.A: Once mature they reside in the bone marrow and thymus; primary lymphoid organs are the lymph nodes and spleen
options.B: Once mature they reside in the bloodstream and lymphatic system; primary lymphoid organs are the bone marrow and thymus
options.C: Once mature they reside in the bloodstream and lymphatic system; primary lymphoid organs are the thymus and spleen
options.D: Once mature they reside in the yolk sac and fetal liver; primary lymphoid organs are the bone marrow and tonsils
options.E: Once mature they reside in the lymphatic system; primary lymphoid organs are the bone marrow and mucosal tissue of the bowel

questions.explanation: Mature immune cells reside in peripheral tissues (bloodstream, lymphatic system). Primary lymphoid organs are the bone marrow and the thymus. A: Bone marrow and thymus are the primary organs; lymph nodes and spleen are secondary. C: The spleen is a secondary lymphoid organ. D: Yolk sac and fetal liver are embryonic sources, and tonsils are secondary organs. E: Mucosal tissue of the bowel is secondary lymphoid tissue.

questions.stem: A child's tonsils enlarge during a throat infection as immune cells do their work there. What kind of organ is the tonsil?

options.A: A site where T cells mature

questions.explanation: Primary lymphoid organs: bone marrow and thymus. Secondary (where cells do their job): lymph nodes, spleen, tonsils, mucosal tissue. A: The thymus, a primary organ. B: Not its role. C: Not its role. E: Not its classification.

questions.stem: Which cell arises from the common lymphoid progenitor?
questions.explanation: HSC → myeloid progenitor (megakaryocyte/erythrocyte, granulocyte/macrophage) and lymphoid progenitor (T, B, NK cells and other ILCs). A: Myeloid. B: Myeloid. D: Myeloid. E: Myeloid.

questions.stem: On the time-after-infection figure, which components act within hours (the first 12 hours) rather than days?

options.A: Epithelial barriers, phagocytes, B lymphocytes, complement and effector T cells
options.B: Phagocytes, dendritic cells, complement, antibodies and NK cells
options.C: Epithelial barriers, effector T cells, dendritic cells and complement
options.D: Epithelial barriers, phagocytes, dendritic cells, complement and NK cells
options.E: Phagocytes, complement, NK cells, antibodies and effector T cells

questions.explanation: The figure places innate immunity (epithelial barriers, phagocytes, dendritic cells, complement, NK cells) in the first 0–12 hours and adaptive immunity (B cells, antibodies, T cells, effector T cells) over days. A: B lymphocytes belong to the adaptive arm that acts over days. B: Antibodies are adaptive and appear over days. C: Effector T cells are adaptive (days). E: Antibodies and effector T cells are adaptive (days).

questions.stem: Which feature belongs to innate rather than adaptive immunity?

options.C: Memory that speeds a second response
options.E: Responses that grow with each exposure

questions.explanation: Innate immunity: first line, recognizes common microbial patterns, rapid, no clonal expansion, no memory, not transferable, shapes adaptive immunity. B: Adaptive. C: Adaptive. D: Adaptive. E: Adaptive.

questions.stem: A host limits damage from an infection by increasing a tissue's capacity to resist microbe-induced injury, without reducing the pathogen load. Which host strategy is this, and how does it differ from the other two?

options.A: Resistance; avoidance relies on barriers and tolerance on effector mechanisms
options.B: Tolerance; avoidance relies on effector mechanisms and resistance on barriers
options.C: Avoidance; resistance relies on barriers and tolerance on effector mechanisms
options.D: Resistance; tolerance relies on barriers and avoidance on antimicrobial proteins
options.E: Tolerance; avoidance relies on barriers and resistance on effector mechanisms

questions.explanation: The three strategies are avoidance (barriers), resistance (effector mechanisms) and tolerance (responses that enhance a tissue's capacity to resist damage induced by microbes). A: Enhancing tissue capacity to resist damage is tolerance; resistance uses effector mechanisms. B: Avoidance is barriers and resistance is effector mechanisms. C: Avoidance means barriers, not enhanced tissue capacity. D: Barriers belong to avoidance, and the scenario describes tolerance.

questions.stem: Which statement about disease tolerance is correct according to the lecture?

options.A: It promotes host health by lowering pathogen fitness through innate and adaptive effector mechanisms
options.B: It promotes host health while having a neutral to positive effect on pathogen fitness
options.C: It is another name for immunological tolerance toward self antigens
options.D: It prevents pathogen entry through physical and chemical barriers
options.E: It protects the host by reducing tissue capacity to respond to damage

questions.explanation: Disease tolerance protects the host by promoting host health while having a neutral to positive effect on pathogen fitness; it is distinct from immunological tolerance. A: Lowering pathogen fitness is resistance; tolerance has a neutral to positive effect on the pathogen. C: The slide stresses that disease tolerance is not to be confused with immunological tolerance. D: That describes avoidance. E: Tolerance enhances the tissue's capacity to resist damage.

questions.stem: Barriers are the "avoidance" level of defense. Which feature makes a barrier chemical rather than physical in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The slide lists physical and chemical barriers, the chemical one being production of antimicrobial proteins. A: Interferons are listed as antiviral activity, not as the chemical barrier. B: This is the NK killing mechanism. D: This is the inflammatory response, not a barrier. E: Complement is listed as a separate innate mechanism.

questions.stem: Which cell arises from the common myeloid progenitor?
questions.explanation: The common myeloid progenitor gives macrophages, granulocytes (basophils, eosinophils, neutrophils), mast cells and dendritic cells. A: Lymphoid. B: Lymphoid. C: Lymphoid. E: Lymphoid.

questions.stem: Monocytes and macrophages can both phagocytose. Why do macrophages do most of the phagocytosis?

options.C: Macrophages are more numerous in blood

questions.explanation: Macrophages reside in almost all tissues, where most infections occur; they phagocytose and orchestrate the response by producing inflammatory mediators. A: They can phagocytose. C: They reside in tissues. D: Not stated. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: Tissue macrophages can arise by two routes. Which pair is correct?

options.A: During embryonic development, or from circulating monocytes that migrate into tissues and differentiate
options.B: During embryonic development, or from circulating neutrophils that migrate into tissues and differentiate
options.C: From the common lymphoid progenitor, or from circulating monocytes that differentiate in blood
options.D: From dendritic cells in tissues, or from the yolk sac after birth
options.E: From mast cells that mature in peripheral tissues, or from fetal liver monocytes in adult blood

questions.explanation: Macrophages either arise during embryonic development or from circulating monocytes that migrate to tissues, where they differentiate. B: Neutrophils die after migrating to tissues; monocytes are the precursors. C: Macrophages are myeloid, and monocytes differentiate after migrating to tissues. D: Dendritic cells are a separate phagocyte class, and yolk sac origin is embryonic. E: Mast cells are a separate lineage.

questions.stem: Within hours of a skin abscess forming, which cell, the most numerous innate cell, dominates the site?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils: mainly circulating, migrate to tissues then die; short-lived; the most numerous innate cells and the main phagocytes. A: Resident, but not the most numerous. B: Parasites and allergy. C: Virus-infected and tumor cells. D: Antigen presentation.

questions.stem: Dendritic cells are the third class of phagocytic cell. What is their main role?
questions.explanation: Dendritic cells migrate from the marrow to tissues; their main role is producing mediators and presenting antigen (the best APCs), not clearance. A: Not their main role. B: Mast cells. D: Plasma cells. E: NK cells.

questions.stem: Which statement about dendritic cells is correct?

options.A: They are the third class of phagocytic cells, arise from the common lymphoid progenitor, and lack phagocytic ability
options.B: They are granulocytes with a granular cytoplasm that defend against parasites too large to ingest
options.C: They migrate as immature cells to skin, intestines and airway mucosa, where they mature and their granules store histamine and other mediators
options.D: They are the third class of phagocytic cells, migrate from bone marrow to tissues, and are the best antigen-presenting cells
options.E: They are group I innate lymphoid cells with an elaborate membrane that kill without priming

questions.explanation: Dendritic cells are the third class of phagocytic cells (after macrophages and neutrophils), migrate from bone marrow to tissues, and are the best APCs. A: They derive from the common myeloid progenitor and do phagocytose. B: This describes eosinophils and basophils. C: This describes mast cells. E: Group I ILC and killing without priming describe NK cells.

questions.stem: A helminth too large to be ingested by neutrophils or macrophages invades the gut wall. Which cell is specialized to defend against it?
questions.explanation: Eosinophils and basophils defend against parasites too large to be ingested and contribute to allergic inflammation. B: Cannot ingest it. C: Cannot ingest it. D: Not specialized for parasites. E: Antigen presentation.

questions.stem: Where does a mast cell complete its maturation?
questions.explanation: Mast cells leave the marrow immature and mature in tissues (skin, intestines, airway mucosa); histamine granules; defense against worms; type I allergic inflammation. A: It leaves immature. B: T cells. D: Not stated. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: The common lymphoid progenitor gives rise to lymphocytes and to innate lymphoid cells (ILCs). What distinguishes ILCs such as NK cells from lymphocytes?

options.A: They arise from the common myeloid progenitor
options.C: They mature in the thymus before release
options.D: They require priming by dendritic cells

questions.explanation: The common lymphoid progenitor gives antigen-specific lymphocytes but also innate lineages that lack antigen-specific receptors: the innate lymphoid cells, which include NK cells. A: ILCs arise from the common lymphoid progenitor. B: NK cells have numerous granules. C: Thymic maturation is stated for T cells. D: NK cells kill without priming.

questions.stem: A large lymphoid-like cell with a granular cytoplasm that kills certain tumor cells and infected cells is most important in which setting?

options.A: The late adaptive response to viral infections
options.B: The early innate response to viral infections
options.C: The early innate response to parasitic worms
options.D: The clearance of extracellular bacteria by phagocytosis
options.E: The presentation of antigen to naive T cells

questions.explanation: The cell is the NK cell: large lymphoid-like, numerous granules, kills certain tumor and infected cells, and plays an important role in the early innate response to viral infections. A: NK cells are innate and act early. C: Parasitic worms are linked to eosinophils, basophils and mast cells. D: Phagocytosis is the role of macrophages and neutrophils. E: That is the dendritic cell's role.

questions.stem: Which description of cytokines is correct?

options.A: Small lipids of about 25 kDa released constitutively that act by binding specific receptors
options.B: Large proteins of about 250 kDa released in response to an activating stimulus that act as enzymes
options.C: Small proteins of about 25 kDa stored in granules that act by forming membrane pores
options.D: Small proteins of about 25 kDa released in response to an activating stimulus that act by binding specific receptors
options.E: Small proteins of about 2.5 kDa released by lymphocytes in response to a stimulus that act through pattern recognition receptors

questions.explanation: Cytokines are small proteins (about 25 kDa) released by various cells in response to an activating stimulus; they induce responses by binding specific receptors. A: Cytokines are proteins released in response to an activating stimulus. B: They are small (about 25 kDa) and act through receptors. C: Pore formation describes perforin, not cytokines. E: The size given is about 25 kDa, they come from various cells, and they bind their own specific receptors.

questions.stem: A macrophage releases a cytokine that binds receptors on the same macrophage. What is this mode of action called?
questions.explanation: Autocrine: same cell. Paracrine: neighboring cell. Endocrine: distant cell via circulation. B: Neighboring cell. C: Distant cell via circulation. D: Not one of the listed modes. E: Not one of the listed modes.

questions.stem: Which cytokine family includes non-immune growth and differentiation factors such as growth hormone, and how do its receptors signal?

options.A: Hematopoietin family; receptors activate NFκB and IRF transcription factors
options.B: TNF family; receptors associate with JAK tyrosine kinases that activate STAT transcription factors
options.C: Hematopoietin family; receptors associate with JAK tyrosine kinases that activate STAT transcription factors
options.D: Type I interferon family; receptors associate with JAK tyrosine kinases that activate IRF transcription factors
options.E: IL-1 family; receptors associate with STAT kinases that activate JAK transcription factors

questions.explanation: Cytokine families are IL-1, interferons, TNF and hematopoietin. The hematopoietin superfamily includes growth hormone; its receptors are associated with JAK tyrosine kinases, which activate STATs. A: NFκB and IRF are the transcription factors named for TLR signaling. B: JAK-STAT is described for the hematopoietin family. D: Interferons are a separate family, and IRF is named for TLR signaling. E: The family is wrong and JAK/STAT roles are reversed.

questions.stem: Pattern recognition receptors recognize two classes of ligands. Which pairing is correct?

options.A: PAMPs from damaged host tissue and DAMPs from pathogens
options.B: PAMPs from pathogens and DAMPs from damaged host tissue
options.C: PAMPs from pathogens and MMPs from damaged host tissue
options.D: DAMPs from damaged host tissue and cytokines from pathogens
options.E: PAMPs from commensals and HYALs from damaged host tissue

questions.explanation: PRRs recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) and damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). A: The definitions are swapped. C: MMPs are enzymes that cleave ECM, generating DAMPs. D: Cytokines are host mediators, not PRR ligand classes. E: HYALs are hyaluronidases that cleave ECM, not a ligand class.

questions.stem: Under tissue stress or injury, how do resident cells generate DAMPs from the extracellular matrix?

options.A: They release metalloproteinases and hyaluronidases that crosslink ECM components, which then suppress inflammation
options.B: They release perforin and granzymes that cleave ECM components, which then induce inflammation
options.C: They release NADPH oxidase and myeloperoxidase that oxidize ECM components, which then induce apoptosis
options.D: They release histamine and cytokines that dissolve ECM components, which then activate complement
options.E: They release metalloproteinases and hyaluronidases that cleave ECM components, which then induce inflammation

questions.explanation: Resident cells release MMPs (metalloproteinases) and HYALs (hyaluronidases) to cleave ECM components that will induce inflammation. A: The enzymes cleave ECM and the fragments induce inflammation. B: Perforin and granzymes are NK cytotoxic granule contents. C: These are respiratory burst enzymes in phagocytes. D: Not the mechanism described for DAMP generation.

questions.stem: On the DAMP figure, how do apoptosis and necrosis differ?

options.A: Apoptosis gives strong DAMP release with silent removal; necrosis gives little DAMP release
options.B: Apoptosis gives little DAMP release; necrosis gives no DAMP release because the cell lyses
options.C: Apoptosis gives PAMP release with phagocyte activation; necrosis gives DAMP release
options.D: Apoptosis gives little DAMP release with silent removal; necrosis gives strong DAMP release
options.E: Apoptosis and necrosis give equal DAMP release, but necrotic cells are removed silently

questions.explanation: Death for homeostasis (apoptosis) gives little DAMP release and silent removal; death by injury (necrosis) gives strong DAMP release, activating cells through PRRs. A: The amounts are swapped. B: Necrosis (death by injury) gives strong DAMP release. C: Apoptosis leads to silent removal and phagocyte deactivation, and PAMPs come from pathogens. E: Release differs, and silent removal belongs to apoptosis.

questions.stem: PRRs are classified into four main groups by cellular location and function. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
questions.explanation: The four main groups are free receptors in the serum, membrane-bound phagocytic receptors, membrane-bound signaling receptors and cytoplasmic signaling receptors. B: One of the four groups. C: One of the four groups. D: One of the four groups. E: One of the four groups.

questions.stem: Where are Toll-like receptors located?

options.A: Free in the serum and lymph
options.B: In the cytosol of the cell
options.C: On the cell surface or in endosomes
options.D: Inside the nucleus of the cell

questions.explanation: TLRs were the first innate sensors discovered; on the plasma membrane or endocytic vesicles; they mainly sense extracellular microbial products. A: Soluble PRRs. B: NLRs. D: Not stated. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: A virus triggers a Toll-like receptor in an endosome, and the cell starts making type I interferon. Which transcription factor drives this?
questions.explanation: TLRs activate NFκB and IRF → inflammatory cytokines and type I interferons. A: T cell activation. B: Cytokine receptor signaling. C: Th2 differentiation. D: Th1 differentiation.

questions.stem: How many TLRs are expressed in humans and in mice?

options.A: 12 TLRs in humans and 10 in mice
options.B: 10 TLRs in humans and 12 in mice
options.C: 10 TLRs in humans and 10 in mice
options.D: 4 TLRs in humans and 12 in mice
options.E: 12 TLRs in humans and 13 in mice

questions.explanation: There are 10 TLRs expressed in humans and 12 in mice, each recognizing a distinct set of molecular patterns. A: The numbers are reversed. C: Mice have 12. D: Humans have 10. E: The slide gives 10 and 12.

questions.stem: According to the slide, which TLRs sense the lipoteichoic acids of Gram-positive cell walls and the lipopolysaccharide of the Gram-negative outer membrane?

options.C: Lipoteichoic acids: TLR-3 and TLR-4; lipopolysaccharide: TLR-2
options.E: Lipoteichoic acids: TLR-1:TLR-2 and TLR-4; lipopolysaccharide: TLR-4

questions.explanation: As written on the slide, lipoteichoic acids are sensed by TLR-1:TLR-2 and TLR-4, and LPS by TLR-4. Note (outside the slides): standard texts attribute lipoteichoic acid to TLR-2 heterodimers and reserve TLR-4 for LPS; answer the exam from the slide. A: The ligands are swapped relative to the slide. B: LPS is sensed by TLR-4. C: LPS is sensed by TLR-4 and LTA by TLR-1:TLR-2 (and TLR-4 on the slide). D: Not the pairing on the slide.

questions.stem: Which family of innate sensors includes NLRP3, which forms an inflammasome in the cytoplasm?
questions.explanation: NLRs are cytoplasmic sensors; some activate NFκB, others trigger cell death and pro-inflammatory cytokines (NLRP3 inflammasome). A: Membrane or endosomal. B: Phagocytic receptors. C: Phagocytic receptors. E: Bind antibody.

questions.stem: In the overview of innate immune mechanisms, antiviral activity is attributed to which component, and which cell is listed as the link with the adaptive response?
questions.explanation: The scheme lists antiviral activity (interferons) and, under phagocytosis, dendritic cells as the link with the adaptive response; eosinophils are tagged for parasites and NK cells for tumoral and virus-infected cells. B: Complement is a separate entry; antiviral activity is interferons. C: Dendritic cells are labeled as the link with the adaptive response. D: Antiviral activity is interferons, and NK cells are listed for tumoral and virus-infected cells. E: Eosinophils are listed for parasites.

questions.stem: Phagocytes carry receptors that stimulate phagocytosis and intracellular killing, and others that signal for cytokine production. Which option assigns them correctly?

options.A: Complement, Fc and G-protein coupled receptors stimulate phagocytosis; scavenger receptors signal for cytokine production
options.B: Toll-like, NOD-like and scavenger receptors stimulate phagocytosis; Fc receptors signal for cytokine production
options.C: Complement, Fc, scavenger and C-type lectin receptors stimulate phagocytosis; G-protein coupled receptors signal for cytokine production
options.D: G-protein coupled and C-type lectin receptors stimulate phagocytosis; complement receptors signal for cytokine production
options.E: Complement and Fc receptors stimulate cytokine production; C-type lectin and scavenger receptors drive actin remodeling by G proteins

questions.explanation: Receptors that stimulate phagocytosis and intracellular killing include complement receptors, Fc receptors, scavenger receptors and C-type lectin family receptors; G-protein coupled receptors signal through downstream pathways to stimulate cytokine production. A: Scavenger receptors are phagocytic; G-protein coupled receptors are the signaling ones. B: Fc receptors are phagocytic receptors. D: Complement receptors are phagocytic. E: The first group are phagocytic receptors.

questions.stem: Put the steps of phagocytosis in order: (1) fusion of the phagosome with a lysosome, (2) microbe binds phagocyte receptors, (3) killing by lysosomal enzymes, ROS and NO, (4) membrane zips up around the microbe.
questions.explanation: Microbes bind phagocyte receptors, the membrane zips up around the microbe, the phagosome fuses with a lysosome to form the phagolysosome, and microbes are killed by lysosomal enzymes, ROS and NO. A: The membrane zips up to form the phagosome before fusion with the lysosome. C: Binding to receptors comes first. D: Killing happens in the phagolysosome, after fusion. E: Binding precedes zipping and fusion precedes killing.

questions.stem: In the phagolysosome, which enzyme generates nitric oxide, and from which substrate?

options.B: Phagocyte oxidase, converting arginine to citrulline
options.C: Myeloperoxidase, converting hydrogen peroxide to nitric oxide
options.D: Superoxide dismutase, converting arginine to ornithine

questions.explanation: The figure shows killing by ROS (phagocyte oxidase) and NO, the latter produced by iNOS from arginine with citrulline as the by-product. A: The direction is arginine to citrulline. B: Phagocyte oxidase generates ROS from oxygen. C: Myeloperoxidase produces hypochlorous acid. D: Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide to hydrogen peroxide.

questions.stem: A boy has recurrent bacterial and fungal infections because his phagocytes cannot convert O₂ to superoxide during the respiratory burst. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: NADPH oxidase makes superoxide (deficiency = chronic granulomatous disease); SOD → H₂O₂; myeloperoxidase + Cl⁻ → HOCl. A: Makes HOCl later. B: Turns superoxide into H₂O₂. C: Removes H₂O₂. E: Regenerates GSH.

questions.stem: A boy with severe G6PD deficiency has recurrent infections resembling chronic granulomatous disease. Why does his respiratory burst fail?

options.C: Too little NADPH for NADPH oxidase

questions.explanation: The NADPH for the burst comes from G6PD (HMP shunt); glutathione reductase also uses NADPH to regenerate GSH. A: Not caused by G6PD deficiency. B: Not caused by G6PD deficiency. D: Not caused by G6PD deficiency. E: Not caused by G6PD deficiency.

questions.stem: Why are NK cells called "natural" killers?

options.D: They kill through T cell receptors
options.E: They kill after antibody class switching

questions.explanation: NK cells are group I ILCs; they kill tumor cells without priming or clonal expansion, unlike cytotoxic T cells primed by APCs. B: Cytotoxic T cells. C: Not needed. D: No antigen-specific receptors. E: B cells.

questions.stem: Besides direct killing, NK cells enhance the immune response by secreting which cytokines, acting on which cells?

options.A: IFNγ and TNFα, acting on neutrophils and mast cells
options.B: IFNγ and TNFα, acting on macrophages and dendritic cells
options.C: Type I interferons and IL-1, acting on macrophages and dendritic cells
options.D: Perforin and granzymes, acting on macrophages and dendritic cells
options.E: IFNγ and histamine, acting on eosinophils and basophils

questions.explanation: NK cells secrete cytokines such as IFNγ and TNFα, which act on other immune cells like macrophages and dendritic cells. A: The slide names macrophages and dendritic cells. C: The cytokines named are IFNγ and TNFα. D: These are cytotoxic granule contents, not the cytokines. E: Histamine is a mast cell mediator.

questions.stem: What decides whether an NK cell kills a target cell?

options.B: Presentation of peptide on MHC class II
options.E: Deposition of complement on the target

questions.explanation: NK decision = balance of activating and inhibitory receptors; activating receptors recognize molecules on cancer and infected cells. A: NK cells lack one. B: Helper T cells. C: Not needed. E: Not the decision.

questions.stem: A healthy hepatocyte with normal MHC I is not attacked by NK cells, whereas a virus-infected hepatocyte that has lost MHC I is lysed. What explains the killing?

options.A: Priming of the NK cell by the virus
options.C: Viral peptide presented on MHC II

questions.explanation: Inhibitory NK receptors recognize cognate MHC I and switch the NK cell off; infected and cancer cells often lose MHC I. A: Not needed. C: Not how NK cells see targets. D: Not needed. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A transformed cell still expresses MHC class I, yet an NK cell kills it. How is this possible?

options.A: Granzymes first cleave its MHC I molecules
options.B: A T cell receptor recognizes it
options.C: Dendritic cells prime the NK cell

questions.explanation: Transformed or infected cells can increase activating ligands, overriding the inhibitory signal even when MHC I is present. A: Not the mechanism. B: NK cells have none. C: Not needed. D: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Within hours of infection, an NK cell lyses a virus-infected cell. What does it release to do this?
questions.explanation: NK cells release cytotoxic granules with perforin and granzymes, causing lysis. A: Complement. B: Phagocytes. D: Not NK killing. E: Mast cells.

questions.stem: A child born without a thymus has normal B cells. Where would his T cells normally have matured?
questions.explanation: Most immune cells arise from bone marrow; T cells generated in the marrow mature in the thymus. B: Where T cells are generated, not where they mature. C: Secondary organ. D: Secondary organ. E: Not the site.

lectures.title: Complement system
lectures.covers: How complement is activated by the classical, lectin and alternative pathways, what its fragments do, how it is regulated, and the diseases of complement deficiency.

items.p: A group of plasma proteins made by the liver. Most are inactive enzymes (zymogens) that cut and activate one another in a cascade.
Complement belongs to innate immunity: it works even without antibodies. It kills pathogens in three ways.

ul: Opsonization and phagocytosis (C3b)
Inflammation (C3a, C4a, C5a)
Lysis by the membrane attack complex (C5b to C9)

items.p: Names follow the order of discovery, not the order of reaction: C1, C4, C2, C3, C5.
Every pathway ends in a C3 convertase that cleaves C3.

ul: C3a: small peptide, inflammation
C3b: the main effector molecule; binds covalently to the microbe

items.p: Activation stays on the pathogen surface. C4b or C3b that fails to bind is hydrolyzed and inactivated.

table: C1q binds the pathogen or antibody (IgG, IgM) on it
MBL or ficolins bind sugars such as mannose
Spontaneous C3 hydrolysis (tickover), or C3b from other pathways

items.p: The classical convertase is written C4b2b in new texts and C4b2a in older ones.
C1 is the sensor: C1q (recognition, a hexamer of trimers) with the proteases C1r and C1s (a calcium-dependent tetramer).

ul: C1q binds, C1r activates itself, C1r cleaves C1s
C1s cleaves C4, then C2
C4b plus C2b form the C3 convertase

items.p: Mannose-binding lectin (a collectin made in the liver) and three ficolins circulate as pattern recognition receptors.

ul: MBL: low affinity but high avidity for repeated sugars; rises in the acute-phase response
MBL carries MASP proteases. MASP-2 cleaves C4 and C2, like C1s.
Ficolins bind acetylated sugars and are more abundant than MBL

items.p: It needs no early components. It runs at a low level all the time and amplifies the other pathways.

ul: C3b binds factor B; factor D cleaves factor B; result: C3bBb
Properdin (factor P) stabilizes C3bBb. It is the only positive regulator and comes from neutrophil granules.
C3bBb plus another C3b is the C5 convertase

items.p: C5 convertase splits C5. C5a is strongly inflammatory. C5b starts the membrane attack complex.
C9 polymerizes into a pore. Water and ions enter, and the cell swells and bursts. The MAC matters most against Neisseria.
Healthy host cells carry regulators; infected cells lose them.

table: Removes C1r and C1s from C1q
Cofactor for factor I, which cleaves C3b and C4b
Stops C9 joining C5b-8: no MAC

items.p: Most complement deficiencies are autosomal recessive. Two exceptions: properdin deficiency is X-linked recessive, and C1 inhibitor deficiency is autosomal dominant.

ul: MBL or MASP-2 deficiency: respiratory infections in early childhood
Properdin deficiency: Neisseria meningitidis
Early components (C1 to C4): pyogenic infections and lupus, from poor clearance of immune complexes
Terminal components (C5 to C9): recurrent Neisseria infections
C1 inhibitor deficiency: hereditary angioedema. Swelling of skin, gut and larynx. Treat with recombinant C1 inhibitor.
DAF deficiency from an acquired stem-cell mutation: paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria. Hemolysis, thrombosis, marrow failure, dark morning urine.

items.p: Tests: CH50 (or CH100) for overall activity, and C3 and C4 levels.

items.note: The slide dates the discovery of complement by Jules Bordet to the "1980s". The historical date is the 1890s.
The slide attributes angioedema to "C2 kinin, a bradykinin". Standard sources name bradykinin from the kallikrein pathway as the main mediator. Use the slide wording for the exam.

cards.q: The three effector functions of complement, and the fragment for each
cards.a: Opsonization: C3b. Inflammation: C3a, C4a, C5a. Lysis: MAC (C5b–C9).

cards.q: What is the critical step of complement activation?
cards.a: A C3 convertase cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b.

cards.q: C3 convertase of the classical and lectin pathways
cards.a: C4b2b (older texts: C4b2a)

cards.q: C3 convertase of the alternative pathway
cards.a: C3bBb (stabilized by properdin)

cards.q: What does the C1 complex contain?
cards.a: C1q (recognition protein, hexamer of trimers) plus proteases C1r and C1s

cards.q: Order of events after C1q binds
cards.a: C1r autoactivates, cleaves C1s; C1s cleaves C4 then C2.

cards.q: Which protease of the lectin pathway cleaves C4 and C2?
cards.a: MASP-2
Mannose-binding lectin or one of three ficolins binding microbial sugars

cards.q: Two ways the alternative pathway starts
cards.a: Tickover (spontaneous hydrolysis of C3) and C3b supplied by the other pathways (amplification loop)
Factor D

cards.q: The only positive regulator of complement
cards.a: Properdin (factor P), from neutrophil secondary granules
C3bBbC3b

cards.q: What forms the pore of the MAC?
cards.a: Polymerized C9, at the site where C5b bound
Dissociates activated C1r and C1s from C1q
Accelerates decay of the C3 convertases
Blocks C9 from joining C5b-8, preventing the MAC
Cofactor for factor I in cleaving C3b (and C4b)
Properdin: X-linked recessive. C1 inhibitor: autosomal dominant. The rest: autosomal recessive.

cards.q: Properdin deficiency or C5–C9 deficiency predisposes to...
cards.a: Neisseria infections (meningitis, gonorrhea)

cards.q: Why do early classical deficiencies (C1q, C2, C4) cause lupus?
cards.a: Immune complexes are not cleared.
C1 inhibitor deficiency (autosomal dominant); recombinant C1 inhibitor
Acquired stem-cell mutation, loss of DAF, uncontrolled complement on red cells
Hemolytic anemia (dark morning urine), thrombosis, impaired bone marrow function

cards.q: Screening test for overall complement activity
cards.a: CH50 (or CH100), plus C3 and C4 levels

questions.stem: Complement was first described as a heat-labile plasma substance that "complements" the bactericidal activity of immune sera. Which statement reflects how the lecture positions it today?

options.A: An adaptive mechanism that protects against infection once specific antibodies have been produced
options.B: An essential innate mechanism that protects against infection even in the absence of antibodies
options.C: A heat-stable effector of cellular immunity that requires priming by antigen-presenting cells
options.D: An innate mechanism restricted to the classical pathway and dependent on immune sera
options.E: A humoral mechanism whose components are synthesized by plasma cells after antigen exposure

questions.explanation: Complement was discovered through the classical pathway as an effector of the humoral response, but it is an essential mechanism of innate immunity that provides protection in the absence of antibodies. A: It was first seen that way (classical pathway), but it is an essential innate mechanism working without antibodies. C: It is heat-labile and needs no priming. D: Lectin and alternative pathways work without antibody. E: Complement proteins are synthesized by the liver.

questions.stem: Each is an outcome of complement activation EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Outcomes of activation: direct killing (membrane attack), facilitated phagocytosis, inflammation; complement also clears immune complexes and debris. A: Membrane attack. B: C3b. C: C3a, C5a. D: Listed function.

questions.stem: How are complement proteases kept inactive in plasma?

options.E: By sialic acid on their surface

questions.explanation: Complement proteases are inactive pro-enzymes (zymogens) activated by proteolytic cleavage, usually by another complement protein. B: Not the mechanism. C: Not the mechanism. D: They circulate. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Which complement receptors are listed in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The slide lists complement receptors CR1, CR2, CR3 and CR4. A: CR5 is not listed. B: CD59 is a regulator that blocks MAC formation. D: DAF and MCP are regulators. E: MBL is a soluble pattern recognition receptor of the lectin pathway.

questions.stem: Why does C4 act before C2 and C3 in the classical pathway even though its number is higher?

options.A: Complement proteins are named by molecular weight, not by the sequence of reactions
options.B: Complement proteins are named by plasma concentration, from most to least abundant
options.C: C4 belongs to the alternative pathway, which was discovered before the classical pathway
options.D: Complement proteins are named by order of discovery, not by the sequence of reactions
options.E: C4 is a cleavage product of C1 and is renumbered after cleavage

questions.explanation: The names depend on order of discovery rather than the reaction sequence (C1, C4, C2, C3, C5…). A: Naming follows order of discovery. B: Naming follows order of discovery. C: The classical pathway was discovered first and C4 belongs to it. E: C4 is cleaved by C1s; it is not a product of C1.

questions.stem: What is the classical C3 convertase called in current nomenclature?
questions.explanation: Cleavage products take lowercase suffixes; C2 was an exception, now rectified: the classical convertase is C4b2b (formerly C4b2a). B: Alternative C3 convertase. C: A C5 convertase. D: Alternative C5 convertase. E: Tickover convertase.

questions.stem: Which statement about C1q, C1r and C1s is correct?

options.A: They are the cleavage products of C1, named in order of size
options.B: They are alternative pathway proteins named with lowercase letters
options.C: They are the three fragments released when C1 inhibitor acts
options.D: They are isoforms of C1 synthesized by different tissues
options.E: They are not cleavage products; together they constitute C1

questions.explanation: Lowercase suffixes normally mark cleavage products (C3a, C3b), but C1q, C1r and C1s are not cleavage products: they all constitute C1. A: They are an exception to the suffix rule. B: Alternative pathway proteins take capital letters such as factor B and factor D. C: C1 inhibitor dissociates C1r and C1s from C1q but does not generate them by cleavage. D: They are subunits of a single complex.

questions.stem: Proteins of the alternative pathway were discovered later. How are they and their cleavage products designated?

options.A: Capital letters such as factor B and factor D; products B1 and B2
options.B: Numbers such as C6 and C7; products C6a and C6b
options.C: Capital letters such as factor B and factor D; products Ba and Bb
options.D: Lowercase letters such as factor b and factor d; products BA and BB
options.E: Capital letters such as factor P and factor H; products Pa and Hb

questions.explanation: Alternative pathway proteins are designated by capital letters (factor B, factor D); their cleavage products are Ba, Bb, Da, Db. A: Products take lowercase letter suffixes. B: Those are terminal components. D: Factors are capital letters; fragments take lowercase suffixes. E: The examples and products given on the slide are factors B and D, with Ba, Bb.

questions.stem: The critical step of complement activation is cleavage of C3 by a C3 convertase. Which product is the main effector molecule?
questions.explanation: C3a binds specific receptors and helps induce inflammation; C3b is the main effector molecule. A: Small inflammatory peptide. B: Highly inflammatory. C: Inflammatory mediator. E: Starts the MAC.

questions.stem: In classical and lectin activation, bacteria in the bloodstream are coated with C3b while nearby red cells are spared. Why?

options.A: Red cells lack the receptors for C3b
options.B: Activation is confined to the pathogen
options.D: Natural antibodies shield the red cells

questions.explanation: Lectin and classical pathways start with proteins binding pathogen surfaces; C3 activation is confined to the pathogen surface, not plasma or host cells. A: Not the reason. C: Not the stated reason. D: Not the reason. E: Neutrophils release properdin.

questions.stem: Which component of the C1 complex is the recognition protein?
questions.explanation: Classical sensor = C1: C1q recognition protein plus the proteases C1r and C1s. B: Protease. C: Protease. D: Substrate. E: Substrate.

questions.stem: Which structure describes C1q?
questions.explanation: C1q is a hexamer of trimers with globular heads and a collagen-like domain; C1r and C1s form a Ca²⁺-dependent C1s–C1r–C1r–C1s tetramer. A: That describes C1r2s2. B: Not C1q. D: Not C1q. E: Not C1q.

questions.stem: C1q can start the classical pathway in two ways. Which pair is correct, and which part of C1q is shown beside its collagen-like domain?

options.A: Binding directly to pathogen surfaces or to mannose residues; lectin domains
options.B: Binding to antibody bound to pathogens or to free antibody in plasma; globular heads
options.C: Binding to C3b on pathogens or to antibody bound to pathogens; thioester domains
options.D: Binding directly to pathogen surfaces or to antibody bound to pathogens; globular heads
options.E: Binding directly to host cell surfaces or to immune sera; serine protease domains

questions.explanation: C1q binds directly to pathogen surfaces or indirectly to antibody bound to pathogens. The figure labels its globular heads and collagen-like domain. A: Mannose recognition belongs to MBL. B: Free antibody is not described as an activator. C: C3b-driven activation is the alternative amplification loop. E: Activation is on pathogens, and proteases are C1r and C1s.

questions.stem: Antibodies bound to a soluble antigen circulate in plasma. What does the lecture say about classical pathway activation in this setting?

options.A: Activation is stronger than on a pathogen surface
options.B: Activation proceeds through MASP-2 instead of C1s
options.C: Activation needs a single antibody regardless of antibody type
options.D: Activation occurs but C4b is not cleaved
options.E: Activation is physically hard to occur

questions.explanation: Depending on the antibody type, one or several antibodies are needed for activation; if antibodies are bound to soluble antigens, activation is physically hard to occur. A: The slide states the opposite. B: MASP-2 belongs to the lectin pathway. C: The number needed depends on antibody type, and soluble antigen makes activation hard. D: Not what is stated.

questions.stem: When C1s cleaves C4, what does C4b do next?

options.A: Acts as a soluble inflammatory mediator

questions.explanation: C1s cleaves C4 → C4a (inflammatory mediator) + C4b (covalently binds the pathogen); C4b binds C2; C1s cleaves C2 → C4b2b (C3 convertase). A: C4a. C: Needs C2b to form the convertase. D: Not part of the MAC. E: Not the next step.

questions.stem: What happens to C4b that fails to bond rapidly with a pathogen membrane?

options.A: Its thioester bond is hydrolyzed and C4b becomes a soluble C3 convertase
options.B: It binds C2 in plasma and activates C3 in the fluid phase
options.C: It is stabilized by properdin until a pathogen is met
options.D: It is recycled into intact C4 by C1 inhibitor
options.E: Its thioester bond is hydrolyzed and C4b is irreversibly inactivated

questions.explanation: If C4b does not rapidly form the bond with a pathogen membrane, the thioester bond is cleaved by hydrolysis and C4b is irreversibly inactivated. A: Hydrolysis inactivates it. B: Activation is confined to surfaces. C: Properdin stabilizes the alternative convertases. D: C1 inhibitor acts on C1r and C1s.

questions.stem: How many circulating pattern recognition receptors can trigger the lectin pathway?
questions.explanation: The lectin pathway is triggered by four circulating PRRs: MBL and three ficolins (collagen-like lectins). A: MBL and three ficolins. B: MBL and three ficolins. C: MBL and three ficolins. E: MBL and three ficolins.

questions.stem: Which pair gives the PAMP examples used in the lecture with the correct organism group?

options.A: LPS of Gram-positive bacteria and lipoteichoic acid of Gram-negative bacteria
options.B: LPS of Gram-negative bacteria and lipoteichoic acid of Gram-positive bacteria
options.C: Mannose of Gram-negative bacteria and LPS of Gram-positive bacteria
options.D: Lipoteichoic acid of Gram-negative bacteria and peptidoglycan of fungi
options.E: Acetylated sugars of viruses and LPS of Gram-positive bacteria

questions.explanation: PAMPs are repeating molecular patterns on pathogens, such as LPS of Gram-negative bacteria and lipoteichoic acid of Gram-positive bacteria. A: The organism groups are swapped. C: LPS is Gram-negative. D: Lipoteichoic acid is Gram-positive. E: LPS is Gram-negative.

questions.stem: Which statement about mannose-binding lectin is correct?

options.A: It is a collectin synthesized in the liver, composed of 2 to 6 trimers (mainly 3–4)
options.B: It is a ficolin synthesized in the lung, composed of 2 to 6 trimers (mainly 3–4)
options.C: It is a collectin synthesized in the liver, composed of a hexamer of trimers with C1r and C1s
options.D: It is a collectin synthesized by neutrophils and stored in secondary granules
options.E: It is a serine protease synthesized in the liver that cleaves C4 and C2

questions.explanation: MBL is synthesized in the liver; proteins of this type are called collectins. MBL in blood is composed of 2 to 6 trimers (mainly 3–4). B: MBL is a collectin made in the liver; lung synthesis applies to M-ficolin. C: That describes the C1 complex. D: That describes properdin. E: The protease is MASP-2.

questions.stem: How do the carbohydrate-recognition domains of MBL achieve strong binding to microbial surfaces?

options.A: High affinity of each domain but low avidity for repetitive carbohydrate structures
options.B: High affinity of each domain for a single specific peptide antigen
options.C: Low affinity of each domain but high avidity for repetitive carbohydrate structures
options.D: Covalent thioester bonding of each domain to acetylated sugars
options.E: Low affinity and low avidity, compensated by a high plasma concentration

questions.explanation: Carbohydrate-recognition domains have low affinity but high avidity for repetitive carbohydrate structures on microbial surfaces. A: It is low affinity, high avidity. B: MBL recognizes repetitive carbohydrates, not specific peptides. D: Thioester bonding is a property of C4b and C3b. E: MBL is present at low concentration, and avidity is high.

questions.stem: How does the plasma level of MBL behave?

options.A: High at baseline, with production decreased during the acute-phase response to infection
options.B: Low at baseline and unchanged during infection
options.C: Higher than the ficolins at baseline and during infection
options.D: Low at baseline, with production increased during the acute-phase response to infection
options.E: Absent at baseline and produced by lung cells during infection

questions.explanation: MBL is present at low concentration in plasma, but its production is increased in the presence of infection (acute-phase response). A: It is low and increases with infection. B: Production increases in the presence of infection. C: Ficolins are more abundant in plasma. E: MBL is present at low concentration and made by the liver.

questions.stem: Which statement about human ficolins is correct?

options.A: L- and M-ficolin are synthesized in the liver; H-ficolin is secreted by lung and blood cells; they bind acetylated sugars
options.B: L- and H-ficolin are synthesized in the lung; M-ficolin is synthesized in the liver; they bind mannose residues
options.C: L- and H-ficolin are synthesized in the liver; M-ficolin is secreted by lung and blood cells; they bind acetylated sugars
options.D: L-, H- and M-ficolin are synthesized by neutrophils; they bind oligosaccharides containing sialic acid
options.E: L- and H-ficolin are synthesized in the liver; M-ficolin is secreted by lung and blood cells; they bind antibody Fc regions

questions.explanation: L-ficolin and H-ficolin are synthesized in the liver and circulate in blood; M-ficolin is synthesized and secreted by lung and blood cells. Ficolins bind oligosaccharides containing acetylated sugars. A: M-ficolin is the one made by lung and blood cells. B: Sites are swapped, and ficolins bind acetylated sugars. D: Sites are liver, lung and blood cells; the ligand is acetylated sugars. E: Ficolins bind oligosaccharides containing acetylated sugars.

questions.stem: After MBL binds a pathogen, which enzyme cleaves C4 and then C2?
questions.explanation: MBL complexes with MASPs; binding changes MASP-2's conformation, and it cleaves C4 then C2 → C4b2b. MASP-2 is closely related to C1r and C1s. A: Classical pathway. B: Activates C1s. C: Alternative pathway. D: Inactivates C3b and C4b.

questions.stem: Which comparison is correct according to the lecture?

options.A: MASP-2 is closely related to factor D, and MBL is more abundant in plasma than ficolins
options.B: MASP-2 is closely related to C1r and C1s, and ficolins are more abundant in plasma than MBL
options.C: MASP-2 is closely related to C1q, and ficolins are less abundant in plasma than MBL
options.D: MASP-1 is closely related to C1q, and ficolins use a different convertase than MBL
options.E: MASP-2 is closely related to C1r and C1s, and ficolins activate through factor B rather than C4

questions.explanation: MASP-2 is closely related to C1r and C1s. The same process applies for the ficolins, which are more abundant in plasma. A: MASP-2 resembles C1r/C1s, and ficolins are more abundant. C: C1q is the recognition protein; ficolins are more abundant. D: Ficolins follow the same process as MBL. E: Ficolins use the same process (C4, C2).

questions.stem: Which statement about the alternative pathway is correct?

options.A: It was the second to be discovered and does not involve the early complement components
options.B: It was the first to be discovered and does not involve the early complement components
options.C: It was the second to be discovered and starts with C1q binding to antibody
options.D: It was the last to be discovered and depends on MASP-2 cleaving C4
options.E: It was the second to be discovered and uses C4b2b as its convertase

questions.explanation: The alternative pathway was the second to be discovered after the classical pathway and does not involve early complement components. B: The classical pathway was discovered first. C: That is the classical pathway. D: It was second, and MASP-2 belongs to the lectin pathway. E: Its convertases are C3bBb and C3(H2O)Bb.

questions.stem: With no infection or antibody present, small amounts of C3b are formed in plasma all the time. What is this process called?
questions.explanation: Tickover = spontaneous hydrolysis of the C3 thioester to C3(H₂O); without infection the C3b is hydrolyzed and resolved. A: Uses C3b from other pathways. C: Coating of microbes. D: Needs a pathogen. E: Not complement activation.

questions.stem: A small fraction of C3 is spontaneously cleaved to C3b without the presence of the microbe. What is the fate of this C3b?

options.A: With no infection it binds host membranes and activates complement; with a pathogen it is hydrolyzed
options.B: With no infection it accumulates in plasma as a stable convertase; with a pathogen it is inactivated by properdin
options.C: With or without infection it requires antibody before it can bind a membrane
options.D: With no infection it is converted back to C3 by factor D; with a pathogen it is cleaved by C1s
options.E: With no infection it is hydrolyzed and resolved; with a pathogen it binds the membrane and activates complement

questions.explanation: The alternative pathway can be spontaneously activated. C3b becomes hydrolyzed and is resolved if there is no infection; if there is a pathogen, C3b binds its membrane, leading to complement activation. A: The outcomes are reversed. B: The fluid-phase convertases are short-lived and properdin stabilizes them. C: The alternative pathway is antibody-independent. D: Factor D cleaves factor B, and C1s is classical.

questions.stem: In the alternative pathway, which enzyme cleaves factor B bound to C3b?
questions.explanation: Factor B binds C3b and is cleaved by factor D, giving C3bBb (alternative C3 convertase). A: Inactivates C3b. B: Regulator. D: Stabilizes the convertase. E: Classical pathway.

questions.stem: What is the alternative pathway C5 convertase?
questions.explanation: C3bBbC3b is the alternative C5 convertase; C5 → C5a and C5b. A: Alternative C3 convertase. B: Classical C3 convertase. C: Tickover C3 convertase. E: Part of the MAC.

questions.stem: Bacteria coated with C3b are rapidly ingested by neutrophils. Which role of C3b is this?
questions.explanation: C3b binds covalently to the microbial surface as an opsonin; added to the C3 convertase it forms the C5 convertase. B: C5a. C: C3a, C5a. D: C5b–C9. E: Not this role.

questions.stem: When the C5 convertase cleaves C5, how are the products described?

options.A: C5b is highly inflammatory; C5a interacts with other subunits to form the MAC
options.B: C5a is the main opsonin; C5b is released as an anaphylatoxin
options.C: C5a stabilizes the C3 convertase; C5b is the main effector molecule
options.D: C5a is highly inflammatory; C5b interacts with other subunits to form the MAC
options.E: C5a inhibits MAC formation; C5b binds factor B

questions.explanation: C5 convertase cleaves C5 into the highly inflammatory C5a and C5b, which interacts with other subunits to form the MAC, a pore in the cell membrane causing lysis. A: The roles are reversed. B: The opsonin is C3b. C: Properdin stabilizes the convertase and C3b is the main effector. E: CD59 inhibits MAC formation, and factor B binds C3b.

questions.stem: A patient's serum kills Neisseria by punching pores in the bacterial membrane. Which component polymerizes to form these pores?
questions.explanation: C9 polymerizes where C5b has bound, forming a pore for ions and water: osmotic swelling and rupture. A: Starts the MAC. B: Joins C5b. C: Inserts before C9. D: Opsonin.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old has a second episode of meningococcal meningitis. His total hemolytic complement (CH50) is absent. Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.explanation: Terminal component (C5–C9) deficiency impairs the MAC (C5b, C6–C9), giving recurrent Neisseria infections. A: SLE. C: Early-childhood respiratory infections. D: Angioedema. E: PNH.

questions.stem: During a bacterial infection, a complement fragment released near the site strongly recruits neutrophils and triggers mast cells. Which highly inflammatory fragment is it?
questions.explanation: C3a and C5a: inflammation. C3b: opsonization. MAC: lysis. A: Opsonin. B: Starts the MAC. D: Binds the pathogen. E: Forms the pore.

questions.stem: Regarding regulation, which statement is NOT consistent with the lecture?

options.A: Regulators are expressed on infected cells and are absent from normal host cells
options.B: Complement must be controlled so that it is activated on pathogens or damaged host cells
options.C: Once a cell is infected, the regulatory molecules on its surface become absent
options.D: Complement can be activated by dying cells, leading to their phagocytosis
options.E: Clearing dying cells avoids autoimmune responses to released intracellular contents

questions.explanation: Regulators are expressed on the surface of normal cells; once a cell is infected they become absent, leading to complement activation. Dying cells can also activate complement so they are phagocytosed, avoiding autoimmune responses. B: Stated on the slide. C: Stated on the slide. D: Stated on the slide. E: Stated on the slide.

questions.stem: What does properdin do?

options.A: Cleaves factor B bound to C3b

questions.explanation: Properdin (factor P), from neutrophil secondary granules, stabilizes C3bBb and C3(H₂O)Bb; it is the only positive regulator. A: Factor D. B: DAF. C: MCP. E: CD59.

questions.stem: Where does properdin come from?

options.A: Hepatocytes, which secrete it during the acute-phase response
options.B: Neutrophils, which store it in azurophilic granules and release it continuously while at rest
options.C: Lung and blood cells, which secrete it into the circulation
options.D: Macrophages, which express it on their surface as a complement receptor
options.E: Neutrophils, which store it in secondary granules and release it when activated by pathogens

questions.explanation: Factor P is produced by neutrophils and stored in secondary granules, released upon neutrophil activation by pathogens; it can also bind some pathogen membranes, directing the alternative pathway. A: Hepatic acute-phase production was described for MBL. B: The slide says secondary granules and release on activation. C: That describes M-ficolin. D: It is a plasma protein released by neutrophils.

questions.stem: Which regulator dissociates activated C1r and C1s from C1q?
questions.explanation: C1 esterase inhibitor is the serine protease inhibitor that dissociates C1r and C1s from C1q and blocks spontaneous C1 activation. B: Acts on C3 convertases. C: Blocks C9. D: Cleaves C3b and C4b. E: Cofactor for factor I.

questions.stem: A patient's red cells lack a membrane regulator that normally stops C9 from joining C5b-8, so they lyse. Which regulator is missing?
questions.explanation: DAF (decay) destabilizes C3 convertases; MCP is the cofactor for factor I cleavage of C3b and C4b; CD59 blocks C9 association with C5b-8. A: Destabilizes C3 convertases. B: Cofactor for factor I. D: Positive regulator. E: Acts on C1.

questions.stem: A woman and her father both have recurrent attacks of skin and laryngeal swelling from C1 inhibitor deficiency. How is this inherited?
questions.explanation: Most complement deficiencies are autosomal recessive; properdin deficiency is X-linked recessive; C1 inhibitor deficiency is autosomal dominant. A: Properdin deficiency. C: Not complement. D: Not complement. E: PNH.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old has repeated respiratory infections with common extracellular bacteria. Work-up shows an isolated defect of the lectin pathway. Which deficiency fits, and why is early childhood the vulnerable period?

options.A: MBL or MASP-2 deficiency; adaptive immunity is not yet fully developed in early childhood
options.B: MBL or MASP-2 deficiency; maternal antibodies block the classical pathway in early childhood
options.C: Properdin deficiency; adaptive immunity is not yet fully developed
options.D: C2 or C4 deficiency; immune complexes are cleared poorly
options.E: C5–C9 deficiency; the MAC cannot form on encapsulated bacteria

questions.explanation: Deficiency of MASP-2 or MBL alters the lectin pathway and increases susceptibility to respiratory infections by common extracellular bacteria during early childhood, when adaptive immunity is not fully developed. B: The reason given is immature adaptive immunity. C: Properdin deficiency affects the alternative pathway and predisposes to Neisseria meningitidis. D: That combination is linked to systemic lupus. E: Terminal deficiencies give recurrent Neisseria infections.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy develops bacterial meningitis due to Neisseria meningitidis; a maternal uncle had the same infection. Deficiency of which alternative pathway protein fits the inheritance and the infection?
questions.explanation: Properdin (factor P) deficiency is X-linked recessive and makes patients susceptible to Neisseria meningitidis, the main agent of bacterial meningitis. A: Not discussed as a disease; the X-linked deficiency linked to N. meningitidis is properdin. C: Autosomal dominant, causing hereditary angioneurotic edema. D: Lectin pathway defect with early-childhood respiratory infections. E: Early classical defect linked to systemic lupus.

questions.stem: A child with C4 deficiency develops systemic lupus erythematosus. What is the mechanism?

options.A: Excess MAC formation on host cells

questions.explanation: Deficiency of early classical components (C1q, C1r, C1s, C4, C2) causes SLE through defective clearance of immune complexes. A: Not the mechanism. B: Not the mechanism. C: Not the mechanism. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman has recurrent skin swelling, abdominal pain, vomiting and one episode of laryngeal edema; her father had similar attacks. Which treatment replaces what she lacks?
questions.explanation: Hereditary angioneurotic edema: AD C1INH deficiency; massive breakdown of C4 and C2 with C2 kinin; treat with recombinant C1INH. A: Not the missing protein. B: Not the missing protein. D: For infection-prone deficiencies. E: Not relevant.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man has very dark morning urine, fatigue, chronic hemolysis and a recent venous thrombosis. What is the mechanism?

options.A: Inherited DAF deficiency from both parents
options.E: Somatic stem cell mutation causing DAF loss

questions.explanation: DAF deficiency: inherited is uncommon; an acquired somatic mutation in hematopoietic stem cells causes PNH (hemolysis, thrombosis, impaired marrow function, dark morning urine). A: Inherited DAF deficiency is uncommon; this is acquired. B: AIHA. C: Would reduce, not increase, lysis. D: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Besides destruction of red blood cells, which two features characterize paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria in the lecture?

options.A: Thrombosis and impaired bone marrow function
options.C: Recurrent Neisseria infections and impaired bone marrow function
options.D: Systemic lupus and impaired clearance of immune complexes

questions.explanation: PNH is characterized by destruction of red blood cells, blood clots (thrombosis) and impaired bone marrow function. B: Laryngeal edema belongs to C1 inhibitor deficiency. C: Neisseria infections are linked to properdin and terminal deficiencies. D: These are linked to early classical deficiencies. E: These belong to hereditary angioneurotic edema.

questions.stem: A patient with active systemic lupus has low complement levels although she has no inherited deficiency. How does the lecture explain this, and which proteins are low?

options.A: Acquired deficiency: the autoimmune condition blocks hepatic synthesis of complement proteins; C5 and C9
options.B: Inherited deficiency unmasked by infection; C1q and properdin
options.C: Acquired deficiency: the autoimmune condition causes complement proteins to get used up; C3 and C4
options.D: Acquired deficiency: autoantibodies stabilize the C3 convertase; factor B and factor D
options.E: Acquired deficiency: loss of DAF from red cells; C3 and C4

questions.explanation: Complement deficiency may be inherited (most autosomal recessive) or acquired: severe infection or an autoimmune condition such as SLE causes complement proteins to get used up, with C3 and C4 deficiency. A: The mechanism is consumption, and the proteins named are C3 and C4. B: The slide describes acquired consumption of C3 and C4. D: Not the mechanism described. E: DAF loss is the PNH mechanism.

questions.stem: A child has recurrent severe pyogenic infections and a lupus-like illness. Which complement deficiency group fits?
questions.explanation: Early (C1–C4): severe recurrent pyogenic infections and SLE. Terminal (C5–C9): impaired MAC, recurrent Neisseria. A: Neisseria. B: Neisseria. C: Angioedema. D: PNH.

questions.stem: Which blood tests are listed for diagnosing a complement deficiency?

options.A: Overall complement activity (CH50 or CH100) and flow cytometry for CD59 and DAF
options.B: Overall complement activity (CH50 or CH100) and specific protein levels (C3 or C4)
options.C: Antinuclear antibody titer and specific protein levels (C3 or C4)
options.D: Overall complement activity (AH50) and properdin gene sequencing
options.E: C1 inhibitor function assay and bone marrow biopsy

questions.explanation: Diagnosis is by blood analysis: overall complement activity (CH50 or CH100) and specific protein levels (C3 or C4). A: Not listed on the slide. C: Not listed as a complement test. D: Not listed on the slide. E: Not listed on the slide.

questions.stem: How does treatment differ between an underactive and an overactive complement response?

options.A: Underactive: immunosuppressors; overactive: precautionary prophylactic antibiotics; a deficient protein such as C1INH can also be supplemented
options.B: Underactive: recombinant C1INH; overactive: prophylactic antibiotics; a deficient protein such as properdin can also be supplemented
options.C: Underactive: plasma exchange; overactive: immunosuppressors; deficient proteins cannot be supplemented
options.D: Underactive: precautionary prophylactic antibiotics; overactive: immunosuppressors; a deficient protein such as C1INH can also be supplemented
options.E: Underactive: prophylactic antibiotics; overactive: antihistamines; a deficient protein such as C3 can also be supplemented

questions.explanation: Underactive response: treat infections and take precautions with prophylactic antibiotics. Overactive/autoimmune manifestations: immunosuppressors. A deficient protein can also be supplemented, such as C1INH. A: The two are swapped. B: C1INH is the supplementation example, used for C1INH deficiency. C: Supplementation is possible, and plasma exchange is not listed. E: The slide lists immunosuppressors and C1INH.

questions.stem: Each of the following describes the complement proteins in the take-home messages EXCEPT:

options.A: They are circulating proteins synthesized by the liver
options.B: They act as proteases and cleave one another in cascade
options.C: They bind to pathogens as well as immune complexes
options.D: They participate in humoral immunity and alert phagocytes of the innate system
options.E: They are synthesized by plasma cells and act as receptors on lymphocytes

questions.explanation: Complement is a group of circulating proteins that are synthesized by the liver, participate in humoral immunity, act as proteases cleaving one another in cascade, bind pathogens and immune complexes, and alert phagocytes. A: Stated in the take-home messages. B: Stated in the take-home messages. C: Stated in the take-home messages. D: Stated in the take-home messages.

questions.stem: Which inflammatory complement subunits cause vascular changes, according to the list of complement functions?
questions.explanation: Functions include opsonization, clearance of immune complexes and cellular debris, chemotaxis of neutrophils, direct cytolysis through the MAC, and vascular changes caused by the inflammatory subunits C3a, C4a and C5a. A: The b-fragments bind surfaces (opsonization, convertases, MAC). C: C9 forms the pore. D: Only C5a of these is listed. E: C1q is the recognition protein and C5b starts the MAC.

questions.stem: Which surfaces does the alternative pathway detect?

options.A: Surfaces coated with bound IgG or IgM

questions.explanation: Classical: surfaces with bound IgG/IgM. Alternative: surfaces not protected by complement inhibitors. Lectin: surfaces with mannose or acetylated sugars. A: Classical. B: Lectin (MBL). C: Lectin (ficolins). E: Protected host cells.

questions.stem: C1q binds an antibody-coated bacterium. What happens next?

options.B: C4 binds C1q and is cleaved

questions.explanation: C1q binds the pathogen or antibody on it → C1r autoactivates → C1r cleaves C1s → C1s cleaves C4, then C2. A: The order is reversed. B: Later, by C1s. D: Not the sequence. E: Not the sequence.

questions.stem: How does decay-accelerating factor protect host cells?

options.B: It cleaves C3b with factor I
options.C: It blocks C9 binding to C5b-8
options.D: It removes C1r and C1s from C1q

questions.explanation: Decay acceleration: DAF (or CFH, CR1) destabilizes C3 convertases, speeding the dissociation of C3bBb and C4b2b. B: Cofactor activity. C: CD59. D: C1 inhibitor. E: Properdin.

questions.stem: How does membrane cofactor protein (MCP) protect host cells?

options.B: It blocks C9 binding to C5b-8
options.C: It removes C1r and C1s from C1q
options.D: It helps factor I inactivate C3b

questions.explanation: Cofactor activity: MCP (or CFH, CR1) binds C3b and is the cofactor for factor I (CFI) cleavage of C3b or C4b. A: Decay acceleration. B: CD59. C: C1 inhibitor. E: Properdin.

lectures.title: Antigen presentation
lectures.covers: The features of adaptive immunity, how B and T cells recognize antigen, what antigens are, and how MHC class I and II molecules present peptides to T cells.

items.p: Adaptive immunity starts when antigen-presenting cells, having phagocytosed the pathogen, show it to lymphocytes.

ul: Specificity: one receptor specificity per lymphocyte; tells apart closely related epitopes
Diversity: billions of structures recognized, thanks to variable antigen-binding sites
Memory: second responses are faster, larger and often different in quality
Specialization: a different kind of response for each class of microbe
Self tolerance: no harmful response to self
Self-limitation: the response fades and the system returns to rest (homeostasis)
Clonal expansion: the few specific cells multiply; all progeny carry the same receptor

items.p: Memory is the basis of vaccination. Failed tolerance gives autoimmunity.
B cells use immunoglobulin. Membrane-bound it is the B-cell receptor; secreted it is antibody. It binds native antigen, soluble or on a cell.
T cells use the T-cell receptor. It is never secreted and only sees small peptides held on MHC molecules.

ul: Antibody: 2 identical heavy and 2 identical light chains; two antigen-binding sites
Variable regions bind antigen; the constant region talks to effector cells and molecules
Light chains are κ or λ (normal ratio 2:1; an abnormal ratio suggests a B-cell tumor)
Five classes by heavy chain: IgM (μ), IgA (α), IgD (δ), IgE (ε), IgG (γ)
Affinity: strength of one site. Avidity: combined strength of all sites.
TCR: α and β chain, one binding site, about 30,000 copies per cell; CD3 is part of the complex

items.p: Receptor diversity comes from V(D)J recombination: VDJ for the heavy chain (chromosome 14), VJ for light chains (κ on chromosome 2, λ on 22).

items.note: The slide writes "22 (Igγ)" for the second light-chain locus. It is the lambda (λ) light chain.

ul: Helper (CD4) and cytotoxic (CD8) T cells
Regulatory T cells
NKT cells: remove tumor and stressed cells, help prevent autoimmunity, do not recognize MHC II
γδ T cells: rare, at mucosal and epithelial surfaces, counted as innate; drive inflammation and wound healing

items.p: An antigen is any substance that can provoke an immune response: usually a protein, peptide or polysaccharide.

ul: Epitope: the part of the antigen bound by antibody
Hapten: small molecule that is immunogenic only when bound to a carrier protein (the complex is an adduct)
Exogenous: from outside. Endogenous: made inside the cell (metabolism, virus, intracellular bacteria).
Autoantigen: a self molecule attacked when tolerance fails
Neoantigen: product of a tumor-specific mutation
Native antigen: not yet processed. B cells can bind it; T cells cannot.

items.p: Classical APCs are dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells. Dendritic cells capture most protein antigens.
APCs collect antigen in tissues, travel to the draining lymph node, and present peptides on MHC II to naive T cells.
Humoral immunity (B cells, antibody) handles extracellular microbes and toxins. Cell-mediated immunity (T cells) handles microbes hidden inside cells.
MHC is called HLA in humans. The genes are on chromosome 6.

table: Nucleated cells and platelets (not mature red cells)
APCs: dendritic cells, macrophages, monocytes, B cells
α and β chains, both cross the membrane

items.p: HLA genes are polygenic, polymorphic and codominant. The class III region holds genes such as TNF.

items.note: The slide names the small class I chain "β-macroglobulin". The standard name is β2-microglobulin.

items.p: Endogenous (class I): cytosolic protein is tagged with ubiquitin, cut by the proteasome, moved into the ER by TAP and loaded on class I. Class I does not leave the ER without a peptide.
Exogenous (class II): protein is taken into vesicles and digested. Class II arrives with CLIP in its groove; HLA-DM helps swap CLIP for the peptide.
