ul: Signal 1: the TCR binds its peptide on MHC
Signal 2: costimulatory molecules on the T cell bind their ligands on the APC

cards.a: Specificity, diversity, memory, specialization, self tolerance, self-limitation, clonal expansion

cards.q: Why are all cells of a lymphocyte clone specific for the same antigen?
cards.a: Receptor gene rearrangement is an irreversible DNA change passed to all progeny.
Membrane-bound = B-cell receptor; secreted = antibody. The T-cell receptor is never secreted.
2 identical heavy chains + 2 identical light chains (κ or λ), giving two identical binding sites

cards.q: Which antibody region binds antigen, and which interacts with effector cells?
cards.a: Variable (V) regions bind antigen; the constant (C) region is the effector part.

cards.q: Normal κ:λ ratio in humans, and meaning of an abnormal ratio
cards.a: 2:1; an abnormal ratio may indicate a B-cell tumor.
Affinity: strength of a single binding site. Avidity: total strength of all sites together.
Heavy chain: 14. κ light chain: 2. λ light chain: 22.

cards.q: Heavy chain recombination versus light chain recombination
cards.a: Heavy: V-D-J. Light: V-J (no D segment).
α and β chains (disulfide-linked heterodimer), one binding site, associated with CD3

cards.q: What do T cells recognize, compared with B cells?
cards.a: T cells: processed peptide on MHC. B cells: native antigen, no processing needed.
Small molecule that provokes a response only when bound to a carrier protein (complex = adduct)
The surface feature of an antigen that an antibody binds
Dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells

cards.q: Which cells express MHC class I?
cards.a: Nucleated cells and platelets (not mature erythrocytes)

cards.q: Which cells express MHC class II?
cards.a: Antigen-presenting cells: dendritic cells, macrophages, monocytes, B cells

cards.q: MHC I versus MHC II: which T cell?
cards.a: MHC I: CD8 cytotoxic T cells. MHC II: CD4 helper T cells.

cards.q: HLA loci of class I and class II
cards.a: Class I: HLA-A, B, C. Class II: HLA-DR, DP, DQ. Chromosome 6.
One α chain plus β2-microglobulin (encoded on chromosome 15, outside the MHC)
Polygenic, polymorphic, codominant

cards.q: Endogenous antigen pathway in four steps
cards.a: Ubiquitin and proteasome, TAP into the ER, loading on MHC I, display to CD8 T cells
Uptake into vesicles, lysosomal digestion, CLIP exchanged for peptide (HLA-DM), MHC II displays to CD4 T cells

cards.q: What keeps MHC class I in the ER?
cards.a: Lack of a bound peptide: class I leaves the ER only after binding peptide.
Signal 1: TCR binds peptide–MHC. Signal 2: costimulation between T cell and APC.

cards.q: γδ T cells: where and what
cards.a: Mucosal and epithelial sites; innate-like; promote inflammation and wound healing

questions.stem: When innate immunity fails to clear a pathogen, what stimulates the adaptive immune system according to the lecture?

options.A: Complement fragments, after opsonization of the pathogen
options.B: NK cells, after lysis of infected host cells
options.C: Antigen-presenting cells, after phagocytosis of the pathogen
options.D: Memory B cells, after first contact with the pathogen
options.E: Neutrophils, after migration into the draining lymph node

questions.explanation: The adaptive immune system is stimulated by antigen-presenting cells after phagocytosis of the pathogen. A: Complement is an innate effector; the slide names APCs. B: Not the trigger named. D: Memory cells result from an adaptive response. E: APCs carry antigen to lymphoid organs.

questions.stem: Which pair of properties belongs to adaptive but not innate immunity?

options.C: Specificity for epitopes and absence of memory

questions.explanation: Innate: rapid, non-specific, pattern recognition, no memory, not transferable. Adaptive: acquired, specific, targeted, memory, transferable. A: These are innate properties. B: These are innate properties. C: Adaptive immunity has memory as its key feature. D: Adaptive receptor diversity is large.

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as a characteristic of adaptive immunity EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Characteristics: specificity, diversity, memory, specialization, self and non-self recognition (self tolerance), self-limitation and clonal expansion. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: What underlies the specificity of adaptive immunity, the ability to distinguish even closely related molecules?

options.A: Each developing lymphocyte expresses several pattern recognition receptors, encoded in the germline
options.B: Each developing lymphocyte expresses one membrane receptor specificity, produced by antigen-receptor gene rearrangement
options.C: Each developing lymphocyte expresses one membrane receptor specificity, selected by the MHC haplotype of the pathogen
options.D: Each mature lymphocyte changes its receptor specificity after each new exposure to antigen
options.E: Each developing lymphocyte expresses two receptor specificities, one per parental chromosome

questions.explanation: Unlike innate cells with several PRRs, each developing lymphocyte expresses only one membrane receptor specificity and can distinguish slight differences between epitopes; this comes from antigen-receptor gene rearrangement. A: That describes innate cells. C: Specificity comes from receptor gene rearrangement. D: Rearrangement is irreversible; the clone keeps one specificity. E: The slide states one specificity per lymphocyte.

questions.stem: To what does the lecture attribute the diversity of adaptive immunity?

options.A: Variability in the structure of antigen-binding sites
options.B: Variability in the constant regions of the heavy chains
options.C: Polymorphism of MHC molecules between individuals
options.D: The large number of pattern recognition receptors per cell
options.E: Expansion of memory clones after each exposure

questions.explanation: Diversity (recognition of billions of different structures) is due to variability in the structures of the antigen-binding sites of lymphocyte receptors. B: Constant regions define class, not antigen recognition. C: MHC polymorphism is a separate property. D: That is innate recognition. E: That describes memory.

questions.stem: A nurse gets a hepatitis B booster years after her primary series. Her antibody level rises within days to a higher peak than after the first dose. What makes this possible?
questions.explanation: Secondary responses are more rapid, larger and often qualitatively different; stimulated naive lymphocytes give long-lived memory cells. A: Innate immunity has no memory. C: Gone in infancy. D: Not the mechanism. E: That removes self-reactive cells.

questions.stem: The adaptive system responds in distinct ways to different classes of microbes, or to the same microbe at different stages of infection, maximizing the efficiency of defense. Which characteristic is this?
questions.explanation: Specialization: each type of immune response protects the host against a given class of microbe. A: Specificity is the distinction between closely related molecules. B: Diversity is the size of the recognition repertoire. C: That is waning of the response. D: That is proliferation of antigen-specific cells.

questions.stem: Which pair of definitions is correct?

options.A: Tolerance: unresponsiveness to self molecules; self-limitation: the response wanes with time, restoring homeostasis
options.B: Tolerance: the response wanes with time, restoring homeostasis; self-limitation: unresponsiveness to self molecules
options.C: Tolerance: unresponsiveness to foreign molecules; self-limitation: the response grows with each exposure
options.D: Tolerance: enhanced tissue resistance to damage; self-limitation: unresponsiveness to self molecules
options.E: Tolerance: unresponsiveness to self molecules; self-limitation: deletion of memory cells after infection

questions.explanation: Unresponsiveness to self molecules is tolerance. Self-limitation: the response wanes with time after antigenic stimulation, returning the system to its resting basal state (homeostasis). B: The two definitions are swapped. C: Tolerance concerns self, and growth with exposure is memory. D: The first is disease tolerance from the innate lecture. E: Memory cells are long-lived; self-limitation is return to the basal state.

questions.stem: Why do the progeny of an activated lymphocyte all carry the same antigen receptor?

options.A: Receptor gene rearrangement is repeated identically in each daughter cell
options.B: The antigen selects the same receptor in each daughter cell from several expressed
options.C: The MHC haplotype dictates the receptor sequence
options.D: Receptor gene rearrangement is an irreversible change in the lymphocyte's DNA
options.E: Costimulatory signals fix the receptor after activation

questions.explanation: The gene rearrangement that generates the receptor is irreversible and changes the lymphocyte's DNA, so all progeny express the same receptor: a clone. Because few lymphocytes recognize a given antigen, clonal expansion is needed. A: It is done once and inherited. B: Each lymphocyte expresses one specificity. C: MHC presents peptide; it does not encode the receptor. E: The receptor is fixed during development by rearrangement.

questions.stem: Which adaptive characteristic is exploited by vaccination, and failure of which one leads to autoimmunity?

options.A: Specialization is exploited by vaccination; failure of memory leads to autoimmunity
options.B: Memory is exploited by vaccination; failure of clonal expansion leads to autoimmunity
options.C: Memory is exploited by vaccination; failure of self tolerance leads to autoimmunity
options.D: Diversity is exploited by vaccination; failure of homeostasis leads to immunodeficiency
options.E: Self tolerance is exploited by vaccination; failure of memory leads to immune dysregulation

questions.explanation: The slide links memory with vaccination and self tolerance with immune dysregulation and autoimmunity. A: Vaccination relies on memory; autoimmunity on failed tolerance. B: Autoimmunity is linked to tolerance. D: Not the links shown. E: The links are reversed.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes the T cell receptor from the B cell receptor?

options.C: It has kappa or lambda chains

questions.explanation: Immunoglobulin exists as membrane-bound BCR and secreted antibody; the TCR is only membrane-bound and recognizes peptide on MHC. A: B cells do; T cells need processed peptide. B: The TCR has one. C: Immunoglobulin light chains. E: Both rearrange.

questions.stem: Which part of an antibody interacts with effector molecules and cells?

options.A: The variable region of the arms
options.B: The constant region of the stem

questions.explanation: Antibody: Y-shaped, 2 identical heavy + 2 identical light chains; V regions at the arm ends bind antigen; the C region (stem) interacts with effector molecules and cells. A: Binds antigen. C: Binds antigen. D: Not the effector region. E: Binds antigen.

questions.stem: A patient's serum kappa-to-lambda light chain ratio is 1:6 (normal about 2:1). What might this indicate?
questions.explanation: Light chains are kappa or lambda, normally about 2:1; an abnormal ratio may indicate a B cell tumor. B: T cells make no light chains. C: Unrelated. D: The ratio is far off. E: Unrelated.

questions.stem: A myeloma protein is identified as IgA. Which part of the molecule defines its class?

options.A: The type of light chain it carries
options.B: The variable region of the heavy chain
options.E: The constant region of the heavy chain

questions.explanation: Five classes (IgM, IgA, IgG, IgE, IgD) differ in the constant region of the heavy chain (μ, α, γ, ε, δ). A: Kappa or lambda in any class. B: Determines specificity. C: Not the class. D: Not the class.

questions.stem: An antibody binds a microbial surface with both of its identical sites, holding far more tightly than either site alone. What is this total strength called?
questions.explanation: Affinity is the strength of a single site; avidity is the total strength from both sites. A: Strength of a single site. B: Which epitope is bound. D: Coating for phagocytosis. E: Blocking a microbe or toxin.

questions.stem: Which statement about somatic recombination of immunoglobulin genes matches the lecture?

options.A: Heavy chain: VJ recombination on chromosome 14; light chain: VDJ recombination on chromosome 2 (κ) or 22
options.B: Heavy chain: VDJ recombination on chromosome 14; light chain: VJ recombination on chromosome 2 (κ) or 22
options.C: Heavy chain: VDJ recombination on chromosome 2; light chain: VJ recombination on chromosome 14 (κ) or 22
options.D: Heavy chain: VDJ recombination on chromosome 6; light chain: VJ recombination on chromosome 15
options.E: Heavy chain: VDJ recombination on chromosome 14; light chain: VDJ recombination on chromosome 22 (κ) or 2

questions.explanation: V(D)J recombination: VDJ for IgH (locus on 14q) and VJ for IgL (κ on 2p, the other light chain on 22). Note: the slide writes "22 (Igγ)"; the light chain on chromosome 22 is lambda (λ). A: D segments belong to the heavy chain. C: The heavy-chain locus is on chromosome 14. D: Chromosomes 6 and 15 carry MHC and β2-microglobulin genes. E: Light chains have no D segment and κ is on chromosome 2.

questions.stem: What total number of B-cell receptors is predicted by the model cited in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The total number of BCRs is predicted to exceed 10^18. A: The figure cited is 10^18. B: That is the number of identical TCRs on one T cell. C: The figure cited is 10^18. E: The figure cited is 10^18.

questions.stem: Each T cell carries many copies of one disulfide-linked heterodimer receptor. About how many identical TCRs does it bear?
questions.explanation: TCR: α and β chains, disulfide-linked heterodimer, one binding site; each T cell bears about 30,000 identical TCRs. A: About 30,000. B: About 30,000. C: About 30,000. D: About 30,000.

questions.stem: Which marker is expressed by all T cells as part of the TCR complex?
questions.explanation: All T cells express CD3; mature T cells express CD4 or CD8. A thymocyte that fails TCR β or α gene rearrangement dies. B: Helper T cells. C: Cytotoxic T cells. D: B cells. E: NK cells.

questions.stem: Which statement about NKT cells matches the lecture?

options.A: They eliminate tumor cells and stressed cells, help avoid autoimmunity, and recognize peptide on MHC II
options.B: They carry a unique TCR, are found at mucosal and epithelial sites, and promote wound healing
options.C: They eliminate tumor and stressed cells, help avoid autoimmunity, and do not recognize MHC II
options.D: They suppress other T cells and are the main mediators of self tolerance
options.E: They kill infected cells after priming and express CD8

questions.explanation: NKT cells: role in eliminating tumor cells and cells stressed by trauma or temperature, role in avoiding autoimmunity; they do not recognize MHC II. A: The slide stresses they do not recognize MHC II. B: That describes γδ T cells. D: That suggests regulatory T cells. E: That describes cytotoxic T cells.

questions.stem: Which statement about γδ T cells is correct?

options.A: Low-abundance cells at mucosal and epithelial sites with a unique TCR; an innate component
options.B: Abundant cells in lymph nodes with a unique TCR; a component of adaptive immunity that provides memory
options.C: Low-abundance cells at mucosal sites without a TCR; a component of innate immunity that kills by perforin
options.D: Low-abundance cells in the thymus with the αβ TCR; they suppress inflammation to promote tolerance
options.E: Circulating helper cells with a unique TCR that recognize peptide on MHC II and activate B cells

questions.explanation: γδ T cells express a unique TCR, are of low abundance (mucosal and epithelial sites), are a component of innate immunity, induce inflammation to promote infection clearance and promote wound healing. B: They are of low abundance, at mucosal/epithelial sites, and counted as innate. C: They do express a (unique) TCR. D: They induce inflammation to promote infection clearance. E: That is the helper T-cell role.

questions.stem: Which term names the surface feature of an antigen that an antibody binds?
questions.explanation: Epitope = the molecular surface feature of an antigen bound by an antibody. A: A small molecule needing a carrier. B: The hapten–carrier complex. D: Not the term used. E: A tumor antigen.

questions.stem: A small drug molecule provokes an immune response only after binding a serum protein. What is the drug called?
questions.explanation: A hapten is a small molecule that is immunogenic only with a carrier protein; the complex is an adduct. A: The surface feature bound. B: The drug–protein complex. C: A tumor antigen. E: A self protein.

questions.stem: Match the antigen types with their definitions.

options.A: Endogenous antigen: normal self protein attacked when tolerance is altered; autoantigen: generated within cells by intracellular infection
options.B: Endogenous antigen: generated within cells by metabolism or intracellular infection; autoantigen: normal self protein attacked when tolerance is altered
options.C: Exogenous antigen: generated within cells by viral infection; endogenous antigen: enters by inhalation, ingestion or injection
options.D: Neoantigen: normal self protein in a tumor; autoantigen: tumor-specific mutated protein
options.E: Native antigen: peptide already processed by an APC; endogenous antigen: unprocessed protein in plasma

questions.explanation: Exogenous antigens enter from outside; endogenous antigens are generated within previously normal cells (metabolism, viral or intracellular bacterial infection); autoantigens are normal self proteins attacked when tolerance is altered. A: The definitions are swapped. C: The definitions are swapped. D: Neoantigens come from tumor-specific mutations. E: A native antigen is not yet processed.

questions.stem: Which statement about tumor antigens (neoantigens) is correct?

options.A: They result from a tumor-specific mutation and are hidden from MHC molecules, so tumors cannot be recognized
options.B: They are normal self proteins presented on MHC class I, and tumors are reliably killed once they appear
options.C: They result from viral infection of normal cells and are presented on MHC class II exclusively
options.D: They are unprocessed proteins that activate T cells directly without MHC
options.E: They result from a tumor-specific mutation and are expressed on MHC class I and II, yet many tumors evade recognition

questions.explanation: Neoantigens result from a tumor-specific mutation during malignant transformation; despite expressing them on MHC class I and II, many tumors have developed ways to evade recognition and killing. A: They are expressed on MHC I and II. B: They are mutated, and many tumors evade killing. C: They arise from mutation in malignant transformation. D: T cells need processed peptide on MHC.

questions.stem: In a lymph node, an intact bacterial toxin that no APC has processed activates B cells but not T cells. What explains the difference?

options.B: T cells lack CD3 in lymph nodes
options.C: The toxin acts as a hapten
options.D: B cells express MHC class I

questions.explanation: T cells cannot bind native antigen; B cells can be activated by native antigen without processing. B: All T cells express CD3. C: It is a whole protein. D: Not the reason. E: T cells need processed peptide on MHC.

questions.stem: A splinter carries bacteria into the skin. Which cells mainly capture the microbial protein antigens and carry them to where the response starts?
questions.explanation: Protein antigens are captured mainly by dendritic cells and concentrated in peripheral (secondary) lymphoid organs, where responses start. A: Phagocytose, but do not carry antigen to lymph nodes. B: Histamine release. D: Barrier cells. E: Parasites.

questions.stem: A hepatitis virus replicates inside hepatocytes, out of reach of antibodies. Which arm of immunity clears it?
questions.explanation: Humoral immunity (B cells, antibodies) handles extracellular microbes and toxins; cell-mediated immunity (T cells) handles intracellular microbes inaccessible to antibodies. A: Antibodies cannot reach it. B: Not the main arm here. C: Cannot reach it. D: Not the main arm here.

questions.stem: Which cell is a classical antigen-presenting cell?
questions.explanation: Classical APCs: dendritic cells, B cells, macrophages; they process protein antigen into peptides presented on MHC II. A: Not a classical APC. C: Not an APC. D: Not an APC. E: Not a classical APC.

questions.stem: After collecting antigen in a peripheral tissue, where does an APC go?

options.A: To the bone marrow, a primary lymphoid organ where naive T cells are generated
options.B: To the thymus, where naive T cells mature
options.C: It stays in the tissue and waits for memory T cells
options.D: To the draining lymph node, where naive T cells circulate
options.E: To the bloodstream, where it presents antigen to neutrophils

questions.explanation: APCs are bone marrow-derived, seed peripheral tissues, collect antigens and traffic to secondary lymphoid organs (they drain to the neighboring lymph node where naive T cells circulate). A: APCs traffic to secondary lymphoid organs. B: The thymus is a primary organ. C: APCs drain to lymph nodes. E: Presentation is to lymphocytes in lymphoid organs.

questions.stem: A patient receives red cells from a donor whose HLA alleles differ from his own, yet his CD8 T cells do not attack the transfused red cells. Why?

options.A: Red cells express MHC class II instead
options.B: Mature erythrocytes lack MHC class I
options.C: Red cells hide MHC I behind glycocalyx
options.D: CD8 T cells recognize MHC II
options.E: Red cells present peptides to CD4 cells

questions.explanation: MHC I is on nucleated cells and platelets, not mature erythrocytes; MHC II is on APCs (monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, B cells). A: MHC II is on APCs. C: Not the reason. D: They recognize MHC I. E: They are not APCs.

questions.stem: The HLA genes on chromosome 6 encode MHC molecules. Which coreceptor binds MHC class II?
questions.explanation: MHC II is bound by CD4 on helper T cells; MHC I by CD8 on cytotoxic T cells. A: Binds MHC I. B: Part of the TCR complex. C: B cell marker. E: NK marker.

questions.stem: Which HLA locus is a major class II locus?
questions.explanation: Class I major A, B, C; minor E, F, G. Class II major DR, DP, DQ; minor DM, DO. A: Minor class II. B: Minor class I. C: Major class I. D: Minor class I.

questions.stem: What does the HLA class III region contain?

options.A: The minor class II loci HLA-DM and HLA-DO
options.C: Immune and non-immune genes, such as TNF
options.D: The immunoglobulin heavy-chain V, D and J segments
options.E: The minor class I loci HLA-E, HLA-F and HLA-G

questions.explanation: The class III region includes both immune and non-immune associated genes like the tumour necrosis factor gene and heat shock proteins' genes. A: These are class II. B: That gene is on chromosome 15. D: Those are on chromosome 14. E: These are class I.

questions.stem: How does MHC class II differ structurally from MHC class I?

options.A: Both of its chains span the membrane
options.B: It has a single MHC-encoded chain
options.D: Its groove is formed by proximal domains
options.E: Its second chain is encoded on chromosome 15

questions.explanation: MHC I: one α chain with a smaller non-MHC chain (chromosome 15). MHC II: α and β chains, both MHC-encoded and spanning the membrane. B: That is class I. C: Both have one. D: Distal domains form it. E: That is class I.

questions.stem: In both MHC classes, which domains form the peptide-binding groove?
questions.explanation: Membrane-proximal domains resemble Ig domains; membrane-distal domains form the peptide groove. A: Membrane-proximal; resemble Ig. B: Anchor the molecule. D: Inside the cell. E: Not described.

questions.stem: MHC class II molecules present antigens from which source, and how long is the bound peptide on the slide?

options.A: From inside the cell; a 14–20 amino acid long peptide
options.B: From outside the cell; a 4–6 amino acid long peptide
options.C: From the cytosol via TAP; a 30–40 amino acid long peptide
options.D: From outside the cell; an intact native protein
options.E: From outside the cell; a 14–20 amino acid long peptide

questions.explanation: Cells engulf and destroy pathogens and present antigens to CD4+ helper T cells on MHC class II, which holds a 14–20 amino acid long peptide. A: Class II presents antigens from outside the cell. B: The slide gives 14–20. C: TAP serves class I. D: MHC binds peptides.

questions.stem: A child's cells display the HLA products inherited from both parents. Which term describes this?
questions.explanation: HLA genetics: polygenic, polymorphic (most people heterozygous at each locus), codominant. B: Many alleles per gene. C: Several genes per class. D: One allele expressed. E: Not a term used.

questions.stem: Each of the following is a feature of peptide–MHC interaction EXCEPT:

options.A: Each MHC molecule displays one peptide at a time
options.B: Each MHC molecule binds one specific peptide with a fast off-rate
options.C: Many different peptides can bind the same MHC molecule
options.D: Peptides are acquired during intracellular assembly
options.E: Stable surface expression of an MHC molecule requires bound peptide

questions.explanation: Features: broad specificity, one peptide at a time, MHC binds only peptides, peptide is loaded during intracellular assembly, stable surface expression requires peptide, and a very slow off-rate. A: A listed feature. C: A listed feature (broad specificity). D: A listed feature. E: A listed feature.

questions.stem: A virus replicates in the cytosol of an epithelial cell. Put the endogenous presentation steps in order: (1) transport of peptides into the ER by TAP, (2) proteasomal degradation of ubiquitinated protein, (3) surface expression to CD8+ T cells, (4) assembly of peptide–class I complexes.
questions.explanation: Endogenous pathway: cytosolic proteins are ubiquitinated and degraded by the proteasome, peptides are transported into the ER by TAP, loaded onto class I, and expressed on the surface for CD8+ T cells. MHC class I molecules do not leave the ER unless they bind peptides. A: Proteasomal degradation precedes TAP transport. B: Peptides must enter the ER before loading. C: Loading in the ER precedes surface expression. E: Assembly follows peptide generation and transport.

questions.stem: In the exogenous pathway, what occupies the MHC class II groove before peptide loading?
questions.explanation: Exogenous: uptake into vesicles, endosomal processing, class II with CLIP exchanged for peptide via HLA-DM, then CD4 T cells. B: Endogenous pathway transporter. C: Catalyzes the exchange. D: Endogenous pathway tag. E: Endogenous pathway.

questions.stem: How are innate immune receptors generated?
questions.explanation: Innate receptors are germline encoded and non-clonal; adaptive receptors arise by somatic rearrangement, clonally, and respond slowly (1–2 weeks). A: Adaptive receptors. B: Adaptive. C: B cells. D: B cells.

questions.stem: Which set contains effector molecules assigned to innate immunity in the comparison table?

options.A: Complement, antibodies, chemokines and antimicrobial peptides
options.C: Acute-phase reactants, antibodies and growth factors
options.D: Complement, acute-phase reactants and antimicrobial peptides
options.E: Complement, T-cell receptors and antimicrobial peptides

questions.explanation: Innate effector molecules: complement, acute-phase reactants, chemokines, cytokines, growth factors, antimicrobial peptides. Adaptive: antibodies, cytotoxic molecules (granzyme, perforin), cytokines. A: Antibodies are adaptive effector molecules. B: These are listed under adaptive immunity. C: Antibodies are adaptive. E: TCRs are receptors, not listed effector molecules.

questions.stem: According to the comparison table, what are the effects on the host of innate versus adaptive responses?

options.A: Innate: no effect on homeostasis and minimal injury; adaptive: altered homeostasis and bystander activation
options.B: Innate: reactivity against self; adaptive: bystander activation
options.C: Innate: altered homeostasis and bystander activation; adaptive: no effect on homeostasis and minimal injury
options.D: Innate: minimal injury; adaptive: reactivity against self
options.E: Innate: altered homeostasis; adaptive: altered homeostasis with memory loss

questions.explanation: Table: innate responses cause altered homeostasis and bystander activation; adaptive responses have no effect on homeostasis and cause minimal injury; neither is reactive against self. A: Reversed. B: The table lists no self-reactivity for either. D: Neither matches the table. E: Adaptive has no effect on homeostasis in the table.

questions.stem: A naive T cell binds peptide–MHC on an APC, but the APC provides no second signal. What is missing for activation?

options.A: An Fc receptor on the APC
options.C: MHC class II on the T cell

questions.explanation: T cell activation needs signal 1 (TCR with peptide–MHC) and signal 2 (costimulatory molecules on the T cell binding ligands on the APC). A: Not the second signal. C: Not required. D: Not required. E: CD3 is on T cells.

questions.stem: Which T cell type eliminates tumor cells and cells stressed by trauma or temperature, and does not recognize MHC II?
questions.explanation: T cell types: helper, cytotoxic, regulatory, NKT, γδ. NKT cells eliminate tumor and stressed cells, avoid autoimmunity and do not recognize MHC II. A: Recognizes MHC II. B: Suppresses responses. D: Mucosal; innate-like; wound healing. E: Recognizes MHC I.

questions.stem: Lipopolysaccharide combines lipid with polysaccharide. What kind of antigen is it?
questions.explanation: Antigens are typically proteins, peptides or polysaccharides; lipids and nucleic acids combine with them to form complex antigens such as LPS. A: Needs a carrier. B: A self protein. C: Tumor-specific. E: A hapten–carrier complex.

questions.stem: MHC class I has one MHC-encoded α chain. On which chromosome is its smaller partner chain encoded?
questions.explanation: MHC I: one α chain (chromosome 6) non-covalently associated with a non-MHC chain encoded on chromosome 15. (Slide 36 calls it "β-macroglobulin"; the standard name is β2-microglobulin, so the name is not tested.) A: The MHC itself. B: Immunoglobulin heavy chain. C: Kappa light chain. D: β-globin.

lectures.title: B cells and antibodies
lectures.covers: The humoral response: how B cells are activated with and without T-cell help, what happens in the germinal center, and what each antibody class does.

items.p: A T cell needs two signals: its receptor on peptide–MHC, then costimulation. It then proliferates, makes cytokines and becomes an effector cell.

ul: CD28 (T cell) binds B7 (APC): the costimulatory signal
CD40L (activated CD4 T cell) binds CD40 on B cells, macrophages and dendritic cells
Signal 1 without proper costimulation can lead to anergy

items.p: Cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells with perforin (holes) and enzymes that trigger apoptosis.
B cells are made and mature in the bone marrow. Naive B cells carry IgM and IgD (by alternative splicing) and meet antigen in peripheral lymphoid tissue.

ul: Follicular B cells: the majority; T-dependent responses to proteins; long-lived plasma cells
Marginal zone and B-1 cells: T-independent responses to lipids, polysaccharides, nucleic acids
Memory B cells: membrane-bound antibody, long life

summary.h: Two ways to activate a B cell

items.p: Signal 1 always comes from the B-cell receptor. Signal 2 differs.

ul: T-independent: repetitive non-protein antigens cross-link receptors (TI-2) or add a TLR signal (TI-1). Little or no memory.
T-dependent: protein antigens. The B cell presents peptide to a Tfh cell and receives CD40L and cytokines.

items.p: Complement helps: CD21 (CR2) binds complement on the microbe and brings CD19 to the receptor, boosting the signal. The coreceptor is CD19, CD21 and CD81.

items.note: The take-home slide lists the coreceptor as "CD19/CD20/CD81" and says T-dependent activation is by "type 2 helper T cells". The detailed slides say CD19/CD21/CD81 and Tfh cells; these match standard texts.

items.p: Fewer than 1 in 10,000 naive T cells recognize a given antigen, so T and B cells must be steered together.

ul: Lymph flow: afferent vessel, subcapsular sinus, cortex, medulla, efferent vessel
Naive T cells sit in T-cell areas; naive B cells in primary follicles
Follicular dendritic cells are not hematopoietic and not phagocytic; they hold antigen on complement receptors for B cells
Activated B and T cells move to the follicle border and meet: linked recognition

items.p: Tfh signals: CD40L gives survival (NFκB, anti-apoptotic proteins). IL-21 gives proliferation and plasma-cell differentiation (STAT3).
First phase: B cells proliferate in the primary focus. Some become plasmablasts: still dividing, secreting mainly IgM, dead within days.

Second phase: other B cells enter the follicle with Tfh cells and build a germinal center. The follicle is now a secondary follicle, with a mantle zone of resting B cells around a light and a dark zone. It disappears 3–4 weeks after exposure.
The enzyme AID mutates the V region (somatic hypermutation), about 1 per 1000 base pairs per division.

ul: Higher affinity: survival, with help from Tfh cells and CD40
No working receptor: apoptosis
Good binders re-enter the dark zone and divide again
Survivors become plasma cells or memory cells

items.p: The V region stays; the constant region changes. It is an irreversible DNA recombination between switch regions (every C gene has one except δ), directed by Tfh cytokines.
Enzymes in order: AID, UNG, APE1. They nick both strands, the DNA between two switch regions is cut out, and the ends are joined.

table: First antibody; pentamer, 10 sites; high avidity; strong complement activator; stays in blood
Main antibody in blood and tissue fluid (about 80%); 3-week life; opsonizes; fixes complement; crosses the placenta; 4 subclasses
Main antibody in secretions and breast milk; neutralizes; monomer or dimer; 2 subclasses
Very low level; bound to mast cells; allergy and parasites
On naive B cells with IgM; hardly secreted

items.p: Antibodies work by neutralization, opsonization and complement activation. In ADCC, NK cells bind the Fc of antibody on a target and kill it; this matters against parasites.

items.note: The slide says IgG crosses the placenta "because of its size". Standard texts attribute transfer to a specific Fc receptor in the placenta.

cards.q: CD28 binds what, and why does it matter?
cards.a: B7 (B7-1, B7-2) on APCs; it is the costimulatory second signal for T-cell activation.

cards.q: CD40L: which cell carries it and what does it bind?
cards.a: Activated CD4 T cells; binds CD40 on B cells, macrophages and dendritic cells.
Th1: IFN-γ. Th2: IL-4, IL-5, IL-13. Th17: IL-17, IL-22.

cards.q: Which T helper subset helps B cells in germinal centers, and with which cytokine?
cards.a: T follicular helper (Tfh) cells; IL-21

cards.q: Which immunoglobulins are on a naive B cell?
cards.a: IgM and IgD (co-expressed by alternative splicing)

cards.q: Which B cells make T-independent responses?
cards.a: Marginal zone B cells and B-1 cells (follicular B cells make T-dependent responses)

cards.q: Typical T-independent antigens, and the catch
cards.a: Repetitive non-protein polymers (polysaccharides, glycolipids, nucleic acids); little or no memory
TI-1: BCR plus another receptor such as a TLR. TI-2: strong cross-linking of BCRs by repetitive polysaccharide.
CD19, CD21 (CR2) and CD81; CD21 binds complement on the microbe
Non-hematopoietic, non-phagocytic, hold antigen on complement receptors for B cells
T and B cells activated by the same antigen meet at the follicle–T-zone border

cards.q: What do CD40L and IL-21 from Tfh cells do to the B cell?
cards.a: CD40L: survival (NFκB, anti-apoptotic). IL-21: proliferation and plasma-cell differentiation (STAT3).
Plasmablast: still dividing, mainly IgM, short-lived, in the primary focus. Plasma cell: long-lived, goes to the bone marrow.

cards.q: What is a secondary lymphoid follicle?
cards.a: A follicle containing a germinal center (mantle zone around light and dark zones)

cards.q: Enzyme of somatic hypermutation, and the region it changes
cards.a: AID (activation-induced cytidine deaminase); the V region, not the C region
Irreversible non-homologous recombination between switch regions; same V region, new constant region

cards.q: Enzymes of class-switch recombination, in order
cards.a: AID, UNG, APE1

cards.q: Which heavy-chain gene has no switch region?
cards.a: δ (IgD is made by alternative splicing, not switching)
Pentamer with 10 binding sites; high avidity; best complement activator; first antibody made
Main antibody of blood and extracellular fluid, about 3-week life, opsonin and complement activator, crosses the placenta

cards.q: IgA: where and how it works
cards.a: Secretions and breast milk; mainly neutralization; monomer or dimer
Very low level; bound to mast cells (and basophils); allergic reactions and parasite defense
Neutralization, opsonization, complement activation
NK cells recognize the Fc of antibody bound to a target and kill it; important against parasites

cards.q: Fate of B cells leaving the germinal center
cards.a: Plasma cells (bone marrow, medullary cords, splenic red pulp) or memory B cells

questions.stem: After receiving signals 1 and 2, what does a T cell do next, and where does signal 2 originate according to the lecture?

options.A: Proliferation, antibody secretion and differentiation into plasma cells; from molecules produced during the innate response
options.B: Proliferation, cytokine production and effector differentiation; from molecules produced during the innate response
options.C: Anergy followed by apoptosis; from molecules produced during the adaptive response
options.D: Somatic hypermutation and class switching; from cytokines released by follicular dendritic cells
options.E: Proliferation, cytokine production and differentiation into its effector state; from peptide bound in the MHC groove

questions.explanation: Through secondary signals the T cell proliferates, produces cytokines and differentiates into its effector state. Signal 2 results from molecules produced during the innate immune response (costimulators, cytokines, complement products). A: Antibody secretion and plasma cells describe B cells. C: Anergy results from negative costimulatory signaling. D: These are B-cell processes. E: Peptide–MHC is signal 1.

questions.stem: A B cell presents antigen to an activated CD4+ helper T cell. Which T cell surface molecule binds CD40 on the B cell to deliver help?
questions.explanation: CD28 on T cells binds B7-1/B7-2 on APCs; CD40L on activated CD4+ T cells binds CD40 on B cells, macrophages and DCs. B: Binds B7 on APCs. C: On APCs, not T cells. D: B cell coreceptor. E: B cell coreceptor.

questions.stem: Besides activation, what can some costimulatory signals produce?

options.A: Negative T-cell signaling with class switching to IgE
options.B: Positive selection of high-affinity T-cell clones in germinal centers
options.C: Irreversible rearrangement of the T-cell receptor genes
options.D: Release of perforin from the antigen-presenting cell

questions.explanation: Some costimulatory signals lead to negative T-cell signaling, resulting in cellular anergy; these pathways may also be involved in generating regulatory cells. A: Class switching is a B-cell event. B: Selection in germinal centers concerns B cells. C: Rearrangement occurs during development. D: Perforin is released by cytotoxic cells.

questions.stem: Which CD4 T cell subset targets extracellular bacteria and fungi?
questions.explanation: Th1: IFN-γ, macrophages. Th2: IL-4/5/13, eosinophils, helminths. Th17: IL-17/22, neutrophils, extracellular bacteria and fungi. A: Intracellular microbes in macrophages. B: Helminths. C: B cell help in germinal centers. E: Suppression.

questions.stem: A child with a helminth infection has high eosinophils and raised IgE. Which CD4 T cell subset drives this response?
questions.explanation: Th2 cells (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13) act on eosinophils, mast cells and basophils against helminths. T follicular helper cells help B cells in germinal centers. A: Intracellular microbes. B: Extracellular bacteria and fungi. D: Germinal center help. E: Suppression.

questions.stem: In the T-cell mediated cytotoxic response, what is the correct sequence?

options.A: Cytotoxic T cell binds the infected cell; an enzyme makes holes in its membrane; perforin enters and promotes apoptosis
options.B: Helper T cell binds the infected cell; perforin makes holes in its membrane; complement enters and causes lysis
options.C: Cytotoxic T cell binds free antigen; antibody makes holes in the microbe; an enzyme enters and promotes necrosis
options.D: Cytotoxic T cell binds the infected cell; perforin makes holes in its membrane; an enzyme enters and promotes apoptosis
options.E: Cytotoxic T cell engulfs the infected cell; lysosomal enzymes digest it in a phagolysosome

questions.explanation: The cytotoxic T cell binds the infected cell (self–nonself complex), perforin makes holes in the infected cell's membrane, an enzyme that promotes apoptosis enters, and the infected cell is destroyed. A: Perforin forms the holes and the enzyme enters. B: The killer is the cytotoxic T cell, and complement is not involved. C: The T cell binds a self–nonself complex on an infected cell. E: Killing is by perforin and enzymes, not phagocytosis.

questions.stem: Where do B cells mature?
questions.explanation: B cells are produced and mature in the bone marrow, then migrate to peripheral lymphoid tissues; antigen binds IgM and IgD on mature naive B cells. A: T cells. B: Where mature B cells meet antigen. C: Not the site. D: Not the site.

questions.stem: How are memory B cells described, and what kinds of antigen do B cells recognize?

options.A: Secreted antibodies and a short lifespan; extracellular soluble antigens and cell surface antigens
options.B: Membrane-bound antibodies and a long lifespan; soluble antigens and cell surface antigens
options.C: Membrane-bound antibodies and a long lifespan; processed peptides on MHC molecules
options.D: No immunoglobulin and a long lifespan; intracellular antigens in the cytosol
options.E: Membrane-bound antibodies and a lifespan of days; soluble antigens exclusively

questions.explanation: Memory B cells have membrane-bound antibodies and a long lifespan. B cells recognize extracellular soluble antigens and cell surface antigens. A: Memory cells carry membrane-bound antibody and are long-lived. C: That is T-cell recognition. D: Memory B cells have membrane Ig, and B cells see extracellular or surface antigen. E: They are long-lived and also recognize cell surface antigens.

questions.stem: On the B-cell receptor, what are Fab and Fc, and how does a naive B cell express IgM and IgD together?

options.A: Fab: antigen-binding fragment; Fc: constant fragment; by alternative splicing
options.B: Fab: constant fragment; Fc: antigen-binding fragment; by alternative splicing
options.C: Fab: antigen-binding fragment; Fc: constant fragment; by class-switch recombination
options.D: Fab: light chain; Fc: heavy chain; by somatic hypermutation
options.E: Fab: antigen-binding fragment; Fc: complement fragment; by V(D)J recombination of a second allele

questions.explanation: Fab = fragment antigen binding; Fc = constant fragment. IgM and IgD are co-expressed through alternative splicing of the heavy-chain transcript (μ and δ constant genes). B: The fragments are swapped. C: IgD co-expression does not involve switch recombination. D: Fab contains parts of both chains, and hypermutation changes V regions. E: Fc is the constant fragment.

questions.stem: Which B cells carry out most T-dependent responses to protein antigens?
questions.explanation: Follicular B cells are the majority and make the bulk of T-dependent responses; marginal zone and B-1 cells make T-independent responses. A: T-independent. B: T-independent. D: Short-lived secretors. E: Secondary responses.

questions.stem: A protein vaccine antigen binds the BCR of a naive follicular B cell. Where does its second activation signal come from?

options.E: MHC class I on dendritic cells

questions.explanation: B cell activation: signal 1 from the BCR; signal 2 from Tfh cells for protein antigens, or from microbial antigens in T-independent activation. A: T-independent; not for protein antigens. B: Not the source. C: Not the source. E: Not the source.

questions.stem: A polysaccharide capsule with highly repetitive units activates B cells directly. What is expected after this activation?
questions.explanation: T-independent activation: the antigen cross-links BCRs (TI-2: repetitive polysaccharides) or acts with a TLR (TI-1); little or no memory. A: Needs T cell help. C: Needs T cell help. D: T-dependent. E: T-dependent.

questions.stem: How do TI-1 and TI-2 activation differ?

options.A: TI-1: BCR plus other receptors such as TLR; TI-2: strong BCR cross-linking by repetitive polysaccharides
options.B: TI-1: strong cross-linking of the BCR by repetitive polysaccharides; TI-2: simultaneous activation of the BCR and TLR
options.C: TI-1: activation by Tfh cells through CD40; TI-2: activation by complement through CD21
options.D: TI-1: activation of follicular B cells; TI-2: activation of plasma cells
options.E: TI-1: protein antigens; TI-2: lipid antigens presented on MHC II

questions.explanation: TI-1: simultaneous activation of BCR and other receptors on B cells (such as TLR). TI-2: strong cross-linking of BCR by repetitive polysaccharides. B: Reversed. C: Tfh help defines T-dependent activation. D: Not the distinction given. E: T-independent antigens are non-protein.

questions.stem: Why must the migration of activated T and B cells in secondary lymphoid organs be precisely regulated?

options.A: More than 1/100 naive T cells recognize a given antigen, so encounters must be limited
options.B: Naive B cells cannot bind antigen until a T cell has processed it
options.C: T cells and B cells recognize different antigens in linked recognition
options.D: Fewer than 1/10,000 B cells express immunoglobulin, so T cells must select them
options.E: Fewer than 1/10,000 naive T cells recognize a given antigen

questions.explanation: The frequency of naive T cells recognizing a particular antigen is extremely low (<1/10,000), so linked recognition requires regulated migration of activated T and B cells into specific locations. A: The frequency is extremely low. B: B cells bind native antigen. C: Linked recognition involves the same antigen. D: The figure refers to naive T cells specific for an antigen.

questions.stem: Trace lymph through a lymph node and state why the node acts as a "settling tank".

options.A: Afferent lymphatics, medulla, cortex, subcapsular sinus, efferent vessel; there are fewer efferent vessels
options.B: Efferent lymphatics, subcapsular sinus, cortex, medulla, afferent vessel; there are fewer afferent vessels
options.C: Afferent lymphatics, subcapsular sinus, cortex, medulla, efferent vessel; there are fewer efferent vessels
options.D: Afferent lymphatics, cortex, subcapsular sinus, medulla, efferent vessel; there are more efferent vessels
options.E: Afferent lymphatics, subcapsular sinus, medulla, cortex, efferent vessel; the capsule is rigid

questions.explanation: Afferent lymphatics bring lymph, which collects in subcapsular sinuses, moves into the cortex then the medulla and exits by the efferent vessel. Fewer efferent vessels let lymph stagnate: a settling tank. A: Cortex precedes medulla after the subcapsular sinus. B: Lymph enters by afferent and leaves by efferent vessels. D: The sinus comes first and efferents are fewer. E: Order and reason are wrong.

questions.stem: Where do naive T and B cells initially sit in a lymph node?

options.A: T cells in the primary lymphoid follicles; B cells in the T-cell areas
options.B: T cells in the medullary cords; B cells in the subcapsular sinus
options.C: T cells and B cells together in germinal centers
options.D: T cells in the T-cell areas; B cells in the primary lymphoid follicles
options.E: T cells in the mantle zone; B cells in the dark zone

questions.explanation: Naive T and B cells entering the node occupy two distinct zones, the T-cell areas and the primary lymphoid follicles (B-cell zones), because of distinct chemokine receptor and chemokine patterns. A: Reversed. B: Not the zones described. C: Germinal centers form after activation. E: These zones belong to an established germinal center.

questions.stem: Which description of follicular dendritic cells is correct?

options.A: Non-hematopoietic, non-phagocytic cells that trap antigen with complement receptors for B cells
options.B: Hematopoietic, phagocytic cells whose long processes present peptide on MHC II to naive T cells
options.C: Non-hematopoietic, phagocytic cells that digest antigen for follicular B cells
options.D: Hematopoietic, non-phagocytic cells that secrete IL-21 for B-cell proliferation
options.E: Non-hematopoietic, non-phagocytic cells that trap antigen through Fc receptors for T cells in the T zone

questions.explanation: FDCs in follicles are of non-hematopoietic origin and non-phagocytic; they bear numerous long processes and trap antigens with complement receptors for access by follicular B cells. B: That describes conventional dendritic cells. C: They are non-phagocytic. D: IL-21 comes from Tfh cells, and FDCs are non-hematopoietic. E: They sit in follicles and use complement receptors for B cells.

questions.stem: After a naive follicular B cell meets its antigen displayed by FDCs or macrophages, where does it go?

options.A: Within a few days to the dark zone of the germinal center
options.B: To the outer follicle, at the interface with the T-cell zone
options.C: Within a few hours to the medullary cords to secrete antibody
options.D: Within a few weeks to the bone marrow as a memory cell
options.E: It stays in the center of the follicle until T cells arrive

questions.explanation: Activated naive follicular B cells migrate within a few hours to the outer follicle, at the interface between the B-cell follicle and the T-cell zone. A: The germinal center forms later. C: Medullary cords receive plasma cells later. D: That is not the first step. E: It migrates to the follicle–T zone interface.

questions.stem: T and B cells activated by the same antigen meet at the border of the follicle. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Naive T cells activated by DCs migrate to the follicle border, where T and B cells activated by the same antigen meet: linked recognition. A: Expansion of fitting clones. B: Germinal center process. C: Change of heavy chain. D: Inside APCs.

questions.stem: Put the T–B interaction in order: (1) B cell proliferation and differentiation, (2) helper T cell expresses CD40L and secretes cytokines, (3) B cell presents antigen to the helper T cell, (4) B cell activated by CD40 engagement and cytokines.
questions.explanation: The B cell presents antigen to the helper T cell; the helper T cell is activated, expresses CD40L and secretes cytokines; the B cell is activated by CD40 engagement and cytokines; then it proliferates and differentiates. A: The B cell first presents antigen to the helper T cell. B: CD40L must be expressed before CD40 is engaged. D: Activation precedes proliferation. E: Presentation comes first.

questions.stem: A patient's B cells cannot respond to IL-21. Which step fails?
questions.explanation: Tfh CD40L–CD40: non-canonical NFκB, anti-apoptotic molecules, survival. Tfh IL-21 → STAT3: proliferation and differentiation into plasma cells. A: Not IL-21 dependent. C: Not IL-21 dependent. D: CD40L–CD40. E: Not IL-21 dependent.

questions.stem: What happens in the primary focus?

options.A: B cells proliferate for several days and some become short-lived plasmablasts
options.B: B cells undergo somatic hypermutation for several weeks, and some become long-lived plasma cells
options.C: B cells rest for several days while T cells proliferate, and class switching is completed
options.D: Resting B cells are displaced to form the mantle zone around light and dark zones
options.E: Memory B cells are selected by follicular dendritic cells and leave by the efferent lymphatic

questions.explanation: In the primary focus B cells proliferate for several days (first phase of the humoral response); some differentiate into antibody-synthesizing plasmablasts. Other B cells go to the follicle and form the germinal center. B: Hypermutation happens in the germinal center. C: B cells proliferate there. D: That describes the germinal center. E: Not what the primary focus is.

questions.stem: What happens to most plasmablasts formed in the primary focus?

options.A: They migrate to the bone marrow
options.D: They die within a few days
options.E: They return to the dark zone

questions.explanation: Plasmablasts secrete antibody (mainly IgM) yet still divide; they die in the primary focus after a few days. Plasma cells are long-lived and migrate to the bone marrow. A: Long-lived plasma cells. B: Not their fate. C: Non-hematopoietic. E: Germinal center centrocytes.

questions.stem: About what share of germinal center lymphocytes are antigen-specific T cells?
questions.explanation: The germinal center is mainly proliferating B cells; antigen-specific T cells are about 10% of its lymphocytes. A: About 10%. B: About 10%. C: About 10%. D: Mostly proliferating B cells.

questions.stem: A lymph node biopsy shows a follicle with a germinal center surrounded by a rim of small resting B cells. What is this rim?
questions.explanation: A follicle with a germinal center is a secondary lymphoid follicle; resting B cells displaced to the periphery form the mantle zone. A: Spleen, outside the mantle. B: T cell area. D: Plasma cells. E: Lymph entry.

questions.stem: When does a germinal center disappear?

options.A: Once plasmablasts form, about 3–4 days after initial exposure
options.B: Once class switching starts, about 3–4 hours after initial exposure
options.C: It persists for life as a secondary follicle
options.D: Once the infection is cleared, about 3–4 weeks after initial exposure
options.E: Once memory cells reach the bone marrow, about 3–4 months after exposure

questions.explanation: The GC shrinks and disappears once infection is cleared (3–4 weeks after initial exposure). A: The germinal center lasts weeks. B: Far too early. C: It shrinks and disappears. E: The time given is 3–4 weeks.

questions.stem: Which B cell coreceptor protein binds complement fragments on a pathogen?
questions.explanation: B cell coreceptor: CD19, CD21 (CR2), CD81. CD21 binds complement fragments on the pathogen; CD19 is phosphorylated by the activated BCR. A: Signals when phosphorylated. B: Part of the complex. D: Receives T cell help. E: On T cells.

questions.stem: Germinal center B cells acquire point mutations in their Ig V regions, but not their C regions, at about 1 per 1000 bp per division. Which enzyme drives this?
questions.explanation: Somatic hypermutation: AID-mediated V-region mutations (1–5 amino acids), about 1/1000 bp per division; they do not extend to the C region. B: Acts after AID in switching. C: Acts after UNG in switching. D: Not named. E: Not named.

questions.stem: At what rate do Ig V-region genes accumulate mutations in germinal center B cells, and what does this mean per division?

options.A: About 1/1000 base pairs per division, giving about a 5% chance of a receptor mutation at each division
options.B: About 1/10^10 base pairs per division, giving about a 50% chance of a receptor mutation
options.C: About 1/10 base pairs per division, so each receptor differs after one division
options.D: About 1/100,000 base pairs per division, giving about a 10% chance of a receptor mutation
options.E: About 1/1000 base pairs per division, giving about a 50% chance of a receptor mutation at each division

questions.explanation: Ig V-region genes mutate at about 1/1000 bp per cell division versus 1/10^10 for the rest of the DNA: about a 50% chance of a receptor mutation at each B-cell division. A: The chance given is about 50%. B: 1/10^10 is the rate for the rest of the DNA. C: The rate is 1/1000. D: Not the figures given.

questions.stem: Which germinal center B cells are positively selected?
questions.explanation: B cells without a functional BCR or with poor antigen uptake die (negative selection); higher-affinity cells are positively selected through Tfh contact and CD40. A: Die by apoptosis. C: Die by apoptosis. D: Positive selection needs Tfh contact. E: Not the criterion.

questions.stem: Where does a centrocyte with an improved receptor go next?
questions.explanation: Cyclic re-entry: centrocytes with better receptors return to the dark zone and divide again as centroblasts; survivors become plasma or memory cells. A: Resting B cells. B: Not the cycle. C: Plasma cells. D: Long-lived plasma cells.

questions.stem: A B cell clone switches from IgM to IgG during a response. What stays the same?
questions.explanation: Isotype switching keeps the same V region (apart from somatic hypermutation) with a different C-region isotype; first IgM and IgD, then IgG, IgA or IgE. B: Changes. C: Changes. D: Changes. E: Change with isotype.

questions.stem: Which statement about the order of immunoglobulin expression is correct?

options.A: The first receptors are IgM and IgG, the first antibody produced is IgD, and IgA or IgE appear later
options.B: Receptors IgM and IgD first; the first antibody produced is IgM; IgG, IgA or IgE come later
options.C: The first receptor is IgG, the first antibody produced is IgG, and IgM appears in secondary responses
options.D: The first receptors are IgM and IgD, the first antibody produced is IgA, and IgM appears later
options.E: The first receptors are IgD and IgE, the first antibody produced is IgM, and IgG appears later

questions.explanation: The first antigen receptors on B cells are IgM and IgD; the first antibody produced in an immune response is IgM. Later the same V region may be expressed in IgG, IgA or IgE. A: The first receptors are IgM and IgD and the first antibody is IgM. C: IgM comes first. D: The first antibody is IgM. E: Naive B cells carry IgM and IgD.

questions.stem: How does class switching differ from co-expression of IgM and IgD?

options.B: It needs no T cell cytokines

questions.explanation: IgM and IgD are co-expressed by alternative splicing; class switching is irreversible non-homologous DNA recombination directed by Tfh cytokines. A: That gives IgD. B: Directed by Tfh cytokines. D: V region unchanged. E: After activation.

questions.stem: Which statement about switch (S) regions is correct?

options.A: Repetitive DNA sequences downstream of each V-region gene except μ, where RNA polymerase can stall
options.B: Unique DNA sequences upstream of each C-region gene including δ, where AID is transcribed
options.C: Repetitive RNA sequences that guide alternative splicing of μ and δ
options.D: Repetitive DNA sequences upstream of each C-region gene except δ, where RNA polymerase can stall
options.E: Repetitive DNA sequences between V, D and J segments that guide somatic hypermutation

questions.explanation: Switch regions are repetitive DNA sequences that guide class switching, found upstream of each Ig C-region gene with the exception of the δ gene. Transcription through them lets RNA polymerase stall, making them substrates for AID, then UNG and APE1. A: They lie upstream of C genes, and the exception is δ. B: They are repetitive and absent before δ. C: Switch regions are DNA and guide recombination. E: They guide class switching.

questions.stem: Which heavy-chain constant gene has no upstream switch region?
questions.explanation: Switch regions are repetitive DNA upstream of each C gene except δ; AID, then UNG, then APE1 make nicks that become double-strand breaks. A: Has one. C: Has one. D: Has one. E: Has one.

questions.stem: A B cell switches from IgM to IgE. What happens to the DNA?

options.A: The Sμ and Sε regions are transcribed together, and the intervening RNA is spliced out
options.B: The V region is replaced by a new V segment next to Cε
options.C: The Sμ and Sε regions are brought together and ligated, and the intervening DNA is excised
options.D: The Sδ and Sε regions are ligated after excision of Cμ
options.E: The Cμ gene is mutated by AID until it encodes ε

questions.explanation: The two S regions are brought together by repair proteins; class switching is completed by excision of the intervening DNA and ligation of the Sε and Sμ regions (switching from IgM to IgE). A: Switching is DNA recombination with excision. B: The V region is unchanged. D: There is no switch region before δ. E: Switching removes intervening DNA; it does not mutate Cμ into Cε.

questions.stem: How many subclasses do IgG and IgA have in humans, and how are IgG subclasses named?

options.A: IgG has four subclasses, IgG1 to IgG4, named in increasing order of serum abundance; IgA has two
options.B: IgG has two subclasses and IgA has four, named by order of discovery
options.C: IgG has three subclasses named by molecular weight; IgA has two
options.D: IgG has four subclasses named by half-life; IgA has one
options.E: IgG has four subclasses, IgG1 to IgG4, named in decreasing order of serum abundance; IgA has two

questions.explanation: IgG has 4 subclasses in humans (IgG1, IgG2, IgG3, IgG4, named by decreasing abundance in serum); IgA has 2 (IgA1, IgA2). A: The order is decreasing abundance. B: Reversed numbers and wrong naming rule. C: IgG has four. D: Naming is by abundance, and IgA has two.

questions.stem: In the first days of an infection, the first antibody secreted is a pentamer with 10 antigen-binding sites. Which class is it?
questions.explanation: IgM: first class produced; pentamer; 10 antigen-binding sites, high avidity; effective complement activation. B: Monomer; later. C: Monomer or dimer. D: Very low levels. E: Little secreted.

questions.stem: Which immunoglobulin is expressed on all naive B cells together with IgM, yet little of it is produced as antibody at any time?
questions.explanation: All naive B cells express surface IgM and IgD. Little IgD antibody is produced at any time. A: IgG is the principal antibody of blood. B: IgA is the principal antibody of secretions. C: IgE is present at very low levels but is not the naive B-cell coreceptor isotype. E: A subclass of IgG.

questions.stem: A newborn has protective antibody against tetanus although he has never been immunized. Which maternal antibody class explains this?
questions.explanation: IgG: principal antibody of blood and tissue fluid; half-life about 3 weeks; opsonizes and activates complement; crosses the placenta. A: Does not cross the placenta. C: Reaches the infant in milk. D: Not protective here. E: Little secreted.

questions.stem: Antibody in breast milk protects a nursing infant's gut. How does this antibody mainly act?
questions.explanation: IgA, the principal antibody of secretions including breast milk, acts mainly by neutralization; it is a weak opsonin and weak complement activator. B: Weak for IgA. C: Weak for IgA. D: Not its main action. E: IgE.

questions.stem: Which antibody class is bound avidly to mast cell receptors?
questions.explanation: IgE: very low serum levels; bound avidly to mast cell (and basophil) receptors; allergic reactions. A: Principal serum antibody. B: Secretions. C: Pentamer. E: Little secreted.

questions.stem: About what share of serum antibody is IgG?
questions.explanation: IgG ~80% (MW 150,000); IgA ~13%; IgM ~6% (MW 900,000); IgD and IgE < 1%. A: IgA. B: IgM. C: About 80%. D: IgD and IgE.

questions.stem: Where do long-lived plasma cells reside?
questions.explanation: After the germinal center, some plasma cells go to the bone marrow (long-lived); others to lymph node medullary cords or splenic red pulp. A: Centroblasts. B: T cell zone. D: T cells. E: Not their home.

questions.stem: A patient with a helminth infection has parasites coated with antibody. NK cells bind the antibody's Fc and release damaging substances. Which mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: ADCC: NK cells recognize the Fc of antibody and release damaging substances; innate effectors can attack pathogens that lack or hide PAMPs; important against parasites. A: Phagocytes ingest coated microbes. B: MAC. C: Blocks binding. E: Antigen-specific T cells.

questions.stem: An antibody binds a bacterial toxin and stops it from attaching to its receptor. Which mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: Antibodies act by neutralization, opsonization and complement activation; which mechanism depends on the heavy-chain isotype. A: Coating for phagocytosis. C: Lysis or inflammation. D: NK cell killing. E: T–B cooperation.

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as influencing the type and quantity of antibody produced EXCEPT:

options.D: The anatomic site where activation occurs
options.E: The MHC class I haplotype of the plasma cell

questions.explanation: Type and quantity of antibodies vary with the type of antigen, prior antigen exposure, involvement of T cells and the anatomic site where activation occurs. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed.

questions.stem: What does the clonal selection hypothesis explain, according to the take-home messages?

options.A: Random mutations during clonal expansion yield higher-affinity B cells, making secondary responses effective
options.B: Random mutations during clonal expansion yield B cells with new specificities, which is why primary responses are so fast
options.C: Directed mutations by antigen yield B cells with lower affinity, which limits autoimmunity
options.D: Class switching during clonal expansion yields IgM memory, which is why secondary responses are slower
options.E: Negative selection in the thymus removes B cells, which is why tolerance is maintained

questions.explanation: During clonal selection, random mutations during clonal expansion produce B cells with increased antibody-binding affinity; this may explain why secondary immune responses are so effective at preventing reinfection. B: The gain is affinity, and the benefit is for secondary responses. C: Mutations are random and higher affinity is selected. D: Not the hypothesis. E: Not what is described.

questions.stem: Besides CD40L and IL-21, activated Tfh cells secrete cytokines such as IL-6 and TGF-β. What do these signals regulate?

options.A: The affinity of each binding site for its epitope
options.B: The survival of B cells through non-canonical NFκB
options.D: The migration of B cells to the T-zone interface
options.E: The cross-linking of B-cell receptors by antigen

questions.explanation: Tfh cells secrete additional cytokines (IL-6, TGF-β and others) that provide signals regulating the type of antibodies produced. A: Affinity is changed by somatic hypermutation and selection. B: That is the CD40L–CD40 effect. D: Migration is chemokine-driven. E: That depends on the antigen.

questions.stem: Which T cell molecule binds B7-1 and B7-2 on antigen-presenting cells to give the costimulatory signal?
questions.explanation: CD28 on T cells binds B7-1/B7-2 on APCs (costimulation); CD40L on activated CD4+ T cells binds CD40 on B cells. A: Binds CD40. B: TCR complex. C: Binds MHC II. E: B cell coreceptor.

questions.stem: A capsular polysaccharide triggers antibody without T cell help. Which B cells mainly respond?
questions.explanation: T-independent responses to multivalent antigens (lipids, polysaccharides, nucleic acids) come from marginal zone B cells and B-1 cells in mucosal sites. A: T-dependent protein responses. C: T-dependent. D: Secondary responses. E: Short-lived secretors.

questions.stem: What does CD40L–CD40 signaling from a Tfh cell mainly give the B cell?
questions.explanation: Tfh CD40L–CD40: non-canonical NFκB, anti-apoptotic molecules, B cell survival. IL-21 → STAT3: proliferation and plasma cell differentiation. B: IL-21 via STAT3. C: IL-6, TGF-β. D: The BCR. E: CD21.

lectures.title: Artificial immunity and vaccines
lectures.covers: Active versus passive immunity, herd immunity, the types of vaccine with their strengths and limits, adjuvants, and vaccination against cancer.

items.p: Passive immunity is borrowed antibody. It works at once but is temporary and leaves no memory.
Active immunity is the person's own response. It takes time but usually lasts, with memory.

table: Maternal antibody; IgA in breast milk and colostrum

items.p: A non-pathogenic biological product that imitates the pathogen's antigens. It induces protection without causing the disease, and it must pass clinical trials like any drug.
An ideal vaccine is safe, effective, long-lasting, easy to give, heat-stable, cheap and easy to mass-produce. Latency and antigenic variation of the pathogen make vaccines harder to design.
When enough people are immune, transmission stops and the unprotected are protected indirectly.

ul: Highly transmissible disease (measles): about 95% coverage needed
Less transmissible (polio, rubella, diphtheria): about 85% may be enough

table: Whole organism destroyed by chemicals, heat or radiation
Stable; weak response; boosters. Hepatitis A, rabies, injectable polio and influenza
Strong, lasting immunity in 1–2 doses; needs refrigeration; can revert; avoid in the immunocompromised. Measles, mumps, chickenpox, yellow fever, BCG
Few side effects; weak, needs adjuvant. Hepatitis B
T-independent: no memory, low affinity, no response under 2 years. Pneumococcus 23
Polysaccharide linked to a protein carrier
T-dependent: memory, works in infants. Hib
Immunity to the toxin, not the microbe. Diphtheria, tetanus
Harmless virus carrying the antigen gene
Strong response without adjuvant; pre-existing immunity to the vector is a problem
DNA or mRNA encoding the antigen
Fast to design. Pfizer and Moderna mRNA vaccines

items.p: DNA vaccines are stable at room temperature but must reach the nucleus. RNA vaccines act in the cytoplasm but are less stable.

items.note: The slide says inactivated vaccines "do not require refrigeration"; in practice most still need a cold chain. The slide also lists cholera among toxoid vaccines; standard sources describe cholera vaccines as killed or live oral vaccines.

summary.h: Live versus non-live in weak immune systems

ul: Live vaccines can replicate without control in immunocompromised patients
Non-live vaccines are safe for them, but may not protect if B cells are missing (B-cell or combined immunodeficiency)

items.p: Adjuvants make a vaccine more immunogenic. They behave like PAMPs: they wake up innate immunity and antigen-presenting cells.

ul: Delivery systems: concentrate and display the antigen
Immune potentiators: activate innate immunity directly
In routine use: aluminum salts

items.p: Other ingredients are preservatives, emulsifiers (polysorbate 80) and stabilizers (gelatine, sorbitol). The main concern is allergy.

ul: Prevent infections that cause cancer: HPV 16 and 18 (cervix), hepatitis B (liver)
Make "cold" tumors visible to the immune system ("hot"), so checkpoint blockade can work

items.note: The slide groups Helicobacter pylori (stomach cancer) with cancer-causing viruses. It is a bacterium, and no vaccine against it is licensed.

cards.q: Passive immunity: definition and two limits
cards.a: Transfer of preformed antibodies; temporary and no memory.
Maternal antibody; IgA in breast milk and colostrum
Pooled immune globulin (IVIG), antivenin
Indirect protection of susceptible people because transmission is interrupted

cards.q: Vaccine coverage needed for measles versus polio or rubella
cards.a: About 95% versus about 85%

cards.q: Two pathogen features that make vaccines difficult
cards.a: Latency and antigenic variation
Weak immune response; booster doses needed
Hepatitis A, rabies, injectable polio, injectable influenza, typhoid
Strong cellular and antibody responses; long-term immunity after 1–2 doses
Need refrigeration, can revert to virulence, dangerous in immunocompromised patients
Measles, mumps, chickenpox, yellow fever, BCG, oral polio, nasal influenza

cards.q: Why does a plain polysaccharide vaccine work poorly in infants?
cards.a: The response is T-independent: no memory, no affinity maturation, no response under 2 years.

cards.q: What does conjugating a polysaccharide to a protein carrier achieve?
cards.a: A T-dependent response: memory, affinity maturation, protection in infants (example: Hib)

cards.q: Toxoid vaccines: how made, and what immunity
cards.a: Toxin inactivated with formalin; immunity to the toxin's effects (diphtheria, tetanus)

cards.q: Subunit vaccine example and its weakness
cards.a: Hepatitis B; poor immunogenicity, so adjuvants are needed

cards.q: Viral vector vaccines: advantage and drawback
cards.a: Strong humoral and cellular response without adjuvant; pre-existing immunity to the vector (solved with simian adenovirus)
DNA: stable at room temperature, must enter the nucleus. RNA: no nucleus needed, less stable.
Enhance immunogenicity by acting like PAMPs: activate innate immunity and APCs
Aluminum salts (alum)
HPV 16/18 (cervical cancer) and hepatitis B (liver cancer)

cards.q: Are non-live vaccines safe in immunodeficiency?
cards.a: Yes, but they may not protect when B cells are lacking.

questions.stem: A hiker bitten by a viper receives antivenin. Which type of immunization is this?
questions.explanation: Passive immunization transfers preformed antibody: temporary, no memory. Artificial passive: immune gamma globulin, antivenin, IVIG. A: Maternal antibody. B: Vaccination. D: Infection. E: Population protection.

questions.stem: How does active immunization differ from passive immunization?

options.A: The person receives preformed antibodies, typically giving long-term immunity
options.B: The person's own immune system is stimulated, but immunity is lost once the antibodies are destroyed
options.C: The person receives primed T cells from an immunized donor
options.D: The person's innate system is stimulated without any adaptive response
options.E: The person's own immune system is stimulated, typically giving long-term immunity

questions.explanation: Active immunization occurs with exposure of an unimmunized individual to a pathogenic agent; the immune system develops immunity, typically long-term. A: Preformed antibodies define passive immunization. B: That is the limitation of passive immunity. C: Not the definition given. D: Active immunization develops adaptive immunity.

questions.stem: Which is an example of natural passive immunity?
questions.explanation: Natural passive: maternal Ig to the child, IgA in breast milk and colostrum. A: Artificial passive. C: Natural active. D: Artificial active. E: Artificial passive.

questions.stem: What distinguishes vaccination from natural infection?

options.C: Innate activation with no adaptive response

questions.explanation: Natural active immunity = infection; artificial active = vaccination, which mimics stimulation without active disease. A: Passive immunization. B: Passive. C: Not vaccination. E: Passive.

questions.stem: Which statement about vaccines matches the lecture's definition?

options.A: A non-pathogenic biological product that, like other drugs, requires clinical trials
options.B: A pathogenic biological product that causes mild disease and, unlike other drugs, is exempt from clinical trials
options.C: A preparation of preformed antibodies that neutralizes the pathogen on later exposure
options.D: A non-pathogenic chemical that blocks pathogen replication during infection
options.E: A biological product that confers protection without inducing an immune response

questions.explanation: A vaccine is a biological product that safely induces an immune response conferring protection on subsequent exposure; it is non-pathogenic, mimics pathogenic antigens, and requires validation through clinical trials. B: It is non-pathogenic and needs clinical trials. C: That is passive immunization. D: That describes an antimicrobial drug. E: Protection comes from the induced immune response.

questions.stem: An infant too young for the measles vaccine avoids infection because almost everyone around her is vaccinated. What protects her?
questions.explanation: Herd immunity: transmission is interrupted, indirectly protecting susceptible people. A: Not the mechanism. B: Not the mechanism. C: She was not infected. D: She received no antibody.

questions.stem: Roughly what vaccine coverage is needed to prevent outbreaks of a highly transmissible pathogen such as measles?
questions.explanation: About 95% for highly transmissible pathogens (measles); about 85% may suffice for polio, rubella or diphtheria. A: Enough for less transmissible pathogens. C: Too low. D: Too low. E: Higher than needed.

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as a requirement of an ideal vaccine EXCEPT:

options.A: Safety, without interfering with the host's immune response
options.C: Manufacture on a large scale at low cost
options.D: Replication in the host to maintain antigen exposure
options.E: Efficacy with a persistent immune response

questions.explanation: Requirements: safety, efficacy, nature and persistence of the immune response, easy administration and thermal stability, large-scale manufacture, low cost. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: Which two pathogen properties are named as challenges to vaccine efficacy and long-term immunity?

options.A: The ability to induce latency and a polysaccharide capsule
options.B: Antigenic variation and a large genome
options.C: The ability to induce latency and antigenic variation

questions.explanation: The ability of pathogens to induce latency or to mutate (antigenic variation) negatively affects vaccine efficacy and long-term immunity. A: The second factor named is antigenic variation (mutation). B: Latency is the other factor. D: Not the factors named. E: Not the factors named.

questions.stem: For the same pathogen there may be several vaccine types. In the generation scheme of vaccine types, which assignment is correct?

options.A: First: live attenuated and inactivated; second: subunit, toxoid, conjugate; third generation: DNA and vector
options.B: First generation: subunit and toxoid; second: live attenuated and inactivated; third generation: conjugate
options.C: First generation: live attenuated and toxoid; second: inactivated and conjugate; third generation: subunit
options.D: First generation: DNA and recombinant vector; second: subunit; third generation: live attenuated
options.E: First generation: live attenuated and inactivated; second: DNA and viral vector; third generation: toxoid and conjugate

questions.explanation: First generation: live attenuated, inactivated. Second generation: subunit, toxoid, conjugate. Third generation: DNA, recombinant vector. For the same pathogen there may be several vaccine types. B: The first two generations are swapped. C: Toxoid and subunit are second generation. D: Reversed. E: Second and third are swapped.

questions.stem: A patient receives an inactivated rabies vaccine. Why does he need several doses?

options.A: The virus may revert to virulence
