options.C: The vaccine lacks an antigen gene

questions.explanation: Inactivated vaccines: the whole organism is destroyed by chemicals, heat or radiation; responses are weak, so boosters are needed (rabies, hepatitis A, typhoid). A: Live vaccines. B: Not the reason. C: Not the reason. D: Not relevant in adults.

questions.stem: Which list contains inactivated vaccines given as examples in the lecture?

options.A: Hepatitis A, measles and oral polio
options.B: Hepatitis B, rabies and yellow fever
options.C: Hepatitis A, rabies and injectable polio

questions.explanation: Examples: typhoid, hepatitis A, rabies, injectable polio (versus the oral live form), injectable influenza (versus the live nasal spray). A: Measles and oral polio are live vaccines. B: Hepatitis B is a subunit vaccine and yellow fever is live. D: Mumps and the nasal influenza spray are live. E: BCG and chickenpox are live attenuated.

questions.stem: Why are live attenuated vaccines easier to produce for viruses than for bacteria?

options.A: Viruses grow faster in culture, so weakening takes less time
options.B: Bacteria cannot be cultured outside a host
options.C: Viral antigens are more immunogenic than bacterial antigens
options.E: Bacteria revert to virulence less often than viruses

questions.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines are easily produced when the pathogen is a virus and hard when it is a bacterium, because viruses have fewer genes, making viral characteristics easier to control. A: The reason given is the smaller number of genes. B: Not the reason given. C: Not the reason given. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: A patient on chemotherapy asks about a yellow fever vaccine before travel. Which feature makes this vaccine risky for him?

options.A: It is a live attenuated vaccine

questions.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines give strong immunity after one or two doses (yellow fever) but are harmful in immunocompromised patients. B: Not the risk. C: It is not. D: It is not. E: It is not.

questions.stem: Which drawback is specific to live attenuated vaccines?
questions.explanation: Live attenuated: harmful in the immunocompromised, need refrigeration, possible reversion to virulence. A: Inactivated vaccines. C: Subunit vaccines. D: Polysaccharide vaccines. E: Viral vector vaccines.

questions.stem: What is BCG?
questions.explanation: BCG: a weakened bovine tuberculosis bacterium; used in many European countries, rarely in the US. A: It is live and bovine. B: Not a toxoid. C: Not a polysaccharide. E: Not nucleic acid.

questions.stem: Which vaccine type usually needs an adjuvant because it is poorly immunogenic?
questions.explanation: Subunit vaccines contain only pieces (usually protein fragments): fewer side effects, but poor immunogenicity needs adjuvants (hepatitis B). A: Strong responses. B: No adjuvant needed. C: Carrier protein boosts it. D: Strong responses.

questions.stem: How does a plain polysaccharide vaccine such as Pneumococcus 23 stimulate the immune system?

options.A: B cells respond in a T cell-dependent manner, giving memory and high-affinity antibody
options.B: T cells respond directly to the polysaccharide on MHC II
options.C: A T cell-independent B-cell response with low-affinity antibody
options.D: NK cells respond through Fc receptors, giving ADCC
options.E: B cells respond after the carrier protein is processed

questions.explanation: Polysaccharide vaccines are made from surface polysaccharides of invasive bacteria (meningococci, pneumococci) and stimulate B cells in a T-independent manner: poor immunogenicity and low-affinity antibody. A: That is the conjugate vaccine response. B: Polysaccharides are not presented to T cells this way. D: Not the mechanism. E: A plain polysaccharide vaccine has no carrier protein.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old receives a plain polysaccharide vaccine. What response is expected?

options.B: Memory B cells with high affinity

questions.explanation: Plain polysaccharide vaccine: no memory B cells, short-lived antibody, no affinity maturation, no response in infants under 2 years. B: Not with polysaccharide. C: T-independent. D: Short-lived. E: Not with polysaccharide.

questions.stem: What makes the Hib conjugate vaccine effective in infants?
questions.explanation: Conjugate vaccine: the weak polysaccharide is linked to a strong protein carrier (tetanus or diphtheria toxoid), giving a T-dependent response with memory. A: Not the key change. C: Not live. D: Does not fix the problem. E: Not the key change.

questions.stem: Which feature does a conjugate vaccine add over a plain polysaccharide vaccine?
questions.explanation: Conjugate response: affinity maturation, memory B cells, long-lived antibody, improved responses in infants. A: Polysaccharide. B: Polysaccharide. C: Polysaccharide. D: Polysaccharide.

questions.stem: A farmer is immunized with a formalin-treated tetanus toxin. What does this protect him against?
questions.explanation: Toxoid vaccines: toxins inactivated with formalin, non-toxic but immunogenic; immunity to the toxin's effects, not the infection (diphtheria, tetanus). A: Toxoids do not prevent infection. B: Not affected. D: Not the target. E: Not the target.

questions.stem: A new vaccine uses a harmless modified virus carrying the gene for a target antigen and induces strong antibody and T cell responses without an adjuvant. Which vaccine type is it?
questions.explanation: Viral vector vaccines: a modified virus carries the target antigen gene; strong humoral and cellular responses without an adjuvant. A: Needs adjuvants. C: Inactivated toxin. D: T-independent. E: Weak responses.

questions.stem: An adenovirus-vectored vaccine works poorly in people with prior immunity to human adenovirus. How is this overcome?

options.C: Give a higher human adenovirus dose

questions.explanation: Vectors include influenza, VSV, measles virus and adenovirus; pre-existing immunity to human adenovirus is overcome with simian adenovirus. B: Not the fix. C: Still neutralized. D: Not the fix. E: Not the fix.

questions.stem: What is the main advantage of nucleic acid vaccines?
questions.explanation: Nucleic acid vaccines (DNA or RNA) give humoral and cellular responses; versatile and quick to adapt (Pfizer and Moderna mRNA). A: Inactivated vaccines. B: Polysaccharide vaccines. C: Toxoids. E: Delivery is poor.

questions.stem: What advantage does an RNA vaccine have over a DNA vaccine?

options.A: It is stable at room temperature
options.B: It is a live attenuated agent
options.C: It needs no delivery into cells
options.D: It induces antibody without T cells
options.E: It need not reach the nucleus

questions.explanation: DNA vaccines are stable at room temperature; RNA vaccines do not need to reach the nucleus. A: DNA vaccines are. B: Not live. C: It must enter cells. D: Not the advantage.

questions.stem: In the table of advantages and disadvantages, which disadvantages are listed for nucleic acid vaccines?

options.A: Weak immunogenicity and requirement for multiple immunizations
options.B: Poor delivery into cells, DNA integration risk, poor mRNA stability
options.C: High storage requirements, poor safety and toxic reversal risk
options.D: Weak and short immunity with requirement for adjuvants
options.E: High purity requirements and possible pre-existing immunity

questions.explanation: Nucleic acid vaccines: high potency, rapid and cost-efficient development; disadvantages are poor intracellular delivery, potential carcinogenesis risk for DNA vaccines due to chromosomal integration, and poor stability of mRNA vaccines. A: Listed for inactivated virus vaccines. C: Listed for attenuated virus vaccines. D: Listed for protein subunit vaccines. E: Listed for viral vector vaccines.

questions.stem: A child with a combined immunodeficiency needs immunization advice. What is the concern with non-live vaccines in him?
questions.explanation: Non-live vaccines pose no risk to the immunocompromised but may not protect in B cell or combined immunodeficiency. B: Non-live vaccines cannot. C: Live vaccines. D: Not non-live. E: Not non-live.

questions.stem: How do adjuvants enhance a vaccine's immunogenicity?

options.B: By preserving the vaccine from microbes
options.C: By activating innate immunity like PAMPs
options.D: By stabilizing the antigen with gelatin

questions.explanation: Adjuvants enhance immunogenicity; they can act like PAMPs, activating innate immunity and APCs (delivery systems and immune potentiators; aluminum salts routinely). A: Not adjuvants. B: Preservatives. D: Stabilizers. E: Emulsifiers.

questions.stem: Adjuvants fall into two classes. Which pairing of class and role is correct?

options.A: Delivery systems activate the innate immune system directly; immune potentiators concentrate and display antigens
options.B: Delivery systems are cytokines; immune potentiators are cationic microparticles
options.C: Delivery systems preserve the vaccine; immune potentiators stabilize it
options.D: Delivery systems concentrate and display antigens; immune potentiators activate the innate immune system directly
options.E: Delivery systems carry the antigen gene; immune potentiators are viral vectors

questions.explanation: Delivery systems (such as cationic microparticles) concentrate and display antigens in repetitious patterns and help localize them. Immune potentiators (such as cytokines or PRR ligands) activate the innate immune system directly. A: Reversed. B: The examples are swapped. C: Those are roles of preservatives and stabilizers. E: Not adjuvant classes.

questions.stem: Which adjuvants are used routinely in licensed vaccines, and which other vaccine components are mentioned with an allergy warning?

options.A: Polysorbate 80 as adjuvant; aluminum salts as stabilizers
options.B: Gelatine as adjuvant; liposomes as preservatives
options.C: Tetanus toxoid as adjuvant; formalin as emulsifier
options.D: Cytokines as routine adjuvants; aluminum hydroxide as preservative
options.E: Aluminum salts; emulsifiers such as polysorbate 80, and stabilizers

questions.explanation: Aluminum salts (aluminum hydroxide, aluminum phosphate, alum) are routine adjuvants; liposome-based adjuvants and oil-in-water emulsions were licensed more recently. Vaccines also contain preservatives, emulsifiers (polysorbate 80) and stabilizers (gelatine, sorbitol): be aware of allergies. A: Aluminum salts are the adjuvants. B: Gelatine is a stabilizer. C: Tetanus toxoid is a carrier protein in conjugate vaccines. D: Aluminum salts are the routine adjuvants.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl receives a vaccine against HPV16 and HPV18. Which cancer will it help prevent?
questions.explanation: Cancer vaccination targets cancer-causing infections: HPV16/18 (cervical cancer), hepatitis B (liver cancer); it may also make "cold" tumors "hot" for checkpoint blockade. A: Hepatitis B. B: Not listed. D: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: What is the second strategy of vaccination against cancer?

options.A: Making "cold" tumors "hot" and amenable to checkpoint blockade
options.B: Inducing tolerance in "hot" tumors to convert them into "cold" tumors resistant to checkpoint blockade
options.C: Transferring preformed antibodies against tumor antigens
options.D: Attenuating tumor cells by culture and injecting them live
options.E: Blocking herd transmission of tumor cells

questions.explanation: Vaccines can induce immune responses in "cold" tumors that do not appear immunogenic on their own, potentially converting them to "hot" tumors amenable to checkpoint blockade therapy. B: Reversed. C: That would be passive immunization. D: Not described. E: Not applicable.

lectures.title: Hypersensitivity
lectures.covers: Immune tolerance and the four Gell and Coombs types of hypersensitivity: mechanisms, timing, clinical examples and how type I is diagnosed.

items.p: Immune tolerance is an active state of unresponsiveness to specific antigens. Self-tolerance means no response to the body's own antigens; when it fails, the result is autoimmunity.
Hypersensitivity is an excessive reaction to an antigen that is normally harmless. It can be mild (urticaria) or life-threatening (anaphylaxis), local or systemic.

summary.h: The four types at a glance

table: Allergic rhinitis, asthma, food allergy, anaphylaxis
Transfusion reaction, Rh disease, Goodpasture, Graves, myasthenia gravis
Contact dermatitis, tuberculin test, graft rejection

items.p: Types I, II and III need antibody. Type IV is T cells and cytokines.
First exposure sensitizes. Th2 cells (driven by IL-4) make B cells switch to IgE, and IgE coats mast cells and basophils through the high-affinity receptor FcεRI.
On re-exposure the allergen cross-links IgE and the cells degranulate within minutes.

ul: Preformed: histamine, tryptase, chymase
Newly made: prostaglandins, leukotrienes (strong bronchoconstrictors), Th2 cytokines
IL-5: eosinophils. IL-13: mucus and smooth-muscle contraction.
Early phase: starts in 5–30 minutes, lasts about an hour
Late phase: starts in 2–7 hours, lasts days; eosinophils and neutrophils are recruited

items.p: Atopy is the inherited tendency to make IgE against common allergens. IgE has the lowest plasma level, the shortest half-life (about 2 days) and does not cross the placenta.

ul: Skin tests: prick, scratch or intradermal. Read the wheal and redness at 15–20 minutes.
Controls: histamine (positive) and saline (negative)
Antihistamines give false negatives
Allergen-specific IgE in blood: preferred when anaphylaxis is a real risk
Total IgE: often high, but a normal value does not exclude allergy
Tryptase: marker of mast-cell activation
Provocation test and elimination diet when the picture is unclear

items.p: Antibody binds an antigen fixed on a cell or tissue. Three possible results:

ul: The cell is destroyed quietly (opsonization and phagocytosis, or ADCC)
Complement is activated and inflammation follows
The cell survives but works abnormally

items.p: Examples of abnormal function: in Graves disease the antibody stimulates the TSH receptor; in myasthenia gravis it blocks the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor.
Goodpasture syndrome: antibody against basement membrane in lung and kidney, with lung bleeding and glomerulonephritis.
Rh disease: a sensitized Rh-negative mother makes antibody against the D antigen on fetal red cells.
Complexes of antibody and soluble antigen settle in vessel walls, joints, glomeruli and alveoli. Complement is activated and inflammation damages the tissue.

ul: Arthus reaction: local. Antigen injected into the skin of someone who already has antibody. Local vasculitis 4–12 hours later (seen rarely after tetanus or diphtheria toxoid).
Serum sickness: systemic. Large dose of foreign protein such as antivenom. Fever, rash and joint pain 7–10 days later. Stop the agent.
Lupus: complexes with anti-nuclear antibodies

items.p: Two phases: sensitization (7–10 days, memory T cells form), then damage 1–2 days after the next contact.

ul: CD4 T cells: delayed-type hypersensitivity. IL-12 gives Th1 cells, IFN-γ calls in macrophages, and their enzymes and oxygen radicals injure tissue. IL-6 gives Th17 cells, and IL-17 calls in neutrophils.
CD8 T cells: direct killing. Graft rejection, Hashimoto disease.

items.p: Remember the 5 Ts: T cells, Transplant rejection, TB skin test, Touching (contact dermatitis), Terminal (delayed).
The patch test diagnoses contact dermatitis. Poison ivy acts through urushiol, a chemical that alters self proteins.

items.note: The slide names type IV "cytotoxic T lymphocyte mediated". The detailed slides and standard texts split it into CD4-mediated (delayed-type) and CD8-mediated (cytotoxic) reactions.

cards.a: An active state of unresponsiveness to specific antigens; loss of self-tolerance gives autoimmunity.

cards.q: Gell and Coombs: the four types in one line each
cards.a: I: IgE, immediate. II: antibody against cell-bound antigen. III: immune complexes. IV: T cells, delayed.
Types I, II and III (type IV is T-cell mediated)

cards.q: Which cytokine drives Th2 differentiation and IgE switching?
cards.a: IL-4

cards.q: The receptor that holds IgE on mast cells
cards.a: FcεRI (high-affinity IgE receptor)

cards.q: What triggers mast-cell degranulation in type I?
cards.a: The allergen cross-links IgE already bound to the cell.
Histamine and neutral proteases (tryptase, chymase)
IL-5: eosinophil growth, activation and survival. IL-13: mucus and smooth-muscle contraction.

cards.q: Early versus late phase of type I
cards.a: Early: 5–30 minutes, about an hour. Late: 2–7 hours, lasts days, eosinophils and neutrophils.
Genetic predisposition to make IgE against common allergens (asthma, rhinoconjunctivitis, atopic dermatitis)
Lowest plasma level, shortest half-life (about 2 days), no placental transfer

cards.q: When is an allergy skin test read, and with which controls?
cards.a: 15–20 minutes; histamine positive control, saline negative control

cards.q: Common cause of a false-negative skin test
cards.a: Antihistamines taken beforehand

cards.q: Which test when anaphylaxis risk is high?
cards.a: Allergen-specific IgE in blood, instead of skin testing
Mast-cell activation; a high level signals risk of severe reactions

cards.q: Three outcomes of antibody binding to a cell (type II)
cards.a: Destruction without inflammation, complement activation with inflammation, or dysfunction without destruction
Antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor: hyperthyroidism
Antibodies block postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors: weakness and fatigue
Antibodies against basement membrane of lung and kidney: lung bleeding and glomerulonephritis

cards.q: How do immune complexes injure tissue (type III)?
cards.a: They deposit in vessels, joints, glomeruli and alveoli and activate complement.
Local type III: antigen injected into skin of a sensitized person; vasculitis in 4–12 hours
Systemic type III after foreign protein (antivenom): fever, rash, joint pain at 7–10 days; stop the agent

cards.q: Two forms of type IV hypersensitivity
cards.a: CD4: delayed-type hypersensitivity (macrophages). CD8: direct cytotoxicity.
IL-12 → Th1 → IFN-γ → macrophages → TNF-α, IL-1β → tissue damage
T cells, Transplant rejection, TB skin test, Touching (contact dermatitis), Terminal (delayed)
Patch test

questions.stem: How does the lecture define immune tolerance?

options.A: A passive absence of lymphocytes specific for an antigen not yet encountered
options.B: An excessive reaction to naturally harmless antigens
options.C: A waning of the response after the antigen is cleared
options.D: A genetic tendency to produce IgE to common allergens
options.E: An active state of unresponsiveness to specific antigens

questions.explanation: Immune tolerance is an active state of unresponsiveness to specific antigens that prevents destructive over-reactivity. Self-tolerance means no response to antigens produced by the body itself; its failure is autoimmunity. A: Tolerance is described as an active state. B: That is hypersensitivity. C: That is self-limitation. D: That is atopy.

questions.stem: Which statement about hypersensitivity is correct?

options.A: An excessive reaction to naturally harmless antigens
options.B: A deficient reaction to pathogenic antigens that range from viruses to helminths
options.C: An appropriate reaction to self antigens that is limited to the skin
options.D: An excessive reaction that is life-threatening in each case, as in urticaria
options.E: A reaction that requires injection of the allergen to occur

questions.explanation: Hypersensitivity is an inappropriate excessive reaction to naturally "harmless" antigens, ranging from mild (cutaneous urticaria) to life-threatening (anaphylaxis); symptoms can be local or systemic. B: Hypersensitivity is an excessive, inappropriate reaction. C: It is inappropriate and can be systemic. D: Severity ranges from mild (urticaria) to life-threatening (anaphylaxis). E: Exposure can also be by ingestion, inhalation or contact.

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as a route of exposure to allergens EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Exposure to allergens can occur through ingestion, inhalation, injection and physical contact. Allergens can be environmental (dust, pollens, food products) or drug components. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: On what basis does the Gell and Coombs classification group hypersensitivity reactions into four types?

options.A: The organ affected and the severity of the reaction
options.B: The route of exposure and the dose of the allergen
options.C: The mechanism involved and the time taken for the reaction
options.D: The antibody class involved and the patient's age at onset
options.E: The chemical nature of the antigen and its molecular weight

questions.explanation: Based on the Gell and Coombs classification (early 1960s), reactions are grouped into 4 types according to the mechanism involved and the time taken for the reaction. A: Not the basis given. B: Not the basis given. D: Not the basis given. E: Not the basis given.

questions.stem: A boy develops glomerulonephritis two weeks after a streptococcal throat infection. What mechanism causes the kidney damage?
questions.explanation: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a type III (immune complex) reaction. A: Type I. C: Goodpasture (type II). D: Type IV. E: Type IV.

questions.stem: What mediates type IV hypersensitivity?
questions.explanation: Types I, II and III are antibody-mediated; type IV is mediated by T cells and cytokines. A: Type I. B: Type II. C: Type III. E: Not a type.

questions.stem: Which antigen form is targeted in type II hypersensitivity?
questions.explanation: Type I: IgE, soluble antigen. Type II: IgG or IgM, cell-bound antigen. Type III: IgG and IgM, soluble antigen. Type IV: T cells. A: Type III. B: Type I. C: Type IV. D: Type IV (CD8).

questions.stem: Which disease is classified as type IV hypersensitivity?
questions.explanation: Type I: anaphylaxis, hay fever. Type II: mismatched transfusion, HDN. Type III: post-streptococcal GN, RA, SLE. Type IV: multiple sclerosis, contact dermatitis, TB test. B: Type III. C: Type I. D: Type II. E: Type III.

questions.stem: Put the steps of a type I reaction in order: (1) mast cell degranulation on re-exposure, (2) activation of Th2 cells and B cells, (3) mast cell sensitization by IgE.
questions.explanation: Step 1: activation of Th2 cell and B cell. Step 2: mast cell sensitization. Step 3: re-exposure to antigen and degranulation. A: Th2 and B-cell activation must produce the IgE first. B: Sensitization precedes degranulation. D: Degranulation is the last step. E: Th2 and B-cell activation comes first.

questions.stem: Which cytokine is crucial for differentiation of Th0 into Th2 cells?
questions.explanation: IL-4 is crucial for the differentiation of Th0 to Th2. A: IL-12 drives Th1 differentiation in the DTH scheme. C: IL-6 drives Th17 differentiation in the DTH scheme. D: IL-5 acts on eosinophils. E: IL-13 promotes mucus production and smooth muscle contraction.

questions.stem: A man stung by a bee collapses within 5 minutes with hypotension and wheezing. Which type of hypersensitivity is this?
questions.explanation: Type I is immediate, within minutes of contact; it includes atopy and anaphylaxis. B: Cell-bound antigen. C: Immune complexes; hours to days. D: Delayed, days. E: Type III, 7–10 days.

questions.stem: A woman with a known peanut allergy reacts within minutes of eating a cookie containing peanut. Why is the reaction so fast?

options.E: IgE is already bound to mast cells

questions.explanation: Sensitization: IgE coats mast cells and basophils; on re-exposure the allergen cross-links IgE and the cells degranulate (histamine, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, tryptase, PAF). A: It is preformed. B: Mast cells do. C: Not the mechanism. D: It is preformed.

questions.stem: What produces the late-phase reaction in type I hypersensitivity?

options.A: Histamine from basophils dilates vessels within minutes
options.B: Immune complexes deposit in vessel walls and fix complement
options.C: Mast-cell chemokines recruit eosinophils and neutrophils
options.D: Th1 cells recruit macrophages through IFN-γ
options.E: IgE is produced de novo by plasma cells at the site

questions.explanation: Mast cells secrete chemokines and other pro-inflammatory mediators, recruiting eosinophils and neutrophils by chemotaxis: the late-phase reaction, with tissue damage and inflammation. A: That is the immediate phase. B: That is type III. D: That is the DTH mechanism. E: Not the mechanism of the late phase.

questions.stem: Which list contains clinical conditions due to type I hypersensitivity?

options.A: Allergic rhinitis, serum sickness and food allergies
options.D: Allergic rhinitis, asthma and food allergies
options.E: Food allergies, Arthus reaction and allergic rhinitis

questions.explanation: Clinical conditions: allergic rhinitis, anaphylaxis, asthma and food allergies. A: Serum sickness is type III. B: Contact dermatitis is type IV. C: Goodpasture syndrome is type II. E: The Arthus reaction is type III.

questions.stem: What is atopy?

options.A: An acquired tendency to produce IgG4 after repeated allergen exposure
options.B: A genetic predisposition to produce IgE to common allergens
options.C: A deficiency of IgE with recurrent parasitic infection
options.D: A delayed T-cell reaction of the skin to contact allergens
options.E: A genetic predisposition to form immune complexes with drugs

questions.explanation: Atopy is the personal tendency (genetic predisposition) to produce IgE antibodies in response to common allergens, with increased risk of asthma, rhinoconjunctivitis or atopic dermatitis. A: Atopy is a genetic tendency to produce IgE. C: Atopy involves IgE production. D: That is contact dermatitis (type IV). E: That is not atopy.

questions.stem: Which antibody class has the lowest plasma level and the shortest half-life (about 2 days)?
questions.explanation: IgE: lowest plasma concentration, shortest half-life (about 2 days), no transplacental transfer. A: About 3 weeks. B: Not the shortest. C: Not the shortest. D: Not the one described.

questions.stem: To which receptor does IgE bind, and on which cells besides mast cells and basophils is it expressed?

options.A: The high-affinity FcεRI; eosinophils and airway smooth muscle
options.B: The low-affinity FcγR; neutrophils, macrophages and NK cells
options.C: The high-affinity FcεRI; red cells, platelets and plasma cells
options.D: Complement receptor CR2; B cells and follicular dendritic cells
options.E: The high-affinity FcεRI; expressed on mast cells and no other cell

questions.explanation: IgE binds the high-affinity FcεRI on basophils, mast cells and eosinophils, and also on airway smooth muscle cells, endothelial cells and epithelial cells. B: That is an IgG receptor. C: Not the cells listed. D: CR2 binds complement fragments. E: It is also on basophils, eosinophils and several tissue cells.

questions.stem: Which mediator is stored preformed in mast cell granules?
questions.explanation: Preformed: histamine and the neutral proteases tryptase and chymase; lipid mediators and Th2 cytokines are also released. A: Lipid mediator, made on activation. B: Lipid mediator, made on activation. D: Lipid mediator, made on activation. E: Not listed as preformed.

questions.stem: Besides IgE cross-linking, which mechanisms can activate mast cells?

options.A: T-cell receptor ligation and CD28 costimulation
options.C: Immune complex deposition and C1 inhibitor binding
options.D: Binding of IgM pentamers to Fc receptors
options.E: Perforin and granzyme release from NK cells

questions.explanation: Mast cells can also be activated through other mechanisms, including complement activation and TLR stimulation. A: Those activate T cells. C: Not the mechanisms named. D: Not named. E: Not named.

questions.stem: An asthmatic patient has marked airway eosinophilia. Which cytokine drives it?
questions.explanation: IL-5: growth, differentiation, activation and survival of eosinophils. IL-13: mucus production and smooth muscle contraction. A: Mucus and smooth muscle contraction. B: Th2 differentiation and IgE. C: Neutrophils. E: Th1, macrophages.

questions.stem: How do the primary and secondary reactions of type I hypersensitivity differ in the lecture figure?

options.A: Primary: begins in 5–30 minutes, lasts about an hour; secondary: begins within 2–7 hours, lasts for days
options.B: Primary: begins within 2–7 hours, lasts for days; secondary: begins in 5–30 minutes, lasts about an hour
options.C: Primary: begins in 5–30 seconds, lasts a minute; secondary: begins in 7–10 days
options.D: Primary: begins in 4–12 hours; secondary: begins in 1–2 days
options.E: Primary: begins in 5–30 minutes, lasts for days; secondary: begins within 2–7 hours, lasts about an hour

questions.explanation: Primary reaction: begins in 5–30 minutes, lasts about an hour (vasodilation, bronchoconstriction, endothelial retraction with leaky vessels and edema). Secondary reaction: begins within 2–7 hours, lasts for days (recruitment of leukocytes; prostaglandins and leukotrienes, the latter excellent bronchoconstrictors). B: Reversed. C: Not the times given. D: These are Arthus and type IV timings. E: Durations are swapped.

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as a way to test for type I hypersensitivity EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Type I is tested by diagnostic skin testing, immunology laboratory tests, provocation testing and elimination diet. The patch test is used for contact dermatitis (type IV). A: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: When is an immediate skin test read, and which tests are epicutaneous?

options.A: At 15 to 20 minutes; the intradermal test and the patch test
options.B: At 48 to 72 hours; the skin prick test and the scratch test
options.C: At 1 to 2 minutes; the intradermal test
options.D: At 15 to 20 minutes; the skin prick test and the scratch test
options.E: At 4 to 12 hours; the scratch test and the intradermal test

questions.explanation: Small amounts of allergen are introduced into the skin; the wheal and erythema are read at 15 to 20 minutes, when maximal. Epicutaneous tests: skin prick and scratch; the other is the intradermal test. A: The epicutaneous tests are prick and scratch. B: Immediate tests are read at 15–20 minutes. C: Reading is at 15–20 minutes, and the intradermal test is not epicutaneous. E: Not the timing given.

questions.stem: How do the skin prick test and the scratch test differ?

options.A: Prick: a scratch of about 1 cm is made, then allergen is applied; scratch: allergen is applied, then a lancet pricks
options.B: Prick: allergen is injected with a tuberculin syringe; scratch: allergen is applied under a patch
options.C: Prick: read at 15 minutes; scratch: read at 48 hours
options.D: Prick: uses histamine as allergen; scratch: uses saline as allergen
options.E: Prick: allergen is applied, then a lancet pricks the skin; scratch: a scratch of about 1 cm is made, then allergen is applied

questions.explanation: Skin prick test: tiny amounts of allergens are applied and a lancet pricks the surface so extracts can enter. Scratch test: a scratch (about 1 cm) is made and the allergen is then applied. A: Reversed. B: Injection is the intradermal test. C: Both are immediate tests. D: Those are the controls.

questions.stem: A patient took an antihistamine on the morning of skin prick testing. What is expected?

options.A: A wheal at the saline control

questions.explanation: False negatives: prior antihistamines. False positives: bleeding, irritant extracts. Controls: histamine (positive) and saline (negative). A: Not caused by antihistamines. B: The wheal is suppressed. D: Not the effect. E: Causes false positives, not this.

questions.stem: How is the intradermal skin test performed?

options.A: Application of allergen under an occlusive patch on the back for two days
options.B: A lancet prick through a drop of allergen on the forearm
options.C: Inhalation of nebulized allergen with spirometry
options.D: Injection of allergen on the back or arm with a tuberculin syringe
options.E: Injection of histamine into the dermis with a tuberculin syringe

questions.explanation: Intradermal test: small amounts of the allergen are injected intradermally on the back or the arm using a tuberculin syringe; read at 15 to 20 minutes. A: That is patch testing. B: That is the skin prick test. C: That would be a provocation test. E: Histamine is the positive control.

questions.stem: What does an elevated serum tryptase indicate?

options.A: Eosinophil activation, with increased risk of parasitic infection
options.B: Mast cell activation, with increased risk of severe reactions
options.D: T-cell sensitization to a contact allergen

questions.explanation: Tryptase is a marker of mast cell activation; elevated levels indicate an increased risk for severe reactions. A: Tryptase is a mast-cell marker. C: Not what tryptase shows. D: Not what tryptase shows. E: Not the meaning given.

questions.stem: A patient with a previous near-fatal reaction to peanuts needs confirmation of the allergy. Which test is preferable, and why?

options.A: Allergen-specific IgE in blood, given the anaphylaxis risk
options.B: Intradermal skin test, because it is the most sensitive in-vivo test
options.C: Total IgE level, because a normal value rules out allergy
options.D: Patch test, because it detects delayed reactions
options.E: Oral provocation, because history and tests agree

questions.explanation: The assay for allergen-specific IgE antibodies in blood is preferable to in-vivo skin testing when the risk of anaphylaxis is considerable. B: In-vivo testing is avoided when anaphylaxis risk is considerable. C: A normal total IgE does not rule out allergy. D: Patch testing is for contact dermatitis. E: Provocation is used when they disagree, and carries risk.

questions.stem: How should a normal total IgE level be interpreted in a patient with suspected allergy?

options.B: It indicates a type IV mechanism
options.C: It indicates a false-negative skin test
options.D: It predicts a severe reaction on re-exposure
options.E: It does not rule out allergy

questions.explanation: Total IgE is often elevated in allergic patients, but normal IgE levels do not rule out allergy. A: Stated otherwise on the slide. B: Not implied. C: Not implied. D: Tryptase, not total IgE, is tied to severe reactions.

questions.stem: When is a provocation test performed, and how does an elimination diet work?

options.A: When history and confirmatory tests agree; suspected foods are given in increasing doses
options.B: When skin testing is positive; suspected foods are avoided for life
options.C: When history and confirmatory tests disagree; suspected foods are removed, then re-introduced
options.D: When tryptase is elevated; suspected foods are injected intradermally
options.E: When total IgE is normal; suspected foods are applied under a patch

questions.explanation: Provocation tests may be performed when the clinical history and the primary confirmatory tests are discordant. In an elimination diet, suspected food allergens are eliminated then re-introduced and reactions are observed. A: Provocation is for discordant results. B: The diet involves re-introduction. D: Not the method. E: Not the method.

questions.stem: Antibodies binding cell-bound antigens can have three consequences. Which is listed as occurring WITHOUT cell destruction?
questions.explanation: Type II outcomes: (1) cell destruction without inflammation (opsonization and phagocytosis, or antibody-dependent cytotoxicity); (2) complement activation and inflammation; (3) cellular dysfunction without cell destruction. A: This destroys the cell without inflammation. B: This destroys the cell. C: This destroys the cell with inflammation. E: That is type III.

questions.stem: A Rh-negative woman delivers her second Rh-positive baby, who develops hemolytic anemia. What causes it?

options.A: Maternal IgE against fetal red cells
options.C: Maternal T cells crossing the placenta
options.E: Maternal IgG against fetal D antigen

questions.explanation: Rh isoimmunization (type II): the mother is sensitized by the first Rh-positive delivery; her antibodies attack the paternally inherited D antigen on fetal red cells. A: Not type I. B: Not the mechanism. C: Not the mechanism. D: Reversed.

questions.stem: A young man has hemoptysis and rapidly progressive kidney failure from antibodies attacking lung and kidney. What is the antibody target?
questions.explanation: Goodpasture (anti-GBM) syndrome: antibodies attack basement membrane in lungs and kidneys: lung bleeding, glomerulonephritis, kidney failure. A: Graves disease. C: Myasthenia gravis. D: Rh disease. E: SLE.

questions.stem: A woman has hyperthyroidism caused by autoantibodies. What do the antibodies do?

options.B: Kill thyroid cells via CD8 T cells

questions.explanation: Graves: antibodies stimulate the TSH receptor (hyperthyroidism). Myasthenia gravis: antibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors block transmission. B: Hashimoto disease. C: Myasthenia gravis. D: Not the mechanism. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A woman with nephritis and arthritis is found to have systemic immune complex disease. Which antibody mainly marks systemic lupus erythematosus?
questions.explanation: Type III: immune complexes deposit in vessels, synovium, glomeruli and alveoli; localized form Arthus, systemic forms serum sickness and SLE (mainly antinuclear antibodies). A: Goodpasture. B: Graves. D: Myasthenia gravis. E: Rh disease.

questions.stem: Which classification of type III reactions is correct?

options.A: Localized: Arthus reaction; systemic: serum sickness and SLE (anti-nuclear antibodies)
options.B: Localized: serum sickness; systemic: Arthus reaction and SLE
options.C: Localized: SLE; systemic: Arthus reaction and contact dermatitis
options.D: Localized: Arthus reaction; systemic: Goodpasture syndrome and Graves disease
options.E: Localized: tuberculin reaction; systemic: serum sickness

questions.explanation: Localized type III: Arthus reaction. Systemic: serum sickness and systemic lupus erythematosus (autoantibodies, mainly anti-nuclear antibodies, deposit in several organs). B: Arthus is local; serum sickness is systemic. C: SLE is systemic and contact dermatitis is type IV. D: Those are type II. E: The tuberculin reaction is type IV.

questions.stem: What is required for an Arthus reaction, and how does it manifest?

options.A: Intradermal antigen in a person not exposed before; local wheal appearing within minutes
options.B: Inhaled antigen in a sensitized person; systemic fever and polyarthritis after a week
options.C: Contact with a hapten on the skin; induration after 1–2 days
options.D: Intravenous foreign serum in large amounts; glomerulonephritis
options.E: Intradermal antigen in a previously sensitized person; local vasculitis of dermal vessels

questions.explanation: The Arthus reaction is in-situ formation of antigen–antibody complexes after intradermal injection of antigen in a previously sensitized person (high antigen and high antibody): local vasculitis from complexes in dermal vessels, with complement activation and recruitment of PMNs. A: Prior sensitization is required, and a wheal within minutes is type I. B: That resembles serum sickness. C: That is type IV. D: That is serum sickness.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old develops severe pain, swelling, induration and hemorrhage at the injection site 8 hours after a tetanus toxoid booster. Which reaction is this?
questions.explanation: Arthus reaction: localized type III, in-situ complexes in a sensitized person; after tetanus or diphtheria toxoid, 4–12 hours after vaccination. A: Minutes, systemic. B: Systemic, 7–10 days. C: Type IV, 1–2 days. E: Infection.

questions.stem: What causes serum sickness?

options.A: Small amounts of intradermal antigen in a sensitized person
options.C: Large amounts of poorly catabolized foreign serum or protein
options.D: Re-exposure to a contact allergen on the skin
options.E: Cross-linking of IgE by a drug hapten

questions.explanation: Serum sickness is a systemic type III reaction due to administration of large amounts of poorly catabolized foreign serum or proteins (antitoxin, antivenom); it first appeared after therapeutic horse antiserum. A: That is the Arthus setting. B: That is SLE. D: That is type IV. E: That is type I.

questions.stem: Ten days after receiving horse antivenom, a patient develops fever, rash and painful joints. Why did symptoms take this long?

options.A: T cells had to be sensitized first
options.B: Antibodies had to be made first

questions.explanation: Serum sickness: systemic type III after foreign serum or protein; symptoms 7–10 days later (time to make antibody); treatment is to withdraw the agent, plus symptomatic drugs. A: Type IV. C: Not the reason. D: Not the reason. E: Not the reason.

questions.stem: How long does the sensitization phase of type IV hypersensitivity take?
questions.explanation: Type IV: sensitization on primary contact (memory T cells, 7–10 days); secondary contact gives tissue damage within 1–2 days. B: Type I. C: Arthus reaction. D: The secondary-contact phase. E: Too long.

questions.stem: Which T cells mediate delayed-type hypersensitivity?
questions.explanation: Type IV subtypes: CD4-mediated delayed-type hypersensitivity; CD8-mediated cytotoxicity. A: Cell-mediated cytotoxicity. B: Not T cells. C: Not the subtype named. D: Not the subtype named.

questions.stem: Two days after weeding, a gardener has an itchy, blistering rash exactly where poison ivy touched her forearms. Which cells drive this reaction?
questions.explanation: Contact dermatitis ("touching") is type IV delayed-type hypersensitivity: urushiol alters self proteins, and CD4+ Th1 cells activate macrophages via IFN-γ, 1–2 days after re-exposure. A: Type I; minutes. C: Type II. D: Type III. E: Type I late phase.

questions.stem: In the Th1 route of delayed-type hypersensitivity, which cytokine activates macrophages?
questions.explanation: Th1 route: IL-12 → Th1 → IFN-γ → macrophages; TNF-α and IL-1β recruit more cells; ROS and lysosomal enzymes damage tissue. Th17 route: IL-6 → Th17 → IL-17 → neutrophils. A: Induces Th1 cells. B: Th17 route, neutrophils. C: Th2. E: Eosinophils.

questions.stem: In the second DTH route shown in the lecture, which cytokines and cells are involved?

options.A: IL-12 induces Th17 cells, whose IL-17 recruits macrophages
options.B: IL-6 induces Th1 cells, whose IFN-γ recruits neutrophils
options.C: IL-6 induces Th17 cells, whose IL-17 recruits neutrophils
options.D: IL-4 induces Th17 cells, whose IL-5 recruits eosinophils
options.E: IL-17 induces Th17 cells, whose IL-6 recruits neutrophils

questions.explanation: Th cells exposed to IL-6 become Th17 cells; IL-17 recruits neutrophils, leading to inflammation and tissue damage. A: IL-6 is the inducer, and neutrophils are recruited. B: IL-6 leads to Th17. D: That mixes in the Th2 pathway. E: The cytokines are swapped.

questions.stem: A nurse develops an itchy vesicular rash on both hands two days after starting to use latex gloves again. Which test confirms the cause?
questions.explanation: Latex contact dermatitis is type IV (DTH); the patch test diagnoses contact dermatitis and finds allergens missed by blood or prick tests. B: Type I. C: Mast cell activation. D: Type I. E: Type I.

questions.stem: Forty-eight hours after an intradermal tuberculin test, a health worker has a 15-mm raised, indurated lesion. Which reaction is this?
questions.explanation: The tuberculin skin test gives a raised, indurated lesion: CD4-mediated delayed-type hypersensitivity (type IV). A: Minutes. C: Hours, hemorrhagic. D: Type II. E: Type III.

questions.stem: Which conditions are given as examples of CD8+ T cell-mediated cytotoxicity?

options.A: Graft rejection after transplant and Graves disease
options.B: Contact dermatitis and the tuberculin reaction
options.D: Graft rejection after transplant and Hashimoto disease

questions.explanation: CD8 cells recognize antigens on cells, causing direct cell destruction. Examples: graft rejection post transplant, Hashimoto disease. A: Graves disease is type II. B: These are DTH (CD4+) examples. C: Myasthenia gravis is type II. E: Serum sickness is type III.

questions.stem: Poison ivy causes contact dermatitis. Which substance is responsible, and to which source of type IV antigens does it belong?

options.A: Urushiol; an autoantigen exposed by tissue injury
options.B: Tuberculin; an antigen from an intracellular pathogen
options.C: Histamine; a preformed mediator in the leaf oil
options.D: Urushiol; a soluble antigen that forms immune complexes
options.E: Urushiol; a foreign chemical that alters self proteins

questions.explanation: Sources of type IV antigens: foreign agents that alter self antigens (urushiol in the surface oil of poison ivy leaves), autoantigens, and antigens from intracellular pathogens causing prolonged infection (mycobacterium). A: It is a foreign chemical altering self proteins. B: Tuberculin relates to mycobacteria. C: Not the mechanism. D: The reaction is T-cell mediated.

questions.stem: Which substance is used as the positive control in skin prick testing?
questions.explanation: Controls: positive histamine (1.8 or 10 mg/mL), negative saline; test sites are spaced apart. A: Negative control. B: Measured in serum. D: Not the control given. E: The test itself.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has drooping eyelids and weakness that worsens through the day. Her antibodies block neuromuscular transmission. What do they target?
questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis (type II): antibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic ACh receptors block neuromuscular transmission: weakness and fatigue. A: Graves disease. B: Goodpasture. C: Not the lecture's example. D: Nicotinic.

questions.stem: What is the main treatment of serum sickness?
questions.explanation: Serum sickness: withdraw the agent; anti-inflammatory drugs and antihistamines relieve symptoms. B: Not the treatment given. C: Not the treatment given. D: Type I. E: Not relevant.

lectures.title: Primary immunodeficiencies
lectures.covers: Inborn errors of immunity: warning signs, classification, the main combined and antibody deficiencies with their genes, chronic granulomatous disease, and treatment options.

items.p: Primary immunodeficiencies (inborn errors of immunity) are genetic disorders of immune development or function. Secondary immunodeficiency is acquired: drugs, cancer, malnutrition, HIV.
Together they affect at least 1 in 1000 to 1 in 5000 people. The 2024 classification lists 559 entities in 10 groups.

Patients get recurrent or opportunistic infections. Many also show failure to thrive, allergy, lymphoproliferation, autoinflammation or autoimmunity. Immune deficiency and autoimmunity often occur together.

ul: Four or more new ear infections in a year
Two or more serious sinus infections or pneumonias in a year
Two or more months of antibiotics with little effect
Failure to gain weight; persistent thrush; recurrent deep abscesses
Need for intravenous antibiotics; deep-seated infections
Family history

items.p: Diagnosis: history, flow cytometry, immunoglobulin levels, genetic testing. Earlier diagnosis means better survival.
The T-cell defect harms both cellular and antibody immunity. Babies look well at birth, then develop opportunistic infections.
Never give live vaccines or non-irradiated blood products. Cure is by stem-cell transplantation or gene therapy.
SCID means very low T cells. Subtypes are named by which cells remain.
The γ chain is shared by the receptors for IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15 and IL-21.
ADA deficiency: first PID gene defect described; high adenosine and deoxyadenosine. Treat with matched transplant, PEG-ADA enzyme replacement or gene therapy.
Omenn syndrome: partial (hypomorphic) RAG defect. Red, peeling skin, eosinophilia, large nodes, liver and spleen.

summary.h: Combined deficiencies with T cells present

ul: Hyper-IgM syndrome: CD40L (X-linked) or CD40 (autosomal recessive). T and B cells cannot cooperate. IgM normal or high; IgG, IgA and IgE very low; no germinal centers.
MHC class II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome II): mutated transcription factors such as CIITA. CD4 cells and antibody responses fail, but the T-cell count is normal.

items.p: Cellular immunity is normal. Symptoms begin after 6 months, when maternal IgG fades.
Typical infections: sinuses, ears and lungs, with pneumococcus, Haemophilus influenzae and Staphylococcus aureus. Treatment is immunoglobulin replacement.

ul: X-linked agammaglobulinemia (Bruton): BTK mutation. Pre-B cells cannot mature. No B cells, no plasma cells, no immunoglobulin.
Common variable immunodeficiency: B cells present, low switched antibodies. Mostly sporadic, cause usually unknown; about 20% have autoimmunity.
Chronic granulomatous disease: defective NADPH oxidase, so no respiratory burst. Diagnosed with the dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow test: normal neutrophils turn DHR fluorescent, patient cells do not.
Familial Mediterranean fever: MEFV gene, pyrin protein, overactive inflammasome.
Immunoglobulin replacement: antibody deficiencies
Stem-cell transplantation or gene therapy: SCID and CID
Enzyme replacement: ADA deficiency
Thymus transplantation: FOXN1 deficiency, DiGeorge syndrome
Small molecules such as JAK inhibitors: selected dysregulation disorders

cards.a: Primary: genetic. Secondary: acquired (immunosuppressive drugs, cancer, malnutrition, HIV).

cards.q: Most severe and most common groups of PID
cards.a: Most severe: combined immunodeficiencies. Most common: antibody deficiencies (about 50%).

cards.q: Two things never to give a child with SCID or CID
cards.a: Live virus vaccines and non-irradiated blood products

cards.q: What defines SCID among combined immunodeficiencies?
cards.a: T-cell lymphopenia
T− B− NK+ SCID; autosomal recessive (V(D)J recombination fails)
γ chain (IL2RG) deficiency: X-linked, T− B+ NK−

cards.q: Which receptors share the common γ chain?

cards.a: T− B− NK− SCID, autosomal recessive; toxic purine metabolites (adenosine, deoxyadenosine)
HLA-identical transplant (first choice), PEG-ADA enzyme replacement, gene therapy
Hypomorphic RAG mutations: erythroderma, eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, infections
CD40L (X-linked, type 1) or CD40 (autosomal recessive, type 3)
Normal or high IgM; very low IgG, IgA, IgE; normal B-cell count; no germinal centers
No MHC class II expression (transcription factor genes such as CIITA); CD4 and antibody defects with a normal T-cell count

cards.q: Why do antibody deficiencies appear after 6 months of age?
cards.a: Maternal IgG transferred across the placenta declines.
Sinopulmonary infections and otitis with extracellular bacteria (pneumococcus, H. influenzae, S. aureus)
BTK; pre-B cells cannot mature, so no B cells, plasma cells or immunoglobulin
B cells present but poor antibody production; mostly sporadic; about 20% autoimmunity; treated with immunoglobulin

cards.q: Chronic granulomatous disease: defect and test
cards.a: NADPH oxidase; dihydrorhodamine (DHR) flow cytometry

cards.q: Familial Mediterranean fever: gene and protein
cards.a: MEFV; pyrin (overactive inflammasome)
Hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation or gene therapy, as early as possible
Partial, not complete, loss of gene function

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as a cause of secondary (acquired) immunodeficiency EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Secondary immunodeficiencies are acquired (immunosuppressive treatment, cancer, malnutrition, viral infection such as HIV). Primary immunodeficiencies are genetic. B: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: How are inborn errors of immunity defined, and what is their estimated collective prevalence today?

options.A: Rare genetic disorders of immune development or function; 1/10,000 to 1/50,000
options.B: Acquired disorders of immune function after infection; at least 1/1000 to 1/5000
options.C: Common polygenic disorders of antibody production; about 1/100
options.D: Rare genetic disorders of immune development or function; at least 1/1000 to 1/5000
options.E: Rare genetic disorders limited to T cells; about 1/1,000,000

questions.explanation: Inborn errors of immunity (PIDs) are a heterogeneous group of rare genetic disorders affecting development and/or function of the immune system. Traditional estimate: 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 50,000 births; collective prevalence now at least 1/1000–1/5000. A: That is the traditional estimate. B: They are genetic. C: Not the definition or figure given. E: They form a heterogeneous group, and the figure is wrong.

questions.stem: Besides recurrent or opportunistic infections, which non-infectious manifestations may PID patients show?

options.A: Failure to thrive, obesity, lymphopenia in each case, and hypertension
options.B: Failure to thrive, allergy, lymphoproliferation or autoimmunity
options.C: Tall stature, allergy and resistance to autoimmunity
options.E: Autoinflammation, deafness in each case, and renal stones

questions.explanation: Non-infectious manifestations: failure to thrive, allergy, lymphoproliferation, autoinflammation and/or autoimmunity. Some forms are syndromic. A: Not the list given. C: Autoimmunity is a manifestation, not something patients resist. D: Not the list given. E: Not the list given.

questions.stem: According to the Jeffrey Modell Foundation's ten warning signs, which finding should raise suspicion of a PID?

options.A: Two new ear infections within one year
options.C: Two weeks on antibiotics with good effect
options.D: One sinus infection within one year
options.E: Four or more new ear infections within one year

questions.explanation: Ten warning signs include: four or more new ear infections in a year, two or more serious sinus infections, two or more months on antibiotics with little effect, two or more pneumonias in a year, failure to gain weight, recurrent deep abscesses, persistent thrush, need for IV antibiotics, two or more deep-seated infections, family history. A: The threshold for children is four or more. B: The sign is two or more pneumonias within a year. C: The sign is two or more months on antibiotics with little effect. D: The sign is two or more serious sinus infections within a year.

questions.stem: What is the "new paradigm" of PIDs adopted since the mid 2010s?

options.A: Immunodeficiency and autoimmunity are opposite, mutually exclusive states
options.B: PIDs are infections of the immune system by opportunistic organisms
options.C: Dysregulation gives both infection susceptibility and autoimmunity
options.D: Autoimmunity protects PID patients from infection
options.E: PIDs are limited to antibody deficiency

questions.explanation: Old paradigm: underactive system = immunodeficiency, overactive = autoimmunity. New paradigm: the two overlap; dysregulation of immune function often produces increased susceptibility to infection as well as autoimmunity/autoinflammation. A: That is the old paradigm. B: They are genetic disorders. D: Not the paradigm. E: The field covers many categories.

questions.stem: Which entity is paired with the year shown on the lecture's timeline?
questions.explanation: Timeline: SCID 1950, XLA 1952, CGD 1954, X-linked hyper-IgM 1961, ADA SCID molecular basis 1972. A: 1972 is the molecular basis of ADA SCID. C: CGD is dated 1954. D: SCID is dated 1950. E: It is dated 1961.

questions.stem: Which set contains "new warning signs" beyond infection?

options.A: Autoimmune cytopenia, unusual pathogens and endocrinopathy
options.C: Restricted pathogen pattern and cancer predisposition

questions.explanation: New warning signs: autoimmune cytopenia, lymphoproliferation, cancer predisposition, eczema/erythroderma, endocrinopathy, enteropathy/IBD, systemic autoimmunity/vasculitis. A: Unusual pathogens belong to the classical infectious signs. B: Severe infections are classical signs. C: The first is a classical infectious sign. E: Recurrent infections are classical signs.

questions.stem: How many PID entities does the IUIS 2024 classification recognize, and in how many tables?
questions.explanation: IUIS 2024 (published April 2025): 559 different PID entities in 10 tables/categories sharing similar phenotypes or molecular bases. B: There are 10 categories. C: The number is 559. D: Not the figures given. E: Not the figures given.

questions.stem: Which group of primary immunodeficiencies is the most common?
questions.explanation: IUIS 2024 lists 559 PIDs in 10 categories; combined immunodeficiencies are the most severe and antibody deficiencies the most common (about 50%). A: The most severe. B: Less common. C: Less common. D: Less common.

questions.stem: In a child with suspected primary immunodeficiency, which test counts the lymphocyte subsets?
questions.explanation: Diagnosis rests on history, flow cytometry, Ig levels and genetic testing; it guides therapy (IVIG, HSCT, gene therapy, prophylaxis, small molecules). A: Measures antibody, not cells. B: Finds the mutation. D: Not the test given. E: Not a diagnostic test for PID.

questions.stem: In the transplantation data shown, which children had the lowest survival (50%)?

options.A: Those younger than 3.5 months without infection at transplantation
options.B: Those older than 3.5 months with active infection at transplantation
options.C: Those older than 3.5 years with no infection
options.D: Those transplanted in the first month of life
options.E: Those younger than 3.5 months with resolved infection

questions.explanation: Age at transplantation and infection status significantly affect survival; it was lowest (50%) in children older than 3.5 months with active infection at the time of transplantation. A: Early transplantation without infection gives the best survival. C: The cut-off is 3.5 months, with active infection. D: Early is better. E: Not the lowest group.

questions.stem: A newborn with severe combined immunodeficiency looks healthy at birth. What appears over the following months?
questions.explanation: CID/SCID: defective T cell development or function impairs both cellular and humoral immunity; patients are asymptomatic at birth, then develop opportunistic infections. A: Autoinflammatory disease. B: CGD. D: Antibody deficiency, later. E: Not SCID.

questions.stem: An infant with suspected SCID needs a platelet transfusion and is due for routine immunization. Which precautions are needed?

options.A: Avoid inactivated vaccines and irradiated blood products
options.B: Give live vaccines early to stimulate T cells
options.C: Avoid IVIG and antibiotics before transplantation
options.D: Give non-irradiated platelets to supply donor lymphocytes
options.E: Avoid live virus vaccines and non-irradiated blood products

questions.explanation: Live virus vaccines and non-irradiated blood or platelet transfusions are dangerous in CID. A: The danger is with live vaccines and non-irradiated products. B: Live vaccines are dangerous. C: Not stated. D: Non-irradiated products are dangerous.

questions.stem: What distinguishes SCID within the combined immunodeficiencies?

options.A: B-cell lymphopenia with normal T cells
options.B: Normal T-cell numbers with impaired function
options.C: Absent NK cells in each subtype

questions.explanation: Both CID and SCID are defects of adaptive immunity, but SCID forms are characterized by T-cell lymphopenia. Subtypes are B+/B− and NK+/NK−. A: SCID is defined by low T-cell numbers. B: That describes CID with residual T cells. C: NK cells may be present or absent. E: Not SCID.

questions.stem: Which interventions are curative for SCID and CID?
questions.explanation: Curative interventions are HSCT and gene therapy, both with a high risk of morbidity and mortality; early diagnosis allows treatment at a young age and raises survival. B: Supportive, not curative. C: Thymus transplantation is for FOXN1 deficiency and DiGeorge syndrome. D: PEG-ADA applies to ADA deficiency. E: Live vaccines are dangerous.

questions.stem: An infant with SCID has no T cells but normal numbers of B cells and NK cells. Which defect fits this pattern?
questions.explanation: SCID arises from four mechanisms: rearrangement machinery (RAG: T−B−NK+), cytokine signaling (γ chain, JAK3: T−B+NK−), CD3 genes (T−B+NK+) and lymphocyte survival (ADA: T−B−NK−). A: T−B−NK+. B: T−B+NK−. D: T−B−NK−. E: B cells absent, T cells normal.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old has severe fungal, viral and bacterial infections, rash and chronic diarrhea. T and B cells are absent; NK cells are present. Which defect of the V(D)J rearrangement machinery fits?
questions.explanation: RAG1/RAG2 deficiency (chr. 11p12, autosomal recessive) impairs V(D)J rearrangement: T−B−NK+ SCID with onset at 2–3 months; susceptibility to opportunistic pathogens or live-vaccine organisms is pathognomonic. A: That gives T−B+NK− SCID. C: That gives T−B−NK− SCID. D: That gives T−B+NK+ SCID. E: That gives absent B cells with normal T cells.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old boy has T−B+NK− SCID; his mother's brother died of infections in infancy. Which gene is most likely mutated?
questions.explanation: γ chain deficiency: IL2RG on Xq13; X-linked recessive T−B+NK− SCID; the most common SCID except in consanguineous populations (JAK3 deficiency uses the same pathway). A: T−B−NK+, autosomal recessive. B: T−B−NK−, autosomal recessive. C: T−B+NK+. D: B cells absent, T cells normal.

questions.stem: The common γ chain is part of the receptor for which cytokine?
questions.explanation: The γ chain is shared by the IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15 and IL-21 receptors. A: Not a γ-chain receptor. B: Not a γ-chain receptor. C: Not a γ-chain receptor. E: Not a γ-chain receptor.

questions.stem: Which SCID phenotype results from defects in the genes encoding the CD3 molecules?
questions.explanation: CD3 gene defects give T−B+NK+ SCID. B: RAG deficiency. C: γ chain deficiency. D: ADA deficiency. E: Not a SCID phenotype given.

questions.stem: A 3-week-old has T−B−NK− SCID with raised blood deoxyadenosine. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: ADA deficiency: first genetic defect described in PID; ADA on 20q13; AR T−B−NK− SCID; onset in the first month in 85–90%; raised adenosine and 2′-deoxyadenosine. A: NK cells present. B: B cells only. D: CGD. E: T−B+NK−.

questions.stem: Which laboratory findings are listed for ADA deficiency?

options.A: Hypergammaglobulinemia, normal CD4/CD8 ratio, low adenosine and 2'-deoxyadenosine
options.B: Normal or increased IgM with deficient IgG, IgA and IgE
options.C: Absent B cells with normal pre-B cells in marrow
options.D: Eosinophilia with elevated IgE and erythroderma

questions.explanation: Labs: hypogammaglobulinemia, reversed CD4+/CD8+ ratio, elevated serum adenosine and 2'-deoxyadenosine. A: The opposite pattern. B: That is hyper-IgM syndrome. C: That is XLA. D: That suggests Omenn syndrome.

questions.stem: What is the treatment of choice for ADA-deficient SCID?
questions.explanation: ADA-SCID: HLA-identical BMT is the treatment of choice; enzyme replacement with weekly PEG-ADA and gene therapy are alternatives. A: An alternative. B: An alternative. C: Not curative. E: FOXN1, DiGeorge.

questions.stem: How do CIDs differ mechanistically from SCIDs in the lecture?

options.A: Defects in early T-cell development leave no T cells
options.B: Residual T cells with impaired function
options.C: Defects in B-cell maturation leave T cells intact
options.D: Defects in phagocyte killing leave lymphocytes intact
options.E: Defects in complement leave adaptive immunity intact

questions.explanation: CID: defects altering the later stages in T-cell development or signaling give residual T cells with impaired function. A: That describes SCID. C: That describes antibody deficiency. D: That describes CGD. E: Not CID.

questions.stem: A boy has recurrent infections with a normal B cell count, high IgM and very low IgG, IgA and IgE; his maternal uncle had the same disease. Lymph nodes lack germinal centers. Which molecule is defective?
questions.explanation: CD40L deficiency (Xq26): X-linked hyper-IgM type 1; defective T–B cooperation, no germinal centers, no isotype switching. CD40 deficiency is AR (type 3). B: Autosomal recessive hyper-IgM type 3. C: No B cells. D: Bare lymphocyte syndrome. E: CGD.

questions.stem: Which statement about MHC class II deficiency is correct?

options.A: Bare lymphocyte syndrome II: mutations in the HLA-DR structural genes; X-linked SCID
options.B: Hyper-IgM syndrome type 3: mutations in CD40; autosomal recessive CID
options.C: Bare lymphocyte syndrome II: mutations in TAP; defective CD8 cells with normal antibodies
options.D: Omenn syndrome: hypomorphic RAG mutations; autosomal recessive
options.E: Bare lymphocyte syndrome II: CIITA-type transcription factor mutations; AR CID

questions.explanation: MHC class II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome II): genes CIITA, RFXANK, RFX5, RFXAP encode transcription factors regulating MHC II expression; AR CID with defective antigen presentation, defective activation and development of CD4+ cells and defective antibody production. A: The genes encode transcription factors, and inheritance is AR. B: A different entity. C: The defect is in MHC II expression, affecting CD4 cells and antibody production. D: A different entity.

questions.stem: An infant with combined immunodeficiency has a normal total CD3 T cell count, and his T cells proliferate normally to PHA, but CD4 help is lacking. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: MHC II deficiency (bare lymphocyte syndrome II; CIITA, RFXANK, RFX5, RFXAP): defective antigen presentation and CD4 development; unlike SCID, total CD3 count is normal and T cells respond to PHA. A: T cells absent. B: T cells absent. D: T cells absent. E: B cell defect.

questions.stem: What is preserved in predominantly antibody deficiencies?
questions.explanation: Antibody deficiencies: defective production of IgG, IgA, IgM or high-affinity antibody, with normal cellular immunity. A: Defective. C: Can be defective. D: Can be defective. E: Often impaired.

questions.stem: A boy was well until 7 months of age and then developed recurrent otitis media and pneumonia. Why do antibody deficiencies present at this age?

options.A: Maternal IgA in breast milk declines after 6 months
options.C: Live vaccines are first given after 6 months
options.D: Transplacental maternal IgG declines after 6 months
options.E: B cells first leave the marrow after 6 months

questions.explanation: Clinical manifestations start after the age of 6 months, when transplacentally derived maternal IgG levels decline. A: The reason given is decline of transplacental IgG. B: Not the reason. C: Not the reason. E: Not the reason.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old boy with X-linked agammaglobulinemia has another severe infection. Which organism is typical?
questions.explanation: Antibody deficiencies: extracellular bacteria (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, S. aureus); recurrent sinopulmonary infections, otitis media, conjunctivitis. B: T cell defects. C: Phagocyte defects. D: T cell defects. E: T cell defects.

questions.stem: About what share of primary immunodeficiencies are antibody deficiencies?
questions.explanation: Antibody deficiencies are the most common PIDs, about 50% (WHO); treatment is immunoglobulin replacement and supportive care. A: About 50%. B: About 50%. C: About 50%. E: About 50%.

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as a molecular basis of antibody deficiency EXCEPT:

options.B: Defective activation of B cells by T cells
options.C: Defective NADPH oxidase in B cells
options.D: Inability to secrete Ig or defects in class switching

questions.explanation: Bases: absence of B cells; defect in activation of B cells by T cells or absence of T helper cells; inability to secrete Igs or class-switch defects; over-activation of suppressive T cells. A: Listed. B: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: An adult has recurrent sinusitis and pneumonia, low IgG and IgA, and B cells at 5% of lymphocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Absent B cells: XLA and AR forms (BLNK, μ heavy chain); B cells > 1%: CVID. B: B cells absent. C: Infancy, T cells absent. D: Phagocyte defect. E: Combined defect in infancy.

questions.stem: A boy has no circulating B cells and no plasma cells, but normal pre-B cells in his marrow. Which gene is mutated?
questions.explanation: XLA (Bruton): BTK gene (Xq21.3–22); X-linked recessive; no Ig, plasma cells or circulating B cells; normal pre-B cells (block in pre-B maturation). A: γ chain SCID. B: Hyper-IgM. C: T−B− SCID. D: FMF.

questions.stem: About what share of patients with CVID have an autoimmune condition?
questions.explanation: CVID: common, variable etiology; low switched isotypes, impaired specific antibody; mostly sporadic, familial forms often AD; ~20% have autoimmunity. A: About 20%. C: About 20%. D: About 20%. E: About 20%.

questions.stem: To what can immune dysregulation disorders be due?

options.A: Defective phagocytosis, defective complement or absent B cells
options.B: Excess tolerance, excess apoptosis or decreased signaling
options.D: Defective V(D)J recombination or ADA deficiency

questions.explanation: Immune dysregulation disorders lead to autoimmune manifestations as well as increased susceptibility to infection; they can be due to defective tolerance, defective apoptosis or increased cellular signaling. A: These define other PID groups. B: The opposite of what is listed. D: These cause SCID. E: Not genetic dysregulation.

questions.stem: What is the underlying defect in chronic granulomatous disease?

options.E: Defective BTK signaling in pre-B cells

questions.explanation: CGD is a primary immunodeficiency of phagocyte function due to defective NADPH oxidase (phox). B: The defect named is NADPH oxidase. C: That is ADA-SCID. D: That is FMF. E: That is XLA.

questions.stem: A boy has recurrent abscesses. When his neutrophils are stimulated with PMA, they fail to convert dihydrorhodamine to fluorescent rhodamine. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: DHR assay: stimulated phagocytes make superoxide that reduces DHR to fluorescent rhodamine; no fluorescence = defective NADPH oxidase (CGD). A: B cell defect. B: T cell defect. C: Switching defect. D: Autoinflammatory.

questions.stem: Which categories make up the autoinflammatory diseases?

options.A: Periodic fever syndromes, antibody deficiencies and complement deficiencies
options.B: Type I interferonopathies, SCID and phagocyte defects
options.C: Sterile inflammation of joints, hyper-IgM and XLA
options.D: Periodic fever syndromes and type I interferonopathies
options.E: Periodic fever syndromes, CVID and bone marrow failure

questions.explanation: Autoinflammatory diseases: periodic fever syndromes, systemic inflammation with urticarial rash, sterile inflammation of the skin/bone/joints, type I interferonopathies. A: The latter are separate PID groups. B: The latter are separate groups. C: The latter are other entities. E: The latter are separate groups.

questions.stem: Which protein is encoded by the MEFV gene?
questions.explanation: Familial Mediterranean fever: MEFV (16p13.3) encodes pyrin; mutations increase inflammasome activation. A: Not MEFV. C: BTK. D: ADA. E: MHC II regulation.

questions.stem: For which conditions is thymus transplantation used?

options.A: ADA deficiency and γ chain deficiency

questions.explanation: Thymus transplantation is used in very few specific cases: FOXN1 deficiency and DiGeorge syndrome. A: These are treated by HSCT, gene therapy or enzyme replacement. B: These receive immunoglobulin replacement. C: Not treated by thymus transplantation. D: Not listed.

questions.stem: Which statement about immunoglobulin replacement and CVID matches the lecture?

options.A: Immunoglobulin substitution cures CVID, so HSCT is not performed
options.B: Immunoglobulin substitution is contraindicated in XLA
options.C: HSCT is first-line in antibody deficiencies, with IVIG for 26% of failures
options.D: Ig substitution is standard, yet 26% of CVID patients undergo HSCT
options.E: Immunoglobulin substitution replaces HSCT in SCID

questions.explanation: Immunoglobulin substitution is adopted in patients with antibody deficiencies; 26% of patients with CVID still undergo HSCT. Patients with SCID and CID require HSCT. A: 26% still undergo HSCT. B: It is the treatment for antibody deficiencies. C: Reversed. E: SCID and CID require HSCT.

questions.stem: Which class of drugs is given as the example of targeted therapy with small molecules, and what guides the choice among them?

options.A: JAK inhibitors; patient age and blood group
options.C: JAK inhibitors; toxicity profile and disease

questions.explanation: Targeted therapies with small molecules: JAK inhibitors; the choice can be driven by the different toxicity profiles, availability of formulations and the disease to treat. A: Not the criteria listed. B: Not the example given. D: Not the example given. E: Not the example given.

questions.stem: What is a hypomorphic mutation?

options.A: One causing partial loss of gene function
options.B: One causing complete loss of gene function
options.C: One causing gain of a new function
options.E: One with no effect on the protein

questions.explanation: A hypomorphic mutation causes a partial loss of gene function (reduced expression or reduced functional performance, but not complete loss): one gene, different severities. B: That is a null (amorphic) mutation. C: Not hypomorphic. D: Not hypomorphic. E: Not hypomorphic.

questions.stem: An infant has desquamating erythroderma, recurrent pneumonia, chronic diarrhea, eosinophilia, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Which genetic change is most likely?

options.A: Null mutations in the IL2RG gene

questions.explanation: Omenn syndrome: severe but incomplete T cell impairment, mostly hypomorphic RAG1/RAG2 mutations (partial loss of function); AR. A: Classic γ chain SCID. C: ADA-SCID. D: XLA. E: FMF.

questions.stem: A girl has T−B+NK− SCID, but her IL2RG gene is normal. Which kinase in the same cytokine signaling pathway is most likely deficient?
questions.explanation: JAK3 deficiency is discussed with γ chain deficiency: the γ chain signals through JAK3; both give T−B+NK− SCID (JAK3 is autosomal, so girls are affected). A: B cell signaling. B: Not discussed with the γ chain. C: Not discussed with the γ chain. E: Not the γ chain partner.

lectures.title: Primary immunodeficiencies: cases
lectures.covers: Five teaching cases that link a clinical picture to its diagnosis: chronic granulomatous disease, Wiskott-Aldrich, Chediak-Higashi, X-linked SCID and hyper-IgE syndrome.

items.p: Each case has one clue that points to the diagnosis. Learn the clue, the confirming test and the gene.

table: Aspergillus pneumonia, normal blood count and antibodies
Eczema, infections, few and small platelets
Pale skin and hair, infections, giant granules
Infections from 3 months, no T cells, B cells present
Cold staphylococcal abscesses, fractures, huge IgE

items.p: A teenage gardener nearly dies of Aspergillus pneumonia. Blood count and immunoglobulins are normal, so the defect is in phagocyte killing.
His neutrophils do not reduce DHR, and neither do his brother's. His mother and sister each have two populations of cells: they are carriers. The disease is X-linked.
A boy with eczema, recurrent infections, bloody diarrhea and petechiae. His platelets are very few and abnormally small. Later he develops autoimmune hemolytic anemia (positive Coombs test).

ul: Antibodies: normal IgG, low IgM, high IgA and IgE; poor vaccine responses
Gene: WAS, X-linked. The protein WASP is found in white cells and megakaryocytes, which explains both problems.
A rare recessive form is caused by WIPF1
Treatment: stem-cell transplantation

items.note: The slide gives a later platelet count of "150000 per uL" while describing platelets as still low. That value is within the normal range; it is probably a typing error.

items.p: A girl of related parents with ear and lung infections, easy bruising, sensitivity to light, and skin and hair lighter than her family. Antibodies, complement and DHR are normal. The smear shows giant granules in white cells.

ul: Autosomal recessive; gene LYST, needed for vesicle trafficking
Neutrophils migrate poorly; NK and cytotoxic T cells kill poorly
Partial albinism: melanocytes cannot hand over their melanosomes
Bleeding: platelet dysfunction
Later: progressive neurological disease, and an accelerated phase with lymphocyte infiltration and pancytopenia

items.p: A boy who was well at birth. From 3 months: cough, ear infections, pneumonia, thrush, poor growth. He has very few lymphocytes, no CD3 cells, normal B cells and few NK cells: X-linked SCID.

A boy with eczema from the first month, repeated staphylococcal skin infections that are not red, hot or painful, pneumonias, fractures after minor injury, a prominent forehead and a wide nose. IgE is enormously raised, with eosinophilia.

ul: Triad: staphylococcal skin abscesses, pneumonia, very high IgE
Also Candida infections; little fever or inflammation
Most common form: autosomal dominant STAT3 mutation (dominant negative), with bone and dental features
Recessive forms (for example DOCK8) have no skeletal features
IL-17 normally recruits phagocytes and drives defensin production in skin

cards.q: Severe Aspergillus infection with normal blood count and immunoglobulins: think of...
cards.a: Chronic granulomatous disease; confirm with the DHR test

cards.q: DHR test: two populations of neutrophils in a mother means...
cards.a: She is a carrier of X-linked chronic granulomatous disease.
Eczema, recurrent infections, thrombocytopenia with small platelets
Normal IgG, low IgM, high IgA and IgE
WAS (protein WASP, in white cells and megakaryocytes); X-linked recessive
Recurrent bacterial infections, partial oculocutaneous albinism, bleeding tendency; later neurological decline
Giant cytoplasmic granules in leukocytes; LYST (vesicle trafficking); autosomal recessive

cards.q: Why is the skin pale in Chediak-Higashi?
cards.a: Melanocytes cannot transfer melanosomes to keratinocytes.

cards.q: Boy with no CD3 cells, normal B cells, low NK cells
cards.a: γ chain deficiency (X-linked SCID)
Staphylococcal skin abscesses ("cold"), pneumonia, very high IgE

cards.q: Hyper-IgE syndrome: most frequent gene and extra features
cards.a: STAT3, autosomal dominant (dominant negative); bone fragility and dental anomalies

cards.q: Why are abscesses "cold" in hyper-IgE syndrome?
cards.a: Patients do not mount strong inflammatory responses (no redness, warmth or fever).

questions.stem: A 15-year-old boy working with a gardening crew develops respiratory failure. Imaging shows large cotton-ball densities in both lungs; needle aspiration grows Aspergillus fumigatus. CBC and immunoglobulins are normal. Which test is most appropriate next?

options.B: Lymphocyte subset count for CD3 cells

questions.explanation: Severe Aspergillus infection with normal CBC and immunoglobulins suggests chronic granulomatous disease; the DHR test was performed in the patient and his family. B: CBC is normal and the fungal lung infection points to a phagocyte defect. C: That is the clue for Chediak-Higashi syndrome. D: That is the clue for hyper-IgE syndrome. E: That is the clue for Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome.
