questions.stem: A boy with Aspergillus pneumonia and his brother show no DHR reduction; their mother and sister each show two populations of neutrophils. What is the mother's status?
questions.explanation: Patient and brother do not reduce DHR; mother and sister have two cell populations (lyonization): X-linked CGD, confirmed by sequencing. A: She would show no reduction. B: Two populations mean a carrier. C: DHR is not the test for this. D: The sister shares the pattern.

questions.stem: A 20-month-old boy has eczema since 6 months, recurrent ear and respiratory infections, bloody diarrhea and petechiae. Platelet count is 10,000/µL and platelets are abnormally small. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.explanation: Recurrent infections, eczema, bloody diarrhea and severe thrombocytopenia with abnormally small platelets in a male infant: Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. A: Eczema and infections occur, but small platelets with thrombocytopenia point elsewhere. B: That shows albinism and giant granules. C: No thrombocytopenia or eczema. E: No thrombocytopenia or eczema.

questions.stem: A boy with Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome becomes pale with dark urine at 18 months; hemoglobin is 5 g/dL and the direct Coombs test is positive. Which complication of his disease is this?

options.A: Anemia from chronic blood loss in stool

questions.explanation: A positive direct Coombs test demonstrated autoimmune hemolytic anemia, treated with steroids. A: The positive Coombs test shows antibody-mediated hemolysis. C: Not the complication described. D: Not shown. E: He is 18 months old.

questions.stem: A boy with eczema, recurrent infections and small platelets is diagnosed with Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome. Which immunoglobulin result is expected?
questions.explanation: Wiskott–Aldrich: normal IgG, low IgM, high IgA and IgE; poor response to polysaccharide vaccines; normal B/T numbers; abnormal T cell proliferation. A: IgA is high. B: IgE is high. D: IgG is normal. E: IgG is normal.

questions.stem: Why does a WAS mutation cause both immunodeficiency and thrombocytopenia?

options.A: WASP is expressed in endothelial cells and hepatocytes
options.B: WASP is a platelet surface receptor for von Willebrand factor
options.C: WASP is required for V(D)J recombination in lymphocytes and megakaryocytes
options.D: WASP is a complement regulator on platelets
options.E: WASP is expressed in white blood cells and megakaryocytes

questions.explanation: Gene WAS (Xp11.23), X-linked recessive. The protein WASP is expressed in white blood cells and megakaryocytes, hence immunodeficiency and thrombocytopenia. The patient received HSCT. A: Not the cells named. B: Not its described role. C: Not its described role. D: Not its described role.

questions.stem: Which gene causes the autosomal recessive form of Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome?
questions.explanation: X-linked WAS (Xp11.23) encodes WASP; the AR form is WIPF1, encoding WASP-interacting protein (WIP). A: X-linked form. C: Chediak–Higashi. D: Hyper-IgE syndrome. E: γ chain SCID.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl of consanguineous parents has recurrent ear infections, pneumonia, easy bruising, photophobia, and skin and hair much lighter than her family. Immunoglobulins, complement and DHR are normal. Which finding on the blood smear clinches the diagnosis?

options.A: Abnormally small platelets with a low count

questions.explanation: Peripheral smear showed giant cytoplasmic granules in her leukocytes, positive for myeloperoxidase: Chediak-Higashi syndrome. Labs: mild neutropenia, normal Ig, complement and DHR. A: That is Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. B: Lymphocyte numbers were normal. C: Not the finding. E: That fits hyper-IgE syndrome.

questions.stem: What causes the bleeding tendency in Chediak–Higashi syndrome?
questions.explanation: Chediak–Higashi: very rare, severe AR; recurrent bacterial infections, partial oculocutaneous albinism, bleeding from platelet dysfunction. A: Wiskott–Aldrich. B: Hemophilia A. D: Not the cause. E: Not the cause.

questions.stem: The girl with Chediak-Higashi syndrome received a bone marrow transplant. What happened in adolescence, as is typical of the disease?

options.B: Recurrence of pyogenic infections with loss of the graft
options.C: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia with positive Coombs test

questions.explanation: Years later she developed a progressive neurological disease (weakness, tremors, ataxia). Most patients who survive into adolescence develop neurological defects: cerebellar ataxia, CNS atrophy, seizures, peripheral neuropathy, cognitive defects. B: The course described is neurological. C: That was the Wiskott-Aldrich case. D: That belongs to hyper-IgE syndrome. E: That was the CGD case.

questions.stem: What is the "accelerated" complication that most patients with Chediak-Higashi syndrome undergo at some point?

options.A: Uncontrolled eosinophil proliferation with very high IgE
options.B: Loss of germinal centers with hypogammaglobulinemia

questions.explanation: Most patients undergo uncontrolled lymphocyte proliferation and lymphohistiocytic infiltration, with fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and pancytopenia. A: Not CHS. B: Not CHS. C: Not CHS. D: Not CHS.

questions.stem: Which gene is mutated in Chediak–Higashi syndrome?
questions.explanation: CHS1/LYST governs vesicle formation and trafficking; mutations cause aberrant vesicle fusion and poor lysosome transport. A: Wiskott–Aldrich. B: Hyper-IgE syndrome. D: X-linked CGD. E: γ chain SCID.

questions.stem: Which immune function is severely impaired in Chediak–Higashi syndrome?
questions.explanation: CHS: reduced chemotaxis and migration of neutrophils and monocytes; severely impaired cytotoxicity of cytotoxic T cells and NK cells. A: Immunoglobulins are normal. C: DHR is normal. D: Complement is normal. E: Not the defect.

questions.stem: Why do patients with Chediak-Higashi syndrome have light skin and hair?

options.B: Melanocytes are absent from the skin
options.C: Tyrosinase is deficient, so melanin is not made

questions.explanation: The pigmentation defect is due to the inability of melanocytes to transfer melanosomes (pigment-containing granules) to keratinocytes and other epithelial cells. B: Melanocytes are present; transfer fails. C: Not the mechanism given. D: Not the mechanism given. E: Not the mechanism given.

questions.stem: A boy, normal at birth, has cough from 3 months, recurrent otitis, bilateral pneumonia, oral thrush and failure to thrive. Lymphocytes are 760/µL with no CD3 cells, a normal B-cell count and a low NK-cell count. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.explanation: No CD3 cells, normal B cells and low NK cells (T−B+NK−) in a boy, with decreased IgG and IgA: γ chain deficiency. A: B cells would be absent and NK cells present. B: B cells would be absent as well. C: NK cells would be normal. E: T cells would be normal and B cells absent.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy has had severe eczema since the first month, recurrent Staphylococcus aureus skin infections without redness, pain or warmth, two pneumonias, two fractures after minor trauma, a prominent forehead and a wide nasal bridge. Which laboratory result is expected?

options.D: High IgM with low IgG and IgA

questions.explanation: Labs: hypereosinophilia (7%), IgE 36,698 (normal 0–200), IgG and IgA normal, IgM slightly high; sequencing showed a heterozygous STAT3 mutation: hyper-IgE syndrome with cold abscesses and bone fragility. A: That is Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome. C: That is CGD. D: That is hyper-IgM syndrome. E: That is Chediak-Higashi syndrome.

questions.stem: A boy with hyper-IgE syndrome has had repeated staphylococcal abscesses. Which other organism is he particularly prone to?
questions.explanation: HIES triad: recurrent staphylococcal skin abscesses, pneumonia, very high IgE; susceptibility to S. aureus and Candida albicans; weak inflammatory responses. B: T cell defects. C: Not listed. D: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Which statement about the genetics of hyper-IgE syndrome is correct?

options.A: The autosomal recessive STAT3 form is the most frequent and spares the skeleton
options.B: The autosomal dominant DOCK8 form is the most frequent and includes skeletal features
options.C: The X-linked STAT3 form affects boys and spares the teeth
options.D: The autosomal dominant STAT3 form is a gain of function limited to the skin
options.E: The autosomal dominant STAT3 form (dominant negative) is the most frequent

questions.explanation: The AD form is the most frequent (familial or sporadic): STAT3 with a dominant negative effect; multisystemic presentation with immune defects, bone fragility and dental anomalies. AR forms (such as DOCK8 deficiency) lack skeletal manifestations. A: The STAT3 form is autosomal dominant with bone fragility. B: DOCK8 deficiency is an AR form without skeletal manifestations. C: STAT3 HIES is autosomal dominant with dental anomalies. D: The effect is dominant negative and multisystemic.

questions.stem: Why does impaired IL-17 function contribute to skin and mucosal infections in hyper-IgE syndrome?

options.A: IL-17 drives class switching to IgE and eosinophil survival
options.B: IL-17 activates macrophages to kill intracellular microbes
options.C: IL-17 induces germinal centers and affinity maturation
options.D: IL-17 recruits phagocytes and promotes defensin production
options.E: IL-17 inhibits neutrophil migration to limit abscesses

questions.explanation: IL-17 is important for mucosal and epithelial immunity, for recruiting phagocytic cells to the site of infection, and for defensin production (skin immunity). A: Those are IL-4 and IL-5 functions. B: That is the IFN-γ role. C: That is the Tfh/IL-21 role. E: IL-17 recruits phagocytic cells.

lectures.title: Immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence
lectures.covers: How labeled antibodies are used to locate a protein in tissue: antibody types, the three staining methods, fluorescence microscopy, the laboratory protocol and its pitfalls.

items.p: Immunohistochemistry finds a specific protein where it sits, in fixed tissue or cells, using an antibody that carries a visible label.
It tells you which protein, where, when, and whether two proteins sit together (co-localization).

ul: Clinic: typing cancers by their molecular markers; identifying cell types (CD4, CD7)
Research: presence, distribution, subcellular location and changes of a protein
Specificity: a binding site reacts with one determinant
Cross-reactivity: it reacts with more than one
Affinity: the strength of one site binding one determinant

items.p: Direct: the labeled antibody binds the antigen itself.
Indirect: an unlabeled primary antibody (say, from rabbit) binds the antigen. A labeled secondary antibody against rabbit antibodies then binds the primary.

table: Amplifies weak signals; tolerates small antigen changes
Highly specific; low background; reproducible; unlimited supply

ul: Immunofluorescence: fluorescent label, fluorescence microscope
Immunoenzymological: enzyme label (horseradish peroxidase, alkaline phosphatase), often with biotin-streptavidin; colored precipitate or emitted light
Immunoelectron microscopy: electron-dense label (ferritin, colloidal gold) seen as black dots

items.p: A fluorochrome absorbs light at one wavelength and emits at a longer one (lower energy).
The microscope has two filters. The first lets through only the exciting light. The second blocks it and lets through only the emitted light.

ul: DAPI: DNA dye, blue under UV
GFP: a fluorescent protein, not a dye
Photobleaching (fading): use less light for less time, more fluorophore, or sturdier fluorophores
Fix (formaldehyde), dehydrate (alcohol), clear (xylene), embed (paraffin), cut 1–10 μm sections, mount
Antigen retrieval: heat or protease uncovers the epitopes
Block endogenous biotin and enzymes, and non-specific sites
Primary antibody, then labeled secondary antibody, then detection
Strong background: endogenous biotin or enzymes, cross-reacting antibodies
Weak staining: poor enzyme activity or weak primary antibody
Autofluorescence: from the tissue or the fixation

items.p: Always run a positive and a negative control. Related antibody techniques are flow cytometry, Western blotting and ELISA.

cards.a: A specific antigen in situ, in fixed tissue or cells, using a labeled antibody
Direct: labeled antibody binds the antigen. Indirect: unlabeled primary antibody, then a labeled secondary antibody against the primary's species.
One determinant only; more than one determinant; strength of a single site–determinant bond
Amplify weak signals and tolerate antigen variation; more false positives and batch-to-batch variability
Highly specific, low background, reproducible, unlimited supply; may not work across species
Immunofluorescence, immunoenzymological staining, immunoelectron microscopy
Absorbs light at one wavelength and emits at a longer wavelength

cards.q: Roles of the two filters in a fluorescence microscope
cards.a: First: passes only exciting light. Second: blocks it and passes only emitted light.
DAPI: blue DNA dye excited by UV. GFP: a green fluorescent protein, not a dye.
Less intense or shorter illumination, more fluorophore, more robust fluorophores
Horseradish peroxidase and alkaline phosphatase (with biotin-streptavidin)
Ferritin or colloidal gold; seen as small black dots
Fixation, dehydration, clearing (xylene), paraffin embedding, sectioning, mounting
Heat or protease treatment that makes epitopes available to the antibody

cards.q: Common causes of high background in IHC
cards.a: Endogenous biotin or enzymes, and cross-reacting antibodies (fix with blocking and antibody dilution)

questions.stem: What is immunohistochemistry?

options.A: In-situ detection of a specific antigen in fixed tissue with an antibody
options.B: Detection of a specific antigen in a tissue lysate after gel electrophoresis
options.C: Detection of a soluble antigen in serum in a coated microplate
options.D: Counting of labeled cells in suspension passing a laser
options.E: Detection of a nucleic acid sequence in fixed tissue with a probe

questions.explanation: IHC is the in-situ detection of a specific antigen/protein in fixed tissue sections and cells using an antibody, visualized with a microscope. B: That is Western blotting. C: That is ELISA. D: That is flow cytometry. E: IHC detects antigen with antibody.

questions.stem: What did Albert Coons achieve in 1941?

options.A: Produced the first monoclonal antibody from a single clone
options.B: Described the hinge and Fc regions of immunoglobulin G
options.C: Localized mycobacterial antigens with an enzyme-labeled antibody
options.D: Localized pneumococcal antigens with a FITC-labeled antibody
options.E: Developed the electron microscope for colloidal gold labels

questions.explanation: Coons (1941) localized pneumococcal antigens in infected tissues using a fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)-labeled antibody. A: Not what is attributed to Coons. B: Not what is attributed to Coons. C: The antigen was pneumococcal and the label fluorescent. E: Not what is attributed to Coons.

questions.stem: A pathologist wants a permanent colored stain that can be read with an ordinary light microscope. Which antibody label fits?
questions.explanation: Labels: fluorescent dyes (fluorescence microscopy), electron-dense particles (electron microscopy), enzymes such as HRP and alkaline phosphatase, radioactive elements. A: Needs a fluorescence microscope. C: Electron microscopy. D: Electron microscopy. E: Not a colored stain.

questions.stem: An antibody raised against one protein also stains an unrelated protein that shares a similar determinant. Which property explains the extra staining?
questions.explanation: Cross-reactivity: an antibody combining site reacts with more than one antigenic determinant. Specificity: with only one. A: Reaction with only one determinant. B: Strength of one site–determinant reaction. D: Two proteins at the same site. E: Unmasking epitopes.

questions.stem: Two antibodies bind the same single epitope, but one stays bound far more strongly than the other. Which property differs?
questions.explanation: Affinity is the strength of the reaction between a single antigenic determinant and a single combining site. Specificity is reaction with only one determinant. A: Both bind the same single epitope. B: No second determinant is involved. C: Not a binding property. D: A property of the antigen.

questions.stem: Which questions can an IHC experiment answer about a protein?

options.A: Where and when it is expressed; co-localization
options.B: Its full amino acid sequence and exact molecular weight
options.C: Its gene copy number and mutations
options.D: Its concentration in serum over time

questions.explanation: IHC shows who is the target, where it is expressed (localized expression), when (time-specific) and co-localization, in fixed tissue or cells. B: Not provided by IHC. C: Not provided by IHC. D: IHC works on fixed tissue. E: Not provided by IHC.

questions.stem: Why is IHC used in clinical histopathology?

options.B: To sequence tumor DNA for mutations
options.C: To type cancers from molecular markers
options.D: To culture tumor cells for drug testing
options.E: To count circulating tumor cells in blood

questions.explanation: Clinical use: diagnosis of abnormal cells, such as specific cancer types based on molecular markers (breast, lung, prostate) and cell-type biomarkers (CD4, CD7). Research use: presence, tissue distribution, subcellular localization, expression changes, co-localization. A: Not an IHC use. B: Not an IHC use. D: Not an IHC use. E: That would be flow cytometry.

questions.stem: In indirect IHC of a human tissue with a rabbit primary antibody, what is the secondary antibody?

options.A: A marker-coupled antibody directed against the human antigen
options.B: An unlabeled antibody directed against human antibodies
options.C: A marker-coupled rabbit antibody against a second epitope
options.D: A marker-coupled antibody directed against rabbit antibodies
options.E: A marker-coupled antibody directed against mouse antibodies

questions.explanation: Direct IHC: a marker-coupled antibody binds the antigen. Indirect IHC: a primary antibody (e.g. rabbit) binds the antigen and marker-coupled secondary antibodies directed against rabbit antibodies bind the primary. A: That would be direct IHC. B: The secondary carries the marker and targets the primary's species. C: The secondary recognizes the rabbit antibody. E: It must match the species of the primary.

questions.stem: What defines a monoclonal antibody?
questions.explanation: Polyclonal: a mixture from different clones, different affinities and epitopes. Monoclonal: identical copies from one clone, one subtype, a single epitope. A: Polyclonal. C: Polyclonal. D: Polyclonal. E: Polyclonal advantage.

questions.stem: A lab uses a polyclonal antibody to detect a low-abundance protein whose sequence varies between individuals. Which drawback should they expect?

options.B: Too weak a signal for rare targets

questions.explanation: Polyclonal: amplifies low-expression signals, tolerates polymorphism, robust; but more false positives from cross-reaction and batch-to-batch variability. A: A monoclonal problem. B: Polyclonals amplify the signal. C: A monoclonal problem. D: Monoclonal.

questions.stem: Each of the following is an advantage of monoclonal antibodies EXCEPT:

options.A: Detection across a range of species

questions.explanation: Monoclonals: highly specific, less background, less cross-reactivity, homogeneous and reproducible, unlimited supply; but so specific that they are less likely to detect across a range of species. B: Listed advantage. C: Listed advantage. D: Listed advantage. E: Listed advantage.

questions.stem: A lab detects an antigen with a fluorochrome-tagged antibody and views it under a UV microscope. Which staining method is this?
questions.explanation: Three staining methods: immunofluorescence (fluorochrome, UV microscope), immunoenzymological staining, immunoelectron microscopy. A: Enzyme labels. B: Electron-dense labels. C: Not tissue staining. D: Not tissue staining.

questions.stem: Which statement about fluorochromes is correct?

options.A: They absorb light at one wavelength and emit at a shorter wavelength
options.B: They emit light without needing excitation
options.C: They absorb electrons and appear as black dots
options.D: They absorb light at one wavelength and emit at a longer wavelength
options.E: They convert a substrate into a colored precipitate

questions.explanation: Fluorochromes absorb light at one wavelength and emit light at a longer wavelength (fluorescence); the emitted photon is necessarily of lower energy than the absorbed one. A: The emitted photon has lower energy, so longer wavelength. B: Excitation is required. C: That describes electron-dense labels. E: That describes enzyme labels.

questions.stem: Which statement about green fluorescent protein (GFP) is correct?

options.A: It is a blue DNA dye
options.E: It is a synthetic cyanine dye

questions.explanation: GFP is a fluorescent protein, not a dye; DAPI is a DNA dye absorbing UV and fluorescing blue; Cy3, Cy5 and Alexa dyes were developed for fluorescence microscopy. A: DAPI. C: HRP or AP. D: Gold or ferritin. E: Cy3, Cy5.

questions.stem: In a fluorescence microscope, what does the second filter do?

options.A: Passes the exciting light and blocks the emitted wavelengths
options.B: Passes just the wavelengths that excite the dye
options.C: Blocks the exciting light and passes the emitted wavelengths
options.E: Blocks ultraviolet and infrared light equally

questions.explanation: Two sets of filters: the first passes only the wavelengths that excite the dye; the second blocks this light and passes only the wavelengths emitted when the dye fluoresces. A: Reversed. B: That is the first filter. D: Not a fluorescence microscope function. E: Not its described role.

questions.stem: In the composite micrograph of a mitotic cell, which structures are shown by which probes?

options.A: Microtubules red, centromeres green, DNA blue with DAPI
options.B: Microtubules green, centromeres red, DNA blue with DAPI
options.C: Microtubules blue with DAPI, centromeres red, DNA green
options.D: Microtubules green, centromeres blue with DAPI, DNA red
options.E: Microtubules green with GFP, centromeres red, DNA unstained

questions.explanation: Spindle microtubules: green fluorescent antibody; centromeres: red fluorescent antibody; DNA of the condensed chromosomes: blue dye DAPI. A: The antibody colors are swapped. C: DAPI stains DNA. D: DAPI stains DNA. E: DNA is stained blue with DAPI.

questions.stem: A fluorescent signal fades while the slide is being examined. Which measure does NOT reduce this problem?

options.A: Lengthening the time of light exposure
options.B: Reducing the intensity of light exposure
options.E: Shortening the time of light exposure

questions.explanation: Photobleaching solutions: reduce the intensity or time-span of light exposure, increase the concentration of fluorophores, use more robust fluorophores less prone to bleaching. B: A listed solution. C: A listed solution. D: A listed solution. E: A listed solution.

questions.stem: A protocol uses a biotinylated secondary antibody, streptavidin coupled to HRP, and a substrate that leaves a violet precipitate. Which method is this?
questions.explanation: Immunoenzymological staining: HRP or alkaline phosphatase; biotin–streptavidin; colorimetric (violet precipitate) or chemiluminescent (light at 425 nm) detection. A: Fluorochrome labels. B: Electron-dense labels. C: Fluorochrome on the primary. D: Not tissue staining.

questions.stem: How does a colloidal gold label appear in immunoelectron microscopy?
questions.explanation: Immunoelectron microscopy: electron-dense labels (ferritin, colloidal gold) on the antibody's Fc (direct) or on anti-immunoglobulin (indirect), seen as small black dots. A: Fluorochrome. B: Enzyme colorimetry. D: DAPI. E: Chemiluminescence.

questions.stem: Put the steps of sample preparation in order: (1) paraffin embedding, (2) fixation with formaldehyde, (3) clearing with xylene, (4) dehydration with alcohol, (5) sectioning with a microtome.
questions.explanation: Fixation (formaldehyde), dehydration (alcohol), removal of ethanol with an organic solvent (xylene), embedding (paraffin), sectioning (microtome), mounting on slides. A: Dehydration with alcohol precedes xylene, which removes the ethanol. B: Fixation comes first. C: Xylene comes before embedding. E: Embedding precedes sectioning.

questions.stem: Formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded sections show no staining with a validated antibody because fixation has masked the epitopes. Which step helps?

options.E: Rapid freezing of the tissue block

questions.explanation: Antigen retrieval: heating or protease treatment makes the epitopes available for antibody binding. B: Reduces background. C: Removes alcohol. D: Covers nonspecific sites. E: An alternative to embedding, not a rescue.

questions.stem: A liver section stained with a biotin–streptavidin method shows strong signal in every hepatocyte, even on the slide without primary antibody. Which step was missed?
questions.explanation: Block endogenous biotin and endogenous enzymes (peroxidases, AP) before the primary antibody; preparation must keep morphology, architecture and antigenicity. A: Unmasks epitopes. B: Not the cause. C: Not the cause. E: Not the cause.

questions.stem: What is the usual thickness of tissue sections for immunohistochemistry?
questions.explanation: Sections are 1–10 μm thick; embedding media (resins, waxes) harden by cooling or polymerization; fixatives formaldehyde, glutaraldehyde. A: Too thin. B: Too thick. D: Too thick. E: Too thick.

questions.stem: An IHC slide shows staining everywhere, masking the target. Which change reduces this background?
questions.explanation: A blocking buffer covers reactive sites; background is reduced by diluting antibodies or changing incubation time and temperature. A: Raises background. C: Not a remedy. D: Raises signal everywhere. E: Not a remedy.

questions.stem: A frozen section treated with no antibody at all glows green under the fluorescence microscope. What is the cause?
questions.explanation: Problems: strong background (endogenous biotin or enzymes, cross-reactivity), weak staining, nonspecific binding, autofluorescence (from the tissue or the fixation). A: Needs an antibody. B: Loss of signal. C: Enzyme methods. D: Weak staining.

questions.stem: Which controls should every immunostaining experiment include?
questions.explanation: The immunostaining concept also underlies flow cytometry, Western blotting and ELISA; variables include tissue, fixation, pre-treatment and antibody; use positive and negative controls. A: Not controls. C: Not controls. D: Not the control given. E: Not controls.

questions.stem: Which technique applies the same labeled-antibody concept to proteins separated by gel electrophoresis and transferred to a membrane?
questions.explanation: Other applications of the immunostaining concept: flow cytometry, Western blotting and ELISA. A: Antigen in plate wells. B: Cells in suspension. C: Tissue sections. E: Ultrastructure.

lectures.title: CBC, blood smear and anemia classification
lectures.covers: How blood cells are made, what a complete blood count and a smear tell you, how anemia is defined (WHO 2024) and classified, and the first steps of the work-up.

items.p: A stem cell gives a myeloid and a lymphoid line. Growth factors steer each lineage.

ul: Red cells: erythropoietin (kidney; rises with hypoxia and anemia)
Platelets: thrombopoietin
Neutrophils: G-CSF. Eosinophils: IL-5. Basophils: IL-3. Monocytes: M-CSF.

items.p: Red cell precursors mature in the marrow for about 5 days. Their cytoplasm turns from blue (RNA) to pink (hemoglobin) and the nucleus is expelled. The reticulocyte spends 1–2 days in blood; the mature cell lives 120 days.
Iron is needed for hemoglobin; B12 and folate for DNA.

table: Average red cell size; the most useful index

ul: Hematocrit is roughly 3 × hemoglobin
In children the lower limit of MCV is about 70 + age in years
White cells 4.5–11 × 10⁹/L: neutrophils 40–70%, lymphocytes 20–40%, monocytes 3–8%, eosinophils 1–6%, basophils under 2%
Platelets 150–450 × 10⁹/L; lifespan 7–10 days

items.p: Four globin chains, each with a heme (iron in protoporphyrin IX) that binds one oxygen molecule.

ul: α genes: chromosome 16. β genes: chromosome 11.
HbF = α2γ2. HbA = α2β2. HbA2 = α2δ2.
The γ-to-β switch happens around birth, so β-chain diseases appear after about 6 months

items.p: The reticulocyte count shows what the marrow is doing. It is the best single test to separate failed production from destruction or loss.

ul: High: bleeding or hemolysis
Low or "normal" despite anemia: marrow failure or ineffective erythropoiesis
Ret-He: early sign of iron-restricted red cell production

items.p: Read where cells just touch (the monolayer). Bluish cells (polychromasia) mean many reticulocytes.

table: Thalassemia, liver disease, HbC, after splenectomy
HUS, TTP, DIC, mechanical heart valve
Hemolysis, marrow stress; normal in newborns

items.p: Anemia is a hemoglobin more than 2 standard deviations below the mean for age and sex, adjusted for altitude and smoking.
Severe anemia is below 7.0 in children under 5 and in pregnancy, and below 8.0 otherwise. Iron deficiency is the leading cause worldwide.
Use mechanism (less production, destruction, loss) and cell size together.

ul: Microcytic (MCV under 80): iron deficiency, thalassemia, late anemia of inflammation, lead, sideroblastic anemia
Normocytic: use reticulocytes. Low: marrow failure. High: bleeding or hemolysis. Normal: early anemia of inflammation.
Macrocytic (MCV over 100): megaloblastic (B12, folate, drugs) or not (alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia)
Confirm anemia with the right threshold
History: diet, bleeding, jaundice, drugs, lead, family (early gallbladder or spleen removal suggests hemolysis)
Examination: pallor, jaundice, bleeding, large liver, spleen or nodes
Simple tests: CBC with indices, reticulocyte count, smear

items.p: Slow-onset anemia can be well tolerated even at a very low hemoglobin.
Without inflammation: ferritin 20 ng/mL or less in children, 30 or less in adults. With inflammation in adults: ferritin under 100 or transferrin saturation under 20%.
The lecture case: a 4-year-old on cow's milk, Hb 6.0, MCV 70. Severe microcytic anemia from iron deficiency. Oral iron brings reticulocytes up within a week.

cards.q: Where is erythropoietin made, and what raises it?
cards.a: Mainly the kidney; hypoxia and anemia

cards.q: Lifespan of red cells, reticulocytes in blood, and platelets
cards.a: 120 days; 1–2 days; 7–10 days

cards.q: MCV: normal range and child's lower limit
cards.a: 80–100 fL; in children about 70 + age in years
Variation in red cell size (anisocytosis); normal 12–15%
About 3 × hemoglobin
α on chromosome 16; β on chromosome 11

cards.q: Composition of HbA, HbA2 and HbF
cards.a: HbA α2β2; HbA2 α2δ2; HbF α2γ2

cards.q: Why do β-chain disorders show after 6 months?
cards.a: The γ-to-β switch occurs around birth, so HbF protects early on.

cards.q: Most informative test to tell production failure from destruction
cards.a: Reticulocyte count
Reticulocytosis
Microangiopathic hemolysis (HUS, TTP, DIC) or a mechanical heart valve
G6PD deficiency or other oxidant hemolysis
Thalassemia, liver disease, HbC, after splenectomy
Hereditary spherocytosis and immune hemolysis
Marrow fibrosis or infiltration (also thalassemia)
Hb more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex, adjusted for altitude and smoking

cards.q: WHO 2024 anemia cutoffs: 6–23 months, 24–59 months, 5–11 years
WHO 2024 anemia cutoffs: women, men, pregnancy
cards.a: Women 12.0; men 13.0; pregnancy 11.0 (10.5 in the 2nd trimester)
Iron deficiency, thalassemia, late anemia of inflammation, lead poisoning, sideroblastic anemia
Alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia, drugs
Hemorrhage or hemolysis
Children ≤ 20 ng/mL; adults ≤ 30 ng/mL
Ferritin < 100 ng/mL or transferrin saturation < 20%

cards.q: First sign of response to oral iron
cards.a: Reticulocytosis within about a week

questions.stem: Which growth factor is matched with the lineage it steers?
questions.explanation: EPO red cells, TPO platelets, G-CSF neutrophils, IL-5 eosinophils, IL-3 basophils, M-CSF monocytes, IL-7 B and T cells, IL-15 NK cells. A: Basophils are steered by IL-3 and T cells by IL-7. B: IL-3 is for basophils and IL-7 for B and T cells. D: Reversed. E: Reversed.

questions.stem: Which cell directly precedes the reticulocyte in erythropoiesis?
questions.explanation: Proerythroblast → basophilic → polychromatic → orthochromatic erythroblast → reticulocyte → mature red cell. A: One step earlier. B: Two steps earlier. C: The first stage. E: Platelet lineage.

questions.stem: How long does each stage of a red cell's life last?

options.A: Marrow about 1–2 days; reticulocyte in blood 5 days; mature cell 120 days
options.B: Marrow about 5 days; reticulocyte in blood 1–2 days; mature cell 120 days
options.C: Marrow about 5 days; reticulocyte in blood 7–10 days; mature cell 120 days
options.D: Marrow about 5 days; reticulocyte in blood 1–2 days; mature cell 60 days
options.E: Marrow about 15 days; reticulocyte in blood 1–2 hours; mature cell 100 days

questions.explanation: Bone marrow about 5 days, reticulocyte in blood 1–2 days, mature red cell 120 days; about 1% of red cells are replaced daily. A: The first two are swapped. C: 7–10 days is the platelet lifespan. D: The lifespan is 120 days. E: Not the figures given.

questions.stem: An early red cell precursor has deep blue cytoplasm. What gives it this color?
questions.explanation: Cytoplasm shifts from blue (RNA, ribosomes) to pink (hemoglobin); the nucleus condenses and is extruded. B: Makes the cytoplasm pink. C: Not the cause. D: Not the cause. E: Not the cause.

questions.stem: A man moves to a high-altitude city and his hematocrit rises. Which organ mainly makes the hormone driving this?
questions.explanation: Erythropoietin is made mainly by the kidney; it rises with hypoxia and anemia and drives red cell production. A: Not the main source. B: The target, not the source. C: Not the source. D: Not the source.

questions.stem: Which factors does the lecture give for normal erythropoiesis, apart from erythropoietin?

options.A: Iron for DNA; B12 and folate for hemoglobin; thyroxine and testosterone accelerate it
options.B: Iron for hemoglobin; B12 and folate for DNA; cortisol and estrogen accelerate it
options.C: Copper for hemoglobin; vitamin K for DNA; insulin accelerates it
options.D: Iron for hemoglobin; B12 and folate for DNA; thyroxine and testosterone accelerate it
options.E: Iron for hemoglobin; vitamin C and zinc for DNA; thyroxine slows it

questions.explanation: Iron is needed for hemoglobin, B12 and folate for DNA; thyroxine and testosterone accelerate erythropoiesis. A: Roles of iron and vitamins are swapped. B: The hormones named are thyroxine and testosterone. C: Not the factors given. E: Not the factors given.

questions.stem: What must an ageing red cell retain to keep circulating, and what removes it when this is lost?

options.A: It must keep its nucleus to pass the spleen; neutrophils remove old cells
options.B: It must stay deformable to pass the spleen; macrophages remove old cells
options.C: It must stay rigid to resist the spleen; complement lyses old cells
options.D: It must keep its ribosomes; the liver filters old cells
options.E: It must stay deformable to pass the kidney; podocytes remove old cells

questions.explanation: Cells must stay deformable to pass the spleen; macrophages remove old cells. A: Mature red cells have no nucleus, and macrophages remove them. C: Deformability is required. D: Not as described. E: The spleen and macrophages are named.

questions.stem: Which statement about the complete blood count is correct?

options.A: The reticulocyte count is part of each differential
options.B: The differential lists red cell indices
options.C: The reticulocyte count is reported on request
options.D: MPV is a red cell index
options.E: RDW describes variation in platelet size

questions.explanation: CBC: red cell count, Hb/hematocrit, indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC, RDW), reticulocyte count on request; white cell count and differential; platelet count and MPV. A: It is on request. B: The differential lists white cell types. D: MPV is mean platelet volume. E: RDW concerns red cells.

questions.stem: Normal CBC values depend on age and sex. On which additional factors does hemoglobin depend (WHO 2024)?
questions.explanation: Normal values depend on age and sex, and hemoglobin also on altitude and smoking. A: WHO 2024 makes no adjustment for ethnicity. B: No adjustment for inflammation. C: Not listed. D: Neither is adjusted for.

questions.stem: Which description of the mature red cell is correct?

options.A: A 7–8 µm biconcave disc without nucleus or mitochondria
options.B: A 7–8 µm biconcave disc with mitochondria but no nucleus
options.C: A 12–15 µm sphere without nucleus or ribosomes
options.D: A 2–3 µm disc with a small surface-to-volume ratio
options.E: A 7–8 µm biconcave disc that divides in the circulation

questions.explanation: Red cells are flexible 7–8 µm biconcave discs with a large surface-to-volume ratio, about 5 million/µL, lifespan 120 days, with no nucleus, ribosomes or mitochondria. B: Mitochondria are absent. C: Size and shape are wrong. D: Size is 7–8 µm and the ratio is large. E: It cannot divide or make protein.

questions.stem: Which statement about hemoglobin is correct?

options.A: About 270 million molecules per red cell; each heme (iron + protoporphyrin IX) binds four O₂
options.B: About 27,000 molecules per red cell; each globin binds one O₂ directly
options.C: About 270 million molecules per red cell; two globin chains carry one shared heme
options.D: About 2.7 billion molecules per red cell; heme is copper + protoporphyrin IX
options.E: About 270 million molecules per red cell; each heme (iron + protoporphyrin IX) binds one O₂

questions.explanation: About 270 million Hb molecules per red cell; 4 globin chains (2 α + 2 non-α), each carrying a heme group (iron + protoporphyrin IX); each heme reversibly binds one O₂. A: Each heme binds one O₂. B: Number and binding site are wrong. C: There are four chains, each with a heme. D: Heme contains iron.

questions.stem: How is hematocrit defined, and how does it relate to hemoglobin?

options.A: Percentage of blood volume occupied by plasma; about 3 × Hb
options.B: Percentage of blood volume occupied by red cells; about Hb ÷ 3
options.C: Average hemoglobin concentration in red cells; about 3 × Hb
options.D: Percentage of blood volume occupied by red cells; about 3 × Hb
options.E: Number of red cells per microliter; about 10 × Hb

questions.explanation: Hematocrit is the percentage of blood volume occupied by red cells, approximately 3 × Hb. Adult Hb: males 13.5–18 g/dL, females 12–15 g/dL. A: It is the red cell fraction. B: It is about three times the Hb. C: That is the MCHC. E: Not the definition.

questions.stem: On which chromosome is the α-globin gene cluster?
questions.explanation: Chromosome 16: α cluster (ζ, α2, α1). Chromosome 11: β cluster (ε, Gγ, Aγ, δ, β). A: β-globin cluster. B: Not a globin cluster. D: Not a globin cluster. E: Not a globin cluster.

questions.stem: Which hemoglobin has the composition α2δ2?
questions.explanation: Embryonic: Gower 1, Gower 2, Portland. Fetal: HbF (α2γ2). Adult: HbA (α2β2), HbA2 (α2δ2). A: α2γ2. C: α2β2. D: Embryonic. E: Embryonic.

questions.stem: An infant with severe β-thalassemia is well at birth and becomes symptomatic after about 6 months. Why?

options.A: HbF does not need β chains

questions.explanation: The γ-to-β switch occurs around birth; as HbF (α2γ2) declines, β-chain disorders appear after about 6 months. B: Not the reason. C: Embryonic hemoglobins disappear early. D: Not the reason. E: Not the reason.

questions.stem: Which red cell index measures variation in cell size?
questions.explanation: MCV 80–100 fL (most useful); RDW 12–15% (anisocytosis); MCH 27–31 pg; MCHC 32–36 g/dL. A: Average volume. B: Hb weight per cell. C: Hb concentration per cell. E: Share of blood volume.

questions.stem: What is the lower limit of normal MCV for a 4-year-old child?
questions.explanation: In children the lower limit of normal MCV is about 70 + age in years (until about 80 fL). A: 70 + age. B: The adult limit. D: Too low. E: 70 + 4.

questions.stem: Which condition gives a low or inappropriately normal reticulocyte count?
questions.explanation: Reticulocytes show marrow activity: increased in blood loss and hemolysis; decreased or inappropriately normal in marrow failure and ineffective erythropoiesis. B: Reticulocytes rise. C: Reticulocytes rise. D: Reticulocytes rise. E: Reticulocytes rise.

questions.stem: After chemotherapy, which reticulocyte parameter is the earliest sign of marrow recovery?
questions.explanation: The immature reticulocyte fraction (IRF) is the earliest sign of marrow recovery; Ret-He (CHr) is an early marker of iron-restricted erythropoiesis. A: Marker of iron-restricted erythropoiesis. C: Rises later. D: Not a marrow recovery marker. E: Not a marrow recovery marker.

questions.stem: Which white cell type predominates in the blood of young children and of adults?

options.A: Neutrophils predominate in young children; lymphocytes in adults
options.B: Monocytes predominate in young children; neutrophils in adults
options.E: Lymphocytes predominate in young children; neutrophils in adults

questions.explanation: Normal WBC count is 4.5–11.0 × 10⁹/L; lifespan from a few hours to about 15 days. Lymphocytes predominate in young children, neutrophils in adults. A: Reversed. B: Not as stated. C: Neutrophils predominate in adults. D: Lymphocytes predominate in young children.

questions.stem: Which adult differential count is normal?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils 40–70%, lymphocytes 20–40%, monocytes 3–8%, eosinophils 1–6%, basophils under 2%. A: The first two are swapped. B: Lymphocytes and monocytes are swapped. C: Not the ranges given. E: Monocytes are 3–8%.

questions.stem: In which condition are basophils increased, according to the white cell overview?
questions.explanation: Basophils release histamine and heparin, take part in hypersensitivity and are increased in myeloproliferative neoplasms. Eosinophils rise in allergy, parasites and some cancers. A: That is listed for eosinophils. B: Neutrophils are the first-line defense. D: Not listed for basophils. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Which statement about platelets is correct?

options.A: Fragments of megakaryocyte nuclei; lifespan 7–10 days; regulated by thrombopoietin
options.B: Fragments of megakaryocyte cytoplasm; lifespan 7–10 days; regulated by thrombopoietin
options.C: Fragments of megakaryocyte cytoplasm; lifespan 120 days; regulated by erythropoietin
options.D: Small nucleated cells; lifespan 1–2 days; regulated by G-CSF
options.E: Fragments of monocyte cytoplasm; lifespan 7–10 days; regulated by M-CSF

questions.explanation: Platelets (150–450 × 10⁹/L, lifespan 7–10 days) are produced by fragmentation of megakaryocyte cytoplasm; they are small and non-nucleated; production is regulated by thrombopoietin. A: They come from cytoplasm and have no nucleus. C: Lifespan and hormone are wrong. D: They are non-nucleated. E: The parent cell is the megakaryocyte.

questions.stem: What does polychromasia on a blood smear indicate?
questions.explanation: Polychromasia: bluish-grey red cells reflecting reticulocytosis. A: Not what polychromasia reflects. B: That is suggested by teardrop cells. C: Not what polychromasia reflects. D: That is suggested by bite cells.

questions.stem: Which area of a blood smear should be read?

options.A: The monolayer, where cells just touch and pallor is visible
options.B: The thick end, where cells overlap and morphology is concentrated
options.C: The thin end, where cells are flattened and pallor is lost
options.D: Any area, since morphology is uniform along the slide
options.E: The edges, where white cells are spread out

questions.explanation: Read in the monolayer: cells just touch and central pallor is visible. Too thick: cells overlap. Too thin: cells flattened, pallor lost. B: Overlap hides morphology. C: Too thin. D: It is not uniform. E: Not the area recommended.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old with a large spleen has many teardrop cells on the smear. Which process do they suggest?
questions.explanation: Teardrop cells (dacrocytes): marrow fibrosis or infiltration, thalassemia. A: Bite cells. B: Schistocytes. C: Pencil cells. E: Target cells.

questions.stem: Each of the following is a cause of target cells EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Target cells (codocytes) are seen in thalassemia, liver disease, HbC and after splenectomy. B: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: Besides HbSS, in which genotype are sickle cells (drepanocytes) seen?
questions.explanation: Sickle cells: HbSS, HbSC and HbS/β-thalassemia. A: No sickle allele. B: No sickle allele. D: α-thalassemia. E: No sickle allele.

questions.stem: A smear shows small, dense red cells without central pallor, and the DAT is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Spherocytes (small, dense, no central pallor): hereditary spherocytosis and immune hemolysis; a positive DAT points to immune. A: DAT negative. C: Bite cells. D: Pencil cells, pale cells. E: Target cells.

questions.stem: In which condition are pencil cells seen?
questions.explanation: Elliptocytes (ovalocytes) are seen in hereditary elliptocytosis; pencil cells in iron deficiency. A: Spherocytes are seen. B: Bite cells are seen. C: Schistocytes are seen. D: Teardrop cells are seen.

questions.stem: A patient becomes jaundiced after taking an oxidant drug; the smear shows red cells with a bite-shaped defect at the edge. Which diagnosis is suggested?
questions.explanation: Bite cells (degmacytes) are seen in G6PD deficiency and other oxidant hemolysis. B: Spherocytes would be seen. C: Schistocytes would be seen. D: Sickle cells would be seen. E: Target and teardrop cells would be seen.

questions.stem: A man with a mechanical aortic valve has anemia, and the smear shows helmet-shaped fragments. What are these cells?
questions.explanation: Schistocytes (helmet and triangle fragments): microangiopathic hemolysis (HUS, TTP, DIC) and mechanical heart valves. A: Small, round, no pallor. C: Oxidant hemolysis. D: Thalassemia, liver disease. E: Marrow fibrosis.

questions.stem: What does the lecture conclude about AI tools such as CytoDiffusion in smear review?

options.A: A replacement for the clinician once sensitivity exceeds 0.9
options.B: A tool no better than chance at detecting unseen blasts
options.C: A second reader that does not replace the clinician
options.D: A tool validated for routine use in diverse populations
options.E: A tool that cannot explain which image regions drive its calls

questions.explanation: CytoDiffusion (2025) reached 0.91 sensitivity for unseen abnormal cells at 0.96 specificity (0.28 for a standard classifier). It flags uncertain cells and shows heat maps; it does not replace the clinician and needs further testing. A: It does not replace reading the smear in clinical context. B: That describes the standard vision-transformer classifier (0.28). D: It still needs testing in diverse populations. E: It shows heat maps.

questions.stem: How is anemia defined?

options.A: Hb more than 1 SD below the mean for age and sex, adjusted for ethnicity
options.B: Hb below 12 g/dL at any age
options.C: Hematocrit more than 2 SD below the mean, adjusted for weight
options.D: Red cell count below 4 million/µL, adjusted for altitude
options.E: Hb more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex

questions.explanation: Anemia: hemoglobin more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex in a healthy reference population, adjusted for altitude and smoking. It is the most common blood disorder worldwide. A: The definition uses 2 SD and no ethnicity adjustment. B: Thresholds vary with age and sex. C: The definition uses Hb. D: The definition uses Hb.

questions.stem: Which example shows that hemoglobin must be read in context?

options.A: Hb 14 g/dL is normal in any 2-year-old
options.B: Hb 7.5 g/dL means severe anemia in a 2-month-old preterm infant
options.C: Hb 11 g/dL means anemia in a second-trimester pregnancy
options.D: Hb 14 g/dL can mean anemia with cyanotic heart disease
options.E: Hb 12.5 g/dL is normal in an adult man

questions.explanation: Hb 7.5 g/dL can be normal for age in a 2-month-old preterm infant (physiologic nadir); Hb 14 g/dL can mean anemia in a 2-year-old with cyanotic heart disease. A: Not with cyanotic heart disease. B: It can be the physiologic nadir. C: The cutoff there is 10.5. E: The cutoff for men is 13.0.

questions.stem: Which statement about the global burden of anemia is correct?

options.A: 1.92 billion people (24.3%) in 2021; malaria is the leading cause
options.B: 192 million people (2.4%) in 2021; dietary iron deficiency is the leading cause
options.C: 1.92 billion people (28.2%) in 2021, up from 24.3% in 1990
options.D: 3.9 billion people (48%) in 2021; B12 deficiency is the leading cause
options.E: 1.92 billion people (24.3%) in 2021; dietary iron deficiency is the leading cause

questions.explanation: 1.92 billion people had anemia in 2021 (24.3%, down from 28.2% in 1990). Dietary iron deficiency leads all causes. Most affected: children under 5, adolescent girls and women of reproductive age, pregnant women. A: The leading cause is dietary iron deficiency. B: The figures are 1.92 billion and 24.3%. C: Prevalence fell from 28.2% to 24.3%. D: Not the data given.

questions.stem: According to WHO 2024, which hemoglobin value defines anemia?

options.A: Below 10.5 g/dL at 6–23 months; below 11.5 g/dL at 5–11 years
options.B: Below 11.0 g/dL at 6–23 months; below 11.5 g/dL at 5–11 years
options.C: Below 10.5 g/dL at 6–23 months; below 12.0 g/dL at 5–11 years
options.D: Below 11.5 g/dL at 6–23 months; below 10.5 g/dL at 5–11 years
options.E: Below 10.0 g/dL at 6–23 months; below 11.0 g/dL at 5–11 years

questions.explanation: WHO 2024: 6–23 months <10.5; 24–59 months <11.0; 5–11 years <11.5; 12–14 years and non-pregnant women <12.0; men <13.0; pregnancy 1st and 3rd trimester <11.0, 2nd trimester <10.5. B: The 6–23 month cutoff was lowered to 10.5. C: 12.0 applies from 12 years. D: Reversed. E: Not the cutoffs.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has a hemoglobin of 6.0 g/dL. How is this graded by WHO 2024?
questions.explanation: At 24–59 months: anemia <11.0, mild 10.0–10.9, moderate 7.0–9.9, severe <7.0. From 5 years and in adults the severe cutoff is <8.0. A: 6.0 is below 7.0. B: The severe cutoff under 5 years is 7.0; 8.0 applies from 5 years. D: 6.0 is far below. E: She is in the 24–59 month group.

questions.stem: Which change did WHO make in 2024?

options.A: Altitude adjustment now starts at 1000 m
options.B: Altitude adjustment now starts at 500 m
options.D: An adjustment for ethnicity was added
options.E: An adjustment for inflammation was added

questions.explanation: Changes: cutoff for 6–23 months lowered from 11.0 to 10.5; new second-trimester cutoff 10.5; altitude adjustment starts at 500 m (was 1000 m); smoking adjustment kept; no adjustment for ethnicity or inflammation. A: It was 1000 m and is now 500 m. C: It was kept. D: There is no adjustment for ethnicity. E: There is no adjustment for inflammation.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with cyanotic heart disease has a hemoglobin of 14 g/dL. How is this interpreted?
questions.explanation: Hb must be read in context: 14 g/dL can be anemia in a cyanotic child; 7.5 g/dL can be normal in a 2-month-old preterm (physiologic nadir). A: Cyanosis needs a higher Hb. B: Not at this level in cyanosis. C: Not suggested. E: Not suggested.

questions.stem: Which findings point specifically to iron deficiency among the symptoms of anemia?
questions.explanation: Digestive: anorexia, nausea; pica and glossitis in iron deficiency. Other systems: fatigue, dyspnea, tachycardia, flow murmur, pallor, impaired T-cell and macrophage function. A: General cardiorespiratory signs. B: General nervous system symptoms. C: General signs. D: A general sign of anemia.

questions.stem: A child with a hemoglobin of 5 g/dL from long-standing iron deficiency is playful and hemodynamically stable. Which determinant of severity explains this?
questions.explanation: Severity depends on how low the Hb is, how fast it fell (slow-onset anemia can be well tolerated even at very low Hb) and comorbidities. A: The level is very low yet tolerated. B: Not a determinant listed. C: Not a determinant listed. E: Not a determinant listed.

questions.stem: Which simple labs complete the diagnostic approach after confirming anemia, history and examination?

options.A: CBC with indices, ferritin and bone marrow aspirate
options.B: CBC with indices, reticulocyte count and blood smear
options.C: Blood smear, hemoglobin electrophoresis and B12
options.D: Reticulocyte count, Coombs test and LDH
options.E: CBC with indices, lead level and CRP

questions.explanation: Approach: confirm anemia, focused history, thorough exam, simple labs (CBC and indices, reticulocyte count, blood smear). A: Not the first simple labs. C: Not the first simple labs. D: Not the first simple labs. E: Not the first simple labs.

questions.stem: In the family history of an anemic child, what does an early cholecystectomy in a relative suggest?

options.A: An inherited bleeding disorder in the family

questions.explanation: Family history: early splenectomy or cholecystectomy (early gallstones suggest hemolysis), early hysterectomy (may suggest a bleeding disorder), autoimmune disease, consanguinity, ethnic origin. Patient history includes neonatal jaundice, dark urine, transfusions, lead, milk intake, pica. A: That is suggested by early hysterectomy. B: Not the association. D: Not the association. E: Not the association.

questions.stem: How are skin bleeding lesions classified by size?

options.A: Petechiae up to 2 mm; purpura 3–10 mm; ecchymosis over 1 cm
options.B: Petechiae 3–10 mm; purpura up to 2 mm; ecchymosis over 1 cm
options.C: Petechiae up to 2 mm; purpura over 1 cm; ecchymosis 3–10 mm
options.D: Petechiae up to 2 cm; purpura 3–10 cm; ecchymosis over 10 cm
options.E: Petechiae up to 5 mm; purpura 5–20 mm; ecchymosis over 5 cm

questions.explanation: Petechiae ≤2 mm (pinpoint, flat, non-blanching); purpura 3–10 mm; ecchymosis >1 cm; hematoma: raised, palpable collection of clotted blood. B: The first two are swapped. C: The last two are swapped. D: The units are wrong. E: Not the sizes given.

questions.stem: Which mouth findings are sought on examination of an anemic patient?

options.E: Petechiae of the palate and tonsillar exudate

questions.explanation: Mouth: glossitis (smooth, sore tongue) and angular cheilitis. Other signs: icterus, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, leg ulcers, abnormal facies. A: Not the findings listed. C: Not the findings listed. D: Not the findings listed. E: Not the findings listed.

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as a cause of microcytic anemia EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Microcytic: iron deficiency, thalassemia, late anemia of inflammation, lead poisoning, sideroblastic anemia. Hypothyroidism causes non-megaloblastic macrocytosis. A: Listed. B: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation. Hb 11 g/dL, MCV 104 fL; vitamin B12 and folate are normal. Which cause of her macrocytosis is most likely?
questions.explanation: Megaloblastic: B12 or folate deficiency, drugs. Non-megaloblastic: alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, myelodysplasia, drugs. B: B12 is normal. C: Folate is normal. D: Microcytic. E: Microcytic.

questions.stem: A patient has a normocytic anemia with high reticulocytes, high LDH and low haptoglobin. Which category fits?
questions.explanation: Normocytic: low reticulocytes = marrow failure or ineffective erythropoiesis; high = hemorrhage or hemolysis; normal = early anemia of inflammation. A: Low reticulocytes. B: Low reticulocytes. C: Normal reticulocytes. E: Microcytic, low reticulocytes.

questions.stem: To decide between production failure and increased destruction, which test is the most informative?
questions.explanation: The reticulocyte count shows how active the marrow is: low in production failure, high in destruction or loss. A: It classifies size, not mechanism. B: Not the answer given. C: Helpful, but the count is the most informative here. D: Not the answer given.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old with no inflammation has her ferritin checked. At or below which level is she iron deficient (ASH 2026)?
questions.explanation: ASH 2026 (no inflammation): children ≤ 20 ng/mL (was ≤ 12); adults, menstruating and pregnant ≤ 30 (up to ≤ 50 with symptoms or risk). A: The old threshold. B: Adults. C: Adults with symptoms or risk factors. E: Adults with inflammation.

questions.stem: How should the ASH 2026 ferritin thresholds be applied?

options.A: With inflammation use ferritin < 100 ng/mL or TSAT < 20%; a threshold prompts assessment
options.B: With inflammation in adults use ferritin < 30 ng/mL; a threshold mandates iron treatment
options.C: With or without inflammation the same threshold applies
options.D: Higher cutoffs carry no risk and rest on high-certainty evidence

questions.explanation: The thresholds apply only without inflammation. With inflammation (adults): ferritin <100 ng/mL or TSAT <20%. A threshold prompts assessment, not automatic iron; higher cutoffs risk overdiagnosis and iron overload, especially in children; most evidence is low certainty. B: The inflammation criterion is <100 or TSAT <20%, and a threshold prompts assessment only. C: Thresholds apply only without inflammation. D: They risk overdiagnosis and iron overload; evidence is mostly low certainty. E: Not the criterion.

questions.stem: What did the 2026 NHANES analysis of children aged 5–14 show?

options.A: Iron supply falters at ferritin < 15 µg/L, lowering prevalence from 30% to 9%
options.B: Iron supply falters at ferritin < 100 µg/L in boys aged 5–7
options.C: Iron supply falters at ferritin < 24 µg/L, raising prevalence from 9% to 30%
options.D: Iron supply falters at ferritin < 24 µg/L, detected by reticulocyte count
options.E: Iron supply is normal until ferritin < 5 µg/L

questions.explanation: In 3,765 healthy US children, the ferritin level at which red cell iron supply first falters (by zinc protoporphyrin) was <24 µg/L: 30% iron deficient versus 9% with the old cutoff (about 15). Girls aged 12–14 were most affected. A: The physiologic cutoff is <24 and prevalence rises. B: Not the finding; girls 12–14 were most affected. D: It was identified with zinc protoporphyrin. E: Not the finding.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old girl, fed mostly cow's milk since age 1, is markedly pale with Hb 6.0 g/dL, MCV 70 fL and normal white cells and platelets. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Severe (Hb 6.0) microcytic anemia (below ~74 fL) from excess cow's milk with few solids: nutritional iron deficiency. A: Screened for, but not the most likely. C: Not this severe. D: No inflammation. E: Rare.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old fed mostly cow's milk has iron deficiency anemia. Besides poor iron intake, how else does cow's milk worsen her anemia?
questions.explanation: Cow's milk can cause occult intestinal blood loss. Expect low reticulocytes, pencil cells, high RDW, low Ret-He; confirm with ferritin ≤ 20 ng/mL and CRP; screen for lead. A: Not stated. B: Not stated. C: Not stated. D: Not stated.

questions.stem: After starting oral iron, limiting cow's milk and adding iron-rich foods, what response is expected?

options.A: A rising hemoglobin within 1–2 days, then reticulocytosis after a month
options.B: Reticulocytosis within about 1 week, then a rising hemoglobin within weeks
options.C: Reticulocytosis within about 1 day, with a normal hemoglobin by 1 week
options.D: No reticulocyte change; ferritin normal within a week
options.E: Reticulocytosis within about 1 week; iron can then be stopped

questions.explanation: Expect reticulocytosis within about 1 week and a rising Hb within weeks; continue iron to replete stores. A: Reticulocytes rise first. C: Too fast. D: Not the expected course. E: Iron is continued to replete stores.

questions.stem: In which situation are nucleated red cells on a blood smear a normal finding?
questions.explanation: Nucleated red cells (normoblasts) are seen in hemolysis, marrow stress or infiltration, and are normal in newborns. A: Not normal at that age. B: Not stated as normal. D: Not stated as normal. E: Not stated as normal.

questions.stem: How should a newly found anemia be classified?

options.A: By MCV first, then mechanism if needed

questions.explanation: Classify two ways at once: by mechanism (decreased production, hemolysis, loss) and by MCV (microcytic < 80, normocytic 80–100, macrocytic > 100 fL). A: Both at the same time. B: That grades severity. C: Not the classification. E: Part of the work-up, not the classification.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old with suspected nutritional iron deficiency is about to start iron. Which tests confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Expect low reticulocytes, pencil cells, high RDW, low Ret-He; confirm with ferritin ≤ 20 ng/mL, checking CRP for inflammation; screen for lead. B: For thalassemia. C: Not needed. D: For macrocytosis. E: For hemolysis.

lectures.title: Microcytic anemias
lectures.covers: Iron deficiency in depth (iron handling, hepcidin, causes, diagnosis, 2026 screening and treatment), plus thalassemia trait, anemia of inflammation, lead poisoning and sideroblastic anemia.

items.p: Small red cells mean too little hemoglobin per cell. Ask which ingredient is missing.

ul: Iron deficiency: not enough iron
Thalassemia: not enough globin
Anemia of inflammation: iron locked away by hepcidin
Lead poisoning: heme synthesis blocked
Sideroblastic anemia: iron cannot be put into heme

items.p: In children, iron deficiency and thalassemia trait are by far the most common.
Food is the only source and the body can barely excrete iron, so balance is set at the gut.

ul: Absorbed in the duodenum and upper jejunum: 1–2 mg a day
Vitamin C helps; phytates, tea, calcium and dairy hinder
Heme iron (meat, fish) is absorbed better than plant iron
The marrow needs about 25 mg a day; almost all of it is recycled from old red cells by macrophages
Carried on transferrin, stored as ferritin

items.p: Ferroportin is the only door by which iron leaves a cell. Hepcidin, made by the liver, locks that door.

ul: Low hepcidin (iron deficiency, anemia, hypoxia, active marrow via ERFE): more absorption and release
High hepcidin (inflammation via IL-6, iron overload): iron trapped in gut cells and macrophages; oral iron poorly absorbed

items.p: Deficiency comes before anemia: first ferritin falls, then transferrin saturation and Ret-He, and only last the hemoglobin and MCV.
Always find the cause.

ul: Low intake: breastfeeding without iron after 4–6 months; too much cow's milk (over about 700 mL a day)
Blood loss: heavy periods, gut bleeding
High demand: prematurity, growth, pregnancy
Poor absorption: celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, H. pylori, bariatric surgery

items.p: Iron deficiency in the first 3 years can harm brain development permanently, even without anemia.
Beyond pallor and fatigue: spoon nails, sore tongue, cracked mouth corners, hair loss, pica (including ice), restless legs.

ul: Ferritin: best single test. Low means deficiency. It rises with inflammation, so check CRP.
2026 thresholds: children 20 ng/mL or less; adolescents and adults 30 or less
Transferrin saturation under 20%; high RDW; low MCV; pencil cells; platelets often raised

items.p: Screen with CBC plus ferritin (not hemoglobin alone): breastfed infants at 9–12 months, formula-fed at 15–18 months, adolescent girls by age 14.

ul: Children: 3 mg/kg elemental iron once a day. Adolescents: 65 mg once a day.
Empty stomach, away from milk; vitamin C helps
Continue at least 3 months to refill stores
Reticulocytes peak at days 5–10; hemoglobin rises in 2–4 weeks
No response at 1 month: check adherence first, then ongoing loss, malabsorption, inflammation, wrong diagnosis
Intravenous iron: intolerance, failure of oral iron, malabsorption, heavy ongoing loss
Heavy periods: test for von Willebrand disease. Pica: test blood lead.

items.p: Confirm with hemoglobin electrophoresis. Do not give iron for microcytosis until deficiency is proven.

The second most common anemia: kidney disease, cancer, autoimmune disease, chronic infection. Normocytic at first, microcytic later; ferritin normal or high. Treat the disease; give intravenous iron if there is true deficiency (ferritin under 100 or saturation under 20%).
Children under 3 are most at risk, and iron deficiency increases lead absorption. Sources: old paint, kohl, remedies, contaminated spices.

ul: Often silent; abdominal pain, constipation, irritability, developmental delay, wrist or foot drop
Lead blocks ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase; zinc protoporphyrin rises
Basophilic stippling (pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase blocked); lead lines on X-ray
No safe level; reference value 3.5 µg/dL

items.note: The slide also lists ALA synthase among the enzymes inhibited by lead. Standard texts name ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase.

items.p: Iron enters the erythroblast but cannot be made into heme. Ferritin and saturation are high; the marrow shows ring sideroblasts (Prussian blue).

ul: Inherited: X-linked ALAS2 (responds to vitamin B6)
Acquired: isoniazid, linezolid, alcohol, lead, myelodysplasia, copper deficiency, zinc excess

cards.a: Iron deficiency, thalassemia, anemia of inflammation (late), lead poisoning, sideroblastic anemia

cards.q: Where is iron absorbed, and what helps or hinders?
cards.a: Duodenum and proximal jejunum; vitamin C helps; phytates, tea, calcium, dairy hinder
Binds ferroportin and causes its destruction, trapping iron in gut cells and macrophages

cards.q: What lowers and what raises hepcidin?
cards.a: Lowers: iron deficiency, hypoxia, ERFE. Raises: inflammation (IL-6), iron overload.
Iron depletion (low ferritin), iron-deficient erythropoiesis (low TSAT, low Ret-He), iron deficiency anemia
Absolute: body iron too low. Functional: iron present but locked in stores (inflammation, kidney disease).

cards.q: Ferritin in iron deficiency versus anemia of inflammation
cards.a: Low versus normal or high (transferrin saturation is low in both)
Koilonychia, glossitis, angular stomatitis, hair loss, pica and pagophagia, restless legs

cards.q: Milk and iron deficiency: the limits
cards.a: No cow's milk before 12 months; no more than about 24 oz (700 mL) a day afterwards
CBC + ferritin (with CRP): breastfed at 9–12 months, formula-fed at 15–18 months, adolescents by age 14
Children 3 mg/kg elemental iron once daily; adolescents 65 mg once daily; at least 3 months
Reticulocyte peak at days 5–10; hemoglobin rises in 2–4 weeks; stores refilled after 3 months

cards.q: Most common cause of failure of oral iron
cards.a: Non-adherence or underdosing
Oral intolerance, no response, malabsorption (IBD, celiac, bariatric surgery), ongoing losses
Hypophosphatemia
Trait: high RBC count, normal RDW, normal ferritin, Mentzer < 13. Iron deficiency: the opposite.
Normocytic then microcytic, low reticulocytes, low TSAT, normal or high ferritin, high hepcidin
ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase (zinc protoporphyrin rises)

cards.q: Why basophilic stippling in lead poisoning?
cards.a: Lead inhibits pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase, so ribosomal RNA clumps.
Abdominal pain, constipation, irritability, developmental delay, wrist or foot drop, lead lines on X-ray

cards.q: Sideroblastic anemia: hallmark and iron tests
cards.a: Ring sideroblasts in marrow; high ferritin and transferrin saturation
X-linked ALAS2 mutation; also give B6 with isoniazid-related cases

cards.q: Adolescent with iron deficiency and heavy periods: screen for...
cards.a: von Willebrand disease

cards.q: Toddler with iron deficiency and pica: test...
cards.a: Blood lead level

questions.stem: A man on isoniazid develops a microcytic anemia, and his marrow shows ring sideroblasts. Which step of hemoglobin synthesis fails?
questions.explanation: Each microcytic anemia lacks one ingredient: iron (deficiency), globin (thalassemia), iron locked by hepcidin (inflammation), heme synthesis blocked (lead), iron not inserted into heme (sideroblastic). B: Thalassemia. C: Iron deficiency. D: Anemia of inflammation. E: Lead (basophilic stippling).

questions.stem: Which microcytic anemias dominate in children, and which is more common in adults?

options.A: Anemia of inflammation and lead poisoning dominate in children; iron deficiency in adults
options.B: Sideroblastic anemia dominates in children; thalassemia trait in adults
options.C: Thalassemia trait dominates at each age
options.D: Iron deficiency and thalassemia trait dominate in children; inflammation in adults
options.E: Iron deficiency and lead poisoning dominate in children; sideroblastic anemia in adults

questions.explanation: In children, iron deficiency and thalassemia trait dominate; anemia of inflammation is more common in adults. A: Not as stated. B: Not as stated. C: Not as stated. E: Not as stated.

questions.stem: How common is iron deficiency in US toddlers, and why does it matter beyond anemia?

options.A: About 15%; cognitive deficits resolve fully once hemoglobin is normal
options.B: About 1.5%; cognitive deficits may persist after correction
options.C: About 50%; growth is affected but cognition is spared
options.D: About 15%; the main risk is iron overload from treatment
options.E: About 15%; cognitive deficits may persist after correction

questions.explanation: About 15% of US toddlers and about 11% of non-pregnant adolescent girls have iron deficiency. It is linked to neurodevelopmental and cognitive deficits that may persist even after anemia is corrected. A: Deficits may persist. B: The figure is about 15%. C: Not the data given. D: Not the concern stated.

questions.stem: A regular blood donor still has a normal hemoglobin and MCV. As her iron stores fall, which test turns abnormal first?
questions.explanation: Stage 1, iron depletion: low ferritin, normal Hb and MCV. Stage 2, iron-deficient erythropoiesis: low TSAT, low Ret-He, high ZPP. Stage 3, anemia: low Hb, microcytosis, high RDW. A: Stage 2. C: Stage 3. D: Stage 3. E: Stage 3.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease has adequate total body iron, but circulating iron is low because it is locked in stores. Which term applies?
questions.explanation: Absolute iron deficiency: total body iron too low (poor intake, blood loss, malabsorption, rapid growth). Functional iron deficiency: iron adequate but locked in stores (inflammation, chronic kidney disease, high hepcidin). A: Total body iron would be too low. B: That is stage 1 of absolute deficiency. D: That is a rare inherited disorder. E: Iron is not inserted into heme there.

questions.stem: Each of the following is a listed role of iron EXCEPT:

options.A: Oxygen delivery to muscle by myoglobin

questions.explanation: Iron is needed for hemoglobin, myoglobin, mitochondrial enzymes (ATP), immunity and brain growth (myelination, neurotransmitters). A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: Which statement about dietary iron is correct?

options.A: Non-heme iron from plants is more bioavailable than heme iron
options.B: Heme iron comes from fortified cereals and legumes
options.C: Heme iron from meat and fish is more bioavailable
options.D: Heme and non-heme iron are absorbed equally
options.E: Non-heme iron is found in meat, poultry and fish

questions.explanation: Heme iron (meat, poultry, fish) has higher bioavailability; non-heme iron (plants, cereals, legumes, fortified foods) lower. A: Reversed. B: Those supply non-heme iron. D: Heme iron is absorbed more easily. E: Those supply heme iron.

questions.stem: A vegetarian woman with iron deficiency asks how to take her oral iron. Which advice improves absorption?

options.E: Take it with a calcium tablet

questions.explanation: Iron is absorbed mainly in the duodenum and proximal jejunum; vitamin C increases absorption; phytates, tea, calcium and dairy reduce it. B: Dairy reduces absorption. C: Tea reduces absorption. D: Phytates reduce absorption. E: Calcium reduces absorption.

questions.stem: During which period may the effects of iron deficiency on the brain be irreversible, even without anemia?
questions.explanation: Effects of deficiency at 0–36 months may be irreversible, even without anemia. Iron deficiency also causes more severe infections (reduced bactericidal activity of macrophages). A: Not the window given. B: Not the window given. C: The window is 0–36 months. D: Not the window given.

questions.stem: Which figures describe daily iron traffic?

options.A: Gut absorbs about 25 mg; marrow uses 1–2 mg; macrophages recycle 1–2 mg
options.B: Gut absorbs 1–2 mg; marrow uses 25 mg; macrophages recycle 25 mg
options.C: Gut absorbs 1–2 g; marrow uses about 25 g; macrophages recycle about 25 g
options.D: Gut absorbs 3–4 mg; marrow uses about 2 g; macrophages recycle 1–2 mg
options.E: Gut absorbs 1–2 mg; marrow uses about 25 mg; kidneys excrete about 25 mg

questions.explanation: Gut absorbs 1–2 mg/day; transferrin carries only 3–4 mg at a time; marrow uses about 25 mg/day; red cells hold about 2 g; spleen macrophages recycle about 25 mg/day. Total body iron 3–4 g. A: Reversed. C: The units are milligrams. D: Not the figures given. E: The body has very limited excretion.

questions.stem: Why is the gut the control point of iron balance?

options.A: The kidneys excrete excess iron when ferritin is high
options.C: Iron is lost freely in bile
options.E: The body recycles iron but has very limited excretion

questions.explanation: The body recycles iron but has very limited excretion; balance is set at the gut by hepcidin. Daily losses of 1–2 mg are replaced by absorbing the same amount. A: There is very limited excretion. B: Not a mechanism. C: Not as stated. D: They recycle about 25 mg/day.

questions.stem: Which cell is matched with its role in iron handling?

options.C: Enterocyte: senses iron and makes hepcidin

questions.explanation: Enterocyte absorbs iron and releases it through ferroportin; hepatocyte stores iron and makes hepcidin; macrophage recycles iron from old red cells and releases it through ferroportin; erythroblast takes iron in through transferrin receptor 1. A: Enterocytes and macrophages export through ferroportin. B: That is the enterocyte. C: That is the hepatocyte. E: ERFE comes from red cell precursors.

questions.stem: During a severe infection, a patient's plasma iron falls within hours as hepcidin rises. What happens at the cell surface?

options.A: Transferrin receptor 1 is shed from cells
options.E: Iron is excreted in the urine

questions.explanation: Ferroportin is the only iron export door; hepcidin binds it, it is internalized and destroyed, iron is trapped and blood iron falls. A: Not the mechanism. B: Not the mechanism. D: Not the mechanism. E: Excretion is very limited.

questions.stem: Which signal lowers hepcidin?
questions.explanation: Hepcidin falls with iron deficiency, anemia or hypoxia, and active erythropoiesis (ERFE); it rises with iron overload and inflammation (IL-6). A: Raises hepcidin. C: Raise hepcidin. D: Raises hepcidin. E: Raises hepcidin.

questions.stem: A patient with active rheumatoid arthritis takes oral iron without benefit. Which mediator explains the poor absorption?
questions.explanation: Inflammation and infection (IL-6) raise hepcidin: the door locks, iron is trapped in stores, blood iron falls, and oral iron is poorly absorbed. B: That would increase absorption. C: Not the mechanism. D: Not the mechanism. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Which test best separates iron deficiency anemia from anemia of inflammation?
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency: hepcidin low, stores empty, ferritin low. Inflammation: hepcidin high, stores full but locked, ferritin normal or high. TSAT is low in both. A: Low in both. B: Can be low in both. C: Low in both. D: Low in both.

questions.stem: Which cause of iron deficiency acts by decreasing absorption?
questions.explanation: Decreased absorption: celiac disease, IBD, atrophic gastritis, H. pylori, bariatric surgery, rarely IRIDA. Decreased intake: exclusive breastfeeding without iron after 4–6 months, excess cow's milk. Blood loss: heavy menses, GI loss, frequent sampling. Increased demand: growth, pregnancy, prematurity. A: Blood loss. B: Increased demand. D: Decreased intake. E: Blood loss.

questions.stem: Above which daily volume does milk intake put a toddler at high risk of iron deficiency (AAP 2026)?
questions.explanation: High risk: cow's milk before 12 months, or more than 24 oz (about 700 mL) a day of cow's or plant milk; also preterm infants, exclusively breastfed infants without iron after 4–6 months, menstruating adolescents, low-iron diets, pregnancy. A: The limit given is 24 oz. C: The limit given is 24 oz. D: The limit given is 24 oz. E: Cow's milk is allowed after 12 months within the limit.

questions.stem: Which sign comes from iron deficiency itself and can appear before anemia?
questions.explanation: Signs from iron deficiency itself: glossitis, angular stomatitis, koilonychia, hair loss, pica including pagophagia, poor memory, restless legs. A: From anemia. B: From anemia. C: From anemia. E: From anemia.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has a transferrin saturation of 12%, RDW 18% and ferritin 8 ng/mL. Which other result is expected?
questions.explanation: Iron deficiency: ferritin low, TSAT < 20%, soluble transferrin receptor raised, MCV and MCH low, RDW > 16%, Ret-He low; microcytic hypochromic smear with pencil forms. B: Ret-He is low. C: TIBC rises in iron deficiency. D: MCH is low. E: Pencil forms are expected.

questions.stem: What is typical on the blood smear and platelet count in iron deficiency anemia?

options.A: Microcytic hypochromic cells and target cells; platelets often low
options.B: Macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils; platelets normal
options.D: Basophilic stippling and schistocytes; platelets low
options.E: Microcytic hypochromic cells and pencil forms; platelets often raised

questions.explanation: Smear: microcytic, hypochromic cells, pencil forms; platelets often raised. A: Platelets are often raised, and pencil forms are typical. B: That is megaloblastic anemia. C: That suggests hemolysis. D: Not iron deficiency.

questions.stem: A woman with active lupus and heavy menses has a ferritin of 60 ng/mL. Why can iron deficiency not be excluded?

options.E: Ferritin is cleared by the kidney

questions.explanation: Ferritin is the best single marker of body iron, but as an acute-phase reactant a normal value cannot exclude deficiency in inflammation; check CRP. A: It rises. C: It reflects stores. D: Not the reason. E: Not the reason.

questions.stem: How should blood for transferrin saturation be drawn?

options.A: After a meal rich in iron
options.B: After an oral iron dose, to test absorption
options.C: At any time; TSAT does not vary
