questions.explanation: TSAT reflects iron available for red cell production; draw fasting and avoid iron or multivitamins beforehand. A: It should be fasting. B: Iron should be avoided beforehand. C: Fasting is advised. E: Not advised.

questions.stem: In an adult with inflammation, below which ferritin value is iron deficiency suspected (2026)?
questions.explanation: 2026 thresholds: children ≤ 20; adolescents and adults ≤ 30 (up to ≤ 50 with symptoms or risk); adults with inflammation < 100 or TSAT < 20%. A: Children without inflammation. B: Adults without inflammation. D: Adults with symptoms or risk factors. E: Not a threshold given.

questions.stem: When does AAP 2026 advise screening for iron deficiency?

options.A: Breastfed infants at 9–12 months; adolescents by age 14
options.B: Breastfed infants at 15–18 months; adolescents at menarche
options.C: Each infant at 12 months by hemoglobin; no adolescent screening
options.D: Breastfed infants at 9–12 months; adolescents after age 18
options.E: Preterm infants at 2 weeks; adolescents yearly from age 10

questions.explanation: Screen breastfed infants at 9–12 months; formula-fed infants at 15–18 months after the switch to cow's or plant milk; children with risk factors yearly to age 4; adolescents with CBC + ferritin ≥1 year after menarche or by age 14, yearly if heavy bleeding. B: 15–18 months is for formula-fed infants. C: That is the replaced 2010 approach. D: Screening is by age 14. E: Preterm infants start iron by 2 weeks; that is not screening.

questions.stem: Which tests does AAP 2026 use for screening?

options.C: Ferritin by itself without a CBC
options.E: CBC and blood lead in each child

questions.explanation: Test CBC and ferritin (not Hb alone) and add CRP, because inflammation makes ferritin falsely reassuring. This replaces the 2010 report and Hb-only screening at 12 months. A: That is the replaced approach. C: CBC and ferritin are both used. D: Not the screening tests. E: Lead is tested with iron deficiency or pica.

questions.stem: Which preventive measure is matched with the right group?

options.A: Exclusively breastfed infants: iron 3 mg/kg/day from birth
options.B: Preterm infants: iron 1 mg/kg/day from 6 months
options.D: Exclusively breastfed infants: iron 1 mg/kg/day by 4 months
options.E: Toddlers: cow's milk from 6 months, unlimited

questions.explanation: Prevention: delayed cord clamping; preterm infants 2–3 mg/kg/day by 2 weeks; exclusively breastfed infants 1 mg/kg/day by 4 months; no cow's milk before 1 year and limit to about 24 oz a day; iron-rich foods; iron for pregnant women. A: The dose is 1 mg/kg/day by 4 months. B: Preterm infants get 2–3 mg/kg/day by 2 weeks. C: Delayed cord clamping is advised. E: No cow's milk before 1 year; limit to about 24 oz.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old weighing 14 kg has iron deficiency anemia. What daily dose of elemental iron is given?
questions.explanation: Treatment: 3 mg/kg elemental iron once daily for children (3 × 14 = 42 mg); 65 mg once daily for adolescents; at least 3 months, then recheck ferritin. A: That is 1 mg/kg (prevention). B: Adolescent dose. D: 2 mg/kg. E: Too high.

questions.stem: How should oral iron be taken, and what should families be warned about?

options.A: With milk to protect the stomach; dark stools and tooth staining
options.B: With tea or calcium; constipation exclusively
options.C: On an empty stomach, away from vitamin C; red urine
options.D: With meals rich in phytates; no warnings needed
options.E: On an empty stomach, away from milk; dark stools and tooth staining

questions.explanation: Give on an empty stomach, away from milk and dairy; vitamin C helps. Warn about dark stools and tooth staining. Every-other-day dosing may be better tolerated (AGA 2024). A: Milk reduces absorption. B: These reduce absorption. C: Vitamin C helps. D: Phytates reduce absorption.

questions.stem: A toddler with iron deficiency has Hb 6.5 g/dL and is clinically stable. How should she be managed?

options.D: Observation without iron until ferritin returns

questions.explanation: Severe anemia (Hb ≤7 g/dL): clinically stable, oral iron with close follow-up; unstable, slow transfusion in small aliquots. Follow up at 1 and 3 months. B: Transfusion is for unstable patients, slowly in small aliquots. C: In children IV iron is for specialist referral in specific indications. D: Treatment is indicated. E: That is for unstable patients.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with iron deficiency anemia starts oral iron. When do reticulocytes peak?
questions.explanation: Days 1–3: feels better. Days 5–10: reticulocyte peak. 2–4 weeks: Hb rises (≥ 2 g/dL at 1 month in severe anemia). ≥ 3 months: stores refilled. A: The child feels better. B: Hemoglobin rises. D: Stores refilled. E: Too late.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin has not risen after 1 month of oral iron. What should be checked first?
questions.explanation: No rise in Hb after 1 month: check the dose and adherence first (non-adherence or underdosing is the most common cause), then ongoing loss, malabsorption, inflammation or another diagnosis. A: Wrong diagnosis is considered after adherence. C: Malabsorption is considered after adherence. D: IRIDA is rare. E: Not the first step.

questions.stem: Each of the following is an indication for intravenous iron EXCEPT:

options.B: No response to an adequate oral trial
options.C: Celiac disease or bariatric surgery blocking absorption
options.D: Ongoing losses that oral iron cannot match
options.E: Mild anemia in a patient who has not yet tried oral iron

questions.explanation: IV iron: oral intolerance, no response to an adequate trial, conditions blocking absorption (IBD, celiac disease, bariatric surgery), ongoing losses. Children are referred to a specialist. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed.

questions.stem: Which practical point about intravenous iron is correct?

options.C: Products needing many small infusions are preferred
options.E: Newer oral formulations outperform ferrous sulfate

questions.explanation: Prefer products that replace the deficit in 1–2 infusions; most reactions are infusion reactions, not true anaphylaxis; ferric carboxymaltose can cause hypophosphatemia (check phosphate with repeated doses); no oral formulation beats ferrous sulfate, which is the cheapest. A: The risk named is hypophosphatemia. B: Most are infusion reactions. C: Prefer replacement in 1–2 infusions. E: No oral formulation beats ferrous sulfate.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl with heavy menstrual flow has Hb 9 g/dL and MCV 70 fL. Besides confirming iron deficiency with ferritin and CRP, which condition should be screened for?
questions.explanation: Case 1: iron deficiency anemia from heavy menstrual bleeding; screen for von Willebrand disease; confirm ferritin <30 ng/mL with CRP; treat with 65 mg elemental iron daily and manage the bleeding. B: A cause of malabsorption, not suggested by heavy bleeding. C: Suggested by pica in toddlers. D: Not suggested by the bleeding history. E: The lecture names von Willebrand disease.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old on large amounts of cow's milk craves ice, soil and paper. Hb is 8.0 g/dL and MCV 65 fL. Which additional test is needed?
questions.explanation: A toddler with pica: check blood lead; lead and iron deficiency often coexist (iron deficiency increases lead absorption). A: Not the priority here. B: Not indicated. C: Macrocytic anemia. D: Not indicated.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old has Hb 11.8 g/dL, MCV 64 fL, RBC count 6.0 million/µL, RDW 13% and normal ferritin. What is the next test?
questions.explanation: Thalassemia trait: high RBC count, normal RDW, normal ferritin, Mentzer index < 13; confirm by Hb electrophoresis or HPLC. A: Iron is not given without proven deficiency. C: Not needed. D: Not suggested. E: Microcytosis, not macrocytosis.

questions.stem: A routine blood count shows an MCV of 68 fL in a well child, and no other tests have been done. The parents ask for iron. What is the best response?

options.C: Give a single IV iron dose
options.E: Start iron and recheck in a year

questions.explanation: Never give iron for microcytosis without confirming iron deficiency (thalassemia trait is the main mimic). A: Not without confirming deficiency. B: Not without confirming deficiency. C: Not without confirming deficiency. E: Not without confirming deficiency.

questions.stem: Which new thalassemia treatment is matched with its nature?

options.A: Mitapivat: CRISPR gene editing; exa-cel: oral pyruvate kinase activator
options.B: Luspatercept: oral iron chelator; mitapivat: erythroid maturation agent
options.C: Mitapivat: oral pyruvate kinase activator; exa-cel: CRISPR gene editing
options.D: Exa-cel: erythroid maturation agent; luspatercept: gene editing
options.E: Mitapivat: hepcidin mimetic; exa-cel: stem cell donor graft

questions.explanation: Exa-cel (Casgevy, FDA Jan 2024): CRISPR gene editing for transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia, age ≥12, about 9 in 10 transfusion-independent. Mitapivat (FDA Dec 2025): first oral drug, a pyruvate kinase activator. Luspatercept: erythroid maturation agent. A: Reversed. B: Luspatercept is the erythroid maturation agent. D: Reversed. E: Not their nature.

questions.stem: Which anemia is the second most common worldwide?
questions.explanation: Anemia of inflammation is the second most common anemia (CKD, cancer, autoimmune disease, chronic infection): normocytic early, microcytic late. B: Not second. C: Not second. D: Rare. E: Not second.

questions.stem: A man with active Crohn's disease has anemia of inflammation, but his ferritin is 60 ng/mL and transferrin saturation 15%. What is the best treatment for the iron problem?
questions.explanation: Anemia of inflammation: treat the disease; look for coexisting iron deficiency (ferritin < 100 or TSAT < 20%); IV iron if deficient (IBD blocks absorption). A: Poorly absorbed with high hepcidin. B: Iron deficiency first. C: Not indicated. E: Coexisting deficiency needs iron.

questions.stem: Each of the following is a listed source of lead EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Sources: old lead-based paint and dust, kohl, traditional remedies, industry, auto-repair work, contaminated spices and foods. A: Listed. B: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: Why are children under 3 most vulnerable to lead, and how does iron status matter?

options.A: Low gastric acid and a mature blood–brain barrier; iron deficiency reduces lead absorption
options.B: Hand-to-mouth activity, immature blood–brain barrier; iron deficiency increases lead absorption
options.C: Higher lead excretion; iron overload increases lead absorption
options.D: Hand-to-mouth activity; iron status has no effect

questions.explanation: Children under 3: more hand-to-mouth activity, immature blood–brain barrier, and iron deficiency increases lead absorption. A: Reversed on both counts. C: Not as stated. D: Iron deficiency increases absorption. E: Not as stated.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old living in an old house has abdominal pain, constipation, irritability and developmental delay. Which additional sign of high lead levels does the lecture list?
questions.explanation: Lead poisoning is often silent; features include abdominal pain, constipation, irritability, developmental delay, encephalopathy at high levels, and wrist and foot drop. Effects are often irreversible. B: A sign of iron deficiency. C: Not listed. D: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old has abdominal pain, constipation and a microcytic anemia with low reticulocytes. Which smear finding points to lead poisoning?
questions.explanation: Lead: microcytic anemia, low reticulocytes, coarse basophilic stippling, high blood lead and ZPP, metaphyseal lead lines. A: Iron deficiency. B: Thalassemia. C: Not lead. D: Microangiopathy.

questions.stem: What is the CDC blood lead reference value, and who should be tested?

options.A: 3.5 µg/dL; children with iron deficiency or pica
options.C: 3.5 µg/dL; adults with occupational exposure exclusively

questions.explanation: There is no safe blood lead level. CDC reference value: 3.5 µg/dL. Test children with iron deficiency or pica. B: The reference value is 3.5, and testing is broader. C: Children with iron deficiency or pica are tested. D: The value is 3.5. E: The value is 3.5.

questions.stem: Which enzymes of heme synthesis does lead inhibit?
questions.explanation: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase (the slide also lists ALA synthase); ALA accumulates, iron cannot be inserted, so zinc is: zinc protoporphyrin rises (iron deficiency raises it too). A: Not listed. B: Not listed. C: These degrade heme. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Inhibition of which enzyme by lead causes basophilic stippling?
questions.explanation: Lead inhibits pyrimidine 5′-nucleotidase, so ribosomal RNA aggregates: basophilic stippling. A: Blocks iron insertion. C: Blocks heme synthesis. D: Mutated in X-linked sideroblastic anemia. E: Degrades heme.

questions.stem: What was the source of the 2023–2024 US lead outbreak described in the lecture?
questions.explanation: 566 cases were linked to cinnamon applesauce pouches (cinnamon adulterated with lead chromate, food fraud); 96% were children under 6. FDA action levels for lead in baby food are 10–20 ppb (Jan 2025). A: Not the source of that outbreak. B: Not the source of that outbreak. D: Not the source of that outbreak. E: Not the source of that outbreak.

questions.stem: Which inherited form of sideroblastic anemia responds to pyridoxine?
questions.explanation: Inherited: X-linked ALAS2 mutations (milder, pyridoxine-responsive) and autosomal recessive SLC25A38 (severe, transfusion-dependent). A: Severe and transfusion-dependent. B: That is IRIDA. C: That is Chediak-Higashi syndrome. D: Not listed.

questions.stem: A patient treated for tuberculosis develops microcytic anemia with high ferritin and high TSAT. Which drug is a listed cause, and which other acquired causes are named?

options.A: Rifampin; also copper excess and zinc deficiency
options.B: Isoniazid; also copper deficiency and zinc excess
options.C: Isoniazid; also iron deficiency and thalassemia

questions.explanation: Acquired sideroblastic anemia: drugs and toxins (isoniazid, linezolid, alcohol, lead), myelodysplastic syndrome, copper deficiency, zinc excess. A: The metal imbalances are reversed and rifampin is not listed. C: Those are separate microcytic anemias. D: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: A marrow stained with Prussian blue shows erythroblasts with iron-laden mitochondria ringing the nucleus. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Sideroblastic anemia: high ferritin and TSAT; ring sideroblasts (iron-laden mitochondria around the nucleus, Prussian blue). Treat: remove the agent, pyridoxine, transfusion and chelation if needed. A: Absent marrow iron. B: Not ring sideroblasts. C: Iron in macrophages. E: Not ring sideroblasts.

lectures.title: Hemolytic anemias
lectures.covers: How to recognise hemolysis and classify it (intrinsic or extrinsic, intravascular or extravascular), then the extrinsic causes: autoimmune, transfusion-related, newborn, drug-induced, microangiopathic (DIC, TTP, HUS) and their treatments.

items.p: A red cell lives about 120 days and must squeeze through vessels narrower than itself.

ul: About 40% more surface area than its volume needs, and a low internal viscosity
Membrane: a lipid bilayer tied by vertical links (ankyrin, band 3, 4.1R) to a spectrin skeleton
No nucleus, no mitochondria. About 90% of glucose goes to glycolysis (ATP, NADH, 2,3-BPG), about 10% to the pentose phosphate pathway (G6PD, NADPH, glutathione)
With age, macrophages trim the membrane; the cell turns spherical and is removed

table: Oxidant damage, Heinz bodies, bite cells

items.p: Hemolysis is a shortened red cell lifespan. It becomes hemolytic anemia only when destruction outpaces what the marrow can replace.
The marrow can raise output several-fold. In compensated hemolysis hemoglobin stays normal and the only clues are reticulocytosis, jaundice or gallstones.
Macrophages break old red cells down. Globin becomes amino acids, iron returns on transferrin, and the heme ring becomes biliverdin, then unconjugated bilirubin carried on albumin.
The liver conjugates it; gut bacteria make urobilinogen; stercobilin colours stool and urobilin colours urine.
In hemolysis every step speeds up: high indirect bilirubin, more urobilinogen, pigment gallstones.
High indirect bilirubin has three causes: hemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis, and a conjugation defect (Gilbert, Crigler–Najjar).

ul: Intrinsic: the red cell is faulty (membrane, enzyme, hemoglobin). Usually inherited. PNH is the exception: acquired, yet intrinsic.
Extrinsic: a healthy cell is attacked from outside (immune, mechanical, infectious, toxic). Usually acquired.

table: ABO reaction, G6PD crisis, TTP, PNH, malaria

items.p: Extravascular is the more common site. Both show reticulocytosis, high indirect bilirubin and high LDH.

summary.h: Proving it and finding the cause

items.p: Step 1, is it hemolysis?

ul: Reticulocytes up (can be low early, or with parvovirus B19)
Indirect bilirubin and LDH up
Haptoglobin down: the most sensitive marker
Urine hemosiderin: chronic intravascular hemolysis
Usually normocytic; MCV may be slightly high because reticulocytes are large

items.p: Step 2, what is the cause?

ul: Direct antiglobulin test (DAT): IgG or C3 already on the patient's red cells. The indirect test looks for antibodies in the serum (screening, crossmatch).
Smear, coagulation tests (DIC), ADAMTS13 under 10% (TTP)
EMA binding and high MCHC (hereditary spherocytosis); G6PD assay after the acute episode; flow cytometry for PNH

items.p: Rule out bleeding in any sudden anemia. Other cytopenias, big nodes or recurrent infections point to a systemic disease.

table: Mycoplasma, EBV; clonal B cells in older adults

ul: Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria: a child after a viral illness, biphasic IgG (Donath–Landsteiner), intravascular, self-limited
Evans syndrome: AIHA plus immune thrombocytopenia; screen for immune dysregulation
Warm AIHA: corticosteroids first; rituximab early if severe; splenectomy less often. Nipocalimab blocks FcRn and lowers IgG.
Cold agglutinin disease: avoid cold, warm fluids and blood, rituximab. Sutimlimab blocks C1s.

Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (within 24 hours): ABO mismatch, usually a clerical error. The recipient's IgM fixes complement: fever, flank pain, hypotension, red urine, DIC. Stop the transfusion and keep the line open.
Delayed reaction (3–14 days): a returning alloantibody (Kidd, Rh); extravascular; falling hemoglobin and a newly positive DAT
Hyperhemolysis in sickle cell disease: the patient's own cells are destroyed too; avoid further transfusion
Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn: maternal IgG crosses the placenta. Rh(D) is the most severe, ABO the most common and usually mild. Prevent with anti-D immunoglobulin.

Drugs: ceftriaxone, piperacillin, cefotetan (immune complex, intravascular, severe); high-dose penicillin (adsorbed on the cell, extravascular); methyldopa, fludarabine, checkpoint inhibitors (true autoantibody). Stop the drug.

items.p: Schistocytes plus low platelets mean a thrombotic microangiopathy until proven otherwise.

table: Treat the cause; platelets, plasma, cryoprecipitate

ul: TTP: without ADAMTS13, ultra-large von Willebrand multimers form platelet-rich clots. Untreated mortality is about 90%, so treat on suspicion.
Typical HUS (about 90%): a young child 5–10 days after bloody diarrhea (E. coli O157:H7). No antimotility drugs.
Atypical HUS: uncontrolled alternative complement pathway. Eculizumab or ravulizumab, after meningococcal vaccination.
Other mechanical or toxic causes: prosthetic valves, march hemoglobinuria, malaria, Clostridium perfringens, venoms, burns, spur cells in severe liver disease
Treat the cause
Folic acid in chronic hemolysis
Transfuse carefully (restrictive threshold: hemoglobin under 7 g/dL in most stable adults, 8 with heart disease)
Splenectomy for selected cases, after vaccination; cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallstones
Newer drugs: mitapivat for pyruvate kinase deficiency; iptacopan, danicopan and crovalimab for PNH; recombinant ADAMTS13 for congenital TTP

cards.a: Hemolysis: shortened red cell lifespan. Hemolytic anemia: destruction outpaces the marrow's ability to compensate.
The marrow keeps up, so there is no anemia: only reticulocytosis, jaundice or gallstones

cards.q: How does the red cell use glucose?
cards.a: About 90% anaerobic glycolysis (ATP, NADH, 2,3-BPG); about 10% pentose phosphate pathway (G6PD, NADPH, glutathione)

cards.q: G6PD deficiency versus pyruvate kinase deficiency: mechanism and site
cards.a: G6PD: oxidant stress, Heinz bodies, bite cells, mostly intravascular. PK: low ATP, rigid cells, removed by the spleen.
Heme → biliverdin → unconjugated bilirubin (on albumin) → conjugated in the liver → urobilinogen (gut) → stercobilin (stool), urobilin (urine)

cards.q: Three causes of a high indirect bilirubin
cards.a: Hemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis, conjugation defects (Gilbert, Crigler–Najjar)
Intrinsic: defective red cell (membrane, enzyme, hemoglobin), usually inherited. Extrinsic: outside factor (immune, mechanical, infectious, toxic), usually acquired.

cards.q: Which intrinsic hemolytic anemia is acquired?
cards.a: Paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (complement-sensitive red cells)
Free plasma hemoglobin, hemoglobinuria, later hemosiderinuria, very low or absent haptoglobin, schistocytes
Milder and chronic, no free hemoglobin, spherocytes; warm AIHA, hereditary spherocytosis

cards.q: Laboratory signs shared by both sites of hemolysis
cards.a: Reticulocytosis, high indirect bilirubin, high LDH, raised urobilinogen

cards.q: Most sensitive laboratory marker of hemolysis
cards.a: Low haptoglobin

cards.q: When can reticulocytes be low despite hemolysis?
cards.a: Early on, or with marrow suppression such as parvovirus B19
Direct: IgG or C3 already on the patient's red cells. Indirect: antibodies in the patient's serum (antibody screen, crossmatch).
IgG at 37 °C; DAT IgG with or without C3; extravascular in the spleen with spherocytes

cards.q: Cold agglutinin disease: antibody, DAT, clue
cards.a: IgM below about 30 °C fixing complement; DAT C3 only; acrocyanosis; Mycoplasma or EBV if secondary
Child after a viral infection; biphasic IgG (Donath–Landsteiner); acute intravascular hemolysis, self-limited
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia plus immune thrombocytopenia; screen for immune dysregulation

cards.q: First-line treatment of warm AIHA, and the targeted drugs for warm and cold disease
cards.a: Corticosteroids (rituximab early if severe). Nipocalimab (FcRn blocker) for warm AIHA; sutimlimab (C1s blocker) for cold agglutinin disease.

cards.q: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction: cause and first step
cards.a: ABO incompatibility, usually a clerical error (recipient IgM, complement, intravascular). Stop the transfusion, keep the IV line.
3–14 days later; anamnestic alloantibody (Kidd, Rh); extravascular; falling hemoglobin, jaundice, new positive DAT

cards.q: Hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn: most severe, most common, prevention
cards.a: Rh(D) most severe; ABO most common and usually mild; anti-D immunoglobulin for Rh(D)-negative mothers

cards.q: Drug-induced immune hemolysis: three mechanisms with a drug each
cards.a: Drug-dependent antibody (ceftriaxone), drug adsorption (high-dose penicillin), autoantibody (methyldopa)
Thrombotic microangiopathy until proven otherwise
DIC: prolonged PT/aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer. TTP: ADAMTS13 < 10%, normal coagulation, brain and heart. HUS: kidney injury, normal coagulation.
ADAMTS13 < 10% leaves ultra-large vWF multimers, giving platelet-rich microthrombi. Plasma exchange, corticosteroids, rituximab, caplacizumab; start on suspicion.
Typical (about 90%): Shiga toxin, 5–10 days after bloody diarrhea, supportive, no antimotility drugs. Atypical: alternative complement pathway; C5 inhibitor after meningococcal vaccine.

cards.q: General treatment principles in chronic hemolysis
cards.a: Treat the cause, folic acid, careful transfusion, splenectomy for selected cases after vaccination, cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallstones

questions.stem: Which structural feature lets a red cell pass vessels narrower than itself?

options.A: About 40% excess surface area for its volume
options.B: About 40% excess volume for its surface area
options.C: A rigid membrane that resists shear
options.D: High cytoplasmic viscosity from a high MCHC

questions.explanation: The red cell has about 40% excess surface area (about 140 µm² for about 90 fL), low cytoplasmic viscosity (regulated MCHC) and a strong yet deformable membrane. B: The excess is in surface area. C: It must be deformable. D: Viscosity is kept low. E: Red cells have no mitochondria.

questions.stem: Why are old red cells removed from the circulation?

options.B: The nucleus reappears and stiffens the cell
options.C: ATP rises and the pump overworks
options.D: Complement lyses cells older than 120 days
options.E: Trimmed membrane makes them more spherical

questions.explanation: With age, macrophages trim small pieces of membrane, so old cells become more spherical and are removed. A: That is oxidant damage. B: Mature red cells have no nucleus. C: Not the mechanism given. D: Not the mechanism given.

questions.stem: Which statement about the red cell membrane is correct?

options.A: An actin network is tied to the bilayer by horizontal links such as hemoglobin
options.B: A spectrin network is tied to the bilayer by vertical links such as ankyrin and band 3
options.C: A spectrin network floats free of the bilayer
options.D: The bilayer is three-dimensional and rigid

questions.explanation: The lipid bilayer is anchored to the skeleton by vertical links (ankyrin and 4.1R complexes, band 3). The cytoskeleton is a 2-dimensional elastic network of spectrin; defects cause spherocytosis and elliptocytosis. A: Not as described. C: It is anchored by vertical links. D: The skeleton is a 2-dimensional elastic network. E: Ankyrin is a linking protein.

questions.stem: How does the red cell use glucose?

options.A: About 10% in glycolysis; about 90% in the pentose phosphate pathway
options.B: About 50% in glycolysis; about 50% in the Krebs cycle
options.C: About 90% in glycolysis; about 10% in the pentose phosphate pathway

questions.explanation: About 90% of glucose goes through anaerobic glycolysis (ATP, NADH, 2,3-BPG, lactate) and about 10% through the pentose phosphate pathway (G6PD, NADPH, reduced glutathione). A: Reversed. B: There are no mitochondria. D: There are no mitochondria. E: Not as described.

questions.stem: Which product of glycolysis is matched with its function in the red cell?
questions.explanation: ATP powers the Na⁺/K⁺ pump and keeps the cell flexible; NADH keeps heme iron as Fe²⁺ (no methemoglobin); 2,3-BPG helps hemoglobin release O₂; NADPH from the pentose phosphate pathway gives reduced glutathione. A: That is NADH. B: That is ATP. C: That is NADPH and reduced glutathione. E: Lactate leaves the cell.

questions.stem: A child has chronic hemolysis. His red cells make too little ATP, become rigid, and are removed by the spleen. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: PK deficiency: too little ATP, rigid cells removed by the spleen (extravascular). G6PD deficiency: oxidant stress, Heinz bodies, bite cells, mostly intravascular. A: Oxidant stress, Heinz bodies, mostly intravascular. B: Oxidant defense. C: Methemoglobin reduction. D: Basophilic stippling.

questions.stem: When does hemolysis become hemolytic anemia?

options.A: When the red cell lifespan falls below 120 days

questions.explanation: Hemolysis is a shortened red cell lifespan from premature destruction; hemolytic anemia occurs when destruction outpaces the marrow's ability to increase production. A: That defines hemolysis. B: That shows marrow response. C: That is a sign of hemolysis. E: That is a marker, not the definition.

questions.stem: A patient has reticulocytosis, mild jaundice and gallstones but a normal hemoglobin. Which term applies?
questions.explanation: Compensated hemolysis: the marrow can raise output several-fold, so hemolysis may cause no anemia, only reticulocytosis, jaundice or gallstones. B: Hemoglobin is normal. C: Reticulocytes would not be raised. D: Reticulocytes would be low. E: Not the picture.

questions.stem: Which sequence describes the breakdown of the heme ring?

options.A: Unconjugated bilirubin, biliverdin, conjugation in the gut, urobilinogen in the liver
options.B: Biliverdin, unconjugated bilirubin on albumin, conjugation in the liver, urobilinogen in the gut
options.C: Biliverdin, conjugated bilirubin on albumin, deconjugation in the liver, stercobilin in urine
options.E: Biliverdin, urobilin in the spleen, bilirubin in the gut

questions.explanation: In macrophages, globin goes to amino acids, iron to transferrin, and the heme ring to biliverdin then unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin carried on albumin. The liver conjugates it; gut bacteria make urobilinogen; stercobilin colours stool and urobilin urine. A: Biliverdin comes first and conjugation is hepatic. C: Albumin carries unconjugated bilirubin; stercobilin is in stool. D: Not the order. E: Not the order.

questions.stem: Which type of gallstone is a consequence of chronic hemolysis?
questions.explanation: In hemolysis every step speeds up: high indirect bilirubin (jaundice), more urobilinogen in stool and urine, and pigment gallstones. A: Not the type linked to hemolysis. B: Those are renal. D: Those are renal. E: Not the type linked to hemolysis.

questions.stem: Which cause of hemolysis is extrinsic?
questions.explanation: Intrinsic: defective red cells (membrane, enzyme, hemoglobin), usually inherited; PNH is acquired intrinsic. Extrinsic: immune, mechanical, infectious, toxic, usually acquired. A: Intrinsic membrane defect. B: Intrinsic enzyme defect. C: Intrinsic hemoglobin defect. D: Acquired, but intrinsic.

questions.stem: Which site of hemolysis is the most common?
questions.explanation: Extravascular hemolysis (macrophages of the spleen, liver and marrow) is the most common. A: Less common. B: That is ineffective erythropoiesis. D: Not a site of hemolysis. E: Not as stated.

questions.stem: What makes paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria unusual among intrinsic hemolytic anemias?

options.A: It is an inherited extrinsic disorder
options.B: It is the sole enzyme defect
options.D: It is an acquired intrinsic disorder

questions.explanation: Acquired intrinsic: PNH, with complement-sensitive red cells. Other intrinsic causes are usually inherited. A: It is acquired and intrinsic. B: It involves complement-sensitive red cells. C: Not stated; it is a red cell defect. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: Which causes are classed as macroangiopathic hemolysis?

options.C: Warm and cold red cell autoantibodies

questions.explanation: Extrinsic: immune (autoimmune, alloimmune, drug-induced), microangiopathic (DIC, TTP, HUS), macroangiopathic (prosthetic heart valves, hypersplenism), other (infections, toxins, venoms, liver and renal disease, burns). A: These are microangiopathic. C: These are immune. D: These are infections. E: Listed under other causes.

questions.stem: Which findings point to intravascular and not extravascular hemolysis?
questions.explanation: Intravascular: often acute and severe, raised free plasma Hb, hemoglobinuria (red–brown), hemosiderinuria later, haptoglobin very low or absent, schistocytes. Extravascular: mild to moderate, often chronic, no free Hb, haptoglobin normal or low, spherocytes. B: These suggest extravascular hemolysis. C: Seen in both. D: Seen in both. E: Seen in both.

questions.stem: Which disorder typically causes intravascular hemolysis?
questions.explanation: Intravascular: ABO reaction, G6PD crisis, TTP, PNH, malaria. Extravascular: warm AIHA, hereditary spherocytosis. A: Extravascular. B: Extravascular. C: Extravascular. E: Extravascular.

questions.stem: Which finding occurs in both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis?
questions.explanation: Both sites: reticulocytosis, high indirect bilirubin, high LDH, urobilinogen. A: Intravascular. B: Intravascular, later. D: Intravascular. E: Extravascular.

questions.stem: What must be ruled out in any acute-onset anemia before attributing it to hemolysis?
questions.explanation: Rule out bleeding in any acute-onset anemia. Hemolysis presents with anemia symptoms plus jaundice, dark or red urine, fever, chills, abdominal and back pain, splenomegaly and gallstones. A: Not acute in onset. C: Not acute in onset. D: Not acute in onset. E: Not acute in onset.

questions.stem: A child with autoimmune hemolytic anemia also has immune thrombocytopenia. What is this combination called, and what should be looked for?
questions.explanation: Evans syndrome is autoimmune hemolytic anemia plus immune thrombocytopenia; screen for immune dysregulation. Other red flags: recurrent infections, family history, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, masses. A: The search is for immune dysregulation. B: HELLP occurs in pregnancy. C: That is a microangiopathy with kidney injury. D: That is a separate entity.

questions.stem: Which marker is the most sensitive for hemolysis?
questions.explanation: Haptoglobin binds free Hb and is the most sensitive marker (low in hemolysis). Also: high reticulocytes, indirect bilirubin and LDH; plasma or urine Hb in intravascular hemolysis; urine hemosiderin in chronic intravascular hemolysis. B: Released from red cells but not the most sensitive. C: From heme breakdown but not the most sensitive. D: Marks chronic intravascular hemolysis. E: Reflects large reticulocytes.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic hemolysis and normal B12 and folate has an MCV of 104 fL. What explains it?
questions.explanation: Anemia in hemolysis is usually normocytic; the MCV can be slightly high because reticulocytes are large. A: Spherocytes are small. B: Not the mechanism. C: Not the mechanism. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Why may the MCV be slightly high in hemolytic anemia?

options.E: Schistocytes are counted as large cells

questions.explanation: Anemia is usually normocytic; MCV may be slightly high because reticulocytes are large. B: Not the reason given. C: Spherocytes are small. D: Not the reason given. E: They are fragments.

questions.stem: Which test is matched with the diagnosis it points to?
questions.explanation: DAT: immune hemolysis. Coagulation tests, fibrinogen, D-dimer: DIC. ADAMTS13 <10%: TTP. Hb electrophoresis: sickle cell disease, thalassemia. EMA binding, osmotic fragility, high MCHC: hereditary spherocytosis. Enzyme assays: G6PD, PK. Flow cytometry: PNH. A: PNH uses its own flow cytometry. B: It points to TTP when below 10%. C: It points to immune hemolysis. D: They point to DIC.

questions.stem: When should G6PD activity be measured in a patient with acute hemolysis?

options.B: Before any transfusion, within the hour

questions.explanation: G6PD and PK enzyme assays detect enzyme deficiencies; test G6PD after the acute episode. A: The assay is advised after the episode. B: Not the advice given. D: Not the advice given. E: Not the advice given.

questions.stem: Before a transfusion, the blood bank screens the patient's serum for red cell antibodies. Which test is used?
questions.explanation: DAT detects IgG or C3 on the patient's red cells; IAT detects antibodies in serum, used for antibody screening and crossmatch. A: Detects antibody already on the red cells. C: HS. D: HS. E: TTP.

questions.stem: A woman with lupus has anemia, spherocytes on the smear and a DAT positive for IgG. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Warm AIHA: most common; IgG at 37 °C; DAT IgG ± C3; extravascular, spleen makes spherocytes; secondary causes include lupus. B: DAT C3 only; IgM. C: Biphasic IgG in children. D: DAT negative. E: Schistocytes.

questions.stem: An elderly man has bluish fingers and ears in cold weather with anemia. The DAT is positive for C3 only. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.explanation: Cold agglutinins: IgM binds below about 30 °C and fixes complement; DAT C3 only; mainly extravascular (liver); acrocyanosis on cold exposure. Primary CAD is a clonal B-cell disorder in older adults; secondary to Mycoplasma or EBV. A: DAT would show IgG. B: That occurs in children after viral infection. D: DAT is not the diagnostic test there. E: Not the picture.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old has sudden red urine and anemia a week after a viral illness. A biphasic IgG antibody is found. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.explanation: Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria: biphasic IgG (Donath–Landsteiner) after viral infection in children; acute intravascular hemolysis, usually self-limited. A: That involves IgM, typically in older adults. C: Not a biphasic antibody. D: That follows bloody diarrhea with kidney injury. E: That is AIHA with immune thrombocytopenia.

questions.stem: What is first-line treatment of warm AIHA?
questions.explanation: Warm AIHA: corticosteroids first line; add rituximab early in severe disease; then immunosuppressants; splenectomy less often. A: Used less often, later. B: That is for TTP. C: That is for cold agglutinin disease. E: That is a C5 inhibitor for PNH and atypical HUS.

questions.stem: How is cold agglutinin disease managed?

options.A: Corticosteroids first line; splenectomy if refractory

questions.explanation: Cold agglutinin disease: avoid cold; warm IV fluids and blood; rituximab-based therapy targets the B-cell clone. A: That is the warm AIHA approach. B: That is for TTP. C: That prevents Rh(D) sensitization. D: Not sufficient.

questions.stem: Which new drug is matched with its target and disease?

options.A: Nipocalimab: C1s, cold agglutinin disease; sutimlimab: FcRn, warm AIHA
options.B: Nipocalimab: C5, PNH; sutimlimab: factor B, PNH
options.C: Sutimlimab: vWF, TTP; nipocalimab: ADAMTS13, TTP
options.D: Nipocalimab: FcRn, warm AIHA; sutimlimab: C1s, cold agglutinin disease
options.E: Nipocalimab: CD20, warm AIHA; sutimlimab: CD20, cold agglutinin disease

questions.explanation: Nipocalimab (FDA Aug 2026): first approved drug for warm AIHA; blocks FcRn, lowering IgG autoantibodies. Sutimlimab (FDA Feb 2022): first for cold agglutinin disease; blocks C1s of the classical pathway. A: Reversed. B: Not their targets. C: Not their targets. E: CD20 is the rituximab target.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes into a red cell transfusion a woman develops fever, chills, dyspnea, red urine and a blood pressure of 55/40 mm Hg. What is the usual cause of this reaction?

options.E: ABO mismatch from a clerical error

questions.explanation: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (within 24 h): usually ABO-incompatible blood from a clerical or identification error; recipient IgM anti-A/B fix complement, causing intravascular hemolysis with fever, chills, flank pain, dyspnea, hypotension, red urine, DIC and renal failure. A: That causes a delayed reaction at 3–14 days. B: Not the cause given. C: Not an acute reaction. D: That causes HDFN.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes into a red cell transfusion, a woman develops fever, flank pain, red urine and hypotension. What is the first step?

options.E: Finish the unit, then send samples

questions.explanation: AHTR: stop the transfusion, keep the IV line, recheck identity, fluids for urine output, notify the blood bank. A: Stop it. C: Stop it. D: Stop it. E: Stop it.

questions.stem: A chronically transfused patient develops jaundice, a falling hemoglobin and a newly positive DAT 8 days after transfusion. Which mechanism fits?

options.A: Anamnestic rise of an alloantibody such as Kidd

questions.explanation: Delayed reaction (3–14 days): anamnestic rise of an alloantibody (e.g. Kidd, Rh) from earlier transfusion or pregnancy; extravascular; falling Hb, jaundice, new positive DAT. Prevent with extended antigen matching. B: That causes an acute reaction. C: Not the mechanism. D: That is PNH. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: What is hyperhemolysis in sickle cell disease, and how is it handled?

options.A: Donor red cells are destroyed, patient cells spared; transfuse more
options.B: Patient red cells sickle in the spleen; exchange transfusion
options.C: Donor and patient red cells are destroyed; avoid further transfusion
options.D: Donor platelets are destroyed; give platelets
options.E: Complement lyses donor cells; give eculizumab first line

questions.explanation: Hyperhemolysis in sickle cell disease: donor and patient cells are destroyed; avoid further transfusion if possible. A: Patient cells are destroyed too, and transfusion is avoided. B: That is sequestration. D: Not hyperhemolysis. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: In hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, which antigen system causes the most severe disease?
questions.explanation: HDFN: maternal IgG crosses the placenta; Rh(D) most severe, ABO most common (usually mild); prevent with anti-D immunoglobulin for Rh(D)-negative mothers. B: The most common, usually mild. C: Not stated. D: Not stated. E: Not stated.

questions.stem: How does a positive DAT change the management of neonatal jaundice (AAP 2022)?

options.A: It is reassuring, so phototherapy thresholds are higher
options.C: A neurotoxicity risk: lower phototherapy thresholds
options.E: It has no effect on thresholds

questions.explanation: Isoimmune hemolysis (positive DAT) is a neurotoxicity risk factor: lower phototherapy thresholds, and escalate care as bilirubin nears the exchange level. A: It lowers the thresholds. B: Care is escalated as bilirubin nears the exchange level. D: Phototherapy is used earlier. E: It lowers them.

questions.stem: A child given ceftriaxone develops sudden, severe intravascular hemolysis. What is the mechanism?
questions.explanation: Drug-dependent antibodies (immune complex): intravascular, severe (ceftriaxone in children, piperacillin, cefotetan). Drug adsorption: high-dose penicillin, extravascular. A: High-dose penicillin; extravascular. B: Not ceftriaxone. C: G6PD deficiency. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: What does the combination of schistocytes and thrombocytopenia mean?
questions.explanation: Schistocytes + thrombocytopenia = thrombotic microangiopathy until proven otherwise (DIC, TTP, HUS; also malignant hypertension, HELLP, drugs, transplant-associated TMA). A: That gives spherocytes and a positive DAT. B: That gives spherocytes. C: Not the meaning. D: Not the meaning.

questions.stem: A septic patient has schistocytes, low platelets, a prolonged PT and low fibrinogen. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: DIC: prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer. TTP and HUS: coagulation tests normal. A: Coagulation tests normal. C: Coagulation tests normal. D: Coagulation tests normal. E: No coagulopathy.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman has high fever, hypotension, coma, diffuse ecchymoses and low hemoglobin, white cells and platelets. The smear shows schistocytes. Which results and treatment are expected?

options.A: Normal fibrinogen and ADAMTS13 below 10%; plasma exchange
options.D: Normal PT and high haptoglobin; observation
options.E: Low fibrinogen, high D-dimer; treat the sepsis

questions.explanation: Severe infection with DIC: systemic activation of coagulation and fibrinolysis. Diagnosis: low platelets, prolonged PT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, schistocytes (ISTH score). Treat the cause; support with platelets, plasma or cryoprecipitate for bleeding. A: That is TTP. B: That is warm AIHA. C: That is STEC-HUS. D: Not DIC.

questions.stem: What does ADAMTS13 normally cleave?
questions.explanation: ADAMTS13 cleaves ultra-large vWF multimers; activity < 10% gives platelet-rich microthrombi (TTP); untreated mortality ~90%. B: Not its substrate. C: Not its substrate. D: Not its substrate. E: Not its substrate.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has fever, confusion, schistocytes, platelets of 15 × 10⁹/L and normal coagulation tests. The ADAMTS13 result is pending. What is the next step?
questions.explanation: TTP: plasma exchange, corticosteroids plus rituximab, caplacizumab; start on clinical suspicion (PLASMIC score). A: Start on clinical suspicion. B: Not the treatment. C: Not the treatment. E: Atypical HUS.

questions.stem: For which condition was recombinant ADAMTS13 approved in 2023?
questions.explanation: Recombinant ADAMTS13 (Adzynma, FDA Nov 2023): first enzyme replacement for congenital TTP, in adults and children. A: Standard treatment there is plasma exchange with immunosuppression. B: That is treated with C5 inhibitors. D: Not its indication. E: That is sutimlimab.

questions.stem: Which triad defines hemolytic uremic syndrome?

options.A: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and fever with coma
options.B: Microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury
options.C: Hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes and low platelets
options.D: Immune hemolysis, immune thrombocytopenia and neutropenia
options.E: Anemia, prolonged PT and low fibrinogen

questions.explanation: HUS triad: microangiopathic hemolytic anemia + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury. A: That suggests TTP. C: That is HELLP. D: That is not HUS. E: That suggests DIC.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old develops pallor and oliguria one week after bloody diarrhea. Which drugs should be avoided?
questions.explanation: STEC-HUS (~90%): young children, 5–10 days after bloody diarrhea; supportive care; avoid antimotility drugs. B: Supportive care. C: Not listed. D: Supportive care. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: A child with atypical HUS is to start a C5 inhibitor. Which vaccine is given first?
questions.explanation: Atypical HUS: uncontrolled alternative complement pathway; eculizumab or ravulizumab; vaccinate against meningococcus first. A: Not the required one. C: Not the required one. D: Not the required one. E: Not the required one.

questions.stem: Which cause of extrinsic hemolysis is matched with its category?

options.A: March hemoglobinuria: infection; spur cells: burns
options.D: March hemoglobinuria: mechanical; spur cells: liver

questions.explanation: Mechanical: prosthetic valves, march hemoglobinuria, ECMO. Infections: malaria, Clostridium perfringens, babesiosis. Toxins and venoms: snake and spider venom, copper, arsenic. Burns. Liver disease: spur cells (acanthocytes). Hypersplenism. A: Not as listed. B: Reversed. C: Reversed. E: Reversed.

questions.stem: A child with hereditary spherocytosis becomes suddenly more anemic with a very low reticulocyte count after a viral illness. Which complication is this?
questions.explanation: After a viral illness: paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria, or parvovirus B19 aplastic crisis in chronic hemolysis. Newborns: HDFN, G6PD deficiency and hereditary spherocytosis can cause severe jaundice. A: That gives acute intravascular hemolysis in a previously well child. B: That follows transfusion in sickle cell disease. C: That adds immune thrombocytopenia. D: Not the complication named.

questions.stem: Which supplement is given in chronic hemolysis?
questions.explanation: Treatment principles: treat the cause, folic acid in chronic hemolysis, immunosuppression for immune causes, careful transfusion, chelation, splenectomy for selected cases (vaccinate first). A: Not routine; risk of overload. B: Not routine. D: Not relevant. E: Not relevant.

questions.stem: What red cell transfusion threshold does AABB 2023 give for most hospitalized, stable adults?

options.A: A liberal threshold of Hb below 10 g/dL
options.B: A restrictive threshold of Hb below 5 g/dL
options.C: Hb below 8 g/dL for each patient
options.E: A restrictive threshold of Hb below 7 g/dL

questions.explanation: AABB 2023: restrictive threshold Hb <7 g/dL for most hospitalized, stable adults; 8 g/dL with cardiovascular disease or orthopedic surgery; always weigh symptoms. A: The threshold is restrictive. B: Not the value given. C: 8 g/dL applies with cardiovascular disease or orthopedic surgery. D: Not the guidance given.

questions.stem: Which targeted therapy is matched with its target in PNH?
questions.explanation: PNH: iptacopan (factor B, oral), danicopan (factor D, oral add-on), crovalimab (C5, subcutaneous); earlier standards eculizumab and ravulizumab (C5). Mitapivat: pyruvate kinase activator for PK deficiency and thalassemia. A: That is danicopan. C: That is crovalimab, eculizumab or ravulizumab. D: That is iptacopan. E: Mitapivat is a pyruvate kinase activator.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old woman has pallor, dark urine and icteric sclerae with a high indirect bilirubin. Besides hemolysis, which causes of high indirect bilirubin does the lecture list?

options.B: Biliary obstruction and acute viral hepatitis

questions.explanation: High indirect bilirubin: hemolysis, ineffective erythropoiesis, Gilbert or Crigler–Najjar. Her most likely diagnosis is hemolytic anemia; next tests: reticulocytes, LDH, haptoglobin, smear, DAT. B: These raise direct bilirubin. C: These raise direct bilirubin. D: Not listed. E: That raises direct bilirubin.

questions.stem: Besides DIC, TTP and HUS, which conditions are listed as causes of microangiopathic hemolysis?

options.B: Warm AIHA and cold agglutinin disease

questions.explanation: Other microangiopathic causes: malignant hypertension, HELLP, drugs (e.g. calcineurin inhibitors), transplant-associated TMA. A: These are macroangiopathic causes. B: These are immune causes. D: These are enzyme defects. E: These are membrane defects.

questions.stem: Two days after starting an oxidant drug, a man has dark urine; a supravital stain shows Heinz bodies and the smear shows bite cells. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: G6PD deficiency: oxidant stress, Heinz bodies, bite cells, mostly intravascular hemolysis. A: Rigid cells, extravascular. B: Glycolysis. C: Basophilic stippling. E: Methemoglobinemia.

lectures.title: Normocytic and macrocytic anemias
lectures.covers: The reticulocyte-and-MCV approach to anemia, then the normocytic causes (chronic disease, kidney disease, pure red cell aplasia) and the macrocytic causes (B12 and folate deficiency, myelodysplasia, alcohol and liver disease, hypothyroidism).

items.p: Anemia is a low red cell mass or hemoglobin: more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex. Age, sex, Tanner stage, altitude and heredity shift the normal value.
The number is judged against need. A hemoglobin of 7.5 g/dL is normal in a 2-month-old premature infant; 14 g/dL is anemic in a 2-year-old with cyanotic heart disease.
WHO 2024 cutoff for men: hemoglobin under 13 g/dL or hematocrit under 39%.

items.note: The slide gives the WHO cutoff for women as under 11.9 g/dL (hematocrit under 36%). WHO states 12.0 g/dL for non-pregnant women; worth checking with the lecturer.

items.p: Think of mechanism (production, loss, breakdown) and cell size together. Three things matter most: the history, the CBC with reticulocytes, and the smear.

ul: Reticulocytes raised: hemolysis or blood loss
Reticulocytes normal or low: sort by MCV

table: Reticulocytes (absolute count over 100,000 = bleeding or hemolysis)

items.p: A high RDW makes iron deficiency likely.
Red cells mature in the marrow for about 3 weeks and live 120 days. As anemia deepens, reticulocytes leave the marrow earlier and circulate longer (1 day at a hematocrit of 45%, 2.5 days at 15%).
Also called anemia of inflammation. Seen with infection, inflammation and cancer, and also obesity, diabetes, heart failure, critical illness and severe trauma.
IL-6 makes the liver release hepcidin. Hepcidin blocks ferroportin in the duodenum and in macrophages, so plasma iron falls within hours.
Hemoglobin 7–11 g/dL, normal MCV (microcytic when long-standing), low reticulocytes.
MCV, serum iron and transferrin saturation can be low in both.

ul: Treat the underlying disease. The aim is fewer symptoms, not a normal hemoglobin.
No iron unless the patient is truly iron deficient
Transfuse for hemoglobin under 7 g/dL, or for symptoms at any level

items.p: Normochromic, normocytic, low reticulocytes. The smear is usually normal; echinocytes appear only in rare severe cases.

ul: Less erythropoietin
Hepcidin not cleared by the kidney
Uremic inhibitors of the marrow, and shorter red cell survival
Marrow fibrosis in some, from secondary hyperparathyroidism

items.p: On dialysis, correct iron deficiency first; then an ESA is first line. Target hemoglobin 10–11.5 g/dL.
Only the red cell line fails: severe anemia, reticulocytes often under 10,000/µL, and almost no erythroid precursors in the marrow.

ul: Congenital: Diamond–Blackfan anemia (usually a high MCV)
Acquired: thymoma, CLL and other blood cancers, solid tumors, HIV, EBV, hepatitis, autoimmune disease, antibodies to EPO after ESA treatment, myelodysplasia
Parvovirus B19 kills red cell precursors directly. Giant proerythroblasts in the marrow suggest it but do not prove it: confirm by PCR.

items.p: Other normocytic causes: heart failure, thyroid, cortisol or androgen deficiency, pregnancy, cancer, marrow infiltration (myelophthisic), old age, HIV.

table: B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, inherited metabolic disease
Reticulocytosis, marrow aplasia, liver disease, drugs and toxins

items.p: In megaloblastic anemia DNA synthesis is impaired, so the nucleus matures more slowly than the cytoplasm: large cells with large, immature nuclei.
Smear: hypersegmented neutrophils, large red cells of varying size, sometimes pancytopenia.
Drugs that cause macrocytosis through DNA metabolism include zidovudine, hydroxyurea, methotrexate, azathioprine and capecitabine.

items.note: Slide 27 lists hypothyroidism under "lipid abnormalities" while slide 44 calls its mechanism unclear.

items.p: B12 needs intrinsic factor from the stomach and a receptor in the ileum.

table: Strict vegetarians, breastfed infants of vegan mothers
Ileal resection, Crohn's disease, Imerslund–Gräsbeck syndrome

items.p: Metformin lowers B12.

Anemia, glossitis, poor appetite and gut symptoms occur in both deficiencies. Numbness and reduced cognition occur only with B12. Cobalamin under 200 pg/mL; homocysteine and methylmalonic acid both high.

ul: Severe or symptomatic anemia, neurologic symptoms, malabsorption or poor adherence: intramuscular 1000 mcg, 1–3 times weekly or daily in week 1, then weekly for up to 4 weeks
Otherwise: weekly injections for 4 weeks then monthly cyanocobalamin (or hydroxocobalamin every 3 months), or 1000–2000 mcg by mouth daily
Marrow recovers within hours; reticulocytes peak at 1 week; counts and MCV normal in 2–3 months; nerves take up to a year

items.note: Slide 33 lists "nitric oxide" as a cause; the standard cause is nitrous oxide. The amounts "1 mg" and "100 mg" beside "Nutritional" are not explained on the slide.

items.p: Develops faster than B12 deficiency.

ul: Poor diet, alcohol
Higher demand: hemolytic anemia, pregnancy, hemodialysis, dermatitis
Malabsorption: celiac disease, tropical sprue, jejunal resection, severe Crohn's disease, short gut, sulfasalazine
Methotrexate

items.p: The blood picture is the same as in B12 deficiency, with no nerve damage. Deficiency in pregnancy raises the risk of neural tube defects.
Serum folate under 2 ng/mL fits deficiency; over 4 makes it unlikely. Homocysteine is high; methylmalonic acid is normal.

ul: Myelodysplastic syndrome: ineffective erythropoiesis in a hypercellular marrow. Anemia is the most common cytopenia; enlarged organs and nodes are uncommon. Smear: dysplastic nucleated red cells, basophilic stippling, bilobed pseudo-Pelger–Huët neutrophils.

Alcohol and liver disease: anemia in 75% of chronic liver disease. Alcohol suppresses red cell production and EPO and reduces B12 absorption; varices bleed; a congested spleen and altered membrane lipids (spur cells) shorten survival.
Hypothyroidism: mechanism unclear; may resolve with thyroxine.

cards.a: Low red cell mass or hemoglobin: Hb more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex (judged against oxygen demand)

cards.q: Three critical aspects in working up anemia
cards.a: Clinical history, CBC with reticulocyte count, peripheral smear

cards.q: Anemia with a raised reticulocyte count means...
cards.a: Hemolysis or blood loss

cards.q: MCV groups and the first test in each
cards.a: < 80 microcytic: ferritin. 80–100 normocytic: reticulocytes. > 100 macrocytic: megaloblastic or not.

cards.q: Normocytic anemia with low reticulocytes: causes
cards.a: Anemia of chronic disease, kidney disease, early iron deficiency, primary marrow disorders (leukemia, MDS, MPN), drugs

cards.q: Mechanism of anemia of chronic disease
cards.a: IL-6 raises hepcidin, which blocks ferroportin in duodenum and macrophages; plasma iron falls within hours

cards.q: Iron deficiency versus anemia of chronic disease: the discriminating tests
cards.a: Iron deficiency: high TIBC, low ferritin, high RDW, hepcidin suppressed. Chronic disease: normal or low TIBC, normal or high ferritin, normal RDW, hepcidin high.

cards.q: Goal of treatment in anemia of chronic disease
cards.a: Treat the underlying condition to relieve symptoms, not to normalize hemoglobin; iron only if truly deficient

cards.q: When to transfuse in anemia of chronic disease (lecturer's note)
cards.a: Hemoglobin under 7 g/dL, or a symptomatic patient at any hemoglobin

cards.q: Anemia of chronic kidney disease: mechanisms
cards.a: Low EPO, reduced renal clearance of hepcidin, uremic inhibitors, shortened red cell survival

cards.q: Anemia of CKD on dialysis: order of treatment and target
cards.a: Correct iron deficiency first, then ESA first line; target hemoglobin 10–11.5 g/dL
Severe anemia with very low reticulocytes (often < 10,000/µL) and virtual absence of erythroid precursors in the marrow
Diamond–Blackfan anemia (usually high MCV)

cards.q: Marrow clue to parvovirus B19 and how to confirm
cards.a: Giant proerythroblasts (suggestive, not diagnostic); confirm with parvovirus B19 PCR
Megaloblastic usually > 110 fL; non-megaloblastic usually < 105 fL
Impaired DNA synthesis: the nucleus matures more slowly than the cytoplasm (nuclear-cytoplasmic dyssynchrony)
Hypersegmented neutrophils, macrocytes of varying size, sometimes pancytopenia
Diet (vegans), no intrinsic factor (gastrectomy, pernicious anemia), competition (fish tapeworm, blind loop), no receptor (ileal resection, Crohn's, Imerslund–Gräsbeck)

cards.q: What separates B12 deficiency from folate deficiency clinically?
cards.a: Neuropsychological symptoms (numbness, reduced cognition) occur only in B12 deficiency

cards.q: Homocysteine and methylmalonic acid in B12 versus folate deficiency
cards.a: B12: both high. Folate: homocysteine high, methylmalonic acid normal.

cards.q: When is B12 given by intensive intramuscular course?
cards.a: Symptomatic or severe anemia, neuropsychiatric symptoms, possible malabsorption, concern about adherence
Marrow within hours; reticulocyte peak at 1 week; counts and MCV normal in 2–3 months; nerves up to a year
Poor diet and alcohol; increased demand (hemolysis, pregnancy, hemodialysis); malabsorption (celiac, tropical sprue, jejunal resection); methotrexate, sulfasalazine
> 4 ng/mL: deficiency unlikely. < 2 ng/mL: consistent with deficiency.

cards.q: Folate deficiency in pregnancy raises the risk of...
cards.a: Fetal neural tube defects
Ineffective erythropoiesis with a hypercellular marrow; anemia is the most common cytopenia; pseudo-Pelger–Huët neutrophils, basophilic stippling

cards.q: Why is anemia common in alcoholic liver disease?
cards.a: Suppressed red cell and EPO production, reduced B12 absorption, variceal bleeding, congestive splenomegaly and altered membrane lipids (spur cells)

questions.stem: Which definition of anemia does the lecture give?

options.A: Hemoglobin more than 1 SD below the mean for age and sex
options.B: Hemoglobin more than 2 SD below the mean for weight and height
options.C: Hemoglobin below the 10th percentile for age and sex
options.D: Hematocrit more than 3 SD below the adult mean for sex
options.E: Hemoglobin more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex

questions.explanation: Anemia is a reduction in red cell mass (hematocrit) or hemoglobin, with hemoglobin more than 2 SD below the mean for age and sex. A: The cutoff is 2 SD. B: The reference is age and sex. C: Not the definition given. D: Not the definition given.

questions.stem: Which factor is NOT listed as affecting the normal hemoglobin value?
questions.explanation: The listed factors are age, sex, Tanner stage, altitude and heredity. A: Listed. B: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old with cyanotic heart disease has a hemoglobin of 14 g/dL. How does the lecture classify this child?

options.A: Normal: above the 2 SD cutoff for age and sex
options.B: Anemic: too low for the cellular oxygen demand
options.C: Polycythemic: above the mean for age and sex
options.D: Normal: values of a premature infant apply
options.E: Anemic: more than 2 SD below the mean for age

questions.explanation: Physiologically, anemia is a hemoglobin too low to meet cellular oxygen demands, so 14 g/dL is anemic in cyanotic heart disease. A: The physiologic definition applies here. C: The value is low for this child's needs. D: That is the other example on the slide. E: 14 g/dL is not below the statistical cutoff.

questions.stem: A hemoglobin of 7.5 g/dL in a 2-month-old premature infant is described as:
questions.explanation: The slide uses this example to show that the same number can be normal: 7.5 g/dL is normal for a 2-month-old premature infant. A: Not the point of the example. B: Not the point of the example. C: Not the point of the example. E: The value is normal at this age.

questions.stem: Which cutoffs define anemia in males in the WHO 2024 definition shown?
questions.explanation: WHO 2024: males hemoglobin < 13 g/dL (130 g/L) or hematocrit < 39%. B: 13.5 g/dL is the EBPG and K-DOQI figure for adult men. C: 36% is the hematocrit given for females. D: Not the male values. E: Not the WHO values.

questions.stem: Which is NOT among the listed clinical manifestations of anemia?
questions.explanation: Listed: tiredness, weakness, shortness of breath, pale or yellowish skin, palpitations, dizziness, chest pain, cold hands and feet, headaches. A: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: How are the two classic approaches to anemia (mechanism and red cell size) meant to be used?

options.A: Size first, with mechanism decided after a marrow biopsy
options.B: Mechanism first, with size reserved for microcytic cases
options.C: Both considered together, with the MCV and reticulocyte count
options.D: Size in adults and mechanism in children under 12 years
options.E: Ferritin first, with size and mechanism in unclear cases

questions.explanation: In reality production/loss/breakdown and MCV are considered simultaneously; the lecturer's note says to look at the MCV and the reticulocyte count. A: Both are considered at once. B: Both are considered at once. D: No such split is made. E: Ferritin comes after the MCV in microcytosis.

questions.stem: Which pairing of index and meaning is correct?

options.A: MCH: average hemoglobin concentration per red cell
options.B: MCHC: average hemoglobin content of each red cell
options.C: RDW: variation in hemoglobin content of red cells
options.D: MCHC: average hemoglobin concentration per red cell
options.E: MCV: variation in the volume of the red cells

questions.explanation: MCV is the average volume, MCH the average hemoglobin content, MCHC the average hemoglobin concentration, and RDW the variation in red cell size. A: MCH is the average hemoglobin content. B: That is the MCH. C: RDW measures variation in size. E: MCV is the average volume.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer's handwritten note, a raised RDW in an anemic patient makes which diagnosis more likely?
questions.explanation: The note reads: high RDW = high chance of iron deficiency. The table on slide 17 also gives a raised RDW in iron deficiency and a normal RDW in anemia of chronic disease. A: Not what the note says. B: The RDW is normal in the comparison table. C: Not what the note says. D: Not what the note says.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old woman has a hemoglobin of 9 g/dL. In the ASH approach to anemia, which result is the first branch point?
questions.explanation: The algorithm starts with the reticulocyte count: normal or decreased → MCV; increased → hemolysis or blood loss. B: The second step when reticulocytes are not raised. C: For microcytic anemia. D: Essential, but not the first branch. E: Not a first step.

questions.stem: What are the three critical aspects in the approach to anemia?

options.A: Clinical history, CBC with reticulocytes, marrow biopsy
options.B: Clinical history, CBC with reticulocytes, peripheral smear
options.C: Clinical history, serum ferritin, peripheral blood smear
options.D: Family history, CBC with reticulocytes, electrophoresis
options.E: Physical examination, serum ferritin, marrow biopsy

questions.explanation: Three critical aspects: clinical history, CBC/reticulocytes and the peripheral smear. A: The third is the smear. C: The CBC with reticulocytes is the second. D: Not the three listed. E: Not the three listed.

questions.stem: In that algorithm, anemia with an increased reticulocyte count points to:
questions.explanation: An increased reticulocyte count means hemolysis (extrinsic or intrinsic to the red cell) or blood loss. A: Marrow invasion has a normal or low count. B: Renal disease has a normal or low count. C: B12 deficiency has a normal or low count. E: Thalassemia sits in the microcytic group.

questions.stem: Which condition is listed under normocytic anemia with a normal or decreased reticulocyte count?
questions.explanation: Normocytic: TEC (transient erythroblastopenia of childhood), early ACD, renal and thyroid disease, marrow invasion. A: Listed under microcytic. B: Listed under macrocytic. D: Listed under macrocytic. E: Listed under microcytic.

questions.stem: Where does anemia of chronic disease appear in the MCV groups of the algorithm?
questions.explanation: ACD (early) is in the normocytic group and ACD (late) in the microcytic group. B: Reversed. C: It does not become macrocytic. D: Not as shown. E: It is listed as microcytic when late.

questions.stem: Which order of erythroid maturation is correct?

options.A: Proerythroblast, nuclear extrusion, erythroblast stages, reticulocyte
options.B: Erythroblast stages, proerythroblast, nuclear extrusion, reticulocyte
options.C: Proerythroblast, erythroblast stages, reticulocyte, nuclear extrusion
options.D: Reticulocyte, proerythroblast, erythroblast stages, nuclear extrusion
options.E: Proerythroblast, erythroblast stages, nuclear extrusion, reticulocyte

questions.explanation: MEP, proerythroblast, early, intermediate and late erythroblast, nuclear extrusion, reticulocyte, red cell. A: The nucleus is extruded after the late erythroblast. B: The proerythroblast comes first. C: The reticulocyte has no nucleus. D: The reticulocyte is the last step before the red cell.

questions.stem: The lecturer's note on the step from reticulocyte to red cell names what the reticulocyte still carries. What is it?
questions.explanation: The handwritten note marks ribosomes at the reticulocyte-to-red-cell step. B: Extruded before the reticulocyte stage. C: Denatured hemoglobin, not a normal content. D: Not what the note says. E: Not what the note says.

questions.stem: Which timing of red cell production and survival is shown?

options.A: About 1 week in the marrow; 120 days in blood
options.B: About 3 weeks in the marrow; 90 days in blood
options.C: About 3 days in the marrow; 120 days in blood
options.D: About 3 weeks in the marrow; 120 days in blood
options.E: About 3 months in the marrow; 3 weeks in blood

questions.explanation: Maturation of erythroid precursors and iron uptake take about 3 weeks in the marrow; the red cell lifespan is 120 days. A: Maturation takes about 3 weeks. B: The lifespan is 120 days. C: Maturation takes about 3 weeks. E: Not as shown.

questions.stem: As the hematocrit falls from 45% to 15%, what happens to red cell precursors?

options.A: Marrow time lengthens and blood reticulocyte time shortens
options.B: Marrow time shortens and blood reticulocyte time lengthens
options.C: Marrow time and blood reticulocyte time both shorten
options.D: Marrow time and blood reticulocyte time both lengthen
options.E: Marrow time is unchanged and blood reticulocyte time lengthens

questions.explanation: With worsening anemia, normoblasts and reticulocytes spend less time in the marrow (3.5 to 1.5 days) and reticulocytes more time in blood (1.0 to 2.5 days). A: Reversed. C: Blood time lengthens. D: Marrow time shortens. E: Marrow time falls from 3.5 to 1.5 days.

questions.stem: At a hematocrit of 15%, how long do reticulocytes spend in the blood?
questions.explanation: Blood reticulocyte time rises from 1.0 day (hematocrit 45%) to 2.5 days (hematocrit 15%). A: The value at a hematocrit of 45%. B: The value at a hematocrit of 35% (and the marrow time at 15%). D: The value at a hematocrit of 25%. E: The marrow time at a hematocrit of 45%.

questions.stem: An anemic patient has a low reticulocyte count and an MCV of 72 fL. Which test comes next?
questions.explanation: Microcytic anemia (MCV < 80 fL): check ferritin; low ferritin = iron deficiency. A: For macrocytic anemia. B: Not the first test. C: For hemolysis. D: Not the first test.

questions.stem: Which is NOT among the causes of microcytic anemia with a normal or high ferritin?
questions.explanation: Normal or high ferritin: chronic disease, thalassemias, hemoglobinopathies, lead intoxication, sideroblastic anemia. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: A patient has a normocytic anemia with an absolute reticulocyte count of 180,000/µL. Which cause fits?
questions.explanation: Normocytic anemia with reticulocytes > 100,000/µL: bleeding or hemolysis. A: Low reticulocytes. B: Very low reticulocytes. C: Low reticulocytes. D: Low reticulocytes.

questions.stem: Which is given as an example of a primary bone marrow disorder causing normocytic anemia with low reticulocytes?
questions.explanation: Primary bone marrow disorders: leukemias, MDS, MPN; drugs are listed in the same box. A: An example of anemia of chronic disease. B: Listed with anemia of chronic disease. D: High reticulocytes. E: High reticulocytes.

questions.stem: Beyond the traditional infectious, inflammatory and neoplastic causes, the lecture links anemia of chronic disease to:

options.A: Obesity, diabetes, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, severe trauma
options.B: Obesity, diabetes, heart failure, critical illness, severe trauma
options.C: Alcohol use, diabetes, heart failure, critical illness, burns
options.D: Obesity, hypertension, heart failure, liver disease, trauma
options.E: Asthma, diabetes, heart failure, critical illness, older age

questions.explanation: ACD is also seen in obesity, diabetes mellitus, congestive heart failure, critical illness and severe trauma. A: Hypothyroidism and pregnancy are separate normocytic causes. C: Alcohol and burns are not listed. D: Hypertension and liver disease are not listed. E: Asthma and older age are not listed here.

questions.stem: Which picture is typical of anemia of chronic disease?

options.A: Hemoglobin 7 to 11 g/dL, normal MCV, low reticulocytes
options.B: Hemoglobin 7 to 11 g/dL, normal MCV, high reticulocytes
options.C: Hemoglobin 4 to 7 g/dL, normal MCV, low reticulocytes
options.D: Hemoglobin 7 to 11 g/dL, high MCV, low reticulocytes
options.E: Hemoglobin 11 to 13 g/dL, low MCV, low reticulocytes

questions.explanation: Hemoglobin ranges from 7 to 11 g/dL, with a normal MCV and a low reticulocyte count. B: The reticulocyte count is low. C: The range is 7 to 11 g/dL. D: The MCV is normal. E: The range is 7 to 11 g/dL.

questions.stem: In inflammation, IL-6 makes the liver release hepcidin. Which protein does hepcidin block?
questions.explanation: IL-6 raises liver hepcidin, which blocks ferroportin in the duodenum, iron-recycling macrophages and hepatocytes, so plasma iron falls. A: Not the target. B: Not the target named. C: Storage protein. E: Not the target.

questions.stem: How soon does hypoferremia develop in inflammation?
questions.explanation: Hypoferremia develops within the first few hours. B: It is faster. C: It is faster. D: It is faster. E: Stores are not empty in inflammation.

questions.stem: Besides interleukin-6, what raises hepcidin in the figures on inflammation and kidney disease?

options.A: Impaired liver function reducing hepcidin breakdown
options.D: Duodenal iron loading increasing hepcidin uptake
options.E: Impaired renal function reducing hepcidin clearance

questions.explanation: Impaired renal function reduces hepcidin clearance, so hepcidin accumulates. A: The liver makes hepcidin; clearance is renal. B: Not shown. C: Not shown. D: Not shown.

questions.stem: A woman with active rheumatoid arthritis has Hb 10 g/dL and MCV 78 fL. Which iron study result would point to coexisting iron deficiency rather than anemia of chronic inflammation alone?
questions.explanation: Transferrin (TIBC) is increased in iron deficiency and normal or decreased in anemia of chronic inflammation; MCV, iron and saturation can be low in both. A: Low in both. B: Low in both. D: Fits inflammation. E: Fits inflammation.

questions.stem: Which finding fits anemia of chronic inflammation rather than iron deficiency?
questions.explanation: Anemia of chronic inflammation: hepcidin increased, ferritin normal or increased, RDW normal. Iron deficiency: hepcidin suppressed, ferritin low, RDW increased. A: Iron deficiency. C: Iron deficiency. D: Iron deficiency. E: Iron deficiency.

questions.stem: What is the stated goal of managing anemia of chronic disease?

options.A: Treat the underlying condition and add oral iron until the hemoglobin is normal
options.B: Give an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent to reach a hemoglobin of 13 g/dL
options.C: Treat the underlying condition to reduce symptoms, not to normalize the hemoglobin
options.D: Transfuse red cells to keep the hemoglobin above 10 g/dL
options.E: Give intravenous iron to bring the ferritin above 500

questions.explanation: Primary treatment is directed at the underlying medical condition, to reduce symptoms and improve clinical outcomes, not to normalize the hemoglobin. A: Normalizing hemoglobin is not the goal. B: Normalizing hemoglobin is not the goal. D: Not the stated approach. E: Not the stated approach.

questions.stem: A woman with rheumatoid arthritis has anemia of chronic disease: Hb 9.8 g/dL, ferritin 300 ng/mL, no symptoms. What is done about iron?
questions.explanation: Do not give iron unless the patient is iron deficient; ESAs can be given; transfuse for Hb < 7 g/dL or a symptomatic patient. A: Not without iron deficiency. B: Not without iron deficiency. C: Not without iron deficiency. E: Not without iron deficiency.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with lymphoma has anemia of chronic disease. His hemoglobin is 8.2 g/dL, and he is short of breath at rest with chest pain on minimal effort. Ferritin is 420 ng/mL. What is the best plan?
questions.explanation: Transfuse if Hb < 7 g/dL, or if the patient is symptomatic regardless of the hemoglobin. B: Too slow for symptoms at rest. C: Not iron deficient. D: Symptoms justify transfusion. E: Symptoms need treatment now.

questions.stem: What does the peripheral film show in anemia of chronic kidney disease?

options.A: Often normal; schistocytes in rare severe cases
options.B: Often normal; echinocytes in rare severe cases
options.C: Often normal; spherocytes in rare severe cases
options.D: Usually abnormal, with spur cells in most cases
options.E: Usually abnormal, with target cells in most cases

questions.explanation: Anemia of CKD is normochromic and normocytic with low reticulocytes; the film is often normal, with echinocytes in rare patients with severe kidney failure. A: The cells named are echinocytes. C: The cells named are echinocytes. D: The film is often normal. E: The film is often normal.

questions.stem: Marrow fibrosis described in some patients with chronic kidney disease is related to:
questions.explanation: The marrow is usually normocellular; a hypocellular marrow with relative erythroid hypoplasia and fibrosis related to secondary hyperparathyroidism has been described. A: Causes the anemia, not the fibrosis. B: Shown as suppressing erythropoiesis. C: Not stated. D: Affects iron, not fibrosis.

questions.stem: The figure on chronic kidney disease shows each of the following contributing to anemia EXCEPT:

options.C: Uremic inhibitors acting on the marrow

questions.explanation: Shown: decreased EPO production, reduced renal clearance of hepcidin, uremic inhibitors and shortened red cell survival. Hepcidin reduces duodenal iron absorption. A: Shown. B: Shown. C: Shown. E: Shown.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman on hemodialysis has fatigue. Hb 8.6 g/dL, MCV 86 fL, low reticulocytes, ferritin 40 ng/mL, transferrin saturation 11%. What is the first step?
questions.explanation: On dialysis, treat absolute or functional iron deficiency first; once iron replete, ESAs are first line. A: Replace iron first. C: Not the first step. D: Not indicated. E: Not the first step.

questions.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease is started on an ESA. Which hemoglobin range is targeted?
questions.explanation: Target hemoglobin with ESAs in CKD: 10 to 11.5 g/dL. A: Too high. B: Too high. D: Too low. E: Too low.

questions.stem: A man has Hb 6 g/dL with a reticulocyte count of 5,000/µL; white cells and platelets are normal. What does the marrow most likely show?
questions.explanation: Pure red cell aplasia: severe anemia, reticulocytes often < 10,000/µL, virtual absence of erythroid precursors in the marrow. B: Megaloblastic anemia. C: Sideroblastic anemia. D: Not this picture. E: Expected with high reticulocytes.

questions.stem: In pure red cell aplasia the reticulocyte count is often below:
questions.explanation: The reticulocyte count is profoundly low, often below 10,000/µL. A: The figure is 10,000. B: The figure is 10,000. C: The figure is 10,000. D: The cutoff used in normocytic anemia.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old has severe anemia, very low reticulocytes and an MCV of 105 fL. White cells and platelets are normal. Which diagnosis fits?
questions.explanation: Congenital PRCA is Diamond–Blackfan anemia, usually with a high MCV. A: Microcytic. B: Microcytic. C: Not severe; not macrocytic. E: Needs an underlying hemolytic disease.

questions.stem: Each of the following is listed as a cause of secondary acquired pure red cell aplasia EXCEPT:

options.C: EPO antibodies after treatment with ESAs

questions.explanation: Listed: thymoma, hematologic malignancies (CLL, LGL leukemia, myeloma), solid tumors, infections (HIV, EBV, viral hepatitis), collagen vascular diseases, drugs (EPO antibodies with ESAs), ABO-incompatible marrow transplantation, parvovirus B19, MDS. Fish tapeworm causes B12 deficiency. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed.

questions.stem: How does parvovirus B19 cause pure red cell aplasia?

options.B: It blocks stem cell commitment to the erythroid line
options.C: It is directly cytotoxic to red cell precursors
options.D: It triggers immune attack after thymoma
