questions.explanation: Parvovirus B19 is directly cytotoxic to red blood cell precursors. A: Seen in patients treated with ESAs. B: The mechanism given for MDS. D: A different secondary cause. E: Not the mechanism given.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with HIV has hemoglobin 6.1 g/dL, reticulocytes 4,000/µL, and normal white cells and platelets. The marrow shows almost no erythroid precursors and a few giant proerythroblasts. What is the best next step?

options.B: CT of the chest for thymoma

questions.explanation: Giant proerythroblasts are strongly suggestive of parvovirus infection but not diagnostic, so PCR for parvovirus B19 is done. B: The marrow finding points to parvovirus first. C: The marrow is not megaloblastic. D: Reticulocytes are absent; this is not hemolysis. E: Would not identify the cause.

questions.stem: Which endocrine deficiencies are listed as causes of normocytic anemia?
questions.explanation: Endocrine disorders: thyroid hormone, cortisol and androgen deficiencies. A: Insulin and estrogens are not listed. C: Not the three listed. D: Parathyroid hormone is not listed. E: Aldosterone is not listed.

questions.stem: Which is NOT listed among the other causes of normocytic anemia?
questions.explanation: Other causes: heart failure, endocrine disorders, pregnancy, cancer, myelophthisic anemia, anemia in older patients, HIV infection. Folate deficiency is macrocytic. A: Listed. B: Listed. D: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: Above which MCV does a macrocytic anemia usually point to a megaloblastic cause?
questions.explanation: Macrocytic (MCV > 100) is not the same as megaloblastic: megaloblastic causes usually give MCV > 110 fL; others usually < 105 fL. A: The cut-off for macrocytosis. B: Normal range. C: Non-megaloblastic causes usually stay below this. D: Too high.

questions.stem: Which cause of macrocytosis is grouped with folate and B12 deficiency under defective DNA synthesis?
questions.explanation: Megaloblastic: folate deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency, inherited metabolic disease. Non-megaloblastic: hemolysis/reticulocytosis, marrow hypo/aplasia, liver disease, drugs/toxins. B: Non-megaloblastic. C: Non-megaloblastic. D: Non-megaloblastic. E: Listed on the non-megaloblastic side.

questions.stem: Each of these drugs is listed as causing macrocytosis through abnormal DNA metabolism EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Listed: antiretrovirals (zidovudine), azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine, capecitabine, cladribine, cytosine arabinoside, hydroxyurea, imatinib, sunitinib, methotrexate. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. E: Listed.

questions.stem: Which causes macrocytosis by a shift to immature or stressed red cells?
questions.explanation: Shift to immature or stressed red cells: reticulocytosis and the action of erythropoietin (skip macrocytes, stress erythrocytosis). A: Abnormal DNA metabolism. C: Abnormal DNA metabolism. D: A primary marrow disorder. E: A lipid abnormality.

questions.stem: In the table of mechanisms of macrocytosis, liver disease is placed under:
questions.explanation: Lipid abnormalities: liver disease (the table also puts hypothyroidism here). A: B12, folate and drugs. B: Reticulocytosis and erythropoietin. C: Aplastic anemia, MDS and others. E: Alcohol abuse and myeloma.

questions.stem: Which pair is listed under "mechanism unknown" in the table of macrocytosis?

options.B: Aplastic anemia and red cell aplasia

questions.explanation: Mechanism unknown: alcohol abuse, multiple myeloma and other plasma cell disorders. A: Liver disease is under lipid abnormalities. B: Primary marrow disorders. C: Shift to immature red cells. D: LGL leukemia is a primary marrow disorder.

questions.stem: What is the basic defect in megaloblastic anemia?
questions.explanation: A nutrient needed for DNA synthesis is lacking, so the nucleus lags behind the cytoplasm (nuclear-cytoplasmic dyssynchrony). B: Microcytic anemias. C: Not the defect. D: Not the basic defect. E: Anemia of inflammation.

questions.stem: A patient with a low vitamin B12 has an MCV of 120 fL. Which white cell change is expected on the smear?
questions.explanation: Megaloblastic smear: hypersegmented neutrophils, macrocytosis with variable red cells, occasionally pancytopenia. A: Infection. B: Infection. D: Acute myeloid leukemia. E: CLL.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old vegan has an MCV of 112 fL and numb feet. Which test result is expected?
questions.explanation: B12 is needed for methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA and homocysteine → methionine, so both MMA and homocysteine rise. In folate deficiency MMA is normal. A: Raised in B12 deficiency. C: Ineffective erythropoiesis raises LDH. D: Low before treatment. E: Not expected.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man had a total gastrectomy 6 years ago. He has numbness of both feet, poor concentration and an MCV of 118 fL. Which mechanism explains his deficiency?

options.A: Loss of the ileal receptor for the complex
options.B: Loss of jejunal surface for folate uptake
options.C: Competition for the vitamin by gut bacteria
options.D: Loss of intrinsic factor needed for ileal uptake
options.E: Lack of the plasma carrier transcobalamin II

questions.explanation: Gastrectomy and autoimmune gastritis cause intrinsic factor deficiency. Numbness and reduced cognition point to B12 rather than folate. A: The ileum is intact. B: Folate deficiency has no neurologic signs. C: That is the blind loop mechanism. E: A rare inherited cause.

questions.stem: Which groups have nutritional vitamin B12 deficiency?

options.A: Strict vegetarians and patients with hemolytic anemia
options.B: Malnourished adults and patients on hemodialysis
options.C: Pregnant women and patients with dermatitis
options.E: Strict vegetarians and breastfed infants of vegan mothers

questions.explanation: Nutritional B12 deficiency: strict vegetarians and breastfed infants of vegan mothers. A: Hemolysis raises folate demand. B: Listed for folate. C: Listed for folate. D: Not listed for B12.

questions.stem: How does pernicious anemia cause B12 deficiency?

options.A: Autoimmune gastritis with ileal receptor deficiency
options.B: Autoimmune gastritis with intrinsic factor loss
options.C: Autoimmune ileitis with intrinsic factor deficiency
options.D: Chronic gastritis with competition for B12

questions.explanation: "IF deficiency": gastrectomy and autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anemia). A: The receptor defect is a separate group. C: The disease is gastric. D: Competition is fish tapeworm or blind loop. E: Listed separately under other causes.

questions.stem: Which pair causes B12 deficiency by competition?

options.A: Fish tapeworm and intestinal blind loop

questions.explanation: Competition: fish tapeworm and intestinal blind loop. B: Ileal resection is a receptor deficiency. C: Gastrectomy is intrinsic factor deficiency. D: Tropical sprue is listed for folate. E: Autoimmune gastritis is intrinsic factor deficiency.

questions.stem: Which causes are grouped as "receptor deficiency"?

options.B: Ileal resection, autoimmune gastritis, transcobalamin II deficiency
options.C: Ileal resection, Crohn's disease, Imerslund–Gräsbeck syndrome
options.D: Jejunal resection, Crohn's disease, tropical sprue
options.E: Ileal resection, fish tapeworm, intestinal blind loop

questions.explanation: Receptor deficiency: ileal resection, Crohn's disease, Imerslund–Gräsbeck syndrome (autosomal recessive). A: Gastrectomy is intrinsic factor deficiency. B: Different groups. D: The folate malabsorption list. E: The last two are competition.

questions.stem: The lecturer's note on the treatment slide says Glucophage (metformin) lowers which level?
questions.explanation: The handwritten note: Glucophage lowers B12. B: Not what the note says. C: Not what the note says. D: Not what the note says. E: Not what the note says.

questions.stem: Which feature is specific to cobalamin deficiency and not seen with folate deficiency?
questions.explanation: Neuropsychological symptoms are specific to cobalamin deficiency. The lecturer's note: B12 gives numbness and reduced cognition. A: Not marked as specific. B: Not marked as specific. C: Not marked as specific. E: The blood picture is the same in both.

questions.stem: Which cobalamin level is given for the diagnosis of deficiency?
questions.explanation: Cobalamin level < 200 pg/mL. A: The figure is 200. B: The figure is 200. D: The figure is 200. E: The figure is 200.

questions.stem: Each of the following is a "concerning feature" that calls for initial intramuscular B12 EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Concerning features: symptomatic or severe anemia, neuropsychiatric symptoms, possible malabsorption, concern about adherence. A: Listed. B: Listed. C: Listed. D: Listed.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman with pernicious anemia has paresthesias and a cobalamin of 120 pg/mL. How is B12 given at first?
questions.explanation: With concerning features: 1000 mcg IM 1 to 3 times weekly or daily in week 1, then weekly up to 4 weeks; repeat CBC at 2 to 3 weeks. A: Concerning features need IM. C: Does not treat B12 deficiency. D: Not the regimen. E: Too infrequent at first.

questions.stem: For how long may the initial intramuscular course be continued if neurologic symptoms are improving?
questions.explanation: Duration is typically 4 weeks; if neuropsychiatric or neurologic symptoms are improving it may be continued for up to 3 months. B: The typical duration without that extension. C: Not the figure given. D: Not the figure given. E: Not the figure given.

questions.stem: After 4 weekly intramuscular doses in a patient without concerning features, which maintenance is given?
questions.explanation: IM 1000 mcg weekly for 4 weeks, followed by cyanocobalamin once every month or hydroxocobalamin once every 3 months. A: Reversed. B: Not the intervals given. C: Hydroxocobalamin is given once in 3 months. E: Not the intervals given.

questions.stem: What is the oral or sublingual dose of B12 for patients without concerning features?
questions.explanation: Oral or sublingual: 1000 to 2000 mcg daily, monitoring the CBC and B12 level at 4 to 8 weeks, at 6 months, then annually. A: The dose is daily. B: Ten times too low. C: That is the dietary intake in the absorption figure. D: Far too low.

questions.stem: A patient starts vitamin B12 for megaloblastic anemia. When do reticulocytes peak?
questions.explanation: After B12, megaloblastic changes resolve within hours; reticulocytes peak after 1 week; counts and MCV normalize in 2 to 3 months. A: Marrow changes resolve within hours. B: Earlier. D: When counts normalize. E: Later.

questions.stem: According to the lecturer's note, how fast do problems improve after treating B12 deficiency?

options.A: Reticulocytes within a few hours; neural problems within a week
options.B: Reticulocytes within a few weeks; neural problems within a year
options.C: Reticulocytes within a year; neural problems within a few weeks
options.D: Reticulocytes within a few weeks; neural problems within a month
options.E: Reticulocytes and neural problems both within a few weeks

questions.explanation: The note: in B12 deficiency reticulocytes improve within a few weeks, neural issues within a year. A: Neural recovery is slow. C: Reversed. D: Neural recovery takes up to a year. E: Neural recovery takes up to a year.

questions.stem: Which malabsorptive cause is listed under folate deficiency?
questions.explanation: Folate malabsorption: gluten-sensitive enteropathy, tropical sprue, jejunal resection, severe Crohn's disease, short gut syndrome, sulfasalazine. A: Listed for B12. B: Listed for B12. C: Listed for B12. E: Listed for B12.

questions.stem: How are two drugs classified among the causes of folate deficiency?
questions.explanation: Sulfasalazine is listed under malabsorption; methotrexate under other causes as an anti-folate drug, with alcohol. A: Reversed. B: Metformin was noted for B12. C: Hydroxyurea is not on this slide. D: Sulfasalazine is under malabsorption.

questions.stem: Which set lists states of increased folate demand or requirement?

options.A: Hemolytic anemia, pregnancy, gastrectomy, vegan diet
options.D: Hemolytic anemia, lactation, peritoneal dialysis, obesity

questions.explanation: Increased demand: hemolytic anemias; increased requirements: pregnancy, hemodialysis, dermatitis. A: The last two are B12 causes. C: Iron deficiency and hypothyroidism are not listed. D: Not as listed. E: Aplastic anemia has low red cell turnover.

questions.stem: Compared with B12 deficiency, the lecturer noted that folate deficiency:

options.A: Develops slower; look for it in pregnancy and dialysis
options.B: Develops faster; look for it in strict vegetarians
options.C: Develops faster; look for it in pregnancy and dialysis
options.D: Develops slower; look for it after ileal resection
options.E: Develops at the same rate; look for it in the elderly

questions.explanation: The note: folate deficiency occurs faster than B12 deficiency; look for it in pregnant and hemodialysis patients. A: It occurs faster. B: Vegetarians are at risk of B12 deficiency. D: Ileal resection is a B12 cause. E: It occurs faster.

questions.stem: Which feature separates cobalamin deficiency from folate deficiency?
questions.explanation: The blood picture is the same, but folate deficiency does not cause neuropsychiatric problems such as subacute combined degeneration. B: Both. C: Both. D: Both. E: Both.

questions.stem: Folate deficiency is strongly implicated in a higher incidence of:
questions.explanation: Folate deficiency is strongly implicated in increasing the incidence of fetal neural tube defects. A: Not the association stated. B: Neuropathy belongs to B12 deficiency. C: Not the association stated. D: Not the association stated.

questions.stem: How is the serum folate interpreted?

options.A: > 2 ng/mL: deficiency unlikely; < 1 ng/mL: consistent with deficiency
options.B: > 4 ng/mL: deficiency unlikely; < 3 ng/mL: consistent with deficiency
options.C: > 10 ng/mL: deficiency unlikely; < 4 ng/mL: consistent with deficiency
options.D: > 4 ng/mL: deficiency unlikely; < 2 ng/mL: consistent with deficiency

lectures.title: Thalassemia
lectures.covers: What thalassemia is and how it is inherited, the α and β forms from carrier to transfusion-dependent disease, telling trait from iron deficiency, and treatment: transfusion, chelation, transplant, gene therapy and the newer drugs.

items.p: An autosomal recessive microcytic anemia caused by reduced or absent globin chain synthesis. Carriers are common across the Mediterranean, the Middle East and Asia.
Three steps explain the disease:

ul: Globin imbalance: too few β (or α) chains, so the unpaired partner chains precipitate
Ineffective erythropoiesis: the marrow makes red cell precursors, but most die before they mature
Hemolysis: the damaged cells that do reach the blood are destroyed early

items.p: The lecturer marked the β-thalassemia pathway as very important. Anemia raises erythropoietin; the marrow expands, which deforms bone and increases iron absorption from the gut. Transfusions add more iron. The result is iron overload.

table: Two from each parent; usually deletions

items.p: By severity:

ul: Transfusion-dependent (TDT, formerly β-thalassemia major): regular transfusion to survive
Non-transfusion-dependent (NTDT): β-thalassemia intermedia, HbH disease, moderate HbE/β-thalassemia
Minor: the carrier (heterozygote) state

items.p: Two carriers have a 25% chance of an affected child, 50% of a carrier and 25% of an unaffected child in every pregnancy. Consanguinity raises the risk.

summary.h: α-thalassemia by number of genes lost

table: Hydrops fetalis; fatal without treatment in the womb

items.p: HbH is four β chains. Hb Bart's is four γ chains.
HbH disease flares with fever, infection or oxidant drugs. Diagnosis: HbH inclusions on a supravital stain and an HbH peak on electrophoresis or HPLC. Non-deletional forms are more severe.
The carrier has a mild microcytic anemia that is often mistaken for iron deficiency. The key finding is HbA2 above 3.5%.

ul: Iron deficiency can lower HbA2 and hide the trait: recheck HbA2 after iron is replaced
No treatment, and no iron unless iron deficiency is proven
Genetic counseling for the patient and partner

items.p: Appears at 6–24 months, when fetal γ chains switch off. Pallor, poor feeding, irritability, failure to thrive, jaundice and a large liver and spleen. Without treatment, death usually comes in the first decade.
Under-treated children develop frontal bossing, maxillary overgrowth, a hair-on-end skull X-ray, growth failure, delayed puberty and fractures. Adequate transfusion from infancy prevents this.

ul: Blood count: very low hemoglobin, low MCV and MCH
Smear: microcytosis, target cells, nucleated red cells, basophilic stippling, teardrop cells
Electrophoresis: very high HbF; HbA absent in β⁰ and low in β⁺
DNA studies: identify the mutations for counseling and prenatal diagnosis

items.note: On slide 3 the handwritten label "reticulocytes" points at a cell with a nucleus. A reticulocyte has no nucleus; the cell looks like a nucleated red cell. Worth checking with the lecturer.

items.p: TIF 2025 targets: pre-transfusion hemoglobin 9.5–10.5 g/dL (10–11 with heart disease or extramedullary hematopoiesis), a transfusion every 2–5 weeks, post-transfusion hemoglobin below 13–15 g/dL.
The blood is leukocyte-reduced and matched at least for ABO, Rh and Kell. Irradiation is for specific indications only.
Once transferrin is saturated, non-transferrin-bound iron loads the heart, liver, pancreas, pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid and gonads.

table: Subcutaneous or IV infusion, 5–7 nights a week

ul: Start after 10–20 transfusions or ferritin above 1000 ng/mL
Ferritin at least every 3 months; yearly MRI from age 8–10 for liver iron and cardiac T2*
Monitor the heart (iron cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias), endocrine glands (short stature, delayed puberty, hypothyroidism, diabetes, hypoparathyroidism), bone and liver
Stem cell transplant: offer early, before iron damage, when an HLA-identical donor exists. Risks: graft-versus-host disease, graft failure, infertility.
Gene therapy uses the patient's own stem cells after myeloablation, so there is less immunosuppression and graft-versus-host disease. Lecturer's note: very expensive, highly successful.

table: Lentiviral vector adds a working β-globin gene
CRISPR editing turns fetal hemoglobin back on

items.p: TIF 2025: gene therapy is the best option from age 14, or when there is no HLA-identical sibling donor.

ul: Luspatercept: traps TGF-β family ligands that block late red cell maturation. 1 mg/kg under the skin every 3 weeks, adults. Watch blood pressure and clots, especially after splenectomy.
Mitapivat: an oral pyruvate kinase activator for adults with α- or β-thalassemia.

items.p: β-thalassemia intermedia has a later onset and a milder chain imbalance. Iron overload still develops, from increased gut absorption, even without transfusion.

ul: Complications: thrombosis (especially after splenectomy), pulmonary hypertension (screen with echocardiography), bone disease, extramedullary masses, leg ulcers, gallstones
Transfuse for a defined goal, then reassess: poor growth or delayed puberty, anemia that affects daily life, a growing spleen, complications, surgery, pregnancy, infection
Monitor iron with liver iron on MRI, not ferritin alone. Chelate at liver iron of 5 mg Fe/g or more, or ferritin of 800 ng/mL or more

items.p: HbE/β-thalassemia (HbE is a β26 Glu→Lys variant, common in Southeast Asia): mild at hemoglobin 9–12, moderate at 6–7 (NTDT), severe at 4–5 g/dL (TDT).

Splenectomy is done less often than before. Indications: massive spleen or hypersplenism, rising transfusion needs despite adequate therapy, or failure to thrive when transfusion and chelation are unavailable.

ul: Vaccinate first: pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib. Penicillin afterwards.
Risks: overwhelming sepsis, thrombosis, pulmonary hypertension

items.p: Prevention: community awareness, premarital screening, genetic counseling, prenatal and preimplantation diagnosis.

ul: First national report: 425 patients, 66% TDT and 34% NTDT, spread evenly across the country
Parents were first-degree relatives in 53%
21 mutations found; IVSI-110 is the most common
Transplant programs: 40 children with a projected 5-year survival of 90%; national program, 10 children, all cured

items.note: Slide 31 gives the mutation counts out of 227 chromosomes, but the printed percentages (for example 67 = 33.0%) do not match that total. The ranking is not affected.

cards.a: Autosomal recessive microcytic anemia from reduced or absent globin chain synthesis
Globin imbalance (unpaired chains precipitate), ineffective erythropoiesis (precursors die before maturing), hemolysis

cards.q: Two sources of iron overload in β-thalassemia
cards.a: Chronic transfusions, and increased gut iron absorption driven by marrow expansion
β: one gene on chromosome 11. α: four genes on chromosome 16 (two from each parent).
β-thalassemia intermedia, HbH disease, moderate HbE/β-thalassemia
1 silent carrier; 2 trait (mild microcytic anemia); 3 HbH disease; 4 Hb Bart's (hydrops fetalis)

cards.q: HbH and Hb Bart's: chain composition
cards.a: HbH = four β chains. Hb Bart's = four γ chains.

cards.q: Key lab finding in the β-thalassemia carrier
cards.a: HbA2 above 3.5%
MCV ÷ RBC count. Over 13: iron deficiency. Under 13: β-thalassemia trait.

cards.q: RBC count and RDW: iron deficiency versus β-thalassemia trait
cards.a: Iron deficiency: low RBC count, high RDW. Trait: normal or high RBC count, normal RDW.

cards.q: Why recheck HbA2 after iron repletion?
cards.a: Iron deficiency can lower HbA2 and mask β-thalassemia trait

cards.q: Why does TDT appear at 6–24 months?
cards.a: Fetal γ chains switch off and β chains are needed
Frontal bossing, maxillary overgrowth, hair-on-end skull, growth failure, delayed puberty, fractures, extramedullary hematopoiesis
Very high HbF; HbA absent (β⁰) or low (β⁺); variable HbA2
Pre-transfusion Hb 9.5–10.5 g/dL (10–11 with heart disease or extramedullary hematopoiesis); every 2–5 weeks; post-transfusion below 13–15 g/dL

cards.q: When to start chelation in TDT
cards.a: After 10–20 transfusions or ferritin above 1000 ng/mL

cards.q: Deferoxamine: route and what to watch
cards.a: Subcutaneous or IV infusion 5–7 nights a week; hearing, vision, growth, local reactions

cards.q: Deferiprone: route and what to watch
cards.a: Oral, three times daily; agranulocytosis and neutropenia (weekly counts), arthropathy

cards.q: Deferasirox: route and what to watch
cards.a: Oral, once daily; kidney and liver function, GI upset
Ferritin at least every 3 months; annual MRI from age 8–10 for liver iron and cardiac T2*
Traps TGF-β family ligands that block late red cell maturation; corrects ineffective erythropoiesis

cards.q: When to offer stem cell transplant
cards.a: Early, before iron damage, when an HLA-identical donor exists
Beti-cel: lentiviral vector adds a working β-globin gene. Exa-cel: CRISPR editing reactivates fetal hemoglobin (age 12 and over).

cards.q: Why iron overload in β-thalassemia intermedia without transfusion?
cards.a: Increased intestinal iron absorption
Liver iron 5 mg Fe/g or more, or ferritin 800 ng/mL or more (monitor with MRI, not ferritin alone)
HbH (β4) inclusions on supravital stain; HbH peak on electrophoresis or HPLC; genetic testing
Vaccinate first (pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib); penicillin prophylaxis afterwards

cards.q: Most common β-thalassemia mutation in Lebanon
cards.a: IVSI-110 (21 mutations found in Lebanon)

lectures.title: Sickle cell disease
lectures.covers: The sickle mutation and genotypes, the acute and chronic complications (infection, splenic sequestration, pain, acute chest syndrome, stroke), screening and diagnosis, and treatment: hydroxyurea, transfusion, transplant, gene therapy and the newer drugs.

items.p: An inherited disorder with chronic hemolytic anemia, vaso-occlusive crises, organ damage and a shortened life. About 8 million people are affected, mostly where malaria is endemic.
Inheritance is autosomal recessive: two sickle genes, or one sickle gene and one thalassemia gene.
High HbF and coinherited α-thalassemia make the disease milder.
A point mutation puts valine in place of glutamic acid at position 6 of the β chain. HbS forms polymers when it loses oxygen, and the red cell sickles.

ul: Hemolysis gives anemia and fatigue
Vaso-occlusion gives pain and organ damage
Around both: inflammation, endothelial dysfunction and a tendency to clot

items.p: Lecturer's note: it is a systemic disease. Complications start in childhood and last for life: stroke, retinopathy, hearing loss, acute chest syndrome, pulmonary hypertension, gallstones, kidney damage, avascular necrosis and priapism (a painful sustained erection).

summary.h: Infection and a sudden drop in hemoglobin

items.p: The spleen stops working in early childhood. Encapsulated bacteria (pneumococcus, Haemophilus, meningococcus) and Salmonella can kill within hours. Penicillin, vaccines, newborn diagnosis and family education cut deaths.

Acute splenic sequestration is a sudden enlargement of the spleen with a hemoglobin fall of 2 g/dL or more. It can cause shock and death and recurs in up to 67%. The lecturer noted that infections trigger it. Parents are taught to feel the spleen.

table: Red cells trapped in the spleen
Parvovirus B19 stops red cell production
Donor and own cells destroyed after transfusion
Careful small-volume transfusion; splenectomy if recurrent
Transfusion; keep away from pregnant contacts

items.p: Small volumes are used in sequestration because the trapped cells return to the circulation.

Dactylitis is painful swelling of the hands and feet from vaso-occlusion of the small bones. It is often the first complication, peaks between 6 months and 2 years, and is usually bilateral (lecturer's note). Early dactylitis may signal a more severe course.
Pain is the most common complication and the top reason children with SCD use health care (not the top cause of death).

ul: Triggers: cold, stress, illness, dehydration, high altitude
Acute pain: severe, needs an unplanned visit. Chronic pain: on most days for 6 months.
Acute pain is an emergency: first analgesic within 1 hour, reassess every 30–60 minutes
Opioids titrated to effect; NSAIDs for 5–7 days; low-dose ketamine if opioids fail
Use incentive spirometry throughout to prevent acute chest syndrome

items.p: A new lung infiltrate plus chest pain, fever, fast breathing, wheeze, cough or low oxygen. It can come with a pain crisis or on its own.
It is the second cause of hospital admission and the leading cause of death in adults with SCD (mortality up to 9%).

ul: Treat with incentive spirometry, antibiotics, oxygen, careful analgesia and transfusion
Hydroxyurea reduces recurrence

items.p: Without screening, 11% of children with HbSS have a stroke by age 20, and more than half recur without treatment.

ul: Children: usually ischemic. Silent infarcts affect learning.
Adults: hemorrhagic stroke in young adults; ischemic stroke at 35–65 years
Transcranial Doppler every year from age 2 to 16 in HbSS and HbSβ⁰
At least one MRI without sedation at early school age
Velocity of 200 cm/s or more: regular transfusions cut the stroke risk by age 18 from 11% to 1.9% (STOP trial)

items.note: The handwritten note on slide 15 says the Doppler measures "cerebral artery diameter". The test measures blood flow velocity (cm/s), as on slide 16. The note "treat: ↑Hb and ↓HbSC" most likely means lowering sickle hemoglobin (HbS); HbSC is a separate genotype. Worth checking with the lecturer.

ul: Anemia is normocytic in HbSS and microcytic in HbS/β-thalassemia
Smear: sickle cells, target cells, Howell–Jolly bodies (the spleen is not working), nucleated red cells
Electrophoresis or HPLC: high HbS, often raised HbF; high HbA2 in HbS/β-thalassemia

table: Penicillin; full vaccines including pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib, flu
Stop penicillin if no splenectomy and no invasive pneumococcal infection

items.p: Today 93.9% of children with HbSS or HbSβ⁰ reach age 18. The move from pediatric to adult care is a high-risk period.
Hydroxyurea is the backbone. It raises HbF, lowers white cells and improves red cell hydration. It is safe from 9 months of age.

ul: Start early and give the maximum tolerated dose
It cuts pain crises, acute chest syndrome, admissions, transfusions and Doppler velocities
Stop it before pregnancy
REACH (2024): escalating to 20–35 mg/kg/day beat a fixed 17.5 mg/kg/day, with 79% less acute chest syndrome and no extra toxicity

table: Acute chest syndrome, sudden fall in hemoglobin, before major surgery, selected pregnancies
Stroke or abnormal Doppler, multi-organ failure, complications despite hydroxyurea

items.p: Lecturer's note: for regular transfusion, use exchange transfusion if possible. Match Rh (C, E) and K antigens to prevent alloimmunization. Watch for iron overload and hyperhemolysis. Minor surgery needs no transfusion.
Stem cell transplant is the established cure: about 95% with a matched sibling, best done young and before organ damage.

items.note: Slide 25 says about 1 in 3 patients has a matched sibling donor. Most sources give a lower figure (under 20%). Not tested in the questions.

items.p: Gene therapy (FDA, December 2023, age 12 and over) uses the patient's own stem cells, so no donor and no graft-versus-host disease. Busulfan is still needed.

table: CRISPR cuts the BCL11A switch; fetal hemoglobin turns back on
97% free of pain crises for 12 months
A viral vector adds a new β-globin gene

items.p: Newer drugs have disappointed: L-glutamine has a modest effect, crizanlizumab lost its EU approval, voxelotor was withdrawn worldwide, mitapivat gave mixed results. Lecturer's note: hydroxyurea is best.

ul: 387 patients, clustered in the North (42.5%) and South (28.4%); high consanguinity; gene influx from neighboring countries
Newborn screening of 10,095 babies: 2.1% had an abnormal hemoglobin (3.5% in the North); HbS was 81% of them, HbD 12%
Prevention: awareness, carrier screening in high school, premarital testing, prenatal or preimplantation diagnosis

cards.a: Sequestration: large spleen, high reticulocytes. Aplastic crisis: spleen unchanged, reticulocytes very low.
Urgent, careful small-volume transfusion (trapped cells return to the circulation); splenectomy if recurrent

Cold, stress, illness, dehydration, high altitude

2nd cause of hospitalization; leading cause of death in adults with SCD

cards.a: Children: usually ischemic. Young adults: hemorrhagic. Age 35–65: ischemic.
Yearly from age 2 to 16 in HbSS and HbSβ⁰; abnormal at 200 cm/s or more

cards.a: Regular transfusions: stroke risk by age 18 falls from 11% to 1.9% (STOP)
Sickle cells, target cells, Howell–Jolly bodies, nucleated red cells

cards.a: Start by 2 months; stop at age 5 if no splenectomy and no invasive pneumococcal infection
Raises HbF; lowers white cells; improves red cell hydration
Start early (safe from 9 months) and escalate to the maximum tolerated dose; stop before pregnancy
Acute chest syndrome, sudden fall in hemoglobin, before major surgery, selected pregnancies
Stroke or abnormal transcranial Doppler, multi-organ failure, complications despite hydroxyurea

cards.a: Rh (C, E) and K
Exa-cel: CRISPR cuts BCL11A so HbF turns back on. Lovo-cel: viral vector adds a β-globin gene (boxed warning for blood cancer).
Patient's own cells: no donor, no graft-versus-host disease; still needs myeloablative busulfan
