questions.stem: Roughly what share of people with the factor V Leiden mutation are homozygous?
questions.explanation: About 1% of people with the mutation are homozygous. A: About 1%. B: About 1%. C: About 1%. E: About 1%.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman on oral contraceptives is heterozygous for factor V Leiden. What is her relative risk of a first venous thrombosis?
questions.explanation: Relative risk: FVL heterozygous 7, OCP 4, both 35 (0.29% per year), FVL homozygous 80. A: FVL heterozygous alone. B: OCP alone. D: The combined risk is far higher. E: FVL homozygous.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman is homozygous for factor V Leiden. What is her yearly incidence of a first venous thrombosis?
questions.explanation: FVL homozygous: relative risk 80, 0.5–1.0% per year. A: FVL heterozygous. C: FVL heterozygous with OCP. D: Normal. E: OCP alone.

questions.stem: A man is heterozygous for factor V Leiden and takes no estrogen. What is his relative risk of a first venous thrombosis?
questions.explanation: Heterozygous FVL: relative risk 7 (0.06% per year); homozygous 80. B: Hyperhomocysteinemia. C: Heterozygous with OCP. D: Homozygous. E: OCP alone.

questions.stem: Which of these carries the lowest relative risk of a first venous thrombosis?
questions.explanation: Relative risks: hyperhomocysteinemia 2.5, OCP 4, FVL heterozygous 7, with OCP 35, homozygous 80. A: 4. B: 7. D: 35. E: 80.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has a DVT. Her prothrombin level is about 30% above normal, and her factor V gene is normal. Which mutation is most likely?
questions.explanation: Prothrombin G20210A, a G-to-A change at nucleotide 20210, raises prothrombin levels by ~30%. A: Factor V gene normal. C: Factor V gene normal. D: Does not raise prothrombin. E: Does not raise prothrombin.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with a DVT receives unfractionated heparin, but his aPTT barely changes even at high doses. Which inherited thrombophilia best explains this?
questions.explanation: Heparin binds antithrombin and amplifies its action ~1000-fold; with too little antithrombin, heparin works poorly. A: Heparin acts through antithrombin. B: Heparin acts through antithrombin. C: Heparin acts through antithrombin. D: Heparin acts through antithrombin.

questions.stem: Which activated factor is NOT a target of antithrombin?
questions.explanation: Antithrombin irreversibly binds thrombin (IIa), IXa, Xa, XIa and XIIa. Va is inactivated by activated protein C. A: Target. B: Target. C: Target. E: Target.

questions.stem: How does heparin enhance antithrombin?

options.A: It raises antithrombin synthesis in the liver
options.C: It activates protein C on endothelium
options.E: It binds and blocks tissue factor

questions.explanation: Heparin binds antithrombin, changing its shape so it binds thrombin and other serine proteases more avidly (~1000-fold). A: It acts on the existing molecule. C: Thrombomodulin does that. D: Activated protein C does that. E: Not its action.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman has had two DVTs. Protein C activity is low; antithrombin and APC-resistance tests are normal. Which control step is lost?

options.A: Inactivation of factors IXa and Xa
options.D: Inactivation of factors Va and VIIIa

questions.explanation: Activated protein C, with protein S, inactivates Va and VIIIa. Protein C deficiency removes this control. A: Antithrombin targets. B: Antithrombin is normal. C: Not a control step. E: Not a control step.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with systemic lupus has a DVT and a persistent lupus anticoagulant. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: APS may be primary or secondary to lupus. Thrombosis plus a persistent lupus anticoagulant in lupus = secondary APS. A: No heparin exposure. B: Not suggested. C: Not suggested. D: Not suggested.

questions.stem: A healthy 25-year-old blood donor has a positive anticardiolipin test once. What is the best interpretation?

options.A: It occurs in 1–5% of healthy people

questions.explanation: Anticardiolipin and lupus anticoagulant antibodies are found in 1–5% of young, apparently healthy people. B: Needs a clinical criterion and a repeat test. C: Not by itself. D: No clinical event. E: Unrelated.

questions.stem: Which event meets the Sapporo vascular thrombosis criterion?

options.C: One small-vessel thrombosis in a kidney

questions.explanation: Clinical criterion 1: one or more episodes of arterial, venous or small-vessel thrombosis, in any tissue or organ. A: Not thrombosis of the listed vessels. B: Bleeding, not thrombosis. D: Not thrombosis. E: Not a listed criterion.

questions.stem: Which pregnancy history meets the Sapporo clinical criteria?

options.A: Delivery at 33 weeks for severe preeclampsia
options.B: Delivery at 36 weeks for severe preeclampsia
options.E: Three miscarriages with a septate uterus

questions.explanation: Pregnancy morbidity: ≥ 1 unexplained death of a normal fetus at ≥ 10 weeks; ≥ 1 premature birth at ≤ 34 weeks from severe preeclampsia, eclampsia or placental insufficiency; ≥ 3 unexplained consecutive miscarriages before 10 weeks. B: At or before 34 weeks. C: Three or more. D: At or beyond 10 weeks. E: Anatomic causes must be excluded.

questions.stem: A 31-year-old woman has had three consecutive miscarriages at 7, 8 and 9 weeks. Uterine imaging, hormones and both parents' karyotypes are normal. Anticardiolipin IgG is high on two tests 8 weeks apart. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Three or more unexplained consecutive miscarriages before 10 weeks is a clinical criterion; aCL in medium or high titer twice ≥ 6 weeks apart is a lab criterion. APS = 1 clinical + 1 lab. A: Not tested; aCL explains it. C: Not tested; aCL explains it. D: Not tested; aCL explains it. E: Not tested; aCL explains it.

questions.stem: A 36-year-old woman had an ischemic stroke. Anticardiolipin IgM is high at diagnosis and again 3 weeks later. What is still needed to diagnose antiphospholipid syndrome?

options.A: A positive lupus anticoagulant as well
options.C: A repeat test 6 or more weeks later

questions.explanation: The lab criterion needs aCL (IgG and/or IgM, medium or high titer) on ≥ 2 occasions ≥ 6 weeks apart. Her stroke meets the clinical criterion. A: One lab criterion is enough. B: One event is enough. D: APS can be primary. E: At least 6 weeks apart.

questions.stem: A woman has a positive lupus anticoagulant on two tests 8 weeks apart but has never had a thrombosis or pregnancy loss. How is she classified?
questions.explanation: APS = 1 clinical criterion + 1 laboratory criterion. Antibodies alone are not the syndrome. A: Needs a clinical criterion. B: Needs a clinical criterion and lupus. C: Not a category. E: Antibodies are acquired.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with a DVT has a prolonged aPTT that does not correct on 1:1 mixing but shortens with excess phospholipid. She has not received heparin. What is present?
questions.explanation: LA: prolonged phospholipid-dependent test, no correction on mixing with normal platelet-poor plasma, shortening with excess phospholipid, other coagulopathies excluded. A: Not phospholipid-dependent. B: Would correct on mixing. C: No heparin was given. D: Would correct on mixing.

questions.stem: A patient's prolonged aPTT corrects on mixing with normal plasma. What is the next step in a lupus anticoagulant work-up?

options.D: A dilute Russell's viper venom time

questions.explanation: Mix corrects → incubated mixing study: no correction → phospholipid dependence; correction → factor assays. A: Done when the mix does not correct. C: Stop when both screening tests are normal. D: Done when the aPTT is normal. E: Not the next step.

questions.stem: A prolonged aPTT corrects on mixing and also on an incubated mix. What comes next?

options.B: A dilute Russell's viper venom time

questions.explanation: A mix that corrects (also after incubation) points to a factor deficiency: factor assays identify it. A: For a mix that does not correct. B: A screening test. C: Correction points away from an inhibitor. D: Already done.

questions.stem: In a lupus anticoagulant work-up the aPTT is normal. What is the next step?

options.C: A dilute Russell's viper venom time

questions.explanation: Test 1 (aPTT) normal → test 2 (dRVVT); if both normal, stop. A: For an abnormal screening test. B: Later in the algorithm. D: Only if test 2 is also normal. E: After a mix that does not correct.

questions.stem: Each is a screening test for lupus anticoagulant EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Screening tests: aPTT, kaolin clotting time, dilute Russell's viper venom time, dilute PT, Textarin time. A: Screening test. B: Screening test. C: Screening test. E: Screening test.

questions.stem: Before a lupus anticoagulant is confirmed, which condition must be excluded?
questions.explanation: The last step is to exclude other coagulopathies, such as a factor VIII inhibitor or heparin. B: Does not prolong the aPTT this way. C: Does not prolong the aPTT this way. D: Does not prolong the aPTT this way. E: Does not prolong the aPTT this way.

questions.stem: A 43-year-old woman presents with syncope. She had coronary stents at 31 and a pulmonary embolism at 33. Now she has bilateral leg DVTs, a pulmonary embolism, and a cool right foot with absent distal pulses. Which abnormality best explains both her arterial and venous clots?
questions.explanation: Lupus anticoagulant and hyperhomocysteinemia cause arterial and venous thrombosis; FVL, G20210A and the deficiencies cause venous thrombosis. A: Venous. C: Venous. D: Venous. E: Venous.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man had a myocardial infarction last year and now has a DVT. Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin tests are negative twice. Which abnormality best explains both events?
questions.explanation: Hyperhomocysteinemia and lupus anticoagulant cause arterial and venous thrombosis. With LA excluded, hyperhomocysteinemia remains. B: Venous. C: Venous. D: Venous. E: Venous.

questions.stem: Each causes venous but not arterial thrombosis EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Hyperhomocysteinemia (and lupus anticoagulant) cause arterial and venous thrombosis. A: Venous. B: Venous. C: Venous. D: Venous.

questions.stem: Among patients with venous thrombosis, which defect is found most often?

options.E: Antithrombin, protein C or S deficiency

questions.explanation: In venous thrombosis: FVL 12–40%, hyperhomocysteinemia 10–20%, APS 10–20%, G20210A 6–18%, antithrombin/protein C/protein S deficiency 5–15%. A: 6–18%. B: 10–20%. D: 10–20%. E: 5–15%.

questions.stem: What share of patients with venous thrombosis carry prothrombin G20210A?
questions.explanation: Prothrombin G20210A is found in 6–18% of patients with venous thrombosis. A: Factor V Leiden. B: Hyperhomocysteinemia or APS. C: Antithrombin, protein C and S deficiencies. E: FVL among inherited thrombophilias.

questions.stem: Each is a reason to test for thrombophilia EXCEPT:

options.C: A first DVT after surgery at 70
options.E: A sister with a PE at age 30

questions.explanation: Work-up: young age, unusual location, repeated unprovoked events, family history of clots at a young age. Testing is usually not the answer. A: Young age. B: Unusual location. D: Listed. E: Family history at a young age.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man has a first DVT after a long-haul flight. His brother had a pulmonary embolism at 30 and his father a DVT at 35. Which feature most supports a thrombophilia work-up?
questions.explanation: Indications: young age, unusual location, repeated unprovoked events, family history of venous or arterial clots at a young age. A: A provoking factor, not an indication. C: A leg DVT is a usual site. D: This is his first. E: Not an indication.

questions.stem: In the 43-year-old woman with syncope, coronary stents at 31 and two PEs, which feature most supports a thrombophilia work-up?

options.A: A family history of breast cancer
options.E: Repeated thrombosis at a young age

questions.explanation: Indications: young age, unusual location, repeated unprovoked events, family history of clots at a young age. A: Not an indication. B: A risk factor, not an indication. C: Not an indication. D: Not an indication.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman of Chinese descent has a right leg DVT at 30 weeks of her first pregnancy. She took oral contraceptives for years. Family and medical history are noncontributory; CBC, PT and aPTT are normal. Which test is most appropriate before anticoagulation?

options.B: Factor V Leiden and prothrombin gene analysis
options.D: Protein C, protein S and antithrombin levels

questions.explanation: Her DVT has a clear trigger (pregnancy; estrogen exposure is a listed acquired risk factor), the site is usual, it is her first event, and there is no family history of clots. The slides give no answer key; this follows the work-up slide: thrombophilia testing is usually not the answer. B: A provoked first clot; testing is usually not the answer. C: No other APS feature. D: Not indicated for a provoked clot. E: Not indicated.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer develops a DVT while still walking normally. Which arm of Virchow's triad does his cancer mainly add?
questions.explanation: Malignancy is an acquired thrombophilia: a hypercoagulable state, the "abnormal blood" arm of Virchow's triad. A: He is mobile; the cancer acts on the blood. B: Not the main effect. C: Not an arm of the triad. E: Not an arm of the triad.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has had two DVTs. Protein C activity is normal, but activated protein C works poorly because its cofactor is low. Which protein is deficient?
questions.explanation: Activated protein C needs protein S to inactivate Va and VIIIa. Hereditary protein S deficiency is an inherited thrombophilia. B: Neutralizes thrombin. C: Activates protein C. D: Contact cofactor. E: Starts coagulation.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old on heparin for 6 days develops an arterial thrombosis, and his platelet count has fallen from 250 to 95 × 10⁹/L. Which risk factor for thrombosis is this?
questions.explanation: HIT is an acquired thrombophilia (with APL, MPD, estrogens, malignancy, surgery, immobility). A: Heparin resistance, not a falling platelet count. C: Venous; no platelet fall. D: Venous; no platelet fall. E: No hemolysis is described.

lectures.title: Overview of hemostasis
lectures.covers: The phases and players of hemostasis, the endothelium, platelet receptors and vWF, the coagulation cascade and cell-based model, the natural brakes and fibrinolysis, bleeding patterns, and reading PT, aPTT and the other screening tests.

items.p: Hemostasis stops bleeding after injury without blocking the vessel. It is quick, localized, carefully regulated and balanced, and it happens in phases.

ul: Vasoconstriction of the damaged vessel
Primary hemostasis: the platelet plug
Secondary hemostasis: the fibrin clot
Tertiary hemostasis: fibrinolysis

items.p: It balances procoagulant and anticoagulant forces. Four main players: blood vessels, platelets, coagulation factors and the fibrinolytic system. Bleeding comes from a fragile vessel, too few or faulty platelets, a missing clotting factor, or a fibrinolysis defect.

table: Smooth surface: platelets do not stick
Nitric oxide and prostacyclin: dilate, inhibit platelets
Tissue factor exposed: starts the cascade
vWF released: glue between platelet and collagen
Thrombomodulin: switches thrombin to an anticoagulant role
TFPI: blocks the first step of the cascade

ul: Injury exposes subendothelial collagen → platelet adhesion
Platelets anchor through GPIb binding vWF
Activated GPIIb-IIIa binds fibrinogen and links platelets → aggregation
The plug appears in 3–5 minutes. It is soft and easily washed away, so a fibrin mesh must reinforce it.

table: Aggregation; the major platelet membrane protein

items.p: A large multimeric glycoprotein made by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes. ADAMTS-13 cleaves it to normal-sized multimers.
Three functions:

ul: Platelet adhesion: a bridge between platelets and the endothelium
Platelet aggregation
Fibrin clot formation: it carries factor VIII and cuts its clearance about 5-fold

items.p: Lecturer's note: von Willebrand disease is a mixed disorder. It affects primary (platelet) and secondary (factor VIII) hemostasis.

items.caption: Coagulation cascade with the lecturer's notes

ul: Intrinsic: XII → XI → IX; IXa with VIIIa activates X. Measured by the aPTT (plasma exposed to contact activators).
Extrinsic: tissue factor (III) with VIIa activates X. Measured by the PT (plasma exposed to tissue factor).
Common: Xa with Va turns prothrombin into thrombin; thrombin turns fibrinogen into fibrin; XIIIa cross-links it. The thrombin time measures fibrinogen → fibrin.

items.p: Lecturer's notes: a prolonged PTT with bleeding means factor VIII, IX or XI. The PT gives the INR. If the PT, aPTT, thrombin time and everything else are normal, think of factor XIII.
Secondary hemostasis is a series of interactions between factors on tissue factor-bearing cells and activated platelets.

table: VIIa/TF activates X and IX; a little thrombin
Thrombin activates platelets and cofactors (V, VIII freed from vWF, XI)
Tenase (IXa + VIIIa) and prothrombinase (Xa + Va) make a large thrombin burst

items.p: The fibrin clot forms in 5–10 minutes.

table: Substrate; low in liver disease and DIC
Vitamin K dependent; target of warfarin
Not in blood; exposed by injury
Removed by citrate in blood tubes
Shortest half-life; first to fall on warfarin
Cross-links fibrin; normal PT and aPTT

items.p: There is no factor VI: it turned out to be activated factor V.

items.note: Slide 12 says factor VIII is "not made in liver". Standard sources: VIII is made mainly by liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (not hepatocytes), so its level holds up in liver disease. Not tested as worded.

items.caption: Four brakes keep the clot at the injury

ul: Flow washes activated factors downstream; the liver clears them
TFPI blocks the TF–VII pathway and stops initiation
Antithrombin mops up thrombin and Xa
Protein C + protein S destroy Va and VIIIa
The intact wall carries thrombomodulin and heparan sulphate

items.p: If one brake fails, the patient clots: antithrombin, protein C or protein S deficiency, factor V Leiden.

Fibrinolysis: as the vessel heals, plasminogen activators turn plasminogen into plasmin inside the clot. Plasmin slowly dissolves fibrin into fibrin degradation (split) products. Deficiency of these regulators raises the risk of thrombosis.
Disorders are inherited or acquired: primary (platelet), secondary (factor), or mixed (both, e.g. vWD).

table: Petechiae, purpura, nosebleeds, heavy periods, gum bleeding

summary.h: History and exam in a bleeding child

ul: Bleeding: nose, gums, bruising, joints and muscles, heavy periods; neonatal bleeding; after dental extraction, surgery, circumcision or trauma; transfusions
Clues to other causes: pallor and infections; weight loss, night sweats, fever, lymphadenopathy, masses (malignancy); diet, drugs, travel
Family: consanguinity, bleeding relatives, hysterectomy at a young age. A negative family history does not exclude an inherited disorder.
Exam: general appearance and hemodynamics, fever, petechiae to hematomas, retinal hemorrhages, hemarthrosis and contractures, lymph nodes, liver and spleen, masses, bone deformities or absent bones

table: Warfarin, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease
XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, I
Hemophilia A or B, XI or XII deficiency, heparin, vWD, lupus anticoagulant
VII deficiency, early warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency, early liver disease
Liver disease, DIC, full warfarin, X, V, II or fibrinogen deficiency
Platelet disorder, vWD, vessel wall, factor XIII deficiency

items.p: Mixing study: mix the patient's plasma 1:1 with normal plasma. Correction = a missing factor; no correction = an inhibitor (antibody).

items.note: The platelet range here is 150–400 × 10⁹/L; the next lecture gives 150–450. Reference ranges vary by laboratory.

cards.a: Vasoconstriction → primary (platelet plug) → secondary (fibrin clot) → tertiary (fibrinolysis)
Blood vessels, platelets, coagulation factors, fibrinolytic system
Smooth surface; NO and prostacyclin; heparan sulphate (activates antithrombin); thrombomodulin; TFPI

cards.q: Injured endothelium: what is exposed or released?
cards.a: Collagen (platelets bind), tissue factor (starts cascade), vWF (glue); endothelin constricts
Adhesion: GPIb–vWF, GPIa-IIa–collagen. Aggregation: GPIIb-IIIa–fibrinogen.
Collagen receptor that promotes activation of GPIIb-IIIa and GPIa-IIa

cards.q: Platelet plug versus fibrin clot timing
cards.a: Plug 3–5 minutes; fibrin clot 5–10 minutes
Endothelial cells and megakaryocytes; ADAMTS-13 cleaves it to normal-sized multimers
Platelet adhesion (bridge), platelet aggregation, carries factor VIII (cuts its clearance 5-fold)

cards.q: Why is vWD a mixed disorder?
cards.a: It affects primary (platelet adhesion) and secondary (factor VIII) hemostasis

cards.q: PT versus aPTT: trigger and factors
cards.a: PT: tissue factor; VII, X, V, II, I. aPTT: contact activators; XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II, I.

cards.q: Prolonged aPTT with bleeding: which factors?
cards.a: VIII, IX or XI

cards.q: Bleeding with normal PT, aPTT, thrombin time and platelets?
cards.a: Think factor XIII deficiency (fibrin not cross-linked)
Initiation (TF-bearing cell) → amplification (platelets and cofactors activated) → propagation (thrombin burst on platelets)

cards.q: Which factor falls first on warfarin, and why?
cards.a: Factor VII: shortest half-life (isolated PT prolongation early)

cards.q: Which factor is removed by citrate tubes?
cards.a: Factor IV (calcium)

cards.q: Why is there no factor VI?
cards.a: It was found to be activated factor V
Flow (liver clears factors), TFPI, antithrombin (thrombin, Xa), protein C + S (Va, VIIIa)
Plasminogen activators → plasmin → dissolves fibrin → fibrin degradation products
Primary: immediate, mucocutaneous, petechiae, small cuts bleed. Secondary: delayed, joints/muscles/deep, small cuts normal.
0.8–1.2 untreated; target usually 2–3
Heparin; low or abnormal fibrinogen
Factor VII deficiency, early warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency, early liver disease

cards.q: PT and aPTT both normal but bleeding: causes
cards.a: Platelet disorder, vWD, vessel wall disorder, factor XIII deficiency
Corrects = factor deficiency; does not correct = inhibitor (antibody)

questions.stem: Hemostasis stops bleeding after injury. What else defines a normal hemostatic response?

options.A: It seals the injury without blocking the vessel
options.B: It seals the vessel along its whole length
options.C: It acts through platelets without any fibrin
options.D: It activates coagulation throughout the blood
options.E: It replaces the vessel wall with fibrin

questions.explanation: Hemostasis is the process of stopping bleeding without blocking a vessel after injury. It is quick, localized, carefully regulated, balanced, and occurs in phases. B: The response is localized; the vessel stays open. C: The fibrin mesh is needed to reinforce the plug. D: Hemostasis is localized, not systemic. E: The clot is later dissolved as the vessel heals.

questions.stem: A vessel is cut. Which event comes first in hemostasis?
questions.explanation: Phases: vasoconstriction, then the platelet plug (primary), the fibrin clot (secondary), and fibrinolysis (tertiary). A: Primary hemostasis follows vasoconstriction. B: Secondary hemostasis. C: Propagation phase of secondary hemostasis. D: Tertiary hemostasis, last.

questions.stem: Which phase of hemostasis is called tertiary hemostasis?
questions.explanation: Primary = platelet plug; secondary = fibrin clot; tertiary = fibrinolysis. A: The first phase. B: Primary hemostasis. C: Secondary hemostasis. E: Final step of secondary hemostasis.

questions.stem: Besides blood vessels, platelets and coagulation factors, which is the fourth main player in hemostasis?
questions.explanation: Four main players: blood vessels, platelets, coagulation factors, fibrinolytic system. Bleeding can come from a fragile vessel, too few or faulty platelets, a missing clotting factor, or a defect in fibrinolysis. A: Not one of the four players. B: Not one of the four players. D: Not one of the four players. E: Not one of the four players.

questions.stem: A man with normal platelets and normal clotting factors bleeds easily. Which cause fits this picture?
questions.explanation: Bleeding can come from a fragile vessel, too few or faulty platelets, a missing clotting factor, or a defect in fibrinolysis. With normal platelets and factors, the vessel is the remaining player. A: His platelets are normal. C: His factors are normal. D: A platelet problem. E: A factor problem.

questions.stem: Which endothelial product dilates the vessel and inhibits platelets?
questions.explanation: Intact endothelium: smooth surface, nitric oxide and prostacyclin (dilate, inhibit platelets), heparan sulphate (activates antithrombin), thrombomodulin, TFPI. A: Constricts the injured vessel. B: Switches thrombin to an anticoagulant role. C: Starts the cascade. D: Glue between platelet and collagen.

questions.stem: How does heparan sulphate on intact endothelium prevent clotting?
questions.explanation: Heparan sulphate activates antithrombin, which blocks thrombin. A: Activated protein C does this. B: TFPI does this. D: Nitric oxide and prostacyclin. E: ADAMTS-13 does this.

questions.stem: Which endothelial molecule switches thrombin from a procoagulant to an anticoagulant role?
questions.explanation: Thrombomodulin on intact endothelium switches thrombin to an anticoagulant role. A: Activates antithrombin. C: Blocks the first step of the cascade. D: Dilates and inhibits platelets. E: Dilates and inhibits platelets.

questions.stem: Which endothelial inhibitor blocks the first step of the coagulation cascade?

options.C: Activated protein C with protein S

questions.explanation: TFPI blocks the TF–FVII pathway and stops initiation. B: Mops up thrombin and Xa. C: Destroys Va and VIIIa. D: Switches thrombin's role. E: Starts fibrinolysis.

questions.stem: Seconds after a vessel is injured, which endothelial product makes it constrict?
questions.explanation: Injured endothelium: collagen exposed, tissue factor exposed, vWF released, vessel constricts (endothelin), protective molecules lost. A: Dilates. B: Dilates. C: Anticoagulant. E: Anticoagulant.

questions.stem: At a site of vessel injury, which event starts the coagulation cascade?
questions.explanation: Injury exposes tissue factor, which starts the coagulation cascade; exposed collagen binds platelets. A: Primary hemostasis. C: Glue for platelet adhesion. D: Vasoconstriction. E: Loss of protection, not the trigger.

questions.stem: Platelets first anchor to an injured vessel through which interaction?
questions.explanation: Injury exposes subendothelial collagen; platelets anchor through GPIb binding vWF; activated GPIIb-IIIa binds fibrinogen and links platelets (aggregation). A: Aggregation, not anchoring. B: GPVI binds collagen. C: GPIa-IIa binds collagen. E: Not the anchoring step shown.

questions.stem: A patient's platelets stick normally to collagen but cannot bind fibrinogen. Which step of primary hemostasis fails?
questions.explanation: GPIIb-IIIa binds fibrinogen, linking platelets together: platelet aggregation. A: Adhesion to collagen is normal. B: Endothelin, not platelets. D: Factor XIIIa. E: Endothelial injury.

questions.stem: How long after injury does the platelet plug normally appear?
questions.explanation: The platelet plug appears in 3–5 minutes; the fibrin clot in 5–10 minutes. B: Too early. C: The fibrin clot. D: Too late. E: Too late.

questions.stem: Which platelet receptor binds collagen and promotes activation of GPIIb-IIIa?
questions.explanation: GPVI is a collagen receptor that promotes activation of GPIIb-IIIa and GPIa-IIa. A: vWF receptor, adhesion. B: Collagen receptor for adhesion. C: The fibrinogen receptor itself. D: Part of the vWF receptor complex.

questions.stem: Which receptor is the major platelet membrane protein?
questions.explanation: GPIIb-IIIa, the fibrinogen receptor that mediates aggregation, is the major platelet membrane protein. A: vWF receptor. C: Collagen receptor. D: Collagen receptor. E: Not the major membrane protein.

questions.stem: Platelet GPIa-IIa mediates which step?
questions.explanation: GPIa-IIa is a collagen receptor that mediates adhesion. A: GPIIb-IIIa. B: GPIb. C: Not a receptor role shown. D: GPVI activates GPIa-IIa, not the reverse.

questions.stem: Which cells make von Willebrand factor?
questions.explanation: vWF is a large multimeric glycoprotein made in endothelial cells and megakaryocytes. A: Not hepatocytes. B: Not macrophages. D: Not liver cells. E: Not fibroblasts.

questions.stem: A patient has no ADAMTS-13 activity. What accumulates in the plasma?
questions.explanation: ADAMTS-13 cleaves vWF to normal-sized multimers; without it, very large multimers persist. A: vWF carries factor VIII. B: Plasmin acts on fibrin. C: These come from ADAMTS-13 cleavage. E: Not the substrate of ADAMTS-13.

questions.stem: A man has very low von Willebrand factor. Why is his factor VIII level also low?

options.A: vWF normally slows factor VIII clearance
options.B: vWF is needed for factor VIII synthesis
options.C: vWF activates factor VIII on platelets
options.D: Factor VIII is used up in platelet plugs
options.E: Anti-vWF antibodies also bind factor VIII

questions.explanation: vWF carries factor VIII and decreases its plasma clearance about 5-fold. B: vWF carries VIII; it does not make it. C: Thrombin activates VIII. D: Not the mechanism. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Each is a function of von Willebrand factor EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: vWF promotes platelet adhesion (bridge), platelet aggregation, and fibrin clot formation by carrying factor VIII and decreasing its clearance. Thrombomodulin activates protein C. A: Adhesion. B: A vWF function. C: A vWF function. E: A vWF function.

questions.stem: Why is von Willebrand disease a mixed disorder of hemostasis?

options.A: It lowers both platelets and fibrinogen
options.B: It blocks both GPIIb-IIIa and GPVI
options.C: It affects platelet adhesion and factor VIII
options.D: It activates both plasmin and thrombin
options.E: It inhibits both ADAMTS-13 and protein C

questions.explanation: Lecturer's note: vWD is mixed; it affects primary (platelet) and secondary (factor VIII) hemostasis. A: Neither is the defect. B: Those are platelet receptors, not vWF. D: Not the mechanism. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: Why is a platelet plug not enough to stop bleeding?

options.A: It forms after the fibrin clot
options.E: It is soft and easily washed away

questions.explanation: The platelet plug is soft and easily washed away; a fibrin mesh from the cascade reinforces it. A: The plug comes first. B: It persists until reinforced. C: Adhesion needs vWF, not fibrin. D: Hemostasis is localized.

questions.stem: Which factor starts the intrinsic pathway?
questions.explanation: Intrinsic pathway: XII → XI → IX (with VIIIa) → X. Extrinsic: TF + VIIa → X. Common: Xa + Va → thrombin → fibrin; XIIIa cross-links it. A: Extrinsic pathway. C: Activated by XIa. D: Common pathway. E: Cross-links fibrin.

questions.stem: A patient's factor deficiency prolongs the aPTT but leaves the PT normal. Which pathway is affected?
questions.explanation: Normal PT with prolonged aPTT points to the intrinsic pathway only (VIII, IX, XI, XII). B: Prolongs the PT. C: Prolongs both. D: Not measured by aPTT. E: Not measured by aPTT.

questions.stem: The PT measures how long plasma takes to clot after it is exposed to what?
questions.explanation: The PT measures time to clot when plasma is exposed to tissue factor; the aPTT when exposed to substances that activate contact factors. A: The aPTT. C: The thrombin time. D: Platelet aggregation testing. E: Platelet testing.

questions.stem: The aPTT is started by substances that activate which group of factors?
questions.explanation: The aPTT measures time for plasma to clot when exposed to substances that activate contact factors. A: Starts the PT. B: Not the trigger. C: Not part of the aPTT. E: Not part of the aPTT.

questions.stem: Which step does the thrombin time measure?
questions.explanation: Thrombin time: fibrinogen to fibrin conversion. A: Upstream of the test. B: Upstream of the test. C: Fibrinolysis. D: Factor XIII; not measured.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy has joint bleeds. His aPTT is prolonged and his PT is normal. A deficiency of which factor fits?
questions.explanation: Lecturer's note: a prolonged PTT with bleeding means factor VIII, IX or XI. Factor XI deficiency usually causes mild bleeding. B: Prolongs the PT. C: Normal PT and aPTT. D: Prolongs both. E: Prolongs both and the thrombin time.

questions.stem: A patient bleeds after surgery. His platelet count, PT, aPTT and thrombin time are normal, but his fibrin is not cross-linked. Which factor is deficient?
questions.explanation: Lecturer's note: if PT, aPTT, thrombin time and everything else are normal, think of factor XIII, which cross-links fibrin. A: Prolongs the aPTT. B: Prolongs the PT. D: Prolongs the thrombin time. E: Prolongs PT and aPTT.

questions.stem: In the cell-based model of coagulation, where does initiation occur?
questions.explanation: Initiation occurs on a TF-bearing cell; amplification activates platelets and cofactors; propagation generates large amounts of thrombin on the platelet surface. A: Propagation. B: Antithrombotic surface. C: Not in the model. E: The end product.

questions.stem: During propagation in the cell-based model, where is the large burst of thrombin made?

options.B: In free plasma away from cells
options.C: On activated platelets at the injury

questions.explanation: Propagation: large amounts of thrombin generated on the platelet surface at the injury site. A: Initiation; small amounts. B: Coagulation occurs on cell surfaces. D: Antithrombotic. E: Not in the model.

questions.stem: In the amplification phase, what does the first small amount of thrombin do?

options.B: Activates factor VII on the TF-bearing cell

questions.explanation: Amplification: platelets and cofactors (V, VIII released from vWF, XI) are activated, setting the stage for large-scale thrombin generation. A: That follows the thrombin burst. B: Initiation. C: Thrombomodulin does this on endothelium. D: XIIIa, at the end.

questions.stem: Which complex on the activated platelet activates factor X during propagation?
questions.explanation: Tenase (IXa + VIIIa) activates X on the platelet; prothrombinase (Xa + Va) makes the thrombin burst. A: Turns prothrombin into thrombin. C: Initiation, on the TF-bearing cell. D: Activates protein C. E: Inhibits thrombin.

questions.stem: After injury, about how long does the fibrin clot take to form?
questions.explanation: The fibrin clot occurs in 5–10 minutes; the platelet plug appears in 3–5 minutes. B: The platelet plug. C: Too early. D: Too late. E: Too late.

questions.stem: Blood for clotting tests is drawn into citrate tubes. Which factor does the citrate remove?
questions.explanation: Factor IV is calcium, used by both pathways and removed by citrate in blood tubes. A: Fibrinogen. B: Tissue factor, not in blood. C: Proaccelerin. E: Fibrin-stabilizing factor.

questions.stem: A patient starts warfarin. Two days later his PT is prolonged but his aPTT is still normal. What explains this?

options.A: Factor VII is not made in the liver
options.C: Factor IX is not vitamin K dependent
options.D: Heparin is needed to prolong the aPTT
options.E: Factor VII has the shortest half-life

questions.explanation: Factor VII has the shortest half-life and is the first to fall on warfarin, so early warfarin prolongs only the PT. A: It is a vitamin K-dependent liver factor. B: Warfarin blocks vitamin K-dependent synthesis. C: It is. D: Not the reason.

questions.stem: Proconvertin is the common name of which factor?
questions.explanation: V proaccelerin, VII proconvertin, VIII antihemophilic, IX Christmas, X Stuart–Prower, XI plasma thromboplastin antecedent, XIII fibrin-stabilizing. A: Proaccelerin. C: Stuart–Prower factor. D: Plasma thromboplastin antecedent. E: Christmas factor.

questions.stem: Which factor sits where the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways meet?
questions.explanation: Factor X (Stuart–Prower) is where the two pathways meet. A: Intrinsic. B: Extrinsic. D: Downstream, in the common pathway. E: Intrinsic.

questions.stem: Why is there no factor VI?

options.A: It was found to be activated factor V
options.B: It was found to be activated factor VII
options.C: It was found to be tissue factor
options.D: It was found to be calcium
options.E: It was found to be fibrinogen

questions.explanation: Factor VI does not exist; it was found to be activated factor V. B: It was Va. C: That is factor III. D: That is factor IV. E: That is factor I.

questions.stem: Which clotting factor is absent from circulating blood until injury exposes it?
questions.explanation: Tissue factor (III) is not in blood; it is exposed by injury. A: Circulating substrate. C: In plasma. D: Carried by vWF in plasma. E: In plasma.

questions.stem: A septic man has oozing from line sites. Platelets are 40 × 10⁹/L, PT and aPTT are prolonged, fibrinogen 0.8 g/L, and D-dimer is high. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Low fibrinogen (normal 2–4 g/L) is seen in DIC and severe liver disease; DIC prolongs PT and aPTT, consumes platelets and raises D-dimer. A: Prolongs the PT, not the aPTT. B: Isolated aPTT; normal fibrinogen. D: Normal PT and aPTT. E: Normal PT, aPTT and fibrinogen.

questions.stem: Activated factors that escape the injury are washed downstream by flow. Which organ clears them?
questions.explanation: Flow washes activated factors downstream and the liver cleans them: one of four brakes that keep the clot at the injury. B: Not shown as the clearing organ. C: Not shown as the clearing organ. D: Not shown as the clearing organ. E: Not shown as the clearing organ.

questions.stem: A woman with inherited antithrombin deficiency has a DVT. Besides thrombin, which activated factor is poorly neutralized?
questions.explanation: Antithrombin mops up thrombin and factor Xa. A: Destroyed by protein C + S. B: Destroyed by protein C + S. C: Blocked by TFPI. E: Not a target shown.

questions.stem: A newborn with severe protein C deficiency has widespread clotting. Which activated factors escape inactivation?
questions.explanation: Protein C + protein S destroy factors Va and VIIIa. A: Antithrombin targets. B: TFPI. C: Not protein C targets. D: Antithrombin.

questions.stem: Failure of a natural brake on coagulation causes thrombosis in each of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: If one brake fails the patient clots: antithrombin, protein C or protein S deficiency, or factor V Leiden. Factor XI deficiency causes mild bleeding. A: A failed brake. B: A failed brake. D: A failed brake. E: Va resists the protein C brake.

questions.stem: Which enzyme dissolves the fibrin clot as the vessel heals?
questions.explanation: Plasminogen activators turn plasminogen into plasmin within the clot; plasmin slowly dissolves fibrin. B: Activates plasminogen. C: Makes fibrin. D: Cross-links fibrin. E: Inhibits thrombin.

questions.stem: A patient with a pulmonary embolus receives a tissue plasminogen activator. Which product rises in his blood as the clot dissolves?
questions.explanation: Plasmin dissolves fibrin into fibrin degradation (split) products; D-dimer measures fibrin breakdown. A: Not a breakdown product. B: Converted to plasmin. C: Not a breakdown product. E: Not a breakdown product.

questions.stem: A deficiency of a fibrinolysis regulator protein most likely causes which problem?
questions.explanation: Deficiency of any of the regulator proteins of clot lysis increases the risk of thrombosis. A: Factor problem. B: Platelet problem. C: Not the effect. D: Not the effect.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old girl has petechiae and gum bleeding that starts right after she brushes her teeth. Which part of hemostasis is most likely defective?
questions.explanation: Primary (platelet or vessel) disorders: immediate, spontaneous mucocutaneous bleeding with petechiae. Secondary (factor) disorders: delayed joint, muscle and deep tissue bleeds. A: Delayed deep bleeds. C: Tertiary hemostasis. D: Thrombosis, not bleeding. E: Not mucocutaneous bleeding.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy develops a swollen knee several hours after a fall. Small cuts stop bleeding normally. Which disorder fits best?
questions.explanation: Clotting factor problems: bleeding delayed by hours into joints, muscles and deep tissue; bleeding after small cuts usually normal. Classic example: hemophilia A and B. A: Primary pattern. B: Primary pattern. D: Vessel disorder. E: Vessel disorder.

questions.stem: A woman has heavy periods and nosebleeds. Which other finding would point to a platelet or vessel problem rather than a factor deficiency?
questions.explanation: Platelet or vessel problems: immediate bleeding from skin and mucosa, petechiae, purpura, nosebleeds, heavy periods, gum bleeding, prolonged bleeding after small cuts. A: Factor pattern. B: Factor pattern. C: Factor pattern. D: Factor pattern.

questions.stem: A 15-year-old girl has heavy periods, nosebleeds and a recent knee hemarthrosis. How is her bleeding pattern classified?
questions.explanation: Mixed platelet and coagulation disorders combine mucocutaneous and deep tissue bleeds (e.g., vWD). B: No joint bleeds. C: No mucocutaneous bleeds. D: Not joint bleeds. E: Not this picture.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy has profuse epistaxis. Which history item best points to an inherited bleeding disorder?
questions.explanation: History includes bleeding in the neonatal period and after dental extraction, surgery, circumcision or trauma, alongside questions for malignancy (weight loss, night sweats, fever, masses) and diet, drugs and travel. A: Malignancy. B: Malignancy. C: Infection. E: Infection or malignancy.

questions.stem: A child with epistaxis also has bruises. Which history item suggests a malignancy?
questions.explanation: Weight loss, night sweats, fever, lymphadenopathy, masses and a distended abdomen raise concern for malignancy. A: Bleeding disorder. C: Bleeding disorder. D: Factor deficiency. E: Mucocutaneous bleeding.

questions.stem: Which family history item suggests an inherited bleeding disorder?

options.A: Early heart attack in the father
options.C: Iron deficiency in a vegetarian mother
options.D: Hysterectomy at a young age in an aunt

questions.explanation: Family history: consanguinity, bleeding in parents, siblings and relatives, hysterectomy at a young age. A: Thrombosis, not bleeding. B: Hemolysis. C: Diet. E: Not relevant.

questions.stem: A boy has recurrent hemarthroses, but his family history is negative. What is the best interpretation?

options.C: An inherited disorder is still possible
options.E: A vessel disorder is most likely

questions.explanation: A negative family history does not exclude an inherited bleeding disorder. A: Not established by family history. B: A negative history does not exclude it. D: It is needed. E: Joint bleeds point to factors.

questions.stem: When examining a child with bleeding, each of the following is specifically sought EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Exam: general appearance, fever or hypothermia, skin bleeding, retinal hemorrhages, hemarthrosis and contractures, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, masses, bone deformities or absent bones. A: Sought. B: Sought. C: Sought. D: Sought.

questions.stem: A man with cirrhosis and a large spleen has a platelet count of 70 × 10⁹/L. What is the main mechanism?
questions.explanation: A low platelet count (normal 150–400 × 10⁹/L) comes from marrow failure, destruction or splenic pooling. B: Not the main mechanism here. C: Not suggested. D: Not suggested. E: Not suggested.

questions.stem: A man on warfarin for atrial fibrillation is monitored with the INR. What is the usual target?
questions.explanation: INR = PT standardized between laboratories; 0.8–1.2 untreated; used to monitor warfarin, usual target 2–3. A: Normal untreated range. C: Too low. D: Higher than the usual target. E: Too high.

questions.stem: A patient on unfractionated heparin has a normal fibrinogen level. Which test is prolonged?
questions.explanation: Thrombin time is prolonged by heparin and by low or abnormal fibrinogen; heparin also prolongs the aPTT. A: A count, not a time. B: Fibrin breakdown. D: Normal by the stem. E: Warfarin monitoring.

questions.stem: A healthy woman at 30 weeks of pregnancy has a mildly raised D-dimer and no symptoms. What is the best interpretation?

options.B: It confirms a deep vein thrombosis

questions.explanation: D-dimer measures fibrin breakdown (normal < 500 µg/L) and rises in thrombosis, DIC, pregnancy, infection and surgery. B: D-dimer is not specific. C: D-dimer is not specific. D: Measured separately. E: Not measured by D-dimer.

questions.stem: A man with a mild bleeding tendency has a prolonged aPTT and a normal PT. Which cause fits?
questions.explanation: Normal PT + prolonged aPTT (intrinsic only): hemophilia A or B, factor XI or XII deficiency, heparin, vWD, lupus anticoagulant. A: Prolongs the PT. B: Prolongs the PT. C: Normal tests. E: Prolongs both.

questions.stem: A man with early liver disease has a coagulation screen. Which result is expected first?

options.A: A prolonged aPTT with a normal PT
options.E: A prolonged PT with a normal aPTT

questions.explanation: Prolonged PT + normal aPTT (extrinsic only): factor VII deficiency, early warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency, early liver disease. A: Intrinsic pattern. B: Not the early pattern. C: Not the early pattern. D: Not the early pattern.

questions.stem: A patient bleeds. PT and aPTT are prolonged; the thrombin time and fibrinogen are normal. A single deficiency of which factor fits?
questions.explanation: Both prolonged: common pathway or several factors (liver disease, DIC, full warfarin, deficiency of X, V, II or fibrinogen). A normal thrombin time and fibrinogen leave X, V or II. A: PT only. C: aPTT only. D: Normal tests. E: Prolongs the thrombin time.

questions.stem: A girl has heavy periods and easy bruising. Her platelet count is normal, and her PT and aPTT are normal. Which diagnosis remains possible?
questions.explanation: Both normal = not a factor problem: platelet disorder, vWD, vessel wall disorder, factor XIII deficiency. B: Prolongs the aPTT. C: Prolongs the PT. D: Prolongs the PT. E: Prolongs the PT.

questions.stem: A boy's prolonged aPTT corrects after his plasma is mixed 1:1 with normal plasma. What does this show?
questions.explanation: Mixing study: mix 1:1 with normal plasma and repeat. Correction = a factor is missing; no correction = an inhibitor (an antibody). A: It would not correct. B: An inhibitor. C: An inhibitor. D: Not tested by aPTT.

questions.stem: A woman's prolonged aPTT does not correct on a 1:1 mix with normal plasma. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: If the mix does not correct, an inhibitor (an antibody) is present; if it corrects, a factor is missing. A: Would correct. B: Would correct. C: Would correct. E: Normal aPTT.

questions.stem: A man has taken warfarin for six months. Both PT and aPTT are prolonged. What is the best explanation?

options.A: A factor VIII inhibitor has developed

questions.explanation: Early warfarin lowers factor VII first (PT only); the full warfarin effect lowers several vitamin K-dependent factors (II, IX, X too), so both PT and aPTT are prolonged. A: Would not prolong the PT. B: Not suggested. D: That is DIC. E: Normal PT and aPTT.

questions.stem: A boy with severe factor VIII deficiency bleeds into a knee. In the cell-based model, which phase fails?
questions.explanation: Propagation needs the tenase complex (IXa + VIIIa) on activated platelets to make the large thrombin burst; without VIII, the burst fails. A: VIIa/TF still makes a little thrombin. C: Primary hemostasis is intact. D: Factor XIIIa. E: Fibrinolysis.

questions.stem: A woman not on heparin has a prolonged PT, aPTT and thrombin time. A single deficiency of which factor fits?
questions.explanation: Thrombin time measures fibrinogen to fibrin; it is prolonged by heparin or low or abnormal fibrinogen. Fibrinogen deficiency also prolongs PT and aPTT. B: Normal thrombin time. C: Normal thrombin time. D: Normal thrombin time. E: PT only.

questions.stem: Months after a DVT, a man's clot has not dissolved. A defect in which protein best explains this?
questions.explanation: Tissue plasminogen activators turn plasminogen into plasmin within the clot, and plasmin slowly dissolves fibrin. A: Neutralizes thrombin; does not dissolve fibrin. B: Destroys Va and VIIIa; does not dissolve fibrin. C: Cross-links fibrin. E: Stops initiation.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has mucocutaneous bleeding. His platelets lack GPIb. Which step of hemostasis fails?
questions.explanation: GPIb is the vWF receptor; platelets anchor to the endothelium through GPIb binding vWF (adhesion). A: GPIIb-IIIa. B: Endothelin. C: Endothelial injury. D: Factor XIIIa.

questions.stem: A child bleeds after a tooth extraction. His PT is prolonged and his aPTT is normal. A deficiency of which factor fits?
questions.explanation: Prolonged PT + normal aPTT (extrinsic only): factor VII deficiency, early warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency, early liver disease. A: Prolongs the aPTT. C: Prolongs the aPTT. D: Prolongs the aPTT. E: Normal PT and aPTT.

lectures.title: Disorders of hemostasis
lectures.covers: Case-based review of platelet disorders (thrombocytopenia, ITP, HIT, DIC, TTP, HUS, inherited platelet function disorders), coagulation disorders (vitamin K deficiency, factor XIII deficiency, liver disease), von Willebrand disease, vessel wall disorders, and bedside clues to the diagnosis.

items.p: Epistaxis in children is mostly local (upper respiratory infection, allergy), but it can be a bleeding disorder.
Red flags: epistaxis lasting > 30 minutes, recurrent or severe enough to need red cell transfusions; severe anemia.
Suspect a severe bleeding disorder with: early onset, prolonged, recurrent or postoperative bleeding, need for transfusions, positive family history.
Inherited disorders: infancy and early childhood, bleeding in males (X-linked, e.g. hemophilia), past postoperative bleeding, positive family history.

table: Male toddler, deep tissue or joint bleeding
Girl with heavy periods and mucocutaneous bleeding
Well, one bleeding site (e.g. one nostril)

items.p: Platelets: 2–3 µm, non-nucleated fragments of megakaryocytes; production regulated by thrombopoietin; normal count 150–450 × 10⁹/L.
Defects are acquired or inherited, of number (thrombocytopenia; thrombocytosis, reactive or primary) or function (receptors: Bernard–Soulier, Glanzmann; release/storage; biochemical pathways).

table: Marrow failure (aplastic anemia, MDS, myelofibrosis, leukemia), megaloblastic anemia, infections, drugs (chemotherapy, ethanol, sulfas), radiotherapy
Cirrhosis with portal hypertension, splenic tumor, sickle cell disease. 30% of platelets sit in a normal spleen, 90% in an enlarged one; often with anemia or leukopenia

items.note: Slide 5 gives a platelet life span of 5–7 days; most references give about 7–10 days. Not tested.

items.p: The most common acquired autoimmune bleeding disorder of childhood. Isolated thrombocytopenia (< 100 × 10⁹/L) with no other cause: a diagnosis of exclusion.

ul: Peaks at 2–5 years; more cases in spring and early summer
About 80% primary; secondary with SLE, APS, CVID, CLL, Evans, ALPS, HIV, hepatitis C, H. pylori, vaccines, infection
Mechanism: increased destruction (autoantibodies, macrophage phagocytosis, cytotoxic T cells) and decreased production (impaired megakaryocyte maturation)
Course: ~70% resolve within 6 months; chronic (> 12 months) in 20–30% of children
Presentation: sudden mucocutaneous bleeding in a well child (petechiae, purpura, gums, nose, GI, hematuria, heavy periods); intracranial hemorrhage very rare; fatigue in 22%
Case: platelets 4,000/mm³, high MPV, large platelets = young platelets → increased destruction (lecturer's notes)

items.p: Severe = clinically significant bleeding requiring treatment. Refractory = significant thrombocytopenia and/or bleeding despite first- and second-line therapies.

Reconsider ITP with: recurrent infections and eczema, bone pain, constitutional symptoms, family history, dysmorphic features, organomegaly, marked lymphadenopathy or masses, anemia or neutropenia, blasts. A normal exam with isolated thrombocytopenia supports ITP.

items.note: Slide 18 says "most children are asymptomatic"; most references describe mild mucocutaneous bleeding as the usual presentation. Not tested.

ul: Goal: a platelet count with adequate hemostasis, not a normal count
Decide on bleeding severity (not the count alone), preference, quality of life and durable response
Traditional: observation, steroids, IVIG, anti-D immunoglobulin, splenectomy
Novel: rituximab (anti-CD20), thrombopoietin receptor agonists
2019 paradigm: observe mild ITP → short steroids when treatment is needed → TPO-RA if first line fails
An immune reaction 5–15 days after heparin
IgG binds the platelet factor 4–heparin complex and platelets → platelet activation, thrombocytopenia, more thrombin
Result: thrombosis (DVT, PE, cerebral venous sinus, limb, stroke, MI)
Treatment: stop heparin and give a non-heparin anticoagulant

items.note: Slide 21 says HIT leads to "bleeding and thrombosis"; standard sources stress thrombosis, with bleeding uncommon despite the low count. Only thrombosis is tested.

items.p: Schistocytes + thrombocytopenia = thrombotic microangiopathy until proven otherwise.

table: Sepsis, trauma, cancer, obstetric, transfusion reaction
Anti-ADAMTS13 antibody, or ADAMTS13 gene variants
Shiga toxin (STEC, Shigella), or complement dysregulation (atypical)

items.p: DIC: coagulation and fibrinolysis activated inside vessels → thrombosis, bleeding, organ damage. Fever, profuse bleeding, shock, multi-organ failure, purpura fulminans. Labs: low platelets, prolonged PT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, schistocytes. Treat the cause; platelets, plasma or cryoprecipitate (fibrinogen-rich) for bleeding.
TTP: rare; ADAMTS13 normally cleaves large vWF multimers. Treatment: supportive, plasmapheresis (removes anti-ADAMTS13 antibodies), immunosuppressants, ADAMTS13 replacement.
HUS: MAHA + thrombocytopenia + acute kidney injury; 90% after Shiga toxin-producing E. coli or Shigella dysenteriae; typically children; clinical diagnosis; supportive care.

Rare bleeding disorders with mucocutaneous bleeding and usually a normal count. Mostly acquired: aspirin, NSAIDs, penicillin, cephalosporins, anticonvulsants; uremia, liver disease, autoimmune disease. Inherited forms are mostly AR with early-onset bleeding.
All three are AR; GT and BSS occur in about 1 in 1 million. Among rare bleeding disorders, factor VII deficiency is reported most often.
Diagnosis: early-onset bleeding, family history, normal PT and aPTT, abnormal platelet function studies, absent glycoproteins on flow cytometry, genetic testing in selected cases.
Treatment by bleeding severity: platelet transfusion; recombinant factor VIIa if platelet-refractory.
Case: a man with lifelong transfusion-dependent nosebleeds, normal platelet count and size, normal PT and aPTT → Glanzmann thrombasthenia (worked out; the slides give no answer).
Inherited: hemophilia (separate lecture), other factor deficiencies. Acquired: warfarin, heparin, chemotherapy; vitamin K deficiency; DIC; inhibitors; liver disease.

ul: Hemophilia case: a 15-month-old boy, swollen knee and forehead hematoma, bleeding maternal uncle, normal CBC and PT, prolonged aPTT
Factor XIII deficiency case: bleeding after tonsillectomy, delayed umbilical cord bleeding, poor wound healing, miscarriages, consanguinity; platelets, PT, aPTT, thrombin time and smear all normal

items.p: Vitamin K deficiency:

ul: Vitamin K (fat soluble; leafy vegetables, colonic bacteria) is needed for II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S
Causes: low intake (breast milk), poor absorption (celiac disease, cystic fibrosis), newborns, prolonged antibiotics, warfarin
Most common in newborns (hemorrhagic disease of the newborn); late form up to 3 months
PT prolonged first (isolated early), then PTT; treat with vitamin K and the cause

items.note: Slide 37 places intracranial and retroperitoneal bleeding in the "early form, 1–7 days". Most references split it into early (< 24 h), classic (2–7 days, GI, skin, umbilical) and late (2–12 weeks, often intracranial). Timings and sites are not tested.

items.p: Liver cirrhosis:

ul: Lower synthesis of most factors except VIII; portal hypertension → big spleen traps platelets
Bilirubin up, albumin down, PT and aPTT prolonged
Fresh frozen plasma (all clotting factors) for active bleeding
Vitamin K corrects the PT in vitamin K deficiency, not in liver failure. A low factor V points to liver failure (V is not vitamin K dependent).

items.note: The slide 45 figure lists "↓ AST and ALT" in late cirrhosis; transaminases are usually normal or mildly raised then rather than low. Not tested.

items.p: The most common congenital bleeding disorder (~1%, males and females equally). A quantitative or qualitative vWF defect → poor platelet adhesion and a secondary coagulation defect. Mostly asymptomatic; found through family history or preoperative screening. Mucocutaneous bleeding (joints in type 3), prolonged bleeding time and aPTT.
Think of vWD in every adolescent girl with heavy periods, iron deficiency and no gynecologic cause.
Case: a 14-year-old girl with heavy periods, nosebleeds, a hemarthrosis, an aunt with an early hysterectomy, normal platelets and PT, prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing.

table: Marked lack of vWF and FVIII; hemophilia-like
Loss of high-molecular-weight multimers, low activity
vWF binds GPIb too avidly; sometimes thrombocytopenia
Poor vWF binding to FVIII; low FVIII, normal vWF activity; suspect in females with isolated FVIII deficiency

items.p: Treatment:

ul: Desmopressin (DDAVP) for type 1 and most type 2: endothelial release of vWF, vWF/FVIII up 2–5-fold
vWF replacement for non-responders and severe cases
Antifibrinolytics for mucosal bleeding; platelet transfusion in type 2B
Bypassing agents (rFVIIa, PCC) in severe cases and with inhibitors to infused vWF
Supportive: no contact sports, aspirin or NSAIDs; estrogen or endometrial ablation for heavy periods

items.note: The backup table (slide 52) lists DDAVP for type 2B. Standard guidance usually avoids DDAVP in 2B because it can worsen thrombocytopenia. Not tested; ask the lecturer.

summary.h: When the vessel is the problem

table: Purpura on buttocks and legs, arthritis, abdominal pain, nephritis; commonest childhood vasculitis
Normal platelets and clotting; check urine
Perifollicular bleeding, corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums
Diet history; response to vitamin C
Stretchy skin, hypermobile joints, bruising, poor wound healing
Recurrent epistaxis, telangiectasia on lips and fingers, AVMs in lung, liver, brain
Flat purple patches on forearms and hands

items.p: Coagulation occurs on the surfaces of platelets and endothelial cells.

cards.a: > 30 minutes, recurrent, needs red cell transfusion; severe anemia
Decreased production, increased destruction (immune or nonimmune), splenic sequestration

cards.q: Share of platelets in a normal versus an enlarged spleen
cards.a: About 30% versus 90%
DIC, TTP, HUS
Isolated thrombocytopenia < 100 × 10⁹/L with no other cause; a diagnosis of exclusion
~70% resolve within 6 months; chronic (> 12 months) in 20–30%
Newly diagnosed 0–3 months; persistent 3–12 months; chronic ≥ 12 months
Increased destruction (antibodies, macrophages, cytotoxic T cells) and impaired megakaryocyte maturation
Infections with eczema, bone pain, constitutional symptoms, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, anemia or neutropenia, blasts
Observe mild ITP → short steroids → TPO receptor agonist
IgG against PF4–heparin activates platelets → thrombosis; stop heparin, give a non-heparin anticoagulant
Low platelets, prolonged PT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, schistocytes

cards.q: DIC versus TTP versus HUS: key separators
cards.a: DIC: prolonged PT/aPTT. TTP: ADAMTS13 < 10%, brain and heart. HUS: Shiga toxin, kidney injury.
Plasmapheresis, immunosuppressants, ADAMTS13 replacement, supportive care
MAHA, thrombocytopenia, acute kidney injury; 90% after Shiga toxin (EHEC, Shigella)
AR; absent GPIIb/IIIa; normal count and size; aggregates with ristocetin only
AR; absent GPIb/IX/V; low count, large platelets; no aggregation with ristocetin
AR; no alpha granules; large gray platelets, low count; myelofibrosis, splenomegaly
Aspirin, NSAIDs, penicillin, cephalosporins, anticonvulsants; uremia, liver disease, autoimmune disease
Delayed umbilical cord bleeding, poor wound healing, miscarriages; all screening tests normal
Factors II, VII, IX, X; proteins C and S
Breast milk, malabsorption (celiac, CF), newborns, prolonged antibiotics, warfarin

cards.q: Liver failure versus vitamin K deficiency
cards.a: Vitamin K corrects the PT only in deficiency; low factor V points to liver failure
Factor VIII
~1%, most common congenital bleeding disorder; adolescent girl with heavy periods and iron deficiency
1: mild deficiency (70–80%, AD). 2: qualitative (15–20%). 3: marked vWF + FVIII deficiency (AR).
2B: vWF binds GPIb too avidly, low platelets. 2N: poor binding to FVIII, low FVIII.
Types 1 and most 2; releases endothelial vWF, raises vWF/FVIII 2–5-fold

cards.q: Vessel disorders: HSP, scurvy, EDS, HHT, senile purpura
cards.a: Immune complexes; vitamin C/collagen; inherited collagen; abnormal vessels; connective tissue loss

questions.stem: An 8-year-old girl has had a nosebleed for an hour. Which feature is a red flag for a bleeding disorder?
questions.explanation: Red flags: long-lasting (> 30 minutes), recurrent, severe epistaxis needing red cell transfusions, and severe anemia. A: Points to a local cause. B: A common local cause. C: A common local cause. D: Reassuring.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of nosebleeds in children?
questions.explanation: Epistaxis is common in children and mostly due to local conditions such as upper respiratory infections and allergy, but it can be due to a bleeding disorder. A: Possible, but less common. C: Possible, but less common. D: Rare. E: Rare.

questions.stem: Which hormone regulates the differentiation and proliferation of platelet precursors?
questions.explanation: Platelets are small (2–3 µm), non-nucleated fragments of megakaryocytes; their production is regulated by thrombopoietin. B: Red cells. C: Neutrophils. D: Eosinophils. E: Lymphocytes.

questions.stem: A child has a platelet count of 900 × 10⁹/L during recovery from pneumonia. How is this classified?
questions.explanation: Platelet number problems: thrombocytopenia (decreased production, increased destruction, splenic sequestration) and thrombocytosis (reactive or primary). A: A marrow disorder, not a response to illness. B: Lowers the count. D: Not a number problem. E: A function problem.

questions.stem: Bernard–Soulier syndrome and Glanzmann thrombasthenia are which kind of platelet defect?
questions.explanation: Function defects: receptors (Bernard–Soulier, Glanzmann), release/storage, biochemical pathways. A: E.g. gray platelet syndrome. B: Another function group. C: A number problem. E: A number problem.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old has macrocytic anemia, neutropenia and a platelet count of 40 × 10⁹/L. The marrow shows dysplasia. What is the mechanism of his thrombocytopenia?
questions.explanation: MDS: a clonal stem cell disorder with ineffective hematopoiesis, marrow dysplasia and cytopenias, with a risk of AML. It lowers platelets by decreased production. A: Not suggested by dysplasia. B: No splenomegaly given. C: Not suggested. D: Not suggested.

questions.stem: Each causes thrombocytopenia by decreased marrow production EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Decreased production: marrow failure, megaloblastic anemia, infections, drugs (chemotherapy, ethanol, sulfas), radiotherapy. Cirrhosis lowers platelets by splenic sequestration. A: Decreased production. C: Decreased production. D: Decreased production. E: Decreased production.

questions.stem: A man with cirrhosis has a large spleen, platelets of 60 × 10⁹/L and mild leukopenia. About what share of his platelets may be held in the spleen?
questions.explanation: About 30% of platelets are sequestered in the spleen normally and 90% with splenic enlargement; anemia and/or leukopenia often accompany it. A: The normal share. B: Below the share given for enlargement. D: Too low. E: Below the share given for enlargement.

questions.stem: Which disorder lowers the platelet count by splenic sequestration?
questions.explanation: Splenic sequestration: cirrhosis with portal hypertension and splenomegaly, splenic tumor, splenic malfunction in sickle cell disease. B: Decreased production. C: Immune destruction. D: Nonimmune destruction. E: Decreased production.

questions.stem: A healthy 18-year-old has sudden oral bleeding and petechiae, no organomegaly, platelets of 4,000/mm³, normal Hb and WBC, a high MPV and large platelets on the smear. What is the mechanism?
questions.explanation: Lecturer's notes: immune thrombocytopenia; large platelets = young platelets. The marrow is producing, so the platelets are being destroyed. A: Large young platelets show an active marrow. B: No splenomegaly. C: Not the cause. E: Not the cause.

questions.stem: A girl with immune thrombocytopenia has large platelets on her smear. What do they indicate?

options.C: Clumping of platelets in the tube
options.D: Old platelets pooled in the spleen
options.E: Young platelets from an active marrow

questions.explanation: Lecturer's notes: in ITP the platelet count falls and platelet size rises; large platelets are young platelets. A: Gray platelet syndrome. B: Bernard–Soulier syndrome. C: An artefact, not size. D: Not the explanation.

questions.stem: Which cause of increased platelet destruction is nonimmune?
questions.explanation: Immune: ITP, HIT, SLE. Nonimmune: DIC (a mixed platelet and coagulation disorder), TTP, HUS. B: Immune. C: Immune. D: Immune complexes. E: Immune.

questions.stem: Immune thrombocytopenia is defined by an isolated platelet count below what level?
questions.explanation: ITP: isolated thrombocytopenia (< 100 × 10⁹/L) without other causes; a diagnosis of exclusion. A: The lower limit of normal. B: Too low. D: Too low. E: Too low.

questions.stem: A 4-year-old has petechiae and a platelet count of 12 × 10⁹/L. How is ITP diagnosed?
questions.explanation: ITP is a diagnosis of exclusion: isolated thrombocytopenia in the absence of other causes or associated disorders. A: Not the basis of diagnosis. C: Not routinely. D: Used for function disorders. E: Used for inherited disorders.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old has just been diagnosed with ITP. About what is the chance of spontaneous resolution within 6 months?
questions.explanation: Childhood ITP is mostly self-limited, with ~70% spontaneous resolution in 6 months; chronic ITP (> 12 months) in 20–30%. A: Too low. B: Too low. C: Too high. E: Too low.

questions.stem: About what share of children with ITP develop chronic ITP?
questions.explanation: Chronic ITP (lasting > 12 months) is seen in 20–30% of children. B: Too low. C: Too low. D: Too high. E: The share that resolves.

questions.stem: At what age does childhood ITP peak?
questions.explanation: Childhood ITP incidence is highest at about 2–5 years and falls after that. A: Lower than the peak. B: After the peak. C: After the peak. D: Lowest.

questions.stem: Childhood ITP shows seasonal variability. When are cases most frequent?
questions.explanation: Monthly cases peak from about March to July and are lowest around October. A: The lowest months. B: Not the peak. D: Falling to the lowest point. E: Before the peak.

questions.stem: A child's ITP was diagnosed 5 months ago. How is it classified now?
questions.explanation: New classification: newly diagnosed 0–3 months, persistent 3–12 months, chronic ≥ 12 months. A: 0–3 months. C: 12 months or more. D: Needs failure of first- and second-line therapy. E: Needs clinically significant bleeding requiring treatment.

questions.stem: Which term describes ITP with clinically significant bleeding despite first- and second-line therapies?
questions.explanation: Refractory: persistent clinically significant thrombocytopenia and/or bleeding despite first- and second-line therapies, requiring treatment. Severe: clinically significant bleeding requiring treatment. A: Bleeding requiring treatment, not failed therapy. B: Duration ≥ 12 months. C: Duration 3–12 months. E: Duration 0–3 months.

questions.stem: Under the old classification, ITP became chronic after how long?
questions.explanation: Old: acute 0–6 months, chronic ≥ 6 months. New: chronic ≥ 12 months. B: End of the new "newly diagnosed" period. C: The new definition. D: Not used. E: Not used.

questions.stem: About what share of ITP is primary?
questions.explanation: Primary ITP ~80%; the rest is secondary (SLE 5%, APS, CVID, CLL, Evans, ALPS, HIV, hepatitis C, H. pylori, vaccines, systemic infection). A: Too low. C: Too high. D: Too low. E: Too low.

questions.stem: A woman with ITP is found to have Helicobacter pylori infection. How is her ITP classified?
questions.explanation: Secondary ITP causes include H. pylori, SLE, APS, CVID, CLL, ALPS, HIV, hepatitis C, vaccines and systemic infection. A: Defined by duration. B: Needs autoimmune hemolysis or neutropenia. C: Defined by failed treatment. E: No drug given.

questions.stem: Besides increased destruction, which mechanism lowers the platelet count in ITP?

options.A: Pooling of platelets in the spleen
options.D: Lack of folate for DNA synthesis

questions.explanation: ITP: increased destruction (autoantibodies, macrophage phagocytosis, cytotoxic T cells) and decreased production (impaired megakaryocyte maturation). A: Not the mechanism shown. B: TTP and DIC. C: Not the mechanism shown. D: Megaloblastic anemia.

questions.stem: In ITP, which cells phagocytose antibody-coated platelets?
questions.explanation: Antibody-coated platelets are taken up by macrophages (APCs), which present platelet antigens (epitope spreading). A: Not shown. B: Not shown. D: Make the autoantibodies. E: Not shown.

questions.stem: In ITP, which T cells destroy platelets directly?
questions.explanation: Tc-cell (CD8)-mediated platelet destruction is one of the mechanisms; Th cells help B cells make autoantibodies. A: Help B cells. C: Not shown. D: Not shown. E: Not shown.

questions.stem: Which bleeding manifestation is very rare in childhood ITP?
questions.explanation: ITP: mucocutaneous bleeding (petechiae, purpura, gum bleeding, epistaxis, GI, hematuria, heavy menses). Lecturer's note: intracranial hemorrhage is very rare. B: The most typical sign. C: Common. D: Common. E: Common.

questions.stem: About what share of children with ITP report fatigue?
questions.explanation: Fatigue is seen in 22% of children with ITP, related to the disease and its treatment. A: Too low. B: Too high. C: Too high. D: Too low.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old has petechiae and a platelet count of 15 × 10⁹/L. Which finding should make you reconsider ITP?
questions.explanation: Reconsider the diagnosis with recurrent infections, eczema, bone pain, constitutional symptoms, family history, dysmorphic features, organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, other cytopenias or blasts. A: Typical of ITP. B: Typical mucocutaneous bleeding. C: Supports isolated thrombocytopenia. E: Supports ITP.

questions.stem: A child has petechiae and a platelet count of 20 × 10⁹/L. Which additional finding argues most against ITP?
questions.explanation: ITP is isolated thrombocytopenia. Concomitant anemia or neutropenia warrants broader evaluation (e.g. marrow failure, malignancy). A: Young platelets fit ITP. B: Fits isolated thrombocytopenia. D: Supports ITP. E: Mucocutaneous bleeding fits ITP.

questions.stem: Which history best fits ITP in a child?

options.A: Sudden bleeding in a well child

questions.explanation: Lecturer's note: ITP = sudden onset of mucocutaneous bleeding. A normal exam with isolated thrombocytopenia supports it. B: Factor deficiency. C: Inherited disorder. D: Malignancy. E: Reconsider ITP.

questions.stem: What is the goal of ITP treatment?
questions.explanation: Goal: achieve a platelet count associated with adequate hemostasis. The decision to treat rests on bleeding severity, not count alone. A: Not required. C: Not the goal. D: Not the goal. E: Not the goal.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with new ITP has a platelet count of 25 × 10⁹/L and a few petechiae, with no mucosal bleeding. What is the best management?
questions.explanation: 2019 paradigm: observe mild ITP → short steroids when treatment is needed → TPO-RA if first-line therapy fails. Treatment is indicated in mucosal bleeding with platelets < 10 × 10⁹/L. A: Not needed for mild ITP. B: Not first line. D: Not first line. E: Not indicated.

questions.stem: An adult's ITP fails a short course of steroids and she needs further treatment. What is the next step in the 2019 paradigm?
questions.explanation: 2019 treatment paradigm: observe mild ITP → short steroids when treatment is needed → TPO-RA if first-line therapy fails. A: Short steroids only, then a TPO-RA. B: Not ITP treatment. C: Not the next step given. E: TTP.

questions.stem: Rituximab treats ITP by targeting which molecule?
questions.explanation: Novel ITP therapies: rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody) and thrombopoietin receptor agonists. A: Not the target. B: Not the target. C: T cells. D: CD40 ligand.

questions.stem: Each is a traditional ITP treatment EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Traditional: observation, steroids, IVIG, anti-D IG, splenectomy. Novel: rituximab, TPO receptor agonists. B: Traditional. C: Traditional. D: Traditional. E: Traditional.

questions.stem: A child with ITP has platelets of 30 × 10⁹/L and no bleeding; another has platelets of 30 × 10⁹/L and heavy gum bleeding. What mainly decides who is treated?
questions.explanation: The decision to treat is based on bleeding severity and not just the platelet count, plus family/patient preference, QoL and evidence of durable response. A: The same in both. B: Not the basis. D: Not the basis. E: Not the basis.

questions.stem: A man receiving heparin after hip surgery has his platelets fall from 250 to 90 × 10⁹/L on day 7, then develops a DVT. What is the mechanism?
questions.explanation: HIT: an immune reaction 5–15 days after heparin; IgG binds the platelet factor 4/heparin complex and platelets, activating them, lowering their count and raising thrombin generation. A: Not HIT. B: HIT is immune. C: Not this picture. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A patient develops heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with a new thrombus. What is the treatment?
questions.explanation: Treatment: stop heparin and give a non-heparin anticoagulant. A: Not the treatment given. C: Still heparin. D: Not relevant. E: The clot needs treatment.

questions.stem: Besides lowering the platelet count, what do HIT antibodies do?
questions.explanation: The IgG–PF4/heparin complex activates platelets, causes thrombocytopenia and increases thrombin generation, leading to thrombosis. A: Not the effect. B: Not the effect. C: TTP. D: Not the effect.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man has had fever and chills for a day and is now comatose and hypotensive with diffuse ecchymoses. Hb, WBC and platelets are low; PT and aPTT are prolonged; CRP is high. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Lecturer's note: sepsis/infection with DIC. Sick appearance, fever, shock and purpura point to DIC. A: Does not explain the coagulopathy. C: Does not explain the picture. D: PT and aPTT would be normal. E: Not a new illness with shock.

questions.stem: In DIC, which process is abnormally activated inside the vessels together with coagulation?
questions.explanation: DIC: a systemic, life-threatening process in which coagulation and fibrinolysis are abnormally activated within the vasculature, causing thrombosis, bleeding and end-organ damage. B: Not the defining process. C: Not the defining process. D: Not the defining process. E: Not the defining process.

questions.stem: Each is a recognized trigger of DIC EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Triggers: sepsis, trauma, cancer, obstetric complications, severe transfusion reactions. A: A trigger. B: A trigger. D: A trigger. E: A trigger.

questions.stem: A septic patient has low platelets, a prolonged PT and schistocytes. Which other result fits DIC?
questions.explanation: DIC: low platelets, prolonged PT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer, schistocytes. A: D-dimer is high. B: TTP. C: Immune hemolysis. E: Low fibrinogen prolongs it.

questions.stem: A woman with DIC after placental abruption is bleeding, with a fibrinogen of 0.6 g/L. Which product best replaces fibrinogen?
questions.explanation: Treat the cause; supportive care with platelets, plasma or cryoprecipitate (a plasma product rich in fibrinogen) for bleeding. A: Replaces platelets. B: Replaces red cells. C: Not a clotting product. D: Not the treatment.

questions.stem: What is rapidly spreading skin bleeding and necrosis in DIC called?
questions.explanation: DIC presents with fever, profuse bleeding, shock, multi-organ failure, thrombosis, and purpura fulminans (rapidly spreading skin bleeding and necrosis). B: Vasculitis. C: Loss of connective tissue. D: Not this finding. E: Scurvy.

questions.stem: What is the main treatment of DIC?
questions.explanation: Treat the cause; give platelets, plasma or cryoprecipitate for bleeding as supportive care. A: TTP. C: Not the treatment. D: Not the treatment. E: Not the treatment given.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman has confusion, fever, schistocytes and a platelet count of 15 × 10⁹/L. PT and aPTT are normal. ADAMTS13 activity is 4%. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: TTP: microscopic clots in small vessels, intravascular hemolysis and organ damage (kidney, heart, brain); ADAMTS13 < 10%; normal PT and aPTT. A: PT and aPTT prolonged. B: ADAMTS13 normal or mildly low. C: No schistocytes. E: No heparin exposure.

questions.stem: A woman with acquired TTP has antibodies against ADAMTS13. Which treatment removes them?
questions.explanation: TTP treatment: supportive care, plasmapheresis to reduce circulating antibodies against ADAMTS13, immunosuppressants, ADAMTS13 replacement. A: Not the treatment. B: Not the treatment given. D: Kidney support. E: Not relevant.

questions.stem: Why do platelet clots form in TTP?
questions.explanation: ADAMTS13 cleaves large vWF multimers into smaller units; when it is inhibited, large multimers persist and clots form in small vessels. A: DIC. B: HUS. C: HIT. D: Factor V Leiden.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old has had several episodes of TTP. Antibodies to ADAMTS13 are absent and its activity is very low. What is the cause?
questions.explanation: TTP triggers: anti-ADAMTS13 autoantibody (immune) or ADAMTS13 gene variants (congenital). B: Atypical HUS. C: Typical HUS. D: HIT. E: DIC.
