questions.stem: A 4-year-old has bloody diarrhea, then pallor, platelets of 40 × 10⁹/L, schistocytes and a rising creatinine. PT and aPTT are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: HUS: triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia and acute kidney injury; typically children. A: ADAMTS13 < 10%; brain and heart. B: PT and aPTT prolonged. C: No hemolysis. E: Normal platelets.

questions.stem: What usually triggers hemolytic uremic syndrome in a child?
questions.explanation: About 90% of HUS follows infection with a Shiga toxin-producing bacterium: enterohemorrhagic E. coli or Shigella dysenteriae. A: TTP. B: Atypical HUS. C: DIC. D: HIT.

questions.stem: A child has HUS without diarrhea, and stool tests for Shiga toxin are negative. What is the likely mechanism?
questions.explanation: HUS triggers: Shiga toxin (STEC) or complement dysregulation (atypical HUS). A: TTP. B: HIT. D: DIC. E: Not a TMA.

questions.stem: How is typical hemolytic uremic syndrome treated?
questions.explanation: HUS: diagnosis based on the clinical scenario; treatment supportive. A: TTP. C: Not the treatment given. D: Not the treatment given. E: Not the treatment given.

questions.stem: A patient has schistocytes and a low platelet count. What should be assumed until proven otherwise?
questions.explanation: Schistocytes + thrombocytopenia = thrombotic microangiopathy until proven otherwise (DIC, TTP, HUS). A: No schistocytes in ITP. B: Spherocytes, not schistocytes. C: Not schistocytes. E: Not to be assumed.

questions.stem: Which laboratory feature best separates DIC from TTP and HUS?
questions.explanation: DIC: PT/aPTT prolonged, fibrinogen low. TTP and HUS: normal PT/aPTT. A: All three. B: All three. C: Hemolysis in all three. D: Hallmark of HUS.

questions.stem: Which organ involvement is the hallmark of TTP?
questions.explanation: Organ hallmark: DIC, bleeding and clotting with shock; TTP, brain, heart and fever; HUS, acute kidney injury. B: The kidney is the hallmark of HUS. C: Not a hallmark. D: Not a hallmark. E: Not a hallmark.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man has GI bleeding and lifelong nosebleeds that needed platelet and red cell transfusions. His platelet count, PT and aPTT are normal, and his platelets are of normal size. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Red flags: severe mucocutaneous bleeding, transfusion dependence, normal platelet count. Glanzmann thrombasthenia: normal count and size, absent GPIIb/IIIa. A: Low count, large platelets. B: Low count, large gray platelets. D: Low count. E: Prolonged aPTT; joint bleeds.

questions.stem: A patient's platelets lack GPIIb/IIIa. What do aggregation studies show?
questions.explanation: Glanzmann thrombasthenia: aggregation only with ristocetin. Bernard–Soulier: aggregation with all agonists except ristocetin. A: Bernard–Soulier syndrome. C: Gray platelet syndrome. D: Not with absent GPIIb/IIIa. E: Aspirin effect.

questions.stem: A boy has lifelong mucosal bleeding, platelets of 60 × 10⁹/L and giant platelets. His platelets do not aggregate with ristocetin. Which glycoprotein is missing?
questions.explanation: Bernard–Soulier syndrome: absent or decreased GPIb/IX/V (the vWF receptor), defective adhesion, low count, large platelets, aggregation with all agonists except ristocetin. B: Glanzmann thrombasthenia. C: Collagen receptor. D: Collagen receptor. E: Not the defect.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old has lifelong nosebleeds, platelets of 70 × 10⁹/L and large platelets. Aggregation with ADP and collagen is normal, but absent with ristocetin. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: BSS: AR, absent GPIb/IX/V, low count, large platelets, no aggregation with ristocetin. A: Normal count and size. B: Normal aggregation. C: Reduced response to collagen. D: Not a platelet disorder.

questions.stem: A child has mucocutaneous bleeding, splenomegaly and marrow fibrosis. Her platelets are few, large and gray. What do they lack?
questions.explanation: Gray platelet syndrome: AR; absent alpha granules and defective secretion; bleeding plus myelofibrosis and splenomegaly; low count; large gray platelets; reduced aggregation with collagen. A: Not the defect. B: Bernard–Soulier syndrome. D: Glanzmann thrombasthenia. E: Not the defect.

questions.stem: How are Glanzmann thrombasthenia, Bernard–Soulier syndrome and gray platelet syndrome inherited?
questions.explanation: All three are AR, with early-onset mucocutaneous bleeding. A: Not as given. B: Hemophilia. C: Not as given. E: Not as given.

questions.stem: A man on long-term dialysis bleeds from his gums. Platelet count, PT and aPTT are normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Platelet function disorders: mucocutaneous bleeding, usually normal count; mostly acquired (drugs; uremia, liver disease, autoimmune disease). A: Count is normal. C: Inherited, severe, from childhood. D: Prolongs the PT. E: Prolongs the aPTT.

questions.stem: Each drug can impair platelet function EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Drugs: aspirin, NSAIDs, penicillin, cephalosporins, anticonvulsants. Warfarin acts on vitamin K-dependent factors. A: Impairs platelet function. B: An NSAID; impairs platelet function. C: Impairs platelet function. E: Impair platelet function.

questions.stem: About how common are Glanzmann thrombasthenia and Bernard–Soulier syndrome?
questions.explanation: Platelet function disorders are rare bleeding disorders, a small share of congenital bleeding disorders; incidence approximately 1 in 1 million. A: Far too common. C: Too common. D: The frequency of vWD. E: Too common.

questions.stem: In a global survey of rare bleeding disorders, which was reported most often?
questions.explanation: Rare bleeding disorders: FVII 6,264, FXI 5,192, Glanzmann 2,179, FV 1,560, FX 1,427, FXIII 1,126, Bernard–Soulier 361. A: Second. B: Less common. D: Less common. E: Least of those shown.

questions.stem: A boy with severe mucocutaneous bleeding has a normal count but abnormal platelet function studies. Which test shows a missing platelet glycoprotein?
questions.explanation: Diagnosis: abnormal platelet function studies; decreased or absent platelet glycoproteins on flow cytometry; genetic testing in selected cases. B: Shows size, not glycoproteins. C: Factor inhibitor versus deficiency. D: Not the test. E: Fibrinogen to fibrin.

questions.stem: A man with Glanzmann thrombasthenia keeps bleeding despite platelet transfusions. What is the next treatment?
questions.explanation: Treatment is guided by bleeding severity: platelet transfusion, recombinant factor VII for platelet-refractory cases, supportive care. A: Factors are normal. B: Fibrinogen. C: Factors are normal. D: vWD.

questions.stem: A 15-month-old boy has a painful swollen left knee and a large forehead hematoma. His maternal uncle has a bleeding disorder. CBC, PT and smear are normal; the aPTT is prolonged. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Red flags: a male toddler with joint swelling and a large hematoma, a positive maternal family history, isolated prolongation of the aPTT. A: Mucocutaneous bleeding. B: Normal CBC. D: Prolonged PT. E: Normal aPTT.

questions.stem: A boy and his maternal uncle both have hemophilia. Which inheritance explains this?
questions.explanation: Inherited bleeding disorders: bleeding in males suggests sex-linked recessive diseases such as hemophilia. A: Would affect the father's side too. C: Passed father to son, not via the mother. D: Not hemophilia. E: Not inherited this way.

questions.stem: Which is an acquired disorder of secondary hemostasis?
questions.explanation: Acquired: drugs (warfarin, heparin, chemotherapy), vitamin K deficiency, DIC, inhibitors of coagulation, liver disease. Inherited: hemophilia, other factor deficiencies. A: Inherited. B: Inherited. C: Platelet disorder. E: Platelet disorder.

questions.stem: An 18-year-old girl bleeds after a tonsillectomy. She had delayed umbilical cord bleeding, poor wound healing and two miscarriages; her parents are first cousins. Platelets, PT, aPTT, thrombin time and smear are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Red flags: severe bleeding with a normal coagulation profile, delayed umbilical cord and post-surgical bleeding, poor wound healing, recurrent miscarriages. Diagnosis: factor XIII deficiency. B: Mild; no umbilical bleeding pattern. C: Mucocutaneous; no wound-healing defect. D: Prolonged PT. E: Prolonged aPTT if low VIII.

questions.stem: Besides factors II, VII, IX and X, vitamin K is needed to make which proteins?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is needed for factors II, VII, IX and X and proteins C and S. A: Not vitamin K dependent. B: Not vitamin K dependent. C: Not vitamin K dependent. D: Not vitamin K dependent.

questions.stem: Besides green leafy vegetables, what is a source of vitamin K?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is fat soluble, found in green leafy vegetables and synthesized by colonic bacteria. A: The liver uses it; does not make it. C: Vitamin D. D: Not a source. E: Not given as a source.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with celiac disease has bruising and a prolonged PT. What is the cause?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K deficiency causes: low intake (breast milk), poor absorption (celiac disease, cystic fibrosis), newborns, prolonged antibiotics, warfarin. A: Not suggested. B: Not suggested. C: Would prolong the aPTT. E: Normal PT.

questions.stem: A 6-week-old exclusively breastfed baby who did not receive vitamin K at birth has bruising and oozing. The PT is prolonged. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K deficiency is most common in newborns (hemorrhagic disease of the newborn); breast milk is low in vitamin K; the late form can occur as late as 3 months. B: Normal PT. C: Normal PT. D: Normal PT. E: Normal PT.

questions.stem: An ICU patient on broad-spectrum antibiotics for three weeks develops a prolonged PT. What is the most likely cause?

options.E: Loss of vitamin K from gut bacteria

questions.explanation: Prolonged antibiotic intake reduces vitamin K made by colonic bacteria; the PT is prolonged first (isolated in the early stage), then the PTT. A: Not suggested. B: Would prolong the aPTT. C: Prolongs the aPTT. D: Not the mechanism given.

questions.stem: A jaundiced man has a prolonged PT that stays prolonged after intravenous vitamin K. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Vitamin K corrects the PT in vitamin K deficiency but not in liver failure. A: Vitamin K would correct it. B: Vitamin K would correct it. D: Vitamin K would correct it. E: Vitamin K would correct it.

questions.stem: A man with a prolonged PT may have liver failure or vitamin K deficiency. Which result points to liver failure?
questions.explanation: A low factor V points to liver failure, since factor V does not depend on vitamin K. A: Low in both. C: Low in both. D: Low in both. E: Low in both.

questions.stem: Which clotting factor is NOT reduced in cirrhosis?
questions.explanation: Liver cirrhosis lowers the synthesis of most coagulation factors except factor VIII. A: Reduced. B: Reduced. C: Reduced. D: Reduced.

questions.stem: A man with cirrhosis is actively bleeding. His PT and aPTT are prolonged. Which product replaces the clotting factors?
questions.explanation: Management of active bleeding in liver failure: fresh frozen plasma, which contains all the clotting factors. B: Mainly fibrinogen. C: Platelets. D: Does not correct liver failure. E: Not a clotting product.

questions.stem: A man with cirrhosis has thrombocytopenia. What is the mechanism?
questions.explanation: Portal hypertension → splenic enlargement → the spleen traps platelets → thrombocytopenia. A: Not the mechanism shown. B: TTP, HUS, DIC. C: Affects factors. E: Not suggested.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old girl has syncope, heavy periods, recurrent nosebleeds and a hemarthrosis. Her paternal aunt had an early hysterectomy for heavy bleeding. Hb is 5 g/dL; platelets and PT are normal; the aPTT is prolonged and corrects on mixing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Red flags: combined mucocutaneous and joint bleeding, heavy menstrual bleeding, early hysterectomy in an aunt, prolonged aPTT. Diagnosis: vWD. A: Unlikely in a girl with mucosal bleeding. B: Normal platelets. D: Normal aPTT. E: Normal aPTT.

questions.stem: Which is the most common congenital bleeding disorder?
questions.explanation: vWD is the most common congenital bleeding disorder, seen in about 1% of the population, males and females equally. B: Less common. C: Less common. D: Rare. E: Rare.

questions.stem: About what share of the population has von Willebrand disease?
questions.explanation: vWD affects about 1% of the population, males and females equally; most are asymptomatic and found through family history or preoperative screening. A: Too low. B: Too high. D: Too low. E: Too high.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl has had heavy periods since menarche and has iron deficiency. A pelvic ultrasound is normal. Which test is most appropriate next?
questions.explanation: Think of vWD in every adolescent girl with heavy periods, iron deficiency and no gynecologic cause. A: Not for this picture. B: Not indicated. C: Not the first thought. D: Not indicated.

questions.stem: Which type of von Willebrand disease is most common?
questions.explanation: Type 1: mild deficiency of vWF, 70–80% of cases, AD. A: 10–20%. B: About 5%. C: Rare and severe. E: Rare.

questions.stem: A child of consanguineous parents has severe mucosal bleeding and hemarthroses. vWF is undetectable and factor VIII is very low. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Type 3: marked deficiency of both vWF and FVIII, AR, severe mucocutaneous and hemophilia-like bleeding. A: vWF would be normal. C: Mild deficiency. D: vWF activity normal. E: Qualitative; sometimes low platelets.

questions.stem: What defines type 2 von Willebrand disease?

options.C: A marked lack of vWF and VIII

questions.explanation: Type 2: qualitative defects of vWF, 4 subtypes, 15–20% of cases, mostly AD. B: Type 1. C: Type 3. D: TTP. E: Not type 2.

questions.stem: A woman with von Willebrand disease has intermittent thrombocytopenia. Her vWF binds platelet GPIb too avidly. Which subtype is this?
questions.explanation: Type 2B (about 5%, AD): increased affinity of vWF for platelet GPIb, sometimes thrombocytopenia. A: Loss of large multimers. B: Low activity. C: Poor binding to factor VIII. D: Mild quantitative deficiency.

questions.stem: A woman has an isolated low factor VIII and normal vWF activity. Her vWF binds factor VIII poorly. Which subtype is this?
questions.explanation: Type 2N: rare, suspect in females with isolated FVIII deficiency; reduced binding of vWF to FVIII; normal vWF activity; AR; treated with DDAVP or FVIII concentrates. A: Low vWF activity. B: Increased GPIb binding. C: Low vWF activity. E: Absent vWF.

questions.stem: A patient with von Willebrand disease has low vWF activity because the high-molecular-weight multimers are missing. Which subtype is this?
questions.explanation: Type 2A (10–20% of vWD): low vWF activity due to loss of high-molecular-weight multimers; normal-to-low FVIII. A: Increased GPIb binding. B: Low activity with normal multimers. D: Poor factor VIII binding. E: Absent vWF.

questions.stem: A girl with type 1 von Willebrand disease needs a dental extraction. Which drug raises her own vWF level?
questions.explanation: Desmopressin (DDAVP) for types 1 and most type 2 promotes endothelial release of vWF and raises vWF/FVIII 2–5-fold. A: An antifibrinolytic. C: A bypassing agent. D: For heavy periods. E: Not relevant.

questions.stem: A girl with von Willebrand disease has repeated gum bleeding. Which add-on treatment targets mucosal bleeding?
questions.explanation: Antifibrinolytics are used for mucosal bleeding in vWD. A: Not relevant. B: Not routine in vWD. D: Not the treatment given. E: Not relevant.

questions.stem: A man with severe von Willebrand disease has developed inhibitors to infused vWF and is bleeding. Which treatment is used?
questions.explanation: Bypassing agents (rFVIIa, prothrombin complex concentrate) in severe cases and with inhibitors to infused vWF. A: Inhibitors block it. B: Not for severe cases with inhibitors. C: Not the treatment given. D: Not the treatment given.

questions.stem: Besides avoiding contact sports, which advice is part of supportive care in von Willebrand disease?
questions.explanation: Supportive: no contact sports, aspirin or NSAIDs; estrogen therapy or endometrial ablation for heavy menstrual bleeding. A: Iron deficiency is common. C: Used for heavy periods. D: Not advised. E: Not relevant.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old has purpura on the buttocks and legs, knee pain and abdominal pain. Platelets and clotting tests are normal. Which test is most important next?
questions.explanation: IgA vasculitis (Henoch–Schönlein purpura): small-vessel immune complex disease with purpura on the buttocks and legs, arthritis, abdominal pain and nephritis; check the urine for blood and protein. B: Platelets are normal. C: Clotting is normal. D: Platelets are normal. E: Not indicated.

questions.stem: A man with alcohol use disorder has perifollicular bleeding, corkscrew hairs and swollen bleeding gums. Which deficiency is most likely?
questions.explanation: Scurvy: vitamin C deficiency, defective collagen; perifollicular bleeding, corkscrew hairs, swollen bleeding gums; dramatic response to vitamin C. A: Prolonged PT, no corkscrew hairs. B: Macrocytic anemia. C: Macrocytic anemia. E: Not this picture.

questions.stem: A teenager has hyperextensible skin, hypermobile joints, easy bruising and poor wound healing. What is the mechanism of the bleeding?
questions.explanation: Ehlers–Danlos syndrome: inherited collagen defect; hyperextensible skin, hypermobile joints, easy bruising, poor wound healing. A: Scurvy. B: IgA vasculitis. C: Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. D: Platelet disorder.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old has recurrent nosebleeds, small red spots on his lips and fingertips, and a lung arteriovenous malformation. His father had the same. What is the mechanism of his bleeding?
questions.explanation: HHT: abnormal vessel development; recurrent epistaxis, telangiectasia on lips and fingers, AVMs in lung, liver and brain, family history. A: Ehlers–Danlos syndrome. B: vWD; no vascular malformations. D: IgA vasculitis. E: Senile and steroid purpura.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old woman on long-term prednisone has flat purple patches on the backs of her hands and forearms. Platelets and clotting tests are normal. What is the best management?
questions.explanation: Senile and steroid purpura: loss of supporting connective tissue; flat purple patches on the forearms and hands; tests normal; reassurance. B: Scurvy. C: vWD. D: Platelets are normal. E: Not indicated.

questions.stem: Each feature should raise suspicion of a severe bleeding disorder EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Suspect a severe bleeding disorder with early onset, prolonged, recurrent or postoperative bleeding, need for PRBC and other blood products, positive family history. Bleeding from a single site in a well child suggests a local cause. A: Suspicious. C: Suspicious. D: Suspicious. E: Suspicious.

questions.stem: Which feature favors an inherited bleeding disorder?

options.A: Onset after starting a new drug

questions.explanation: Inherited bleeding disorders: presentation in infancy and early childhood, bleeding in males (sex-linked), previous postoperative bleeding, positive family history. A: Acquired. B: Acquired. C: Acquired (DIC). E: Often ITP.

questions.stem: A well-looking boy has repeated bleeding from the right nostril. The rest of the exam is normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Well looking, bleeding from a single site only: local cause (e.g. unilateral epistaxis). B: Petechiae expected. C: Usually several sites. D: Deep tissue or joint bleeding. E: Sick looking, organomegaly.

questions.stem: A sick-looking 5-year-old has petechiae, lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Sick looking with lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly: malignancy. Well child with petechiae: ITP. A: Well looking, normal exam. C: Joint and deep bleeding. D: Mucocutaneous bleeding. E: Umbilical and surgical bleeding.

questions.stem: On which cell surfaces does coagulation take place?
questions.explanation: Coagulation occurs on the surfaces of platelets and endothelial cells. A: Not red cells. B: Not neutrophils. C: Hepatocytes make factors. D: Not red cells.

lectures.title: Laboratory bleeding measures
lectures.covers: Which test probes which phase of hemostasis: platelet count and smear, PFA-100, PT, aPTT, thrombin time and fibrinogen, the PT/aPTT grid, mixing studies, factor assays, the VWF panel and pre-analytical errors.

items.p: Every lab test probes one of the three phases of hemostasis.

table: Platelet count and smear, PFA-100/200, VWF panel
PT, aPTT, thrombin time, fibrinogen, mixing study, factor assays

items.p: A platelet count of 20,000/µL disrupts primary hemostasis.

ul: Typical adult range 150–450 × 10⁹/L: below 150 = thrombocytopenia, above 450 = thrombocytosis
Usually the first screen in a bleeding workup: fast, and it excludes quantitative platelet problems
The smear asks: is the low count spurious from EDTA clumping? Are platelets giant, dysplastic or clumped? Any other CBC clue (anemia, leukocytosis, pancytopenia)?

items.p: Reduced platelet function (uremia, aspirin) adds bleeding risk at every count. A normal count with abnormal bleeding should raise suspicion of a functional platelet defect or VWD.

ul: Citrated blood is drawn through a collagen-coated membrane under high shear; the closure time is measured
Cartridges: collagen/epinephrine and collagen/ADP. It simulates adhesion, activation and aggregation.
Screens platelet function, not number
Prolonged closure time: VWD, aspirin/NSAID effect, significant inherited platelet dysfunction
Limits: a normal PFA does not exclude mild VWD or mild platelet defects. Low hematocrit, low platelet count and pre-analytical problems prolong it.

items.p: Abnormal PFA + normal count → platelet function or VWF problem → next test: VWF panel.

table: Extrinsic + common pathway; isolated prolongation = factor VII; reported as the INR (warfarin)
Primary hemostasis (platelets, VWD) or a vascular cause
Hemophilia A or B, factor XI or XII deficiency, lupus anticoagulant
Factor VII deficiency, early warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency
Liver disease, DIC, vitamin K deficiency or higher-dose warfarin; isolated X, II or V deficiency

ul: Infant boy bleeding after a heel stick, isolated long aPTT, normal platelets → hemophilia A or B (XII → XI → VIII/IX → X)
Warfarin, isolated long PT → extrinsic pathway (factor VII) and the INR
Decompensated cirrhosis oozing from IV sites, both prolonged → liver disease (a global process)

items.p: Patient plasma + normal plasma 1:1, then re-test.

table: Normal plasma supplied the missing factor → factor deficiency
Something in the patient's plasma also blocks the normal plasma → inhibitor (lupus anticoagulant, factor antibody)

items.p: Ordered after an isolated prolonged aPTT and a mixing study that corrects. They show which factor (VIII, IX, XI, XII) and how severe.

summary.h: The bleeding workup and the VWF panel

items.p: Bleeding history → platelet count → PT + aPTT → PFA-100 → VWF panel.

Opening case: a 19-year-old with nosebleeds since childhood, easy bruising and heavy periods (mucocutaneous, immediate). The first test is the platelet count and smear. Platelets 260,000/µL, PT 12.5 s and aPTT 34 s were normal; the PFA-100 closure time was markedly prolonged → VWF panel. A normal count and normal PT/aPTT do not rule out VWD.

ul: Type 1: partial quantitative deficiency, most common (~75%)
Type 2: qualitative (functional) defect, several subtypes
Type 3: severe, near-total deficiency; rare

items.p: They silently distort coagulation results.

ul: EDTA tube used instead of citrate
Citrate tube only half-filled
Sample left 6 hours at room temperature before testing

items.note: The slides ask which tests are distorted and in which direction but give no answer. Standard laboratory practice (not from the slides): an underfilled citrate tube has too much citrate for the plasma and falsely prolongs the PT and aPTT; an EDTA sample is rejected for clotting tests; a long delay at room temperature lets labile factors (mainly factor VIII) decay and can falsely prolong the aPTT. Only the underfilled tube is tested.

cards.q: Which phase does each test probe?
cards.a: Platelet count, smear, PFA-100, VWF panel: primary. PT, aPTT, thrombin time, fibrinogen: secondary.
150–450 × 10⁹/L; below 150 thrombocytopenia, above 450 thrombocytosis
≥ 50,000 minimal; 20,000–50,000 minor bleeding after trauma; < 20,000 spontaneous; < 5,000 severe, possibly life-threatening

cards.q: What adds bleeding risk at any platelet count?
cards.a: Reduced platelet function (uremia, aspirin)

cards.q: Why is the CBC and smear the first test in a bleeding workup?
cards.a: Fast, and it excludes quantitative platelet problems

cards.q: Low count in a well patient with clumps on the smear?
cards.a: Spurious count from EDTA clumping

cards.q: Normal platelet count but abnormal bleeding: think of?
cards.a: A functional platelet defect or VWD
Citrated blood through a collagen-coated membrane (collagen/epinephrine, collagen/ADP) under high shear; closure time measured

cards.q: PFA-100: causes of a prolonged closure time
cards.a: VWD, aspirin/NSAID, significant inherited platelet dysfunction; also low hematocrit, low count, pre-analytical problems
A normal result does not exclude mild VWD or mild platelet defects

cards.q: Abnormal PFA-100 with a normal count: next test?
cards.a: VWF panel (VWF antigen, ristocetin cofactor activity, factor VIII activity)

cards.q: PT versus aPTT versus thrombin time
cards.a: PT: extrinsic + common. aPTT: intrinsic + common. TT: fibrinogen → fibrin.
Hemophilia A or B, factor XI or XII deficiency, lupus anticoagulant
Factor VII deficiency, early warfarin, early vitamin K deficiency

cards.q: PT and aPTT both prolonged: causes
cards.a: Liver disease, DIC, vitamin K deficiency or higher-dose warfarin; isolated X, II or V deficiency

cards.q: PT and aPTT both normal but bleeding: think of?
cards.a: Primary hemostasis (platelets, VWD) or a vascular cause
Patient + normal plasma 1:1, re-test. Corrects = factor deficiency; no correction = inhibitor (lupus anticoagulant, factor antibody)

cards.q: When is a factor assay ordered?
cards.a: After an isolated prolonged aPTT and a mixing study that corrects; it shows which factor and how severe
Severe < 1%, moderate 1–5%, mild 5–40%
Bleeding history → platelet count → PT + aPTT → PFA-100 → VWF panel
VWF antigen (amount), ristocetin cofactor activity (function), factor VIII activity (VWF stabilizes it)
Type 1 partial quantitative (~75%); type 2 qualitative; type 3 near-total, rare

cards.q: Three pre-analytical errors in coagulation testing
cards.a: EDTA tube instead of citrate; half-filled citrate tube; 6 hours at room temperature before testing

questions.stem: A 30-year-old has a platelet count of 20,000/µL with a normal PT and aPTT. Which phase of hemostasis is most directly disrupted?
questions.explanation: Platelets form the first plug, so a low count disrupts primary hemostasis. Every laboratory test probes one phase: primary, secondary or fibrinolysis. B: Secondary hemostasis; the PT and aPTT are normal. C: Clot breakdown, not plug formation. D: Not what the count reflects. E: The factor XIII step of the fibrin clot.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old on warfarin has a prolonged PT, a normal aPTT and a normal platelet count. Which pathways does the abnormal test measure?
questions.explanation: The PT measures the extrinsic and common pathways. An isolated prolonged PT points to the extrinsic pathway (factor VII) and is reported as the INR. A: The aPTT (intrinsic), which is normal. B: The PFA-100. C: Not measured by the PT. E: The thrombin time.

questions.stem: Which test measures the conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin?
questions.explanation: Four basic tests: PT (extrinsic + common), aPTT (intrinsic + common), thrombin time (common pathway, fibrinogen → fibrin), fibrinogen concentration (substrate for clot formation). A: Extrinsic and common pathways. B: Intrinsic and common pathways. D: Platelet function. E: One intrinsic factor.

questions.stem: An adult's platelet count is 480 × 10⁹/L. How is this classified?
questions.explanation: Typical adult range 150–450 × 10⁹/L: below 150 = thrombocytopenia, above 450 = thrombocytosis. A: The upper limit is 450 × 10⁹/L. B: Clumping lowers the count. C: A count says nothing about function. D: Lowers the count.

questions.stem: A healthy 40-year-old with no bleeding history has a platelet count of 45 × 10⁹/L on an EDTA sample. The smear shows large platelet clumps. What is the most likely explanation?
questions.explanation: The smear checks whether the count is spurious because of EDTA clumping, and whether platelets are giant, dysplastic or clumped. A: Clumps on the smear explain the low count. C: No other cytopenia and no bleeding. D: No splenomegaly; clumps explain it. E: Clumps are not giant single platelets.

questions.stem: Why is the CBC with smear usually the first test in a bleeding workup?

options.A: It quickly excludes a platelet number problem
options.B: It measures platelet adhesion under shear
options.C: It detects mild von Willebrand disease

questions.explanation: The CBC + smear is usually the first screen in a bleeding workup because it is fast and helps exclude quantitative platelet problems. B: The PFA-100. C: Needs the VWF panel. D: The PT. E: The mixing study.

questions.stem: A man has a platelet count of 35,000/µL. What bleeding is expected at this count?
questions.explanation: Bleeding risk: ≥ 50,000/µL minimal; 20,000–50,000/µL minor bleeding after trauma; < 20,000/µL spontaneous bleeding; < 5,000/µL severe, possibly life-threatening spontaneous bleeding. A: At or above 50,000/µL. B: Below 20,000/µL. C: Below 5,000/µL. E: A clotting factor pattern.

questions.stem: Below which platelet count does spontaneous bleeding become expected?
questions.explanation: Below 20,000/µL: spontaneous bleeding; below 5,000/µL: severe, possibly life-threatening spontaneous bleeding. A: Below this, bleeding after trauma. B: Minimal risk. D: The lower limit of normal. E: Severe, possibly life-threatening bleeding.

questions.stem: A child has a platelet count of 4,000/µL. Which bleeding risk does this carry?
questions.explanation: Below 5,000/µL the risk is severe, possibly life-threatening spontaneous bleeding. A: 20,000–50,000/µL. B: ≥ 50,000/µL. C: Understates the risk. D: A clotting factor pattern.

questions.stem: Two patients have platelet counts of 30,000/µL. One has end-stage renal disease and bleeds more. What explains the difference?
questions.explanation: Reduced platelet function (e.g. due to uremia or aspirin use) adds risk of bleeding in each platelet count range. A: Not the uremic effect. C: Not the explanation given. D: The counts are equal. E: Would not increase bleeding.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman has lifelong nosebleeds and gum bleeding. Her platelet count, PT and aPTT are normal. Which disorder is most likely?
questions.explanation: A normal count with abnormal (lifelong mucocutaneous) bleeding should raise suspicion of a functional platelet defect or VWD. A: Male, joint and deep bleeding, prolonged aPTT. B: Prolonged PT. C: Low count. E: Prolonged PT.

questions.stem: What does the PFA-100 closure time assess?
questions.explanation: PFA-100/200 screens platelet adhesion/aggregation function under high shear: not the number, the function. A: The platelet count. B: The thrombin time. C: A factor assay. D: Fibrinolysis.

questions.stem: PFA-100 cartridges pair epinephrine or ADP with which substance?
questions.explanation: Citrated blood is drawn through a collagen-coated membrane under high shear (collagen/epinephrine and collagen/ADP cartridges), and closure time is measured. A: The PT trigger. C: The thrombin time reagent. D: The substrate, not the coating. E: Used in VWF activity testing.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old taking daily aspirin has a normal platelet count, PT and aPTT. Which result is most likely abnormal?
questions.explanation: A prolonged closure time supports a platelet-type problem: VWD, aspirin/NSAID effect, or significant inherited platelet dysfunction. B: Fibrinogen to fibrin. C: Not affected by aspirin. D: Not affected by aspirin. E: No prolonged clotting time to mix.

questions.stem: A boy with mild mucocutaneous bleeding has a normal PFA-100 closure time. Which condition is still possible?
questions.explanation: Important limits: a normal PFA does not exclude mild VWD or mild platelet defects. Low hematocrit, low platelet count and pre-analytical issues can prolong it. A: Severe; would prolong closure time. B: Significant inherited dysfunction prolongs it. D: A low count prolongs it. E: A low hematocrit prolongs it.

questions.stem: A woman with a hematocrit of 18% has a normal platelet count, takes no drugs and has a normal VWF panel. Her PFA-100 closure time is prolonged. What best explains it?
questions.explanation: Low hematocrit, low platelet count and pre-analytical issues can prolong the PFA closure time. A: The PFA does not test factors. C: The PFA does not test factors. D: Affects the aPTT. E: Not a cause.

questions.stem: A patient has an abnormal PFA-100 and a normal platelet count. What does this suggest?

options.D: A defect of the vessel wall
options.E: A platelet function or VWF problem

questions.explanation: The PFA-100 screens function, not quantity. With a normal count, an abnormal result points to a platelet function or VWF-related problem; the next test is the VWF panel. A: The count is normal. B: The PFA does not test factors. C: Not tested by the PFA. D: Not tested by the PFA.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman has had nosebleeds since childhood, easy bruising and heavy menstrual bleeding. The exam is otherwise normal. What is the best first laboratory test?
questions.explanation: Bleeding history → platelet count/smear → PT + aPTT → PFA-100 → VWF panel. The count and smear is the right first move. A: Come after the count. B: Comes after the PFA-100. D: Not the first move. E: Not a first test.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman has lifelong mucocutaneous bleeding. Platelets are 260,000/µL, PT 12.5 s and aPTT 34 s. The PFA-100 closure time is markedly prolonged. What is the next test?
questions.explanation: A normal platelet count and normal PT/aPTT did not rule out VWD: the abnormal PFA-100 led to the VWF panel (VWF antigen, VWF activity/ristocetin cofactor, factor VIII activity). A: aPTT normal; mucocutaneous pattern. B: Nothing prolonged to mix. C: The count is normal. E: Fibrinogen to fibrin.

questions.stem: In what order is a bleeding workup built?
questions.explanation: Algorithm: bleeding history → platelet count → PT + aPTT → PFA-100 → VWF panel. B: History comes first. C: History and count come first. D: The count precedes the PFA. E: History comes first.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy has prolonged bleeding after a heel stick. The PT is normal, the aPTT prolonged and the platelet count normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Isolated prolonged aPTT → intrinsic pathway factors (XII → XI → VIII/IX → X): hemophilia A (VIII) or B (IX). A: Prolongs the PT. C: Prolongs the PT too. D: Prolongs the PT first. E: Normal aPTT.

questions.stem: An infant's isolated prolonged aPTT corrects on 1:1 mixing with normal plasma. Which test identifies the missing factor and its severity?
questions.explanation: Factor assays are ordered after an isolated prolonged aPTT and a mixing study that corrects: they pinpoint which factor (VIII, IX, XI, XII) and how severe. A: How much VWF is present. B: Platelet function. C: Fibrinogen to fibrin. E: Already shows a deficiency.

questions.stem: A boy's factor VIII activity is 0.6%. How is his deficiency graded?
questions.explanation: Factor activity level determines severity: severe < 1%, moderate 1–5%, mild 5–40%. B: 1–5%. C: 5–40%. D: Not a severity grade. E: Not a severity grade.

questions.stem: A boy's factor IX activity is 3%. How is his deficiency graded?
questions.explanation: Severe < 1%, moderate 1–5%, mild 5–40%. A: < 1%. B: 5–40%. D: Not a severity grade. E: Not a severity grade.

questions.stem: Each prolongs the aPTT with a normal PT EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: PT normal + aPTT prolonged: hemophilia A/B, factor XI or XII deficiency, lupus anticoagulant. Factor VII deficiency prolongs the PT alone. A: Intrinsic factor. B: Intrinsic factor. C: Isolated prolonged aPTT. D: Factor IX, intrinsic.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman has a prolonged aPTT and a normal PT. The aPTT stays prolonged after 1:1 mixing with normal plasma. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: No correction on mixing = an inhibitor in the patient's plasma (e.g. lupus anticoagulant, factor antibody). B: Would correct on mixing. C: Would correct on mixing. D: Prolongs the PT. E: Prolongs the PT.

questions.stem: A prolonged aPTT corrects after 1:1 mixing with normal plasma. What does this suggest?
questions.explanation: Corrects: normal plasma supplied the missing factor → the patient is missing a clotting factor. A: Would not correct. B: Does not affect the aPTT. C: Not tested by mixing. E: Affects the PFA, not mixing.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man has new large bruises. His aPTT is prolonged with a normal PT and does not correct after 1:1 mixing. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Does not correct: something in the patient's plasma actively blocks normal plasma too → an inhibitor (e.g. lupus anticoagulant, factor antibody). A: Would correct. B: Would correct. D: Prolongs the PT. E: Prolongs the PT.

questions.stem: In a mixing study, patient plasma is mixed with normal plasma in what ratio before re-testing?
questions.explanation: Patient plasma + normal plasma, 1:1, then re-test. A: Not the ratio. C: Not the ratio. D: The citrate-to-blood ratio of the tube. E: Not the ratio.

questions.stem: Why does a mixing study fail to correct when an inhibitor is present?

options.A: Normal plasma lacks the missing factor
options.B: The inhibitor destroys platelets in the tube
options.E: The inhibitor also blocks the normal plasma

questions.explanation: Does not correct: something in the patient's plasma is actively blocking normal plasma too → an inhibitor is present. A: It supplies it. B: Plasma test; no platelets. C: Not the reason. D: Not the reason.

questions.stem: An isolated prolonged PT in a patient on warfarin reflects a fall in which factor?
questions.explanation: Isolated prolonged PT → think extrinsic pathway (factor VII) and the INR. A: Intrinsic; aPTT. B: Intrinsic; aPTT. D: Intrinsic; aPTT. E: Intrinsic; aPTT.

questions.stem: Which value derived from the PT is used to monitor warfarin?
questions.explanation: Isolated prolonged PT → think extrinsic pathway (factor VII) and the INR. A: The intrinsic test. B: Fibrinogen to fibrin. C: Platelet function. D: Fibrin breakdown.

questions.stem: A patient on long-term antibiotics with poor intake has a prolonged PT and a normal aPTT. If the cause is not corrected, which change follows?
questions.explanation: Early vitamin K deficiency prolongs the PT alone (factor VII); more severe vitamin K deficiency prolongs both PT and aPTT. A: Not a vitamin K effect. C: Fibrinogen is not vitamin K dependent. D: Platelet function. E: Not vitamin K dependent.

questions.stem: A patient with decompensated cirrhosis oozes from IV sites. PT and aPTT are prolonged and platelets are low-normal. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Both prolonged → think common pathway or a global process (liver disease, DIC, vitamin K deficiency). B: The aPTT would be normal. C: The PT would be normal. D: Normal PT and aPTT. E: Isolated aPTT.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old with lifelong bleeding has a prolonged PT and aPTT that correct on mixing. Liver tests and fibrinogen are normal and he takes no drugs. Which single deficiency fits?
questions.explanation: Prolonged PT with prolonged PTT: combined deficiencies (liver disease, DIC, vitamin K deficiency) or isolated deficiencies of factor X, II or V. A: PT alone. B: aPTT alone. C: aPTT alone. E: Both normal.

questions.stem: Each prolongs both the PT and the aPTT EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Early warfarin effect prolongs the PT alone (with factor VII deficiency and early vitamin K deficiency). Both prolonged: liver disease, DIC, vitamin K deficiency/warfarin (higher dose), factor X, II or V deficiency. A: Global process. C: Global process. D: Common pathway. E: Common pathway.

questions.stem: A septic patient oozes from IV lines. PT and aPTT are prolonged and the platelet count is low. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Both prolonged → a global process such as liver disease, DIC or vitamin K deficiency; the low count fits DIC. A: PT and aPTT normal. B: Thrombosis; not this picture. C: PT alone; count normal. D: Normal PT and aPTT.

questions.stem: An elderly woman has flat purple patches on her forearms. Platelet count, PT and aPTT are normal. Where is the problem most likely?
questions.explanation: Both normal: consider primary hemostasis (platelets, VWD) or a vascular cause. B: PT normal. C: aPTT normal. D: Both normal. E: Both normal.

questions.stem: A patient has a prolonged PT and aPTT. Which result points to a fibrinogen problem rather than a factor X deficiency?
questions.explanation: The thrombin time tests the last step (fibrinogen → fibrin); fibrinogen concentration is the substrate. Factor X acts before thrombin, so the thrombin time stays normal in factor X deficiency. A: Platelet function. B: Not specific. C: Both are deficiencies. E: Unrelated.

questions.stem: Which VWF panel test measures how well VWF functions?
questions.explanation: VWF panel: VWF antigen (how much), VWF activity/ristocetin cofactor (how well it functions), factor VIII activity (VWF stabilizes factor VIII). A: How much VWF is present. B: The carried factor. D: Not part of the panel. E: Not part of the panel.

questions.stem: Why does a VWF panel include factor VIII activity?

options.D: VWF is made from factor VIII

questions.explanation: The panel measures VWF antigen, VWF activity (ristocetin cofactor) and factor VIII activity, because VWF stabilizes factor VIII. A: Reversed. C: ADAMTS-13 does. D: Separate proteins. E: VWF binds GPIb.

questions.stem: A woman with heavy periods has VWF antigen and VWF activity both mildly and proportionally reduced. Which type of von Willebrand disease is most likely?
questions.explanation: Type 1: partial quantitative deficiency, the most common (~75%). B: Function low out of proportion to antigen. C: Near-total deficiency. D: Not suggested. E: Not a VWD type.

questions.stem: A man's VWF antigen is normal, but his ristocetin cofactor activity is markedly reduced. Which type of von Willebrand disease is most likely?
questions.explanation: Type 2: a qualitative/functional defect (several subtypes): VWF is present but works poorly. A: Antigen and function fall together. B: Antigen near-absent. C: Not suggested. E: Not a VWD type.

questions.stem: A child with severe bleeding has nearly undetectable VWF antigen and activity and a very low factor VIII. Which type of von Willebrand disease is this?
questions.explanation: Type 3: severe, near-total deficiency, rare. Factor VIII is low because VWF stabilizes it. A: Partial deficiency. B: Qualitative defect. D: Not suggested. E: Not a VWD type.

questions.stem: About what share of von Willebrand disease is type 1?
questions.explanation: Type 1 is the most common (~75%). A: Too low. B: Too low. C: Too high. D: Too low.

questions.stem: A citrate tube for coagulation tests is only half-filled with blood. What is the expected effect?
questions.explanation: The slides pose this without an answer; standard laboratory practice: an underfilled tube has excess citrate for the plasma volume, which binds the calcium added in the test, so clotting times are falsely prolonged. A: A count is not run on this tube. B: Not the effect. C: Not the effect. E: The ratio matters.

questions.stem: Each is a pre-analytical error that can distort coagulation results EXCEPT:

options.A: A lupus anticoagulant in the sample
options.B: An EDTA tube used instead of citrate
options.D: Six hours at room temperature before testing

questions.explanation: Pre-analytical errors silently distort coagulation results: tube switch (EDTA instead of citrate), underfilled citrate tube, delayed transport (6 hours at room temperature). A lupus anticoagulant is a true patient inhibitor, not a sampling error. B: Wrong tube. C: Wrong ratio. D: Delayed transport. E: Factors consumed in the tube.

lectures.title: Hemophilia
lectures.covers: Hemophilia A and B: inheritance, severity, joint and life-threatening bleeds, diagnosis, prophylaxis and factor dosing, treatment by bleed site, inhibitors and bypassing agents, emicizumab, novel therapies, and acquired hemophilia.

ul: X-linked recessive bleeding disorder: absent or low factor VIII (hemophilia A) or factor IX (hemophilia B)
Lifelong joint, muscle and deep tissue bleeding
The second most common bleeding disorder after VWD; hemophilia A is ~80% of patients
Congenital: F8/F9 mutations on the X chromosome; males are affected in > 99% of cases. Inherited in 2/3; about 1/3 of patients have a new mutation (no family history).
Severe hemophilia A: inversion in intron 22 of F8. Hemophilia B: about 2/3 have missense mutations.
Acquired: a rare autoimmune disorder with autoantibodies against factor VIII

items.p: Case: a 2½-year-old boy with a growing forehead hematoma without trauma, easy bruising, a painful swollen knee at 18 months and a bleeding maternal uncle. Hb 9.5 g/dL, normal platelets and PT, prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing. Factor VIII 0.5% = severe hemophilia A.

items.note: Slide 4 places both F8 and F9 at Xq28. Standard sources: F8 is at Xq28, F9 at Xq27. Not tested.

items.p: Baseline factor levels generally match bleeding severity.

table: Spontaneous joint and muscle bleeds without trauma
Occasional spontaneous bleeds; prolonged bleeding after minor trauma or surgery
Spontaneous bleeding rare; severe bleeding with major trauma or surgery

items.p: Hemarthrosis is the most common bleed (70–80% of all bleeds).

ul: Early signs: worsening pain, tingling or a bubbling feeling, less range of motion
Later: limited movement, swelling, numbness, warm skin
Target joint: bleeding into the same joint ≥ 3 times in 6 months → progressive damage, crippling arthropathy, muscle atrophy

items.caption: Repeated hemarthrosis leads to hemophilic arthropathy

items.p: Blood in the joint → inflammation → synovitis and more bleeding → cartilage loss and joint-space narrowing → contractures, muscle atrophy and chronic pain. Damage is permanent and often needs surgery; its extent tracks the frequency of bleeding.

items.note: Slide 8 gives joint sites as ankle 42%, elbow 21%, knee 20%, shoulder 4%, hip 4%, wrist 2%. Many standard sources name the knee as the most commonly affected joint overall (the ankle leads in young children). The ranking is not tested.

table: Muscle and nerve damage if untreated

ul: Clues: bleeding after circumcision or umbilical cord separation; joint, muscle or deep tissue bleeds; positive family history; ecchymoses, hemarthrosis, arthropathy, muscle atrophy
Labs: prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing; FVIII or FIX < 40%; normal VWF antigen and activity; mutated F8/F9
A normal aPTT does not exclude mild hemophilia
If in doubt: factor VIII level → if normal, factor IX → if both normal, factor XI

items.p: WFH 2020: prophylaxis is the standard of care everywhere, and it beats on-demand therapy (treating bleeds when they happen).

ul: Regular, long-term prophylaxis keeps joints and muscles working, prevents chronic arthropathy and gives a good quality of life
Start early: ideally before age 3 or after the first joint bleed (primary prophylaxis)
Aim for trough levels high enough to prevent all bleeds (often ≥ 3–5%)
Dose by the patient's pharmacokinetics

items.p: Case continued: standard half-life factor VIII 3 times a week plus extra doses for bleeds, a central venous catheter, and family teaching on adherence.

ul: Treat at home within 2 hours of onset, supervised by the comprehensive care team
Medicines: factor replacement, cryoprecipitate (FVIII, fibrinogen, factor XIII, VWF, fibronectin), desmopressin, antifibrinolytics
WFH prefers factor concentrates to cryoprecipitate or FFP (quality, safety, efficacy); those are for when nothing else is available or affordable
Treat veins with care

items.p: Peak level: 15–30 minutes after infusion.
Example: a 20-kg boy needing a 40 IU/dL rise of factor VIII needs 40 ÷ 2 × 20 = 400 units; factor IX needs twice that per kg.

table: Urgent factor replacement before any evaluation, until bleed-free
Factor until bleed-free + RICE + analgesia + physiotherapy
Antifibrinolytics and supportive care; factor for severe refractory bleeds

items.p: Continuous factor infusion is recommended around surgery or for a severe bleed.

items.note: Slide 16 also lists treatment durations and target peak levels (e.g. intracranial 10–14 days, 50–80/80–100%). These differ from the WFH 2020 tables cited on the slide, so they are not tested.

ul: RICE, physiotherapy, noncontact sports
No NSAIDs or aspirin; control pain
Psychosocial support, vaccinations, patient and family education
Monitor: bleeds, musculoskeletal status, inhibitor development, transfusion-related infections, quality of life

items.p: Prerequisites for care: a multidisciplinary team (hematologists, orthopedic surgeons, physiotherapists, genetic counselors, nurses, psychologists, social workers), management protocols, a coagulation lab able to test for inhibitors, concentrates and antifibrinolytics, and a registry of treatment and bleeding records.
Case continued: at 12 years, the adherent boy has profuse rectal bleeding (Hb 5.0 g/dL) that continues despite factor VIII given to 80–100%. Cause: an inhibitor.

ul: Neutralizing antibodies bind FVIII/FIX and stop it binding to platelet surfaces and other clotting factors
Frequency in severe disease: ~25% in hemophilia A, ~5% in hemophilia B
Titer in Bethesda units: low < 5 BU, high > 5 BU
Consequences: uncontrollable bleeding, progressive joint damage, poor quality of life, very high cost, premature death (hemophilia A-related death 41.7% with inhibitors vs 12.0% without)

items.p: Treatment:

ul: Very high doses of factor for a long time
Bypassing agents: activated prothrombin complex; recombinant factor VIIa
Factor VIII mimetic: emicizumab

items.p: rFVIIa binds tissue factor and makes a little thrombin; at high (pharmacological) doses it activates factor X directly on activated platelets, bypassing VIII and IX → thrombin burst → stable plug.

items.caption: Emicizumab bridges factor IXa and factor X

items.p: Emicizumab: a subcutaneous bispecific monoclonal antibody that mimics FVIIIa. It binds FIXa and FX so that FIXa activates FX.

items.note: Slide 20 says activated prothrombin complexes contain activated II, VII, IX and X. Standard sources describe them as mostly non-activated II, IX and X with activated VII. Not tested.

items.p: Limits of standard half-life factor VIII:

ul: IV route: needs venous access, a heavy treatment burden, poor adherence
Rapid elimination: repeated infusions each week, a fluctuating effect
Immunogenicity: alloantibodies → treatment failure, need to bypass FVIII and remove the antibodies

items.p: Extended half-life concentrates mean fewer doses: rFIX half-life 4–5 times longer, rFVIII 1.4–1.5 times longer. Gene therapy offers a potential cure (lasting production of the patient's own FVIII or FIX).
Shared decision-making: seek participation → help explore and compare options → assess preferences → reach a joint decision → evaluate the decision.

Case 2: a 65-year-old woman with 12 hours of abdominal distension, 2 weeks of bruising and hip pain, and 5 years of joint pains and rash. No family history. Hb 5.5 g/dL, normal PT, markedly prolonged aPTT that does not correct on mixing, FVIII < 1%, very high inhibitor titer; ultrasound shows a massive abdominal hematoma.

ul: A rare, potentially life-threatening autoimmune disorder: autoantibodies against clotting factors, most often FVIII
A disease of older people: > 80% of cases are ≥ 65 years
An underlying condition in 50%: pregnancy, autoimmune disorders, malignancy, drug allergy
Treatment: as for congenital hemophilia with inhibitors, plus treating the underlying disease

cards.a: A: factor VIII deficiency (~80%). B: factor IX deficiency. Both X-linked recessive.

cards.q: Hemophilia: share with a new mutation
cards.a: About 1/3 (no family history); inherited in 2/3

cards.q: Genetic defect in severe hemophilia A
cards.a: Inversion in intron 22 of F8

cards.q: Main mutation type in hemophilia B
cards.a: Missense (about 2/3)
Severe < 1%, moderate 1–< 5%, mild 5–< 40%
Severe: spontaneous joint/muscle bleeds. Moderate: occasional spontaneous, prolonged after minor trauma. Mild: bleeding with major trauma or surgery.

cards.q: Early signs of a joint bleed
cards.a: Worsening pain, tingling or bubbling, less range of motion
≥ 3 bleeds into the same joint in 6 months

cards.q: Share of bleeds that are hemarthroses

cards.a: Intracranial, neck/throat (airway), gastrointestinal

cards.q: Deep muscle bleeds: sites and risk
cards.a: Iliopsoas, calf, forearm; muscle and nerve damage if untreated
Prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing; FVIII or FIX < 40%; normal VWF antigen and activity

cards.q: Suspected hemophilia: order of factor levels
cards.a: Factor VIII → if normal, IX → if both normal, XI. A normal aPTT does not exclude mild hemophilia.

cards.q: WFH prophylaxis: when to start and trough target
cards.a: Ideally before age 3; trough often ≥ 3–5%; dose by pharmacokinetics
Prophylaxis (regular, long-term) is the standard of care; on-demand = treating bleeds as they occur

cards.q: When should a bleed be treated?
cards.a: At home within 2 hours of onset
FVIII: 1 unit/kg raises ~2 IU/dL. FIX: 1 unit/kg raises ~1 IU/dL.

cards.q: Half-lives of factor VIII and IX
cards.a: VIII 8–12 h; IX 18–24 h. Peak 15–30 min after infusion.
FVIII, fibrinogen, factor XIII, VWF, fibronectin (no factor IX)

cards.q: Intracranial bleed in hemophilia: first step
cards.a: Urgent factor replacement before any evaluation
Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin
~25% severe hemophilia A, ~5% severe B. Low < 5 BU, high > 5 BU.
Very high-dose factor long term; bypassing agents (aPCC, rFVIIa); emicizumab
High doses activate factor X directly on activated platelets, bypassing VIII and IX → thrombin burst
Subcutaneous bispecific antibody that bridges FIXa and FX (mimics FVIIIa)
rFIX 4–5 times longer; rFVIII 1.4–1.5 times longer
Autoantibodies, mostly against FVIII; > 80% aged ≥ 65; 50% have a cause (pregnancy, autoimmune, malignancy, drug allergy); aPTT does not correct on mixing

questions.stem: A 2½-year-old boy has a forehead hematoma that has grown for a day without trauma. He bruises easily and had a painful swollen knee at 18 months. His maternal uncle has a bleeding disorder. Platelets and PT are normal; the aPTT is prolonged and corrects on mixing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A male toddler with deep and joint bleeding, a maternal uncle affected, and an isolated prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing: hemophilia. A: Mucocutaneous; usually not hemarthrosis. B: Normal platelet count. D: Prolongs the PT. E: Would not correct on mixing.

questions.stem: A boy with recurrent hemarthroses has a factor VIII level of 0.5%. How is his disease classified?
questions.explanation: FVIII 0.5% = severe hemophilia A (< 1%). A: 1–< 5%. B: 5–< 40%. C: Factor IX, not VIII. D: Factor IX, not VIII.

questions.stem: A boy has hemophilia, an X-linked recessive disorder; his maternal uncle is also affected. His mother has never bled. What is her most likely status?
questions.explanation: Hemophilia is X-linked recessive; with an affected maternal uncle the mother most likely carries the mutated F8/F9 gene and passes it to her son. B: She has never bled. C: The uncle points to her side. D: Less likely with an affected uncle. E: She has never bled.

questions.stem: In what share of cases does hemophilia affect males?
questions.explanation: X-linked recessive in 2/3 of cases; F8/F9 mutations on the X chromosome affect males in > 99% of cases. A: Too low. C: Too low. D: The share that is inherited. E: Too low.

questions.stem: Hemophilia is the second most common bleeding disorder after which disorder?
questions.explanation: Hemophilia is the 2nd most common bleeding disorder after VWD. A: A rare bleeding disorder. B: A rare bleeding disorder. C: A rare platelet disorder. E: A rare bleeding disorder.

questions.stem: About what share of people with hemophilia have hemophilia A?
questions.explanation: Hemophilia A makes up ~80% of the total hemophilia population. B: Too low. C: The share with hemophilia B. D: Too high. E: Too low.

questions.stem: A boy with severe hemophilia A has no family history of bleeding. Both parents are well. What best explains this?
questions.explanation: About 1/3 of patients have novel mutations; inheritance explains the other 2/3. A: Hemophilia is X-linked. B: A father gives his son a Y. C: Rare; a disease of old age. E: Not the usual explanation.

questions.stem: Which F8 gene defect is associated with severe hemophilia A?
questions.explanation: Severe hemophilia A is associated with an inversion in intron 22 of the F8 gene. A: Not described. C: Hemophilia B. D: von Willebrand disease. E: Not described.

questions.stem: Which mutation type is found in about two thirds of patients with hemophilia B?
questions.explanation: Around 2/3 of patients with hemophilia B have missense mutations. A: Severe hemophilia A. B: Not the majority. D: Not the majority. E: Not described.

questions.stem: A man with hemophilia A has a factor VIII level of 15%. Which bleeding pattern is expected?

options.E: Bleeding with major surgery or trauma

questions.explanation: Mild (5–< 40%): spontaneous bleeding rare; severe bleeding with major trauma or surgery. Baseline FVIII/IX levels generally correlate with bleeding severity. A: Severe (< 1%). B: Moderate (1–< 5%). C: Moderate (1–< 5%). D: Not the mild pattern.

questions.stem: A boy has spontaneous knee and ankle bleeds without trauma. Which factor VIII level is most likely?
questions.explanation: Severe hemophilia (< 1%): spontaneous joint/muscle bleeding in the absence of trauma. B: Occasional spontaneous bleeding. C: Spontaneous bleeding rare. D: Normal or near normal. E: Normal.

questions.stem: Which severity group makes up the largest share of patients with hemophilia?
questions.explanation: Severe 53%, mild 28%, moderate 19% of patients. A: 28%. B: 19%. C: Not a severity group. E: Rare.

questions.stem: A boy with severe hemophilia feels tingling and a bubbling sensation in his knee. The knee is not yet swollen. What is happening?
questions.explanation: Early signs: worsening pain, tingling or bubbling, decreased range of motion. Later: limited movement, swelling, numbness, warm skin. A: Late, after repeated bleeds. B: Fever, swelling, warmth. D: Not in the joint. E: Not the picture.

questions.stem: A boy with hemophilia has bled into his right ankle four times in five months. What is this joint called?
questions.explanation: Target joint: bleeding in the same joint ≥ 3 times over a 6-month period, leading to progressive joint damage, crippling arthropathy and muscle atrophy. A: Not the term. C: Not the term. D: The end result, not the definition. E: A late consequence.

questions.stem: What share of all bleeds in hemophilia are joint bleeds?
questions.explanation: Hemarthrosis is the most common type of bleeding, 70–80% of all bleeds. A: Muscle bleeds. B: Neck/throat and GI. C: Intracranial. D: Too low.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old with severe hemophilia has a narrowed knee joint space and a contracture after years of bleeds into that knee. Which process links the bleeds to the damage?
questions.explanation: Blood in the joint → inflammation → synovitis and recurring hemarthrosis → loss of cartilage, narrowing of joint space → contractures, muscle atrophy, chronic pain; permanent arthropathy often requiring surgery. A: Gout. B: Not the cycle. D: Rheumatoid arthritis. E: Not the cycle.

questions.stem: What does the extent of hemophilic joint disease correlate with?

options.A: The half-life of the factor used

questions.explanation: The extent of joint disease correlates with the frequency of bleeding. A: Not the stated correlation. B: Not the stated correlation. C: Not the stated correlation. D: Normal in hemophilia.

questions.stem: A boy with severe hemophilia develops a neck swelling and stridor after a throat infection. What is the main danger?
questions.explanation: Neck/throat bleeding is a life-threatening medical emergency leading to airway obstruction. A: Intracranial bleeding. B: Joint bleeding. C: Deep muscle bleeding. E: Gastrointestinal bleeding.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old with severe hemophilia has an iliopsoas bleed. If untreated, what is the main risk?
questions.explanation: Muscles, especially deep compartments (iliopsoas, calf, forearm), 10–20% of bleeds: can result in muscle and nerve damage if left untreated. B: Neck/throat bleeding. C: Joint bleeding. D: Intracranial bleeding. E: Gastrointestinal bleeding.

questions.stem: Which bleed in hemophilia is classified as life-threatening?
questions.explanation: Life-threatening: intracranial, neck/throat, gastrointestinal. Serious/debilitating: joints, muscles, mucous membranes. A: Serious/debilitating. C: Serious/debilitating. D: Mucous membranes; serious. E: Serious/debilitating.

questions.stem: A male newborn bleeds heavily after circumcision. Platelets and PT are normal; the aPTT is prolonged and corrects on mixing. Which level is measured first?
questions.explanation: If in doubt, do the FVIII level; if normal, the FIX level; if both normal, FXI. A: Second, if VIII is normal. B: Third, if VIII and IX are normal. D: Normal aPTT in XIII deficiency. E: Would prolong the PT.

questions.stem: A boy with suspected hemophilia has a prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing and a normal factor VIII level. Which test comes next?
questions.explanation: FVIII level first; if normal, FIX level; if both normal, FXI. B: After IX. C: Not in the sequence. D: The PT is normal. E: Not the next step.

questions.stem: A boy with prolonged bleeding has normal factor VIII and factor IX levels and a prolonged aPTT. Which level is measured next?
questions.explanation: If FVIII is normal, do FIX; if both are normal, do FXI. A: Extrinsic; PT. C: Normal aPTT. D: Would prolong the PT. E: Would prolong the PT.

questions.stem: A boy whose maternal uncle has mild hemophilia A bleeds heavily after a tooth extraction. His aPTT is normal. What is the next step?
questions.explanation: A normal aPTT does not exclude mild hemophilia; if in doubt, do the FVIII level. A: A normal aPTT does not exclude mild hemophilia. B: Not suggested. C: Not the question here. E: Not the question here.

questions.stem: Which laboratory result is expected in hemophilia A?
questions.explanation: Labs: prolonged aPTT corrected by mixing studies; decreased FVIII or FIX (< 40%); normal VWF Ag/VWF activity; mutated F8/F9 gene. A: Normal in hemophilia. B: Normal in hemophilia. C: Corrects (a deficiency). D: Below 40% in hemophilia.

questions.stem: Hemophilia is defined by a factor VIII or IX level below what value?
questions.explanation: Decreased FVIII or FIX (< 40%); mild hemophilia is 5–< 40%. A: Too high. C: Too low. D: Too high. E: Too low.

questions.stem: The parents of a 2-year-old with severe hemophilia A ask whether to give factor only when he bleeds. What does the WFH recommend?
questions.explanation: Prophylaxis is the standard of care: regular, long-term prophylaxis preserves musculoskeletal function, prevents chronic arthropathy and ensures good quality of life. Prophylaxis is superior to on-demand therapy. B: Treating bleeds when they occur; inferior. C: Should start early. D: Concentrates preferred. E: Not for severe hemophilia.

questions.stem: Primary prophylaxis in severe hemophilia should ideally start before what age?
questions.explanation: Prophylaxis should start early, ideally before the age of 3 or after the first joint bleed (primary prophylaxis). A: Not the stated age. B: Too late. D: Too late. E: Too late.

questions.stem: Which trough factor level does WFH prophylaxis usually aim for?
questions.explanation: Aim for target factor trough levels high enough to prevent all bleeds (often ≥ 3–5%), with pharmacokinetic-guided dosing. A: The upper limit of mild hemophilia. B: Too high for a trough. C: Higher than the usual aim. D: Severe range.

questions.stem: How should prophylaxis doses be individualized?
questions.explanation: PK-guided dosing: individualize dosing to the patient's pharmacokinetics. A: Normal in hemophilia. B: Not used. C: Normal in hemophilia. E: Not used.

questions.stem: A toddler with severe hemophilia A starts standard half-life factor VIII three times a week, and a central venous catheter is inserted. Why is the catheter needed?
questions.explanation: Standard half-life FVIII is given IV and eliminated quickly, so repeated infusions are needed each week: venous access, treatment burden, adherence. B: It is IV; emicizumab is subcutaneous. C: Not the reason. D: Not the reason. E: Not the reason.

questions.stem: A boy with hemophilia feels an ankle bleed starting at home in the evening. What does WFH advise?

options.B: Infuse factor at home within 2 hours
options.C: Go to the clinic the next morning
options.E: Take ibuprofen and rest the ankle

questions.explanation: Treat bleeds at home within 2 hours of onset under supervision of the comprehensive care team. A: Treat at onset. C: Too late. D: Factor is needed. E: NSAIDs are avoided.

questions.stem: Cryoprecipitate contains each of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Cryoprecipitate contains FVIII, fibrinogen, factor XIII, VWF and fibronectin, so it does not treat hemophilia B. A: Present. B: Present. D: Present. E: Present.

questions.stem: Why does WFH prefer clotting factor concentrates to cryoprecipitate or plasma?
questions.explanation: WFH: concentrates are preferred over cryoprecipitate/FFP because of concerns about quality, safety and efficacy; those are used only if they are the only available or affordable options. A: Cryoprecipitate/FFP are used when affordable. B: Not the reason. C: Still IV. D: Inhibitors arise to concentrates.

questions.stem: A 20-kg boy with severe hemophilia A needs his factor VIII level raised by 40 IU/dL. About how many units of factor VIII are needed?
questions.explanation: 1 FVIII unit/kg raises plasma FVIII by ~2 IU/dL: 40 ÷ 2 = 20 units/kg × 20 kg = 400 units. A: Uses 1 IU/dL per unit/kg. B: Uses 4 IU/dL per unit/kg. C: Too many. E: Too few.

questions.stem: A 30-kg boy with hemophilia B needs his factor IX level raised by 40 IU/dL. About how many units of factor IX are needed?
questions.explanation: 1 FIX unit/kg raises plasma FIX by ~1 IU/dL: 40 units/kg × 30 kg = 1,200 units. B: Uses 2 IU/dL per unit/kg (factor VIII). C: Too many. D: Too few. E: Too few.

questions.stem: Why is factor VIII infused more often than factor IX?

options.A: It raises levels less per unit
options.B: It needs vitamin K to work
options.C: It is cleared by the kidney

questions.explanation: Half-life of factor VIII 8–12 hours; of factor IX 18–24 hours. A: It raises them more (2 vs 1 IU/dL). B: Neither needs it after infusion. C: Not the reason. D: Not the reason.

questions.stem: A boy receives an IV dose of factor VIII for a bleed. When should a blood sample be drawn to check the peak level?
questions.explanation: Peak clotting factor level: 15–30 minutes after infusion. A: Too late. C: The half-life of FVIII. D: The half-life of FIX. E: Too early.

questions.stem: A teenager with hemophilia has knee pain after a joint bleed. Which analgesic should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Supportive therapy: RICE, physiotherapy, noncontact sports, no NSAIDs or aspirin, pain control, psychosocial support, vaccinations, education. A: Safe for pain. B: Not an antiplatelet drug. D: Not an antiplatelet drug. E: Not an antiplatelet drug.

questions.stem: Which sport best suits a boy with severe hemophilia?
questions.explanation: Supportive therapy includes physiotherapy and noncontact sports. A: Contact sport. B: Contact sport. C: Contact sport. E: Contact sport.

questions.stem: People with hemophilia are monitored regularly for each of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Monitor regularly for bleeds, musculoskeletal complications, inhibitor development, transfusion-related infections and quality of life. A: Monitored. B: Monitored. D: Monitored. E: Monitored.

questions.stem: A boy with severe hemophilia A falls and develops a severe headache and vomiting. What is the first step?
questions.explanation: Intracranial bleeding: urgent clotting factor replacement before evaluation and until bleed-free. A: Treatment comes first. B: Life-threatening bleed. C: The platelets are normal. E: Not for severe hemophilia.

questions.stem: A boy's knee hemarthrosis is treated with factor until bleed-free, RICE and analgesia. What else belongs in the plan?
questions.explanation: Joints: urgent clotting factor replacement until bleed-free + RICE + analgesia + physiotherapy. A: Added for neck/throat bleeds. B: Platelets are normal. C: Not deficient. D: Not indicated.

questions.stem: A man with hemophilia has a gastrointestinal bleed. Besides urgent factor replacement, which treatment is added?
questions.explanation: Gastrointestinal: same as intracranial (urgent factor replacement) plus antifibrinolytics. Neck/throat: plus antifibrinolytics/antibiotics. B: Platelets are normal. C: Not deficient. D: Not the added treatment. E: Added for neck/throat bleeds.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with severe hemophilia A and no inhibitor is scheduled for knee surgery. How is factor VIII best given around the operation?
questions.explanation: Continuous CFC infusion is recommended for perioperative management or a severe bleed. A: Levels fall within hours. C: Prevention is needed. D: Concentrates are preferred. E: Not for severe hemophilia.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old with severe hemophilia A, fully adherent to prophylaxis, has profuse rectal bleeding. Hb is 5.0 g/dL. Bleeding continues despite factor VIII given to a level of 80–100%. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: A proportion of patients develop neutralizing anti-factor antibodies (inhibitors) that make factor treatment ineffective. A: The family is fully adherent. B: Target level reached. D: Not suggested. E: Not suggested.

questions.stem: In which unit is the strength of a factor VIII inhibitor reported?
questions.explanation: Low-titer: < 5 Bethesda units (BU); high-titer: > 5 BU. A: Factor levels. B: Clotting times. C: Factor levels. E: Not used.

questions.stem: A patient with hemophilia A has an inhibitor titer of 12 Bethesda units. How is it classified?
questions.explanation: Low-titer < 5 BU; high-titer > 5 BU. A: Not a category used. B: Bethesda measures neutralizing activity. C: Not a factor inhibitor. D: Not a titer category.

questions.stem: About what share of patients with severe hemophilia A develop inhibitors?
questions.explanation: Inhibitor formation: ~25% of patients with severe hemophilia A and ~5% with severe hemophilia B. B: Severe hemophilia B. C: Too high. D: Too low. E: Too high.

questions.stem: How do neutralizing inhibitors reduce the effect of infused factor VIII?

options.B: They block its binding to platelets

questions.explanation: Neutralizing antibodies bind FVIII/FIX and prevent it from binding to platelet surfaces or other clotting factors. A: Not the mechanism. C: Not the mechanism. D: Not the mechanism. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: In severe hemophilia A, what share of patients with inhibitors had a hemophilia-related death, compared with 12% without?
questions.explanation: Inhibitors bring uncontrollable bleeding, progressive joint damage, poor quality of life, very high cost and premature death (41.7% vs 12.0%). A: Without inhibitors. B: Inhibitor frequency. C: Hemophilia B inhibitors. D: Too high.

questions.stem: A man with severe hemophilia A and a high-titer inhibitor is bleeding. Which agent bypasses the need for factors VIII and IX?
questions.explanation: Bypassing agents: activated prothrombin complexes and rFVIIa, which directly activates factor X, bypassing the need for factors VIII and IX. A: Neutralized by the inhibitor. B: Raises FVIII; neutralized. C: Contains FVIII. E: Not missing.

questions.stem: Besides bypassing agents and emicizumab, which strategy treats a factor VIII inhibitor?

options.A: High doses of factor VIII long term
options.C: Daily oral vitamin K for months

questions.explanation: Treatment of inhibitors: very high doses of CFC for a long time, bypassing agents, factor VIII mimetics (emicizumab). B: Not a strategy given. C: Not relevant. D: Not relevant. E: Raises FVIII; neutralized.

questions.stem: At pharmacological doses, how does recombinant factor VIIa stop bleeding?

options.A: It activates factor IX on endothelium
options.C: It activates factor X on platelets
options.D: It bridges factor IXa and factor X
options.E: It inhibits plasmin in the clot

questions.explanation: rFVIIa binds TF and makes a little thrombin; at pharmacological doses it directly activates factor X on the surface of activated platelets → thrombin burst → stable hemostatic plug. A: Not the mechanism. B: Not the mechanism. D: Emicizumab. E: Antifibrinolytics.

questions.stem: How does emicizumab work?

options.A: It activates X on platelet surfaces
options.B: It bridges factor IXa and factor X
options.E: It supplies activated factors II and X

questions.explanation: Emicizumab is a bispecific antibody that mimics FVIIIa: it binds FIXa and FX, bringing them close enough for FIXa to activate FX. A: rFVIIa. C: Not a factor. D: Not the mechanism. E: Activated prothrombin complexes.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with hemophilia A and an inhibitor fears IV infusions. Which agent is given subcutaneously?
questions.explanation: Emicizumab is a subcutaneous monoclonal antibody that mimics the role of FVIIIa. A: IV. B: IV. D: IV; neutralized. E: IV; hemophilia B.

questions.stem: Compared with standard products, extended half-life recombinant factor IX lasts about how much longer?
questions.explanation: Extended half-life CFCs decrease dosing frequency: rFIX half-life is 4–5-fold and rFVIII 1.4–1.5-fold longer. A: Extended half-life FVIII. B: Too low. C: Too high. D: Too high.

questions.stem: Which treatment offers a potential cure for hemophilia?
questions.explanation: Gene therapy offers a potential cure through transfer of the missing/mutated gene, giving sustained endogenous FVIII/FIX production. B: Prophylaxis, not cure. C: Prophylaxis, not cure. D: Treats bleeds. E: Not a cure.

questions.stem: Besides a multidisciplinary team, which is a prerequisite for hemophilia care?

options.D: A lab able to test for inhibitors

questions.explanation: Prerequisites: a multidisciplinary team, management protocols, a coagulation lab capable of testing for inhibitors, CFCs/hemostatic agents/antifibrinolytics, a registry of treatment data and bleeding records. A: Not listed. B: Not listed. C: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Which limitation of standard half-life factor VIII causes repeated infusions every week?
questions.explanation: Standard half-life FVIII: IV administration (venous access, burden, poor adherence), rapid elimination (repeated IV infusions, fluctuating effect), immunogenicity (allo-antibodies → treatment failure). A: Causes treatment failure. C: Causes access problems. D: A result, not the cause. E: Not the cause.

questions.stem: In shared decision-making, which step comes right after assessing the patient's preferences?
questions.explanation: Seek participation → help explore and compare options → assess preferences → reach a joint decision → evaluate the decision. A: The first step. B: Before assessing preferences. D: The last step. E: Not a step.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman has 12 hours of abdominal distension, 2 weeks of bruising and hip pain, and 5 years of joint pains and rash. No relative bleeds. Hb is 5.5 g/dL, PT normal; the aPTT is markedly prolonged and does not correct on mixing. Ultrasound shows a massive abdominal hematoma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An older adult with new severe bleeding, a negative family history and an aPTT that does not correct on mixing (FVIII < 1%, very high inhibitor titer): acquired hemophilia. A: Mixing would correct. B: Causes clotting, not massive bleeding. C: Prolongs the PT. D: Mixing would correct.

questions.stem: An older woman with acquired hemophilia A and long-standing autoimmune joint disease is bleeding. Besides bypassing agents, what is essential?
questions.explanation: Acquired hemophilia treatment: the same as congenital hemophilia with inhibitors plus treatment of the underlying disease. A: Neutralized by the inhibitor. B: Neutralized. C: Not deficient. E: Platelets are normal.

questions.stem: Two months after delivery, a 30-year-old woman has extensive bruising. Her aPTT is prolonged with a normal PT and does not correct on mixing; factor VIII is very low. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Acquired hemophilia is due to an underlying condition in 50% of cases: pregnancy, autoimmune disorders, malignancy, drug allergy. A: Prolongs the PT. C: Mixing would correct. D: Mixing would correct. E: Mixing would correct.

questions.stem: Which group most often develops acquired hemophilia?
questions.explanation: Acquired hemophilia is a disease of old age: > 80% of cases are ≥ 65 years. B: Congenital hemophilia presents then. C: Not the typical group. D: Not the typical group. E: Not the typical group.

questions.stem: Against which factor are the autoantibodies of acquired hemophilia most often directed?
questions.explanation: Acquired hemophilia: autoantibodies (inhibitors) against plasma clotting factors, most frequently FVIII. A: Less often. B: Less often. D: Less often. E: Less often.

lectures.title: Disorders of white blood cells
lectures.covers: Non-malignant WBC disorders: leukocytosis and its forms, leukemoid and leukoerythroblastic reactions, neutropenia (ANC grades, drug, infection, congenital, immune, margination), lymphopenia, and neutrophil function defects (LAD, Chediak-Higashi, CGD).

ul: Adult WBC 4,000–11,000/µL (4.0–11.0 ×10⁹/L). Know the normal ranges for age before calling a count abnormal.
About 90% of WBCs sit in the marrow, 2–3% circulate, 7–8% are in tissues. WBC life span 11–16 days, mostly in the marrow.
The marrow pool can raise circulating WBCs 2–3-fold within a few hours.
Neutrophils are ~60% of adult WBCs: 9 days in the marrow, 3–6 hours in blood, 1–4 days in tissue.
