questions.stem: A volunteer donates one unit of whole blood for a trauma patient. Which of the following is NOT part of that unit as collected?
questions.explanation: Whole blood (500 mL) contains red cells, white cells, platelets and plasma. Cryoprecipitate is prepared later from plasma. A: Part of whole blood. B: Part of whole blood. C: Part of whole blood. D: Part of whole blood.

questions.stem: Which blood component is transfused most often?
questions.explanation: Transfusion of RBCs is the most common. A: Less often. C: Less often. D: Less often. E: Less often.

questions.stem: How does apheresis differ from whole blood donation?

options.B: The whole unit is spun into its components
options.C: Plasma is fractionated into clotting factors
options.D: Red cells are irradiated before storage
options.E: The donor gives a larger single volume

questions.explanation: Apheresis: one component (platelets, red cells or plasma) is collected and the rest returned to the donor. Whole blood: the unit is spun and separated into its components. B: Whole blood donation. C: Plasma processing. D: Processing, not collection. E: Not the difference.

questions.stem: Which product is prepared from donated plasma?
questions.explanation: Plasma gives fresh frozen plasma, prothrombin complex concentrate, cryoprecipitate, clotting factors, immunoglobulins and albumin. A: From whole blood or plateletpheresis. B: Red cell product. C: Cellular product. E: Red cell product.

questions.stem: How are apheresis platelets stored?
questions.explanation: Platelets: room temperature with agitation, given over 15–30 min. A: Red cells and whole blood. B: Fresh frozen plasma. D: Cryoprecipitate. E: Prothrombin complex concentrate.

questions.stem: A unit of packed red cells is issued from the blood bank. At what temperature is it stored?
questions.explanation: Whole blood and packed red cells: +1 to +6 °C, given within 4 hours. A: Platelets. C: Fresh frozen plasma. D: Cryoprecipitate. E: Prothrombin complex concentrate.

questions.stem: A man with liver failure and DIC has several low clotting factors and is bleeding. Which product fits?
questions.explanation: FFP (clotting factors, albumin, immunoglobulins; ≤ −25 °C; 30 min): DIC, liver failure, multiple clotting factor deficiencies. A: VWF, VIII, XIII deficiencies. B: Thrombocytopenia. C: No clotting factors. E: Immune cytopenia, immune deficiency.

questions.stem: A man on warfarin has an intracranial bleed. Which product gives rapid reversal?
questions.explanation: PCC (factors II, VII, IX, X, proteins C and S; slow IV push): life-threatening bleeding, rapid warfarin reversal. A: VWF, VIII, XIII. B: Not for warfarin reversal. C: No clotting factors. D: Not a factor product.

questions.stem: Which protein is present in prothrombin complex concentrate?
questions.explanation: PCC contains factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins S and C. Cryoprecipitate carries VIII, XIII and VWF. B: Cryoprecipitate. C: Cryoprecipitate. D: Cryoprecipitate. E: No concentrate exists.

questions.stem: A woman with von Willebrand disease bleeds during surgery, and no factor concentrate is available. Which blood component supplies VWF?
questions.explanation: Cryoprecipitate (10–20 mL; ≤ −18 °C): factor VIII, XIII and VWF deficiencies, trauma, DIC, unavailable factor concentrate. A: II, VII, IX, X. B: Not the VWF source. D: No clotting factors. E: No clotting factors.

questions.stem: For which factor is no clotting factor concentrate available?
questions.explanation: Clotting factor concentrates: all clotting factors except FV; used for disorders of secondary hemostasis. A: Concentrate exists. B: Concentrate exists. C: Concentrate exists. D: Concentrate exists.

questions.stem: Immunoglobulin products used for immune cytopenias are made mostly of which class?
questions.explanation: Immunoglobulins: mostly IgG; 2–6 °C; given over 3 h; immune cytopenia and immune deficiencies. A: Not the main class. B: Not the main class. D: Not the main class. E: Not the main class.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with sickle cell disease and a stroke starts chronic transfusion with phenotype-matched red cells. What is being matched?

options.A: All antigens on the red cell surface
options.B: The genetic sequences at the antigen loci
options.C: A group of antigens from one gene
options.D: A surface molecule defined by an antibody
options.E: The ABO and RhD group of the donor

questions.explanation: RBC phenotype: combination of antigens on the RBC surface. Genotype: genetic sequences at the loci for blood group antigens. B: Genotype. C: Blood group system. D: A red cell antigen. E: Part of the phenotype.

questions.stem: What is a blood group system?

options.A: The antigens on a person's red cells
options.B: Antigens from one gene or linked genes
options.C: DNA sequences at blood group loci
options.D: A surface sugar defined by an antibody
options.E: The antibodies found in a person's plasma

questions.explanation: Blood group system: a group of ≥ 1 antigens controlled by a single gene or a cluster of closely linked genes. ISBT 2024: 366 antigens, 47 systems. A: Phenotype. C: Genotype. D: A red cell antigen. E: Not the definition.

questions.stem: How many blood group systems does the ISBT list (2024)?
questions.explanation: ISBT working group 2024: 366 human red cell antigens and 47 blood group systems. A: Number of antigens. B: ABO and Rh groups. C: ABO groups. E: Not the value.

questions.stem: Besides pretransfusion testing, blood typing is used to assess the risk of which disease?
questions.explanation: Blood typing: pretransfusion testing, organ transplantation, evaluation of transfusion reactions and risk of HDFN. A: Membrane defect. B: Enzyme defect. C: Acquired clonal defect. D: Not assessed by typing.

questions.stem: The ABO genes are located on which chromosome?
questions.explanation: ABO: the most important blood group system; genes on chromosome 9; involved in severe hemolytic reactions and HDFN. A: HFE. C: β-globin. D: α-globin. E: Not ABO.

questions.stem: Which is the most important antigen of the Rh system?
questions.explanation: Rh is the 2nd most important system; major antigens D (most important), C, c, E, e. A: Major, less important. B: Major, less important. D: Minor system (Kell). E: Minor system (Duffy).

questions.stem: Which is a minor but clinically significant blood group system?
questions.explanation: Major systems: ABO and Rh. Minor clinically significant systems: Kell, Kidd, Duffy, MNS. A: Major system. B: Major system. C: Not a red cell system. E: Platelet antigens.

questions.stem: A patient's red cells agglutinate with anti-B and anti-Rh reagents but not with anti-A. What is the blood group?
questions.explanation: Agglutination means the red cells carry the antigen bound by the reagent antibody: B antigen and Rh antigen present, A absent. B: Would agglutinate with anti-A. C: Would agglutinate with anti-A. D: Would not agglutinate with anti-B. E: Would agglutinate with anti-A, not anti-Rh.

questions.stem: A woman is blood group O. Which antibodies are present in her plasma?
questions.explanation: If an antigen is on a person's red cells, the matching antibody is absent from plasma. Group O cells lack A and B, so plasma has anti-A and anti-B. A: Group B. B: Group A. D: Group AB. E: Not naturally present.

questions.stem: In an emergency with no time for typing, which red cells can be given to any recipient?
questions.explanation: O negative is the universal donor: no A, B or Rh (D) antigen on the red cells. B: Carries A and B antigens. C: Universal recipient type. D: Carries A antigen. E: Carries B antigen.

questions.stem: A stable 60-year-old inpatient with AML has Hb 7.4 g/dL, no bleeding and no heart disease. What is the best decision?
questions.explanation: AABB restrictive threshold: Hb < 7 g/dL for most hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults, including those with hematologic or oncologic disease. Decisions rest on the clinical context, not Hb alone. A: Above the restrictive threshold of 7. B: Above the threshold. C: Fresh units are not needed. D: No indication given.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with coronary artery disease is about to have major surgery. His Hb is 7.6 g/dL. What is the best decision?

options.A: Wait until Hb is below 7 g/dL

questions.explanation: Higher threshold, Hb < 8 g/dL, in selected patients with cardiovascular disease or undergoing major surgery. A: A higher threshold applies. B: Not for anemia. C: Not indicated. E: Not for anemia.

questions.stem: For most hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults, red cells are transfused below which hemoglobin?
questions.explanation: Restrictive threshold: Hb < 7 g/dL for most stable hospitalized adults and critically ill but stable children; < 8 g/dL with cardiovascular disease or major surgery. A: Cardiovascular disease or major surgery. C: Too high. D: Too high. E: Too low.

questions.stem: A resident asks the blood bank for red cells stored less than 10 days for a stable inpatient with anemia. Which units are appropriate?
questions.explanation: RBC units can be used within their approved shelf life; fresh (< 10 days) units are not routinely necessary. A: Fresh units are not routinely necessary. B: Not advised. C: Not advised. D: Not advised.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old with pre-B-cell ALL needs a lumbar puncture. Below what platelet count should platelets be given first?
questions.explanation: AABB: lumbar puncture, transfuse at < 20 ×10⁹/L. A: Major non-spine surgery. B: Prophylaxis during chemotherapy. D: Preterm neonates. E: Not a threshold.

questions.stem: A man receiving chemotherapy for AML has a platelet count of 12 ×10⁹/L and no bleeding. What is the best decision?
questions.explanation: Hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia on chemotherapy or allogeneic SCT without bleeding: transfuse at < 10 ×10⁹/L. A: Threshold is < 10. C: No indication. D: No indication. E: No bleeding.

questions.stem: A woman needs a major abdominal operation (not involving the spine). Platelets should be raised above what level?
questions.explanation: AABB: major surgery not involving the spine, transfuse at < 50 ×10⁹/L. A: Lumbar puncture. B: Prophylaxis on chemotherapy. C: Preterm neonates. E: Not the threshold.

questions.stem: In a preterm neonate without major bleeding, platelets are transfused below what level?
questions.explanation: Preterm neonates without major bleeding: transfuse at < 25 ×10⁹/L. B: Adults on chemotherapy. C: Major surgery. D: Lumbar puncture. E: Too high.

questions.stem: A woman with TTP has a platelet count of 9 ×10⁹/L and no bleeding. Why are platelets withheld?
questions.explanation: Avoid platelet transfusion in TTP and HIT, except for life-threatening bleeding or urgent procedures: platelet activation. A: Not the reason. B: Not the reason. C: Not the reason. E: Not the reason.

questions.stem: A patient with ALL receives leukocyte-depleted red cells. Which risk does leukocyte depletion lower?
questions.explanation: Leukocyte depletion: significant reduction in CMV transmission, WBC immunization and febrile reactions. A: Irradiation. B: Not affected. D: Volume-related. E: Plasma proteins.

questions.stem: Which cellular blood component is not leukocyte-depleted?
questions.explanation: All cellular blood components, except granulocyte concentrates, must be leukocyte depleted (< 5 ×10⁶ WBCs per component). B: Must be depleted. C: Must be depleted. D: Cellular; depleted. E: Must be depleted.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old on chemotherapy for ALL needs red cells. Which processing step stops donor T cells from dividing in him?
questions.explanation: Irradiation prevents donor T lymphocytes from dividing in the recipient and decreases GVHD. Indications include children on chemotherapy. A: Lowers CMV, immunization and fever. C: Antigen matching. D: Compatibility. E: Infections.

questions.stem: What does irradiation do to the shelf life of red cells?
questions.explanation: Irradiation decreases RBC shelf life to 28 days. A: Not the value. B: Not the value. C: Not the value. D: It is shortened.

questions.stem: Which patient needs irradiated blood products?

options.B: Adult with a bleeding peptic ulcer

questions.explanation: Irradiation: HSCT candidates and recipients, children on chemotherapy, primary immune deficiency, aplastic anemia on IST. B: Not listed. C: Not listed. D: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Which infection is part of the pretransfusion screen of donated blood?
questions.explanation: Infectious screen: HIV, HBV, HCV, HTLV and others. A: Not listed. B: Not listed. C: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: A red cell unit has been out of the refrigerator for 45 minutes before the nurse is ready to start it. What should be done?
questions.explanation: Discard a pack that has been at room temperature > 4 h, out of the refrigerator > 30 min, opened, or shows signs of deterioration. A: Out of the fridge > 30 min. B: Out of the fridge > 30 min. C: Out of the fridge > 30 min. D: Out of the fridge > 30 min.

questions.stem: Before hanging a red cell unit, the nurse sees pink plasma above the red cells. What does this mean?
questions.explanation: Pink plasma means hemolysis: do not use. Any bag that fails a check is returned to the blood bank and never transfused. A: Milky plasma. B: The bag must not be used. D: Not the meaning. E: Look for large clots.

questions.stem: Which solution may run in the same tubing as a red cell unit?
questions.explanation: Only 0.9% sodium chloride, ABO-compatible plasma or albumin should be hung in the same tubing with a PRBC unit; avoid mixing medications with blood. A: Not allowed. C: Not allowed. D: No medications. E: No medications.

questions.stem: In adults, at what rate is a red cell unit started for the first 15 minutes?
questions.explanation: 1–2 mL/min (60–120 mL/h) for the first 15 minutes, then as rapidly as tolerated, not exceeding 4 hours. A: Too fast. B: Too fast. C: Too slow. E: Too fast.

questions.stem: A child with severe anemia shows signs of hypoxia. How much of the red cell transfusion is given quickly?
questions.explanation: Quickly give the first 5 mL/kg of PRBCs to relieve hypoxia, then slowly. If still critically low, give a second 5–10 mL/kg. B: Too much. C: Too little. D: Too much. E: The rest goes slowly.

questions.stem: For how long after a red cell transfusion is the patient monitored for reactions?

options.A: Up to 6 hours after it ends
options.B: Up to 30 min after it ends
options.C: Up to 24 hours after it ends
options.D: Up to 2 hours after it ends
options.E: Up to 12 hours after it ends

questions.explanation: Monitor the patient during transfusion and up to 30 minutes after its end: vital signs and signs of acute transfusion reactions. A: Not the value. C: Not the value. D: Not the value. E: Not the value.

questions.stem: An Rh-negative young woman needs a platelet transfusion and only Rh-positive platelets are available. What is the concern?

options.A: Hemolysis from anti-D in platelet plasma
options.E: Rh immunization from red cell stroma

questions.explanation: Platelets contain enough red cell stroma (membrane fragments) to stimulate Rh immunization. A: Not the concern. B: Not the concern. C: Not related to Rh. D: Not the concern.

questions.stem: A platelet transfusion should be completed within what time?
questions.explanation: Complete platelet infusion within 30 minutes (15–30 min). A: Red cells. B: Immunoglobulin. D: Not the value. E: Not the value.

questions.stem: A child becomes febrile, hypotensive and shaky with chills 5 minutes after a platelet transfusion starts. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Transfusion-transmitted infection is mostly reported with platelet transfusion (bacterial contamination): rapid fever, chills, hypo- or hypertension, septic shock. A: Benign; no shock. B: No fever; IgA deficiency. C: Respiratory picture. E: Hypertension, volume.

questions.stem: Bacterial contamination of a transfused unit is suspected. What confirms the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Culture of the blood pack confirms the diagnosis. A: Hemolysis. C: TRALI or TACO. D: Compatibility. E: Anaphylaxis.

questions.stem: A patient has suspected bacterial contamination after a platelet transfusion. The transfusion is stopped and cultures are sent. What else is started promptly?
questions.explanation: Stop the transfusion, assess and stabilize, notify the blood bank, culture patient and bag, and start IV antibiotics promptly. A: Anaphylaxis. B: Urticarial reaction. D: AHTR. E: TA-GVHD.

questions.stem: Thirty minutes into a red cell transfusion, a postpartum woman has fever, chills, flushing, dyspnea and red urine. BP 55/40 mmHg. PT and aPTT are prolonged, fibrinogen is low and D-dimer is high. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: AHTR: incompatible blood → recipient antibodies against donor antigens → intravascular hemolysis; fever, chills, flushing, dyspnea, back pain, red urine; DIC, shock, organ failure. A: No hemolysis or shock. B: Hives only. C: No red urine or DIC. D: Days to weeks later.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?
questions.explanation: AHTR: commonest cause is infusion of incompatible (most likely ABO) blood due to clerical or nursing error. B: FNHTR. C: TRALI. D: Infection. E: Urticarial reaction.

questions.stem: A patient has an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction. After the transfusion is stopped, which treatment is specific to this reaction?
questions.explanation: Treatment: AHTR, aggressive hydration and diuresis. ATR: epinephrine, steroids, vasopressors. UTR: antihistamines. FNHTR: antipyretics. TA-GVHD: steroids and immune suppressants. A: Anaphylaxis. B: Urticarial reaction. D: FNHTR. E: TA-GVHD.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with hereditary IgA deficiency receives plasma. Within minutes she has wheeze, stridor, hives and hypotension. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: ATR: most often in hereditary IgA deficiency with anti-IgA antibody after IgA-containing products; wheezing, laryngeal edema and hypotension in severe cases. A: Hives without wheeze or hypotension. B: Fever, red urine. C: Pulmonary edema within 6 h. E: Fever, chills.

questions.stem: A woman has an anaphylactic transfusion reaction with stridor and hypotension. Which drug is given?
questions.explanation: ATR: epinephrine, steroids, vasopressors, respiratory support. A: Urticarial reaction. C: FNHTR. D: TACO. E: Infection.

questions.stem: Anaphylactic transfusion reactions are seen most often in patients with which condition?
questions.explanation: ATR: most often in patients with hereditary IgA deficiency who make anti-IgA antibody and then receive IgA-containing products. A: Not the risk group. B: Not the risk group. C: Not the risk group. D: Not the risk group.

questions.stem: Forty minutes into a red cell transfusion, a man develops itchy hives on one arm. Vital signs are normal and there is no wheeze. The transfusion is paused and an antihistamine given; he stays symptom-free for 30 minutes. What next?
questions.explanation: UTR: urticaria or itching within minutes; antihistamines, resume transfusion if no symptoms after 30 min. Permanent stop needs features such as hives over > 2/3 of the body. B: Localized hives allow resuming. C: Anaphylaxis. D: AHTR. E: Infection.

questions.stem: What causes urticarial transfusion reactions?

options.D: Recipient IgE against a donor protein
options.E: Recipient antibodies to donor red cells

questions.explanation: UTR: quite common; mostly caused by preformed recipient IgE antibody interacting with a donor allergen or protein. A: Anaphylactic reaction. B: FNHTR. C: TRALI. E: AHTR.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old with iron deficiency anemia from heavy menstrual bleeding receives red cells. An hour in, she develops fever, chills and malaise; BP and urine are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: FNHTR: the most common reaction; fever, chills, malaise; a diagnosis of exclusion. A: No hypotension or red urine. B: No wheeze or hypotension. C: Respiratory signs. D: Days later.

questions.stem: What causes a febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction?

options.C: Recipient IgE against a donor protein
options.D: Donor T cells dividing in the host

questions.explanation: FNHTR is caused by cytokines released from donor leukocytes during storage; prevented by leukocyte filters. A: ATR. C: UTR. D: TA-GVHD. E: AHTR.

questions.stem: Which measure prevents febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reactions?
questions.explanation: FNHTR prevention: use of leukocyte filters. A: Prevents TA-GVHD. B: TACO. D: TACO. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Which is the most common transfusion reaction?
questions.explanation: FNHTR is the most common transfusion reaction. B: Quite common. C: Rarer. D: Rarer. E: Rarer.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old with AML has fever, rash, vomiting, diarrhea, pancytopenia and very high liver enzymes. Ten days ago he received a non-irradiated red cell unit at a small hospital. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: TA-GVHD: donor T lymphocytes in a host with weak immunity; fever, rash, diarrhea, vomiting, hepatic dysfunction and pancytopenia 10–30 days after transfusion. A: Rash, diarrhea and liver injury after transfusion point elsewhere. C: No rash or pancytopenia. D: Within hours. E: Within minutes.

questions.stem: Transfusion-associated graft versus host disease is fatal mostly because of what?
questions.explanation: TA-GVHD has a high fatality rate, mostly due to pancytopenia. B: Not the main cause. C: Not the main cause. D: Not the main cause. E: Not the main cause.

questions.stem: Which patient is at risk of transfusion-associated graft versus host disease?

options.E: An athlete with a femoral shaft fracture

questions.explanation: At risk: premature and LBW infants, children with PID, organ transplant recipients, patients on chemotherapy or IST. Prevented by irradiated products. A: Normal immunity. B: Normal immunity. D: Normal immunity. E: Normal immunity.

questions.stem: Two hours into a plasma transfusion, a patient develops sudden dyspnea, hypoxia and diffuse bilateral infiltrates. BP is 100/60 mmHg and the JVP is normal. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: TRALI: sudden dyspnea, hypoxia, pulmonary edema and diffuse infiltrates within 6 h of any plasma-containing product. A: Hypertension, raised JVP. B: Wheeze, urticaria. C: Red urine. E: Fever without lung injury.

questions.stem: What is the mechanism of TRALI?

options.A: Recipient antibodies against donor red cells
options.D: Donor T cells attacking the host

questions.explanation: TRALI: donor antibodies attack recipient WBCs and pulmonary endothelial cells, increasing pulmonary vascular permeability. A: AHTR. B: TACO. C: UTR. D: TA-GVHD.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old with heart failure receives 3 red cell units rapidly. Four hours later he has dyspnea, BP 175/95 mmHg, raised JVP, basal crackles and frothy pink sputum. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: TACO: rapid large-volume transfusion → acute LVF and pulmonary edema within 12 h; hypertension, raised JVP, basal crackles, frothy pink sputum. B: Normal JVP; no hypertension. C: Hypotension, wheeze. D: Red urine, hypotension. E: Fever, chills.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old develops transfusion-associated circulatory overload. After stopping the transfusion, which drug is given?
questions.explanation: TACO management: stop the transfusion, give oxygen and diuretics, respiratory support as needed. A: Anaphylaxis. B: Urticarial reaction. C: FNHTR. E: TA-GVHD.

questions.stem: What is the leading cause of transfusion-related death?
questions.explanation: TACO: leading cause (32% of fatalities). TRALI: second (21%). A: Second leading cause (21%). B: Less common. C: Rare. D: Less common.

questions.stem: An 85-year-old with heart failure and chronic kidney disease needs two units of red cells. How should they be given?

options.B: Transfuse one unit at a time

questions.explanation: TACO prevention: transfuse one unit at a time, slow the rate, give a diuretic in patients at risk. A: Prevents TA-GVHD. C: Prevents FNHTR. D: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes into a red cell transfusion, a patient develops fever and chills. What is the first step?
questions.explanation: First step: stop the transfusion immediately, keep the IV open with 0.9% sodium chloride and see the patient. Early signs of benign and serious reactions are similar. A: Stop first. B: Stop first. D: Stop first. E: Stop first.

questions.stem: What is the cornerstone of preventing transfusion reactions?

options.C: Universal irradiation of red cell units
options.D: Routine use of fresh red cell units

questions.explanation: A restrictive attitude towards transfusion plus pretransfusion testing is the cornerstone of prevention. B: Not the cornerstone. C: Prevents TA-GVHD. D: Not needed. E: Not the cornerstone.

questions.stem: How should an acute transfusion reaction be regarded at its onset?

options.C: Febrile and harmless if vitals are stable
options.D: Infectious until cultures come back negative

questions.explanation: All acute transfusion reactions must be considered potentially serious until proved otherwise; early signs of benign and serious reactions may be similar. A: Early signs are similar. B: Not the rule. C: Not the rule. D: Not the rule.

questions.stem: Which finding means a transfusion must be stopped permanently?

options.D: A few hives on the chest

questions.explanation: Stop permanently: reaction < 15 min after starting, temperature > 39 °C, hypotension or shock, chills, back or chest pain, dyspnea, tachycardia or arrhythmias, flushing or hives over > 2/3 of the body, hemoglobinuria, bleeding from the IV site. A: Mild; can resume. C: Below 39 °C. D: Below 2/3 of the body. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Why does chronic transfusion inevitably cause iron overload?

options.B: Donor red cells release free iron at once

questions.explanation: Iron overload: increased intake (transfusions) or increased absorption with normal intake. Humans have a limited ability to eliminate excess iron. A: Not the reason. B: Not the reason. D: Not the reason. E: Not the reason.

questions.stem: Which condition causes iron overload mainly through increased intestinal absorption rather than transfusion?
questions.explanation: Non-transfusion (increased intestinal iron absorption): hereditary hemochromatosis and ineffective erythropoiesis (NTDT, sideroblastic anemia, CDA, MDS). A: Transfusion-related. B: Transfusion-related. C: Transfusion-related. E: Transfusion-related.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man has fatigue, joint pain, raised liver enzymes, new diabetes and darkened skin. Transferrin saturation is 78% and ferritin 1,800 ng/mL; CRP is normal. Which genotype is most likely?
questions.explanation: HH is AR; homozygosity for C282Y in around 80%, compound heterozygosity C282Y/H63D, other HFE mutations, and less often non-HFE genes. The triad of cirrhosis, diabetes and skin pigmentation = "bronze diabetes". A: Less common. C: Less common. D: No iron overload. E: No iron overload.

questions.stem: On which chromosome is the HFE gene?
questions.explanation: HFE (type 1 HH) lies on the short arm of chromosome 6; inheritance is autosomal recessive. A: ABO. B: β-globin. C: α-globin. E: Not HFE.

questions.stem: What is the most common cause of severe iron overload?
questions.explanation: Hereditary hemochromatosis is the most common cause of severe iron overload. A: Transfusion-related. B: Transfusion-related. C: Ineffective erythropoiesis. D: Less common.

questions.stem: How are most patients with hereditary hemochromatosis first identified?
questions.explanation: Most patients (75%) are asymptomatic and are diagnosed on routine chemistry or a positive family history. B: Classic triad, but late. C: Late. D: Late. E: Late.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old has heart failure, hypogonadism and very high transferrin saturation. He has never been transfused. Which form of iron overload fits his age?
questions.explanation: HH usually presents at 40–50 years, except the juvenile form (10–30 years). Manifestations: cirrhosis, cardiomyopathy, endocrinopathies, hyperpigmentation, HCC, arthropathy. A: Presents at 40–50 years. B: Never transfused. D: Not suggested. E: Never transfused.

questions.stem: Which transferrin saturation supports a diagnosis of hereditary hemochromatosis?
questions.explanation: Labs: transferrin saturation ≥ 45%, serum ferritin ≥ 150–300 ng/mL without inflammation, high liver iron concentration. A: Too low. C: Too low. D: Too low. E: Too low.

questions.stem: A man is newly diagnosed with hereditary hemochromatosis. What is the first-line treatment?
questions.explanation: Treatment: phlebotomy at frequent intervals until iron depletion; chelation; liver transplant for end-stage liver disease and HCC; arthroplasty for severe joint destruction. A: End-stage liver disease or HCC. B: Severe joint destruction. D: Not listed. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: What is the goal of therapy in hereditary hemochromatosis?
questions.explanation: Goal: remove iron before it produces irreversible parenchymal damage. Early diagnosis and iron depletion increase survival. B: Not the goal. C: Damage is irreversible. D: Wrong direction. E: Not the goal.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with hereditary hemochromatosis has end-stage cirrhosis and a small hepatocellular carcinoma. Which treatment addresses his liver disease?
questions.explanation: Liver transplantation is for end-stage liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma in HH. A: Iron depletion; not for end-stage disease. B: Joint destruction. C: Not listed. D: Adds iron.

questions.stem: A preterm newborn on a ventilator needs a red cell transfusion. Which modification of the unit prevents transfusion-associated graft versus host disease?
questions.explanation: TA-GVHD is prevented by irradiated blood products; premature and LBW infants are at risk. A: Lowers CMV, immunization and fever. B: Antigen matching. C: Not needed. E: TACO prevention.

questions.stem: Leukocyte depletion is applied selectively in a hospital. Which patient should receive leukocyte-depleted units?

options.A: A healthy adult having knee surgery
options.C: A young man after a car crash
options.E: An adult with a bleeding peptic ulcer

questions.explanation: Leukocyte depletion should be universal; if selective: infants and neonates, immune deficient patients, SCT recipients and oncology patients, chronically transfused patients. A: Not in the selective list. C: Not in the selective list. D: Not in the selective list. E: Not in the selective list.

questions.stem: A group A patient is given group B red cells by mistake. What destroys the donor red cells?
questions.explanation: AHTR: incompatible (most likely ABO) blood → recipient antibodies against donor antigens → intravascular hemolysis. A group A recipient has anti-B in plasma. A: Act on recipient cells. B: No A antigen on donor cells. C: TA-GVHD. D: Urticarial reaction.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old with β-thalassemia who has never been transfused has a high ferritin and liver iron. What is the mechanism of his iron overload?

options.A: Iron delivered by red cell transfusions

questions.explanation: Non-transfusion-related iron overload (increased intestinal absorption): hereditary hemochromatosis and ineffective erythropoiesis (NTDT, sideroblastic anemia, CDA, MDS). A: Never transfused. B: Not the cause in thalassemia. C: Not the mechanism. E: Not the mechanism.

lectures.title: Cellular therapies in non-malignant hematology
lectures.covers: What counts as cellular therapy, the three platforms (transplant, gene addition, gene editing), why fetal hemoglobin is the target, the ex vivo workflow from mobilization to engraftment, conditioning, trial endpoints, safety, long-term follow-up and the ethics of consent and access.

items.p: Cellular therapy = any treatment that uses living cells as the therapeutic agent: cells that are transplanted, expanded or selected, genetically modified, or given with a conditioning regimen.

ul: Goal: durable disease modification, sometimes after a single treatment. Supportive care manages the consequences; cellular therapy tries to restore normal biology at the source, so fewer transfusions and fewer crises.

Blood disorders begin in the stem cell, so changing the stem cell changes the whole system. HSC self-renewal keeps the pool alive; differentiation produces the myeloid lineage (red cells, platelets, granulocytes, monocytes) and the lymphoid lineage (B and T cells).

table: Infuse healthy donor stem cells to replace a defective marrow (classic allogeneic HSCT)
Isolate or amplify a population (CD34+ cells, T cells) to strengthen or restore function
Add a corrective gene (gene addition) or edit a sequence (CRISPR)
Chemotherapy or radiation to make marrow space so the cells can engraft
Healthy stem cells from a donor (allogeneic) or the patient (autologous) replace a faulty blood-forming system
A viral vector (usually lentiviral) delivers a functional transgene into the patient's own HSCs
A targeted nuclease (CRISPR-Cas9) cuts at a chosen site; the cell's repair machinery rewrites the sequence or regulatory switch — no new gene is added

items.p: Allogeneic versus autologous:

table: Required, to reduce rejection and GVHD
The correction must succeed, and conditioning is still required

items.p: These are defects of HSCs or their progeny, hereditary or acquired. Unlike cancer, the abnormal clone is not the problem — the aim is healthy production across all lineages.

ul: Hemoglobinopathies: sickle cell disease, β-thalassemia — defective globin chains impair red-cell function and survival.
Inherited immunodeficiencies: SCID and related disorders — defective lymphocytes.
Marrow-failure syndromes: Fanconi anemia, aplastic anemia — too few cells of multiple lineages.
Metabolic / storage disorders: Gaucher disease, mucopolysaccharidoses — enzyme deficiencies with toxic substrate accumulation.
Red-cell and platelet disorders: selected congenital hemolytic anemias, thrombocytopenias.

table: Deoxygenated HbS polymerizes into fibers; the cell becomes a rigid fragile sickle
Globin chain imbalance → ineffective erythropoiesis; precursors die in the marrow
Anemia, marrow expansion with skeletal changes, transfusion dependence
Improve the patient's own red-cell production, not just manage the anemia

summary.h: Why fetal hemoglobin is the target

ul: γ-globin is produced in fetal life and switched down after birth, when β-globin takes over; HbF is silenced in most adults.
The strategy: turn the γ-globin switch back on in the patient's own HSCs.
In sickle cell disease: HbF dilutes HbS and inhibits the polymerization that drives sickling.
In β-thalassemia: γ-globin partly replaces the missing β-globin, improving red-cell output.

One regulatory change, broad effect: editing a single control element raises HbF across the whole red-cell lineage instead of repairing each pathogenic base — an indirect correction that works whatever the mutation.

items.caption: The γ-globin switch: silenced after birth, reactivated in an edited HSC

table: A functional gene copy is delivered, usually by a lentiviral vector, and added to the genome
CRISPR-Cas9 cuts at a chosen site; repair alters a sequence or regulatory element
Lyfgenia — lentiviral vector adding a modified β-globin gene for sickle cell disease
Casgevy — edits the BCL11A erythroid enhancer to reactivate HbF
Random integration site; expression not precisely controlled
Targeted edit of a chosen element
Off-target edits, genomic rearrangements, p53 selection

items.p: Seven stages: mobilize → collect CD34+ → edit or transduce → release testing → condition the patient → reinfuse → monitor engraftment.

ul: Mobilization: agents such as G-CSF and plerixafor push HSCs out of the marrow niche into the blood.

Apheresis: the machine separates a CD34-enriched product and returns the remaining blood components. CD34 is a surface marker enriched on HSCs; the product is not pure (progenitors, lymphocytes, residual blood cells).
Collection gates: adequate cell dose (enough to survive manufacturing losses and still engraft), viability (dead cells cannot self-renew), sterility and traceability.
Collection is the first quality gate: a failure there cannot be rescued later — it means repeat mobilization, delay, or a product with lower engraftment potential.

items.note: Slide 14 lists G-CSF and plerixafor together as mobilizing agents. Outside the slides, G-CSF is avoided in sickle cell disease because it can precipitate severe crises; plerixafor-based mobilization is used instead. Not tested.

items.p: Manufacturing and release testing:
Activate and maintain with cytokines → deliver the edit (lentiviral vector or ribonucleoprotein complexes) → wash and formulate → cryopreserve or infuse fresh → release testing.

table: The product contains the intended CD34+ HSC population
High proportion of living cells, typically ≥ 70% post-thaw
Functional capacity to engraft and produce red cells (surrogate assays)
% of alleles modified; correlates with HbF induction potential
Leftover vector or CRISPR components below threshold

summary.h: Conditioning is part of the therapy

ul: Chemotherapy clears the hematopoietic niches and suppresses the recipient's immune system, creating marrow space so corrected HSCs can engraft. Without it, the infused cells have little room to establish durable hematopoiesis.
Toxicities: cytopenias, infection risk, mucositis, infertility, organ toxicity, hospitalization.
A perfect product does not erase conditioning risk. The patient still faces the full intensity of the regimen, which is why the decision to proceed is individualized in a non-malignant disease.

summary.h: Engraftment, lineage output and trial endpoints

items.p: Infusion → homing to the marrow niche → self-renewal → lineage output (erythroid, myeloid, megakaryocytic, lymphoid).

ul: Benefit builds slowly: mature blood cells have finite lifespans and are replaced gradually, so transfusion support and monitoring continue through the transition.

table: Hemoglobin and HbF; hemolysis markers (LDH, bilirubin, reticulocytes); organ function
Transfusion independence; vaso-occlusive events; quality of life; hospitalizations
Engraftment kinetics (stem-cell take and lineage output); durability (years-long persistence)

items.note: Slide 18 scores these endpoints out of 10 in a bar chart with no explanation of where the scores come from. The endpoints are worth knowing; the numbers are not tested.

items.p: Risk depends on the whole platform — conditioning regimen, cell product and molecular strategy — not on the editing enzyme alone.

table: Conditioning causes cytopenias, mucositis, organ toxicity, hospitalization
Mild fever and chills up to anaphylactoid responses; monitor during and after reinfusion
The period before engraftment is the highest-risk window
A guide RNA may match similar sequences elsewhere → indels, deletions, translocations. Tested by in silico prediction, unbiased assays and karyotyping
Double-strand breaks → translocations and deletions beyond the cut site; p53-mediated selection shapes which cells survive
Gene addition only: integration can disrupt a gene or activate an oncogene → clonal expansion

ul: Edited HSCs self-renew for years, so monitoring must extend far beyond the infusion date: FDA guidance describes up to 15 years for certain gene-therapy products, watching for off-target edits, clonal expansion and insertional oncogenesis, and tracking durability of benefit.
"One-time administration" does not mean "one-time responsibility." Effects, intended and unintended, may appear months or years later.

Somatic, not germline. The edit is confined to the patient's blood-forming cells and is not passed to offspring; heritable germline editing is not part of approved cellular therapies, and consent must say so.
Fertility: conditioning can threaten fertility, so preservation is discussed before treatment (it adds cost and time).
Children: parents or guardians give permission; the child gives assent when developmentally appropriate. Both are documented.
Access: specialized centers, travel burden, insurance authorization, fertility-preservation cost and caregiver support decide who is actually treated. Eligibility is not purely medical.
None of the three platforms is reversible: engrafted donor cells, an integrated transgene and a genomic edit all persist.

items.p: Reasoning checklist:

ul: Which cell is abnormal — erythroid, myeloid, lymphoid, or the stem cell itself?
Is the goal replacement, addition or editing?
Autologous or allogeneic?
What conditioning is required, and what does it cost the patient?
Which outcome proves benefit (beyond surrogate markers)?
What monitoring is needed, and for how long?

questions.stem: Which feature makes a treatment a cellular therapy?

options.A: A viral vector is injected into the bloodstream
options.B: Living cells are the therapeutic agent
options.C: A missing protein is replaced by infusion
options.D: A cytotoxic drug clears the marrow
options.E: A monoclonal antibody blocks a surface receptor

questions.explanation: Cellular therapy encompasses any treatment that uses cells as the therapeutic agent, whether transplanted, expanded or selected, genetically modified, or combined with a conditioning regimen. A: Describes in vivo gene transfer, not a cell product. C: Protein replacement therapy. D: Conditioning chemotherapy. E: Antibody therapy.

questions.stem: What is the stated goal of cellular therapy in non-malignant hematology?

options.C: Permanent suppression of the immune system

questions.explanation: The goal is durable disease modification, sometimes after a single treatment; unlike supportive care it restores normal biology at the source. A: Supportive care, which these therapies aim to reduce. B: These diseases are not malignant. C: Immunosuppression controls GVHD, not a goal. E: These therapies aim beyond symptom control.

questions.stem: A therapy changes one control element in the genome of a patient's stem cells without inserting a new gene. Which strategy is this?

options.A: A regulatory switch is rewritten at a chosen site
options.B: A functional transgene is inserted into the genome
options.C: A lentiviral vector carries a new gene copy
options.D: Donor stem cells replace the marrow compartment
options.E: Collected T cells are amplified in culture

questions.explanation: Gene editing uses targeted nucleases to rewrite a selected genomic sequence or regulatory switch, with no whole new gene added. B: Gene addition. C: Gene addition. D: Transplantation. E: Expansion and selection.

questions.stem: Which property of hematopoietic stem cells makes a single administration potentially durable?
questions.explanation: HSC self-renewal keeps the stem-cell pool alive, so edited or transplanted HSCs persist and keep producing blood cells for years. A: Produces mature cells that die and are replaced. B: Mobilization moves them there for collection. D: A silencer of γ-globin, not a durability mechanism. E: Stem cells do not become the niche.

questions.stem: From which lineage do monocytes and macrophages arise?
questions.explanation: Myeloid pathway: red cells, platelets, granulocytes, monocytes and macrophages. Lymphoid pathway: B cells and T cells. A: B and T cells. B: Marrow microenvironment. C: Vessel lining. D: Connective tissue.

questions.stem: A laboratory isolates CD34+ cells from a collection and amplifies them in culture. Which cellular therapy strategy is this?
questions.explanation: Expand or select: isolate or amplify specific cell populations such as CD34+ cells or T cells to strengthen or restore function. A: Supplies a transgene with a vector. B: Rewrites a genomic sequence. C: Creates marrow space before infusion. E: Uses donor stem cells.

questions.stem: A collected stem-cell product goes straight to infusion with no laboratory manufacturing step. Which platform is this?
questions.explanation: In the comparison table, HSC transplantation involves no manufacturing (cells are collected fresh); only graft processing is done. A: Ex vivo transduction and complex release testing. B: Ex vivo editing with guide RNA and Cas9. D: Culture in the laboratory. E: Manufactured before reinfusion.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old with transfusion-dependent β-thalassemia will receive his own hematopoietic stem cells after laboratory editing. Which complication does this avoid?
questions.explanation: Autologous cells eliminate donor matching and GVHD; the patient receives his own edited cells, with no allogeneic immune response. B: Conditioning is still given. C: Can follow any cell product. D: A conditioning toxicity. E: A risk of the editing platform.

questions.stem: After allogeneic transplantation a patient takes long-term drugs that autologous platforms do not require. Which drugs?
questions.explanation: Long-term immunosuppressive drugs are often needed after allogeneic transplant to control graft-versus-host disease. A: Treat iron overload. C: Used before collection. D: Control bleeding. E: Support cells in culture.

questions.stem: A child with sickle cell disease has no suitable HLA-matched donor. Which platform avoids the donor requirement?
questions.explanation: Gene addition and CRISPR editing both use autologous cells, so no donor is needed; HSC transplantation requires a matched related or unrelated donor. A: Needs a donor. B: Needs a donor. C: Needs a donor. D: Needs a donor.

questions.stem: How do the non-malignant targets of cellular therapy differ from leukemia?

options.A: The abnormal clone is not the problem
options.B: The hematopoietic stem cell is unaffected
options.C: The marrow is replaced by fibrosis

questions.explanation: These disorders arise from defects in HSCs or their progeny; unlike cancer the abnormal clone is not the problem, and the goal is to restore healthy blood-cell production across all lineages. B: Defects lie in HSCs or their progeny. C: Not the described mechanism. D: Conditioning is still required. E: Allogeneic transplant is one option.

questions.stem: Which disease group is targeted because defective globin chains impair red-cell function and survival?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobinopathies (sickle cell disease and β-thalassemia) are listed as targets because defective globin chains impair red-cell function and survival. A: Defective lymphocytes. B: Insufficient production of several lineages. C: Enzyme deficiencies with substrate accumulation. D: A platelet lineage defect.

questions.stem: An infant with severe combined immunodeficiency is referred for cellular therapy. Which lineage is defective?
questions.explanation: Inherited immunodeficiencies such as SCID are listed among the targets: defective lymphocytes fail to mount immune responses. A: Red cell production. C: Platelet production. D: Granulocytes and monocytes. E: The marrow niche.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with short stature, absent thumbs and pancytopenia is assessed for cellular therapy. Which marrow-failure syndrome is this?
questions.explanation: Marrow-failure syndromes listed are Fanconi anemia and aplastic anemia: the marrow cannot produce sufficient blood cells of multiple lineages. A: No congenital anomalies. B: Metabolic and storage disorder. D: Hemoglobinopathy. E: Inherited immunodeficiency.

questions.stem: A toddler has an enzyme deficiency that lets toxic substrate build up in his tissues. Which listed target is this?
questions.explanation: Metabolic and storage disorders such as Gaucher disease and the mucopolysaccharidoses are enzyme deficiencies that accumulate toxic substrates in tissues. A: Marrow failure. B: Hemoglobinopathy. C: Marrow failure. E: Immunodeficiency.

questions.stem: A boy with sickle cell disease develops an ischemic pain crisis after a night of hypoxia. Which molecular event begins the cascade?

options.B: Loss of spectrin from the red cell membrane
options.D: Complement deposition on the red cell
options.E: Antibody binding to the red cell surface

questions.explanation: When HbS gives up oxygen the molecules stack into long fibers; the fibers bend the erythrocyte into a rigid fragile sickle, causing hemolysis and vaso-occlusion. A: Not the sickling mechanism. B: Hereditary spherocytosis. D: Immune hemolysis. E: Immune hemolysis.

questions.stem: A child with β-thalassemia major has a hypercellular marrow, severe anemia and a low reticulocyte count. What drives this ineffective erythropoiesis?

options.B: Loss of the CD34 surface marker
options.C: Failure of the γ-globin switch at birth

questions.explanation: Reduced or absent β-globin impairs hemoglobin assembly; the globin chain imbalance triggers ineffective erythropoiesis, so precursors die in the marrow. B: A stem-cell marker, not a cause. C: Persistent HbF would help, not harm. D: Not the described mechanism. E: Affects surviving circulating cells.

questions.stem: A child with untreated β-thalassemia has frontal bossing and widened facial bones. Which process explains these skeletal changes?
questions.explanation: Ineffective erythropoiesis drives marrow expansion and skeletal changes, alongside chronic anemia and growth delay. A: A sickle cell complication. B: Infection. C: Not a described effect. D: Not the described mechanism.

questions.stem: Which gene product takes over from γ-globin after birth?
questions.explanation: During fetal life γ-globin chains are produced; after birth the β-globin gene takes over and this developmental switch silences HbF in most adults. A: Expressed before and after birth. C: A minor adult chain, not the switch partner. D: Embryonic. E: Embryonic.

questions.stem: After therapy a boy with sickle cell disease has an HbF of 35% and no further pain crises. Which change explains the benefit?

options.A: HbF corrects the β-globin point mutation
options.B: HbF displaces HbS from the red cell
options.E: HbF blocks iron loading of the red cell

questions.explanation: Increased HbF levels dilute hemoglobin S and inhibit the polymerization that drives sickling and vaso-occlusion. A: Reactivating HbF repairs no DNA base. B: HbS remains in the cell. C: No conversion occurs. E: Unrelated to sickling.

questions.stem: Two patients with different β-globin mutations both improve after the same BCL11A-targeted therapy. Why does one edit work for both?

options.A: It repairs each pathogenic base in the β-globin gene
options.B: It replaces the entire β-globin locus
options.C: It silences the mutant β-globin allele
options.E: It raises HbF across the red-cell lineage

questions.explanation: One regulatory change has a broad effect: editing a single control element can raise HbF across the entire red-cell lineage rather than repairing each pathogenic mutation. A: Base-by-base repair is what this strategy avoids. B: No locus replacement occurs. C: Silencing the mutant allele is not the mechanism. D: Gene addition, a different platform.

questions.stem: Lyfgenia delivers a modified β-globin gene into a patient's own stem cells with a lentiviral vector. Which long-term risk belongs to this platform?

options.B: Off-target cleavage by a guide RNA

questions.explanation: For gene-addition platforms, vector integration can disrupt endogenous genes or activate an oncogene, leading to clonal expansion or insertional oncogenesis. A: The cells are autologous. B: Editing platforms. D: Follows double-strand breaks in editing. E: No donor is involved.

questions.stem: A product reactivates fetal hemoglobin by editing the BCL11A erythroid enhancer. Which product is it?
questions.explanation: Casgevy edits the BCL11A erythroid enhancer to reactivate fetal hemoglobin production; Lyfgenia is the gene-addition example. A: Adds a modified β-globin gene with a lentiviral vector. C: An iron chelator. D: A complement inhibitor. E: A mobilizing agent.

questions.stem: In the ex vivo workflow, which step immediately follows quality-control release testing?
questions.explanation: The seven stages run: mobilize, collect CD34+ cells, edit or transduce, release testing, condition the patient, reinfuse, monitor engraftment. B: Stage 2. C: Stage 3. D: Stage 6, after conditioning. E: Stage 1.

questions.stem: Before collection a patient is given a drug for several days and his circulating CD34+ count rises sharply. Which drug was given?
questions.explanation: Mobilizing agents such as G-CSF and plerixafor push HSCs out of the marrow niche into the bloodstream, increasing the circulating stem cells available for collection. A: A thrombopoietin receptor agonist. B: An anti-CD20 antibody. C: An iron chelator. E: A corticosteroid.

questions.stem: During apheresis for a gene therapy, what does the machine give back to the patient?
questions.explanation: Apheresis draws blood, separates the CD34+ cells and returns the remaining blood components to the patient, yielding a concentrated stem-cell product. A: That is kept for manufacturing. C: A drug given beforehand. D: Used later in the laboratory. E: Given after manufacturing.

questions.stem: What does the CD34 marker identify in the collected product?
questions.explanation: CD34 is a surface marker enriched on human HSCs; the goal is a product with enough viable CD34+ cells to reconstitute all blood lineages. A: Not the enriched population. B: There is no donor in an autologous product. D: Niche cells, not collected. E: Not the marker's target.

questions.stem: Besides stem cells and progenitors, what else does the apheresis product contain?
questions.explanation: The apheresis product is not a pure stem-cell suspension: it also contains progenitor cells, lymphocytes and residual blood cells. B: Remain in the niche. C: Remain in the bone. D: Not in blood. E: Added later in the laboratory.

questions.stem: A cell product is recalled and the team must show which patient it came from and every step it passed through. Which collection parameter allows this?
questions.explanation: Traceability is a chain of identity linking each product to the patient and every manufacturing step, protecting safety and quality control. A: Functional capacity to engraft. lectures.title: Hemoglobin structure and function
lectures.covers: The red cell and its metabolism, the structure of hemoglobin and its heme pocket, the adult hemoglobins, T and R states with cooperative oxygen binding, the dissociation curve and P50, the four negative regulators, CO2 carriage with the Bohr and Haldane effects, and the biochemistry of carbon monoxide, thalassemia and sickle cell disease.

summary.h: The red cell and its metabolism

ul: Blood cells are erythrocytes, leukocytes and thrombocytes, all from hematopoietic stem cells in the marrow. Low tissue oxygen makes the kidney release erythropoietin, which drives red cell production.

A red cell is a flexible biconcave disk, 6–8 microns across and 2 microns thick. Its three jobs: carry oxygen from lungs to tissues, buffer the blood by binding protons, and so allow CO2 to travel as bicarbonate.
With no internal organelles its metabolism is limited, and glycolysis is the main energy pathway. Lactate production regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can keep running.

table: Reduces methemoglobin (Fe³⁺) back to the ferrous state
The major allosteric effector of oxygen binding
Regenerates reduced glutathione, protecting membrane lipids and proteins from oxidation

items.caption: Red cell pathways: glycolysis with its two shunts

ul: About 270 million hemoglobin molecules per red cell, carrying around 98% of the oxygen in blood. At that concentration solubility depends on side-chain placement: hydrophobic residues buried in the core, hydrophilic residues on the water-exposed surface.
One molecule = 4 heme groups (iron + porphyrin ring) + 4 globin chains. Heme sits in a hydrophobic pocket, its iron coordinated to the proximal histidine, and is not covalently linked to the globin.
Each heme reversibly binds one O2, so the tetramer carries four.
The globin genes are switched on chronologically through development.

table: α chains 141 amino acids, non-α chains 146
Tetramer of two heterodimers, with allosteric interactions
Higher O2 affinity: it binds 2,3-BPG weakly
Plasma glucose over the last 2–3 months; 6.5% or more is diagnostic for diabetes

ul: Hemoglobin handles three diffusible ligands: O2 (delivery), CO2 (elimination) and NO (vascular tone).

summary.h: Binding oxygen: T, R and cooperativity

ul: The iron stays ferrous throughout: hemoglobin carries oxygen without oxidizing its heme. Oxyhemoglobin is the bound form, deoxyhemoglobin the unbound one.
In the lungs O2 binds, the inter-dimer bonds break, the dimers rotate on each other and hemoglobin shifts to R. In the tissues O2 is released and it returns to T.
Cooperativity: once the first O2 binds, the remaining hemes bind faster. That communication between the four hemes is heme-heme interaction, and it makes the curve sigmoid.

Pulse oximetry uses red light (about 660 nm) and infrared (about 940 nm). Oxyhemoglobin lets red light through and absorbs more infrared, so arterial blood looks bright red; deoxyhemoglobin absorbs more red, so venous blood looks darker.
About 98% saturation in the lungs at an arterial pO2 of 95 mmHg; 75% in peripheral tissues at a pO2 of 40 mmHg, so 25% of the load is delivered at rest.
The plateau between 70 and 100 mmHg is a safety margin: a fall from 100 to 50 mmHg costs only about 15% of saturation.
P50 is the pO2 at which hemoglobin is half-saturated, so it is a direct expression of affinity.

items.p: CO2, H+, Cl⁻ and 2,3-BPG all lower hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen.

table: Binds the central cavity between the two β chains, stabilizing T and promoting delivery to tissues. In the lungs the pO2 is high enough to load O2 anyway. Without BPG, hemoglobin loads oxygen more readily
Stabilizes T by strengthening the inter-subunit bonds and 2,3-BPG binding — the Bohr effect
Binds the N terminus of the globins as carbaminohemoglobin, stabilizing T

ul: HbF binds 2,3-BPG weakly, which is why it holds oxygen more tightly than HbA.

summary.h: Carrying CO2, and the Bohr and Haldane effects

table: Form of CO2 leaving the tissues
Bicarbonate, after carbonic anhydrase hydrates CO2

ul: Inside the red cell the H+ is buffered by hemoglobin and phosphate; the bicarbonate leaves to buffer the blood against other metabolic acids.
Chloride shift: bicarbonate leaving the cell in the tissues is matched by Cl⁻ entering, keeping the charge balanced.
At the lungs the whole equilibrium reverses: CO2 is released, H+ recombines with bicarbonate, and hemoglobin loses H+ so it binds oxygen more readily.
Bohr effect: H+ (and CO2) lower O2 affinity by stabilizing T. Haldane effect: oxygen binding in the lungs shifts hemoglobin to R, releasing H+ and CO2 and helping CO2 unloading.

table: Right shift (Bohr); CO2 and H+ bind the globin portion and alter its conformation
Right shift; rises with chronic hypoxia — altitude, smoking, COPD
The more active the tissue, the higher its pCO2, H+ and temperature, so more O2 is released at the same pO2

ul: The logic of altitude: lower pO2 means less saturation leaving the lungs, so BPG rises to squeeze more oxygen out in the tissues.

Carbon monoxide: colorless, odorless, can be fatal. It binds the oxygen sites 200–250 times more strongly than O2, so it outcompetes oxygen, and its conformational effect shifts the curve left, so what is still carried is released less readily.

items.note: Slide 36 calls CO's affinity "several orders of magnitude" higher and then gives 200–250 times. Only the 200–250 figure was tested.

ul: Erythropoietin doping: more circulating red cells means thicker blood and thrombosis risk, with better aerobic capacity. EPO also drives cell-survival pathways through its receptor, so it may promote cancer; in cancer patients EPO-like drugs shortened survival or sped tumor growth, and have carried an FDA boxed warning since 2007.

table: Quantitative: too little of a normal chain
Gene deletions in most α-thalassemias; point mutations affecting transcription, splicing or translation in most β-thalassemias
Amino acid substitution, deletion or elongation
Unpaired chains precipitate and damage the membrane: early death in the marrow or rapid removal from the circulation
Abnormal solubility (sickle cell), unstable hemoglobin, or altered oxygen affinity

ul: The two overlap: some hemoglobinopathies also reduce chain output and so are thalassemias too, but most are not.

items.p: A 19-year-old with lifelong hemolysis has a crisis the night after a hot hike at 2,000 m with little water. Hb 8.2 g/dL, high reticulocytes and LDH, unconjugated bilirubin. Electrophoresis: no HbA, about 90% HbS, 8% HbF, 2% HbA2 — homozygous HbSS.

ul: The mutation: each β chain carries glutamate to valine at position 6. Losing glutamate's negative charge is why HbS runs differently on the gel, and valine is hydrophobic sitting on a surface that should be hydrophilic.

The switch: in the T state a hydrophobic pocket on the β chain is exposed; the valine of one HbS slots into that pocket on a neighbour and the molecules stack into long rigid fibers. In the R state the pocket is hidden and oxygenated HbS stays soluble. Fibers therefore form wherever oxygen is released.
The cells become stiff and sticky: they block small vessels (ischemic pain) and are destroyed early (hemolysis, jaundice).

table: Higher temperature, CO2 and H+: right shift
HbS more concentrated, fibers form much faster

ul: Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Carriers (HbAS) have about 40% HbS, usually no symptoms, and some protection against severe malaria.
HbF protects because γ chains do not join the fibers, so babies are well until HbF falls; hydroxyurea raises HbF to prevent crises.

Crisis treatment: pain relief, IV fluids, warmth, oxygen if the saturation is low, and treat any infection. Bone marrow transplant can be curative, and the CRISPR gene therapy approved in 2023 reactivates HbF in the patient's own stem cells.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old has had pale skin, yellow sclerae and episodes of bone pain since childhood, and a crisis follows a hot high-altitude hike with little water. Which property of his hemoglobin explains this?

questions.explanation: A typical red cell is a flexible biconcave disk with a diameter of 6–8 microns and a thickness of 2 microns. A: Thinner than described. B: Thicker than described. C: That is the lower end of the diameter. D: That is the upper end of the diameter.

options.B: Buffering the blood by binding protons

options.C: Its lifespan is too short for enzymes to work
