questions.stem: A man is given a drug that oxidizes the iron of his hemoglobin. Which form of hemoglobin results?
questions.explanation: Methemoglobin is the ferric (Fe3+) form of hemoglobin. A: Hemoglobin with oxygen bound. B: The unbound form. C: Hemoglobin with CO2 at the N terminus. E: Hemoglobin with carbon monoxide bound.

questions.stem: Which glycolytic product reduces methemoglobin back to the ferrous state?
questions.explanation: The NADH produced in glycolysis is used to reduce the ferric form of hemoglobin, methemoglobin, to the normal ferrous state. A: From the hexose monophosphate shunt, used to regenerate glutathione. C: The energy currency of glycolysis. D: The end product of anaerobic glycolysis. E: An allosteric effector of oxygen binding.

questions.stem: Which pathway produces 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate?
questions.explanation: Glycolysis branches into a side pathway, the Rapoport-Luebering shunt, in which 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate is produced. B: Generates NADPH. C: Needs mitochondria. D: Handles oxidative stress. E: Recycles lactate in the liver.

questions.stem: A man's red cells lyse after an oxidant drug because reduced glutathione cannot be replenished. Which pathway has failed?
questions.explanation: The hexose monophosphate shunt generates NADPH, which protects red cell membrane lipids and proteins from oxidation through regeneration of reduced glutathione. A: Supplies energy and NADH. C: Makes 2,3-BPG. D: Needs mitochondria. E: A hepatic pathway.

questions.stem: About how many hemoglobin molecules does one red cell contain?
questions.explanation: There are around 270 million hemoglobin molecules per red cell. A: Far fewer than described. B: Far fewer than described. C: Fewer than described. D: More than described.

questions.stem: What proportion of the oxygen in blood is carried by red cells?
questions.explanation: Red cells transport around 98% of the oxygen present in the blood. A: Understates the share. B: Understates the share. D: Understates the share. E: A small share is dissolved in plasma.

questions.stem: How does hemoglobin stay soluble at the concentration found inside a red cell?

options.A: Hydrophilic side chains lie on the surface
options.B: The heme pockets open onto the surface
options.C: Disulfide bridges link the four chains
options.D: The tetramer carries no net charge

questions.explanation: Because of the high hemoglobin concentration, solubility is helped by the distribution of side chains: hydrophobic residues sit in the interior core and hydrophilic residues on the water-exposed surface. B: Heme sits in a hydrophobic pocket. C: The chains are not linked this way. D: Not the described mechanism. E: That describes HbA1c.

questions.stem: How many heme groups does one hemoglobin molecule contain?
questions.explanation: One hemoglobin molecule has 4 heme groups (iron plus a porphyrin ring) and 4 globin chains. A: That is myoglobin. B: Fewer than in the tetramer. C: More than in the tetramer. E: More than in the tetramer.

questions.stem: A variant hemoglobin loses its heme because one residue in the pocket is replaced. Which residue normally coordinates the heme iron?
questions.explanation: Heme sits in a hydrophobic pocket with its iron coordinated to the proximal histidine, and it is not covalently linked to the globin. B: Not the coordinating residue. C: A surface charge, not a ligand. D: The CO2 binding site. E: Not the coordinating residue.

questions.stem: How is heme held in the globin chain?

options.C: By an ester link to a serine
options.D: By a pocket, with no covalent bond
options.E: By a peptide bond to the chain

questions.explanation: Heme sits in a hydrophobic pocket and is not covalently linked to the globin. A: Heme is not covalently linked here. B: Not the attachment described. C: Not the attachment described. E: Not the attachment described.

questions.stem: How many oxygen molecules can one hemoglobin tetramer transport?
questions.explanation: Each heme group reversibly binds one oxygen molecule, so the tetramer transports four. A: Each heme binds one. B: Fewer than the tetramer carries. C: More than the tetramer carries. D: More than the tetramer carries.

questions.stem: Which chromosome carries the α-globin-like genes?
questions.explanation: In adults the globin part is one pair of α-globin-like chains (chromosome 16) and one pair of β-globin-like chains (chromosome 11). A: Carries the β-globin-like genes. B: Not a globin locus here. D: Not a globin locus here. E: Not a globin locus here.

questions.stem: Which chromosome carries the β-globin-like genes?
questions.explanation: The β-globin-like gene cluster lies on chromosome 11; the α-globin-like cluster lies on chromosome 16. A: Carries the α-globin-like genes. C: Not a globin locus here. D: Not a globin locus here. E: Not a globin locus here.

questions.stem: Electrophoresis in a healthy adult shows a band making up 2–3% of total hemoglobin. Which chain composition does it have?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin A2 is α2δ2 and makes up 2–3% of total hemoglobin; HbA (α2β2) is 96–97% and HbF (α2γ2) under 1%. A: HbA, 96–97% of the total. B: HbF, under 1% in an adult. C: HbA1c. E: Not an adult hemoglobin here.

questions.stem: A newborn's hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly than his mother's does. Which hemoglobin is responsible?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin F (α2γ2) makes up under 1% of adult hemoglobin and has a higher oxygen affinity. B: The main adult hemoglobin. C: A minor adult hemoglobin. D: Glycated HbA. E: An abnormal hemoglobin.

questions.stem: A patient's HbA1c is 7.4%. What does this value reflect?

options.A: Plasma glucose over the last 24 hours
options.B: Iron stores over the last 3 months
options.C: Plasma glucose over the last 2–3 months

questions.explanation: HbA1c is glycated HbA β chains and measures plasma glucose over the last 2–3 months; a value of 6.5% or more is diagnostic for diabetes. A: A single glucose measurement does that. B: Ferritin reflects iron stores. D: Not what the test measures. E: HbF is measured separately.

questions.stem: How many amino acids are in an α-globin chain?
questions.explanation: Primary structure: α chains have 141 amino acids and non-α chains 146. A: The length of a non-α chain. C: Not the stated length. D: Not the stated length. E: Not the stated length.

questions.stem: Which level of globin structure describes the tetramer of two heterodimers?
questions.explanation: Quaternary structure is the tetramer of two heterodimers, with allosteric interactions between them. A: The amino acid sequence. B: Helical segments joined by loops. C: Globular folding of one subunit. D: Not a level of globin structure.

questions.stem: Which diffusible ligand does hemoglobin carry to help control vascular tone?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin interacts with three diffusible ligands: O2 for delivery, CO2 for elimination and NO for control of vascular tone. A: Carried for elimination by the lungs. B: Carried for delivery to tissues. D: A poison, not a physiological ligand. E: Leaves the red cell to buffer the blood.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin shuttles oxygen all day without its heme carrier being oxidized. In which state does the iron stay?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin transports O2 from the lungs to peripheral tissues without oxidation of its heme carrier: the iron remains in the ferrous state. A: Hemoglobin with ferric iron is methemoglobin, which cannot carry oxygen. C: Not a biological form here. D: Not a form described. E: Iron stays in the ring.

questions.stem: A pulse oximeter emits infrared light at roughly which wavelength?
questions.explanation: A pulse oximeter uses two lights: red at about 660 nm and infrared at about 940 nm. A: Not a wavelength used. B: Not a wavelength used. C: That is the red light. D: Not a wavelength used.

questions.stem: Why does venous blood look darker than arterial blood?

options.E: Venous blood has a lower hematocrit

questions.explanation: Oxygenated hemoglobin lets red light through and absorbs more infrared, so arterial blood looks bright red; deoxygenated hemoglobin absorbs more red light, so venous blood looks darker. A: Bilirubin is a plasma pigment. B: Acidity does not change the colour. C: Methemoglobin is a small fraction. E: The hematocrit is not the reason.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin reaches a pulmonary capillary and oxygen binds. What happens first to the tetramer?
questions.explanation: Binding of O2 induces changes that break the inter-dimer bonds; the dimers then rotate relative to each other and hemoglobin shifts to the R state. B: Oxidation would give methemoglobin. C: BPG binds the deoxygenated form. D: The tetramer stays intact. E: That happens in the tissues.

questions.stem: What does rotation of the two dimers on each other achieve?

options.A: It exposes the heme iron to plasma
options.B: It converts α chains into β chains

questions.explanation: The dimers rotate on each other to increase and decrease the inter-dimer distance, which facilitates the uptake and release of O2. A: Heme stays in its pocket. B: Chains are not interconverted. C: BPG stays in the cell. E: The histidine stays coordinated.

questions.stem: Which hemoglobin conformation has relatively low oxygen affinity?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin exists in two alternating conformations: T (taut) deoxygenated with relatively low O2 affinity and R (relaxed) oxygenated with high affinity. A: The oxygenated, high-affinity conformation. C: HbA1c, not a conformational state. D: CO2 bound at the N terminus. E: Methemoglobin.

questions.stem: Hemoglobin reaches the lungs, binds oxygen and its dimers rotate. Which conformation does it now hold?
questions.explanation: Hemoglobin picks up O2 in the lungs; binding breaks the inter-dimer bonds, the dimers rotate and hemoglobin shifts to the R (relaxed) state with higher O2 affinity. A: The deoxygenated conformation it has just left. B: Formed when CO2 binds in the tissues. D: Methemoglobin, which carries no oxygen. E: HbA1c, unrelated to conformation.

questions.stem: A hemoglobin dissociation curve is sigmoid rather than a straight line. What produces its steep middle section?

options.A: 2,3-BPG is displaced from the central cavity
options.C: The heme iron changes oxidation state
options.E: The first oxygen bound speeds the rest

questions.explanation: Once the first O2 binds, binding of O2 to the remaining hemes is accelerated, which gives the steeply rising section of the sigmoid curve. A: BPG release is not the mechanism. B: A separate reaction. C: The iron stays ferrous. D: Part of the chloride shift.

questions.stem: What is the communication between the four hemes of hemoglobin called?
questions.explanation: The acceleration of O2 binding after the first heme is occupied suggests communication between the four hemes, referred to as heme-heme interaction. B: Describes a negative effector. C: The effect of H+ on affinity. D: The exchange of Cl- for bicarbonate. E: Oxygen-driven CO2 release.

questions.stem: Which ion is one of the four primary negative regulators of hemoglobin's oxygen affinity?
questions.explanation: The four primary negative regulators are CO2, H+, Cl- and 2,3-BPG. A: Not one of the four. B: Not one of the four. C: Not one of the four. D: Not one of the four.

questions.stem: A variant hemoglobin has lost the positive charges in the cleft between its β chains and binds 2,3-BPG poorly. Which site is affected?

options.A: The heme pocket of each α chain
options.B: The central cavity between the β chains
options.C: The N terminus of each globin chain
options.E: The surface valine of the β chain

questions.explanation: Between the two beta chains is the binding site for 2,3-BPG, which is synthesized through the Rapoport-Luebering shunt. A: Occupied by heme. C: The CO2 binding site. D: Not the BPG site. E: That is the HbS substitution.

questions.stem: How does 2,3-BPG change oxygen handling?

options.C: It displaces CO2 from the N terminus
options.E: It blocks chloride entry into the cell

questions.explanation: When BPG binds it stabilizes the T state, promoting delivery of O2 to the tissues; in the lungs the pO2 is high enough to force O2 loading despite BPG. A: Oxygen binding does that. B: Oxidation gives methemoglobin. C: Not its action. E: Not its action.

questions.stem: A unit of stored blood has lost most of its 2,3-BPG. What follows for its hemoglobin?
questions.explanation: When 2,3-BPG is not available, or not bound in the central cavity, hemoglobin can be converted to HbO2 more readily. A: BPG is what stabilizes the T state. B: A right shift needs more BPG, not less. D: CO2 carriage is separate. E: Oxidation is a separate process.

questions.stem: Why does fetal hemoglobin hold oxygen more tightly than HbA?

options.D: It is glycated at its β chains

questions.explanation: HbF binds 2,3-BPG weakly, so less of it is held in the low-affinity T state. B: Ferric iron carries no oxygen. C: HbF is α2γ2. D: HbF has no β chains. E: Chloride lowers affinity.

questions.stem: Blood leaving an exercising muscle carries a large CO2 load. In which form is most of it travelling?
questions.explanation: CO2 is hydrated by carbonic anhydrase to carbonic acid, then converted to H+ and bicarbonate: about 70% of the total. A: Only 5–10%. B: Only 20–25%. C: The heme site carries oxygen. D: That is the 2,3-BPG site.

questions.stem: What share of CO2 travels as carbaminohemoglobin?
questions.explanation: CO2 is transported dissolved (5–10%), as carbaminohemoglobin (20–25%) and as bicarbonate (70%). A: The dissolved fraction. C: Not a stated fraction. D: The bicarbonate fraction. E: Not a stated fraction.

questions.stem: In a tissue capillary some CO2 binds hemoglobin directly rather than becoming bicarbonate. Where does it attach?
questions.explanation: CO2 binds directly to the N terminus of globins to form carbaminohemoglobin, which stabilizes the T state. A: That site carries oxygen. B: That is the 2,3-BPG site. D: That residue holds the heme iron. E: That is the HbS substitution.

questions.stem: What effect does carbaminohemoglobin formation have on hemoglobin?
questions.explanation: CO2 binds the N terminus of globins to form carbaminohemoglobin and stabilize the T state. B: Oxygen binding does that. C: CO2 is a negative regulator. D: Oxidation gives methemoglobin. E: CO2 and BPG act at different sites.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the red cell enzyme that converts CO2 to carbonic acid. Which enzyme is blocked?
questions.explanation: CO2 is hydrated by carbonic anhydrase to H2CO3, then converted to H+ and bicarbonate. A: Makes 2,3-BPG. B: Handles peroxides. C: The first step of the HMP shunt. E: Converts pyruvate to lactate.

questions.stem: Hydration of CO2 floods the red cell with H+ yet its pH barely moves. What buffers that H+?
questions.explanation: Within red cells the H+ is buffered by hemoglobin and phosphate, while the bicarbonate is transported into the blood to buffer H+ from other metabolic acids. B: Plasma proteins, outside the cell. C: An enzyme rather than a buffer. D: Handles oxidative stress. E: Ions exchanged, not buffers.

questions.stem: Blood reaches a pulmonary capillary and unloads CO2. Which change then lets hemoglobin bind oxygen more readily?
questions.explanation: In the lungs the equilibrium reverses: hemoglobin loses some of its H+, a feature that allows it to bind oxygen more readily. A: Chloride lowers affinity. C: BPG lowers affinity. D: CO2 is released in the lungs. E: Oxidation gives methemoglobin.

questions.stem: A sprinter's working muscle is acidic. What does the H+ do to the hemoglobin passing through?
questions.explanation: H+ stabilizes the T state by stabilizing the inter-subunit bonds and 2,3-BPG binding, so more oxygen is released. A: Oxidation gives methemoglobin. B: H+ strengthens BPG binding. C: Oxygen binding does that. D: CO2 does that.

questions.stem: What is the effect of pH on hemoglobin's oxygen affinity called?
questions.explanation: The effect of H+ on hemoglobin's oxygen affinity, through stabilization of the T state, is the Bohr effect. A: Oxygen-driven release of H+ and CO2. B: Exchange of Cl- for bicarbonate. D: Cooperativity between hemes. E: The pathway making 2,3-BPG.

questions.stem: In the lungs, oxygen binding makes hemoglobin give up H+ and CO2. What is this called?
questions.explanation: When O2 binds in the lungs, hemoglobin shifts to the R state and releases H+ and CO2, helping CO2 unloading: the Haldane effect. A: The effect of H+ on oxygen affinity. B: Exchange of Cl- for bicarbonate. C: Accelerated binding of later oxygen molecules. E: The pathway making 2,3-BPG.

questions.stem: In a tissue capillary, bicarbonate pours out of the red cell. Why does chloride move in at the same time?

options.E: To carry CO2 to the lungs

questions.explanation: Diffusion of bicarbonate out of red cells in the tissues must be coupled to Cl- movement into them to maintain electrical neutrality: the chloride shift. A: The heme site carries oxygen. C: The enzyme needs no chloride here. D: Chloride stabilizes the T state. E: Bicarbonate does that.

questions.stem: How does chloride lower hemoglobin's oxygen affinity?

options.E: By acidifying the red cell cytosol

questions.explanation: Cl- lowers O2 affinity mainly by binding deoxy-Hb directly, stabilizing the T state. A: BPG binding is not displaced by chloride. B: CO2 does that. D: Oxidation gives methemoglobin. E: H+ acts separately.

questions.stem: Venous blood leaving a resting tissue has a pO2 of 40 mmHg. What is the hemoglobin saturation?
questions.explanation: 75% saturation in the peripheral tissues at a pO2 of 40 mmHg (venous blood); about 98% in the lungs at an arterial pO2 of 95 mmHg. B: Lower than the venous value. C: Lower than the venous value. D: Closer to arterial blood. E: The arterial value.

questions.stem: At what arterial pO2 is hemoglobin about 98% saturated?
questions.explanation: About 98% saturation is reached in the lungs at an arterial pO2 of 95 mmHg. A: Far below the arterial value. B: The venous value. C: Below the arterial value. D: Above the arterial value.

questions.stem: Saturation falls from about 98% in the lungs to 75% in a resting tissue. What fraction of the oxygen load has been delivered?
questions.explanation: Saturation falls from about 98% in the lungs to 75% in the tissues: 25% of the O2 load is released. A: Less than the stated fraction. B: More than the stated fraction. C: That is the venous saturation value. E: That is the arterial saturation value.

questions.stem: What does the plateau of the curve between 70 and 100 mmHg provide?

options.A: Faster release of oxygen in the tissues
options.E: A safety margin against falls in pO2

questions.explanation: The plateau between 70 and 100 mmHg pO2 constitutes a safety mechanism against variations in pO2. A: That happens on the steep part. B: The plateau does not change affinity. C: CO2 transport is separate. D: Unrelated to the plateau.

questions.stem: A patient with lung disease has an arterial pO2 of 50 mmHg instead of 100. Roughly how far does hemoglobin saturation fall?
questions.explanation: If the pO2 dropped from 100 to 50 mmHg there would only be a corresponding drop of about 15% in hemoglobin saturation. A: Understates the fall. B: Overstates the fall. D: Overstates the fall. E: Overstates the fall.

questions.stem: What does P50 express?

options.A: The pO2 at which hemoglobin is half-saturated
options.B: The pO2 of normal venous blood
options.C: The saturation reached at a pO2 of 50 mmHg
options.D: The pO2 at which the curve plateaus
options.E: The partial pressure of CO2 in the tissues

questions.explanation: P50 is an expression of hemoglobin's affinity for O2: the pO2 at which hemoglobin is half-saturated with oxygen. B: A fixed physiological value. C: Reverses the definition. D: The plateau starts around 70 mmHg. E: A different gas.

questions.stem: A patient's hemoglobin has a P50 below the normal value. What does this indicate?
questions.explanation: A low P50 indicates high affinity for oxygen, with the dissociation curve shifted to the left. A: That goes with a high P50. C: That raises P50. D: That raises P50. E: That raises P50.

questions.stem: Through which part of hemoglobin do CO2 and H+ change its conformation?
questions.explanation: pH (Bohr effect) and pCO2 affect P50 because CO2 and H+ bind the globin portion of hemoglobin and alter its conformation. A: Binds oxygen itself. B: Holds the iron. C: The 2,3-BPG site. E: Anchors the heme.

questions.stem: Which change in body state lowers hemoglobin's oxygen affinity by altering its conformation?

options.D: A fall in the white cell count

questions.explanation: A high temperature alters hemoglobin's conformation and raises P50, alongside pH, pCO2 and 2,3-BPG. A: Not a regulator of affinity. B: Not a regulator of affinity. C: Not a regulator of affinity. D: Not a regulator of affinity.

questions.stem: After three weeks at 3,500 m, which red cell change improves oxygen delivery to a climber's tissues?
questions.explanation: 2,3-BPG increases in response to chronic hypoxia (high altitude, smoking, COPD), enhancing dissociation of O2 in the tissues. A: Chloride handling is unchanged. B: CO2 handling is unchanged. C: Methemoglobin carries no oxygen. E: A minor hemoglobin, not an adaptation.

questions.stem: Which group of patients would be expected to have a raised 2,3-BPG from chronic hypoxia?
questions.explanation: 2,3-BPG increases in response to chronic hypoxia: high altitude, smoking and COPD. A: Not listed as a hypoxic stimulus. C: An iron-loading disorder. D: No effect described. E: No effect described.

questions.stem: During hard exercise, muscle takes up more oxygen at an unchanged capillary pO2. Why?

options.C: The P50 falls in the muscle

questions.explanation: The more active a tissue, the greater its pCO2, H+ and temperature; at any given pO2 this makes hemoglobin release more oxygen to the active cells. B: Red cell mass does not change acutely. C: A falling P50 would hold oxygen tighter. D: CO2 handling continues. E: HbF production does not change acutely.

questions.stem: Why does erythropoietin doping raise the risk of thrombosis?

options.C: It raises the circulating red cells

questions.explanation: Erythropoietin increases the number of circulating red cells, making the blood thicker and raising thrombosis risk, while improving aerobic capacity. A: Not the described mechanism. B: Not the described mechanism. D: Not the described mechanism. E: Not the described mechanism.

questions.stem: Why do EPO-like drugs carry an FDA boxed warning in cancer patients?
questions.explanation: EPO also activates cell survival pathways through its receptor; in cancer patients, trials showed EPO-like drugs can shorten survival or speed tumor growth, hence the boxed warning since 2007. A: Not the reported harm. B: Not the reported harm. C: Not the reported harm. D: Not the reported harm.

questions.stem: A man rescued from a smoky basement is confused, and his oxygen saturation reads normal. Why is oxygen delivery to his tissues impaired?

options.A: Carbon monoxide oxidizes the heme iron
options.B: Carbon monoxide shifts the curve to the left
options.C: Carbon monoxide stabilizes the T state

questions.explanation: CO competes with O2 for the binding sites and, through conformational effects, also shifts the dissociation curve to the left, so less O2 is released to the tissues. A: It binds the oxygen site rather than oxidizing iron. C: It has the opposite conformational effect. D: CO2 handling is not the problem. E: That would aid release, not impair it.

questions.stem: How much more strongly does carbon monoxide bind hemoglobin's oxygen-binding sites than oxygen does?
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide has 200 to 250 times higher affinity for the oxygen-binding sites of hemoglobin than O2 has. A: Far below the stated figure. B: Below the stated figure. C: Above the stated figure. E: Above the stated figure.

questions.stem: Which defect defines the thalassemias?

options.A: Reduced production of a globin chain
options.B: An amino acid substitution in a globin chain
options.C: Loss of the heme binding pocket

questions.explanation: Genetic errors resulting in quantitative defects in globin chain production cause the thalassemias. B: That defines a hemoglobinopathy. C: Not the defect described. D: Methemoglobinemia. E: An affinity problem, not a thalassemia.

questions.stem: A child with β-thalassemia major has severe anemia with red cells dying in the marrow. What damages those cells?
questions.explanation: With unbalanced chain synthesis the non-paired globin chains precipitate and damage the cell membrane, causing early cell death in the marrow or rapid removal from the circulation. A: The lesion of sickle cell disease. B: Immune hemolysis. D: Immune hemolysis. E: The lesion of oxidative hemolysis.

questions.stem: Which molecular change underlies most α-thalassemias?
questions.explanation: Thalassemias usually result from underproduction of normal globin proteins, often through gene deletions (most α-thalassemias). A: The usual cause of β-thalassemia. B: The lesion of a hemoglobinopathy. C: A rarer hemoglobinopathy mutation. E: Not a described cause.

questions.stem: Most β-thalassemias result from which kind of mutation?

options.A: Deletions of the whole gene cluster
options.B: Amino acid substitutions on the surface
options.C: Point mutations in the globin gene

questions.explanation: Most β-thalassemias arise from point mutations in the globin gene affecting transcription, splicing or translation. A: The usual cause in α-thalassemia. B: The lesion of a hemoglobinopathy. D: Not a described cause. E: Not a described cause.

questions.stem: What makes a disorder a hemoglobinopathy rather than a thalassemia?

options.A: Too little of a normal chain is made
options.B: It is a qualitative defect of the chain
options.C: The heme group cannot be inserted
options.D: The red cell membrane is abnormal

questions.explanation: Hemoglobinopathies are qualitative defects of the globin chains from substitutions, deletions or elongation; thalassemias are quantitative defects of production. A: That is a thalassemia. C: Not the distinction described. D: A membrane disorder. E: Deletions reduce output, as in α-thalassemia.

questions.stem: Which functional defect does sickle cell anemia represent among the hemoglobinopathies?
questions.explanation: Abnormalities in chain structure give abnormal solubility (sickle cell anemia), unstable hemoglobin or altered oxygen affinity. A: A different functional defect. B: A different functional defect. C: That is a thalassemia. D: Not a listed defect.

questions.stem: Sequencing of a sickle cell patient's β-globin gene shows a single changed codon at position 6. Which substitution is it?
questions.explanation: Each β chain of HbS carries one substitution at position 6: glutamate to valine. B: A different variant. C: The α chain is not affected. D: A different variant. E: Not the substitution described.

questions.stem: Why does HbS move differently from HbA on electrophoresis?

options.A: Valine makes the molecule much larger
options.D: HbS is glycated at the β chains
options.E: The substitution removes a negative charge

questions.explanation: Electrophoresis separates species by charge; losing glutamate's charge is why HbS moves differently on the gel. A: The size change is negligible. B: HbS has normal α chains. C: γ chains belong to HbF. D: That describes HbA1c.

questions.stem: The HbS mutation places a valine on the outside of the molecule. Why does its position matter?

options.A: Valine cannot be reached by antibodies

questions.explanation: Valine is hydrophobic and sits on the surface of the molecule, where hydrophilic residues normally keep hemoglobin soluble. A: Immunity is not involved. B: Heme binding is normal. C: The BPG site is unchanged. E: The chains still pair.

questions.stem: Why do HbS fibers form only when oxygen has been released?

options.A: The valine is buried in the T state
options.B: A hydrophobic pocket is exposed in the T state
options.C: The heme iron is oxidized in the tissues

questions.explanation: In deoxyhemoglobin a hydrophobic pocket on the β chain becomes exposed; the valine of one HbS fits into that pocket on a neighbouring deoxy-HbS and the molecules stack into long rigid fibers. A: The T state exposes the pocket. C: The iron stays ferrous. D: BPG binds the deoxygenated form. E: Chloride does not drive polymerization.

questions.stem: What happens to HbS when it is fully oxygenated?
questions.explanation: In the R state the hydrophobic pocket is hidden, so oxygenated HbS stays soluble. A: Fibers form in the deoxygenated state. B: That is oxidative damage. D: Hemoglobins are not interconverted. E: Heme stays bound.

questions.stem: Why do sickled cells cause both ischemic pain and jaundice?

options.C: They are too small to carry oxygen
options.D: They activate the coagulation cascade directly

questions.explanation: Bent and distorted cells are stiff and sticky: they block small vessels (ischemic pain) and are destroyed early (hemolysis, jaundice). B: Bilirubin comes from their breakdown. C: Size is not the problem. D: Not the described mechanism. E: That is hereditary spherocytosis.

questions.stem: Electrophoresis in a 19-year-old shows no HbA, about 90% HbS, 8% HbF and 2% HbA2. Which condition is this?
questions.explanation: No HbA with about 90% HbS means both β-globin genes carry the sickle mutation: HbSS. A: Would show HbA as well. B: Would show mostly HbA with a raised HbA2. D: Would show a much higher HbF and no HbS. E: Would be mostly HbA.

questions.stem: About what share of hemoglobin is HbS in a person with sickle cell trait?
questions.explanation: Carriers (sickle cell trait, HbAS) have about 40% HbS, usually with no symptoms. B: Below the carrier level. C: Below the carrier level. D: Above the carrier level. E: The level in homozygous disease.

questions.stem: Which advantage do sickle cell carriers have?
questions.explanation: Carriers usually have no symptoms and some protection against severe malaria. A: Not an effect of the trait. B: The trait does not change affinity. C: Not an effect of the trait. E: Not an effect of the trait.

questions.stem: Why does a high fetal hemoglobin level protect a child with sickle cell disease?

options.B: HbF carries its iron in the ferric state
options.C: HbF dissolves the fibers already formed
options.D: HbF blocks the valine from being made
options.E: γ chains do not join the fibers

questions.explanation: HbF protects because γ chains replace β chains and do not join the fibers, so babies are well until HbF falls. A: HbF binds BPG weakly. B: Ferric iron carries no oxygen. C: It prevents rather than dissolves. D: The mutation is unchanged.

questions.stem: A child with four crises a year is started on a drug that raises his fetal hemoglobin. Which drug is it?
questions.explanation: Hydroxyurea raises HbF to prevent crises. A: An iron chelator. C: Supports erythropoiesis. D: A corticosteroid. E: Raises the red cell count.

questions.stem: A patient in a painful sickle crisis has an oxygen saturation of 97% on room air. Which measure belongs in his initial treatment?
questions.explanation: Treatment of a crisis is pain relief, IV fluids, warmth, oxygen if the saturation is low, and treatment of any infection. A: Oxygen is given when the saturation is low. B: Not listed for a routine crisis. C: Prevents crises rather than treating one. D: Treats iron overload.

questions.stem: Which treatment can cure sickle cell disease?
questions.explanation: Bone marrow transplant can be curative, and CRISPR gene therapy approved in 2023 reactivates HbF in the patient's stem cells. A: Reduces crises without curing. B: A temporary measure. C: Supports erythropoiesis. E: Removes excess iron.

questions.stem: Why does dehydration make a sickle crisis worse?
questions.explanation: Dehydration shrinks the red cells; HbS is more concentrated and fibers form much faster. A: Acidosis, not alkalosis, promotes sickling. C: Heat, not cold, was the trigger here. D: A fall would hold oxygen tighter. E: A right shift, not a left shift, is the issue.

questions.stem: Chronic anemia in sickle cell disease raises the 2,3-BPG level. What does this do to oxygen handling?

options.C: It shifts the curve to the right

questions.explanation: Chronic anemia raises 2,3-BPG and shifts the curve right: better O2 delivery, but more deoxy-HbS and so more fiber formation. A: BPG stabilizes the T state. B: BPG does not change HbF. D: CO2 carriage is unaffected. E: Chloride handling is unaffected.

questions.stem: Which feature belongs to β-thalassemia major rather than to sickle cell disease?

options.A: Too few β chains are made
options.B: One amino acid substitution in the β chain
options.C: Polymerization of hemoglobin in the T state
options.D: Pain crises from occluded small vessels
options.E: A hydrophobic residue on the molecule's surface

questions.explanation: Sickle cell disease is a qualitative defect (an abnormal β chain); β-thalassemia major is quantitative (too few β chains from many different mutations). B: The sickle lesion. C: The sickle lesion. D: The sickle presentation. E: The sickle lesion.

lectures.title: Heme metabolism
lectures.covers: How heme is built in eight steps from glycine and succinyl CoA, how ALA synthase is regulated, acute intermittent porphyria versus lead poisoning, and how heme is broken down to bilirubin, conjugated and excreted, with Gilbert syndrome as the case.

summary.h: Heme and where it is made

ul: Heme (Fe-protoporphyrin IX) is the prosthetic group of hemoglobin, myoglobin, mitochondrial and microsomal cytochromes, catalase, peroxidases and tryptophan pyrrolase.

Structure: four pyrrole rings joined by methine bridges (–CH=) form the porphyrin ring, with iron at the center. Eight side chains, two per pyrrole: methyl, vinyl or propionate, in the order MVMVMPPM.
All aerobic cells are presumed able to make heme.

table: Erythroid cells of the bone marrow

ul: Glycine + succinyl CoA, eight reactions. The first and the last three are mitochondrial; the steps in between are cytoplasmic. Heme feeds back negatively on the first enzyme.

items.caption: The eight steps of heme synthesis

table: Hydroxymethylbilane: four PBG head to tail, a linear tetrapyrrole
Uroporphyrinogen III: rearranged and cyclized, octacarboxylate
Coproporphyrinogen III: the four acetate groups lose their carboxyls, tetracarboxylate
Protoporphyrinogen IX: two propionates become vinyls, dicarboxylate
Protoporphyrin IX: six hydrogens removed, the first porphyrin (oxidized)

ul: Without URO-synthase, HMB cyclizes nonenzymatically to uroporphyrinogen I.
Everything before protoporphyrin IX is a porphyrinogen (reduced form).
ALA synthase is rate-limiting and therefore highly regulated. Two isoforms:

table: Repressed by the free heme pool. Induced by fasting and by cytochrome P450-inducing drugs, which use up heme. Repressed by glucose
Erythropoietin and iron: translation stops when iron is low

ul: Defects in ALAS2 cause X-linked sideroblastic anemia.
If a downstream enzyme is partly blocked, heme falls, feedback is lost, ALAS1 is induced and ALA and PBG are overproduced. This is the basis of the acute attack.
Rare disorders, each a deficiency of one heme synthesis enzyme. Usually autosomal dominant or recessive, sometimes sporadic. They show up where the pathway is busiest: bone marrow and liver.
A block causes accumulation of precursors and lack of product, and both can be toxic.

items.note: Only acute intermittent porphyria needs to be known by name; the other porphyria names on the slides are marked FYI.

items.p: A 26-year-old woman has 3 days of severe abdominal pain with vomiting and constipation, a soft abdomen and a normal CT. She began a strict low-calorie diet two weeks ago and a sulfonamide five days ago. Pulse 118, BP 150/95, sodium 126, confusion, weak arms, and urine that turns reddish-brown on standing.

ul: Why now: the sulfonamide induces P450s and fasting induces ALAS1, so the liver is asked for more heme and more ALA enters the pathway.

Urine: ALA high, PBG markedly high, because ALA dehydratase still works and PBG piles up in front of the half-working enzyme. PBG oxidizes on standing to a reddish-brown pigment. No blisters, because the block comes before any porphyrin.
Diagnosis: HMB synthase (PBG deaminase) deficiency, autosomal dominant. Activity is halved and most carriers never have an attack.

table: Drugs that drive ALAS1 (sulfonamides …), fasting, progesterone, alcohol
Abdominal pain, tachycardia, hypertension, neuropathy, confusion, low sodium; no skin signs
Often taken for an acute abdomen or a psychiatric illness; some patients have unnecessary surgery
Stop the trigger, IV glucose, IV hemin (restores heme feedback on ALAS1), then avoid unsafe drugs

ul: Lead strongly inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase. ALA rises in the blood without a rise in PBG.

table: Inherited HMB synthase at half activity
Acquired: lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase
Yes: heme synthesis in red cell precursors is blocked

ul: Urine PBG is the test that separates them.

items.note: Clinical Sciences (microcytic anemia, slide 32) lists ALA synthase as inhibited by lead. This lecture names ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase, which matches standard sources.

ul: Red cells live 120 days. The spleen acts as a sieve for red cell quality; old cells release hemoglobin, which is split into heme and globin.
The porphyrin ring is hydrophobic and must be made soluble to be excreted. This happens in macrophages of the reticulo-endothelial system, mostly in the spleen.

table: Opens the ring; releases Fe²⁺ and CO
Uses NADPH; gives the yellow-red pigment

ul: Bilirubin is a cellular antioxidant: a mildly high level without liver disease may be beneficial.
In hepatocytes, bilirubin UDP-glucuronyltransferase (UGT) adds glucuronic acid, giving bilirubin diglucuronide.
Conjugation makes bilirubin hydrophilic, so it travels in bile without a protein carrier. Unconjugated (indirect) bilirubin is not normally secreted.
Conjugated (direct) bilirubin is actively transported into the bile canaliculi and on to the intestine.
In the gut, bacteria remove the glucuronic acid, and bilirubin becomes urobilinogen, mainly in the colon.

items.caption: The journey of bilirubin from the macrophage to feces and urine

ul: Hyperbilirubinemia gives jaundice: yellow tissues and sclerae. It usually signals liver disease (hepatocellular), obstruction or hemolytic anemia.
Too much unconjugated bilirubin can cross the blood-brain barrier and deposit in the brain: kernicterus.
Labs measure total and direct bilirubin with reactive dyes; indirect bilirubin is calculated as total minus direct. Total bilirubin is normal up to 1.2 mg/dL.

items.p: A 21-year-old student fasting for Ramadan in exam week notices yellow eyes. He feels well, and urine and stools look normal. His eyes turned yellow once before, during a viral illness.

table: Total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL, almost all unconjugated
Bilirubin reaches the liver but leaves it unconjugated
Normal ALT, AST and alkaline phosphatase
Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and stays out of the urine
Rises with fasting or illness, normal when eating

ul: UGT1A1 works at about 30% of normal. Affects about 5–10% of people. Mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, worse with fasting, illness and stress.
Benign: no liver damage, no treatment, only reassurance.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman has severe abdominal pain with a normal CT scan, a pulse of 118/min and a sodium of 126 mmol/L. She started a sulfonamide five days ago, and her urine darkens on standing. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: A neurovisceral attack with hyponatremia and dark urine after a P450-inducing drug is acute intermittent porphyria: HMB synthase (PBG deaminase) works at half activity. A: A block here would keep PBG from rising. C: Lead inhibits it; a block here builds up a porphyrin, not PBG. D: A block here builds up porphyrinogens, which cause skin signs. E: A heme degradation enzyme.

questions.stem: Two weeks into a strict low-calorie diet, a woman with a half-active heme synthesis enzyme has her first attack of abdominal pain. How does fasting set off the attack?

options.C: It depletes pyridoxal phosphate in the liver
options.D: It enlarges the hepatic free heme pool
options.E: It blocks iron entry into mitochondria

questions.explanation: Fasting induces ALAS1 (glucose represses it); more ALA then floods a pathway whose HMB synthase works at half capacity, and ALA and PBG pile up. B: Fasting acts on the first enzyme. C: Not the mechanism. D: Free heme represses ALAS1. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A sulfonamide precipitates an acute attack in a carrier of a heme synthesis defect. What is the first event in the liver?

options.B: The drug displaces heme from hemoglobin
options.C: The drug speeds glucose uptake into hepatocytes
options.D: The drug removes the cofactor of ALA synthase
options.E: Induced cytochrome P450s use up free heme

questions.explanation: Cytochrome P450-inducing drugs such as sulfonamides need heme: the free heme pool falls and ALAS1 is derepressed. A: Lead does that. B: Not the mechanism. C: Glucose represses ALAS1. D: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A woman with known acute intermittent porphyria is admitted after two days of vomiting and eating nothing. Which infusion directly represses her hepatic ALA synthase?
questions.explanation: Fasting induces ALAS1 and glucose represses it, so IV glucose is part of AIP treatment. A: The ALA synthase cofactor. B: Iron is not the treatment. D: Unrelated to heme synthesis. E: Not described as repressing ALAS1.

questions.stem: A woman with an inherited half-active HMB synthase has an attack after starting a sulfonamide. Which urinary compound is most markedly raised?
questions.explanation: In AIP urine ALA is high and PBG markedly high: ALA dehydratase keeps converting the extra ALA into PBG, which then piles up in front of HMB synthase. A: Lies beyond the block. B: Lies beyond the block. C: A heme breakdown product. E: A normal urine pigment.

questions.stem: A woman's fresh urine is pale yellow but turns reddish-brown after standing on the windowsill during an attack of abdominal pain and confusion. What explains the color change?
questions.explanation: On standing, PBG oxidizes to a reddish-brown pigment: that is why the urine darkens in an attack of acute intermittent porphyria. B: Stercobilin colors feces. C: She has no hemolysis. D: Not part of the attack. E: Not the cause here.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old woman in an acute porphyric attack has a markedly raised urine PBG but no blisters or sun sensitivity. Why is her skin spared?

options.A: Her porphyrins are cleared in bile
options.C: Skin damage needs a very high ALA level
options.D: The block lies before any porphyrin forms

questions.explanation: Only the precursors ALA and PBG (neurotoxic) accumulate; the block comes before the porphyrins, which cause photosensitivity. A: Porphyrins are not accumulating. B: Untreated patients also lack skin signs. C: ALA and PBG cause neurological signs. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: A patient with an inherited defect of heme synthesis has neuropathy and confusion but normal skin. Which compounds are accumulating?
questions.explanation: Excess porphyrin precursors (ALA and PBG) are associated with neurological manifestations; excess porphyrins and porphyrinogens cause skin photosensitivity. A: Porphyrinogens cause skin photosensitivity. B: Porphyrinogens cause skin photosensitivity. C: A porphyrin; causes skin photosensitivity. D: Not a heme synthesis intermediate.

questions.stem: A patient with an inherited defect of heme synthesis has skin photosensitivity with blisters but no abdominal pain or neuropathy. Which intermediates are in excess?
questions.explanation: Each enzyme deficiency causes accumulation of intermediates: excess porphyrins/porphyrinogens cause skin photosensitivity, excess ALA and PBG neurological manifestations. A: A precursor; neurological effects. B: Precursors cause neurological effects. D: Heme breakdown products. E: Heme breakdown products.

questions.stem: A woman in an acute porphyric attack keeps vomiting despite IV glucose. Which drug restores heme feedback on hepatic ALA synthase?
questions.explanation: Treatment of an AIP attack: stop the trigger, IV glucose, and IV hemin, which restores heme feedback on ALAS1. A: Iron does not restore heme feedback. C: The ALA synthase cofactor. D: Unrelated to heme synthesis. E: Acts on erythroid cells.

questions.stem: Acute intermittent porphyria is autosomal dominant, yet a patient's father, who carries the same mutation, has never had an attack. What is the explanation?

options.A: His mutation lies in the erythroid isoform
options.B: Men cannot express the mutant HMB synthase
options.C: His bone marrow supplies heme to his liver
options.D: Half the enzyme activity is enough
options.E: He makes no ALA in the liver

questions.explanation: HMB synthase activity is halved and most carriers never have an attack: an attack needs a trigger that drives ALAS1. A: The defect is in HMB synthase, not ALA synthase. B: Not the explanation. C: Heme is made locally. E: He makes ALA normally.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has had two laparotomies for recurrent severe abdominal pain that found nothing. She now has confusion and a sodium of 124 mmol/L. Which condition was most likely missed?
questions.explanation: AIP is often misdiagnosed as an acute abdomen or a psychiatric illness, and some patients have unnecessary surgery. A: Mild jaundice without pain. B: An anemia without attacks. C: No pain attacks. D: Hemolysis without hyponatremia.

questions.stem: Each of the following can trigger an attack of acute intermittent porphyria EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: An attack needs a trigger that drives ALAS1: some drugs (sulfonamides), fasting, progesterone, alcohol. Glucose represses ALAS1. A: A listed trigger. B: A listed trigger. D: A listed trigger. E: A listed trigger.

questions.stem: A woman has severe abdominal pain with vomiting and a normal CT scan. Which additional finding would argue against an acute porphyric attack from HMB synthase deficiency?
questions.explanation: ALA and PBG are neurotoxic: abdominal pain, tachycardia, hypertension, neuropathy, confusion and low sodium, with no skin signs. A: Hypertension fits. C: Tachycardia fits. D: Low sodium fits. E: Neuropathy fits.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old living in an old house with peeling paint has abdominal pain and anemia. Urine ALA is high and urine PBG is normal. Inhibition of which enzyme explains the normal PBG?
questions.explanation: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase (and ferrochelatase): ALA rises in the absence of a rise in PBG. B: A block here would raise PBG. C: A block here would lower ALA. D: Acts beyond PBG. E: A heme degradation enzyme.

questions.stem: A man has abdominal pain and neuropathy, and urine ALA is high. Which urine test best separates acute intermittent porphyria from lead poisoning?
questions.explanation: Urine PBG is high in AIP and normal in lead poisoning (ALA dehydratase is inhibited). A: High in both. C: A heme breakdown product. D: A heme breakdown product. E: Not a porphyria marker.

questions.stem: Why does lead poisoning cause anemia while acute intermittent porphyria does not?

options.A: Lead causes chronic blood loss from the gut
options.B: Lead binds the oxygen site of hemoglobin
options.C: Lead blocks heme synthesis in red cell precursors

questions.explanation: Lead strongly blocks two enzymes in the very cells that make hemoglobin; in AIP half of the HMB synthase activity suffices for red cells. A: Not the mechanism. B: Not the mechanism. D: Not the mechanism. E: Lead inhibits ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase.

questions.stem: In lead poisoning, an acquired porphyria, protoporphyrin IX builds up in red cell precursors although iron is available. Which enzyme is inhibited?
questions.explanation: Ferrochelatase (heme synthetase) inserts ferrous iron into protoporphyrin IX; with ALA dehydratase it is highly sensitive to heavy metals. A: Forms protoporphyrin IX. B: Acts two steps earlier. C: Acts in the cytoplasm. D: Acts in the cytoplasm.

questions.stem: A boy has a lifelong anemia, as did his maternal uncle. Both carry a defect in the erythroid-specific gene for the first enzyme of heme synthesis. Which gene is mutated?
questions.explanation: ALA synthase exists as a housekeeping form (ALAS1) and an erythroid-specific form (ALAS2); defects in ALAS2 cause X-linked sideroblastic anemia. A: The housekeeping isoform. B: Gilbert syndrome. C: AIP; no anemia. E: Not the first enzyme.

questions.stem: A defect in the erythroid-specific ALA synthase causes which disorder?
questions.explanation: Defects in ALAS2 cause X-linked sideroblastic anemia (XLSA). B: HMB synthase deficiency. C: Reduced UGT1A1. D: An enzyme defect of the hexose monophosphate shunt. E: Acquired, not genetic.

questions.stem: Severe vitamin B6 deficiency lowers pyridoxal phosphate in erythroblasts. Condensation of which substrates slows?
questions.explanation: ALA synthase condenses glycine and succinyl CoA into ALA using pyridoxal phosphate as a cofactor. A: Acetyl CoA is not used. B: Serine is not used. C: ALA dehydratase does this. D: HMB synthase.

questions.stem: Which step of heme synthesis is its main point of regulation?

options.A: Insertion of iron into protoporphyrin IX
options.B: Joining two ALA molecules into PBG
options.C: Condensation of glycine with succinyl CoA

questions.explanation: The first enzyme, ALA synthase, is rate-limiting and therefore highly regulated; heme exerts negative feedback on it. A: Ferrochelatase; not rate-limiting. B: ALA dehydratase; not rate-limiting. D: URO-synthase; not rate-limiting. E: Not rate-limiting.

questions.stem: What represses hepatic ALA synthase (ALAS1)?
questions.explanation: Liver ALAS1 is repressed by the hepatic "free heme" pool; P450-inducing drugs and fasting deplete heme and derepress it. B: Controls ALAS2. C: A substrate. D: Controls ALAS2 translation. E: A breakdown product.

questions.stem: A toddler with severe iron deficiency has erythroblasts short of iron. How is their ALA synthase (ALAS2), which is controlled by erythropoietin and iron, affected?

options.C: It is repressed by free heme

questions.explanation: Erythroid ALAS2 is controlled by erythropoietin and iron: translation stops when iron is low. A: That is the transferrin receptor response. C: That controls ALAS1. D: Fasting acts on ALAS1. E: Not the mechanism.

questions.stem: In a liver with a partial block late in heme synthesis, heme output falls. Which change follows directly?
questions.explanation: A block downstream lowers heme, removes feedback and induces ALAS1, overproducing ALA and PBG: the basis of the acute attack. A: Not the consequence. B: A degradation enzyme. C: Not the consequence. E: Unrelated.

questions.stem: All cells with aerobic metabolism are presumed able to make heme. Which cells make the most heme per day?

options.A: Erythroid cells of the bone marrow
options.E: Macrophages of the red pulp in the spleen

questions.explanation: The first major site is the erythroid cells of the bone marrow (about 300 mg/day, mostly for hemoglobin); the second is the liver; adrenals and kidneys also make a sizable amount. B: The second major site. C: A sizable but smaller amount. D: A sizable but smaller amount. E: They break heme down.

questions.stem: Why does the liver need a steady supply of newly made heme?

options.A: Export of heme to developing red cells in marrow

questions.explanation: The liver is the second major site of heme synthesis because the rapid turnover of microsomal cytochromes requires newly formed heme. A: Erythroid cells make their own. B: Bilirubin comes from heme breakdown. C: Not the reason. D: Made in muscle.

questions.stem: Heme is a prosthetic group in each of the following proteins EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Heme functions as a prosthetic group for hemoglobin, myoglobin, mitochondrial and microsomal cytochromes, catalase, peroxidases and tryptophan pyrrolase. A: A heme protein. B: A heme protein. D: A heme protein. E: Heme proteins.

questions.stem: What links the four pyrrole rings of the porphyrin ring?
questions.explanation: Four pyrrole rings are joined by methine bridges (–CH=) to form the porphyrin ring. A: Join amino acids. C: Join cysteines. D: Side chains. E: Join sugars.

questions.stem: How many side chains substitute the porphyrin ring of heme?
questions.explanation: Eight side chains serve as substituents on the porphyrin ring, two on each pyrrole: propionate, methyl or vinyl, in the order MVMVMPPM. A: One per pyrrole is too few. B: Too few. C: Too many. E: Too many.

questions.stem: Which step of heme synthesis takes place in the cytoplasm?

options.A: Condensation of glycine and succinyl CoA

questions.explanation: The first reaction and the last three occur in mitochondria; ALA is transported to the cytoplasm, where ALA dehydratase condenses it into PBG. A: Mitochondrial. C: Mitochondrial. D: Mitochondrial. E: Mitochondrial.

questions.stem: Which reactions of the eight-step heme pathway occur in mitochondria?

options.A: The first and the last three
options.B: The first three and the last
options.C: The first two and the last two

questions.explanation: Heme is made from glycine and succinyl CoA in 8 reactions: the first and the last three occur in mitochondria, those in between in the cytoplasm. B: Reverses the pattern. C: Wrong split. D: Wrong split. E: Wrong split.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the entry of intermediates into mitochondria. After which product would heme synthesis stop?
questions.explanation: Coproporphyrinogen III, the last cytoplasmic product, enters the mitochondrion for the sixth step. A: Further cytoplasmic steps follow. B: Further cytoplasmic steps follow. D: One more cytoplasmic step follows. E: Formed inside mitochondria.

questions.stem: HMB synthase links four PBG molecules head to tail. What does it form?
questions.explanation: Hydroxymethylbilane synthase (PBG deaminase) catalyzes the head-to-tail condensation of four PBG molecules by deaminations into the linear tetrapyrrole hydroxymethylbilane. A: Cyclization is the next step. B: Protoporphyrinogen IX. C: Protoporphyrin IX. E: Four rings are joined.

questions.stem: What does uroporphyrinogen III synthase do to hydroxymethylbilane?

options.A: Removes four carboxyl groups from it
options.B: Removes six hydrogen atoms from it

questions.explanation: URO-synthase catalyzes the rearrangement and rapid cyclization of HMB into uroporphyrinogen III, the asymmetric physiologic porphyrinogen. A: URO-decarboxylase. B: PROTO-oxidase. C: HMB synthase deaminates PBG. D: Ferrochelatase.

questions.stem: A patient has an inherited deficiency of uroporphyrinogen III synthase. What happens to the hydroxymethylbilane she makes?

options.A: It cyclizes nonenzymatically to uroporphyrinogen I
options.B: It is decarboxylated directly to coproporphyrinogen III
options.C: It is split back into porphobilinogen
options.D: It is oxidized to protoporphyrin IX
options.E: It is excreted unchanged as ALA

questions.explanation: Without the enzyme, HMB cyclizes nonenzymatically to uroporphyrinogen I, which is converted to coproporphyrinogen I. B: Needs URO III first. C: Not shown. D: Not shown. E: Not shown.

questions.stem: Which heme synthesis intermediate is a porphyrinogen with eight carboxylate groups?
questions.explanation: Uroporphyrinogen III is an asymmetric octacarboxylate porphyrinogen; COPRO III is tetracarboxylate and PROTO IX dicarboxylate. A: Tetracarboxylate. C: Dicarboxylate. D: A porphyrin. E: A single pyrrole.

questions.stem: Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase removes carboxyl groups from which side chains of uroporphyrinogen III?
questions.explanation: URO-decarboxylase removes the four carboxyl groups of the acetic acid side chains of URO III, forming the tetracarboxylate coproporphyrinogen III. A: COPRO-oxidase acts on these. B: Formed later. D: Link the rings. E: Not present.

questions.stem: Coproporphyrinogen oxidase forms protoporphyrinogen IX, a dicarboxylate porphyrinogen. What change does it make?

options.A: Turns four acetate groups into methyl groups
options.D: Turns two propionates into vinyl groups

questions.explanation: COPRO-oxidase decarboxylates two of the four propionic acid groups to form the two vinyl groups of protoporphyrinogen IX. A: URO-decarboxylase. B: PROTO-oxidase. C: Ferrochelatase. E: URO-synthase.

questions.stem: Protoporphyrinogen oxidase removes six hydrogen atoms from its substrate. What does that make its product?

options.A: The first porphyrinogen of the pathway
options.E: The first porphyrin of the pathway

questions.explanation: PROTO-oxidase forms protoporphyrin IX, a porphyrin (oxidized form), whereas the preceding tetrapyrroles are porphyrinogens (reduced forms). A: URO III is earlier. B: URO III is earlier. C: ALA is made in mitochondria. D: Heme is next.

questions.stem: An enzyme deficiency blocks a multi-step metabolic pathway. Besides a lack of product, what may cause harm?
questions.explanation: Blocks in the pathway usually lead to accumulation of precursors and lack of products, both of which may have toxic effects. A: The product falls. B: Flow is blocked. D: Substrate builds up. E: Not described.

questions.stem: Porphyrias may be inherited or arise sporadically. What do they share?

options.A: A defect in the breakdown of heme to bilirubin
options.E: Loss of one heme synthesis enzyme

questions.explanation: Porphyrias result from the deficiency of a specific enzyme in heme synthesis; they are usually autosomal dominant or recessive, but also sporadic. A: Bilirubin disorders. B: Hemoglobinopathies. C: Not the defect. D: Not the defect.

questions.stem: Porphyrias show up mainly in the tissues where the heme pathway is most active. Which are they?
questions.explanation: The enzymes are arranged sequentially in a pathway that is most active in the bone marrow and liver. B: Not the main sites. C: Where symptoms appear. D: Not the main sites. E: Not the main sites.

questions.stem: Senescent red cells are removed by the splenic sieve. About how long have they circulated?
questions.explanation: Red cells have a lifespan of 120 days; the spleen acts as a sieve that controls red cell quality. A: Far too short. B: Too short. C: Too short. E: Too long.

questions.stem: An old red cell is removed from the circulation and its hemoglobin split into heme and globin. In which cells is the heme turned into bilirubin?
questions.explanation: Heme breakdown to bilirubin occurs in the macrophages of the reticulo-endothelial system, mostly in the spleen. A: They conjugate bilirubin. C: Not the site. D: Not the site. E: They make heme.

questions.stem: Why must heme be modified before it can be excreted?

options.A: Its iron is in the ferric state
options.C: It is too large to filter

questions.explanation: The porphyrin ring is hydrophobic and must be solubilized to be excreted; bilirubin, the yellow product, is secreted in bile. A: Not the reason given. B: Not the reason given. C: Not the reason given. E: Not the reason given.

questions.stem: Where in the macrophage does heme oxygenase open the heme ring?
questions.explanation: Heme is oxidized into biliverdin, with the ring opened by heme oxygenase in the ER. A: Where heme is made. B: Not the site. C: Not the site. D: Not the site.

questions.stem: A patient with brisk hemolysis breaks down much more heme than usual. Which gas, released when heme oxygenase opens the ring, does he produce in excess?
questions.explanation: Heme oxygenase uses O2 to open the ring, releasing Fe2+ and CO and forming biliverdin. B: Not the product. C: Not the product. D: Consumed, not released. E: Released by HMB synthase.

questions.stem: A macrophage cannot supply NADPH to its heme degradation pathway. Which pigment builds up?
questions.explanation: Biliverdin reductase reduces biliverdin to bilirubin using NADPH; without NADPH biliverdin accumulates. A: Its formation needs NADPH. C: Formed in the gut. D: Formed in the gut. E: Formed in the liver.

questions.stem: Why does newly formed bilirubin travel from the spleen to the liver on albumin?

options.D: It must be oxidized on the way
options.E: Albumin carries it to the kidney

questions.explanation: Bilirubin is poorly soluble, so it is transported to the liver by albumin. A: Conjugation happens in the liver. B: Reverses the pathway. D: Not the reason. E: It goes to the liver.

questions.stem: In hepatocytes, which enzyme forms bilirubin diglucuronide?
questions.explanation: In hepatocytes bilirubin is conjugated with glucuronic acid by bilirubin UDP-glucuronyltransferase (UGT), yielding bilirubin diglucuronide. A: Forms bilirubin. C: Opens the heme ring. D: Not the conjugating enzyme here. E: Heme synthesis.

questions.stem: What does conjugation with glucuronic acid allow bilirubin to do?

options.B: Bind albumin more tightly in plasma
options.D: Travel in bile without a protein carrier
options.E: Leave the liver back into plasma

questions.explanation: Conjugation increases hydrophilicity, so bilirubin can be transported in bile without a protein carrier; unconjugated bilirubin is not normally secreted. A: Unconjugated bilirubin does that. B: Albumin carries unconjugated bilirubin. C: Not described. E: Not the purpose.

questions.stem: Which form of bilirubin is actively transported into the bile canaliculi?
questions.explanation: Conjugated (direct) bilirubin is actively transported into the bile canaliculi and then into bile to the intestine. A: Unconjugated; not secreted. B: Reduced before it leaves the macrophage. C: Formed in the gut. D: Formed in the gut.

questions.stem: A lab reports total bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL (normal up to 1.2) and direct bilirubin 0.2 mg/dL. What is the calculated indirect bilirubin?
questions.explanation: Total and direct bilirubin are measured with reactive dyes; indirect bilirubin is calculated as total minus direct. B: The direct value. C: Half the total. D: The excess above normal. E: Adds instead of subtracts.

questions.stem: A 21-year-old fasting during Ramadan notices yellow eyes in exam week. Total bilirubin is 3.2 mg/dL, almost all unconjugated; hemoglobin, reticulocytes, LDH, ALT, AST and alkaline phosphatase are normal. Which enzyme is underactive?
questions.explanation: Gilbert syndrome: bilirubin UDP-glucuronyltransferase (UGT1A1) works at about 30% of normal, so bilirubin reaches the liver but leaves it unconjugated. A: Production is normal. B: Production is normal. D: Heme synthesis. E: Hemolysis is excluded.

questions.stem: A young man with yellow sclerae has a high unconjugated bilirubin, but his hemoglobin, reticulocyte count and LDH are normal. What do these normal values show?

options.D: Bilirubin is made at a normal rate

questions.explanation: Normal hemoglobin, reticulocytes and LDH mean red cells are not destroyed faster than usual: bilirubin is made at a normal rate, so the hold-up is in the liver or beyond. A: They do not measure conjugation. B: Alkaline phosphatase reflects that. C: ALT and AST reflect that. E: Not measured.

questions.stem: A man with Gilbert syndrome has a total bilirubin of 3.2 mg/dL. Why is his urine dipstick negative for bilirubin?

options.A: The renal tubules convert bilirubin to urobilin
options.E: Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin

questions.explanation: Unconjugated bilirubin is bound to albumin and poorly water-soluble, so it stays out of the urine. A: Urobilin comes from urobilinogen. B: Not the reason. C: Not the reason. D: Stercobilin is fecal.

questions.stem: A healthy 21-year-old has mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that rises with fasting and illness; liver enzymes and blood count are normal. What is the management?
questions.explanation: Gilbert syndrome is benign: no liver damage and no treatment needed, only reassurance. A: No liver damage. C: For porphyric attacks. D: For iron overload. E: No hemolysis.

questions.stem: In Gilbert syndrome, what is the residual activity of bilirubin UDP-glucuronyltransferase?
questions.explanation: Reduced activity of UGT1A1, to about 30% of normal. A: Too low. B: Too low. D: Too high. E: Too high.

questions.stem: About how many people have Gilbert syndrome?
questions.explanation: Gilbert syndrome is common: about 5 to 10% of people; mild unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia worse with fasting, illness and stress. B: Too rare. C: Too rare. D: Too rare. E: Too common.

questions.stem: Why may a mildly high bilirubin without liver disease benefit health?

options.C: Bilirubin protects red cells from lysis

questions.explanation: Bilirubin is a cellular antioxidant: mildly high levels in the absence of liver disease have beneficial health effects. A: Not described. B: Not described. C: Not described. D: Not described.

questions.stem: A newborn's hyperbilirubinemia climbs very high, almost all unconjugated, and he develops neurological signs. What explains them?
questions.explanation: Excessive unconjugated bilirubin can cross the blood-brain barrier and accumulate in the brain: kernicterus. A: Liver failure. B: ALA and PBG. C: Lead. E: Benign.

questions.stem: Jaundice can be a sign of each of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Jaundice is usually a symptom of an underlying disorder: liver disease, obstruction or hemolytic anemia; Gilbert syndrome also causes it. A: A listed cause. B: A listed cause. D: A listed cause (hepatocellular jaundice). E: Unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia.

questions.stem: After a long course of broad-spectrum oral antibiotics, which step of bilirubin handling falls?
questions.explanation: In the intestine bacteria deconjugate bilirubin and convert it to urobilinogen; fewer bacteria means less urobilinogen. A: Hepatic. C: In plasma. D: In macrophages. E: Hepatic.

questions.stem: In the intestine, what removes glucuronic acid from bilirubin?
questions.explanation: In the intestine, glucuronic acid is removed by bacteria: bilirubin is deconjugated and then converted to urobilinogen. B: Not the agent. C: Removes glutamates from folate. D: Not the agent. E: Not the agent.

questions.stem: Where is most urobilinogen formed?
questions.explanation: Bilirubin is converted to urobilinogen mainly in the colon but also in the small intestine. A: Mostly colon. C: Bilirubin is conjugated there. D: Bilirubin is made there. E: Urobilin is made there.

questions.stem: Which pigment gives feces their typical color?
questions.explanation: Some urobilinogen is oxidized by bacterial enzymes to stercobilin, which is excreted and gives feces their typical color. A: Colors urine. B: An earlier product. C: Its precursor. E: Deconjugated in the gut.

questions.stem: Urobilinogen reabsorbed into the portal blood reaches the kidney. What does it become there?
questions.explanation: Some urobilinogen enters the portal blood, where it is recycled or goes to the kidneys and is converted to urobilin, which gives urine its color. A: Formed in the gut. B: An earlier product. D: An earlier product. E: A heme precursor.

questions.stem: A patient with blistering skin lesions has an inherited deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. Which intermediate accumulates?
questions.explanation: A block leads to accumulation of the substrate before it: URO-decarboxylase acts on uroporphyrinogen III, a porphyrinogen, and excess porphyrinogens cause skin photosensitivity. B: The product, which falls. C: A precursor further back. D: A precursor further back. E: Formed later.

questions.stem: A child with abdominal pain is being worked up for acute intermittent porphyria or lead poisoning. Which finding points to lead?
questions.explanation: Lead blocks ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase in red cell precursors and causes anemia; in AIP half of HMB synthase activity suffices, so there is no anemia. A: Present in both. B: Present in both. C: Present in both. D: From PBG, which lead does not raise.

questions.stem: A man in an acute attack of intermittent porphyria is given intravenous hemin. Which enzyme is it meant to switch down?
questions.explanation: IV hemin restores heme feedback on ALAS1, cutting the flood of ALA and PBG. A: Controlled by erythropoietin and iron. C: Already half-active. D: Converts ALA to PBG. E: Breaks heme down.

questions.stem: A student has yellow sclerae. Total bilirubin is 4.0 mg/dL with direct bilirubin 0.3 mg/dL; hemoglobin, reticulocytes, ALT, AST and alkaline phosphatase are normal. Where is the problem?
questions.explanation: The raised bilirubin is almost all indirect while production is normal and the liver is uninjured: bilirubin reaches the liver but leaves it unconjugated. A: Reticulocytes and hemoglobin are normal. B: Alkaline phosphatase is normal. C: Production is normal. E: They act after bile secretion.

questions.stem: An inflammatory response has already eliminated a bacterial agent. Which step comes next in the sequence described in the notes?
questions.explanation: The order is recognition → recruitment → removal → regulation → resolution and repair. Once the agent is removed, the next step is regulation of the response. A: Resolution and repair is the final step and comes after regulation. C: Recruitment comes before removal. D: Recognition is the first step. E: Removal is the step that has just been completed.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Purpose and sequence

questions.stem: Which statement about the components of inflammation is correct?

options.A: Its two components are humoral and cellular, regulated by antibodies and complement
options.B: Its two components are vascular and lymphatic, regulated mainly by histamine
options.C: Its two components are cellular and fibrotic, regulated by cytokines and growth factors
options.D: Its two components are vascular and cellular, both regulated by mediators and adhesion molecules
options.E: Its two components are exudative and proliferative, regulated mainly by adhesion molecules

questions.explanation: Inflammation has a vascular and a cellular component; in acute inflammation both are regulated by chemical mediators and adhesion molecules. A: Humoral versus cellular describes adaptive immunity. B: Lymphatics participate, but the two components are vascular and cellular, and many mediators act. C: Fibrosis is part of repair, not a component of inflammation. E: These are not the two components named, and mediators also regulate the events.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Purpose and sequence

questions.stem: Which cardinal sign is matched with its correct mechanism?

options.A: Calor: increased interstitial pressure on nerves
options.C: Dolor: dilation of vessels with increased flow
options.D: Rubor: leakage of protein-rich fluid into tissue

questions.explanation: Tumor (swelling) is due to extravascular accumulation of fluid. A: Calor comes from increased blood flow; pressure on nerves contributes to pain. C: Dolor comes from interstitial pressure and mediators such as bradykinin; vasodilation causes redness and heat. D: Rubor comes from vessel dilation; fluid leakage causes swelling. E: Functio laesa is loss of function, not vasoconstriction.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Cardinal signs and causes

questions.stem: All of the following are listed as causes of inflammation EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The causes listed are infection, trauma, physical injury (thermal extremes, ionizing radiation), chemical injury, foreign bodies, immunologic injury and tissue death. Apoptosis is not listed; in resolution, neutrophil apoptosis is part of switching inflammation off. A: Foreign bodies are listed. B: Immunologic injury is listed. C: Physical injury from thermal extremes or radiation is listed. E: Tissue death is listed; inflammation occurs in the viable tissue next to it.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Cardinal signs and causes

questions.stem: Which statement about the early vascular changes of acute inflammation is correct?

options.A: Arteriolar dilation begins at once, with no prior change
options.B: A brief vasoconstriction precedes arteriolar dilation
options.D: Dilation is mediated mainly by LTC4, LTD4 and LTE4
options.E: Dilation reduces blood flow, causing pallor and cooling

questions.explanation: Acute inflammation begins with a brief vasoconstriction followed by arteriolar dilation and increased blood flow, producing redness and warmth; histamine is an important mediator. A: A brief vasoconstriction comes first. C: The vasoconstriction is brief. D: LTC4, LTD4 and LTE4 are vasoconstrictors. E: Dilation increases flow, causing redness and warmth.

questions.stem: All of the following are mechanisms of increased vascular permeability EXCEPT:

options.E: VEGF-induced transcytosis and leaky new vessels

questions.explanation: The mechanisms listed are endothelial-cell contraction with widened gaps, direct endothelial injury, leukocyte-mediated injury, and VEGF-induced transcytosis with leaky new vessels. PECAM-1 mediates leukocyte transmigration, not fluid leakage. A: Endothelial contraction is listed. C: Direct endothelial injury is listed. D: Leukocyte-mediated injury is listed. E: VEGF effects are listed.

questions.stem: A child has an infected wound on the foot and a tender, enlarged inguinal lymph node. What is the main reason more microbes and debris reach that node during acute inflammation?

options.A: Leukocytes carry microbes into veins draining to the node
options.B: Lymphatic valves fail and lymph flows back
options.C: Increased extracellular fluid increases lymph drainage
options.D: Lymph nodes produce chemokines that pull microbes toward them
options.E: Increased capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes microbes into nodes

questions.explanation: In inflammation extracellular fluid increases, so lymph drainage increases. Leukocytes, debris and microbes are carried with the lymph, and the draining nodes may become inflamed and painful (lymphadenitis). A: Leukocytes travel in lymph, not veins, to the node. B: Valve failure is not described. D: Chemokines organize lymphoid tissue but do not pull microbes into nodes. E: Drainage is the route described, not capillary pressure into nodes.

questions.stem: During leukocyte recruitment, which event directly precedes firm adhesion?
questions.explanation: The order is margination → pavementing → rolling → adhesion → transmigration, so rolling comes right before adhesion. A: Pavementing precedes rolling. B: Margination is the first step. C: Transmigration follows adhesion. D: Chemotaxis is the movement toward the injury after emigration.

questions.stem: Which pairing of adhesion molecule and its binding partner is correct?
questions.explanation: E- and P-selectins on endothelium bind oligosaccharides such as sialyl-Lewis X on leukocytes. A: The leukocyte selectin binds endothelial mucin-like GlyCAM-1. C: ICAM-1 is endothelial and binds leukocyte integrins. D: VCAM is endothelial and binds leukocyte integrins. E: PECAM-1 binds PECAM-1 on both cells; GlyCAM-1 is endothelial.

questions.stem: A drug blocks the integrins LFA-1, MAC-1 and VLA-4. Which step would be most directly impaired?
questions.explanation: Integrins on leukocytes bind endothelial ICAM-1/2 and VCAM, producing firm adhesion before transmigration. A: Rolling depends on selectins. B: Margination happens as blood flow changes, before binding. D: Pavementing is lining of the endothelium before rolling. E: Phagolysosome formation occurs inside the phagocyte.

questions.stem: Which statement about P-selectin is correct?

options.A: Stored in Weibel–Palade bodies and platelet α-granules
options.B: Induced on neutrophils by IL-1 and TNF
options.C: Stored in platelet dense granules and neutrophil granules
options.D: Binds GlyCAM-1 on high endothelial venules
options.E: Relocated to the surface by C5a and LTB4

questions.explanation: P-selectin is stored in endothelial Weibel–Palade bodies and platelet α-granules, and relocates to the plasma membrane after stimulation by histamine and thrombin. B: P-selectin is endothelial and platelet, not neutrophil. C: Dense granules are not its store. D: GlyCAM-1 is the ligand of the leukocyte selectin; P-selectin binds sialyl-Lewis X. E: The relocating stimuli are histamine and thrombin.

questions.stem: Which molecule is expressed on both leukocytes and endothelial cells?
questions.explanation: PECAM-1 (CD31) is expressed on both leukocytes and endothelial cells and mediates transmigration. B: ICAM-2 is endothelial. C: E-selectin is endothelial. D: VLA-4 is a leukocyte integrin. E: GlyCAM-1 is an endothelial mucin-like molecule.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a chemotactic factor for neutrophils?
questions.explanation: The listed neutrophil chemotactic factors are bacterial products, C5a, LTB4, HETE and kallikrein. LTC4 is a vasoconstrictor, bronchoconstrictor and permeability mediator. A: Kallikrein is listed as chemotactic. C: HETE is listed as chemotactic. D: C5a is the main complement chemotactic factor. E: Bacterial products are listed.

questions.stem: Which statement about phagocytosis is correct?

options.A: Opsonins dissolve particles before they are engulfed
options.B: The phagosome forms by fusion of two lysosomes
options.D: IgM and C5a are the most important opsonins
options.E: Monocytes are poor phagocytes compared with lymphocytes

questions.explanation: Pseudopods enclose the particle in a phagosome, which fuses with lysosomes to form a phagolysosome; this is associated with degranulation. A: Opsonins coat and immobilize particles on the phagocyte surface. B: The phagosome forms from the engulfing pseudopods. D: The most important opsonins are IgG and C3b. E: Neutrophils and monocytes–macrophages are the main phagocytes.

questions.stem: In which setting is leukocyte-mediated injury especially likely to worsen tissue damage after the original insult?

options.B: Serous blister formation after a burn
options.C: Lymphatic drainage of a resolving abscess wall

questions.explanation: Leukocytes damage host tissue during clearance of necrotic tissue, including after myocardial infarction, especially with reperfusion; also in infection, autoimmune reactions and allergic disease such as asthma. B: A serous blister is a cell-poor exudate. C: Lymphatic drainage is part of resolution. D: Neutrophil apoptosis ends the response. E: Macrophage clearance is part of resolution.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

questions.stem: The most important substances released by activated leukocytes that injure host tissue are:

options.A: Histamine and serotonin from leukocyte granules

questions.explanation: The most important injurious leukocyte products are lysosomal enzymes (in the granules) and reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. A: Histamine and serotonin come from mast cells, basophils and platelets. B: PGI2 and NO are endothelial and protective. C: Lipoxins resolve inflammation and antiproteases protect tissue. D: C3b and IgG are opsonins.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

questions.stem: Which statement about neutrophils in acute inflammation is correct?

options.A: They dominate the focus for the first 2–3 days, then are replaced by lymphocytes
