options.B: Early neutrophilia comes from division of mature circulating neutrophils
options.C: They are the main cells in viral infections
options.D: Neutrophilia is a typical response to parasitic infestation
options.E: Early neutrophilia comes from the marrow postmitotic reserve pool, with more band forms

questions.explanation: Early neutrophilia comes from release of the bone marrow postmitotic reserve pool, with more immature band neutrophils. A: Neutrophils dominate the first 24 hours and are replaced by monocytes–macrophages after 2–3 days. B: Mature neutrophils do not divide. C: Lymphocytes dominate many viral infections. D: Parasites cause eosinophilia.

questions.stem: Why are monocytes–macrophages better suited than neutrophils to the later phase of an inflammatory focus?

options.A: They live longer, divide in tissue and engulf larger particles
options.B: They arrive first and degranulate within minutes of injury
options.C: They die after a single burst, which limits tissue damage
options.D: They are the main source of histamine in the tissue
options.E: They release lipoxins that recruit more neutrophils

questions.explanation: Monocytes–macrophages engulf larger particles, are longer-lived, and can divide and proliferate in the inflamed tissue. B: Neutrophils arrive first. C: Dying after one burst describes neutrophils. D: Histamine comes from mast cells, basophils and platelets. E: Lipoxins help resolve inflammation.

questions.stem: Which cell is matched with the setting in which it is prominent?

options.B: Eosinophils – allergic reactions and parasitic infestations
options.C: Lymphocytes – the first 24 hours of acute inflammation
options.D: Neutrophils – chronic inflammation alongside plasma cells

questions.explanation: Eosinophils are prominent in allergic reactions and parasitic infestations. A: Lymphocytes are prominent in viral infections; basophilia occurs in CML. C: Neutrophils dominate the first 24 hours. D: Chronic inflammation features lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells. E: Monocytes become prominent after 2–3 days.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Cells in acute and chronic inflammation

questions.stem: Which statement about the inflammatory cells is correct?

options.A: Eosinophils are the main source of histamine
options.B: Chronic inflammation is dominated by mononuclear cells
options.C: Basophilia is the typical response to allergic reactions
options.D: Neutrophils are capable of dividing in the inflamed tissue
options.E: Monocytes predominate in the first 24 hours

questions.explanation: Lymphocytes, along with monocytes–macrophages and plasma cells, are the most prominent cells in chronic inflammation. A: Mast cells and basophils are the histamine sources. C: Allergy causes eosinophilia; basophilia is from CML and myeloproliferative diseases. D: Macrophages, not neutrophils, can divide in the tissue. E: Neutrophils predominate in the first 24 hours.

questions.stem: Which mediator is matched with its correct origin category?
questions.explanation: Endogenous mediators are cell-derived or plasma-protein-derived; bradykinin comes from the plasma kinin system. A: Histamine is cell-derived (mast cells, basophils, platelets). B: C5a comes from plasma complement proteins. C: Microbial peptides are exogenous mediators. D: PAF is made from cell membrane phospholipids.

questions.stem: Histamine release from mast cells and basophils is triggered by all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Triggers are antigen binding to IgE on mast cells and basophils, C3a and C5a, physical stimuli, and cytokines or products from inflammatory cells. C3b is an opsonin. A: IgE-bound antigen is a trigger. C: Physical stimuli are triggers. D: C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins that trigger release. E: Cytokines and inflammatory-cell products are triggers.

questions.stem: Which statement about histamine and serotonin is correct?

options.A: Serotonin comes from platelets and acts like histamine
options.B: Serotonin comes from mast cells and opposes histamine
options.C: Histamine comes from basophils but not from platelets
options.D: Histamine acts mainly by damaging arteriolar endothelium
options.E: Serotonin is the main trigger of mast cell degranulation

questions.explanation: Histamine is released from mast cells, basophils and platelets and acts especially through endothelial contraction in postcapillary venules. Serotonin, released from platelets, has effects similar to histamine. B: The doc gives platelets as the serotonin source, with similar effects. C: Platelets also release histamine. D: Histamine acts by endothelial contraction in postcapillary venules. E: Degranulation triggers are IgE-bound antigen, C3a/C5a, physical stimuli and cytokines.

questions.stem: Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid, the precursor of which mediators?
questions.explanation: Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids; the COX pathway makes prostaglandins and thromboxanes, and the lipoxygenase pathway makes leukotrienes and lipoxins. A: Bradykinin and kallikrein belong to the kinin system. C: Histamine and serotonin are preformed amines. D: NO is made by endothelial cells, not from arachidonic acid. E: C3a and C5a are complement fragments.

questions.stem: Which arachidonic acid product is matched with the correct pathway and action?
questions.explanation: Endothelial PGI2 is a COX product, a powerful vasodilator and inhibitor of platelet aggregation. A: TxA2 is a COX product. B: LTB4 is a lipoxygenase product. D: Lipoxins come from 5-HPETE (lipoxygenase) and help resolve inflammation. E: HETE is a lipoxygenase product and is chemotactic.

questions.stem: Which statement about the lipoxygenase pathway is correct?

options.B: It is not the pathway blocked by aspirin

questions.explanation: Aspirin inhibits the cyclooxygenase pathway. The lipoxygenase pathway produces HPETEs, LTB4 (chemotactic), LTC4/LTD4/LTE4 (bronchoconstriction, vasoconstriction, permeability) and lipoxins (help resolve inflammation). A: TxA2 is a COX product. C: PGI2 is a COX product. D: Only LTB4 is described as chemotactic; LTC4–LTE4 constrict and increase permeability. E: Lipoxins help resolve inflammation.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma has an attack after allergen exposure, with bronchoconstriction and increased vascular permeability that persist after antihistamine treatment. Which group of mediators best explains the persistent effects?
questions.explanation: LTC4, LTD4 and LTE4 are potent vasoconstrictors, bronchoconstrictors and mediators of increased permeability (the slow-reacting substance of anaphylaxis). A: LTB4 and HETE are chemotactic for neutrophils. B: PGI2 and NO are vasodilators. C: Lipoxins help resolve inflammation. E: TxA2 and serotonin are platelet products; neither is the slow-reacting substance.

questions.stem: Which statement about platelet-activating factor is correct?

options.A: It is a peptide cleaved from kininogen by kallikrein
options.B: It inhibits platelets and causes bronchodilation in asthma
options.C: It is a lipoxygenase product of leukocytes
options.D: It is a plasma protein made by the liver
options.E: It is more potent than histamine in increasing permeability

questions.explanation: PAF is generated from membrane phospholipids in several cell types. It stimulates platelets, causes bronchoconstriction, increases permeability, and is described as substantially more potent than histamine in increasing permeability and vasodilation. A: That describes bradykinin. B: PAF stimulates platelets and causes bronchoconstriction. C: PAF comes from membrane phospholipids; it is not a leukotriene. D: PAF is a lipid made by cells, not a hepatic protein.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: PAF, cytokines and chemokines

questions.stem: Which effect is NOT attributed to IL-1 and TNF in the notes?
questions.explanation: IL-1 and TNF reduce, not increase, endothelial thromboresistance, which promotes thrombosis. A: Acute-phase responses are listed. B: Adhesion molecule synthesis is listed. C: Neutrophil degranulation is listed. D: Fever and cachexia are systemic effects listed.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: PAF, cytokines and chemokines

questions.stem: Besides attracting selected leukocyte populations, chemokines:
questions.explanation: Chemokines are small proteins that primarily attract selected leukocytes; they support recruitment and the normal organization of cells in lymphoid tissues. A: Fever and acute-phase responses come from IL-1 and TNF. B: The opsonins are IgG and C3b. D: The MAC is C5b–9. E: NO and PGI2 inhibit platelet aggregation.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: PAF, cytokines and chemokines

questions.stem: Nitric oxide contributes to endothelial thromboresistance by:
questions.explanation: NO, made by endothelial cells, relaxes smooth muscle, inhibits platelet aggregation (thromboresistance) and participates in microbial killing. B: NO does not cleave PGI2. C: P-selectin relocation is caused by histamine and thrombin. D: Factor XIIa starts the kinin and coagulation systems. E: TxA2 promotes aggregation.

questions.stem: Which statement about reactive oxygen species is correct?

options.A: They are synthesized by phospholipase A2 in neutrophils
options.B: At low levels they cause tissue injury; at high levels they amplify signals
options.C: At low levels they increase chemokine and adhesion molecule expression
options.E: They are neutralized mainly by α1-antitrypsin

questions.explanation: ROS are made by NADPH oxidase. At low levels they increase chemokine, cytokine and adhesion molecule expression; at higher levels they injure tissue. A: ROS come from NADPH oxidase. B: The relationship is reversed. D: Catalase detoxifies H2O2. E: α1-antitrypsin is an antiprotease; ROS are handled by SOD, catalase and glutathione peroxidase.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old non-smoker develops panacinar emphysema. Uninhibited activity of which enzyme, from leukocyte granules, explains the lung destruction?
questions.explanation: Lysosomal enzymes are checked by antiproteases; α1-antitrypsin is the major inhibitor of neutrophil elastase. Its deficiency in the lung lets leukocyte proteases destroy tissue, causing panacinar emphysema. B: MPO generates hypochlorous acid; it is not the protease checked by α1-antitrypsin. C: Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid. D: NADPH oxidase generates ROS. E: Kallikrein makes bradykinin.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

questions.stem: Which statement about substance P is correct?

options.A: It is a lipid mediator generated by phospholipase A2
options.B: It transmits pain and regulates vascular tone and permeability
options.C: It is an acute-phase protein produced by hepatocytes in the liver
options.D: It is an anaphylatoxin formed during complement activation
options.E: It is stored in Weibel–Palade bodies with P-selectin

questions.explanation: Neuropeptides such as substance P transmit pain signals and regulate vascular tone and permeability; nerve fibers producing them are prominent in the lung and GI tract. A: Lipid mediators are arachidonic acid metabolites and PAF. C: Acute-phase proteins include CRP and fibrinogen. D: The anaphylatoxins are C3a and C5a. E: Weibel–Palade bodies store P-selectin.

questions.stem: Activated Hageman factor (factor XIIa) directly activates all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Factor XIIa initiates the kinin system (prekallikrein → kallikrein), the intrinsic coagulation pathway and the plasminogen system, which in turn activate complement. The COX pathway starts from arachidonic acid released by phospholipase A2. B: The kinin system is initiated by XIIa. C: XIIa activates intrinsic coagulation. D: XIIa activates the plasminogen system. E: Prekallikrein conversion is part of the kinin system.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Kinin and complement systems

questions.stem: Which statement about the kinin system is correct?

options.A: Bradykinin is cleaved from prekallikrein by factor XIIa
options.B: Kallikrein is a vasoconstrictor that opposes bradykinin
options.C: Bradykinin is the chemotactic product of the system
options.D: Kininogen is released from mast cell granules
options.E: Kallikrein cleaves kininogen and is also chemotactic

questions.explanation: Kallikrein, generated from prekallikrein, cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen to bradykinin; kallikrein can also act as a chemotactic factor. Bradykinin causes permeability, arteriolar dilation and pain. A: Bradykinin comes from kininogen, cleaved by kallikrein. B: Kallikrein is chemotactic, not a vasoconstrictor. C: Kallikrein, not bradykinin, is the chemotactic factor. D: Kininogen is a plasma protein.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Kinin and complement systems

questions.stem: Which action of C5a is described in the notes?
questions.explanation: C5a is chemotactic, releases histamine (including from platelet dense granules), induces leukocyte adhesion molecules and activates the lipoxygenase pathway. A: C3b is the opsonin. C: C5b-9 forms pores. D: C5a induces adhesion molecules. E: Factor XIIa converts prekallikrein.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Kinin and complement systems

questions.stem: Which statement about complement in inflammation is correct?

options.A: C3b is the membrane attack complex
options.B: C5b–9 acts as the main opsonin
options.D: C3a is the main chemotactic fragment

questions.explanation: C3a and C5a are anaphylatoxins that trigger mast-cell and basophil degranulation. C5a is also chemotactic; C3b is an opsonin; C5b–9 is the lytic MAC. A: C3b is an opsonin. B: C5b–9 lyses cells. D: C5a is the chemotactic fragment described. E: C5a promotes adhesion-molecule expression.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Kinin and complement systems

questions.stem: Which statement about neutrophil extracellular traps is correct?

options.A: They are formed by fibrin deposited from plasma
options.B: They kill microbes inside the phagolysosome
options.C: They trap microbes in fibrils, limiting spread
options.D: They are released by macrophages after 2–3 days
options.E: They are the main cause of serous effusions

questions.explanation: NETs are extracellular fibrillar networks released by neutrophils that concentrate antimicrobial substances and prevent spread by trapping microbes. A: Fibrin comes from coagulation. B: NETs act outside the cell. D: They are released by neutrophils. E: Serous effusions come from plasma or mesothelium.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old with bacterial pneumonia has fever, weight loss and raised serum CRP, fibrinogen and ferritin. Which is also listed as an acute-phase protein made by the liver under the same stimulus?
questions.explanation: IL-1 and TNF drive hepatic acute-phase proteins: CRP, serum amyloid-associated protein, complement, fibrinogen, prothrombin, α1-antitrypsin, α2-macroglobulin, ferritin and ceruloplasmin. A: Bradykinin is a kinin. C: Albumin is not in the doc' acute-phase list (it falls in inflammation). D: IgG is made by plasma cells. E: Histamine is a vasoactive amine.

questions.stem: Which pair of proteins is listed both as an antiprotease and among the acute-phase proteins?
questions.explanation: α1-antitrypsin and α2-macroglobulin are the antiproteases that check lysosomal enzymes, and both are also in the acute-phase list. A: These are acute-phase proteins but not antiproteases. B: These are acute-phase proteins but not antiproteases. C: These are coagulation-related acute-phase proteins. E: These are antioxidant enzymes.

questions.stem: Which statement about selectins is correct?

options.A: IL-1 and TNF promote their endothelial expression
options.B: They mediate firm adhesion before transmigration
options.C: E-selectin is stored in Weibel–Palade bodies
options.D: They are integrins expressed on leukocytes
options.E: They bind ICAM-1 and VCAM on endothelium

questions.explanation: Selectins mediate rolling; IL-1 and TNF promote endothelial adhesion-molecule expression. E- and P-selectins bind sialyl-Lewis X; P-selectin is stored in Weibel–Palade bodies and platelet α-granules. B: Firm adhesion is mediated by integrins. C: P-selectin is the stored one. D: Integrins are a separate family. E: ICAM-1 and VCAM bind integrins.

questions.stem: Which feature belongs to resolution of acute inflammation rather than to conversion to chronic inflammation?

options.A: Proliferation of fibroblasts and new vessels
options.E: Apoptosis of neutrophils at the site

questions.explanation: Resolution includes decay of mediators, normal permeability, neutrophil apoptosis, anti-inflammatory mediators, lymphatic drainage and macrophage clearance. A: Fibroblast and vessel proliferation mark chronic conversion. B: Lymphocytes replacing neutrophils marks chronic conversion. C: Plasma cells mark chronic conversion. D: Architectural distortion results from scarring.

questions.stem: Which outcome of acute inflammation is correctly defined?

options.A: Fistula – a localized collection of pus in an organ
options.B: Abscess – an abnormal communication between two hollow organs
options.C: Scar – restoration of normal structure and function
options.D: Ulcer – excavation of a surface from necrosis and sloughing

questions.explanation: An ulcer is a local defect or excavation of a surface caused by necrosis and sloughing of inflamed necrotic tissue. A: That defines an abscess. B: That defines a fistula. C: A scar may distort structure or impair function. E: An effusion is fluid in a mesothelial-lined cavity.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Ulcer and other outcomes

questions.stem: Which statement about abscesses is correct?

options.A: They are diffuse exudates spreading along tissue planes
options.B: They are usually caused by viral infections
options.C: Their center contains viable, preserved neutrophils
options.D: They consist mainly of fibrin with few cells
options.E: They may be walled off and replaced by connective tissue

questions.explanation: An abscess is a localized collection of pus within a tissue, organ or confined space; it may become walled off and replaced by connective tissue. A: An abscess is localized. B: Pyogenic bacteria such as staphylococci are the usual cause. C: The center contains necrotic leukocytes and tissue cells; viable neutrophils form the rim. D: That describes fibrinous inflammation.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Purulent inflammation and abscess

questions.stem: Moving outward from the center of an abscess, which sequence is described?

options.A: Necrotic center → neutrophil rim → fibroblastic zone
options.B: Preserved neutrophils → necrotic cells → fibrous capsule
options.C: Fibroblastic proliferation → necrotic cells → preserved neutrophils
options.D: Necrotic cells → fibroblastic proliferation → rim of neutrophils
options.E: Granulation tissue → necrotic cells → rim of lymphocytes

questions.explanation: The center is a mass of necrotic leukocytes and tissue cells, surrounded by a rim of preserved neutrophils; outside, vascular congestion and parenchymal and fibroblastic proliferation indicate chronic inflammation and repair. B: Preserved neutrophils form the rim around the necrotic center. C: Fibroblastic proliferation is the outermost zone. D: Neutrophils lie between the center and the fibroblastic zone. E: Granulation tissue and a lymphocyte rim are not described.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Purulent inflammation and abscess

questions.stem: Which statement about serous inflammation is correct?

options.A: It is defined by deposition of fibrin
options.B: It is rich in neutrophils and liquefied necrotic debris
options.C: It is typical of meningeal inflammation
options.D: Its fluid comes from plasma or mesothelium
options.E: It is the classic pattern of appendicitis

questions.explanation: Serous inflammation is a relatively cell-poor, serum-like, protein-rich exudate; the fluid may come from plasma leakage or mesothelial-cell secretion. A: Fibrin defines fibrinous inflammation. B: That describes pus. C: The meninges are a typical fibrinous site. E: Appendicitis is suppurative.

questions.stem: Five days after a myocardial infarction, a patient has pericardial chest pain. Autopsy weeks later shows a shaggy eosinophilic meshwork on the pericardium. What allowed this exudate to form, unlike a serous one?

options.B: Mesothelial cells secreted fluid after irritation
options.C: Lymphatic drainage of the pericardium increased
options.E: Neutrophils released NETs that trapped proteins

questions.explanation: Fibrinous inflammation follows more severe injury: greater permeability lets large molecules such as fibrinogen pass, and local coagulation deposits fibrin, seen as an eosinophilic meshwork. A: Bacteria would cause purulent inflammation. B: Mesothelial secretion produces serous fluid. C: Increased drainage removes, not deposits, exudate. E: NETs are neutrophil fibrils, not the fibrin meshwork described.

questions.stem: A fibrinous exudate that is not removed undergoes organization. What does organization involve?

options.A: Fibrinolysis followed by clearance by macrophages
options.B: Ingrowth of fibroblasts and vessels, then scarring
options.C: Conversion of fibrin into pus by neutrophils
options.D: Formation of granulomas around the fibrin

questions.explanation: Fibrinous exudates may resolve by fibrinolysis and macrophage clearance; if not, they undergo organization, with ingrowth of fibroblasts and vessels that leads to scarring. A: That is resolution of the exudate, the alternative to organization. C: Pus is not described from fibrin. D: Granulomas are not described. E: Re-epithelialization is not described.

questions.stem: Which statement about purulent inflammation is correct?

options.A: It is cell-poor with sterile fluid
options.B: It mainly affects mesothelium-lined cavities as fibrin
options.C: Its classic example is a burn blister
options.E: It is also called serous inflammation

questions.explanation: Purulent (suppurative) inflammation produces pus. It is most often caused by bacteria that cause liquefactive necrosis (e.g., staphylococci), called pyogenic bacteria; acute appendicitis is a common example. A: That describes serous inflammation. B: That describes fibrinous inflammation. C: Blisters are serous. E: Purulent is also called suppurative.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Purulent inflammation and abscess

questions.stem: Ulceration requires which condition?

options.A: Deposition of fibrin in a body cavity
options.B: Seeding of pyogenic bacteria into deep tissue
options.E: Necrosis and inflammation on or near a surface

questions.explanation: An ulcer is a local defect produced by necrosis and sloughing of inflammatory necrotic tissue; it can occur only when necrosis and inflammation exist on or near a surface. A: That is fibrinous inflammation. B: That produces an abscess. C: That produces a blister (serous). D: Caseating granulomas are not required.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Ulcer and other outcomes

questions.stem: Which statement about the morphologic patterns is correct?

options.C: Serous effusions are rich in neutrophils
options.D: Peptic ulcers show both acute and chronic inflammation
options.E: Abscesses are the typical lesion of fibrinous pericarditis

questions.explanation: In peptic ulcers acute and chronic inflammation coexist: neutrophils and vascular dilation in the acute stage, scarring with lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells with chronicity. A: Fibrinous exudates may organize into scar. B: Blisters are serous. C: Serous fluid has few leukocytes. E: Pericardial exudates are fibrinous.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Ulcer and other outcomes

questions.stem: Restoration of injured tissue to normal structure after inflammation depends mainly on:

options.A: The number of neutrophils recruited and their life span
options.B: The amount of fibrin deposited and how fast it is cleared
options.C: Extent of destruction and regenerative capacity
options.D: The cytokines released and how long fever lasts
options.E: The size of the draining lymph nodes and lymph flow

questions.explanation: Restoration depends on the extent of tissue destruction and the regenerative capacity of the specific tissue. A: Neutrophil numbers do not determine regeneration. B: Fibrin clearance affects fibrinous exudates, not the general rule given. D: Cytokines and fever are systemic effects. E: Lymph flow clears edema but does not determine restoration.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Purpose and sequence

questions.stem: Which term describes leukocytes moving from the central blood flow toward the vessel wall?
questions.explanation: Margination is localization of leukocytes to the outer margin of the blood flow, adjacent to the endothelium. A: Pavementing is lining the endothelial surface. B: Rolling is loose selectin binding along the surface. C: Emigration is passage between endothelial cells into the tissue. E: Chemotaxis is movement toward the injury along a chemical gradient.

questions.stem: Engagement of leukocyte receptors by microbial products leads to "leukocyte activation". Which of the following is NOT one of its listed results?

options.B: Production of substances that destroy microbes

questions.explanation: Activation enhances phagocytosis, production of microbicidal substances and of amplifying mediators (arachidonic acid metabolites and cytokines). Antibodies are made by plasma cells. A: Enhanced phagocytosis is listed. B: Microbicidal substances are listed. D: Arachidonic acid metabolites are listed. E: Cytokines are listed.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Chemotaxis and leukocyte activation

questions.stem: Intracellular killing of phagocytosed microbes is described as:

options.A: Oxygen-dependent through NADPH oxidase, without other routes
options.E: Mediated by nitric oxide from the endothelium

questions.explanation: Intracellular killing in phagocytes uses oxygen-dependent and oxygen-independent mechanisms. A: Oxygen-independent mechanisms also exist. B: Complement acts at the cell surface. C: Antibodies act as opsonins outside the cell. E: Endothelial NO is not the intracellular mechanism described.

questions.stem: Which pair consists of the most important phagocytic cells?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils and monocytes–macrophages are the most important phagocytes. A: Eosinophils are not named as major phagocytes. B: Dendritic cells are not named here. C: Mast cells release histamine. D: Eosinophils and basophils are not the main phagocytes.

questions.stem: Neutrophilia is typical of which pair of conditions?
questions.explanation: Neutrophilia is caused by bacterial infections and other acute inflammation such as infarction. A: Viral infections cause lymphocytosis. B: Hay fever causes eosinophilia. C: These cause monocytosis. E: These cause eosinophilia.

questions.stem: Aspirin's anti-inflammatory action targets which enzyme, and which products fall?
questions.explanation: The cyclooxygenase pathway (COX-1, COX-2) yields thromboxanes and prostaglandins and is inhibited by aspirin. A: Phospholipase A2 is upstream and not the aspirin target. B: Lipoxygenase is not the aspirin target. C: Leukotrienes and HETE are lipoxygenase products. E: Thromboxanes and prostacyclin are COX products.

questions.stem: Prostaglandins (other than TxA2 and PGI2) are listed as causing:
questions.explanation: Prostaglandins induce vasodilation, pain and fever. A: Prostaglandins dilate vessels. B: Chemotaxis is LTB4 and HETE. C: Bronchoconstriction is LTC4, LTD4 and LTE4. D: Platelet aggregation is TxA2.

questions.stem: Which statement about lipoxins is correct?

options.A: They are lipoxygenase products that help resolve inflammation
options.B: They are COX products that cause pain and fever
options.C: They are lipoxygenase products that attract neutrophils strongly
options.D: They are lipoxygenase products causing bronchospasm
options.E: They are COX products that aggregate platelets

questions.explanation: Lipoxins come from the lipoxygenase pathway and generally help resolve inflammation, acting as anti-inflammatory mediators. B: Pain and fever come from prostaglandins. C: LTB4 attracts neutrophils. D: LTC4, LTD4 and LTE4 cause bronchoconstriction. E: TxA2 aggregates platelets.

questions.stem: Which set lists the antioxidant protections against oxygen-derived radicals?
questions.explanation: The antioxidant mechanisms named are superoxide dismutase, catalase (detoxifies H2O2) and glutathione peroxidase. B: NADPH oxidase generates ROS. C: α1-antitrypsin is an antiprotease. D: α2-macroglobulin is an antiprotease. E: Myeloperoxidase is a granule enzyme, not an antioxidant defense.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Leukocyte-mediated tissue injury

questions.stem: Lysosomal enzymes of neutrophils and monocytes reach the extracellular space:

options.A: After cell death and by leakage during phagocytosis
options.B: By IgE-triggered degranulation and after cell death
options.C: Through C5b-9 pores and by leakage from phagosomes
options.D: By the platelet release reaction and after cell death
options.E: Through transcytosis and by leakage from phagosomes

questions.explanation: Lysosomal enzymes may be released after cell death or by leakage during formation of phagocytic vacuoles. B: IgE-triggered degranulation is the mast cell mechanism. C: C5b-9 pores lyse target cells. D: The release reaction is a platelet event. E: Transcytosis is a VEGF permeability mechanism.

questions.stem: Neuropeptide-secreting nerve fibers are especially prominent in:
questions.explanation: Nerve fibers secreting neuropeptides are especially prominent in the lung and GI tract. B: The kidney is not named. C: The skin is not named. D: Liver and spleen are not named. E: The heart is not named.

questions.stem: Which is NOT listed among the systemic effects of inflammation caused by IL-1 and TNF?
questions.explanation: IL-1 and TNF cause fever, cachexia, leukocytosis and hepatic synthesis of acute-phase proteins. Lymphocytopenia is not listed. A: Fever is listed. B: Cachexia is listed. D: Leukocytosis is listed. E: Acute-phase proteins are listed.

questions.stem: An accumulation of fluid in a mesothelium-lined cavity is called:
questions.explanation: Fluid in a mesothelium-lined cavity is an effusion. B: Edema is interstitial fluid. C: Exudate describes protein-rich fluid, not its location. D: Transudate describes low-protein fluid, not its location. E: An abscess is a localized collection of pus.

questions.stem: Fibrinous exudates are characteristic of inflammation of:
questions.explanation: Fibrinous exudates are characteristic of the linings of body cavities: meninges, pericardium and pleura. B: Skin blisters are serous. C: Appendicitis is purulent. D: Skin and stomach are not named. E: Stomach and duodenum give peptic ulcers.

questions.stem: Pus is composed of:

options.B: Lymphocytes, plasma cells and edema fluid
options.E: Neutrophils, necrotic debris and edema fluid

questions.explanation: Pus is an exudate of neutrophils, liquefied debris of necrotic cells and edema fluid. A: Fibrin and red cells are not its components. B: Lymphocytes and plasma cells mark chronic inflammation. C: Giant cells belong to granulomas. D: Eosinophils are not a component.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Purulent inflammation and abscess

questions.stem: Besides mucosal surfaces, where does the doc say ulceration may occur?
questions.explanation: Ulceration requires necrosis and inflammation at or near a surface and may occur in mucosa or in ischemic lower-extremity tissues. A: Fluid in these cavities is an effusion. C: Deep localized pus is an abscess. D: Lymph nodes show lymphadenitis. E: The meninges show fibrinous exudates.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Ulcer and other outcomes

questions.stem: According to the doc, inflammation is a protective response intended to:

options.A: Eliminate the cause of injury and remove necrotic tissue
options.B: Repair tissue before the injurious agent has been removed
options.C: Limit blood flow so that infection cannot spread
options.D: Replace injured tissue by fibrosis from the start
options.E: Generate antibodies against the injurious agent

questions.explanation: Inflammation is a protective response intended to eliminate the initial cause of cell injury and remove necrotic cells and tissues resulting from the original insult. B: Repair (resolution) is the last step, after removal. C: Vasodilation increases blood flow. D: Fibrosis is a possible outcome, not the aim. E: Antibody production is not the definition given.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Purpose and sequence

questions.stem: A patient has a zone of necrotic myocardium. Where do the inflammatory changes develop?

options.A: Within the core of the necrotic tissue
options.B: Once bacteria have colonized the necrotic tissue
options.C: In distant organs through circulating cytokines
options.D: In viable tissue adjacent to the necrotic area
options.E: Throughout the whole organ at the same time

questions.explanation: Tissue death is a cause of inflammation, and inflammation occurs in viable tissue adjacent to necrotic areas. A: Dead tissue cannot mount the response. B: Infection is not required. C: Systemic effects exist, but the local reaction is next to the necrosis. E: The reaction is located at the margin of the necrosis.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Cardinal signs and causes

questions.stem: Which cardinal sign is attributed specifically to increased blood flow?
questions.explanation: The doc attributes rubor to vasodilation and calor (heat) to increased blood flow; the rapid review links redness and warmth to vasodilation and increased local flow. A: Rubor is attributed to vasodilation. B: Tumor is extravascular fluid accumulation. C: Dolor is tissue pressure plus mediators such as bradykinin. E: Functio laesa is loss of function.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Cardinal signs and causes

questions.stem: Which pair of mediators does the doc name as important in increased vascular permeability?
questions.explanation: Increased permeability lets protein-rich fluid leave vessels; histamine and kinins are important mediators. A: Lipoxins resolve inflammation; NO relaxes smooth muscle. B: TxA2 and PGI2 act mainly on vascular tone and platelets. C: These are antioxidant enzymes. D: These are acute-phase proteins.

questions.stem: Inflammation of draining lymph nodes is called:
questions.explanation: Inflammation of lymphatic vessels is lymphangitis; inflammation of draining lymph nodes is lymphadenitis. Nodes may become enlarged and tender. A: Lymphangitis is inflammation of the lymphatic vessels. B: Lymphedema is lymph accumulation, not inflammation. C: Lymphocytosis is increased blood lymphocytes. D: Not a term used for this.

questions.stem: Leukocytes lining up along the endothelial surface, before rolling, is called:
questions.explanation: Leukocytes move toward the wall (margination), line the endothelium (pavementing), roll, adhere firmly, and then cross (transmigration/diapedesis). A: Margination is moving from the central flow toward the wall. B: Rolling follows pavementing. D: Diapedesis is crossing the endothelium. E: Chemotaxis is directed movement along a chemical gradient.

questions.stem: P-selectin moves from its storage granules to the cell surface after stimulation by:
questions.explanation: P-selectin is stored in Weibel–Palade bodies and platelet α-granules and moves to the surface after stimulation by histamine or thrombin. A: IL-1 and TNF promote adhesion-molecule expression in general. B: C5a and LTB4 are chemotactic factors. D: These belong to the kinin system. E: These are opsonins.

questions.stem: Leukocyte integrins bind which endothelial molecules during firm adhesion?
questions.explanation: Firm adhesion is mediated by leukocyte integrins (LFA-1, MAC-1, VLA-4) binding endothelial immunoglobulin-family proteins ICAM-1/ICAM-2 and VCAM. A: Selectins mediate rolling. B: Sialyl-Lewis X is the leukocyte ligand of E- and P-selectin. D: PECAM-1 mediates transmigration. E: Weibel–Palade bodies store P-selectin.

questions.stem: Chemotaxis is best defined as:

options.A: Random leukocyte movement within the central bloodstream
options.C: Directed leukocyte movement along a chemical gradient
options.D: Coating of particles to aid phagocytosis
options.E: Passage of leukocytes between endothelial cells

questions.explanation: Chemotaxis is directed leukocyte movement along a chemical gradient; neutrophil chemoattractants include bacterial products, C5a, LTB4, HETE and kallikrein. A: Chemotaxis is directed, not random. B: That is rolling. D: That is opsonization. E: That is transmigration.

questions.stem: Which group consists entirely of neutrophil chemoattractants named in the doc?
questions.explanation: The neutrophil chemoattractants named are bacterial products, C5a, LTB4, HETE and kallikrein. B: LTC4 is a constrictor, not a chemoattractant. C: C3b is an opsonin. D: Prostacyclin is a vasodilator. E: C3a and serotonin are not in the list.

questions.stem: Which is the correct order of events in phagocytosis?
questions.explanation: Phagocytosis involves recognition and attachment, engulfment by pseudopodia, formation of a phagosome, fusion with lysosomes into a phagolysosome, then killing and degradation. A: Attachment comes before engulfment. B: The phagolysosome forms last. C: A phagosome cannot form before attachment. E: The phagosome forms from the pseudopod engulfment.

questions.stem: How does opsonization help phagocytosis?

options.A: It lyses the particle before it is engulfed
options.B: It attracts phagocytes toward the particle along a gradient
options.C: It fuses the phagosome with lysosomes
options.D: It coats the particle, improving phagocyte attachment

questions.explanation: Opsonization coats a particle to facilitate phagocytosis, improving phagocyte attachment and uptake; important opsonins are IgG and C3b. A: Lysis is the MAC's role. B: That is chemotaxis. C: Fusion is a later step inside the cell. E: ROS come from NADPH oxidase.

questions.stem: During which period do neutrophils predominate in an acute inflammatory focus?
questions.explanation: Neutrophils predominate during the first 24 hours; after about 2–3 days monocytes/macrophages become more prominent. B: Monocytes/macrophages take over after 2–3 days. C: Neutrophils come before macrophages. D: Chronic inflammation features lymphocytes, plasma cells and macrophages. E: Neutrophils undergo apoptosis in resolution.

questions.stem: A shepherd drinks raw goat milk and develops prolonged fever. His blood shows increased monocytes. Which group lists infections that cause the same change?
questions.explanation: Monocytosis can occur in tuberculosis, brucellosis (the likely cause here), typhus and salmonellosis. A: Mumps, rubella and influenza are viral, which makes lymphocytes prominent. B: Allergy and parasites make eosinophils prominent. D: Pyogenic bacteria cause neutrophilia. E: CML causes basophilia.

questions.stem: Basophilia may occur in:
questions.explanation: Mast cells and basophils are histamine sources; basophilia may occur in CML and other myeloproliferative diseases. A: Parasites make eosinophils prominent. B: Bacterial infection causes neutrophilia. C: Viral infections make lymphocytes prominent. D: Infarction causes neutrophilia.

questions.stem: Which statement about nitric oxide is correct?

options.A: It is a platelet product causing arteriolar vasoconstriction
options.B: It is a leukotriene that increases permeability
options.C: It is an antiprotease that blocks elastase
options.D: It is made by NADPH oxidase in neutrophils
options.E: It is endothelial and relaxes vascular smooth muscle

questions.explanation: NO is produced by endothelial cells, relaxes vascular smooth muscle, inhibits platelet aggregation and contributes to microbial killing. A: NO is not a platelet product and dilates vessels. B: Leukotrienes are lipoxygenase products. C: α1-antitrypsin blocks elastase. D: NADPH oxidase generates ROS.

questions.stem: Reactive oxygen species in inflammation are generated through:
questions.explanation: ROS are generated through the NADPH oxidase pathway in activated neutrophils and macrophages. A: COX makes prostaglandins and thromboxanes. B: SOD is an antioxidant defense, not an ROS source. C: Lipoxygenase makes leukotrienes and lipoxins. E: Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid.

questions.stem: Which complement product lyses susceptible cells?
questions.explanation: C5b–9 forms the membrane attack complex, which lyses susceptible cells. A: C5a is an anaphylatoxin and chemotactic factor. B: C3b is an opsonin. D: C3a is an anaphylatoxin. E: C4b is not described in the doc.

questions.stem: All of the following are acute-phase proteins listed in the doc EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The liver increases CRP, serum amyloid-associated protein, complement components, fibrinogen, prothrombin, α1-antitrypsin, α2-macroglobulin, ferritin and ceruloplasmin. Histamine is a vasoactive amine. A: SAA protein is listed. B: Prothrombin is listed. C: Complement components are listed. D: α2-macroglobulin is listed.

questions.stem: Which statement about resolution is correct?

options.B: Neutrophils are replaced by plasma cells
options.D: Pus is walled off by connective tissue
options.E: The surface epithelium necroses and sloughs

questions.explanation: In resolution, mediators decay or are degraded, permeability normalizes, recruitment ceases, neutrophils undergo apoptosis, anti-inflammatory mediators are produced, and lymphatics and macrophages clear fluid and debris. A: That is repair by scarring or chronic inflammation. B: That is conversion to chronic inflammation. D: That is an abscess. E: That is ulceration.

questions.stem: Which outcome is an abnormal communication between two organs, or between an organ and a surface?
questions.explanation: A fistula is an abnormal communication between two organs or between an organ and a surface. A: An ulcer is a surface excavation. C: An abscess is a localized collection of pus. D: A scar results from tissue destruction. E: An effusion is fluid in a mesothelial-lined cavity.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Ulcer and other outcomes

questions.stem: Extensive organization of a fibrinous pericardial exudate can lead to:

options.A: Resolution with complete restoration of the pericardium
options.B: A purulent abscess in the pericardial cavity
options.C: Obliteration of the space and restricted cardiac function

questions.explanation: If fibrin persists, organization (ingrowth of fibroblasts and vessels) can produce scar; extensive organization in the pericardial cavity may obliterate the space and restrict cardiac function. A: Resolution requires fibrin to be degraded and cleared. B: Abscesses need pyogenic bacteria. D: A serous effusion is a different, cell-poor exudate. E: Ulcers form at mucosal or ischemic surfaces.

questions.stem: Acute appendicitis is the doc's common example of:
questions.explanation: Acute appendicitis is a common example of suppurative (purulent) inflammation. A: Serous inflammation is cell-poor, as in blisters. C: Fibrinous inflammation affects the meninges, pericardium and pleura. D: Appendicitis here is acute. E: Peptic ulcer is the ulcer example.

questions.stem: In the doc's rapid review, bronchoconstriction is matched with:
questions.explanation: The integration lists bronchoconstriction → LTC4/LTD4/LTE4 and PAF. A: These are neutrophil chemoattractants. B: These are matched with pain. C: These are matched with fever and the acute-phase response. D: Histamine and kinins are permeability mediators; they are not matched with bronchoconstriction.

questions.stem: In the doc's rapid review, pain (dolor) is matched with:
questions.explanation: Pain is matched with bradykinin, prostaglandins and increased tissue pressure. A: These are matched with redness and warmth. B: These are matched with fever and the acute-phase response. D: These mediate rolling and adhesion. E: These are matched with bronchoconstriction.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Rapid review table

questions.stem: Which statement about the origin of mediators is correct?

options.A: Endogenous mediators are often microbial products
options.B: Exogenous mediators are often microbial products
options.D: Bradykinin is an exogenous, cell-derived mediator
options.E: Histamine is an exogenous, plasma-derived mediator

questions.explanation: Exogenous mediators are often microbial products; endogenous mediators may be cell-derived or plasma-protein-derived. A: Endogenous mediators come from the host. C: Plasma-protein-derived mediators are endogenous. D: Bradykinin is endogenous and plasma-protein-derived. E: Histamine is endogenous and cell-derived.

questions.stem: Which statement about histamine is correct?

options.A: It is released from mast cells, basophils and platelets
options.B: It is released from neutrophils and endothelial cells
options.C: It acts mainly by contracting arteriolar smooth muscle
options.D: It is produced by phospholipase A2 from membranes
options.E: It is generated from kininogen by kallikrein

questions.explanation: Histamine causes vasodilation and increased permeability, especially through endothelial contraction in postcapillary venules, and is released from mast cells, basophils and platelets. B: Neutrophils and endothelium are not listed sources. C: It acts through endothelial contraction in postcapillary venules. D: Phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid. E: That describes bradykinin.

questions.stem: Which cells produce IL-1 and TNF, according to the doc?
questions.explanation: IL-1 and TNF are produced by macrophages and other cells; they drive acute-phase and systemic responses, adhesion molecules, neutrophil degranulation and reduced thromboresistance. A: Platelets are not the source named. B: Hepatocytes make acute-phase proteins in response. C: Plasma cells make antibodies. E: Mast cells are not the source named.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: PAF, cytokines and chemokines

questions.stem: The doc attributes rubor (redness) to:
questions.explanation: Rubor results from vasodilation; calor from increased blood flow; tumor from extravascular fluid; dolor from tissue pressure and mediators such as bradykinin. A: Tissue pressure contributes to dolor. C: Extravascular fluid causes tumor. D: Loss of function is functio laesa. E: Fibrin deposition defines fibrinous inflammation.
questions.source: Acute Inflammation doc: Cardinal signs and causes

questions.stem: Which statement about the onset of chronic inflammation is correct?

options.A: It can occur de novo, with no acute phase
options.B: It requires a failed acute reaction first
options.C: It cannot follow repeated bouts of acute inflammation
options.E: It begins when neutrophils undergo apoptosis

questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation can follow persistent or recurrent injury or an ineffective response, and it can also occur de novo. B: It can occur de novo. C: Repeated acute bouts are a listed cause. D: Infection is one of several etiologies. E: Neutrophil apoptosis is part of resolution.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes chronic nonspecific inflammation from acute inflammation?

options.E: Exudation of protein-rich fluid into tissue

questions.explanation: Chronic nonspecific inflammation shows mononuclear cells, tissue destruction with concomitant repair (new vessels, fibroblasts, fibrosis), and architectural distortion. B: Increased permeability is a hallmark of acute inflammation. C: Leukocyte infiltration occurs in both. D: Mediators act in both. E: Exudation is a hallmark of acute inflammation.

questions.stem: In chronic inflammation, which statement about the macrophage–lymphocyte interaction is correct?

options.B: Macrophages inhibit lymphocytes to limit the response
options.C: Plasma cells arise from activated T lymphocytes in the tissue
options.D: Monocytes enter the tissue without chemotactic signals
options.E: Neutrophils present antigen to B lymphocytes

questions.explanation: Monocytes are recruited by chemotactic factors; macrophage cytokines activate lymphocytes, which in turn release cytokines that activate macrophages; B cells activated by macrophage-presented antigen become plasma cells. B: Macrophages activate lymphocytes. C: Plasma cells come from B cells. D: Chemotactic factors recruit monocytes. E: Macrophages present the antigen.

questions.stem: Which etiology of chronic inflammation is matched with the example given in the notes?
questions.explanation: Chronic cholecystitis due to gallstones is the example of repeated bouts of acute inflammation. A: Gallstone cholecystitis is the repeated-bouts example. B: Asthma is an allergic example. D: Sarcoidosis is granulomatous with unknown cause. E: Peptic ulcer is not given as the toxic example.

questions.stem: Which statement about granulomas is correct?

options.A: Giant cells form from fusion of epithelioid macrophages
options.B: Epithelioid cells are modified surface epithelial cells
options.C: Granulomas are surrounded by a rim of neutrophils
options.D: Giant cells form from fusion of lymphocytes
options.E: Granulomas are made mainly of plasma cells

questions.explanation: Granulomas are nodular collections of epithelioid cells (specialized macrophages) with a lymphocyte rim; giant cells form by fusion of macrophages. B: Epithelioid cells are specialized macrophages. C: The rim is lymphocytes. D: Giant cells come from macrophages. E: Plasma cells are not the main cells.

questions.stem: Which statement about giant cells is correct?

options.A: Langhans giant cells are specific for tuberculosis
options.B: Foreign-body giant cells have nuclei scattered in the cytoplasm
options.C: Foreign-body giant cells have a peripheral horseshoe of nuclei
options.D: Megakaryocytes are pathologic giant cells of granulomas
options.E: Giant cells in herpes come from macrophage fusion

questions.explanation: Foreign-body giant cells have scattered nuclei; Langhans cells have peripheral horseshoe nuclei and are characteristic of, but not specific for, TB. A: Langhans cells are not TB-specific. C: The horseshoe pattern belongs to Langhans cells. D: The notes list megakaryocytes and osteoclasts as normal multinucleated cells. E: Herpes giant cells are infected epithelial cells.

questions.stem: A lymph node biopsy from a patient with fever and cough shows granulomas with central cheese-like necrosis. Which statement about this necrosis is correct?

options.A: It is liquefactive necrosis caused by pyogenic staphylococci
options.B: It is typical of the non-caseating granulomas of sarcoidosis
options.C: It results from T cells killing mycobacteria-laden macrophages
options.D: It results from neutrophil elastase digesting the node
options.E: It is coagulative necrosis from vascular occlusion

questions.explanation: Caseating granulomas are characteristic of TB; caseous necrosis results from T-cell killing of mycobacteria-laden macrophages and from free-radical injury. A: Liquefactive necrosis by pyogenic bacteria produces abscesses. B: Sarcoidosis granulomas are non-caseating. D: Elastase injury is not the mechanism described. E: Ischemic necrosis is not the mechanism in TB.

questions.stem: How does granuloma formation begin?

options.A: Neutrophils present antigen to CD8+ T cells
options.B: B cells present antigen to macrophages
options.C: Macrophages present antigen to CD4+ T cells
options.D: CD8+ T cells kill macrophages, releasing IFN-γ
options.E: Epithelioid cells release IL-1 to recruit T cells

questions.explanation: Poorly digestible antigen is presented by macrophages to CD4+ T cells; T-cell activation releases cytokines (especially IFN-γ) that transform macrophages into epithelioid and giant cells. A: Neutrophils are not the presenting cells. B: Macrophages present to T cells. D: The T cells involved are CD4+, and IFN-γ is released by activated T cells. E: Epithelioid cells are the result, not the starting signal.

questions.stem: Which statement about the etiology of granulomatous inflammation is correct?

options.A: Caseating granulomas are typical of autoimmune diseases
options.B: Sarcoidosis is the prototype of non-caseating granulomas
options.C: Crohn disease is listed as an infectious cause
options.D: Reactions to tumors produce abscesses rather than granulomas
options.E: Cat-scratch disease is caused by a fungus

questions.explanation: Non-caseating granulomas occur in several chronic inflammatory and autoimmune diseases; the prototype is sarcoidosis. A: Autoimmune diseases give non-caseating granulomas. C: Crohn disease is listed under unknown or autoimmune causes. D: Reaction to tumors is a listed cause. E: Cat-scratch disease is caused by a bacterium.

questions.stem: All of the following are listed as infectious causes of granulomatous inflammation EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Infectious causes listed are mycobacteria (M. tuberculosis, M. leprae), fungi (Blastomyces, Histoplasma, Coccidioides), T. pallidum and the cat-scratch bacterium. Staphylococci cause purulent inflammation and abscesses. A: M. leprae is listed. C: Coccidioides is listed. D: T. pallidum is listed. E: Blastomyces is listed.

questions.stem: Which statement about multinucleated cells is correct?

options.A: They are restricted to granulomatous lesions
options.C: They may be seen in virus-infected epithelial cells
options.E: They do not occur in tumors or in viral infections

questions.explanation: Multinucleated giant cells also occur in virus-infected cells (epithelial cells in herpes) and in some tumors; osteoclasts are normal multinucleated cells. A: They also occur outside granulomas. B: Osteoclasts are normal. D: Neutrophils are not multinucleated. E: Some tumors contain them.

questions.stem: When eosinophils are prominent in chronic inflammation, which etiology is most likely?
questions.explanation: When chronic inflammation is due to parasites or allergic disorders, eosinophils are involved and seen at the site. A: Gallstone cholecystitis shows mononuclear cells. B: Foreign bodies cause granulomas with giant cells. D: Mycobacteria cause caseating granulomas. E: Pyogenic bacteria cause purulent inflammation.

questions.stem: Chronic inflammation occurs in which two major patterns?
questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation occurs as chronic nonspecific inflammation and granulomatous inflammation. A: These are acute patterns. B: These are acute outcomes and patterns. C: These are the two granuloma types. E: Purulent is an acute pattern.

questions.stem: In chronic inflammation, antibody-producing plasma cells arise from:

options.A: T lymphocytes activated by macrophage cytokines
options.C: B lymphocytes activated by neutrophil-presented antigen
options.D: B lymphocytes activated by macrophage-presented antigen

questions.explanation: B lymphocyte activation by macrophage-presented antigen forms antibody-producing plasma cells. A: T cells do not become plasma cells. B: Monocytes become macrophages. C: Macrophages, not neutrophils, present the antigen. E: Epithelioid cells are modified macrophages.

questions.stem: Whenever a granuloma is found in a biopsy, which disease should always be excluded?
questions.explanation: The notes state that in the presence of a granuloma, tuberculosis should always be excluded. A: Sarcoidosis is not the disease named for exclusion. B: Histoplasmosis is a cause, but TB is the one named. C: Crohn disease is a cause, but TB is the one named. D: Syphilis is a cause, but TB is the one named.

questions.stem: Which cytokine transforms monocytes and macrophages into epithelioid and giant cells?
questions.explanation: Activated CD4+ T cells release cytokines, especially IFN-γ, which transform monocytes and macrophages into epithelioid and giant cells. A: TNF is not the cytokine named for this transformation. C: IL-1 drives systemic acute-phase effects. D: IL-8 is a neutrophil chemokine. E: Histamine is a vasoactive amine.

questions.stem: Which group lists only the fungi named as causes of granulomatous inflammation?
questions.explanation: The fungi listed are Blastomyces dermatitidis, Histoplasma capsulatum and Coccidioides immitis. A: Treponema is a bacterium. C: Candida is not in the list. D: Aspergillus is not in the list. E: M. leprae is a mycobacterium.

questions.stem: Which of the following is listed as a normal multinucleated cell?
questions.explanation: The notes name megakaryocytes and osteoclasts as normal multinucleated cells. (Standard sources describe megakaryocytes as polyploid with a single multilobed nucleus.) A: Plasma cells have one nucleus. B: Epithelioid cells have one nucleus but can fuse into giant cells. C: Neutrophils have one multilobed nucleus. E: Monocytes have one indented nucleus.

questions.stem: A granuloma contains giant cells whose nuclei form a horseshoe around the periphery. Which statement is correct?

options.A: These are foreign-body cells, specific for retained sutures
options.B: These are Langhans cells, specific for tuberculosis
options.C: These are foreign-body cells, formed from lymphocytes
options.D: These are virus-infected epithelial cells of herpes
options.E: These are Langhans cells, characteristic but not specific for TB

questions.explanation: Langhans giant cells have nuclei in a horseshoe at the periphery and are characteristic of, but not specific for, tuberculous granulomas. A: Foreign-body giant cells have scattered nuclei. B: Langhans cells are not specific for TB. C: Giant cells come from epithelioid macrophages, and foreign-body cells have scattered nuclei. D: Herpes giant cells are infected epithelial cells, not granuloma cells.

questions.stem: Which statement about the causes of granulomatous inflammation is correct?

options.A: Cat-scratch disease is caused by a bacterium
options.B: Crohn disease is listed as an infectious cause
options.C: Mycobacterium leprae is listed as a fungus
options.D: Treponema pallidum is listed as a fungus
options.E: Tumors are not listed as a cause

questions.explanation: Infectious causes are mycobacteria (M. tuberculosis, M. leprae), fungi (Blastomyces, Histoplasma, Coccidioides), Treponema pallidum and the bacterium of cat-scratch disease; Crohn disease and sarcoidosis are unknown/autoimmune causes; reaction to tumors is also listed. B: Crohn disease is under unknown or autoimmune causes. C: M. leprae is a mycobacterium. D: T. pallidum is the bacterium of syphilis. E: Reaction to tumors is listed.

questions.stem: Which pairing of granulomatous cause and its category is correct?

options.D: Retained surgical suture – reaction to tumor

questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis and Crohn disease are listed as unknown or autoimmune causes. A: T. pallidum is a bacterium. B: Coccidioides is a fungus. C: Sarcoidosis is unknown or autoimmune. D: Retained material belongs to the foreign-body category.

questions.stem: Which etiology of chronic nonspecific inflammation is listed?

options.A: A single brief thermal burn of the skin
options.B: Rapid elimination of a pyogenic bacterium
options.C: Spontaneous neutrophil apoptosis at the site
options.E: Prolonged exposure to a nondegradable toxin

questions.explanation: Etiologies are persistent infections, repeated bouts of acute inflammation, autoimmune diseases, allergic diseases and prolonged exposure to toxic (nondegradable) agents. A: A single brief injury usually resolves. B: Elimination of the agent leads to resolution. C: Neutrophil apoptosis is part of resolution. D: Transient histamine release is an acute event.

questions.stem: Non-caseating granulomas are mainly encountered in:

options.B: Pyogenic bacterial abscesses of the skin
options.C: Acute viral infections of the skin

questions.explanation: Non-caseating (epithelioid) granulomas are encountered in several chronic inflammatory diseases, especially autoimmune ones; the prototype is sarcoidosis. Caseating granulomas are typical of TB. A: TB typically gives caseating granulomas. B: Abscesses are purulent. C: Acute viral infections give lymphocytic inflammation. E: Fibrinous pericarditis is a fibrinous exudate.

questions.stem: Chronic inflammation develops when:

options.A: The agent is eliminated within hours
options.B: Neutrophils undergo apoptosis at the site
options.E: The agent persists or cannot be degraded

questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation occurs when the injury is persistent or recurrent, or when the reaction cannot completely degrade the agent (bacteria, tissue debris, foreign bodies). A: Rapid elimination leads to resolution. B: Neutrophil apoptosis is part of resolution. C: Lymphatic drainage is part of resolution. D: Mediator decay is part of resolution.

questions.stem: Besides infectious agents and unknown or autoimmune causes, granulomas also arise from:

options.D: Foreign bodies and reactions to tumors

questions.explanation: The four etiology groups are infectious agents, foreign bodies, unknown or autoimmune causes (sarcoidosis, Crohn disease), and reactions to tumors. A: These are not listed granuloma causes. B: Infarction causes acute inflammation. C: Burns cause serous blisters. E: These relate to eosinophils, not granulomas.

lectures.title: Intro to Biochemistry and Cell Structure

questions.stem: A child with CFTR ΔF508 has no chloride channel at the apical membrane of airway cells, although the mutant protein can still conduct chloride. What happens to the mutant protein?

options.A: It lacks mannose-6-phosphate and is secreted
options.B: It is retained in the ER and degraded (ERAD)
options.C: It is never translated on ER-bound ribosomes
options.D: It is imported into peroxisomes by an SKL signal
options.E: It is retrieved from the Golgi by a KDEL signal

questions.explanation: ΔF508 CFTR is misfolded but functional; ER quality control retains it and degrades it (ERAD), so it never reaches the apical membrane. A: Missing M6P with secretion of the enzymes is I-cell disease. C: CFTR is a membrane protein, made on ER-bound ribosomes. D: SKL targets cytosolic proteins to peroxisomes. E: KDEL retrieval applies to ER-resident proteins, not CFTR.
questions.source: Intro to Biochemistry and Cell Structure, slide 23

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy, developmentally normal until age 6, has progressive loss of vision, hearing and motor skills, with adrenal insufficiency. Plasma very-long-chain fatty acids are elevated. What is the primary defect?
questions.explanation: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy: ABCD1 mutation impairs peroxisomal oxidation of VLCFAs, which accumulate in the nervous system and adrenals; onset at 5–10 years. A: Biogenesis defects (Zellweger) present in infancy and are fatal in the first year. B: Mistargeting of lysosomal enzymes is I-cell disease. C: mtDNA disorders are maternally inherited and don't raise VLCFAs. D: CPT-I carries long-chain, not very-long-chain, fatty acids and causes hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
questions.source: Intro to Biochemistry and Cell Structure, slides 32–34

questions.stem: A mitochondrial myopathy affects a mother and all her children with very different severity. Which statement best explains this pattern?

options.B: Autosomal dominant inheritance with incomplete penetrance
options.D: Mutation in a nuclear gene encoding a mitochondrial protein

questions.explanation: mtDNA comes from the oocyte; differing proportions of mutant mtDNA (heteroplasmy) cause variable severity. B: Would allow paternal transmission. C: Lyonization applies to X-linked genes. D: Nuclear-encoded defects follow Mendelian inheritance. E: Imprinting involves parent-specific gene silencing, not mtDNA.
questions.source: Intro to Biochemistry and Cell Structure, slide 27

questions.stem: A 2-month-old has hypotonia, seizures, dysmorphic features and an enlarged liver. Plasma very-long-chain fatty acids and phytanic acid are elevated, and plasmalogens are low. What is the underlying defect?
questions.explanation: Zellweger syndrome: without functional peroxisomes, VLCFA and phytanic acid oxidation, plasmalogen and bile acid synthesis all fail; fatal in the first year. A: X-ALD affects VLCFA transport only and starts at 5–10 years. B: Refsum disease raises phytanic acid alone, with onset in childhood or adolescence. C: Acid α-glucosidase deficiency is Pompe disease (lysosomal glycogen). D: This is I-cell disease (lysosomal enzyme mistargeting).
questions.source: Intro to Biochemistry and Cell Structure, slides 32, 35

questions.stem: A patient receiving paclitaxel develops neutropenia. How does paclitaxel arrest dividing cells?
questions.explanation: Taxanes stabilize microtubules, freezing the mitotic spindle. A: Blocking polymerization is vincristine/vinblastine (and colchicine). C: Actin isn't the target. D: Dynein isn't directly inhibited. E: Intermediate filaments aren't targeted.

questions.stem: A protein is made with an N-terminal hydrophobic signal sequence and a KDEL sequence near its C-terminus. Where will it finally reside?
questions.explanation: The signal sequence brings it into the ER on ER-bound ribosomes; KDEL keeps it in the ER or returns it from the Golgi. A: Lysosomal proteins need mannose-6-phosphate. B: Peroxisomal proteins carry SKL and are made on free ribosomes. C: Secreted proteins also start with a signal sequence, but KDEL retains this one. E: Nuclear proteins use basic NLS sequences and are made on free ribosomes.

questions.stem: A 14-month-old boy has coarse facial features, restricted joint movement, and developmental delay. Plasma levels of multiple lysosomal hydrolases are markedly elevated. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: I-cell disease: no mannose-6-phosphate tagging in the Golgi, so lysosomal enzymes are secreted into plasma. A: Tay-Sachs. B: Gaucher. D: Hurler. E: Pompe. None of these raise plasma levels of multiple hydrolases.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has eczema, recurrent otitis media, and bloody diarrhea. Platelets are low and small. His maternal uncle had similar problems. Which cellular process is defective?
questions.explanation: Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome (X-linked, WAS protein) disrupts actin organization in blood cells: eczema, infections, thrombocytopenia with small platelets. A: Microtubule defects don't give this triad. B: Dynein defects cause Kartagener syndrome. C: Keratin defects cause epidermolysis bullosa simplex. E: Mistargeting causes I-cell disease.

questions.stem: A lab uses fluorescent annexin V to identify apoptotic cells in culture. What does annexin V binding detect?

options.A: Phosphatidylcholine moved to the inner leaflet
options.C: Phosphatidylserine exposed on the outer leaflet

questions.explanation: PS is normally kept in the inner leaflet by ATP-dependent flippases; its exposure on the outer leaflet is the "eat-me" signal of apoptotic cells, detected with annexin V. A: PC is normally in the outer leaflet; its position isn't the marker. B: Raft cholesterol isn't what annexin V binds. D: Phospholipase C (e.g., C. perfringens alpha toxin) lyses membranes; it isn't an apoptosis marker. E: PI signaling happens on the inner leaflet.

questions.stem: How does cholesterol affect the fluidity of the plasma membrane?

options.A: Less fluid at body temperature; prevents freezing at low temperature
options.B: More fluid at body temperature; tighter packing at low temperature
options.E: No effect on fluidity; it only forms lipid rafts

questions.explanation: Cholesterol is a fluidity buffer: at body temperature it restricts tail movement (less fluid, less permeable), and at low temperature it prevents tight packing. B: That reverses both effects. C: Cis-unsaturated tails and ethanol increase fluidity; cholesterol doesn't. D: At low temperature it keeps the membrane from freezing. E: Rafts are one role, but cholesterol also buffers fluidity.

questions.stem: Which amino acid is most likely to act as a proton donor/acceptor in an enzyme active site at physiological pH?
questions.explanation: Histidine's imidazole pKa (~6) lets it switch between protonated and unprotonated states at pH 7.4. B: Lysine (pKa ~10.5) stays protonated. C: Arginine (pKa ~12.5) is always positive. D: Leucine is nonpolar. E: Glycine has no ionizable side chain.

questions.stem: Proline and glycine both destabilize an α helix, but for different reasons. Why does glycine do so?

options.A: Its rigid ring introduces a kink
options.B: Its bulky side chain clashes with neighbors
options.C: Its charge opposes the helix dipole

questions.explanation: Glycine's side chain is only a hydrogen, so it is unusually flexible and coiling it into a helix is unfavorable. A: The rigid ring and kink describe proline, the helix breaker. B: Glycine has the smallest side chain. C: Glycine's side chain is uncharged. D: Cysteine forms disulfides.

questions.stem: A lab estimates protein concentration in a sample by measuring absorbance at 280 nm. Which residues mainly produce this signal?
questions.explanation: Trp and Tyr absorb strongly at 280 nm. A: Phe absorbs weakly (~257 nm) and leucine not at all. B: Sulfur residues aren't the basis. C: Basic residues don't absorb at 280 nm. E: Neither absorbs at 280 nm.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes the disease-causing prion protein (PrPSc) from normal PrPC?
questions.explanation: PrPSc has the same sequence as PrPC but a β-sheet-rich, insoluble, protease-resistant conformation that templates conversion of PrPC. A, D: The sequence is identical. B: This describes normal PrPC. E: PrPSc is refolded, not unstructured.

questions.stem: Which chaperone binds exposed hydrophobic patches on a nascent polypeptide, keeping it unfolded until synthesis is complete?
questions.explanation: Hsp70 (with Hsp40) holds nascent chains unfolded and prevents aggregation until synthesis is complete. B: The proteasome degrades proteins. C: Ubiquitin tags misfolded proteins for degradation. D: SRP targets ribosomes to the ER. E: Chaperonins form a barrel-shaped protected chamber in which the protein folds.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman has rapidly progressive dementia and myoclonus over 5 months; MRI shows cortical diffusion restriction. At autopsy, the brain shows spongiform change. What is the pathogenic mechanism?

options.B: Trinucleotide repeat expansion in a nuclear gene
options.D: Misfolded protein that converts normal protein to its β-sheet form

questions.explanation: Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease: PrPSc templates PrPC conversion to a β-sheet, protease-resistant form. A: Tau tangles are Alzheimer disease. B: Repeat expansion is Huntington disease. C: Lewy bodies are Parkinson disease. E: JC virus in oligodendrocytes causes PML.

questions.stem: A patient with Z-variant α1-antitrypsin develops cirrhosis. Which mechanism best explains the liver damage?

options.A: Loss of function: low plasma levels leave the liver unprotected
options.C: Toxic gain of function: polymers accumulate in hepatocytes
options.E: ER retention and ERAD of a protein that stays soluble

questions.explanation: Z-variant α1-antitrypsin misfolds and polymerizes in hepatocytes: a toxic gain of function that damages the liver, while its absence from plasma causes emphysema. A: Low plasma levels explain the lung disease, not the liver disease. B: Templated conversion is specific to prions. D: Missing M6P is I-cell disease. E: Retention and degradation without aggregation is ΔF508 CFTR (loss of function).

questions.stem: A patient's missense variant gives a high-confidence AlphaFold model with no visible change in the overall fold. What is the best conclusion?

options.A: It is benign, because the fold is preserved
options.B: It cannot be called benign on this basis
options.C: It is pathogenic, because AlphaFold models are static
options.D: It must lie in an intrinsically disordered region
options.E: The model is invalid for a single protein

questions.explanation: AlphaFold can't reliably predict how a point mutation affects stability or function; a variant can abolish catalysis, binding or trafficking without changing the fold, so conservation and functional data are still needed. A: A preserved fold doesn't mean preserved function. C: Being static is a limitation, not evidence of pathogenicity. D: Disordered regions are where AlphaFold is weak, so a high-confidence model argues against this. E: Single proteins are what AlphaFold predicts best.

questions.stem: In the presence of an inhibitor, an enzyme's Lineweaver–Burk plot shows the same y-intercept but an x-intercept closer to zero. What type of inhibitor is it?
questions.explanation: Same y-intercept = unchanged Vmax; x-intercept (−1/Km) closer to zero = increased Km → competitive. A: Non-competitive raises the y-intercept (↓Vmax) with the same x-intercept. C: Uncompetitive gives parallel lines (both change). D: Irreversible inhibition lowers Vmax. E: An activator wouldn't raise Km.

questions.stem: Blood glucose is ~5 mM between meals. Hexokinase has a Km for glucose of ~0.05 mM and glucokinase ~6 mM. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Glucokinase works near Vmax between meals
options.B: Both work at about half Vmax
options.C: Hexokinase has lower affinity for glucose
options.D: Glucokinase is mainly found in erythrocytes
options.E: Hexokinase works near Vmax between meals

questions.explanation: With [S] ≫ Km (5 vs 0.05 mM), hexokinase is saturated. A: Glucokinase, at [S] below its Km, runs well below Vmax and speeds up as glucose rises after meals. B: Only glucokinase is near half Vmax. C: Hexokinase has the lower Km, so higher affinity. D: Glucokinase is hepatic; RBCs use hexokinase.

questions.stem: Which statement about enzymes as catalysts is correct?

options.C: They lower the activation energy without changing equilibrium
options.D: They are consumed in the reaction
options.E: Their active sites are most complementary to the substrate's ground state

questions.explanation: Enzymes lower activation energy; equilibrium and ΔG are unchanged and the enzyme is regenerated. A: ΔG is unaffected. B: Equilibrium is unaffected. D: Enzymes aren't consumed. E: Active sites best fit the transition state.

questions.stem: An inhibitor binds only to the enzyme–substrate complex. How do apparent Km and Vmax change?
questions.explanation: Uncompetitive inhibition lowers both Vmax and apparent Km (binding ES pulls the equilibrium toward ES). B: That's competitive. C: That's pure non-competitive. D: Inhibitors don't raise Vmax. E: Binding ES necessarily changes kinetics.

questions.stem: A regulatory enzyme gives a sigmoidal velocity vs [S] curve and is inhibited by the final product of its pathway. Which terms best describe it?
questions.explanation: Sigmoidal kinetics = allosteric (usually multisubunit) enzyme; end-product inhibition = feedback inhibition. A: Michaelis–Menten enzymes give hyperbolic curves. C: Zymogens are inactive precursors. D: Isozymes are different proteins catalyzing the same reaction. E: Allosteric enzymes are usually multimeric.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man of East Asian descent develops facial flushing, tachycardia, and nausea after half a glass of wine. Which enzyme variant best explains this?
questions.explanation: Lacking the low-Km (high-affinity) ALDH2 lets acetaldehyde accumulate, causing flushing. A: Low ADH activity would reduce acetaldehyde formation. B: CYP2E1 induction doesn't explain acute flushing. C: Catalase is a minor ethanol pathway. E: Glucokinase is unrelated.

questions.stem: A farmer arrives 12 hours after organophosphate pesticide exposure with salivation, bradycardia and muscle fasciculations. Atropine reduces the secretions, but pralidoxime has no effect. Why?

options.A: Organophosphates are reversible inhibitors that have washed out
options.B: Pralidoxime works only by blocking muscarinic receptors
options.C: Organophosphates block acetylcholine synthesis, not breakdown
options.D: Atropine has already reactivated the enzyme
options.E: The phosphorylated AChE has aged and is permanently inhibited

questions.explanation: Organophosphates phosphorylate the catalytic serine of AChE (irreversible inhibition). Pralidoxime removes the phosphate only before the adduct "ages"; after that, recovery waits on new enzyme over weeks, while atropine still blocks muscarinic effects. A: They are irreversible, covalent inhibitors. B: Blocking muscarinic receptors is atropine's action. C: They block ACh breakdown, so ACh accumulates. D: Atropine is a receptor blocker and doesn't act on AChE.

questions.stem: FAD stays tightly bound to its enzyme throughout catalysis, whereas NAD⁺ binds, is reduced and dissociates. How are these coenzymes classified?
questions.explanation: Coenzymes that associate permanently are prosthetic groups (FAD); those that associate transiently are co-substrates (NAD⁺). A: Reversed. B: Both are organic, vitamin-derived coenzymes, not metal ions. C: The apoenzyme is the protein part; the holoenzyme is protein plus cofactor. E: Allosteric effectors bind a separate site to regulate activity; these take part in the reaction.

questions.stem: Cortisol binds an intracellular receptor that acts as a transcription factor. Which other messenger uses the same receptor superfamily?
questions.explanation: Lipophilic messengers (steroids, thyroid hormone, retinoic acid, vitamin D) cross the membrane and bind the steroid/thyroid hormone receptor superfamily. A: Catecholamines are polar and bind surface receptors. C: Insulin is a polypeptide acting on a surface receptor tyrosine kinase. D: Cytokines are proteins that use surface receptors. E: Acetylcholine acts on surface ion channel (nicotinic) receptors.

questions.stem: Endothelial cells release prostacyclin, which relaxes the adjacent vascular smooth muscle. This is an example of which signaling mode?
questions.explanation: PGI2 from endothelial cells acts on nearby cells of a different type (smooth muscle): paracrine. A: Endocrine signals travel in the blood to distant cells. B: Autocrine acts on the secreting cell or cells of the same type. C: Gap junctions pass small molecules such as Ca²⁺ directly between cells. D: Direct signaling through surface receptors needs cell-to-cell contact, as in the immune system.

questions.stem: Compared with aspirin, a glucocorticoid reduces synthesis of a broader range of eicosanoids, including leukotrienes. Why?

options.B: It inhibits phospholipase C, blocking IP3 and DAG
options.C: It blocks prostaglandin receptors on target cells
options.D: It inhibits phospholipase A2, so arachidonic acid isn't released
options.E: It inhibits adenylyl cyclase in injured cells

questions.explanation: Glucocorticoids inhibit PLA2, which releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipids, so the whole eicosanoid cascade shuts down; aspirin and NSAIDs inhibit only downstream COX. A: Irreversible COX inhibition is aspirin's action, which spares leukotrienes. B: PLC makes IP3 and DAG, not arachidonate. C: Receptor blockade wouldn't reduce synthesis. E: Adenylyl cyclase makes cAMP, not eicosanoids.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old woman has leg weakness that worsens with walking and recovers with rest, slurred speech after long phone calls, and ptosis by evening. What is the mechanism of her disease?

options.A: Antibodies against presynaptic voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels
options.C: Blockade of ACh release by a bacterial toxin
