questions.explanation: Myasthenia gravis: anti-AChR antibodies cross-link receptors, which are endocytosed and degraded, giving fatigable weakness. A: Lambert–Eaton (improves with use). B: Loss of AChE would increase ACh effect. C: Botulism (descending paralysis, not fatigable pattern). D: Demyelination gives a different pattern (e.g., Guillain–Barré).

questions.stem: Cortisol enters a cell and binds the glucocorticoid receptor in the cytoplasm. What happens next?

options.A: The receptor autophosphorylates and recruits Grb2
options.B: The receptor activates Gs, raising cAMP
options.C: The receptor opens an ion channel in the membrane
options.D: Heat shock proteins dissociate, exposing an NLS
options.E: The receptor binds its response element in the cytoplasm

questions.explanation: Cortisol binding changes the receptor's conformation: it releases its heat shock proteins, exposing a nuclear localization signal, then dimerizes and moves to the nucleus to bind the hormone-response element. A: Autophosphorylation and Grb2 are RTK signaling. B: Gs and cAMP are GPCR signaling. C: Ion channel receptors are surface receptors for neurotransmitters. E: The hormone-response element is DNA, in the nucleus.

questions.stem: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies reduce the number of nicotinic ACh receptors. Why does pyridostigmine improve muscle strength?

options.A: It stimulates synthesis of new receptors
options.B: More ACh reaches the remaining receptors
options.C: It blocks binding of anti-receptor antibodies
options.E: It acts directly as a nicotinic agonist

questions.explanation: Pyridostigmine is a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor: ACh accumulates in the cleft, so the fewer remaining receptors are occupied more often. It is symptomatic, so immunosuppressants are added. A: It doesn't increase receptor synthesis. C: Antibody production is reduced by immunosuppressants, not by AChE inhibitors. D: Pyridostigmine is reversible; irreversible AChE inhibitors are nerve agents. E: It acts on the enzyme, not on the receptor.

questions.stem: Cholera toxin and pertussis toxin act on opposite G proteins, yet both raise intracellular cAMP. Which pair of mechanisms is correct?

options.A: Cholera activates Gi; pertussis activates Gs
options.C: Cholera locks Gs active; pertussis blocks Gi
options.D: Cholera blocks Gq; pertussis activates PLC

questions.explanation: Cholera ADP-ribosylates Gαs (no GTPase → stays on); pertussis ADP-ribosylates Gi (can't inhibit AC). A: Reversed. B: PDE isn't the target. D: Gq and PLC aren't involved. E: Both act via G proteins, not AC directly.

questions.stem: A hormone activates a Gq-coupled receptor on a smooth muscle cell. Which second messenger directly releases Ca²⁺ from the ER?
questions.explanation: Gq activates phospholipase C, which cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and DAG; IP3 opens Ca²⁺ channels in the ER. A: DAG stays in the membrane and, with Ca²⁺, activates PKC. B: PIP3 is made by PI3-kinase and serves as a PH-domain docking site. C: cAMP is made by adenylyl cyclase (Gs). D: cGMP is made by guanylyl cyclase.
questions.source: Signal Transduction, VI slide 29; VII slides 8–9

questions.stem: After an RTK autophosphorylates, which protein links it to Ras activation by binding phosphotyrosine through an SH2 domain?
questions.explanation: Grb2 binds phosphotyrosine via SH2 and recruits SOS (a Ras GEF) via SH3. A: Raf acts downstream of Ras. B: STATs bind JAK-phosphorylated cytokine receptors. C: Smad4 is in TGF-β signaling. E: PKA is cAMP-dependent.

questions.stem: TGF-β binds its type II receptor. What is the next step in the pathway?

options.B: Type II receptor phosphorylates type I on serine

questions.explanation: TGF-β receptors are serine/threonine kinases: ligand-bound type II recruits and phosphorylates type I, which phosphorylates an R-Smad; R-Smad joins Smad4 and regulates transcription in the nucleus. A: Tyrosine autophosphorylation is RTK signaling. C: JAK is used by cytokine receptors. D: Smad4 (Co-Smad) is not phosphorylated. E: R-Smad acts in a complex with Smad4.

questions.stem: A 9-month-old boy has recurrent severe infections, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive. He has almost no circulating T cells and his thymic shadow is absent. His maternal uncle died in infancy of infections. Which gene is most likely mutated?
questions.explanation: X-linked SCID: common γ chain (IL2RG) shared by many cytokine receptors. B: ADA deficiency causes autosomal recessive SCID. C: BTK causes X-linked agammaglobulinemia (B cells absent, T cells normal). D: WAS causes eczema, thrombocytopenia, infections. E: CD40L causes hyper-IgM syndrome.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old has multiple café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, and cutaneous neurofibromas. The defective protein normally does what?
questions.explanation: Neurofibromin (NF1) is a Ras GAP; its loss keeps Ras active. A: That's a GEF (e.g., SOS), which activates Ras. B: JAK phosphorylates STATs. C: Gi inhibits adenylyl cyclase. E: Phosphodiesterases degrade cGMP.

questions.stem: A man taking sildenafil uses nitroglycerin for chest pain and becomes severely hypotensive. Which statement explains how the two drugs together raise cGMP?

options.A: NO blocks cGMP breakdown; sildenafil activates guanylyl cyclase
options.B: NO activates adenylyl cyclase; sildenafil blocks cAMP breakdown
options.C: Both activate membrane guanylyl cyclase receptors
options.E: NO activates soluble guanylyl cyclase; sildenafil blocks cGMP breakdown

questions.explanation: Nitroglycerin supplies NO, which activates the cytoplasmic guanylyl cyclase, so more cGMP is made; sildenafil inhibits a cGMP phosphodiesterase, so less is destroyed. Together they cause excessive vasodilation. A: Reversed. B: cAMP isn't the messenger here. C: NO's receptor is the cytoplasmic guanylyl cyclase, and sildenafil acts on the phosphodiesterase. D: Only sildenafil inhibits the phosphodiesterase.

questions.stem: With continuous exposure to epinephrine, a cell's β-adrenergic response fades. Which event underlies this desensitization?

options.B: Grb2 binds phosphotyrosines on the receptor
options.C: β-ARK phosphorylates the receptor, which then binds β-arrestin
options.D: Gαs loses its intrinsic GTPase activity
options.E: PKA dissociates from its anchoring proteins

questions.explanation: β-adrenergic receptor kinase phosphorylates the receptor, creating a binding site for β-arrestin, which blocks further G protein binding; receptors are then endocytosed. A: Phosphodiesterase hydrolyzes cAMP; it isn't a kinase. B: Grb2 binds phosphotyrosines on RTKs. D: Loss of Gαs GTPase (as with cholera toxin) prolongs the signal. E: AKAPs set PKA location, not receptor sensitivity.

questions.stem: After a carbohydrate-rich meal, which change most directly accelerates hepatic glycolysis at the rate-limiting step?
questions.explanation: Insulin raises F2,6BP (PFK-2 kinase active), the most potent PFK-1 activator. A: Citrate inhibits PFK-1. C: ATP inhibits PFK-1. D: G6P inhibits hexokinase, not PFK-1, and wouldn't accelerate glycolysis. E: Acetyl-CoA inhibits PDH, not PFK-1.

questions.stem: In untreated type 1 diabetes, reduced glucose uptake by which tissue contributes to the hyperglycemia?
questions.explanation: Insulin moves GLUT4 to the plasma membrane in skeletal muscle, adipose tissue and heart; without insulin these tissues take up little glucose. A: Erythrocytes use GLUT1, which is insulin-independent. B: Neurons use GLUT3, which is insulin-independent. D: Hepatocytes use bidirectional GLUT2, which is insulin-independent. E: Intestinal uptake uses the Na⁺-coupled SGLT.

questions.stem: During intense exercise, why does skeletal muscle convert pyruvate to lactate?

options.A: To make ATP at the lactate dehydrogenase step
options.B: To relieve ATP inhibition of PFK-1
options.C: To export glucose directly to the liver
options.D: To supply NADH to the respiratory chain
options.E: To regenerate NAD⁺ for glyceraldehyde 3-P dehydrogenase

questions.explanation: NADH production exceeds respiratory chain capacity; the high NADH/NAD⁺ ratio drives pyruvate → lactate, regenerating the limited NAD⁺ that glyceraldehyde 3-P dehydrogenase needs. A: LDH makes no ATP. B: Lactate doesn't regulate PFK-1. C: Lactate, not glucose, goes to the liver (Cori cycle). D: LDH consumes NADH; it doesn't supply it.

questions.stem: What is the net yield of anaerobic glycolysis (glucose → 2 lactate)?
questions.explanation: 4 ATP made − 2 invested = 2 ATP; NADH is reoxidized when pyruvate becomes lactate. B: 4 is gross, not net. C: Aerobic glycolysis to pyruvate nets 2 ATP + 2 NADH. D: Complete oxidation. E: There is a net gain.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic alcohol use is confused and ataxic. He is given thiamine before glucose. Which enzyme requires the coenzyme form of thiamine (TPP)?
questions.explanation: PDH requires TPP (with lipoate, CoA, FAD, NAD⁺); giving glucose without thiamine can worsen Wernicke encephalopathy. A: LDH needs NADH only. B: Pyruvate carboxylase needs biotin. C: GAPDH needs NAD⁺. E: Pyruvate kinase needs no TPP.

questions.stem: A lean 16-year-old has mild, stable fasting hyperglycemia found on routine testing. Her father and grandfather have the same finding and have never needed insulin. An inactivating mutation in which enzyme is most likely?
questions.explanation: MODY2: glucokinase, the high-Km glucose sensor of hepatocytes and pancreatic β cells, is inactivated, giving mild fasting hyperglycemia. B: Low-Km hexokinase is saturated at normal glucose and can't act as a sensor. C: PFK-1 is the rate-limiting step of glycolysis, not the glucose sensor. D: Pyruvate kinase deficiency causes hemolytic anemia. E: Glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke) causes fasting hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: An infant has seizures, developmental delay and microcephaly. CSF glucose is low while blood glucose is normal. A ketogenic diet improves the seizures. Which transporter is deficient?
questions.explanation: GLUT1 haploinsufficiency: glucose doesn't cross the blood–brain barrier in sufficient amounts; ketone bodies from a high-fat diet are an alternative brain fuel. A: GLUT2 serves liver and kidney. B: GLUT3 is neuronal, but the defect here is entry across the blood–brain barrier. D: GLUT4 is the insulin-regulated transporter of muscle, fat and heart. E: SGLT is Na⁺-coupled transport in the intestine, renal tubules and choroid plexus; its loss isn't the known cause of this syndrome.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old has cramps within minutes of sprinting, a "second wind" after slowing down, and dark urine after hard effort. Fasting glucose and liver size are normal. What will a forearm exercise test show?

options.D: Lactate flat; ammonia rises more than normal
options.E: Normal rise of both lactate and ammonia

questions.explanation: McArdle disease (muscle phosphorylase, PYGM): no glucose 1-P from glycogen, so lactate doesn't rise; with ATP regeneration blocked, ADP accumulates, adenylate kinase makes AMP, and AMP deaminase releases extra ammonia. A: Lactate can't rise without glycogenolysis. B: Ammonia rises, typically more than normal. C: Glycolysis from glycogen is blocked. E: A normal result is expected in CPT-II deficiency, not here.

questions.stem: During fasting, glucagon raises cAMP in hepatocytes. Which combination results?
questions.explanation: PKA cascades phosphorylate both: phosphorylase becomes active, synthase inactive, so no futile cycle. A: Dephosphorylation is the insulin/fed state for synthase, and phosphorylase is inactive then. B: Reverses the effect of phosphorylation on each enzyme. D: Not the glucagon effect. E: G6P activation is a fed-state allosteric signal.

questions.stem: A 10-month-old has failure to thrive, hepatosplenomegaly and raised ALT/AST, with normal fasting glucose. Liver biopsy shows PAS-positive material that resists diastase digestion, with early fibrosis. Which enzyme is defective?
questions.explanation: Andersen disease (GSD IV): no branches, so insoluble, diastase-resistant polyglucosan drives fibrosis; degradation is intact, so fasting glucose stays normal early. A: Debranching deficiency (Cori) causes fasting hypoglycemia. B: Synthase deficiency means little glycogen. C: Glycogenin (GYG1) defects affect muscle glycogen storage (GSD XV). E: Von Gierke glycogen has normal structure, with severe fasting hypoglycemia.

questions.stem: Which statement explains why muscle glycogen cannot supply blood glucose?

options.E: Muscle glycogen is stored in lysosomes

questions.explanation: Without glucose 6-phosphatase, G6P can't become free glucose to export; it's used in local glycolysis. A: Muscle has its own phosphorylase (PYGM). C: Muscle glycogen is branched. D: Phosphoglucomutase is present. E: Most glycogen is cytosolic.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old has severe fasting hypoglycemia with seizures, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricemia and hyperlipidemia. Glucagon doesn't raise blood glucose. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: Von Gierke disease (GSD I): glycogen is normal and mobilized, but the final step to free glucose (shared with gluconeogenesis) is blocked; G6P is shunted to lactate, urate and lipid. B: McArdle disease affects muscle only. C: Pompe disease gives cardiomegaly with normal blood glucose. D: Cori disease causes fasting hypoglycemia, but lactate and urate stay normal (outside the slides). E: Andersen disease presents with cirrhosis and normal early glucose.

questions.stem: A 3-month-old has hypotonia and massive cardiomegaly with heart failure. Blood glucose is normal. Muscle biopsy shows glycogen of normal structure inside membrane-bound vacuoles. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: Pompe disease (GSD II, acid maltase/GAA): glycogen accumulates in lysosomal vacuoles; it is the only GSD that is a lysosomal storage disease, with massive cardiomegaly and normal glucose. A: Von Gierke disease causes severe fasting hypoglycemia. C: McArdle disease presents later with exercise cramps. D: Synthase deficiency means little glycogen is stored. E: Hexosaminidase A deficiency (Tay-Sachs) stores ganglioside, not glycogen.

questions.stem: A student sprints shortly after a large carbohydrate meal, while insulin is high. Why does his muscle still break down glycogen?

options.A: Ca²⁺ and AMP activate the phosphorylase system allosterically
options.B: Insulin activates glycogen phosphorylase in muscle
options.D: Glucagon raises cAMP in muscle cells

questions.explanation: Allosteric signals override hormonal ones: contraction releases Ca²⁺, which activates phosphorylase kinase through its calmodulin subunit, and rising AMP activates muscle phosphorylase b without phosphorylation. B: Insulin, through protein phosphatase-1, inactivates phosphorylase. C: G6P inhibits phosphorylase a and activates synthase. D: Glucagon acts on the liver; muscle responds to epinephrine. E: Free glucose inhibits phosphorylase a, and only in liver.

questions.stem: A cell's glycogen is completely depleted, and glycogen synthase cannot start a chain on free glucose. How is the first primer made?

options.A: Branching enzyme transfers glucose onto free glucose
options.B: Debranching enzyme builds a primer from free glucose
options.E: Glycogenin attaches glucose to its own tyrosine and extends it

questions.explanation: Glycogenin autoglucosylates one of its tyrosines using UDP-glucose and builds a short α(1→4) chain that glycogen synthase then elongates; glycogenin stays at the core of the granule. A: Branching enzyme only moves segments of existing chains. B: Debranching enzyme works in degradation. C: This enzyme makes UDP-glucose, not chains. D: Degradation is not a reversal of synthesis; phosphorylase only shortens chains.

questions.stem: A toxin makes the inner mitochondrial membrane permeable to protons. What happens to O₂ consumption and ATP synthesis?
questions.explanation: Uncoupling dissipates the gradient: electron flow (O₂ use) accelerates while ATP synthesis falls and heat rises. B: That pattern fits ETC or ATP synthase inhibitors. C: ATP can't rise without the gradient. D: Not possible. E: The gradient is lost.

questions.stem: Why do electrons from succinate yield fewer ATP (~1.5) than electrons from malate (~2.5)?

options.A: Succinate oxidation makes GTP instead of a reduced coenzyme
options.B: FAD(2H) passes them directly to cytochrome c
options.C: Complex II pumps protons back into the matrix
options.D: Malate dehydrogenase is coupled directly to ATP synthase
options.E: Succinate dehydrogenase passes them via FAD to CoQ, bypassing complex I

questions.explanation: Succinate dehydrogenase (complex II, the only TCA enzyme in the inner membrane) reduces FAD and passes electrons to CoQ, skipping complex I's proton pumping: 6 protons instead of 10. A: GTP comes from succinyl-CoA (succinate thiokinase). B: Electrons from complex II still pass through CoQ and complex III. C: Complex II doesn't pump protons at all. D: Malate's NADH enters at complex I; ATP synthase runs on the proton gradient.
questions.source: Energy Production, IX slides 16–18; VIII slides 29, 39

questions.stem: A child ingests a rodenticide and develops seizures and cardiac arrhythmias. Citrate accumulates in tissues. Which enzyme is inhibited?
questions.explanation: Fluoroacetate → fluorocitrate, which inhibits aconitase, so citrate accumulates. A: Citrate synthase forms fluorocitrate rather than being blocked. B: SDH inhibition would accumulate succinate. D: Cyanide/CO inhibit complex IV. E: Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase.

questions.stem: Cytosolic NADH from glycolysis in skeletal muscle enters mitochondria via the glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle. Approximately how much ATP does each NADH yield?
questions.explanation: The G3P shuttle passes electrons to FAD → CoQ, bypassing complex I (6 protons → ~1.5 ATP). A: Too low. B: 2.5 is via the malate–aspartate shuttle. C: An older textbook value for matrix NADH. E: Too high.

questions.stem: A firefighter rescued from a burning building has headache, confusion, and severe lactic acidosis despite a normal PaO₂. Venous blood looks unusually bright red. Which ETC component is primarily inhibited?
questions.explanation: Cyanide (from burning plastics) and CO inhibit cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV), blocking O₂ use; tissues can't extract O₂ → bright venous blood and lactic acidosis. B: Rotenone inhibits complex I. C: Malonate-type inhibitors affect complex II. D: Antimycin A inhibits complex III. E: Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia. Which blood finding is expected from his vitamin deficiency?
questions.explanation: Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome: thiamine (TPP) deficiency impairs the α-keto acid dehydrogenases (PDH, α-KGDH, branched-chain), so pyruvate, α-ketoglutarate and other α-keto acids accumulate in blood. A: Citrate accumulates when aconitase is blocked (fluoroacetate). B: Methylmalonate rises in vitamin B12 deficiency. D: Succinate would rise with a block at succinate dehydrogenase. E: Pyruvate that can't enter PDH is shunted to lactate, so lactate rises.

questions.stem: α-Ketoglutarate is withdrawn from the TCA cycle for amino acid synthesis, and acetyl-CoA starts to accumulate. Which enzyme mainly restores the cycle?
questions.explanation: Removing any intermediate depletes oxaloacetate, so acetyl-CoA can't enter. Pyruvate carboxylase (biotin, ATP) makes oxaloacetate from pyruvate and is activated by acetyl-CoA, the signal that oxaloacetate is short. A: PDH supplies acetyl-CoA, not 4-carbon intermediates. B: Citrate synthase consumes oxaloacetate. C: PEPCK removes oxaloacetate for gluconeogenesis. D: α-KGDH consumes α-ketoglutarate.

questions.stem: Approximately how many ATP are produced when one acetyl-CoA is oxidized by the TCA cycle and oxidative phosphorylation?
questions.explanation: 3 NADH × 2.5 + 1 FAD(2H) × 1.5 + 1 GTP = 10. A: 12 uses older values (3 ATP per NADH, 2 per FAD(2H)). C: 7.5 counts only the NADH. D: 9 leaves out the GTP. E: 2.5 is the yield of one NADH.

questions.stem: Which enzyme pair together bypasses the irreversible pyruvate kinase step of glycolysis?
questions.explanation: Pyruvate → OAA (pyruvate carboxylase, biotin, ATP) → PEP (PEPCK, GTP). A: G6Pase bypasses hexokinase. C: PDH and citrate synthase are oxidative, not gluconeogenic. D: FBPase bypasses PFK-1; aldolase is reversible. E: These aren't bypass enzymes.

questions.stem: During a prolonged fast, which compound can the liver use for net glucose synthesis?
questions.explanation: Hepatic glycerol kinase phosphorylates glycerol, which is oxidized to DHAP, a glycolytic intermediate. A: Acetyl-CoA's two carbons are lost as 2 CO₂ in the TCA cycle, so there is no net oxaloacetate. B, C: Leucine and lysine are the only exclusively ketogenic amino acids. E: Acetoacetate is a ketone body made from acetyl-CoA and gives no net glucose.

questions.stem: During fasting, which signal most directly activates hepatic pyruvate carboxylase?
questions.explanation: Fatty acid oxidation floods the liver with acetyl-CoA, an allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase. A: Insulin opposes gluconeogenesis. B: F2,6BP inhibits FBPase and activates glycolysis. D: AMP inhibits FBPase. E: Citrate isn't the activator of pyruvate carboxylase.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man is found confused after 2 days of binge drinking with little food. Blood glucose is 40 mg/dL and lactate is elevated. Which change in the liver best explains the hypoglycemia?

options.E: Activation of pyruvate carboxylase by ethanol

questions.explanation: Alcohol dehydrogenase raises the cytosolic NADH/NAD⁺ ratio, blocking lactate → pyruvate and malate → oxaloacetate, so gluconeogenesis fails once glycogen is depleted; mild lactic acidosis follows. B: The ratio rises. C: Induction would increase glucose output. D: Glycogen is depleted after days of little food. E: Ethanol doesn't activate pyruvate carboxylase.

questions.stem: A 6-month-old girl has lactic acidosis, hypotonia, seizures and developmental delay. Lactate, pyruvate and alanine are elevated; blood glucose is normal. Thiamine doesn't help. Which dietary approach is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: PDH deficiency, the most common cause of congenital lactic acidosis: pyruvate can't become acetyl-CoA, so a ketogenic diet supplies acetyl-CoA from fat, bypassing PDH. A: Carbohydrate increases pyruvate and lactate. B: Alanine adds more pyruvate. C: Cornstarch is for von Gierke disease. D: Biotin is the cofactor of pyruvate carboxylase, not PDH.

questions.stem: Glucagon promotes hepatic gluconeogenesis partly by phosphorylating which glycolytic enzyme, inactivating it?
questions.explanation: PKA phosphorylates and inactivates hepatic pyruvate kinase, so PEP isn't lost to pyruvate. A: Hexokinase is regulated by G6P. B: Glucokinase is regulated by its regulatory protein, not PKA phosphorylation. D: Aldolase is unregulated. E: Enolase is unregulated.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old boy has hemolytic anemia, jaundice and splenomegaly. Hemoglobin structure is normal. His red cells have low ATP and have lost their flexibility. Which enzyme is most likely deficient?
questions.explanation: RBCs lack mitochondria and rely on anaerobic glycolysis; pyruvate kinase deficiency accounts for >95% of inherited glycolytic defects, and low ATP makes RBCs rigid, causing hemolysis. A: PDH is mitochondrial, so RBCs don't use it. B: Pyruvate carboxylase is mitochondrial, for gluconeogenesis and anaplerosis. C: Glucose 6-phosphatase is in liver and kidney. D: Glucokinase is in liver and β cells; RBCs use hexokinase.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old is found comatose after sleeping through the night and wakes with IV glucose. Pyruvate, lactate and alanine are high, aspartate is low, and ammonia is raised. Vitamin supplements don't help. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: Without pyruvate carboxylase there is no oxaloacetate: gluconeogenesis fails (fasting hypoglycemia), pyruvate spills to lactate and alanine, and low oxaloacetate means low aspartate for the urea cycle (hyperammonemia). B: PDH deficiency gives lactic acidosis with normal fasting glucose. C: Von Gierke disease doesn't explain the low aspartate and raised ammonia. D: OTC deficiency raises ammonia but not pyruvate or lactate. E: MCAD deficiency gives hypoketotic hypoglycemia with medium-chain acylcarnitines.

questions.stem: Metformin lowers hepatic fatty acid synthesis mainly because AMPK activation causes which change?

options.A: Phosphorylation and inactivation of acetyl-CoA carboxylase
options.B: Allosteric activation of ACC by citrate
options.D: Increased fatty acid synthase expression through SREBP-1

questions.explanation: Metformin raises AMP/ATP, activating AMPK, which phosphorylates and inactivates ACC, so less malonyl-CoA (and less fat) is made. B: Citrate activates ACC, the opposite of AMPK's effect. C: HMG-CoA synthase belongs to ketogenesis. D: SREBP-1 is driven by insulin and would raise synthesis. E: HSL mobilizes stored TAG and isn't the mechanism here.

questions.stem: An 18-month-old vomits and sleeps through breakfast, then is found unresponsive with glucose 1.8 mmol/L. Free fatty acids are high, ketones are low, and the acylcarnitine profile shows medium-chain species. His sister died suddenly in infancy. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: High FFAs show mobilization works; low ketones and medium-chain acylcarnitines show β-oxidation stalling at medium chain length: MCAD deficiency. A: CPT-I deficiency gives low acylcarnitines (they are never made). C: This ketogenesis step wouldn't produce medium-chain acylcarnitines. D: CPT-II deficiency raises C16/C18 acylcarnitines and mainly hits muscle. E: Glycogen phosphorylase deficiency causes fasting hypoglycemia with intact fat oxidation and raised ketones.

questions.stem: Which molecule is both the committed product of fatty acid synthesis and the inhibitor of the carnitine shuttle?
questions.explanation: Malonyl-CoA is made by ACC and inhibits CPT-I, so newly made palmitate cannot be burned. A: Citrate activates ACC and carries acetyl units to the cytosol. B: Acetyl-CoA is the substrate of ACC, not a CPT-I inhibitor. D: Acylcarnitine is the product of CPT-I. E: Long-chain acyl-CoA inhibits ACC and is the CPT-I substrate.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman develops thigh pain and dark urine after a 9-hour hike with little food. CK is 48,000 U/L. She had similar episodes with fasting and fever, never with short intense exercise, and is normal between attacks. Long-chain (C16, C18) acylcarnitines are raised. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Prolonged effort or fasting forces muscle onto long-chain fatty acids, and a CPT-II defect raises long-chain acylcarnitines: CPT-II deficiency. A: McArdle is triggered by brief maximal effort, has a second wind, and CK stays raised between attacks. C: CPT-I deficiency affects the liver and gives low acylcarnitines. D: MCAD gives medium-chain species and presents with infant fasting hypoglycemia. E: Von Gierke gives fasting hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis and hepatomegaly, not recurrent rhabdomyolysis.

questions.stem: A patient with vitamin B12 deficiency excretes methylmalonate. Which step of odd-chain fatty acid oxidation is blocked?
questions.explanation: Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase needs the B12 coenzyme; when it fails, methylmalonate and propionate are excreted. A: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase needs biotin. B: The racemase needs no vitamin cofactor. C: This is the ACC step of fatty acid synthesis (biotin). E: This is ketogenesis, unrelated to B12.

questions.stem: Why can the liver produce ketone bodies but not use them as fuel?
questions.explanation: Liver mitochondria have no thiophorase (succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase), the enzyme that activates acetoacetate to acetoacetyl-CoA in peripheral tissues. B: HMG-CoA synthase is the liver's rate-limiting ketogenic enzyme. C: Hepatocytes have mitochondria (red blood cells don't). D: This enzyme interconverts acetoacetate and 3-hydroxybutyrate, depending on NAD⁺/NADH. E: Ketone bodies are released into blood and used by brain, muscle and kidney.

questions.stem: A patient on fat-free parenteral nutrition for 8 months develops scaly dermatitis. Which fatty acid appears in their blood?
questions.explanation: Without linoleate, desaturases act on oleate instead, producing Mead acid, which is diagnostic of essential fatty acid deficiency. A: Arachidonic acid is made from linoleate, so it falls. B: Phytanic acid accumulates in Refsum disease. C: α-Linolenic acid is an essential fatty acid and would also be absent. D: Very-long-chain fatty acids accumulate in peroxisomal disorders such as Zellweger and X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy.

questions.stem: Adipocytes can store fatty acids as triacylglycerol only when glucose enters them. Why can't they use free glycerol instead?

options.E: Hormone-sensitive lipase is active after meals

questions.explanation: Adipocytes have no glycerol kinase, so glycerol phosphate must come from glucose via DHAP, and glucose enters through insulin-dependent GLUT4; the liver has glycerol kinase. A: They need this enzyme to reduce DHAP, so they have it. B: Fatty acids must be activated to acyl-CoA in all tissues that make TAG. C: Adipocytes do have GLUT4; it is how glucose enters. E: HSL is dephosphorylated and inactive when insulin is high.

questions.stem: A patient with the muscle form of CPT-II deficiency is advised to take medium-chain triglyceride supplements. Why do they help?

options.B: Medium-chain fatty acids inhibit malonyl-CoA formation
options.D: They are converted to muscle glycogen
options.E: They stimulate carnitine synthesis in muscle

questions.explanation: Fatty acids shorter than 12 carbons cross the inner mitochondrial membrane and are activated in the matrix, bypassing CPT-I, the translocase and CPT-II. A: They bypass the defective enzyme; they don't repair it. B: Their oxidation doesn't depend on CPT-I, so malonyl-CoA is irrelevant to them. D: Fatty acids can't make net glucose or glycogen. E: Muscle can't synthesize carnitine; liver and kidney make it.

questions.stem: Which amino acid is unique in undergoing rapid oxidative deamination by glutamate dehydrogenase, releasing free ammonia?
questions.explanation: Most amino groups are funneled to glutamate by transamination, and glutamate is the only amino acid rapidly deaminated oxidatively. A: Alanine gives its amino group to α-KG via ALT. B: Aspartate donates nitrogen at argininosuccinate synthetase in the urea cycle. D: Glutamine is cleaved by glutaminase in the liver. E: Lysine isn't transaminated; it loses its amino group by a different deamination.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old woman who always disliked meat and milk becomes confused and drowsy after starting a high-protein diet. Ammonia is 240 µmol/L, plasma glutamine is high, citrulline and blood urea are low, urine orotic acid is high, and ALT/AST are normal. Her mother's brother died at 4 days of age. What is the diagnosis?

options.B: OTC deficiency in a female carrier

questions.explanation: Low citrulline with high orotic acid means carbamoyl phosphate is made but not passed to ornithine and spills into pyrimidine synthesis; X-linked inheritance explains the affected uncle and the mosaic female carrier. A, C: With CPS I or NAGS missing, no carbamoyl phosphate is made, so orotic acid is low. D: The block is after citrulline, so citrulline would be high. E: Arginase acts last, so citrulline and arginine would not be low.

questions.stem: Why does a protein-rich meal speed up the urea cycle?

options.E: Glutamate and arginine raise N-acetylglutamate, which activates CPS I

questions.explanation: NAGS makes N-acetylglutamate from acetyl-CoA and glutamate, and arginine activates NAGS; the meal supplies both, and N-acetylglutamate is the essential activator of CPS I, the rate-limiting enzyme. A: Arginine activates NAGS, not CPS I directly. B: N-acetylglutamate acts on CPS I. C: The control point is CPS I, the first step, not arginase. D: Arginine, not aspartate, activates NAGS.

questions.stem: Which pair of amino acids is exclusively ketogenic?
questions.explanation: Leucine and lysine are the only exclusively ketogenic amino acids: their carbon skeletons can't make glucose. A, C: These amino acids are glucogenic or both, not exclusively ketogenic. D, E: These yield pyruvate or TCA intermediates, so they are glucogenic.

questions.stem: A newborn screened on day 1 has a normal phenylalanine level. By 6 months, the infant has a musty urine odor, fair hair and light skin, seizures and developmental delay. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency (PKU): Phe builds up and tyrosine, hence melanin, falls. The early test was falsely normal because the mother cleared fetal Phe through the placenta (test after 24-48 h of protein feeding). A: Tyrosinase deficiency causes albinism without a musty odor or Phe accumulation. B: Homogentisic acid oxidase deficiency causes alkaptonuria (dark urine, arthritis later). D: This enzyme gives maple syrup urine disease. E: This enzyme gives homocystinuria.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old has displaced lenses, osteoporosis and a deep vein thrombosis. Plasma methionine is high and cysteine is low. Which enzyme is deficient?
questions.explanation: Cystathionine β-synthase converts homocysteine to cystathionine (toward cysteine); its loss raises homocysteine and methionine and lowers cysteine. Pyridoxine (B6) helps responsive patients. A: PAH deficiency is PKU. B: Homogentisic acid oxidase is defective in alkaptonuria. C: This enzyme is defective in maple syrup urine disease. D: Tyrosinase deficiency causes albinism.

questions.stem: A man with recurrent kidney stones excretes cystine, ornithine, arginine and lysine in his urine. Which statement best explains his disease?

options.A: Transporter shared by gut and kidney; ornithine forms stones
options.C: Urea cycle enzyme defect; arginine forms stones
options.D: Transporter shared by gut and kidney; cystine forms stones
options.E: Neutral amino acid transporter defect; tryptophan is lost

questions.explanation: Cystinuria: a defect in the COAL transport system shared by the small intestine and proximal tubule; only cystine is insoluble enough to precipitate. A: Ornithine doesn't precipitate. B: The same transport systems exist in the intestine. C: It's a transport defect, not a urea cycle disorder. E: Neutral amino acid (tryptophan) loss is Hartnup disorder.

questions.stem: During prolonged exercise, skeletal muscle sends amino nitrogen to the liver as alanine. What does the liver do with alanine's carbon skeleton?

options.A: Transaminates it to pyruvate and makes glucose
options.C: Converts it to glutamine for excretion
options.D: Converts it to lactate for the Cori cycle

questions.explanation: Glucose–alanine (Cahill) cycle: muscle transaminates pyruvate to alanine; the liver transaminates alanine back to pyruvate (ALT) and uses it for gluconeogenesis, returning glucose to muscle. B: Only glutamate undergoes rapid oxidative deamination. C: Glutamine is the other ammonia carrier, made by glutamine synthetase in most tissues. D: The Cori cycle carries lactate from muscle to liver, not the reverse. E: Alanine is glucogenic; leucine and lysine are the only exclusively ketogenic amino acids.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old develops a scaly rash on sun-exposed skin, diarrhea and episodes of confusion after a febrile illness. Urine contains increased neutral amino acids. What links his transport defect to the symptoms?

options.A: Cystine precipitates in skin and gut
options.C: Homogentisic acid deposits in connective tissue
options.D: Tryptophan loss limits niacin and NAD⁺ synthesis

questions.explanation: Hartnup disorder: defective neutral amino acid transport in gut and kidney causes loss of tryptophan, a precursor of niacin (nicotinamide of NAD⁺/NADP⁺), so it mimics pellagra. Treatment: high-protein diet, sun protection, niacin. A: Cystine forms kidney stones in cystinuria. B: PKU causes hypopigmentation, not a pellagra-like picture. C: Homogentisic acid pigments cartilage in alkaptonuria. E: Branched-chain keto acids accumulate in maple syrup urine disease.

questions.stem: Koch's postulates cannot be fulfilled for Mycobacterium leprae. Which postulate fails?

options.A: The organism is present in every case of the disease
options.B: The organism is isolated in pure culture in vitro
options.C: The organism reproduces the disease in laboratory animals
options.D: The organism is re-isolated from the infected animal
options.E: The host produces specific antibodies to the organism

questions.explanation: M. leprae cannot be cultivated on artificial media, so pure culture (postulate 2) fails. A: It is present in every case. C: Failure in lab animals is the N. gonorrhoeae exception (human-only disease). D: Re-isolation is not the stated problem for M. leprae. E: Antibody production is not one of Koch's four postulates.

questions.stem: Bacterial mesosomes are functionally analogous to which eukaryotic structure?
questions.explanation: Mesosomes are invaginations of the bacterial cell membrane carrying respiratory enzymes, so they replace mitochondria (which bacteria lack). A: Bacteria lack a Golgi. B: Lysosomes are digestive organelles, not respiratory. C: Bacteria lack ER. E: Bacteria have their own (70S) ribosomes; these synthesize protein, not energy.

questions.stem: Protein-synthesis inhibitors can be selectively toxic to bacteria because bacterial ribosomes are:
questions.explanation: Bacteria have 70S ribosomes (30S + 50S); human cells have 80S (40S + 60S), so drugs can target one without the other. B: That is the eukaryotic (human) ribosome. C: 40S is a eukaryotic subunit. D: 30S and 50S form the 70S, not 80S, ribosome. E: 40S and 60S are the eukaryotic subunits.

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes helminths from protozoa?

options.B: Ability to cause disease in humans
options.C: Multicellular body with differentiated tissues and organ systems

questions.explanation: Helminths are macroscopic multicellular worms with differentiated tissues and organ systems; protozoa are microscopic single-celled eukaryotes. A: Both are eukaryotes with a true nucleus. B: Both are human pathogens. D: Chitin walls are a fungal feature. E: Both, as eukaryotes, have 80S ribosomes.

questions.stem: Fungal and bacterial cell walls differ in their main structural component. Which pairing is correct?

options.D: Fungi: no cell wall; bacteria: peptidoglycan

questions.explanation: Fungal walls contain chitin; bacterial walls contain peptidoglycan (unique to bacteria). A: Reversed. B: Cellulose is the plant cell-wall component. C: Bacteria do not use cellulose. D: Fungi do have a cell wall; animal cells are the ones without.

questions.stem: Which feature correctly distinguishes viruses from bacteria?

options.C: Viruses contain only one type of nucleic acid, DNA or RNA
options.D: Viruses grow on artificial media such as agar
options.E: Viruses have a peptidoglycan cell wall

questions.explanation: Viruses contain only DNA or RNA inside a protein capsid and are obligate intracellular. A: Viruses have no ribosomes; they use the host's. B: Bacteria divide by binary fission; viruses replicate inside cells. D: Viruses need living cells. E: Viruses have a capsid, not a cell wall.

questions.stem: Which antibiotic binds the same ribosomal subunit as tetracycline?
questions.explanation: Tetracyclines and aminoglycosides (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) bind the 30S subunit. A: Macrolides act on 50S. B: Clindamycin acts on 50S. C: Linezolid acts on 50S. D: Chloramphenicol acts on 50S.

questions.stem: Co-trimoxazole combines a sulfonamide with trimethoprim. Which enzyme does the trimethoprim component inhibit?
questions.explanation: Trimethoprim blocks dihydrofolate reductase (dihydrofolic → tetrahydrofolic acid); with sulfonamides it blocks two sequential folate steps. A: Sulfonamides (PABA analogs) inhibit this earlier step (slide name; standard name dihydropteroate synthase). C: Quinolones inhibit DNA gyrase. D: Rifampicin inhibits RNA polymerase. E: β-lactams inhibit transpeptidase.

questions.stem: Why is nafcillin effective against penicillinase-producing S. aureus while penicillin G is not?

options.A: It binds D-Ala-D-Ala termini instead of PBPs
options.C: Its bulky R side chain blocks β-lactamase access to the β-lactam ring
options.D: It is always given with clavulanic acid
options.E: It binds the altered PBP encoded by mecA

questions.explanation: Steric hindrance from the bulky R group protects the β-lactam ring, so nafcillin is used for S. aureus (except MRSA). A: That is vancomycin. B: That ring is the cephalosporin structure. D: Clavulanate is paired with amoxicillin (Augmentin), not needed for nafcillin. E: mecA-altered PBP is exactly why MRSA resists nafcillin.

questions.stem: Which cephalosporin covers MRSA?
questions.explanation: Ceftaroline (5th generation) covers MRSA but not Pseudomonas. A: Cefazolin is 1st generation. C: Cefaclor is 2nd. D: Ceftriaxone is 3rd. E: Cefepime is 4th; it doesn't cover MRSA.

questions.stem: During an epidemic of cerebrospinal meningitis, healthy close contacts are given oral rifampicin. This use is best described as:
questions.explanation: Chemoprophylaxis = antimicrobials to prevent infection in people not yet infected (also: amoxicillin before dental extraction in heart disease, preoperative use). B: Combinations to prevent resistance are used in TB. C: Superinfection is overgrowth of resistant flora (oral Candida, C. difficile). D: Synergy means two drugs together (e.g. penicillin + aminoglycoside). E: The contacts are not ill.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old with atypical pneumonia fails amoxicillin. Cold agglutinins are positive. Why did amoxicillin fail?

options.A: The organism lacks a cell wall
options.B: The organism carries a β-lactamase R plasmid
options.E: The organism has an mecA-altered PBP

questions.explanation: Mycoplasma pneumoniae naturally lacks a cell wall, so β-lactams have no target (non-genetic resistance by loss of target structure). B: β-lactamase is genetic resistance in wall-bearing bacteria. C: 30S changes affect aminoglycosides/tetracyclines. D: Dormancy is the M. tuberculosis example of non-genetic resistance. E: mecA is the MRSA mechanism.

questions.stem: In an E-test (epsilometer) on an inoculated agar plate, how is the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) read?

options.A: The diameter of the inhibition zone around a disc, in mm
options.B: Comparison of zone size with CLSI tables as S/I/R
options.C: The highest concentration printed on the strip
options.D: The point where the elliptical inhibition zone meets the strip
options.E: The concentration at the tip of the strip after 24 h

questions.explanation: The strip carries an antibiotic gradient; after 24 h at 37 °C a tear-drop zone forms and the zone edge's intersection with the strip is the MIC. A: That is Kirby-Bauer disc diffusion. B: That is how disc diffusion is interpreted. C: The highest concentration is not the MIC. E: The tip has no special meaning; the intersection point does.

questions.stem: Ciprofloxacin kills bacteria by inhibiting which enzyme?
questions.explanation: Quinolones (nalidixic acid, ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin) inhibit DNA gyrase and block DNA synthesis. A: Rifampicin inhibits RNA polymerase. B: Trimethoprim inhibits dihydrofolate reductase. D: β-lactams inhibit transpeptidase. E: Vancomycin physically obstructs glycosyltransferase.

questions.stem: A Staphylococcus aureus isolate is resistant to methicillin and all other β-lactams, though β-lactamase inhibitors do not restore activity. What is the resistance mechanism?

options.C: Loss of the cell wall target
options.D: Decreased permeability of the outer membrane
options.E: Altered penicillin-binding protein from a mecA mutation

questions.explanation: MRSA resists by modifying the target: mecA alters the PBP so β-lactams no longer bind (vancomycin or ceftaroline are used). A: A β-lactamase inhibitor would restore activity. B: Efflux pumps are the quinolone example. C: Loss of target is Mycoplasma. D: S. aureus is Gram-positive and has no outer membrane.

questions.stem: A virus is inactivated by ether. What can you conclude?
questions.explanation: Ether dissolves the lipid envelope; naked viruses resist it. A: Envelope, not nucleic acid type, determines sensitivity. B: Symmetry is unrelated. C: Prions aren't viruses and resist many agents. E: Replication site is unrelated.

questions.stem: Which virus contains single-stranded DNA?
questions.explanation: Parvoviruses are the ssDNA exception. A, B, D: These are dsDNA. C: Reovirus is the dsRNA exception.

questions.stem: Hepatitis D virus can only replicate in cells co-infected with hepatitis B virus. HDV is therefore best described as a:
questions.explanation: Defective viruses need a helper virus (HBV supplies HBsAg). B: Prions lack nucleic acid. C: Viroids are naked RNA in plants. D: Pseudovirions carry host DNA. E: Bacteriophages infect bacteria.

questions.stem: How are naked (non-enveloped) viruses typically released from infected cells?
questions.explanation: Naked viruses exit by lysis. A, D: Budding is how enveloped viruses exit and acquire their envelope. B: Not the typical route. E: Conjugation is bacterial gene transfer.

questions.stem: A pandemic influenza strain emerges with hemagglutinin from an avian virus and other genes from a human virus. Which mechanism produced it?
questions.explanation: Influenza has a segmented RNA genome; co-infection allows segment swapping → shift. A: Drift gives minor seasonal changes. C: Recombination occurs mostly in DNA viruses. D: Interference blocks a second virus. E: Complementation supplies proteins without exchanging genes.

questions.stem: A man dies of encephalitis weeks after a bat bite. Which inclusion bodies are expected in his brain neurons?
questions.explanation: Rabies produces intracytoplasmic Negri bodies. A: Cowdry bodies are intranuclear (herpes). B: Combined inclusions are the measles pattern. C: Syncytia are a cell-fusion cytopathic effect, not inclusions. D: Plaques are foci of dead cells in tissue culture.

questions.stem: In retrovirus replication, which enzyme transcribes viral mRNA and progeny genomes from the integrated proviral DNA?
questions.explanation: After reverse transcription and integration, the provirus is transcribed by the host cell RNA polymerase. B: Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from the RNA genome, the earlier step. C: Retroviruses do not copy RNA from RNA. D: Integrase inserts the DNA but does not transcribe it. E: Retroviruses do not carry a DNA polymerase for transcription.

questions.stem: A virus is inoculated onto the chorioallantoic membrane of a 10-day embryonated egg. Which finding shows viral growth?

options.D: Pocks: white opaque areas on the membrane

questions.explanation: Pocks are white opaque lesions on the transparent CAM from virus-infected cells. A: Plaques are seen in tissue culture. B: Syncytia are a cytopathic effect in cell culture. C: Negri bodies are rabies inclusions in neurons. E: Mucoid colonies are capsulated bacteria on agar.

questions.stem: Herpesviruses and paramyxoviruses usually enter host cells by which mechanism?

options.B: Fusion of the envelope with the cell membrane via F protein

questions.explanation: These enveloped viruses carry F protein and fuse with the cell membrane, releasing the nucleocapsid into the cytoplasm. A: Direct penetration is the bacteriophage example. C: Endocytosis engulfs virions in vesicles; it is not the example given for these viruses. D: Budding is a release step. E: Lysis is how naked viruses are released.

questions.stem: Why does an obligate anaerobe die when exposed to air?

options.A: It lacks catalase and superoxide dismutase to remove toxic O₂ products
options.B: It cannot make ATP without O₂
options.C: O₂ blocks its cell wall synthesis
options.D: It requires O₂ as its final hydrogen acceptor
options.E: It only grows at low O₂ tension

questions.explanation: Superoxide and H₂O₂ accumulate without SOD and catalase. B: Anaerobes make ATP without O₂ (organic or inorganic acceptors). C: O₂ does not block wall synthesis. D: Using O₂ as the hydrogen acceptor defines obligate aerobes. E: Growth at low O₂ tension defines microaerophiles.

questions.stem: In a broth culture, the viable count stays constant while the total count keeps rising. In vivo, this growth phase corresponds to:

options.C: Signs and symptoms such as fever

questions.explanation: This is the stationary phase (multiplication = death from nutrient exhaustion and toxic products), which corresponds to signs and symptoms. A: Incubation = lag phase. B: Invasion = log phase. D: Recovery = decline phase. E: The carrier state is not a growth-curve phase.

questions.stem: Griffith injected mice with live non-capsulated pneumococci plus heat-killed capsulated pneumococci; the mice died. Which gene-transfer process explains this?
questions.explanation: Competent live bacteria took up naked capsule genes from dead cells. A: No phage was involved. B: Conjugation needs live donor contact. D: Transposition moves genes within a cell. E: Lysogenic conversion needs a phage.

questions.stem: Which gene-transfer mechanism requires cell-to-cell contact but not naked DNA or phage?
questions.explanation: Conjugation uses a sex pilus between donor and recipient, with no naked DNA or phage. A: Uses naked DNA and a competent cell. B: Uses a phage. C: A lab form of transformation using naked DNA. D: Occurs in segmented RNA viruses.

questions.stem: A food handler has shed Salmonella Typhi in her stool for 6 years without symptoms. Which type of carrier is she?
questions.explanation: Chronic carriers discharge the organism for a long time; carriers are dangerous because they are asymptomatic, undetected and mobile. A: Incubatory carriers shed during the incubation period. B: Convalescent carriers shed only during recovery after illness. D: Commensals are normal flora. E: Saprophytes live free in nature.

questions.stem: Oral viridans streptococci cause endocarditis after entering the bloodstream. What type of infection is this?
questions.explanation: A commensal becomes pathogenic when it reaches a new site (mouth → heart). B: The trigger here is a new site, not low immunity. C: Zoonoses come from animals. D: Viridans streptococci are commensals, not obligate pathogens. E: A carrier has no disease.

questions.stem: A traveler has diarrhea; stool shows motile pear-shaped trophozoites with flagella and resistant cysts. Which protozoan class is this?
questions.explanation: Giardia lamblia is a flagellate. A: Amebae move with pseudopodia. B: Sporozoa (Plasmodium) are spore-forming. C: Ciliates (Balantidium) have cilia. E: Cestodes are tapeworms (helminths).

questions.stem: In DNA cloning, the insert and plasmid are cut with the same restriction endonuclease. Which enzyme then seals the insert into the plasmid?
questions.explanation: DNA ligase seals the gaps between the sticky ends, forming the recombinant plasmid, which is then transformed into E. coli. A: Reverse transcriptase copies RNA to DNA. B: Restriction endonucleases cut, they do not seal. C: DNA gyrase is the quinolone target. E: Transpeptidase cross-links peptidoglycan.

questions.stem: A helminth is leaf-shaped and flattened with oral and ventral suckers, and has separate sexes. Which is it?
questions.explanation: Leaf-shaped with suckers = trematode (fluke); flukes are hermaphrodites except Schistosoma. A: Fasciola is a hermaphroditic fluke. B, D: These are cestodes (segmented tapeworms with a scolex). C: Ascaris is a nematode, round in cross-section.

questions.stem: Which antiretroviral targets a host-cell protein rather than a viral one?
questions.explanation: Maraviroc blocks host CCR5. A: Enfuvirtide binds viral gp41. B: Zidovudine targets reverse transcriptase. D: Raltegravir targets integrase. E: Nevirapine binds reverse transcriptase.

questions.stem: Why is amantadine ineffective against influenza B?

options.C: Influenza B has an unsegmented genome
options.E: Influenza B has NB protein instead of M2

questions.explanation: Amantadine blocks the M2 ion channel needed for uncoating; influenza B has NB instead. A: Influenza B has neuraminidase (oseltamivir works). B: It has hemagglutinin. C: Its RNA has 8 segments. D: It is enveloped.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old with recurrent herpes labialis no longer responds to acyclovir. Which enzyme change most likely explains this?

options.A: Mutated or absent viral thymidine kinase

questions.explanation: Acyclovir needs viral TK for its first phosphorylation; TK mutations cause resistance (foscarnet is then used). B: Cellular TK doesn't activate acyclovir. C: UL97 activates ganciclovir in CMV. D, E: These aren't herpes targets.

questions.stem: Which anti-herpes drug requires no phosphorylation to act?
questions.explanation: Foscarnet directly inhibits viral polymerases. A, E: Need viral TK. B: Needs UL97. C: Needs cellular kinases.

questions.stem: How does oseltamivir limit influenza infection?

options.E: Blocks fusion of the envelope with the cell

questions.explanation: Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir oral, zanamivir inhaled) trap new virions on the cell. A: HA attachment is not its target. C: That is amantadine. D: Not its target. E: Fusion inhibition is enfuvirtide (HIV gp41).

questions.stem: Zidovudine and nevirapine both inhibit HIV reverse transcriptase. How does zidovudine differ?

options.A: It must be phosphorylated in the cell and terminates the proviral DNA chain
options.B: It binds the enzyme directly and alters its active site
options.C: It blocks integrase from inserting proviral DNA
options.D: It binds gp41 and prevents membrane fusion
options.E: It binds CCR5 on the host cell

questions.explanation: Zidovudine is an NRTI: a nucleoside analog phosphorylated to a fake nucleotide that stops chain elongation. B: That is nevirapine (NNRTI). C: Integrase inhibitors (raltegravir). D: Enfuvirtide. E: Maraviroc.

questions.stem: How do type I interferons released by a virus-infected cell protect neighboring cells?

options.A: They neutralize free virions in the blood
options.B: They activate macrophages as their main action
options.C: They induce proteins that degrade viral mRNA and block viral protein synthesis

questions.explanation: Type I IFN (α, β) binds neighboring cells and induces an antiviral state (viral mRNA degradation, blocked viral protein synthesis) and raises MHC expression. A: Antibodies neutralize virions. B: Macrophage activation is mainly type II (IFN-γ). D: That is maraviroc. E: That is oseltamivir/zanamivir.

questions.stem: Why do influenza A and hepatitis C virus develop antiviral resistance faster than herpesviruses?

options.C: They use host DNA polymerase for replication
options.D: They become latent in sensory neurons

questions.explanation: RNA polymerases lack proofreading, giving high error rates and many resistance mutations. A: RNA viruses have small genomes (<30 kb). B: Faster, not slower, replication increases mutations. C: DNA viruses use host machinery with proofreading, so they mutate less. D: Latency is a herpesvirus feature and does not drive resistance.

questions.stem: After Gram staining, an organism appears pink. Which cell-wall feature explains this?

options.B: Waxy wall rich in mycolic acid
options.C: No cell wall, with sterols in the membrane
options.D: Thin peptidoglycan with an outer membrane

questions.explanation: Gram-negative walls are decolorized by alcohol and take up safranin (pink). A: Gram-positive walls retain the violet. B: Mycolic acid walls (M. tuberculosis) are not Gram-stained; Ziehl-Neelsen is used. C: Wall-less Mycoplasma stain poorly. E: Capsules appear as an unstained halo.

questions.stem: Which component is responsible for fever and shock in Gram-negative sepsis?
questions.explanation: Lipid A is endotoxin, released on lysis. A: Teichoic acid is Gram-positive (adhesion). B: Peptidoglycan isn't the endotoxin. D: The O polysaccharide is the antigenic part. E: Porins are channels.

questions.stem: Surgical instruments are contaminated with Clostridium spores. Which method reliably destroys the spores?

options.B: Autoclaving with steam at 121 °C for 20 minutes

questions.explanation: Spores (dehydrated, calcium dipicolinate, metabolically inert, many layers) resist boiling and chemicals but are killed by autoclaving. A: Spores resist boiling. C: Spores resist chemical sterilization. D: UV kills vegetative bacteria, not reliably spores. E: Lysozyme damages vegetative cell walls (forms L-forms), not spores.

questions.stem: A UTI fails to respond to antibiotics because resistance genes spread from one E. coli strain to another. Which element most likely transferred them?
questions.explanation: Conjugative plasmids (large, F factor/tra gene, common in Gram-negative bacilli) form sex pili and transfer R genes between cells. A: Non-conjugative plasmids cannot transfer under normal conditions. B: Transposons move genes within a cell. C: Ordinary pili mediate adherence; sex pili mediate conjugation. D: Flagella give motility.

questions.stem: Which property distinguishes exotoxins from endotoxins?

options.B: Exotoxins can be converted into toxoids for vaccination
options.D: Exotoxins are released only on cell lysis

questions.explanation: Formalin-treated exotoxins become antigenic, non-toxic toxoids (tetanus, diphtheria). A: Lipid A is endotoxin. C: Exotoxins are heat-labile. D: Exotoxins are secreted by living cells. E: They are strongly immunogenic.

questions.stem: Penicillin-treated Gram-negative bacteria lose their walls but regrow them when the drug is removed. These forms are:
questions.explanation: Wall-deficient L-forms from Gram-negatives are spheroplasts and can revert. A: Mycoplasma genetically lacks a wall and doesn't revert. B: Protoplasts come from Gram-positives. D: Spores are resting forms. E: Acid-fast bacilli have waxy walls.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man has fever, cough, and diarrhea after a hotel stay; the organism grows inside alveolar macrophages by blocking phagosome–lysosome fusion. Which organism shares this survival mechanism?
questions.explanation: Legionella and mycobacteria inhibit phagolysosome fusion. B: Listeria escapes the phagosome into the cytoplasm. C: S. aureus uses protein A and coagulase. D: S. pyogenes uses M protein. E: Neisseria uses pili and IgA protease.

questions.stem: A 2-year-old has repeated pneumococcal infections. Serotype-specific capsule swelling is seen when the isolate is mixed with antiserum. Which property makes the capsule a key virulence factor?

options.B: It degrades secretory IgA at mucosa

questions.explanation: Capsules are antiphagocytic; serotype-specific swelling (Quellung) is the basis of serotyping and vaccines. A: Lipid A is in the Gram-negative outer membrane. B: IgA protease is a Neisseria enzyme. C: Coagulase is a S. aureus enzyme. E: Pili are made of pilin, not capsule.

questions.stem: Staphylococci colonize an IV catheter within a loosely bound polysaccharide layer that protects them from antibiotics and immune cells. This layer is the:
questions.explanation: Slime (glycocalyx) is loosely attached and secreted, binding bacteria to each other and to catheters or valves as a biofilm. B: A capsule is firmly attached and well-defined. C: Staphylococci are Gram-positive with no outer membrane. D: A peptidoglycan cortex is part of a spore. E: Teichoic acid aids adhesion but is part of the cell wall.

questions.stem: A man with a crush injury develops rapidly spreading gas gangrene from Clostridium perfringens. Which enzyme degrades a fatty component of human tissue cell membranes?
questions.explanation: C. perfringens lecithinase degrades lecithin, a fatty component of human tissues. A: Collagenase (also C. perfringens) degrades collagen. B: Hyaluronidase degrades hyaluronic acid. C: Coagulase (S. aureus) converts fibrinogen to fibrin. D: Streptokinase (S. pyogenes) lyses fibrin clots.

questions.stem: An antifungal kills Candida by inhibiting synthesis of β-(1,3)-glucan, a component of the fungal cell wall. Which drug is it?
questions.explanation: Echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) inhibit glucan synthase; they are fungicidal against Candida but only disrupt the growing wall of Aspergillus. A: Polyene; binds membrane ergosterol and forms pores. C: Azole; blocks ergosterol synthesis. D: Converted to 5-FU; disrupts RNA and DNA synthesis. E: Allylamine; inhibits squalene epoxidase.

questions.stem: Which enzyme do azole antifungals such as fluconazole inhibit?
questions.explanation: Azoles inhibit the fungal cytochrome P-450 enzyme 14α-demethylase (lanosterol → ergosterol), damaging the cell membrane; CYP-450 inhibition also explains their drug–drug interactions. A: Target of allylamines (terbinafine). B: Target of echinocandins. C: Blocked by flucytosine's metabolite 5-FdUMP. D: No antifungal class in the lecture targets it.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man with diabetic ketoacidosis develops facial pain, fever and a black necrotic lesion on the nasal mucosa. Biopsy shows broad, irregular, nonseptate hyphae branching at right angles. Blood cultures are negative. Besides correcting the ketoacidosis, what is the most appropriate management?

options.D: Surgical debridement plus lipid amphotericin B
options.E: Amphotericin B plus flucytosine, then fluconazole

questions.explanation: Broad, nonseptate, right-angle hyphae in a diabetic with ketoacidosis indicate mucormycosis (Zygomycetes); treatment combines aggressive surgical debridement with lipid amphotericin B (or posaconazole). Blood cultures are of no benefit. A: Fluconazole is mainly for Candida. B: Echinocandins are not active against Zygomycetes. C: Itraconazole is the usual drug for endemic mycoses. E: Induction regimen for cryptococcal meningitis.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old man with HIV (CD4 count 60/µL) has two weeks of headache and fever. Lumbar puncture shows a high opening pressure, and India ink staining of the CSF shows encapsulated yeasts. Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.C: Amphotericin B plus flucytosine for 14 days

questions.explanation: Cryptococcal meningitis is treated with amphotericin B plus flucytosine for 14 days, then oral fluconazole for 8–10 weeks; CSF is removed to keep pressure below 20 cm H2O. A: Echinocandins are not active against Cryptococcus. B: Fluconazole is the consolidation step, not induction. D: Extended-spectrum triazole aimed at Aspergillus and other moulds. E: Management of mucormycosis.

questions.stem: Which CSF test is the most sensitive for diagnosing cryptococcal meningitis?
questions.explanation: Cryptococcal antigen by latex agglutination in CSF has a sensitivity of >90%. B: India ink shows encapsulated yeasts but is only 50–75% sensitive. C: Galactomannan is a cell-wall antigen used for Aspergillus. D: Distinguishes C. albicans from non-albicans Candida. E: A rapid test to speciate Candida.

questions.stem: Which patient with proven invasive candidiasis should receive an echinocandin rather than fluconazole as initial therapy?

options.A: A patient with mild illness and no previous azole exposure
options.B: A neutropenic patient who is severely ill
options.C: A patient with suspected CNS involvement
options.D: A patient with asymptomatic candiduria and a urinary catheter
options.E: A young non-diabetic patient at low risk for C. glabrata

questions.explanation: Neutropenia, severe illness, or suspected cardiac valve/myocardial involvement call for an echinocandin or an amphotericin formulation first. A, E: These are the criteria for first-line fluconazole. C: Give amphotericin B; echinocandins penetrate the CNS poorly. D: Modify risk factors; it rarely requires treatment.

questions.stem: A farmer from the Mississippi valley has chronic cough and skin lesions. Tissue biopsy shows large (8–15 µm) yeasts with a single daughter cell attached by a broad base. Culture at room temperature grows a mould. Which organism is most likely?
questions.explanation: Blastomyces is a dimorphic endemic fungus of the Ohio/Mississippi valleys: mould in the environment, large yeast with broad-based budding in tissue. A: Same region, but small (2–3 µm) intracellular budding yeasts. B: Not dimorphic; capsule with a narrow pore between mother and daughter. C: US Southwest; non-budding spherules with endospores. D: Latin America; multiple buds on one mother cell.

questions.stem: During treatment of invasive fungal infection, a patient develops a rising creatinine with low serum potassium and magnesium. Which drug is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Polyene toxicity is nephrotoxicity, hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia; lipid (especially liposomal) formulations are less nephrotoxic. A: Echinocandins have a good safety profile. B: Causes bone marrow suppression. C: Causes blurry vision; azoles also cause liver toxicity and drug interactions. E: Azole toxicity is mainly hepatic and drug interactions, not renal wasting.

questions.stem: A researcher measures how quickly an oral drug reaches its peak plasma concentration and how long the kidneys take to clear it. Which field is being studied?
questions.explanation: Absorption and excretion are what the body does to the drug: pharmacokinetics (ADME). A: Pharmacodynamics is what the drug does to the body. B: Pharmacogenomics is how genes change response or dose. C: Pharmacoepidemiology is drug behavior across populations. E: Pharmaceutics is drug formulation and delivery.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes how pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics relate to each other?

options.A: Pharmacokinetics sets the drug concentration at the site of action; pharmacodynamics translates that concentration into an effect
options.B: Pharmacodynamics sets the drug concentration at the site of action; pharmacokinetics translates it into an effect
options.C: Both describe what the body does to the drug
options.D: Pharmacokinetics describes receptor binding; pharmacodynamics describes drug excretion
options.E: Both describe what the drug does to the body

questions.explanation: PK (body → drug) determines the concentration available at the site of action; PD (drug → body) turns that concentration into effect. B: Reverses the two. C: Only PK is what the body does to the drug; PD is the reverse. D: Receptor binding is PD and excretion is PK. E: Only PD is what the drug does to the body; PK is the reverse.

questions.stem: A patient needs a much lower dose of a drug than most patients because of an inherited variant in the gene for the enzyme that inactivates it. Which discipline best explains this?
questions.explanation: Pharmacogenomics explains why a patient's DNA changes their dose. A: Pharmacoepidemiology looks at drug behavior across whole populations, not one patient's genotype. B: Pharmaceutics is formulation and delivery. C: Toxicology is detecting and treating poisoning. D: Pharmacoeconomics asks whether a drug is worth its cost.

questions.stem: A health ministry compares the price and health outcomes of two antihypertensives to decide which one to reimburse. Which discipline does this analysis belong to?
questions.explanation: Pharmacoeconomics asks whether a drug is worth what it costs. A: Pharmacoepidemiology describes how drugs behave across populations, not cost. B: Pharmacy is preparing, verifying and dispensing drugs. D: Pharmaceutics is formulation and delivery. E: Pharmacodynamics is the drug's effect on the body.

questions.stem: Which historical event most directly led to mandatory teratogenicity testing before drug approval?

options.A: Withering's study of foxglove for dropsy
options.C: The compilation of the Ebers Papyrus
options.D: The isolation of aspirin's active compound from willow bark
options.E: Medicinal cultivation of the opium poppy in Sumer

questions.explanation: Thalidomide, given for morning sickness without fetal testing, caused severe limb malformations; mandatory trial phases, teratogenicity testing and informed consent laws followed. A: Withering established systematic dose testing, not teratogenicity rules. C: The Ebers Papyrus is an ancient list of remedies. D: Willow bark is the origin of aspirin, unrelated to fetal safety rules. E: Opium use in Sumer is ancient history with no regulatory consequence.

questions.stem: William Withering's lasting contribution to pharmacology was best described as:

options.A: The first chemical synthesis of a drug
options.B: Creating the first national drug-approval agency
options.D: Systematic dose testing in patients with recorded outcomes
options.E: Introducing informed consent for clinical trials

questions.explanation: Withering spent nearly a decade testing foxglove doses on patients, recording benefit and harm: observe, dose, record, adjust. A: He identified a plant ingredient; he didn't synthesize a drug. B: Drug agencies came later. C: Receptor theory is unrelated to his work. E: Informed consent laws followed thalidomide in the 1960s.

questions.stem: A newborn has severely shortened limbs with the hands attached close to the shoulders. Early in pregnancy, the mother took a sedative prescribed abroad for nausea. The same drug is now used to treat multiple myeloma. Which drug is it?
questions.explanation: Thalidomide, marketed as a sedative for morning sickness, caused severe limb malformations (phocomelia); its current use in multiple myeloma is on the drug-development lecture (L14) slides. The other teratogens below are outside the slides (standard Step 1 facts). A: Isotretinoin causes craniofacial, CNS and cardiac defects. B: Valproate causes neural tube defects. D: Warfarin causes nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses. E: Lithium causes Ebstein anomaly.

questions.stem: Drug X produces 50% of its effect at 1 mg and plateaus at 60% of the maximal tissue response. Drug Y produces 50% of its effect at 10 mg and plateaus at 100%. Which statement is correct?

options.A: X is more potent and more efficacious
options.B: X is more potent; Y is more efficacious
options.C: Y is more potent; X is more efficacious
options.D: Y is more potent and more efficacious
options.E: The two drugs have equal efficacy

questions.explanation: Potency = the dose needed for an effect (X needs less, so it's more potent); efficacy = the maximal effect regardless of dose (Y reaches the higher plateau). A: X's plateau is lower, so it's less efficacious. C: Reverses both properties. D: Y needs a 10× higher dose, so it's less potent. E: The plateaus differ (60% vs 100%).

questions.stem: Propranolol, a beta-blocker, blunts the heart's response to a beta-agonist but triggers no receptor response on its own. In terms of the two receptor properties, propranolol has:
questions.explanation: An antagonist has affinity (it binds, so it can block the agonist) but no intrinsic activity (binding triggers nothing). A: Affinity plus full intrinsic activity is a full agonist (e.g., beta-agonists). B: Partial intrinsic activity is a partial agonist, which would itself produce a submaximal response. C: A drug can't trigger a response without binding first. D: Without affinity it couldn't occupy the receptor and block the agonist.

questions.stem: A new antihypertensive lowers blood pressure markedly in a tightly controlled randomized trial. In routine clinics, its effect is much smaller because patients skip doses and have multiple comorbidities. Which pair of terms describes the trial result and the clinic result?
questions.explanation: Efficacy = whether a drug can work under ideal trial conditions; effectiveness = whether it does work in the real world. B: Potency is the dose needed for an effect, not trial vs real-world performance. C: Reverses the two. D: Cost-effectiveness is value for money (e.g., QALYs). E: Affinity and intrinsic activity are receptor properties.

questions.stem: In the 7-step therapeutic plan, a physician has just chosen the optimal plan for a 70-year-old woman with pneumonia. Which step comes next?
questions.explanation: The order is problem identification → desired outcome → therapeutic tools → therapeutic alternatives → optimal plan → outcome evaluation → patient education. A: Step 1. B: Step 2. D: Step 4, before the plan is chosen. E: Step 3.

questions.stem: A partial agonist is given at a concentration high enough to occupy all of its receptors. Which response is expected?

options.A: Zero response, because it blocks the receptor
options.C: A response above the full agonist's Emax
options.D: A submaximal response, below the full agonist's Emax
options.E: A full response, but only at a higher dose than the full agonist

questions.explanation: Partial agonists can't achieve full Emax even at saturating concentrations. A: Zero response at full occupancy describes an antagonist. B: 100% Emax is a full agonist. C: No agonist exceeds the system's maximal response. E: Needing a higher dose for the same maximum describes lower potency, not partial agonism.

questions.stem: Drug P is a partial agonist and drug F a full agonist at the same receptor. Both produce half of their own maximal effect at 1 mg. Which statement is correct?

options.A: P and F are equally potent, but P is less efficacious
options.B: P is less potent and less efficacious than F
options.C: P and F are equally efficacious, but P is less potent
options.D: P is more potent than F because it reaches its plateau sooner
options.E: P has no intrinsic activity, so it is an antagonist

questions.explanation: Potency is about the dose needed (same here); efficacy is the maximal effect, and a partial agonist can't reach full Emax even at saturating concentrations, yet it may appear equally potent. B: Equal doses for half-maximal effect mean equal potency. C: Reverses the two properties. D: Potency is judged by the dose for a given effect, not by when a lower plateau is reached. E: A partial agonist has some intrinsic activity; an antagonist has none.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man's blood pressure falls from 160/100 to 135/85 mmHg on metoprolol, a beta-blocker. A classmate says metoprolol has "0% efficacy" at the β-receptor. What best reconciles the two?

options.A: Metoprolol is a partial agonist with about 55% relative Emax
options.B: Metoprolol has no affinity for β-receptors; its effect isn't receptor-mediated
options.C: Zero molecular efficacy, yet clinically effective by blocking the receptor
options.D: It is efficacious only in trials; clinic results reflect effectiveness
options.E: It is highly potent, and potency replaces the need for efficacy

questions.explanation: An antagonist has 0% relative Emax at the molecular level but still "works" clinically; clinical and molecular definitions of efficacy differ. A: A partial agonist would itself stimulate the receptor; beta-blockers are antagonists. B: Antagonists have affinity; that's how they block. D: Efficacy vs effectiveness is about trial vs real-world conditions, not molecular vs clinical efficacy. E: Potency is the dose needed for an effect and doesn't explain zero intrinsic activity.

questions.stem: A weak acid drug with a pKa of 4.4 is in gastric juice at pH 1.4. What is the approximate ratio of unionized to ionized drug?
questions.explanation: pKa − pH = 4.4 − 1.4 = 3 = log(HA/A⁻), so HA : A⁻ = 10³ : 1. When pH < pKa, a weak acid is mostly unionized. A: Inverts the ratio; that would apply to a weak base, or to an acid at pH 7.4. B: A difference of 3 log units is 1000, not 100. D: Subtracting the values without taking the antilog. E: 1 : 1 only when pH = pKa.

questions.stem: A patient arrives after an overdose of phenobarbital, a weak acid that is renally excreted. Which intervention will most increase its urinary elimination?

options.A: Ammonium chloride to acidify the urine
options.E: IV sodium bicarbonate to alkalinize the urine

questions.explanation: Alkaline urine ionizes a weak acid, so it can't be reabsorbed across the tubule (ion trapping) and is excreted. A: Acidifying the urine keeps weak acids unionized → more reabsorption, less elimination. B: Metoclopramide speeds gastric emptying; it doesn't affect renal elimination. C: Fluid restriction lowers urine flow. D: Calcium carbonate acts in the gut and doesn't meaningfully trap the drug in urine.

questions.stem: An oral drug has a bioavailability (F) of 20% and a hepatic extraction ratio (ER) of 0.75. What fraction of the dose is absorbed from the gut (f)?
questions.explanation: F = f × (1 − ER) → 0.20 = f × 0.25 → f = 0.80. A: 0.20 × 0.75 multiplies F by ER, the wrong operation. C: 25% is (1 − ER), not f. D: 0.20 × 0.25 multiplies by (1 − ER) instead of dividing. E: Divides F by ER instead of by (1 − ER).

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes active transport from facilitated diffusion?

options.A: It can move drug against its concentration gradient using energy
options.D: It is used by glucose and amino acids
options.E: It occurs at the blood–brain barrier

questions.explanation: Active transport uses energy (ATP) and doesn't need a concentration gradient; facilitated diffusion moves only down the gradient with no energy. B: Both are carrier-mediated. C: Both are saturable. D: Glucose and amino acids are the lecture's examples of facilitated diffusion. E: Carrier-mediated transport of both kinds occurs at the BBB.

questions.stem: A patient has an acute angina attack. Oral nitroglycerin has a bioavailability of only ~10% because of first-pass metabolism. Which route gives the fastest effective relief?
questions.explanation: Sublingual absorption drains into the systemic circulation, bypassing the liver, and nitroglycerin acts within 2–3 minutes. B: Transdermal also avoids first pass, but absorption is very slow; patches are for prevention, not acute attacks. A, D, E: All oral forms pass through the portal circulation, so ~90% is destroyed before reaching the systemic circulation; SR and enteric coating also delay onset.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old starts an oral drug that normally undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism. Compared with a young adult, how is the oral bioavailability likely to change?

options.A: Decreased, because gastric emptying is faster
options.B: Increased, because first-pass metabolism is reduced
options.C: Decreased, because gastric acid is increased
options.D: Unchanged, because first-pass metabolism doesn't change with age
options.E: Decreased, because slower GI motility shortens absorption time

questions.explanation: In the elderly ↓ first-pass metabolism → ↑ bioavailability. A: GI motility is decreased in the elderly, not faster. C: Gastric acid is decreased in the elderly, not increased. D: First-pass metabolism declines with age. E: Slower motility lengthens absorption time.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman takes levothyroxine with breakfast together with her calcium supplement. After 3 months she is still hypothyroid. What is the best advice?

options.A: Double the levothyroxine dose and keep the same timing
options.B: Take it with the largest meal of the day instead
options.C: Crush the tablet and take it with a glass of milk
options.D: Take it fasting, 30 min before breakfast, apart from calcium
options.E: Replace the calcium supplement with an antacid at breakfast
