questions.explanation: Food and calcium reduce levothyroxine absorption; timing and separation fix the problem. A medication failure is often an absorption or interaction issue, not the drug. A: Raising the dose ignores the interaction. B: More food further reduces absorption. C: Milk adds calcium. E: Antacids also bind and reduce absorption.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with acne has no improvement after 2 months of oral doxycycline. She takes each dose with a glass of milk and an antacid for stomach upset. What best explains the treatment failure?

options.A: Chelation of the drug by divalent cations, reducing absorption
options.D: Increased plasma protein binding of the drug
options.E: Bacterial resistance due to efflux pumps

questions.explanation: Tetracyclines (and fluoroquinolones) bind Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ and Fe²⁺ in the gut, forming poorly absorbed chelates. B: Calcium doesn't induce CYP3A4. C: No P-gp induction occurs here. D: Milk doesn't change plasma protein binding. E: Resistance is possible but doesn't explain the clear interaction with milk and antacids.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with cirrhosis and large portosystemic collaterals develops marked toxicity from his usual oral dose of a drug with a high hepatic extraction ratio. The IV dose has never caused problems. What best explains this?

options.A: Reduced gut absorption from bowel-wall edema
options.E: Increased oral bioavailability because portal blood bypasses the liver

questions.explanation: Shunting lets absorbed drug skip first-pass extraction, so oral F rises sharply while the IV dose (no first pass) is unaffected. A: Reduced absorption would lower levels. B: Increased renal clearance would lower levels. C: Enzyme induction would lower levels. D: Slower emptying delays absorption but doesn't raise total exposure this much.

questions.stem: A patient needs a faster onset from an oral analgesic tablet. Which co-administered factor would most speed its delivery to the duodenum for absorption?
questions.explanation: Metoclopramide accelerates gastric emptying, delivering the drug sooner to the upper small intestine, the main absorption site. B: Anticholinergics slow gastric emptying. C: Morphine slows gastric emptying. D: Hot drinks slow emptying; cold drinks speed it. E: Intensive exercise slows emptying; moderate exercise speeds it.

questions.stem: A 60-kg patient receives 600 mg of a drug as an IV bolus. The extrapolated plasma concentration at time zero is 20 mg/L. Where is this drug most likely distributed?

options.D: Concentrated in tissues far beyond body water
options.E: Bound almost entirely to plasma albumin

questions.explanation: Vd = 600 mg / 20 mg/L = 30 L = 0.5 L/kg, close to total body water (~0.55 L/kg). A: Plasma is ~0.05 L/kg. B: ECF is ~0.2 L/kg. D: Tissue concentration gives Vd > ~1 L/kg. E: Extensive albumin binding keeps Vd near plasma volume.

questions.stem: A patient stable on phenytoin (a weak acid, highly bound to albumin) develops severe hepatic disease with low serum albumin. The total phenytoin level is unchanged. What is the main risk?

options.B: Toxicity from an increased free fraction
options.E: No change, because total levels are normal

questions.explanation: Low albumin → fewer binding sites → more free (active) drug even at the same total level. A: Binding falls, not rises. C: Protein binding doesn't govern GI absorption. D: More free drug means more is available to cross into tissues. E: The total level hides the rise in free drug.

questions.stem: A patient on propranolol, a weak base, is admitted with an acute severe illness. How is the free (unbound) fraction of propranolol most likely to change?

options.B: Increase, because α1-acid glycoprotein synthesis falls
options.D: Decrease, because α1-acid glycoprotein synthesis rises
options.E: No change, because weak bases don't bind plasma proteins

questions.explanation: Weak bases bind mainly the positively charged α1-acid glycoprotein, whose synthesis increases during an acute insult → more binding, lower free fraction. A: Albumin falls in acute illness but binds mainly weak acids (phenytoin, salicylates). B: α1-acid glycoprotein rises, not falls. C: Albumin falls, and it isn't propranolol's main carrier. E: Weak bases bind α1-acid glycoprotein (e.g., quinidine, propranolol).

questions.stem: Domperidone, a dopamine antagonist that doesn't cross the blood–brain barrier, still relieves nausea through a central site. What best explains this?

options.A: It is highly lipid-soluble and diffuses through the tight junctions
options.B: The chemoreceptor trigger zone lies where the barrier is leaky
options.C: P-glycoprotein pumps it into the brain
options.D: Brain endothelial MAO and COMT convert it to an active metabolite
options.E: Nausea makes the barrier leaky everywhere

questions.explanation: The BBB is leaky at the chemoreceptor trigger zone, so domperidone (and apomorphine) can act there without entering the rest of the brain. A: If it diffused freely it would cross the BBB everywhere. C: P-gp is an efflux pump that keeps drugs out of the brain. D: Endothelial MAO and COMT neutralize drugs; they are part of the barrier. E: Infection, not nausea, is the pathological factor that makes the barrier leakier.

questions.stem: A pregnant woman takes a weakly basic drug. At equilibrium, the fetal plasma concentration of the drug is higher than the maternal concentration. What best explains this?

options.A: Fetal plasma is more alkaline, trapping the ionized base
options.B: P-glycoprotein actively pumps the drug into the fetus
options.C: The placenta is completely impermeable to acids
options.D: Fetal plasma is slightly more acidic, trapping the ionized base
options.E: Fetal albumin binds bases more strongly

questions.explanation: In the slightly more acidic fetal plasma, a base becomes more ionized and can't diffuse back (ion trapping). A: Alkaline plasma would keep a base unionized. B: P-gp exports drugs and limits fetal exposure. C: The placenta isn't an absolute barrier. E: Albumin binds mainly acids.

questions.stem: After an overdose of imipramine (Vd > 10 L/kg), hemodialysis removes very little drug. What best explains this?

options.A: Imipramine is confined to plasma, bound to albumin
options.B: Imipramine distributes only in total body water
options.C: Most of the drug is concentrated in tissues, so little is in plasma
options.D: A large Vd means the drug is eliminated too quickly to need dialysis
options.E: Imipramine is a large protein that can't cross dialysis membranes

questions.explanation: A Vd far above total body water (> 1 L/kg) means the drug is concentrated in tissues; only a small fraction is in plasma, where dialysis acts. A: Plasma-confined drugs (heparin, insulin) have Vd ~0.05–0.1 L/kg. B: Total body water corresponds to ~0.55 L/kg (e.g., ethanol). D: Vd describes distribution, not speed of elimination. E: Imipramine is a small lipophilic drug, not a protein.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old man with decompensated heart failure and marked peripheral edema receives a standard weight-based IV dose of gentamicin, a water-soluble antibiotic. His peak plasma level is lower than expected. Why?

options.C: Increased P-glycoprotein efflux in the gut
options.D: Faster renal clearance from heart failure
options.E: Increased Vd from expanded extracellular water

questions.explanation: Edema expands extracellular water, so a water-soluble drug spreads into a larger apparent Vd → lower peak concentration. A: Gentamicin has low protein binding, and less binding wouldn't lower the peak. B: There is no first pass after IV dosing. C: Gut P-gp is irrelevant to an IV drug. D: Heart failure tends to reduce renal clearance.

questions.stem: A pilot with allergic rhinitis is switched from diphenhydramine to loratadine and no longer feels drowsy. Which property of loratadine best explains this?

options.A: It doesn't cross the blood–brain barrier well
options.B: It is a competitive H2 antagonist
options.C: It has much lower plasma protein binding
options.D: It is excreted unchanged by the kidney
options.E: It has a very small volume of distribution

questions.explanation: Second-generation H1 antihistamines are less lipophilic and are P-gp substrates, so little reaches the CNS; first-generation agents are lipophilic and cross the BBB. B: Loratadine is an H1 antagonist. C: Lower binding would increase free drug and wouldn't explain less sedation. D: The route of excretion doesn't determine CNS entry. E: A small Vd isn't the reason it spares the brain.

questions.stem: In Parkinson disease, the brain needs more dopamine, yet patients are given levodopa (L-DOPA) rather than dopamine. Why?

options.A: Dopamine is too lipid-soluble and stays in body fat
options.B: L-DOPA is small enough to diffuse through the BBB tight junctions
options.C: L-DOPA enters the brain via LAT1, then becomes dopamine
options.D: The BBB is leaky in Parkinson disease, but only for L-DOPA
options.E: Dopamine crosses the BBB but is pumped back out by P-glycoprotein

questions.explanation: Dopamine can't cross the BBB; L-DOPA is carried across by the LAT1 transporter and then converted to dopamine inside the brain. A: Dopamine is blocked by the BBB, not trapped in fat. B: L-DOPA needs a transporter; it isn't simple diffusion. D: Infection, not Parkinson disease, is the lecture's example of a leakier barrier. E: Dopamine is simply blocked; the lecture lists it among substances that don't cross.

questions.stem: A lipid-soluble drug undergoes a phase I reaction followed by glucuronidation. Compared with the parent drug, the final glucuronide conjugate is most likely:

options.A: More lipid-soluble and reabsorbed in the renal tubule
options.B: Polar, pharmacologically inactive, and excreted in bile or urine
options.C: Chemically reactive and potentially toxic or carcinogenic
options.D: More pharmacologically active than the parent drug
options.E: Stored in body fat until it is metabolized further

questions.explanation: Phase II conjugates are almost always inactive, highly water-soluble, and excreted in bile (> 300 Da) or urine (< 300 Da). A: Both phases decrease lipid solubility, which limits tubular reabsorption. C: Chemically reactive, possibly toxic products are typical of phase I. D: Active metabolites arise mainly from phase I (e.g., codeine → morphine); phase II products are usually inactive. E: Polar conjugates don't accumulate in fat.

questions.stem: Which reaction is a phase II metabolic reaction?
questions.explanation: Acetylation is a conjugation (synthetic) reaction, as are glucuronidation, sulfation, methylation, and glutathione/glycine conjugation. B: Oxidation is phase I (functionalization). C: Hydrolysis is phase I. D: Reduction is phase I. E: Deamination is phase I.

questions.stem: A patient stable on warfarin is started on rifampin for tuberculosis. Two weeks later the INR has fallen below target. What is the mechanism?

options.D: Increased vitamin K synthesis by gut flora
options.E: Induction of hepatic enzymes that metabolize warfarin

questions.explanation: Rifampin is a classic inducer: more microsomal enzyme → faster warfarin clearance → lower levels and INR over time. A: Inhibition would raise the INR. B: Displacement would transiently raise free warfarin and the INR. C: Rifampin doesn't meaningfully block warfarin absorption. D: Not the mechanism of this interaction.

questions.stem: Grapefruit juice markedly raises blood levels of oral felodipine but not of IV felodipine. What explains the difference?
questions.explanation: Grapefruit blocks CYP3A4 in the gut wall, so only orally given drug escapes presystemic metabolism. A: The wrong isoform and site. B: Induction of renal P-gp would lower levels, not raise them. C: Protein displacement wouldn't depend on the route. E: Glucuronidation doesn't happen in plasma and isn't the mechanism.

questions.stem: A patient taking lovastatin develops muscle pain a week after starting erythromycin. Which mechanism best explains this?
questions.explanation: Statins are CYP3A4 substrates ("3A4 SICS"); erythromycin inhibits their metabolism → ↑ statin levels → muscle toxicity. A: Induction would lower statin levels. B: CYP2C9 handles warfarin, NSAIDs and sulfonylureas. C: CYP2D6 handles codeine, antidepressants, tamoxifen and β-blockers. E: CYP2C19 handles PPIs and phenytoin (and clopidogrel, outside the slides).

questions.stem: An 80-year-old taking diazepam nightly becomes increasingly drowsy over several weeks at the same dose. Which combination of age-related changes best explains this?

options.A: ↓ hepatic microsomal activity and ↑ Vd of lipid-soluble drugs

questions.explanation: Aging reduces microsomal (phase I) activity and increases Vd of lipophilic drugs (more fat), so diazepam accumulates with repeated doses. B: Both changes go the other way. C: Diazepam is lipophilic and not cleared unchanged by the kidney; renal function also declines with age. D: Lower absorption would reduce drowsiness. E: More conjugation would speed clearance.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man has a coronary stent placed and is discharged on clopidogrel. His primary physician adds omeprazole for dyspepsia. Months later he has stent thrombosis. Which mechanism most likely contributed?

options.A: Omeprazole induced CYP3A4, accelerating clopidogrel clearance
options.C: Omeprazole raised gastric pH, preventing clopidogrel absorption
options.D: Omeprazole inhibited CYP2C19, reducing activation of clopidogrel

questions.explanation: Clopidogrel is a prodrug activated by CYP2C19; omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19 → less active metabolite → weaker platelet inhibition. A: Omeprazole isn't a meaningful CYP3A4 inducer here. B: Displacement wouldn't reduce antiplatelet effect long-term. C: The interaction is metabolic, not absorption-based. E: The P2Y12 receptor is clopidogrel's target, not omeprazole's.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with chronic heavy alcohol use takes regular therapeutic doses of acetaminophen for a week and develops liver injury. What best explains his susceptibility?

options.A: Alcohol inhibits acetaminophen metabolism, so the parent drug accumulates
options.C: Alcohol increases glucuronidation, making inactive conjugates
options.D: Alcohol decreases the Vd of acetaminophen
options.E: Alcohol induces microsomal enzymes, increasing toxic NAPQI formation

questions.explanation: Chronic alcohol induces microsomal enzymes; acetaminophen is toxified to NAPQI, so induction increases toxicity (the lecture's alcohol → acetaminophen → liver toxicity example). A: Inhibition by chronic alcohol isn't the mechanism, and the parent drug isn't the hepatotoxin. B: Protein displacement doesn't create a toxic metabolite. C: More inactive conjugates would be protective. D: A Vd change doesn't explain hepatotoxicity.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman taking fluoxetine, a CYP2D6 inhibitor, gets almost no pain relief from codeine after a dental extraction. What best explains this?

options.A: Fluoxetine induces codeine metabolism to inactive products
options.B: Fluoxetine displaces codeine from plasma proteins
options.C: Reduced conversion of codeine to morphine, its active metabolite
options.D: Codeine accumulates as the parent drug and blocks opioid receptors
options.E: Fluoxetine inhibits phase II glucuronidation of codeine

questions.explanation: Codeine is converted by CYP2D6 to morphine, which provides the analgesia; inhibiting CYP2D6 reduces this activation. A: Fluoxetine is an inhibitor, not an inducer. B: Displacement would increase free drug, not reduce its effect. D: Codeine isn't a receptor blocker; higher parent levels don't explain lost analgesia. E: Glucuronidation inactivates drugs; inhibiting it wouldn't reduce activation.

questions.stem: Morphine, which is excreted mainly as a glucuronide, is not used as an analgesic during labor. What is the reason?

options.A: Neonatal enzymes are immature, so morphine is cleared slowly
options.B: Neonates have higher CYP3A4 activity, producing toxic metabolites
options.C: Morphine is a prodrug activated only in the fetal liver
options.D: The placenta metabolizes morphine to an active toxin

questions.explanation: Several enzymes have low activity in neonates (especially premature ones) and need at least 8 weeks to reach adult levels, so morphine that crosses to the baby isn't cleared. B: Neonatal enzyme activity is lower, not higher. C: Morphine is already active; codeine is the prodrug example. D: The issue is neonatal clearance, not placental toxification. E: Binding isn't the reason given; reduced metabolism is.

questions.stem: A drug's urine concentration is 20 mg/mL, urine flow is 1 mL/min, and plasma concentration is 0.2 mg/mL. What is its renal clearance?
questions.explanation: Cx = (Ux × V) / Px = (20 × 1) / 0.2 = 100 mL/min. A: Multiplies Ux × V × Px. B: Inverts the ratio (Px / Ux). C: Ux × V is the excretion rate (mg/min), not a clearance. E: Assumes clearance equals GFR without calculating.

questions.stem: A substance is freely filtered at the glomerulus but completely reabsorbed by the tubules, with no secretion. What is its renal clearance?
questions.explanation: If everything filtered is reabsorbed, no plasma is cleared of it; glucose is the classic example. B: Clearance = GFR when a substance is filtered with no reabsorption or secretion (e.g., inulin). C: Clearance ≈ RPF needs filtration plus near-complete secretion. D: Renal clearance can't exceed RPF. E: Urine flow isn't a clearance value here.

questions.stem: A patient overdoses on digitoxin, a drug that undergoes extensive enterohepatic recirculation. Which intervention best increases its elimination?

options.D: Giving a drug that blocks organic cation transporters
options.E: Repeated oral activated charcoal or cholestyramine

questions.explanation: Binding agents in the gut trap drug released into bile, interrupting recirculation → ↑ fecal excretion. A: Urine alkalinization targets renally excreted weak acids. B: β-glucuronidase would free more drug for reabsorption and worsen recirculation. C: Acidification doesn't affect biliary recycling. D: Blocking OCTs would, if anything, reduce renal secretion.

questions.stem: A drug is 95% bound to plasma albumin. Which renal process can still remove it efficiently and lower its plasma concentration toward zero?

options.D: Filtration through pores in the collecting duct
options.E: Diffusion across the glomerular basement membrane

questions.explanation: Carrier-mediated tubular secretion works against the gradient, is the most effective renal elimination mechanism, and can strip drug from plasma. A: Only free drug is filtered, so binding limits filtration (e.g., warfarin). C: Reabsorption returns drug to the blood. D: The collecting duct doesn't filter through pores. E: Albumin-bound drug can't cross the GBM.

questions.stem: Drugs secreted by the same renal tubular carrier can compete with each other. Which pair is most likely to compete for tubular secretion?
questions.explanation: Both are organic anion transporter substrates (PUMA: Penicillin, Uric acid, Methotrexate, Aminohippuric acid). A: Morphine uses organic cation transporters (MATH). B: Amiloride is an OCT substrate. D: Morphine is OCT; uric acid is OAT. E: Triamterene is OCT; aminohippuric acid is OAT.

questions.stem: A drug has a total body clearance of 600 mL/min and a renal clearance of 150 mL/min. What is its nonrenal clearance?
questions.explanation: ClT = ClR + ClNR → ClNR = 600 − 150 = 450 mL/min. B: Repeats the renal clearance. C: That's total clearance. D: Adds instead of subtracting. E: Divides the two values.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old woman on weekly low-dose methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis is started on probenecid for gout. Two weeks later she has mouth ulcers and pancytopenia. What is the most likely mechanism?

options.A: Probenecid induced hepatic metabolism of methotrexate
options.B: Probenecid increased glomerular filtration of methotrexate
options.C: Probenecid displaced methotrexate from P-glycoprotein in the gut
options.D: Probenecid inhibited renal tubular secretion of methotrexate via OATs

questions.explanation: Probenecid competes for basolateral organic anion transporters, reducing secretion of OAT substrates (methotrexate, penicillin) → accumulation and toxicity. A: Induction would lower levels. B: More filtration would lower levels. C: Not the mechanism. E: Probenecid doesn't meaningfully alkalinize urine; alkalinization would actually aid methotrexate excretion.

questions.stem: Para-aminohippuric acid (PAH) is both filtered and almost completely secreted in a single pass through the kidney. Its clearance is therefore used to estimate which quantity?
questions.explanation: Almost all PAH reaching the kidney is removed, so its clearance ≈ renal plasma flow, the theoretical maximum clearance. A: GFR is estimated by inulin or creatinine, which are filtered but not secreted. C: Filtration fraction = GFR/RPF and needs both values. D: Water reabsorption isn't measured by PAH. E: Cardiac output isn't derived from PAH clearance.

questions.stem: A drug has a hepatic extraction ratio of 0.8. Hepatic blood flow is 1.5 L/min. What is its hepatic clearance?
questions.explanation: Liver clearance = flow × ER = 1.5 × 0.8 = 1.2 L/min. A: Uses (1 − ER) instead of ER. C: Assumes complete extraction (ER = 1). D: Calculates 1.5 / 0.8, dividing instead of multiplying. E: Calculates 0.8 / 1.5, dividing ER by flow.

questions.stem: A drug is eliminated by zero-order kinetics with k0 = 10 mg/L per hour, starting at 100 mg/L. How long does it take to fall from 100 to 50 mg/L, and then from 50 to 25 mg/L?
questions.explanation: Zero-order: a constant amount (10 mg/L) is removed each hour, so t½ = 0.5C0/k0: 50/10 = 5 h, then 25/10 = 2.5 h. The half-life shortens as concentration falls. A: A constant half-life is a first-order feature. B: Treats the drug as first-order with a constant half-life; zero-order t½ isn't constant. D: Uses C0/k0 (time to reach zero), not 0.5C0/k0. E: Reverses the trend; zero-order t½ gets shorter, not longer.

questions.stem: A drug follows first-order kinetics with a Vd of 40 L and a clearance of 4 L/h. What is its half-life?
questions.explanation: t½ = 0.693 × Vd / CL = 0.693 × 40 / 4 ≈ 6.9 h. A: Inverts the ratio (CL/Vd × 0.693). B: Omits 0.693 (Vd/CL only). C: Divides by 0.693 instead of multiplying. D: Multiplies 0.693 by Vd but forgets to divide by CL.

questions.stem: A drug with first-order elimination and a half-life of 8 hours is started as a constant IV infusion without a loading dose. About how long until it reaches 95% of its steady-state concentration?
questions.explanation: 95% of Css takes ~4.32 half-lives → 4.32 × 8 ≈ 35 h. B: One half-life gives 50%. C: Two half-lives give 75%. D: Three half-lives give 87.5%. E: ~6.6 half-lives (53 h) is needed for 99%.

questions.stem: A drug given by IV infusion has a Vd of 50 L and a clearance of 5 L/h. A plasma concentration of 10 mg/L is needed quickly. What loading dose should be given?
questions.explanation: Loading dose = Vd × Ctarget = 50 L × 10 mg/L = 500 mg; clearance sets the maintenance rate, not the loading dose. A: Divides Vd by Ctarget. B: CL × Ctarget is the maintenance infusion rate (50 mg/h). C: Multiplies Vd by CL. E: Overestimates by 10×.

questions.stem: An oral drug (F = 0.5) has a clearance of 2 L/h. The target average steady-state concentration is 15 mg/L, given every 12 hours. What maintenance dose is needed?
questions.explanation: Dose = Css × CL × τ / F = 15 × 2 × 12 / 0.5 = 720 mg. A: Ignores F and halves the result. C: Ignores F (the IV dose). D: Omits the dosing interval. E: Corrects for F twice.

questions.stem: A drug following first-order kinetics is given repeatedly at a dosing interval equal to its half-life. What is the accumulation factor (R)?
questions.explanation: Half of each dose is lost per interval → R = 1 / fraction lost = 1 / 0.5 = 2. A: R ≈ 1 only when the interval is ≥ 5 half-lives. B: R = 1.5 needs a longer interval (~1.6 half-lives). C: R = 3 needs an interval shorter than one half-life. D: Not consistent with dosing every half-life.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with epilepsy has a phenytoin level of 12 mg/L. Her dose is increased by about 15%. Two weeks later she has nystagmus and ataxia, and her level is 28 mg/L. What best explains the disproportionate rise?

options.B: Saturation of the metabolizing enzymes (zero-order kinetics)

questions.explanation: At therapeutic levels phenytoin metabolism nears saturation, so elimination becomes constant-amount (zero-order); small dose increases cause large, unpredictable level jumps. A: Auto-induction would lower levels. C: Vd doesn't change with a small dose increase. D: Bioavailability is already high and doesn't explain non-proportional kinetics. E: Not the mechanism for phenytoin's behavior.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with chronic kidney disease (GFR 25 mL/min) needs a renally cleared drug. Compared with a patient with normal kidneys, how should the loading and maintenance doses be adjusted?

options.A: Loading dose decreased; maintenance dose unchanged
options.D: Loading dose unchanged; maintenance dose decreased
options.E: Loading dose increased; maintenance dose decreased

questions.explanation: Loading dose depends on Vd (unchanged), while maintenance dose depends on clearance (reduced in renal failure). A: Reverses the dependencies. B: Lowering the loading dose would delay reaching target levels. C: Higher maintenance doses would cause accumulation and toxicity. E: There is no reason to raise the loading dose.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with severe renal impairment receives repeated doses of meperidine for pain. On day 3 he develops tremor and a seizure, although his meperidine level is in the usual range. What best explains this?

options.A: Accumulation of an active, toxic metabolite
options.C: Reduced volume of distribution of meperidine
options.E: Displacement of meperidine from plasma proteins

questions.explanation: In renal impairment the metabolite normeperidine accumulates; its toxicity is not predicted by parent-drug levels. B: Saturation would raise the parent-drug level. C: A smaller Vd would also raise the parent-drug level. D: Tolerance reduces the effect; it doesn't cause seizures. E: Displacement gives only a transient rise in free drug and wouldn't depend on renal function.

questions.stem: After an IV bolus, a drug's log plasma concentration–time plot shows a steep initial fall followed by a slower straight-line decline. What does the steep initial phase mainly represent?

options.C: Distribution of drug from plasma into tissues

questions.explanation: This is the two-compartment model: a biexponential decline made of two first-order processes, distribution (early, steep) then elimination (later, linear). A: Both phases are first-order in this model; zero-order elimination would not give a biexponential curve. B: An IV bolus has no absorption phase. D: First-pass metabolism applies to oral drugs. E: Enterohepatic recirculation causes secondary peaks, not an initial steep fall.

questions.stem: A 100-mg oral dose of a drug gives an AUC of 20 mg·h/L. A 25-mg IV dose of the same drug gives an AUC of 10 mg·h/L. What is the absolute oral bioavailability?
questions.explanation: F = (AUC_PO/Dose_PO)/(AUC_IV/Dose_IV) = (20/100)/(10/25) = 0.2/0.4 = 0.5. A: Compares doses only (25/100). C: Uses AUC_IV/Dose_IV (10/25) alone as F. D: 100% would mean complete absorption; dose-normalized AUCs (0.2 vs 0.4 per mg) show only half is absorbed. E: Ignores the different doses (20/10).

questions.stem: A generic and a brand-name product of the same drug are each given at 500 mg. Their AUCs are 90 and 100 mg·h/L, with similar Cmax. What is the generic's relative bioavailability, and are the products bioequivalent by the 20% rule?

options.D: Can't be determined without an IV dose

questions.explanation: Relative F = (90/500)/(100/500) = 0.90; a 10% difference is within 20%, so they are considered bioequivalent. A: The 10% difference is within the limit. B: Inverts the ratio and misjudges equivalence. C: Confuses the difference with the ratio. D: Relative bioavailability doesn't need an IV reference; absolute does.

questions.stem: A 500-mg IV dose of an antibiotic is given. Its Vd is 30 L and k is 0.2 h⁻¹. Over 48 h, 300 mg are recovered unchanged in urine. What is its renal clearance?
questions.explanation: ClT = k × Vd = 0.2 × 30 = 6 L/h; fe = 300/500 = 0.6; ClR = 6 × 0.6 = 3.6 L/h. A: That's total clearance. B: That's nonrenal clearance (6 − 3.6). C: That's kR (0.2 × 0.6), not a clearance. E: Halves the correct value.

questions.stem: A patient on a continuous IV infusion has a target Css of 20 mg/L and a clearance of 2 L/h. After acute kidney injury, clearance falls to 1 L/h. What infusion rate now maintains the same Css?
questions.explanation: Infusion rate = Css × CL: 40 mg/h before, 20 × 1 = 20 mg/h now. B: Halves the rate twice. C: The old rate, which would double Css. D: Wrongly increases the rate. E: Divides CL by Css.

questions.stem: A patient's daily dose of a drug is split from one large dose into four smaller doses, keeping the same total daily amount. What is the main pharmacokinetic effect?

options.C: Smaller fluctuation between peak and trough concentrations

questions.explanation: More frequent, smaller doses narrow the Cmax–Cmin swing; the average Css depends only on total dose rate, F, and CL. A: The average is unchanged. B: Time to Css depends on half-life, not dosing frequency. D: Half-life is a drug property. E: F doesn't change with dose splitting.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation starts oral digoxin (half-life ≈ 36 h in her) at a fixed daily maintenance dose without a loading dose. When will her digoxin level approach steady state?

options.E: Never, because digoxin follows zero-order kinetics

questions.explanation: Steady state takes ~4–5 half-lives: 4–5 × 36 h ≈ 6–7.5 days. A: One half-life gives only 50% of Css. B: ~2 half-lives gives ~75%. C: Far longer than 5 half-lives. E: Digoxin follows first-order kinetics at therapeutic doses.
questions.source: Quantitative PK, slide 37; PK Problem Solving, solution 2c

questions.stem: A 400-mg oral dose of a drug (F = 0.5) is given. Total clearance is 10 L/h. Over 48 h, 100 mg of unchanged drug is recovered in the urine. What is the renal clearance?
questions.explanation: Only the absorbed dose (0.5 × 400 = 200 mg) reaches the circulation, so the fraction excreted unchanged = 100/200 = 0.5 and ClR = 0.5 × 10 = 5 L/h. A: Uses 100/400, ignoring F. B: That's total clearance. D: Nonrenal clearance from the uncorrected fraction (10 − 2.5). E: Divides total clearance by F.

questions.stem: A 70-kg patient takes a drug with a Vd of 100 mL/kg and a half-life of 3.5 h (first-order). Taking 0.693 ≈ 0.7, what is its total body clearance?
questions.explanation: Vd = 0.1 L/kg × 70 kg = 7 L; k = 0.7/3.5 = 0.2 h⁻¹; CL = k × Vd = 0.2 × 7 = 1.4 L/h. A: A 10× error in the mL→L conversion. B: Omits 0.693 (7/3.5). C: Divides Vd by k instead of multiplying. D: Forgets to multiply by body weight (0.1 × 0.2).

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is brought in after an intentional ingestion. She has slurred speech, dilated pupils, temperature 40 °C, BP 150/90, HR 120, and RR 36. Which class of agent best explains these findings?
questions.explanation: Mydriasis, hyperthermia, tachycardia, and hypertension point to a stimulant (FAST: free-base cocaine, anticholinergics, sympathomimetics, theophylline). A: Opioids cause miosis, bradypnea, and hypothermia. B: Benzodiazepines cause sedation without hyperthermia or tachycardia. C: Organophosphates cause SLUDGE with miosis and bradycardia. E: β-blockers cause bradycardia and hypotension.

questions.stem: On the lecture's lists of agents causing toxic hypotension and toxic bradycardia, which agent appears on both?
questions.explanation: Clonidine (with calcium channel blockers) is listed for both hypotension and bradycardia. B: Cocaine (free base) causes tachycardia and hyperthermia. C: Theophylline also causes tachycardia and hyperthermia. D: Reserpine is listed for hypotension only. E: Digoxin is listed for bradycardia only.

questions.stem: A patient presents 6 hours after swallowing a large number of tablets. Which statement about emptying the stomach (emesis or lavage) is most accurate?

options.A: It should be done before assessing airway and circulation
options.B: It is most effective 4–8 hours after ingestion
options.C: It enhances elimination of drug already absorbed
options.D: It must be done before any antidote can be given
options.E: Its benefit is now limited; it works mainly within 1–2 hours

questions.explanation: Emptying the stomach is effective only 1–2 h after ingestion; by 6 h most drug has left the stomach. A: Stabilizing vital signs (ABC) always comes first. B: The useful window is 1–2 h, not 4–8 h. C: It prevents absorption; enhanced elimination uses forced diuresis, multiple-dose charcoal, dialysis, hemoperfusion or urine alkalinization. D: Antidotes are given as soon as indicated; they must be used quickly.

questions.stem: Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity by competing at μ-opioid receptors. How is it classified among antidote mechanisms?
questions.explanation: Antidotes that act on receptors are pharmacological antidotes; naloxone displaces opioids from μ receptors. A: Chemical antidotes inactivate the poison itself (e.g., chelators, N-acetylcysteine detoxifying NAPQI). B: Functional antagonists reverse downstream effects through another mechanism. D: Chelators bind metals. E: Elimination enhancers include dialysis, charcoal, and urine alkalinization.

questions.stem: A patient overdoses on a drug with strong antimuscarinic effects. He has hot dry skin, dilated pupils, tachycardia, and urinary retention. Which antidote is indicated?
questions.explanation: Physostigmine, a cholinesterase inhibitor, raises acetylcholine and overcomes the muscarinic block. A: Atropine is itself antimuscarinic and would worsen this; it treats cholinergic (organophosphate) poisoning. C: Naloxone reverses opioids. D: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines. E: Acetylcysteine treats acetaminophen poisoning.

questions.stem: An unresponsive patient arrives with an unknown ingestion. His respirations are shallow and BP is 80/50. What should be done first?

options.A: Identify the exact toxic agent with a urine drug screen

questions.explanation: Treat the patient, not the poison: maintaining respiration and circulation comes first. A: Identification proceeds in parallel and often only the class is found. B: Antidotes must have a clearly defined indication and can themselves be toxic. C: Decontamination follows stabilization and is time-limited. D: Enhanced elimination is for selected poisons after stabilization.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old farmer collapses after spraying crops with an organophosphate. He has salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhea, vomiting, pinpoint pupils, and bradycardia. Which antidote should be given?
questions.explanation: Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, causing cholinergic excess (SLUDGE, miosis, bradycardia); atropine blocks the muscarinic effects. A: Physostigmine also inhibits acetylcholinesterase and would worsen toxicity. C: Naloxone is for opioids; pinpoint pupils alone don't make this opioid toxicity, and opioids don't cause SLUDGE. D: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines. E: Desferrioxamine treats iron poisoning.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old is brought in after swallowing many of his pregnant mother's prenatal vitamins. He has vomiting, bloody diarrhea, and lethargy, with metabolic acidosis. Which antidote is indicated?
questions.explanation: Iron overdose (GI hemorrhage, then acidosis and shock) is treated with the iron chelator deferoxamine. A: Succimer chelates lead and other heavy metals. B: NAC treats acetaminophen. D: Methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia. E: Fomepizole treats methanol and ethylene glycol.

questions.stem: A patient is admitted with a large aspirin overdose. Which measure from the lecture enhances aspirin elimination?

options.A: Sodium bicarbonate infusion to alkalinize the urine

questions.explanation: Alkaline urine ionizes the weak acid aspirin, trapping it in the tubule so more is excreted. B: Acid urine keeps aspirin un-ionized, so more is reabsorbed. C: Stomach emptying works only within 1–2 h. D: Desferrioxamine chelates iron. E: Ethanol is the antidote for methanol and ethylene glycol.

questions.stem: A patient on a usual dose of lisinopril develops a persistent dry cough. A second patient takes twice the prescribed dose of warfarin by mistake and develops a hematoma. Which classification is correct?

options.B: The cough is a medication error; the hematoma is an ADR
options.D: The cough is an ADR; the hematoma is an ADE but not an ADR
options.E: Neither is an adverse drug event

questions.explanation: An ADR occurs at normal doses in normal use (the cough); harm from an overdose is an ADE that the ADR definition excludes. A: Overdose is excluded from the ADR definition. B: The cough involved no error in the process. C: The cough involved no error. E: Both are injuries from drug use, so both are ADEs.

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes type B (bizarre) from type A (augmented) adverse drug reactions?

options.A: Type B reactions are unpredictable from the drug's known pharmacology
options.C: Type B reactions are common but rarely fatal
options.D: Type B reactions resolve with dose reduction
options.E: Type B reactions only appear after drug withdrawal

questions.explanation: Type B reactions are qualitatively abnormal, unpredictable, and not dose-related; rare but with high mortality. B: Dose-dependence characterizes type A. C: Common but rarely fatal describes type A. D: Lowering the dose doesn't prevent type B; the drug must be stopped. E: Reactions on withdrawal are type E.

questions.stem: A patient taking a non-selective β-blocker for angina develops bronchospasm. Which change best prevents this toxicity while keeping the benefit?

options.A: Increase the dose to improve angina control
options.B: Add a second non-selective β-blocker at low dose
options.D: Give the drug by IV infusion

questions.explanation: Benefit (β1, heart) and toxicity (β2, airways) come from different receptor types, so functional selectivity separates them. A: A higher dose worsens β2 blockade. B: Still non-selective. D: The route doesn't change receptor selectivity. E: A muscarinic agonist would worsen bronchoconstriction.

questions.stem: A patient on long-term prednisone stops it abruptly and develops hypotension, weakness, and hyponatremia. How is this reaction classified, and how could it have been prevented?

options.A: Type A; by lowering the dose
options.B: Type B; by never giving the drug again
options.C: Type C; by limiting cumulative use
options.D: Type D; by avoiding the drug in pregnancy
options.E: Type E; by tapering the dose gradually

questions.explanation: Addisonian crisis after steroid withdrawal is an end-of-use (type E) reaction, avoided by tapering. A: Type A is an augmented effect during use. B: Type B is unpredictable and unrelated to stopping. C: Type C relates to cumulative long-term use (e.g., NSAID nephropathy). D: Type D is delayed (carcinogenesis, teratogenesis).

questions.stem: Clavulanic acid has little antibacterial effect alone, but it makes amoxicillin effective against β-lactamase–producing bacteria. Which type of pharmacodynamic interaction is this?
questions.explanation: In potentiation one drug has little or no effect alone yet increases the other's effect. A: Additive means E(A+B) = E(A) + E(B), both active. C: Antagonistic means one reduces the other (naloxone + morphine). D: Synergism needs both drugs active, with a combined effect above the sum (TMP-SMX). E: The lecture classifies it as a PD effect-modification example.

questions.stem: A patient on digoxin starts amiodarone, which displaces digoxin from plasma proteins and also reduces its excretion. What is the expected result?

options.A: Brief rise in free digoxin that settles without a dose change
options.B: Fall in total digoxin with free digoxin unchanged
options.C: Fall in free digoxin as more is excreted; dose must be raised
options.D: Lasting rise in free and total digoxin; dose must be reduced
options.E: Lasting rise in total digoxin only; free digoxin unchanged

questions.explanation: Displacement plus reduced excretion blocks the escape route, so free and total levels both rise and the dose must be adjusted. A: That's displacement alone (e.g., phenytoin): the extra free drug is cleared to a new steady state. B: That's the new steady state after displacement alone, not when excretion is also reduced. C: Excretion is reduced, not increased. E: Free (active) drug rises too.

questions.stem: A patient on lithium for bipolar disorder starts hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension. A week later she has coarse tremor, confusion, and vomiting. What is the mechanism?

options.A: Thiazide inhibits lithium metabolism by CYP3A4
options.E: Pharmacodynamic synergism at the same receptor

questions.explanation: Thiazides (and NSAIDs) reduce renal lithium clearance → accumulation of a narrow-therapeutic-range drug. A: Lithium isn't metabolized by CYP enzymes. C: Lithium isn't protein-bound. D: Absorption is already near complete. E: The interaction is pharmacokinetic (excretion).

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman with osteomyelitis receives IV vancomycin over 10 minutes. Soon after, she develops flushing and pruritus of the face, neck, and upper torso, with mild hypotension. IgE testing is negative. What is the best way to prevent this with future doses?

options.C: Switch to oral vancomycin for osteomyelitis
options.D: Increase the dose and lengthen the interval

questions.explanation: Vancomycin infusion reaction is non-IgE mast-cell histamine release linked to infusion rate (a rapid reaction); slowing the infusion (± antihistamine pretreatment) prevents it. A: It isn't a true allergy, so vancomycin can be continued. B: Epinephrine isn't preventive here. C: Oral vancomycin isn't absorbed and won't treat osteomyelitis. D: Larger doses given fast would worsen it.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman taking a combined oral contraceptive is started on rifampin for latent tuberculosis. Which advice is most appropriate?

options.A: No change needed; rifampin doesn't affect contraceptives
options.B: Stop the contraceptive during treatment, with no other precautions
options.C: Use an additional or alternative non-hormonal contraceptive method
options.E: Take the two drugs at least 2 hours apart

questions.explanation: Rifampin strongly induces CYP450, lowering estrogen/progestin levels and risking contraceptive failure (the effect lasts until induction wears off after stopping). A: The interaction is well established. B: Stopping without an alternative leaves her unprotected. D: A lower dose would make failure worse. E: The interaction is enzyme induction, not absorption, so spacing the doses doesn't help.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man on rifampicin needed a higher warfarin dose to keep his INR in range. Rifampicin is stopped and the warfarin dose is left unchanged. Two weeks later he has gum bleeding and a high INR. What explains this?

options.A: Enzyme levels fall after the inducer is stopped, so warfarin is cleared more slowly
options.B: Rifampicin had displaced warfarin from plasma proteins
options.C: Stopping rifampicin causes enzyme inhibition within hours
options.D: Pharmacodynamic tolerance to warfarin has worn off

questions.explanation: Induction is slow on, slow off: after the inducer is removed, enzyme levels fall over days to weeks, and a warfarin dose raised to overcome induction becomes too high. B: Displacement would raise free warfarin while on rifampicin, not after stopping it. C: Removing an inducer isn't enzyme inhibition, and the change is gradual. D: The higher dose was needed because of faster metabolism (PK), not receptor tolerance. E: Potentiation needs both drugs present; rifampicin is gone.

questions.stem: Drug X has a KD of 1 nM and drug Y a KD of 100 nM at the same receptor. Which statement is correct?

options.A: Y has 100 times higher affinity than X
options.B: X occupies half the receptors at a concentration 100 times lower than Y
options.C: X must have greater efficacy than Y
options.D: X must be a full agonist
options.E: Y reaches a higher maximal binding (Bmax)

questions.explanation: KD is the concentration for half-maximal binding; a lower KD means higher affinity, so X half-saturates at 1 nM vs 100 nM for Y. A: Reverses the relationship. C: Affinity says nothing about efficacy. D: Agonist vs antagonist isn't determined by KD. E: Bmax reflects receptor number, not the drug's KD.

questions.stem: At a receptor with significant constitutive activity, a drug reduces the response below the basal level, even with no agonist present. What is this drug?
questions.explanation: Inverse agonists have negative efficacy, returning constitutively active R# to Ri (e.g., cetirizine at H1). A: A full agonist raises the response to maximum. B: A partial agonist raises it to a submaximal ceiling. C: A neutral antagonist alone leaves basal activity unchanged. E: A physiological antagonist works through a different receptor.

questions.stem: In the presence of a fixed concentration of antagonist, the agonist's log dose–response curve shifts to the right in parallel, and the same maximal response is still reached. Which type of antagonist is this?
questions.explanation: Reversible competitive antagonists are surmountable: a parallel right shift with unchanged Emax. B: An irreversible antagonist lowers the maximum. C: A non-competitive antagonist depresses the slope and the maximum. D: A physiological antagonist acts through another receptor and doesn't produce a simple parallel shift at the same receptor. E: A chemical antagonist inactivates the drug itself.

questions.stem: A reversible competitive antagonist is present at a concentration equal to 4 × its KA. By how much must the agonist concentration be increased to restore the original response?
questions.explanation: Schild: dose ratio = [A]/KA + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5. A: 2-fold applies when [A] = KA. B: Forgets the +1. C: Subtracts 1 instead of adding it. D: Competitive reversible block is surmountable.

questions.stem: Epinephrine reverses histamine-induced bronchoconstriction in anaphylaxis. What type of antagonism is this?
questions.explanation: Two agonists produce opposing effects through different receptors (H1 vs β2): physiological antagonism. A: Chemical means the two drugs combine directly. B: Pharmacokinetic means changing histamine's concentration. D: Epinephrine doesn't compete at H1 receptors. E: Non-competitive antagonism blocks the chain beyond the same agonist's receptor.

questions.stem: For an agonist at cardiac β-adrenoceptors, the EC50 for the contractile response is much lower than the KD for binding. What does this indicate?

options.A: The agonist is a partial agonist
options.C: There is an inverse agonist present

questions.explanation: EC50 < KD means half-maximal response arrives before half the receptors are occupied: a receptor reserve (spare receptors). A: A partial agonist couldn't give the full response even at full occupancy. B: Irreversible binding isn't inferred from EC50 vs KD. C: An inverse agonist would reduce basal activity. E: Desensitization would raise the EC50.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man on chronic methadone maintenance is given buprenorphine in the emergency department for pain. Within minutes he develops yawning, rhinorrhea, piloerection, and abdominal cramps. What best explains this?

options.A: Buprenorphine is a full μ agonist and caused overdose
options.C: Buprenorphine is an inverse agonist at μ receptors
options.E: Buprenorphine is a high-affinity partial μ agonist that displaced methadone

questions.explanation: As a partial agonist with high affinity, buprenorphine displaces the full agonist and gives less receptor activation, acting as an antagonist and precipitating withdrawal. A: Full-agonist overdose causes miosis and respiratory depression, not withdrawal. B: Enzyme induction takes days. C: It isn't classified as an inverse agonist. D: The signs are classic opioid withdrawal, not allergy.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man stops his long-term metoprolol abruptly because he ran out. Two days later he has palpitations, BP 175/100, and chest pain at rest. What is the mechanism?

options.A: Downregulation of β receptors during treatment
options.C: Upregulation of β receptors during chronic blockade

questions.explanation: Chronic blockade upregulates β receptors; when the antagonist is removed, normal catecholamine levels act on excess receptors → overshoot (rebound tachycardia, hypertension, angina). Hence tapering. A: Downregulation follows chronic agonist exposure, not blockade. B: Tachyphylaxis is a fading response during repeated dosing. D: Hypersensitivity is immune-mediated. E: More enzyme would reduce catecholamine effects.

questions.stem: Phenoxybenzamine is given before surgery for pheochromocytoma. A day after the last dose the drug is barely detectable in plasma, yet α-blockade persists. Why?

options.A: It is a reversible competitive antagonist with very high affinity
options.B: It binds covalently, so recovery needs synthesis of new receptors
options.C: It has an active metabolite with a long half-life
options.D: It is a non-competitive antagonist acting beyond the receptor

questions.explanation: Irreversible (covalent) antagonists act until receptors are replaced, so their duration depends on receptor turnover rather than drug elimination. A: A reversible block would fade as plasma levels fall. C: The block persists because the receptors themselves are inactivated, not because of a metabolite. D: Phenoxybenzamine binds the α-receptor itself; non-competitive antagonists (verapamil) act beyond it. E: Up-regulation would increase, not block, the response.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man with a morphine overdose wakes after IV naloxone. Ninety minutes later, with no further opioid use, he is drowsy again with a respiratory rate of 6/min. What best explains this?

options.A: Naloxone is cleared faster than morphine, so morphine regains the receptors
options.B: Naloxone is a partial agonist that adds to respiratory depression
options.C: Tachyphylaxis to naloxone at μ receptors
options.D: Naloxone binds irreversibly and then releases morphine
options.E: Up-regulation of μ receptors by naloxone

questions.explanation: When an agonist and an antagonist compete, concentration decides: as the shorter-acting naloxone is cleared, morphine reoccupies μ receptors and respiratory depression returns. B: Naloxone is a pure antagonist with no intrinsic activity. C: Tachyphylaxis is a fading response to repeated agonist doses, not antagonist clearance. D: Naloxone is a reversible competitive antagonist. E: Up-regulation needs chronic blockade and wouldn't cause respiratory depression.

questions.stem: Which receptor family produces a response within milliseconds because the receptor and the effector are the same protein?
questions.explanation: Ligand-gated ion channels (e.g., nicotinic ACh receptor) open directly on agonist binding, within milliseconds. B: GPCRs work over seconds via G-proteins and second messengers. C: Kinase-linked receptors take hours (gene transcription). D: Cytokine receptors also act over hours. E: Nuclear receptors need transcription and protein synthesis (hours).

questions.stem: Through which G-protein and second-messenger pathway do α1-adrenoceptors and M3 muscarinic receptors act?

options.C: Direct opening of K⁺ channels by the G-protein
options.D: Gq → phospholipase C → IP3 and DAG

questions.explanation: α1 and M3 couple to Gq, activating phospholipase C (IP3/DAG → Ca²⁺). A: Gs/cAMP is used by β-adrenoceptors. B: Gi is used by α2. C: G-protein opening of K⁺ channels is the M2 mechanism in the heart. E: Guanylyl cyclase is linked to ANF receptors and isn't GPCR signaling here.

questions.stem: An asthmatic patient uses a salbutamol inhaler every hour for a day and notices each puff works less well. Which mechanism is mainly responsible for this rapid loss of response?

options.A: Down-regulation by reduced receptor gene expression over weeks
options.B: Receptor phosphorylation by βARK and binding of β-arrestin

questions.explanation: Rapid (seconds–minutes), reversible desensitization: GRK (βARK) phosphorylates the agonist-occupied receptor, then β-arrestin uncouples it from Gs. A: Down-regulation is slower (hours–days). C: Enzyme induction is a PK process that takes days. D: Antibodies aren't the mechanism. E: Glucocorticoids aren't involved, and they tend to restore β-receptor responsiveness.

questions.stem: In a population study, a drug has an ED50 of 10 mg for its therapeutic effect and a TD50 of 400 mg for a toxic effect. What is its therapeutic index?
questions.explanation: TI = TD50 / ED50 = 400 / 10 = 40. A: Inverts the ratio. B: Divides by 100. C: Subtracts instead of dividing. D: Multiplies instead of dividing.

questions.stem: Researchers count how many of 100 patients obtain headache relief at each dose of an analgesic. Which type of curve and parameter are they generating?
questions.explanation: An all-or-none effect counted across a population gives a quantal curve; ED50 is the dose at which 50% respond. A: Graded curves measure response size in one individual (EC50). B: Emax belongs to graded curves. D: KD comes from binding studies. E: Bmax is the binding capacity, not a quantal parameter.

questions.stem: A patient's pain is unchanged when ibuprofen is increased above its usual maximal dose, but he develops dyspepsia. Which concept explains this?
questions.explanation: Above the ceiling dose, further increases give no extra analgesia but add side effects. A: The threshold dose is the lowest dose with a detectable effect. B: Tachyphylaxis is a rapidly fading response to repeated doses. C: Spare receptors increase sensitivity. D: Inverse agonism reduces constitutive receptor activity.

questions.stem: A traveler develops profuse watery diarrhea after drinking contaminated water. Stool contains a toxin that ADP-ribosylates a G-protein α subunit. What is the direct intracellular consequence in enterocytes?

options.A: Inhibition of Gi, preventing cAMP from falling
options.B: Gs locked in the GTP-bound state → persistently ↑ cAMP
options.C: Activation of Gq → ↑ IP3 and Ca²⁺

questions.explanation: Cholera toxin prevents Gsα from hydrolyzing GTP, so adenylyl cyclase stays on → high cAMP → CFTR opening and Cl⁻/water secretion. A: Gi inhibition is pertussis toxin's action. C: Gq isn't the target. D: Heat-stable E. coli toxin raises cGMP; it doesn't lower it. E: CFTR is opened, not blocked.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old nonsmoking woman has lung adenocarcinoma with an activating mutation in a receptor tyrosine kinase that normally binds epidermal growth factor. Which drug directly targets this receptor's kinase activity?
questions.explanation: Erlotinib is an EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor used in EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer. A: Trastuzumab is an antibody against HER2. B: Tofacitinib inhibits JAK (cytokine receptor signaling). D: Imatinib inhibits BCR-ABL. E: Rituximab targets CD20 on B cells.

questions.stem: For the same quantal effect, drug A has an ED50 of 2 mg and drug B an ED50 of 50 mg. Which conclusion is justified?

options.A: A produces a larger maximal effect than B
options.B: A has a wider therapeutic index than B
options.C: B is 25 times more potent than A
options.D: A is 25 times more potent than B
options.E: A is 25 times more selective than B

questions.explanation: Potency compares the doses needed for the same effect: 50 ÷ 2 = 25. A more potent drug isn't necessarily more effective or safer. A: Potency says nothing about maximal effect. B: The therapeutic index also needs the TD50. C: Reverses it; a lower ED50 means higher potency. E: Selectivity compares one drug's ED50 values for two different effects.

questions.stem: A patient with an acute asthma attack receives a systemic glucocorticoid plus an inhaled β2-agonist. Why can't the glucocorticoid be relied on alone for immediate relief?

options.A: Its receptor alters gene transcription, so effects lag 30 min to hours
options.B: Its G-protein-coupled receptor desensitizes within minutes
options.C: It opens a ligand-gated channel that closes within milliseconds
options.D: It is only a partial agonist at β2-adrenoceptors
options.E: Its kinase-linked receptor is rapidly down-regulated

questions.explanation: Glucocorticoids are lipid-soluble and act on intracellular (nuclear) receptors; new proteins must be made, so effects take 30 min to hours and then outlast plasma levels. B: Glucocorticoid receptors aren't GPCRs; desensitization over minutes is a GPCR feature (e.g., β2). C: Ligand-gated channels act in milliseconds and would give rapid relief. D: Glucocorticoids don't act at β2-adrenoceptors. E: They don't act through kinase-linked receptors.

lectures.title: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs

questions.stem: A patient takes acetaminophen tablets bought in the US together with paracetamol tablets bought in Lebanon. How are these two names related?

options.A: Brand name and generic name of the same drug
options.B: Two different drugs of the same class
options.C: USAN and INN of the same drug
options.D: Chemical (IUPAC) name and generic name of the same drug
options.E: INN and proprietary name of the same drug

questions.explanation: Acetaminophen is the US Adopted Name (USAN) and paracetamol is the WHO International Nonproprietary Name (INN); both are generic names for the same drug, so taking both risks a double dose. A: Brand names are Panadol, Tylenol. B: They are one drug. D: The IUPAC name is N-(4-hydroxyphenyl)acetamide. E: Neither is a proprietary (brand) name.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slides 6–7

questions.stem: Before first-in-human dosing, a candidate drug is tested for whether it blocks the cardiac hERG potassium channel and prolongs the QT interval. Which preclinical task category is this?
questions.explanation: Safety pharmacology tests for hazardous acute effects such as arrhythmias and bronchoconstriction; hERG block is the slide's example. B: Genotoxicity and the maximum non-toxic dose. C: Absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion in animals. D: Works out the mechanism of a toxic effect already found. E: Large-scale production, stability and formulation.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slides 15, 17

questions.stem: Of drugs that enter Phase I, at which transition is a drug least likely to move on to the next stage?
questions.explanation: Only ~29% of drugs pass from Phase II to Phase III; Phase II is the first real test of efficacy in patients, and lack of efficacy is the most common reason for failure. A: ~52% move on from Phase I. C: ~58% pass Phase III. D: ~91% of submissions are approved. E: Phase IV happens after approval; it monitors marketed drugs rather than being a development gate.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slides 24–25

questions.stem: A new anti-inflammatory drug is approved after Phase III trials in about 3,000 patients showed no serious hepatic toxicity. Two years after marketing, spontaneous reports reveal fulminant hepatitis in about 1 in 10,000 users. What best explains why the trials missed this reaction?

options.A: Phase I was done in healthy volunteers rather than patients
options.B: The Phase III trials were not double-blinded
options.C: The placebo response masked the adverse effect
options.D: Preclinical carcinogenicity studies last only two years
options.E: About 30,000 patients must be treated to see even one case

questions.explanation: By the rule of three, detecting a 1-in-10,000 reaction needs ~30,000 treated patients; Phase III enrolls 300–3,000, so such reactions appear only after marketing (pharmacovigilance, Phase IV). A: Phase II and III are in patients, and the problem is size. B: Blinding controls bias; it does not create rare events. C: Placebo response concerns perceived benefit, not hepatitis. D: Carcinogenicity is a separate animal tumor test.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slides 42–43

questions.stem: The FDA approves a new monoclonal antibody, a biologic never approved before. How long is the marketing exclusivity granted at approval?
questions.explanation: A new biological product receives 12 years of exclusivity. A: New clinical investigation (e.g., new indication). B: New chemical entity (small molecule). C: Orphan drug (<200,000 US patients). E: Patent term, counted from filing, granted by the patent office, not FDA exclusivity.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slides 46–48

questions.stem: A patent on a lead compound was filed in 2012, and the drug was approved in 2022. Which statement about its US patent protection is correct?

options.A: Up to 5 years may be restored, with at most 14 years left after approval
options.B: It lasts 20 years counted from the date of approval
options.C: It is granted by the FDA at the time of approval
options.D: It can be renewed once for another 20 years
options.E: It is what stops generics from referencing the brand's clinical data

questions.explanation: Patent term restoration can give back part of the time lost in testing and review: no more than 5 years, and no more than 14 years of patent life after approval. B: 20 years, non-renewable, counted from filing. C: Patents come from the USPTO; the FDA grants exclusivity. D: The term is non-renewable. E: That is marketing (data) exclusivity.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slides 46–47

questions.stem: In 1961, thousands of babies were born with limb defects after their mothers took a sedative in pregnancy. What did the US law passed in response add to drug approval?

options.A: Proof of safety before a drug can be marketed
options.B: A shorter approval route for generic drugs
options.D: User fees in exchange for FDA review deadlines
options.E: Proof of efficacy from controlled trials

questions.explanation: The thalidomide disaster led to the 1962 Kefauver–Harris Amendments: proof of efficacy as well as safety, from controlled trials, plus informed consent. A: 1938 Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (after elixir sulfanilamide). B: 1984 Hatch–Waxman Act. C: 2007 FDA Amendments Act. D: 1992 Prescription Drug User Fee Act.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slide 38

questions.stem: In a randomized, placebo-controlled antidepressant trial, patients do not know which treatment they receive, but the psychiatrists rating their mood do. The drug group shows a larger improvement than expected. Which design change best addresses the most likely bias?

options.A: Randomize the patients to treatment groups
options.E: Enroll healthy volunteers instead of patients

questions.explanation: The trial is single-blind, so observer bias remains (raters see what they expect); double-blinding hides the treatment from both patient and observer. A, B: Already randomized and placebo-controlled. D: Crossover makes each patient his or her own control but does not hide the treatment from the rater. E: Efficacy must be tested in patients; this does not remove observer bias.
questions.source: Development, Evaluation and Control of Drugs, slide 26

questions.stem: A tracheal biopsy from a 43-year-old smoker shows stratified squamous epithelium where pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium is expected. Which statement best describes this change?
questions.explanation: Metaplasia is a reversible replacement of one differentiated cell type by another that better tolerates chronic stress; squamous epithelium resists smoke but sacrifices mucociliary function. A: Dysplasia is disordered growth with atypia, not replacement by another normal cell type. C: Hyperplasia increases cell number without changing cell type. D: Metaplasia is reversible if the stimulus is removed. E: Atrophy is shrinkage, not a change of cell type.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p2; tutorial s19, s22

questions.stem: After an acetaminophen overdose, which finding indicates that hepatocytes have crossed into irreversible injury?

options.C: Membrane blebs with loss of microvilli
options.D: Leakage of AST and ALT into blood

questions.explanation: Loss of plasma membrane integrity lets intracellular enzymes leak into the blood: a hallmark of irreversible injury (along with pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis). A: Swelling and ER dilation reflect ion-pump failure and are reversible. B: Fatty change is reversible. C: Blebs form while the membrane is still intact (reversible). E: Chromatin clumping is reversible; pyknosis, karyorrhexis and karyolysis are irreversible.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p4; tutorial s26–30

questions.stem: A 75-year-old man dies 3 weeks after a large stroke. The infarcted area of brain is soft and cystic. Which pattern of necrosis is this?
questions.explanation: Ischemic injury in the CNS produces liquefactive necrosis: tissue is digested into a soft mass that later becomes a cyst. A: Coagulative necrosis is typical of ischemia in other solid organs. B: Caseous necrosis is seen in TB granulomas. D: Fibrinoid necrosis affects vessel walls. E: Fat necrosis occurs in pancreatitis and breast.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p5; tutorial s43

questions.stem: Which feature favors apoptosis over necrosis?

options.A: Apoptotic bodies cleared with little inflammation
options.D: Death of large groups of adjacent cells
options.E: Leakage of cell contents into the blood

questions.explanation: Apoptosis: shrinkage, intact membrane, apoptotic bodies rapidly phagocytosed with minimal inflammation, usually single cells or small clusters. B: Swelling and rupture are necrosis. C: This nuclear sequence (ending in karyolysis) is listed for necrosis; apoptosis shows chromatin condensation and fragmentation. D: Necrosis often affects groups of adjacent cells. E: Leakage of contents is necrosis.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p6–7; tutorial s46

questions.stem: Coronary flow is restored by angioplasty 4 hours after occlusion, but serum troponin rises further and some still-viable myocytes die. Which mechanism best explains this?

options.B: Fatty change from impaired lipid metabolism
options.E: Reperfusion injury from ROS and calcium overload

questions.explanation: Restoring flow to still-viable ischemic tissue can worsen injury: more ROS, calcium overload, inflammation, and complement activation. A: Growth-factor withdrawal isn't the trigger here. B: Fatty change is a reversible accumulation, not a cause of cell death. C: There is no infection; pyroptosis is an inflammasome response to microbes. D: Calcification follows necrosis; it doesn't cause it.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p4; tutorial s40

questions.stem: A lymph node biopsy shows back-to-back follicles. Immunostaining shows strong BCL-2 in the follicle centers, and a t(14;18) translocation is found. What is the effect of BCL-2 overexpression?

options.B: Promotes cytochrome c release from mitochondria

questions.explanation: BCL-2 opposes BAX/BAK, preventing cytochrome c release and intrinsic apoptosis, so B cells survive and accumulate (follicular lymphoma). A: Caspase-8 belongs to the extrinsic (death-receptor) pathway. B: BCL-2 prevents cytochrome c release. D: BCL-2 doesn't activate p53. E: MLKL is activated by RIPK1/RIPK3 in necroptosis.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p6; tutorial s45

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with alcohol use disorder has acute epigastric pain radiating to the back and elevated lipase. At surgery, chalky white deposits are seen in the peripancreatic fat. What process produced them?

options.E: Saponification of fatty acids with calcium

questions.explanation: Enzymatic fat necrosis: pancreatic lipases release fatty acids that bind calcium (saponification), giving chalky white deposits. A: Caseous necrosis is TB. B: Metastatic calcification needs hypercalcemia and occurs in normal tissue. C: Acinar necrosis doesn't produce chalky deposits in fat. D: Fibrinoid necrosis affects vessel walls.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p5; tutorial s48–49

questions.stem: In a macrophage infected with bacteria, inflammasome activation triggers caspase-1, which cleaves gasdermin D. Pores form, the cell swells and ruptures, and IL-1β is released. Which form of cell death is this?
questions.explanation: Pyroptosis: inflammasome → caspase-1 → gasdermin D pores, swelling and rupture; caspase-1 also activates IL-1β and IL-18. A: Necroptosis uses RIPK1/RIPK3 → MLKL. C: Ferroptosis is iron-dependent lipid peroxidation when glutathione-GPX4 defenses fail. D: Apoptosis keeps the membrane intact with little inflammation. E: Autophagy is mainly a survival response.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p7; tutorial s33–34

questions.stem: A 65-year-old with long-standing aortic stenosis has a thick-walled left ventricle. Which change explains the myocardial enlargement?

options.B: Replacement of myocytes by a more resistant cell type
options.C: Disordered myocyte growth with nuclear atypia
options.D: Larger myocytes from more structural proteins and organelles

questions.explanation: Cardiac myocytes have limited capacity to divide, so pressure overload causes hypertrophy: increased synthesis of structural proteins and organelles. A: Hyperplasia requires cells that can divide. B: That is metaplasia. C: That is dysplasia. E: That is fatty change, a form of reversible injury.
questions.source: Cell Injury, notes p1; tutorial s5–6

questions.stem: A 70-year-old has a calcified, stenotic aortic valve. Serum calcium and phosphate are normal. Which process explains the calcification?
questions.explanation: Calcium deposits in damaged tissue with normal serum calcium: dystrophic. B: Metastatic calcification requires hypercalcemia and affects normal tissue. C: Hemosiderin is iron. D: Lipofuscin is wear-and-tear pigment. E: Steatosis is fat.
questions.source: Cell Death and Intracellular Accumulations, slides 30–32

questions.stem: A liver biopsy shows coarse golden-brown granules in hepatocytes that stain blue with Perls stain. Which pigment is it?
questions.explanation: Iron-containing hemosiderin is Prussian/Perls blue positive (e.g., hemochromatosis). A: Lipofuscin is Perls negative. B: Bilirubin is yellow-green and Perls negative. C: Melanin is Perls negative. E: Carbon is black (anthracosis).
questions.source: Cell Death and Intracellular Accumulations, slide 28

questions.stem: A kidney section shows a wedge-shaped pale area where tubular and glomerular outlines are preserved but nuclei are absent, with inflammatory cells at the edge. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Preserved architecture without nuclei = coagulative necrosis from ischemia. A: An abscess destroys architecture. B: Caseous necrosis has granulomas. D: Fat necrosis affects adipose tissue. E: Fibrinoid necrosis is in vessel walls.
questions.source: Cell Death and Intracellular Accumulations, slides 4–5, 11

questions.stem: A lung lymph node from a city dweller has macrophages packed with black pigment. The patient has no respiratory symptoms. What is this?
questions.explanation: Inhaled carbon (exogenous pigment) in macrophages is anthracosis, usually harmless. A: Hemosiderin is golden-brown. B: Melanin is endogenous, mainly in skin. C: Lipofuscin is yellow-brown and intracellular. D: Caseous necrosis is a granulomatous necrosis.
questions.source: Cell Death and Intracellular Accumulations, slides 24–25

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man with multiple myeloma has a serum calcium of 14 mg/dL. Calcium deposits are found in previously normal kidneys, lungs, and gastric mucosa. Which process is this?
questions.explanation: Hypercalcemia causes calcium deposition in normal tissues: metastatic calcification. A: Dystrophic calcification occurs in injured or dead tissue with normal calcium metabolism. C: Psammoma bodies are a form of dystrophic calcification in some tumors (outside slides). D: Saponification is calcium binding fatty acids in necrotic fat, not driven by hypercalcemia. E: Hemosiderin is an iron pigment, not calcium.
questions.source: Cell Death and Intracellular Accumulations, slide 30

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with diabetes and peripheral arterial disease has a black, dry, shriveled toe. Over several days it becomes swollen, moist, and foul-smelling. What best explains the change?

options.B: Trauma caused fat necrosis of the toe

questions.explanation: Dry gangrene is coagulative necrosis of an ischemic limb; superimposed bacterial infection adds liquefactive action of bacteria and leukocytes = wet gangrene. A: Caseous necrosis is seen in TB granulomas. B: Fat necrosis occurs in pancreatitis and breast. D: Fibrinoid necrosis is a vessel-wall pattern. E: Calcification wouldn't make the toe moist and foul-smelling.
questions.source: Cell Death and Intracellular Accumulations, slides 21–22

questions.stem: At autopsy, the heart of an 88-year-old is small and brown. Myocytes contain fine brownish-yellow granules that are negative on Perls stain. What is the pigment?
questions.explanation: Lipofuscin is the brownish-yellow wear-and-tear pigment of aging and atrophy (heart, liver, brain). A: Hemosiderin is Perls/Prussian blue positive. B: Melanin is made by epidermal melanocytes. C: Bilirubin gives a diffuse yellow color (jaundice). D: Carbon is black (anthracosis).
questions.source: Cell Death and Intracellular Accumulations, slides 28, 35

questions.stem: A patient survives a large myocardial infarction. Six weeks later, what will most likely occupy the infarcted area?
questions.explanation: Cardiac myocytes are essentially permanent cells; major loss heals by collagen scar. A: Regeneration is insufficient. B: Gliosis is the CNS response. C: Myocytes don't undergo hyperplasia. E: A granuloma is a macrophage aggregate.

questions.stem: Which growth factor is the major mediator of fibrosis, increasing collagen synthesis while reducing ECM degradation?
questions.explanation: TGF-β is the major mediator of fibrosis: it activates fibroblasts and increases collagen/ECM synthesis while reducing ECM degradation. A: VEGF drives angiogenesis. B: PDGF drives fibroblast migration and proliferation but isn't the main fibrogenic mediator. C: HGF drives hepatocyte proliferation. D: FGF-2 drives fibroblast proliferation and angiogenesis.

questions.stem: A clean surgical incision is sutured. About 3 days later, which finding is expected?

options.E: Regenerated hair follicles in the scar

questions.explanation: By ~day 3 macrophages replace neutrophils and granulation tissue begins to fill the incision. B: Neutrophils dominate in the first 24 h, and epithelium bridges by 24–48 h. C: A mature scar takes ~1 month. D: ~80% strength takes ~3 months. E: Appendages aren't restored in a scar.

questions.stem: A patient on long-term high-dose prednisone has an abdominal wound that separates on postoperative day 7. Which mechanism most contributed?
questions.explanation: Glucocorticoids impair healing by suppressing inflammation and collagen synthesis → weak wound → dehiscence. A: Excess TGF-β causes fibrosis. B: A keloid is excess scar. D: More TIMP activity would favor matrix accumulation. E: Contraction isn't the cause of dehiscence.

questions.stem: Which tissue is composed of stable (quiescent) cells that can re-enter the cell cycle after injury?
questions.explanation: Renal tubular cells are stable: normally in G0, they divide after injury (repair also needs preserved tubular basement membranes). A, C, E: Labile, continuously renewing tissues. D: Mature skeletal muscle fibers don't divide; limited regeneration comes from satellite cells.
questions.source: Tissue Repair, notes p2; tutorial s18

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman has a raised, firm scar on her earlobe one year after piercing. Which finding would identify it as a keloid rather than a hypertrophic scar?

options.A: It extends beyond the original wound
options.B: It is raised above the skin surface
options.C: It formed in a wound under tension
options.E: Granulation tissue rises above the surface

questions.explanation: A keloid extends beyond the original wound boundaries and tends to persist or recur; a hypertrophic scar stays within the wound and may regress. B: Both are raised. C: Tension isn't what defines a keloid. D: Both contain excess collagen. E: That is exuberant granulation tissue, which blocks re-epithelialization.
questions.source: Tissue Repair, notes p8; tutorial s27

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with poor diet has gum bleeding, perifollicular hemorrhages, and a surgical wound that won't heal. Which step of collagen synthesis is impaired?
questions.explanation: Scurvy: vitamin C is needed for hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues, so collagen is weak (bleeding gums, poor wound healing). A: Glycosylation doesn't depend on vitamin C. B: Cleavage of procollagen peptides isn't vitamin C–dependent. C: Lysyl oxidase cross-linking needs copper, not vitamin C (outside slides). E: Glycine repeats are set by the amino-acid sequence, not by vitamin C.

questions.stem: A large open leg wound left after debridement heals by second intention. Compared with a sutured surgical incision, which feature is much more prominent?
questions.explanation: Second intention: larger defect, more inflammation and granulation tissue, a larger scar, and much greater contraction by myofibroblasts (α-smooth muscle actin). A: A thin epidermis isn't a defining feature. B: Appendages aren't restored in a scar. D: Re-epithelialization covers a larger area and takes longer. E: More granulation tissue is needed.
questions.source: Tissue Repair, notes p8; tutorial s7

questions.stem: A patient with chronic hepatitis C develops cirrhosis with fibrous septa and regenerative nodules. Which cells are a major source of the collagen in the septa?
questions.explanation: In chronic liver disease, activated hepatic stellate cells are a major source of collagen. A: Hepatocytes form the regenerative nodules, not the septa. B: Macrophages release profibrotic mediators such as TGF-β but don't mainly deposit collagen. C: Endothelial cells form new vessels. D: Lymphocytes release mediators but don't deposit collagen.
questions.source: Tissue Repair, notes p6; tutorial s22

questions.stem: A 6-year-old has periorbital edema and generalized swelling. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein. What is the main mechanism of the edema?
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome: urinary protein loss lowers plasma oncotic pressure; renal edema is generalized and shows first in loose tissue such as the eyelids. A: Increased hydrostatic pressure follows impaired venous return (heart failure, venous obstruction). B: Lymphatic obstruction is inflammatory, neoplastic, post-surgical, or post-irradiation. D: Increased permeability is inflammatory. E: Arteriolar dilation (e.g., heat) raises hydrostatic pressure; not the cause here.

questions.stem: A pleural fluid sample has high protein content and many inflammatory cells. Which mechanism most likely produced it?

options.B: Increased hydrostatic pressure from heart failure
