questions.explanation: Protein-rich inflammatory fluid is an exudate from increased permeability. A: Low oncotic pressure gives a transudate. B: Heart failure gives a transudate. C: Sodium retention gives a transudate. D: Cirrhosis gives a transudate.

questions.stem: A patient with long-standing right heart failure has a liver with a mottled red and tan cut surface. Microscopy shows centrilobular necrosis and hemorrhage with preserved portal tracts. What is this?
questions.explanation: "Nutmeg liver": venous congestion damages the zone farthest from the blood supply (centrilobular). B: Steatosis is fat accumulation. C: Hepatitis cirrhosis has nodules and fibrous septa. D: Liver infarcts are rare (dual supply). E: Hemochromatosis is iron deposition.

questions.stem: An organ is engorged with blood and has a blue-red (cyanotic) color. Which mechanism and type of blood fit best?
questions.explanation: Congestion is passive: impaired venous outflow fills the organ with deoxygenated blood, giving a blue-red color. A: Active hyperemia (exercise, inflammation) makes tissue red with oxygenated blood. C: Stagnant venous blood is deoxygenated. D: Arteriolar dilation brings in oxygenated blood. E: Lymphatic blockage causes edema, not blood engorgement.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with chronic left heart failure has sputum containing macrophages with golden-brown cytoplasmic granules that stain with Prussian blue. What are these cells?
questions.explanation: Chronic pulmonary congestion ruptures capillaries; alveolar macrophages phagocytose RBCs and store iron as hemosiderin. A: Foam cells contain lipid. B: Anthracotic macrophages contain black carbon (Prussian blue negative). C: Langhans cells are granuloma giant cells. E: Reed–Sternberg cells are Hodgkin lymphoma.

questions.stem: Six months after mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection and radiation, a woman develops persistent swelling of the arm on the same side. What is the mechanism?
questions.explanation: Post-surgical and post-irradiation lymphatic blockage causes lymphedema. A: Hydrostatic causes are impaired venous return (heart failure, venous obstruction) or arteriolar dilation. B: Low oncotic pressure follows hypoproteinemia (nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis, malnutrition). C: Sodium retention is renal and causes generalized edema. D: Increased permeability is inflammatory.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with congestive heart failure has worsening leg edema. Besides raised venous pressure, which additional mechanism, triggered by reduced renal perfusion, worsens the edema?

options.B: Low oncotic pressure from urinary albumin loss

questions.explanation: Heart failure lowers renal perfusion, activating renin–angiotensin–aldosterone and increasing tubular sodium (and water) reabsorption. A: Lymphatic blockage is inflammatory, neoplastic, post-surgical, or post-irradiation. B: Urinary protein loss is nephrotic syndrome. D: Increased permeability is inflammatory. E: Arteriolar dilation is not the renal mechanism.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy has sudden scrotal pain. At surgery the testis is twisted, dark red, and swollen. Why is the infarct hemorrhagic?

options.A: Arterial occlusion in an end-arterial organ
options.B: Septic embolus to the testicular artery
options.D: Venous obstruction with ongoing arterial inflow

questions.explanation: Torsion first compresses thin-walled veins; arterial inflow continues → blood pools → red infarct. A: End-arterial arterial occlusion gives white infarcts. B: No sign of infection; an arterial embolus would give a white infarct. C: Liquefactive necrosis is typical of brain/abscess, not a cause of hemorrhage. E: Arterial thrombosis in a solid organ gives a white infarct.

questions.stem: Which organ most typically develops a pale (white), wedge-shaped infarct after arterial embolism?
questions.explanation: Solid organs with end-arterial supply (kidney, spleen, heart) form white infarcts. B: Lung has dual supply → red infarcts. C: Small intestine has dual supply → red. D: Ovary infarcts are venous (torsion) → red. E: Brain infarcts become liquefactive.

questions.stem: A patient with severe thrombocytopenia has many 1–2 mm red spots on the skin of the legs. What are these lesions?
questions.explanation: Pinpoint 1–2 mm hemorrhages are petechiae. A: Purpura are 3–10 mm. B: Ecchymoses are > 1 cm bruises. C: Hematomas are localized collections within tissue. D: Telangiectasias are dilated vessels, not hemorrhages.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old has black, tarry stools for 3 days. What is the most likely bleeding site?
questions.explanation: Melena = partially digested blood, usually from an upper GI source such as a duodenal ulcer. A: Sigmoid → hematochezia. C: Rectum → hematochezia. D: Anal canal → bright red blood. E: Left colon bleeding → hematochezia.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with atrial fibrillation dies suddenly 6 hours after a large embolic occlusion of a coronary artery. At autopsy, microscopy of the territory shows no definite necrosis. What best explains this?

options.A: The occlusion was not hemodynamically significant
options.B: Dual blood supply protected the myocardium
options.E: Liquefactive necrosis had dissolved the cells

questions.explanation: Histologic evidence of necrosis lags; death within ~12–18 h may show only congestion or pallor. A: A large occlusion is significant. B: The heart has end-arterial coronary supply. D: Myocytes don't regenerate. E: Myocardium undergoes coagulative necrosis.

questions.stem: Two patients have complete occlusion of the same coronary branch. In patient 1 it developed slowly over years; in patient 2 it occurred suddenly from an embolus. Only patient 2 has a large infarct. What best explains the difference?

options.A: Patient 1 has a dual coronary blood supply
options.B: Collaterals had time to enlarge in patient 1
options.D: Venous outflow was obstructed in patient 2

questions.explanation: Slow narrowing allows time for collateral vessels to enlarge; sudden occlusion leaves little time to compensate. A: The heart is an end-arterial organ in both. C: Both have the same tissue type. D: Embolism is arterial, not venous. E: Myocytes don't regenerate enough to prevent infarction.

questions.stem: A bruise on the thigh changes from red-blue to green over several days. Which pigment produces the green color?
questions.explanation: Ecchymosis colors follow hemoglobin breakdown: red-blue/purple, then green (biliverdin), then yellow-brown (bilirubin and hemosiderin). A: Bilirubin gives yellow-brown later. B: Hemosiderin contributes to the late yellow-brown. C: Hemoglobin gives the initial red-blue. E: Lipofuscin is a wear-and-tear pigment, unrelated.

questions.stem: With [K⁺]out = 4 mM and [K⁺]in = 140 mM at 37 °C, what is the approximate K⁺ equilibrium potential?
questions.explanation: E_K = 61.5 × log(4/140) = 61.5 × (−1.54) ≈ −95 mV. A: The sign is wrong; [out] < [in] gives a negative log. B: 61 mV is the coefficient (and ≈ E_Na in magnitude), not the answer. D: −70 mV is the resting Vm, which also reflects Na⁺ and Cl⁻ permeability. E: Uses the divalent coefficient (30.75 mV, z = 2) instead of 61.5 mV.

questions.stem: A neuron rests at −70 mV although its E_K is about −95 mV. What best explains the difference?

options.A: A small resting Na⁺ permeability pulls Vm toward E_Na
options.B: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves equal charge each way
options.C: Resting Cl⁻ permeability exceeds K⁺ permeability
options.D: Voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are inactivated at rest
options.E: K⁺ is at electrochemical equilibrium at −70 mV

questions.explanation: Vm is a permeability-weighted average (GHK); P_K dominates, but resting P_Na is not zero, so Vm sits near, not at, E_K. B: The pump is electrogenic (3 Na⁺ out / 2 K⁺ in). C: P_K : P_Cl ≈ 1 : 0.45; K⁺ dominates. D: At rest Na⁺ channels are closed but available, not inactivated. E: At −70 mV K⁺ still has an outward driving force.

questions.stem: Shortly after an action potential, a nerve fiber fires again only if the stimulus is stronger than normal. What explains this?

options.A: Nearly all voltage-gated Na⁺ channels are still inactivated
options.B: E_Na has fallen because Na⁺ entry abolished the gradient
options.C: The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is saturated after the action potential
options.D: Some Na⁺ channels have recovered, but K⁺ conductance is still high
options.E: Voltage-gated K⁺ channels are all closed

questions.explanation: This is the relative refractory period: partial Na⁺ channel recovery plus lingering K⁺ conductance means a stronger stimulus is needed. A: That is the absolute refractory period, when no stimulus works. B: One AP barely changes ion gradients; E_Na stays positive. C: The pump doesn't set refractoriness. E: K⁺ conductance is elevated, not zero.

questions.stem: A researcher holds a squid axon's membrane at 0 mV and records the current needed to keep it there. After tetraethylammonium is applied internally, the late outward current disappears. Which current did TEA abolish, and what technique was used?

options.B: Ca²⁺ current, using a current clamp
options.C: Cl⁻ current, using a voltage clamp
options.D: Leak current, using a current clamp
options.E: K⁺ current, using a voltage clamp

questions.explanation: Voltage clamp fixes Vm and measures the injected current; internal TEA blocks K⁺ channels, removing the delayed outward K⁺ current. A: TTX blocks Na⁺ channels from outside and wasn't used. B: Holding voltage constant is voltage clamp, not current clamp. C: TEA blocks K⁺ channels, not Cl⁻ channels. D: Wrong technique, and TEA isn't a general leak blocker.

questions.stem: Compared with an action potential, an electrotonic (graded) potential:

options.B: Spreads faster but decays with distance
options.C: Spreads only forward because of refractoriness
options.D: Is regenerated at each patch of membrane

questions.explanation: Electrotonic potentials are conducted faster than APs but attenuate rapidly (decremental), so they suit local integration, not long-distance signaling. A: They have no fixed threshold. C: They can spread both ways; refractoriness applies to APs. D: Regeneration is what makes APs nondecremental. E: They can be depolarizing (Na⁺) or hyperpolarizing (Cl⁻).

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with chronic kidney disease has K⁺ of 7.5 mEq/L and muscle weakness. What is the effect on his skeletal muscle resting membrane potential and excitability?

options.C: Depolarized; reduced excitability due to Na⁺ channel inactivation
options.E: Depolarized; increased excitability due to K⁺ channel inactivation

questions.explanation: High [K⁺]out makes E_K less negative → resting depolarization; sustained depolarization inactivates voltage-gated Na⁺ channels → reduced excitability and weakness. A: Hyperpolarization occurs in hypokalemia. B: Also describes hypokalemia. D: The pump can't offset a large ECF K⁺ rise. E: Reduced, not increased, excitability, via Na⁺ (not K⁺) channel inactivation.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis has demyelinated axon segments. Which change in the demyelinated internode explains slowed or blocked conduction?

options.A: Membrane resistance rises and capacitance falls
options.B: Membrane resistance falls and capacitance rises
options.C: Both membrane resistance and capacitance rise
options.D: Both membrane resistance and capacitance fall
options.E: Nodal Na⁺ channels become permanently inactivated

questions.explanation: Myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance; losing it does the opposite, so local current leaks out and charges the membrane before reaching the next node. A: That is the effect of myelin, which speeds conduction. C, D: Myelin moves the two in opposite directions. E: The problem is internodal current loss, not nodal channel inactivation.

questions.stem: Pulmonary interstitial edema triples the alveolar–capillary diffusion distance, and lung disease halves the surface area. With an unchanged O₂ gradient, O₂ diffusion becomes what fraction of normal?
questions.explanation: Fick: J ∝ A·ΔC/Δx, so J changes by (1/2) × (1/3) = 1/6. B: Accounts only for the distance. C: Accounts only for the area. D: Treats the halved area as doubled. E: Inverts the relationship; thickness and area work in the opposite directions.

questions.stem: Two coupled neurons fire in near-perfect synchrony, and current injected into either one immediately changes the voltage of the other. Their connection most likely:

options.A: Uses ligand-gated channels on the postsynaptic cell
options.B: Requires voltage-gated Ca²⁺ entry to transmit
options.D: Has a delay of about a millisecond

questions.explanation: Gap junctions (connexons) couple cells directly: minimal delay, often bidirectional, synchronize groups of cells. A: Ligand-gated receptors belong to chemical synapses. B: Ca²⁺-triggered transmitter release is the chemical synapse. C: Amplification is possible at chemical synapses; gap junctions are passive. D: A millisecond-range delay is typical of chemical synapses.

questions.stem: Which hormone lowers blood calcium by inhibiting intestinal Ca²⁺ absorption and increasing renal Ca²⁺ excretion?
questions.explanation: Per the lecture, glucocorticoids decrease blood Ca²⁺ by inhibiting intestinal absorption and increasing renal excretion. A: Calcitonin also lowers Ca²⁺, but by inhibiting osteoclasts. B: GH raises Ca²⁺ by increasing intestinal absorption. D: PTH raises Ca²⁺ (bone resorption, renal reabsorption, calcitriol). E: Calcitriol raises Ca²⁺ by increasing intestinal absorption.

questions.stem: A signal opens Ca²⁺ channels for only milliseconds, yet local cytosolic Ca²⁺ rises 10–20-fold. What makes this possible?

options.A: A ~10,000-fold inward Ca²⁺ gradient across PM and ER
options.B: Ca²⁺-binding proteins release their bound Ca²⁺
options.D: Ca²⁺ diffuses freely across the lipid bilayer
options.E: Ca²⁺ enters the cytosol by primary active transport

questions.explanation: Cytosolic Ca²⁺ (~10⁻⁷ M) is ~10,000-fold below ECF and ER Ca²⁺ (~10⁻³ M), so Ca²⁺ rushes into the cytosol as soon as channels open. B: Ca²⁺-binding proteins buffer (take up) Ca²⁺ and blunt the rise. C: Mitochondria take up Ca²⁺ as a removal mechanism. D: Ca²⁺ needs channels to cross. E: Entry is passive through channels; pumps remove Ca²⁺.

questions.stem: In a ventricular myocyte, which event directly triggers release of Ca²⁺ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum?

options.A: IP₃ binding to IP₃ receptors on the SR
options.B: Ca²⁺ entering via L-type channels and opening RyR2

questions.explanation: Trigger Ca²⁺ through L-type channels (LTCC) in the T-tubule opens RyR2 on the SR (calcium-induced calcium release). A: IP₃-gated channels release ER Ca²⁺ in Gq signaling, not the cardiac trigger. C: Phospholamban (PLB) regulates SERCA2a reuptake, i.e. relaxation. D: NCX removes Ca²⁺ during relaxation. E: Troponin binding follows SR release.

questions.stem: Which ECG change and symptom pair fit a plasma calcium of 14 mg/dL?
questions.explanation: Hypercalcemia (depressive effects above ~12 mg/dL) shortens QT and depresses nerves and gut smooth muscle (constipation, sluggish reflexes). A: QT prolongation and tetany suggest hypocalcemia. B: QT shortens in hypercalcemia. C: Tetany is hypocalcemia (~6 mg/dL). E: QT shortens and reflexes become sluggish.

questions.stem: Two days after total thyroidectomy, a 45-year-old woman has perioral tingling and carpal spasm when a BP cuff is inflated. Which change underlies her neuromuscular findings?

options.B: Excess PTH acting on motor neurons
options.C: Loss of calcitonin's effect on nerves

questions.explanation: Inadvertent parathyroid removal → low PTH → hypocalcemia → increased neuronal Na⁺ permeability → easy AP initiation (tetany). A: K⁺ channel block isn't the lecture's mechanism. B: PTH is low, not high. C: Calcitonin loss doesn't cause tetany. D: The problem is low ECF Ca²⁺.

questions.stem: Which protein lowers cytosolic Ca²⁺ by ATP-driven pumping into an intracellular store?
questions.explanation: SERCA is the ER/SR Ca²⁺ pump (regulated by phospholamban in the heart). A: PMCA uses ATP but pumps Ca²⁺ out of the cell. B: NCX uses the Na⁺ gradient to move Ca²⁺ out of the cell. D: Mitochondrial import is driven by the H⁺ gradient, not ATP directly. E: Binding proteins buffer Ca²⁺; they don't transport it.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to measure cytosolic Ca²⁺ with a fluorescent indicator rather than a Ca²⁺-sensitive photoprotein. Which should she use?
questions.explanation: Fura-2 and Fluo-3 are fluorescent Ca²⁺ markers. A: Aequorin is the jellyfish photoprotein, the other measurement method. C: Ryanodine is the plant alkaloid that names the SR release channel. D: TTX blocks Na⁺ channels. E: IP₃ releases ER Ca²⁺; it doesn't measure it.

questions.stem: Which calcium-balance pattern is expected in a healthy 10-year-old during a growth spurt?

options.A: Absorption exceeds urinary excretion; net bone deposition
options.B: Urinary excretion exceeds absorption; net bone deposition
options.C: Urinary excretion exceeds absorption; net bone resorption
options.D: Absorption equals urinary excretion; no net bone change
options.E: Absorption exceeds urinary excretion; net bone resorption

questions.explanation: Growing children are in positive Ca²⁺ balance: intestinal absorption > urinary excretion, and the excess is deposited in bone. B: Negative balance can't fund net deposition. C: Negative balance, seen in pregnancy and lactation. D: Describes a stable adult. E: A positive balance goes into bone, not out of it.

questions.stem: Urea is 45 mg/100 mL in proximal tubular fluid and 15 mg/100 mL in blood. Permeability is 2×10⁻⁵ cm/s and area 100 cm². What is the urea flux?
questions.explanation: J = P·A·ΔC = (2×10⁻⁵ cm/s)(100 cm²)(30 mg/100 mL = 0.3 mg/cm³) = 6×10⁻⁴ mg/s, from higher (lumen) to lower (blood). A: Wrong direction. C: Uses 30 mg/cm³; forgets that 1 mL = 1 cm³ and the /100 mL. D: Uses the lumen concentration (45) instead of the difference. E: Drops the factor of 2 in P.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 19–20

questions.stem: A transport process moves its solute downhill, shows saturation, transports D- but not L-glucose, and is unaffected by ouabain. Which process is it?
questions.explanation: Downhill, carrier-mediated (saturable, stereospecific), no energy → facilitated diffusion. B: Simple diffusion isn't saturable or stereospecific. C: Primary active transport moves solute uphill. D, E: Secondary active transport is uphill and is inhibited by ouabain (loss of the Na⁺ gradient).
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 12, 22, 28

questions.stem: In the intestinal epithelium, which pair of transporters accounts for transcellular glucose absorption?
questions.explanation: Apical SGLT uses the Na⁺ gradient (secondary active); basolateral GLUT2 lets glucose out by facilitated diffusion; the basolateral Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase maintains the gradient. A: Reversed. C: The pump is basolateral, but glucose entry needs SGLT to go uphill. D: NKCC1 and CFTR mediate Cl⁻ secretion. E: H⁺/K⁺-ATPase is the gastric parietal-cell pump.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slide 49

questions.stem: Which epithelium is best suited to maintain a large transepithelial osmotic gradient?
questions.explanation: Tight epithelia maintain steep gradients, and the lecture names the urinary bladder as the tightest of all (claudins set paracellular permeability). A, B, E: Leaky epithelia do bulk, nearly isosmotic transport. C: The colon is tight, but less so than the bladder.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 50–51

questions.stem: In the renal collecting tubule, Na⁺ enters through apical ENaC and is pumped out basolaterally. How is Cl⁻ absorbed with it?

options.C: Paracellularly, driven by a lumen-negative voltage
options.D: Paracellularly, driven by a lumen-positive voltage
options.E: Paracellularly, by solvent drag with water

questions.explanation: The Na⁺/K⁺ pump moves positive charge from lumen to interstitium, making the lumen negative; this drives passive Cl⁻ absorption across the tight junctions. A: There is no primary Cl⁻ pump in this model. B: NKCC2 is the thick ascending limb transporter. D: The lumen becomes negative, and a lumen-positive voltage would hold Cl⁻ in the lumen. E: Solvent drag is described for leaky epithelia like the proximal tubule.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 55, 57

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man has LDL of 350 mg/dL and tendon xanthomas. His LDL receptors bind LDL normally but fail to internalize it. What is the most likely defect?

options.D: Receptor unable to cluster into clathrin-coated pits
options.E: Failure of receptor recycling from endosomes

questions.explanation: In this form of familial hypercholesterolemia the receptor binds LDL but can't enter clathrin-coated pits, so there is no receptor-mediated endocytosis. A: Receptors are present and bind. B: Binding is normal. C: Lipase deficiency acts after internalization. E: Recycling happens after internalization, which never occurs here.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 39–41

questions.stem: A child with cystic fibrosis has thick airway mucus. Which step of airway NaCl secretion is defective?
questions.explanation: Cl⁻ loaded by NKCC1 exits apically via CFTR; the lumen-negative voltage then pulls Na⁺ paracellularly, and water follows. Without CFTR, secretion fails and mucus thickens. A, B: These basolateral steps are intact. C: ENaC mediates Na⁺ absorption, not secretion. D: Paracellular Na⁺ follows Cl⁻ passively; it isn't the primary defect.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 56, 59

questions.stem: Histamine rapidly increases gastric acid secretion. By which type of regulation does it act on the parietal cell?

options.B: Recruitment of H⁺/K⁺-ATPase to the apical membrane
options.E: Inhibition of the pump by omeprazole

questions.explanation: Histamine translocates the H⁺/K⁺ pump to the apical membrane (recruitment of existing transporters). A: Increased synthesis is the aldosterone example (Na⁺/K⁺ pump subunits). C: Post-transcriptional modification is the CFTR example. D: Claudin modulation is the aldosterone/claudin-8 example. E: Omeprazole blocks the pump, lowering acid.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 24, 59

questions.stem: Ouabain is applied to intestinal epithelium, and glucose absorption falls. Why?

options.A: SGLT loses the Na⁺ gradient that drives glucose entry
options.C: SGLT is a P-type ATPase that ouabain inhibits
options.D: Ouabain competes with glucose for SGLT
options.E: Tight junctions open and glucose leaks back

questions.explanation: Ouabain inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; the Na⁺ gradient that powers secondary active SGLT transport collapses. B: GLUT2 isn't the ouabain target. C: SGLT is a cotransporter (secondary active), not an ATPase. D: Ouabain binds the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, not SGLT. E: Ouabain isn't described as acting on tight junctions.
questions.source: Transport Across the Cell Membrane, slides 24–25, 28, 49

questions.stem: Gentle abdominal pressure is painless in a healthy person but very painful over an inflamed appendix. Which mechanism explains this tenderness?

options.A: Referred pain via convergent spinal neurons
options.B: Lowered nociceptor threshold from inflammatory mediators
options.D: Neuropathic pain from direct nerve injury
options.E: Exaggeration by the emotional component of pain

questions.explanation: Sensitization: bradykinin, prostaglandins, leukotrienes and substance P lower the activation threshold of pain pathways; this is the basis of clinical tenderness. A: Referred pain is felt away from the source. C: Opioid circuits diminish pain. D: The nerve itself isn't the source. E: The emotional component varies perception but doesn't explain localized tenderness over inflamed tissue.

questions.stem: Impulses from a stimulated nociceptor spread into neighboring terminal branches and release a peptide that causes vasodilation, neurogenic edema, and mast-cell histamine release. Which peptide?
questions.explanation: Substance P mediates secondary activation: vasodilation, neurogenic edema, histamine from mast cells and serotonin from platelets. A: Bradykinin is produced in damaged tissue, not released from nerve terminals. B: Prostaglandins sensitize terminals but aren't peptides. C: Serotonin is released from platelets in response to substance P. E: β-endorphin is an endogenous opioid that reduces pain.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old woman has severe burning pain along a thoracic dermatome 2 months after a vesicular rash resolved. Light clothing brushing the skin is excruciating. What is this phenomenon?
questions.explanation: After herpes zoster the nerve itself is the source (neuropathic), and very light moving stimuli become painful (allodynia). A: Pain is in the involved dermatome, not referred. B: The inflammation has resolved. D: Not a placebo effect. E: This is somatic and dermatomal, not visceral.

questions.stem: A patient reports less pain after an inert pill he was told is a strong analgesic. Which system most likely mediates this?
questions.explanation: Suggestion and reassurance act through pain-modulation circuits; the pain-diminishing ones use endogenous opioids (the basis of the placebo effect). A: Sensitization increases pain. B: Substance P amplifies pain. C: Prostaglandins sensitize nociceptors. D: Bradykinin causes pain.

questions.stem: A patient with irritation of the diaphragm complains of shoulder pain. What explains this?

options.A: Fibers from both sites converge on a common spinal cell body
options.C: The phrenic nerve itself is the source of the pain
options.D: The organ activates the same CNS cells as its overlying skin

questions.explanation: Referred pain: pain fibers from different locations converge on the same spinal cell, so the brain misattributes the source. B: There is no shoulder pathology to sensitize. C: Neuropathic pain arises from a damaged nerve, not irritation of an organ. D: That is the normal mechanism that localizes deep pain correctly to the overlying skin, not to a distant site. E: Modulation changes intensity, not location.

questions.stem: A bodybuilder training in a 34 °C gym reaches 39 °C, which falls when he rests. Later, with COVID-19, he is again 39 °C. How do the two episodes compare?

options.B: Exercise: raised set point; infection: unchanged set point
options.C: Exercise: unchanged set point; infection: raised set point
options.D: Both: unchanged set point with failed heat loss
options.E: Exercise: lowered set point; infection: raised set point

questions.explanation: Exercise in heat is hyperthermia: heat gain exceeds loss with the set point unchanged. Infection is fever: pyrogens → PGE₂ → raised set point. A, B: Exercise doesn't change the set point. D: Fever does raise the set point. E: The set point isn't lowered in exercise.

questions.stem: A resting person in a room at 22 °C loses most body heat by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: Radiation accounts for about 60% of heat loss at rest. A, C: Conduction and convection are smaller at rest. B: Evaporation (sweating) becomes important in heat and exercise, not at rest in a cool room. D: Respiratory loss is minor.

questions.stem: A tumor destroys the anterior hypothalamus (preoptic area). Which response is most impaired?

options.E: Brown fat thermogenesis in the cold

questions.explanation: Warm-sensitive neurons of the anterior hypothalamus/POA drive heat dissipation: sweating and skin vasodilation. A, C: Shivering and vasoconstriction come from cold-sensitive neurons in the posterior hypothalamus. D, E: These are heat-production and conservation responses, not anterior-hypothalamus heat loss.

questions.stem: At the onset of fever, a patient shivers under blankets although his temperature is 37.5 °C. Why?
questions.explanation: Pyrogens → PGE₂ raise the set point above body temperature, so the body responds as if cold (chills, shivering). A: Set point below body temperature drives heat loss (as when fever breaks). B: Failed heat dissipation is hyperthermia, with an unchanged set point. C: Sweating is a heat-loss response, not the cause of chills. E: Thyroid hormone isn't the trigger.

questions.stem: During general anesthesia with sevoflurane and succinylcholine, a 20-year-old develops rigidity, hypercapnia, and a temperature of 41 °C. Which best describes his thermoregulatory state?

options.A: Fever: pyrogens raise the set point

questions.explanation: Malignant hyperthermia is a cause of hyperthermia listed in the lecture: uncontrolled muscle heat production with no change in set point. A: No pyrogens or PGE₂ are involved, so antipyretics don't help. C: Temperature is high. D: In hyperthermia the set point is unchanged. E: Circadian swing is only ~0.6 °C.

questions.stem: A newborn exposed to cold maintains temperature without shivering. Which mechanism is mainly responsible?
questions.explanation: Non-shivering thermogenesis in brown fat is most important in infants exposed to cold. B: Thyroid hormone mediates long-term cold adaptation, not the newborn's immediate response. C: Vasodilation loses heat. D: Progesterone raises basal temperature in the luteal phase. E: Sweating promotes heat loss.

questions.stem: Sweating during heat stress is reduced by a drug that blocks the transmitter at the sweat gland. Which fibers normally drive this sweating?
questions.explanation: The anterior hypothalamus/POA sends impulses through the spinal cord and sympathetic cholinergic fibers to the sweat glands. A: Circulating epinephrine/norepinephrine can stimulate sweat glands (important in exercise), but the nerve fibers are cholinergic. B: Sweat glands receive sympathetic, not parasympathetic, innervation. D: Somatic fibers supply skeletal muscle. E: Not a sweat-gland pathway.

questions.stem: An 80-year-old man is found outdoors on a winter morning with a core temperature of 28 °C. What is the most likely cause of death if he is not rewarmed?
questions.explanation: Severe hypothermia (27–29 °C) causes cardiac fibrillation; arrhythmias are the common cause of death, and the elderly are a risk group. B: Heat stroke occurs at 40–44 °C. C, D, E: Not the lecture's cause of death in hypothermia.

questions.stem: A 60-kg man (body fluid osmolality 290 mOsm/kg; 60-40-20 rule) has 360 mmol of NaCl added to his ECF. NaCl stays in the ECF. What is his new body fluid osmolality?
questions.explanation: TBW 36 L; total osmoles 36 × 290 = 10,440. NaCl adds 720 mOsm (2 osmoles per mole) → 11,160/36 = 310 mOsm/kg. Water shifts ICF → ECF until both are equal (ICF ≈ 22.5 L, ECF ≈ 13.5 L). A: NaCl is an effective osmole and raises osmolality. B: Counts NaCl as 1 osmole. D: Counts 1 osmole and ignores the water shift (ECF 12 L only). E: Ignores the water shift from the ICF.

questions.stem: A 70-kg man (osmolality 290 mOsm/kg; 60-40-20 rule) rapidly drinks 3 L of water. After full absorption but before any excretion, what is his plasma osmolality?
questions.explanation: Total osmoles 42 × 290 = 12,180; new TBW 45 L → 271 mOsm/kg in all compartments (ICF 30 L, ECF 15 L; water splits 2/3 : 1/3). A: Water dilutes all compartments. C: Keeps all 3 L in the ECF (4060/17). D: Subtracts the water instead of adding it. E: Puts all 3 L into the ICF (8120/31).

questions.stem: Red cells are placed in 300 mM urea. What happens?

options.A: They swell, because urea enters and water follows
options.B: They shrink, because urea draws water out
options.C: No change, because the solution is isosmotic
options.D: No change, because urea is an impermeant solute
options.E: They shrink, then return to normal volume

questions.explanation: 300 mM urea is isosmotic but hypotonic: urea is permeant, equilibrates across the membrane, and exerts no effective osmotic force, so water enters and cells swell (may burst). B: Urea isn't an effective osmole. C: Isosmotic doesn't mean isotonic. D: Urea is permeant. E: There is no initial shrinkage in the lecture's model.

questions.stem: Which IV fluid is approximately isosmotic in the bag, yet expands both ECF and ICF after infusion?
questions.explanation: D5W (~252 mOsm/L) is near-isosmotic, but glucose is metabolized, leaving free water that distributes into ECF and ICF. A: Isotonic saline stays in the ECF. B: 0.45% NaCl also expands both, but it is hyposmotic in the bag (~154 mOsm/L). D: Mannitol is hyperosmotic and shrinks the ICF. E: Lactated Ringer's is clinically isotonic and stays in the ECF.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man with a severe head injury has rising intracranial pressure. IV mannitol is given. Which change explains its immediate effect?

options.A: It enters neurons and raises their osmolality
options.B: It lowers plasma osmolality, so water leaves the brain
options.C: It raises plasma oncotic pressure like albumin
options.D: It crosses the blood–brain barrier and pulls water into the CSF
options.E: It raises plasma osmolality, drawing water out of brain tissue

questions.explanation: Mannitol is poorly permeable, an effective extracellular osmole: it raises plasma osmolality and draws water from brain cells and interstitium (if the BBB is intact), then causes osmotic diuresis. A: It stays extracellular. B: It raises, not lowers, plasma osmolality. C: It is a sugar alcohol, not a protein. D: It works only if the BBB keeps it out.

questions.stem: Which statement about tonicity is correct?

options.A: 150 mM NaCl and 300 mM urea are both isotonic
options.B: Tonicity includes all solutes, permeant or not
options.C: Infused glucose has a sustained osmotic effect in healthy people
options.D: Tonicity depends only on impermeant solutes
options.E: Isosmotic solutions never change cell volume

questions.explanation: Only impermeant (effective) solutes set tonicity. A: The urea solution is hypotonic. B: That describes osmolarity. C: Rapidly metabolized solutes like dextrose have no sustained osmotic effect. E: Isosmotic urea swells cells.

questions.stem: A 70-kg man (osmolality 290 mOsm/kg) receives 2 L of isotonic saline. What are his final ECF and ICF volumes?
questions.explanation: Isotonic saline doesn't change effective ECF osmolality, so no water shifts: all 2 L stay in the ECF (14 → 16 L) and the ICF stays 28 L. B: Splits the saline 1/3 : 2/3 as if it were water. C: Results of adding NaCl alone (water shifts out of cells). D: Water doesn't leave the ICF. E: Puts all the fluid in the cells.

questions.stem: A patient with nephrotic syndrome is losing protein in the urine and develops generalized edema. Which mechanism is primary?
questions.explanation: Loss of plasma protein leaves less oncotic pressure to pull fluid back into capillaries (hypoalbuminemia; kidney or liver disease). A: Raised hydrostatic pressure is heart failure or venous obstruction. C: Increased permeability is inflammation or burns. D: Lymphatic obstruction is node removal or filariasis. E: Plasma osmolality (crystalloid) doesn't drive edema across capillaries; proteins do.

questions.stem: Use the lecture's values: interstitial pressure −3 mmHg, interstitial oncotic 8 mmHg, venous-end capillary pressure 10 mmHg. A patient with liver failure has plasma oncotic pressure 18 mmHg. What is the net pressure at the venous end?
questions.explanation: Outward 10 + 3 + 8 = 21; inward 18; net 3 mmHg outward, so the venous end now filters. A: The normal venous value (plasma oncotic 28). B: Omits interstitial oncotic pressure. C: Treats the −3 mmHg interstitial pressure as an inward force. E: Uses the arterial-end capillary pressure (30 mmHg).

questions.stem: Which structural feature makes hepatic sinusoids the most permeable type of capillary?
questions.explanation: Discontinuous (sinusoidal) capillaries, e.g. liver, have fenestrae plus large gaps. A: Fenestrated capillaries (small intestine, exocrine glands). C: Continuous capillaries (skeletal muscle). D: Blood–brain barrier capillaries. E: The glycocalyx is a barrier, not a source of permeability.

questions.stem: A solute has a reflection coefficient of 0 across a capillary wall. What does this mean?

options.A: It is fully reflected and exerts its full osmotic force
options.B: It crosses as easily as water and exerts no osmotic force
options.C: It crosses faster than water does
options.D: It crosses only by active transport
options.E: It is held back by the glycocalyx

questions.explanation: σ = 0: the solute leaks through as rapidly as water, so its gradient produces no fluid flow. A: That is σ = 1 (no leakage). C: That is a negative σ (rare). D: σ says nothing about active transport. E: Being held back means σ near 1.

questions.stem: According to the revised (Landis–Pappenheimer) model, what happens when capillary pressure is held steadily below plasma oncotic pressure?

options.A: Sustained absorption, as classic Starling predicts
options.B: Increased filtration at the venous end
options.C: No sustained absorption; absorption is only transient

questions.explanation: Real measurements show absorption only transiently, after abrupt drops in capillary pressure, not at steady state, because fluid exchange occurs with the subglycocalyx space. A: The classic prediction that real data contradict. B: Low pressure doesn't raise filtration. D: Lymph flow continues. E: Not predicted by the model.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with right heart failure has bilateral pitting ankle edema. Serum albumin is normal. Which Starling force change is mainly responsible?
questions.explanation: In cardiac failure, raised pressure at the venous end of the capillary favors filtration over absorption. B: Albumin is normal. C: There's no inflammation or toxin. D: Lymphatics are intact. E: Lower interstitial oncotic pressure would oppose edema.

questions.stem: Shortly after losing 1.5 L of blood, a trauma patient's hematocrit begins to fall before any IV fluids are given. Why?

options.E: Absorption of interstitial fluid into plasma

questions.explanation: A sudden drop in capillary pressure (shock) favors absorption of interstitial fluid into capillaries, diluting the red cells. A: Filtration falls. B: Increased permeability would move fluid out of plasma. C: Marrow changes take days. D: Lymphatic obstruction causes edema, not plasma dilution.

questions.stem: After axillary lymph node dissection for breast cancer, a 52-year-old woman develops persistent arm edema. Which Starling change contributes most?
questions.explanation: Normally more fluid is filtered than absorbed, and lymphatics return the excess fluid and protein. With lymphatic blockage, protein accumulates in the interstitium, raising interstitial oncotic pressure. B: Plasma proteins are normal. C: Raised capillary pressure is heart failure. D: Reduced permeability would limit edema. E: The edematous interstitium becomes less negative, not more.

questions.stem: What makes transport through nuclear pore complexes directional?

options.B: Ran-GTP in the nucleus and Ran-GDP in the cytosol
options.C: Ran-GDP in the nucleus and Ran-GTP in the cytosol
options.D: SRP binding the NLS in the cytosol
options.E: An H⁺ gradient across the nuclear envelope

questions.explanation: Ran-GEF is bound to chromatin in the nucleus (makes Ran-GTP) and Ran-GAP is cytosolic (makes Ran-GDP); this gradient drives both import and export. A: Nucleoporins aren't ATP-driven pumps. C: Reversed: GEF is nuclear, GAP is cytosolic. D: SRP targets proteins to the ER; NLSs bind nuclear import receptors. E: An H⁺ gradient drives mitochondrial, not nuclear, import.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 18, 20–21

questions.stem: A drug collapses the H⁺ gradient across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Which step of protein import is directly blocked?

options.A: Signal-sequence translocation through TIM into the matrix

questions.explanation: Translocation of the signal sequence across the inner membrane into the matrix requires the electrochemical H⁺ gradient. B: Release of cytosolic hsp70 depends on ATP hydrolysis, not the H⁺ gradient. C: TOM recognition at the outer membrane comes first and doesn't need the gradient. D: Translation is unaffected. E: Glycosylation is an ER event.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 26–27

questions.stem: A soluble ER chaperone escapes to the Golgi. How is it returned to the ER?

options.A: Its KKXX signal binds COPI coats directly
options.B: The KDEL receptor packages it into COPII vesicles
options.C: The M6P receptor packages it into clathrin vesicles
options.D: The KDEL receptor packages it into COPI vesicles
options.E: Its NLS binds a nuclear import receptor

questions.explanation: Soluble ER residents carry a C-terminal KDEL; the KDEL receptor (high affinity in the Golgi, low in the ER) packages them into retrograde COPI vesicles. A: KKXX binding COPI directly is the route for ER membrane proteins. B: COPII carries cargo forward from ER to Golgi. C: M6P sorts lysosomal hydrolases. E: NLSs target the nucleus.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 51–52

questions.stem: A mutation blocks assembly of COPII coats. What is the most direct consequence?

options.A: Newly made secretory proteins accumulate in the ER
options.B: Escaped ER residents accumulate in the Golgi
options.C: Lysosomal hydrolases are secreted into the blood
options.D: Nuclear proteins remain in the cytosol
options.E: LDL stays bound at the cell surface

questions.explanation: Proteins leave the ER in COPII-coated vesicles, so blocking COPII traps cargo in the ER. B: That would follow a COPI/retrieval defect. C: That is I-cell disease (missing M6P tag). D: That is an NLS/import defect. E: That is a clathrin-coated pit defect.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 44, 50–51

questions.stem: A 1-year-old has coarse facies and skeletal abnormalities. Fibroblasts show large lysosomal inclusions, and plasma lysosomal enzyme activities are markedly elevated. Which feature of these enzymes is normally recognized for tagging?
questions.explanation: I-cell disease: GlcNAc phosphotransferase recognizes a signal patch on lysosomal hydrolases and starts M6P tagging; without it, hydrolases are secreted into the blood. A: KDEL retains soluble ER proteins. B: The N-terminal signal sends them into the ER but doesn't sort them to lysosomes. C: A C-terminal 3-amino-acid signal targets peroxisomes. D: Lysine-rich internal signals are NLSs.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 12, 57–59

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man eats home-canned vegetables and develops descending flaccid paralysis. The toxin cleaves proteins needed for vesicle fusion at the NMJ. Which protein family is targeted?
questions.explanation: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNAREs, which catalyze vesicle fusion with the target membrane, so ACh isn't released. A: Clathrin coats endocytic and TGN vesicles. C: Targeting GTPases help guide vesicles but aren't the toxin target. D: COPII acts at the ER. E: Adaptins link clathrin to cargo receptors.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 47–48

questions.stem: A precursor protein moves from the cytosol into the mitochondrial matrix. Which transport mode is this, and what must the protein do?
questions.explanation: Transmembrane transport: translocators move proteins into a topologically distinct space (ER lumen, mitochondria), and the protein usually must unfold to snake through. A, D: Gated transport is nucleus–cytosol traffic through pores. B: Vesicular transport moves cargo between topologically equivalent compartments (e.g. ER → Golgi). E: Mitochondrial precursors are imported unfolded.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 6–8, 25

questions.stem: A protein's only sorting signal is an N-terminal sequence containing 5–10 hydrophobic amino acids. Where does it most likely end up?
questions.explanation: An N-terminal hydrophobic signal targets the protein to the ER via SRP; without further signals it passes to the Golgi and on to the cell surface by default. A: ER retention needs a C-terminal KDEL. B: Mitochondrial signals alternate positive and hydrophobic residues. C: Peroxisomal signals are C-terminal 3-amino-acid sequences. D: NLSs are internal clusters of positive residues.
questions.source: Intracellular Compartments and Protein Sorting, slides 12, 33, 63

questions.stem: A vessel has a thick media of many smooth muscle layers with scanty elastic fibers, bounded by distinct internal and external elastic laminae. Which vessel is it?
questions.explanation: Muscular (distributing) arteries, e.g., femoral, radial, coronary, have a thick smooth-muscle media and both elastic laminae. A: The aorta is an elastic artery; its media is dominated by fenestrated elastic membranes. C, D: Veins lack distinct internal and external elastic laminae. E: Arterioles have only 2–3 smooth muscle layers.

questions.stem: A biopsy shows capillaries whose endothelial cells are perforated by fenestrae but rest on a continuous basal lamina. Which organ was most likely biopsied?
questions.explanation: Fenestrated (visceral) capillaries have fenestrae with a continuous basal lamina; they occur where exchange is extensive: endocrine glands, intestine, pancreas, renal glomeruli. A, D: Liver and spleen have sinusoidal capillaries (large fenestrae, discontinuous basal lamina). B, C: Lung and muscle have continuous capillaries (no fenestrae).

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes a medium-sized vein from its companion muscular artery?
questions.explanation: In veins the adventitia is the thickest, most prominent layer and the media is thin (2–4 smooth muscle layers). A, B: These describe the artery. D: Vasa vasorum are more numerous in veins. E: Veins have larger, more irregular lumina.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old teacher who stands all day has dilated, tortuous superficial leg veins and ankle edema. What is the primary structural failure?
questions.explanation: Valve failure in leg veins is the basis of varicose veins; the valves are intimal folds. B, C: These are arterial changes. D: Anchoring filaments hold lymphatic capillaries open; their loss would impair lymph drainage, not dilate veins. E: Pericytes surround capillaries and postcapillary venules, not the superficial leg veins.

questions.stem: Veins contain approximately what percentage of the body's total blood volume at any given time?
questions.explanation: The slides state veins hold about 70% of total blood volume (capacitance vessels). A, B, C: Too low. E: Too high; arteries, capillaries and the heart hold the rest.

questions.stem: What keeps lymphatic capillaries open when interstitial pressure rises?

options.A: Anchoring filaments tethering them to connective tissue

questions.explanation: Anchoring filaments pull the endothelium open as tissue swells. B: Lymphatic capillaries lack muscle. C: Their junctions are loose. D: They lack fenestrae. E: Valves occur in larger lymphatics.

questions.stem: Contraction of which structures prevents blood from entering a capillary bed?
questions.explanation: Precapillary sphincters are individual smooth muscle cells around capillaries at their origin from metarterioles; their constriction stops blood entering the bed. A: Muscular venules are downstream of the bed. B: Valves prevent venous backflow. C: Elastic laminae don't contract. D: Vasa vasorum supply the walls of large vessels.

questions.stem: Which combination of features describes the capillaries of the spleen and bone marrow?

options.C: Many large fenestrae; discontinuous basal lamina
options.D: No fenestrae; sparse basal lamina with anchoring filaments
options.E: Smooth muscle layer; continuous basal lamina

questions.explanation: Sinusoidal capillaries (liver, spleen, bone marrow, lymph nodes, adrenal cortex) have many large fenestrae and a discontinuous basal lamina. A: Continuous capillaries. B: Fenestrated capillaries. D: Lymphatic capillaries. E: Capillaries have no muscular layer.

questions.stem: The common carotid artery is classified as which vessel type, with which tunica media?

options.A: Muscular artery; layers of smooth muscle with scanty elastic fibers
options.C: Elastic artery; 2–3 layers of smooth muscle

questions.explanation: The aorta and its major branches (common carotid, subclavian, large pulmonary arteries) are elastic (conducting) arteries; their broad media of fenestrated elastic membranes damps pressure changes with each heartbeat. A: Describes muscular arteries such as the femoral or radial. B: Mismatch; muscular arteries have scanty elastic fibers. C, E: A 2–3-layer smooth muscle media describes arterioles.

questions.stem: A DNA sample is 30% adenine. What percentage is guanine?
questions.explanation: Chargaff: A = T = 30%, so G + C = 40% and G = 20%. A: 30% is thymine. B: 40% is G + C combined. D: 35% splits the remaining 70% without subtracting thymine. E: Halves the correct value.

questions.stem: Five double-stranded DNA fragments of equal length differ only in base composition. Which needs the most heat to denature?
questions.explanation: By Chargaff's rule, 15% A means 30% A–T and 70% G–C, the highest; G–C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds versus 2 for A–T. A: 80% A–T, so only 20% G–C. C: 60% A–T, so 40% G–C. D: 40% G–C. E: 50% G–C.

questions.stem: Which feature is true of the mitochondrial genome but not of the nuclear genome?

options.B: More than 90% of the sequence is noncoding
options.C: Lower mutation rate than the other genome
options.D: Some codons don't follow the universal code

questions.explanation: Per the comparison slide, some mitochondrial codons deviate from the universal code. A: mtDNA is circular; nuclear DNA is linear. B: Only ~3% of mtDNA is noncoding; >90% describes nuclear DNA. C: mtDNA has a higher mutation rate. E: Both genomes are double-stranded.

questions.stem: A drug inhibits histone deacetylases. What is the expected effect on chromatin near target genes?

options.A: Chromatin stays acetylated and open, increasing transcription
options.C: Histone tails keep a stronger positive charge

questions.explanation: Acetylation neutralizes histone tails, loosening chromatin; blocking deacetylation keeps genes active. B: That's the effect of deacetylation. C: Acetylation removes positive charge. D: HDAC inhibition doesn't directly methylate DNA. E: Nucleosomes remain.

questions.stem: At one level of compaction, DNA is about 50 times shorter than its extended form, with about 6 nucleosomes per turn. Which level is this?
questions.explanation: The 2nd level, the 30-nm solenoid, shortens DNA ~50-fold with 6 nucleosomes per turn. A: Nucleosomes (1st level) shorten DNA ~7-fold. B: Loops are the 3rd level, formed by supercoiling the solenoid. C: Euchromatin is the decondensed, transcriptionally active state. D: The octamer is the protein core DNA wraps around in a nucleosome.

questions.stem: Whose X-ray diffraction image (Photo 51) confirmed the helical structure that Watson and Crick had only theorized?
questions.explanation: Franklin's Photo 51 revealed the helical structure. B: Wilkins, her colleague, showed her work to Watson and Crick and shared the 1962 Nobel Prize. C: Stimson showed the bases lie inside the molecule. D: Chargaff described the base-pairing ratios. E: Levene proposed the incorrect tetranucleotide model.

questions.stem: A molecule consists of deoxyribose bonded to adenine, with no phosphate group. What is it?
questions.explanation: Sugar + base = nucleoside, and adenine is a purine. A: A nucleotide also needs a phosphate. C: Adenine is a purine, not a pyrimidine. D: Wrong base class, and there is no phosphate. E: A free base has no sugar.

questions.stem: Humans have about 20,000 genes but more than 160,000 proteins. What mainly explains this?
questions.explanation: Alternative splicing produces several proteins from one gene. A: Pseudogenes don't make functional proteins. C: Gene families are separate genes. D: Housekeeping genes are a category, not a mechanism. E: These are repetitive elements, not a way one gene yields several proteins.

questions.stem: A sequence resembles an active gene but lacks introns and a promoter and ends in a poly(A) stretch. What is it?
questions.explanation: Processed pseudogenes arise by retrotransposition of mRNA, so they lack introns and promoters. A: Nonprocessed pseudogenes keep introns. B: Housekeeping genes are functional. C: Microsatellites are short tandem repeats. D: lncRNA genes are transcribed from promoters.

questions.stem: A forensic lab compares DNA from a crime scene with suspects. Which markers vary most usefully between individuals?
questions.explanation: STR repeat number varies among people, enabling human identification. B: Centromeric repeats aren't used for routine identification. C: SINEs are interspersed retrotransposed elements, not the identification markers. D: Housekeeping exons are highly conserved. E: Telomere sequence is identical across people.

questions.stem: Which RNA acts as the peptidyl transferase during translation and makes up ~80% of cellular RNA?
questions.explanation: rRNA is the catalytic and structural core of ribosomes. A: mRNA is ~3–7% of RNA. B: tRNA is ~10–15%. C: snRNA functions in splicing. E: miRNA regulates gene expression.

questions.stem: A regulatory RNA of 22 nucleotides reduces protein production from a target gene. What is its mechanism?

options.A: Binding complementary mRNA, which RISC then degrades or blocks
options.B: Methylating CpG islands in the target promoter
options.C: Guiding splicing of the target pre-mRNA
options.D: Remodeling chromatin as a capped, polyadenylated transcript
options.E: Acting as a peptidyl transferase on the ribosome

questions.explanation: miRNAs (18–25 nt) act by RNA interference: they bind complementary mRNA, and the RISC complex suppresses translation and promotes degradation. B: Promoter methylation isn't an miRNA function. C: Splicing involves snRNAs. D: That describes lncRNAs (>200 nt). E: Peptidyl transferase activity belongs to rRNA.

questions.stem: Normal fibroblasts stop dividing after a limited number of divisions, but a cancer cell line divides indefinitely while keeping its chromosome ends stable. Which enzyme activity is most likely increased?
questions.explanation: Telomerase adds TTAGGG repeats to chromosome ends; its activity is abundant in cancer and insufficient in aging. A: Ligase joins DNA fragments. B: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling. D: Primase makes RNA primers. E: RNase H removes primers.

questions.stem: A tandem repeat array consists of a 30-bp unit repeated about 100 times (3 kb). How is it classified?
questions.explanation: Minisatellites (VNTRs) have 10–100-bp units in 0.5–30-kb arrays. A: STRs have 2–5-bp units. B: SINEs are interspersed retrotransposed elements <500 bp, not tandem arrays. C: LINEs are ~6-kb interspersed elements. E: Telomeres are 6-bp TTAGGG repeats at chromosome ends.

questions.stem: In C0t analysis, denatured genomic DNA is allowed to reanneal. Which fraction renatures at the lowest C0t values?
questions.explanation: Reassociation rate is proportional to copy number, so highly repetitive satellite DNA renatures first (C0t <10⁻²). A: Unique sequences renature last (C0t 10–10⁴). C: Moderately repetitive DNA renatures at intermediate C0t (10⁻²–10). D: Mostly single-copy genes. E: Mostly single copies too.

questions.stem: Why is the lagging strand synthesized discontinuously?

options.A: DNA polymerase synthesizes only in the 5′→3′ direction
options.B: Helicase unwinds only the lagging-strand template
options.C: Primase can prime only the leading strand
options.D: DNA polymerase reads the template only 5′→3′
options.E: Ligase must seal each fragment before the next begins

questions.explanation: Polymerase adds nucleotides only to a 3′ end (synthesis 5′→3′), so the strand oriented against fork movement is made in Okazaki fragments. B: Helicase unwinds both strands. C: Every new strand needs a primer. D: Polymerase reads the template 3′→5′. E: Ligase joins the fragments afterward.

questions.stem: In which order are RNA primers handled at the end of DNA replication?

options.A: Ligase → RNase H → DNA polymerase I
options.B: RNase H → DNA polymerase I → ligase
options.D: RNase H → DNA polymerase III → topoisomerase
options.E: DNA polymerase I → RNase H → ligase

questions.explanation: Per the lecture: RNase H removes the primers, DNA polymerase I fills the gaps, DNA ligase seals the nicks. A: Nicks can't be sealed before primers are replaced. C: Primase makes primers; it doesn't remove them. D: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling; it doesn't seal nicks. E: Primers must be removed before pol I fills the gap.

questions.stem: A template DNA strand reads 3′-TACGGA-5′. What is the mRNA sequence?
questions.explanation: RNA is complementary to the template and antiparallel, matching the coding strand (5′-ATGCCT-3′) with U for T. A: That's the template itself. B: Reversed. C: Uses T, so it's DNA. E: Wrong orientation.

questions.stem: A mutation changes the intron's first two nucleotides from GU to AU. What is the most likely consequence?

options.C: Abnormal splicing at the donor site
options.D: Premature stop codon in the exon

questions.explanation: GU marks the 5′ (donor) splice site; altering it disrupts splicing (exon skipping or intron retention). A: Capping is independent of splice sites. B: AAUAAA is the poly(A) signal. D: Not a coding change. E: Kozak surrounds the start codon.

questions.stem: Which enzyme ensures each tRNA carries the correct amino acid?
questions.explanation: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases attach each amino acid to its tRNA. A: Peptidyl transferase forms peptide bonds. C: RNA pol III transcribes tRNA genes. D: Release factors end translation. E: Poly(A) polymerase adds the tail.

questions.stem: During elongation, where does an incoming aminoacyl-tRNA bind?
questions.explanation: New aminoacyl-tRNAs enter the A site; the growing chain sits in the P site; empty tRNAs exit from the E site. A: P holds the peptidyl-tRNA. B: E is the exit. D: Cap binding happens at initiation. E: Kozak is an mRNA sequence.

questions.stem: A mutation in the AAUAAA sequence of a gene's 3′ region would most directly impair which step?

options.D: Transcription initiation at the TATA box
options.E: Cleavage and polyadenylation of the pre-mRNA

questions.explanation: AAUAAA signals the endonuclease to cleave and poly(A) polymerase to add the tail. A: Capping is at the 5′ end. B: Branch points are within introns. C: AUG is the start codon. D: TATA is in the promoter.

questions.stem: A point variant changes the codon UGG (Trp) to UGA. What happens when the ribosome reaches this codon?

options.A: A release factor recognizes it and the chain is released
options.B: A tRNA reads UGA as tryptophan by wobble pairing
options.C: The ribosome skips the codon and continues
options.D: A different amino acid is inserted
options.E: Translation continues to the normal stop codon

questions.explanation: UGA is a stop codon (with UAA and UAG); release factors recognize it, water is added instead of a peptide bond, and a truncated protein is released. B: Wobble lets a tRNA read synonymous sense codons; no tRNA reads stop codons. C: Stop codons end translation; they aren't skipped. D: Stop codons don't encode amino acids. E: Translation ends at the new stop codon.

questions.stem: During DNA replication, the error rate falls from about 1 in 10⁴ to about 1 in 10⁸ nucleotides. Which activity is mainly responsible during replication?

options.B: Gap filling by DNA polymerase I

questions.explanation: Per the lecture, DNA polymerase III proofreads during replication, and pol II corrects remaining errors at the end. A: RNase H removes RNA primers. B: Pol I fills gaps left by primers. C: Ligase seals nicks. E: Helicase breaks hydrogen bonds to open the fork.

questions.stem: The variant c.621C>A changes codon UAC (Tyr) to UAA. What type of variant is this?
questions.explanation: UAA is a stop codon, so translation ends early (p.Tyr207X). The slide writes this as c.621U>A; in c. notation DNA bases are used and the changed base is C. A: Synonymous keeps the same amino acid. B: Frameshift needs an indel not divisible by 3. C: Missense substitutes a different amino acid. E: The change is within a codon, not a splice site.

questions.stem: A report reads c.16_17delAG (p.Ser6ProfsX2). Which best describes this variant?

options.A: Frameshift deletion with a premature stop

questions.explanation: Deleting 2 nt shifts the reading frame; 'fs' means frameshift and 'X2' means the stop is at position 2 of the shifted frame (Pro6 = 1, stop at codon 7). B: In-frame deletions remove a multiple of 3 nt. C: Nonsense is a single-base substitution creating a stop. D: Pro6 is only the first changed residue; the frame stays shifted after it. E: The protein is altered.

questions.stem: In the variant c.133C>T (p.Arg45Trp), what do the prefixes c. and p. indicate?

options.B: c. = coding DNA numbering; p. = protein level
options.C: c. = codon number; p. = polypeptide length

questions.explanation: c. numbers the coding DNA (cDNA) sequence and p. gives the protein change. A: Here p. is the protein level, not the short chromosome arm. C: 133 is a nucleotide position; the codon number (45) is in the p. part. D: C>T shows the base change; prefixes give the reference type. E: Genomic numbering uses g.; pathogenicity isn't part of the name.

questions.stem: A variant is found in 8% of the general population. How is it best described?

options.C: A variant of uncertain significance by definition

questions.explanation: A variant in ≥1% of the population is a polymorphism and is more likely benign. A: Common variants are rarely pathogenic for rare disease. B: Frequency doesn't define de novo status. C: VUS is a classification, not set by frequency. D: Somatic status is unrelated.

questions.stem: A woman with AD osteogenesis imperfecta carries a glycine substitution in one COL1A1 allele. The abnormal chains are incorporated into triple helices and disrupt them. What mechanism is this?
questions.explanation: The mutant protein interferes with the normal protein in the multimer. A: Haploinsufficiency is reduced quantity, not interference. B: No novel function is gained. D: Imprinting is parent-of-origin silencing. E: LOH applies to tumor suppressors.
questions.source: Genetic Variability and Disease, slide 37; reading p2

questions.stem: How many disease-causing variants does a typical individual exome contain?
questions.explanation: Of ~20,000 exome variants, only ~1–2 are disease-causing. A: Total variants. B: Non-synonymous. C: Rare variants. D: Homozygous rare variants.

questions.stem: A rare missense variant is found in a gene that fits the patient's phenotype, but the evidence is insufficient to call it either benign or pathogenic. How is it classified?
questions.explanation: A VUS is the middle ACMG category, used when evidence is insufficient either way. A: Likely benign requires evidence favoring benign. B: A polymorphism is defined by frequency ≥1%; this variant is rare. D: Likely pathogenic requires evidence favoring pathogenicity. E: Pathogenic requires strong evidence.

questions.stem: Non-allelic homologous recombination between segmental duplications in opposite orientation on the same chromosome produces:
questions.explanation: Inverted repeats recombine to flip the intervening segment. A, B: Direct repeats yield deletions or duplications. D: SDs on different chromosomes yield translocations. E: NAHR causes structural, not point, changes.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old has slowly progressive distal leg weakness; nerve conduction studies show a demyelinating neuropathy, and he is diagnosed with Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1A. Which genetic change is most likely?
questions.explanation: Most CMT1A is a 1.5-Mb chr17 duplication including PMP22, produced by NAHR between flanking segmental duplications. A: A single PMP22 copy causes HNPP. C: The classic mechanism changes PMP22 dosage; a translocation doesn't. D: Inversions don't change dosage. E: Chromothripsis is a complex multi-rearrangement event, not the usual cause.

questions.stem: Which abnormality would a chromosomal microarray (array-CGH) detect?
questions.explanation: Microarrays detect copy-number changes larger than ~1 kb. A: A balanced translocation has no gain or loss. B: An inversion is balanced too. C: Far below ~1-kb resolution; sequencing is needed. E: Also below the resolution.

questions.stem: Which abnormality is most likely to be missed by a standard karyotype?
questions.explanation: Standard karyotyping resolves only changes >5 Mb; a 1-Mb deletion needs a microarray (>1 kb resolution). A: A whole extra chromosome is visible. B: Large translocations are visible. C: Large inversions are visible. D: Ring chromosomes are visible.

questions.stem: Exome sequencing is done for a child with a rare disease. Which variant is most likely removed at the first filtering step?

options.D: A rare homozygous missense variant in a known disease gene

questions.explanation: The first filter removes common variants (minor allele frequency >1%), which are unlikely to cause a rare disease. A: Rare and predicted damaging, so kept. C: Novel and truncating, so kept. D: Rare and in a disease gene, so kept. E: Rare and predicted damaging, so kept.

questions.stem: Which DNA repair pathway joins double-strand break ends with little or no homology, often leaving small insertions or deletions?
questions.explanation: NHEJ fuses double-strand break ends with little or no homology, especially in G0/G1, leaving insertions or deletions at the junction. B: NAHR needs highly identical segmental duplications. C: FoSTeS is a replication error, not break repair. D: Serial replication slippage is also replication-based. E: Crossing-over is normal meiotic exchange between non-sister chromatids.

questions.stem: Two 15-kb regions on the same chromosome share 97% sequence identity. How are they best classified?
questions.explanation: SDs/LCRs are regions ≥1 kb present in more than one copy with ≥90% identity; they mediate NAHR. B: STRs have 2–5-bp repeat units. C: SINEs are <500 bp. D: VNTR units are 10–100 bp. E: LINEs are ~6 kb interspersed retrotransposons.

questions.stem: A pedigree shows affected individuals in every generation, both sexes affected, and an affected father with an affected son. What is the most likely inheritance?
questions.explanation: Vertical transmission with male-to-male transmission indicates AD. A, B: X-linked inheritance never shows male-to-male transmission. C: AR is horizontal (siblings). E: Mitochondrial disease isn't passed by fathers.
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, reading p1

questions.stem: Two unaffected parents have a child with cystic fibrosis. What is the chance their next child will be an unaffected carrier?
questions.explanation: Each child: 25% affected, 50% carrier, 25% non-carrier. B: 25% is the risk of being affected. C: 75% is the chance of being unaffected. D: 2/3 is the carrier probability for an already unaffected sibling. E: Not all children are carriers.
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, reading p3

questions.stem: A man with Marfan syndrome has an unaffected daughter whose son has Marfan syndrome. What explains the daughter's status?
questions.explanation: She carries the mutation but shows no phenotype: non-penetrance. A: Variable expressivity is differing severity in affected carriers. B: Mosaicism would involve her father's gonads. C: Anticipation is worsening over generations from repeat expansion. D: Pleiotropy is multiple effects of one gene.
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, reading p2

questions.stem: A man with hemophilia A and a non-carrier woman have children. What is the risk to their sons and daughters?

options.B: 50% of sons affected; 50% of daughters carriers
options.C: No sons affected; all daughters carriers

questions.explanation: An affected male gives his X to all daughters (carriers) and his Y to all sons. A: Sons get his Y. B: That's the pattern for a carrier mother. D: Sons aren't carriers. E: Daughters are heterozygous carriers, usually unaffected.
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, reading p3

questions.stem: A girl has progressive proximal weakness and markedly elevated CK. Dystrophin testing shows a pathogenic variant on one X; her father is healthy. Which mechanism best explains her symptoms?
questions.explanation: If most cells inactivate the normal X, a heterozygous female can manifest an X-linked recessive disease. A: UPD is possible but far less common than skewing. C: DMD isn't a repeat disease. D: Pseudodominance relates to consanguinity in AR. E: Dystrophin isn't imprinted.
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, reading p4

questions.stem: Unaffected parents have two children with achondroplasia, both carrying the same FGFR3 mutation. Neither parent has the mutation in blood DNA. What best explains the recurrence?
questions.explanation: A mutation in part of a parent's germline can recur in several gametes. A: Achondroplasia is fully penetrant, so a carrier parent would be affected. B: It's dominant. C: Not a repeat disorder. D: The same gene is involved.
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, reading p2

questions.stem: Hereditary deafness can be caused by mutations in many different genes with AD, AR, or X-linked inheritance. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Different genes causing the same phenotype is locus heterogeneity. A: Allelic heterogeneity is different mutations in one gene. B: Pleiotropy is one gene with multiple effects. D: Variable expressivity is varying severity. E: A phenocopy is a non-genetic mimic (e.g., rubella deafness).
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, reading p5

questions.stem: A healthy woman's brother and maternal uncle both have hemophilia A. Her parents are unaffected. What is the probability that her first son will be affected?
questions.explanation: Her mother is an obligate carrier (affected son and affected brother), so the woman has a 1/2 chance of being a carrier, and a carrier's son has a 1/2 risk: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. A: That's the risk if she were a known carrier. C: 1/8 is the risk for a child of unknown sex. D: 2/3 is the carrier risk of an unaffected sibling in AR disease. E: Unaffected women can still be carriers.
questions.source: Mendelian Patterns and Inheritance, slides 45–46; reading p3–4

questions.stem: Different FGFR3 mutations cause achondroplasia, hypochondroplasia, thanatophoric dysplasia, or craniosynostosis. What does the lecture call this?
questions.explanation: One gene producing several distinct phenotypes is clinical heterogeneity. B: Locus heterogeneity is many genes causing one phenotype (e.g., deafness). C: Penetrance is whether a carrier shows any phenotype. D: Germline mosaicism explains recurrence from unaffected parents. E: A phenocopy is a non-genetic mimic.

questions.stem: A woman with a mitochondrial myopathy has several children with very different severity. Her brother, also affected, has unaffected children. What explains both observations?

options.C: Autosomal dominant inheritance with reduced penetrance

questions.explanation: mtDNA passes only through mothers; heteroplasmy (via the bottleneck) gives variable severity. B: Affected X-linked males would pass it to daughters. C: AD would allow paternal transmission. D: Imprinting depends on parent of origin of a nuclear gene. E: Anticipation needs repeat expansion.
questions.source: Unusual Patterns of Inheritance, slides 7; reading p9–10

questions.stem: A 15q11–13 deletion is found in a child with severe intellectual disability, absent speech, ataxia, seizures, and frequent laughter. On which parental chromosome is the deletion?

options.D: Paternal; UBE3A is expressed only from the paternal copy in brain

questions.explanation: Angelman results from loss of maternal UBE3A expression (maternal deletion in ~70%, paternal UPD, or UBE3A mutation). A: A paternal deletion causes Prader-Willi. B: This region is imprinted. C: A homozygous deletion isn't the mechanism. D: UBE3A is paternally imprinted (silenced) in brain, so the maternal copy is the expressed one.
questions.source: Unusual Patterns of Inheritance, slide 30; reading p8

questions.stem: A hypotonic newborn later develops hyperphagia, obesity, and hypogonadism. FISH for 15q11–13 is normal, but methylation testing is abnormal. What is the most likely mechanism?
questions.explanation: Prader-Willi without a deletion is almost always maternal UPD15 (no paternal copy). A: Paternal UPD15 causes Angelman. B: UBE3A mutations cause Angelman. D: A deletion would show on FISH. E: A maternal deletion causes Angelman and would also show on FISH.
questions.source: Unusual Patterns of Inheritance, slide 30; reading p8

questions.stem: A young man has intellectual disability, a long face, large ears, and macroorchidism. What is the molecular basis?

options.A: CAG expansion in the coding region of huntingtin
options.B: CGG expansion in the FMR1 5′ UTR with methylation and silencing
options.C: CTG expansion in the DMPK 3′ UTR

questions.explanation: Fragile X: a full CGG expansion in the FMR1 5′ UTR (>250 repeats per the slide) is methylated, so FMRP is absent. A: Huntington disease. C: Myotonic dystrophy. D: Friedreich ataxia. E: Prader-Willi/Angelman.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman has premature ovarian failure. Her nephew has fragile X syndrome. What is her most likely genotype?

options.E: Skewed X inactivation of a normal X

questions.explanation: Premutation carriers (59 to ~200 CGG repeats) have a ~20% risk of premature ovarian failure before 40; full-mutation carriers don't. A: Full mutations aren't linked to ovarian failure. B: A normal allele wouldn't explain it. C: UPD of X isn't the mechanism. E: Skewing of a normal X doesn't cause ovarian failure.

questions.stem: Which mtDNA defect is typical of Kearns-Sayre syndrome?
questions.explanation: KSS, Pearson syndrome, and CPEO are caused by single mtDNA deletions. A: MELAS. B: MERRF. C: LHON. D: POLG causes SANDO/MIRAS.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old woman has diabetes and progressive bilateral hearing loss; her mother had the same, and her brother has recurrent stroke-like episodes with lactic acidosis. Which variant is most likely?
questions.explanation: m.3243A>G most often presents as maternally inherited diabetes and deafness, and also causes MELAS. B: MERRF (myoclonus, ragged red fibers). C: NARP. D: LHON. E: Fragile X–associated disorders.

questions.stem: A complete hydatidiform mole has a 46,XX karyotype. What is the parental origin of its genome?

options.C: Maternal with one extra paternal set
options.E: Paternal with one extra maternal set

questions.explanation: Complete moles are androgenetic, so paternal genome leads to placental overgrowth with no fetus. A: Entirely maternal is an ovarian teratoma. B: That's normal. C: That's a partial mole (69,XXY). E: A maternal extra set gives a small placenta.
questions.source: Unusual Patterns of Inheritance, reading p8

questions.stem: A man inherited from his mother an allele that is silenced by maternal imprinting in his somatic cells. What imprint will this allele carry in his sperm?

options.B: Paternal imprint, after erasure and resetting
options.D: Maternal imprint in half of his sperm
options.E: A random imprint set at fertilization

questions.explanation: Imprints are maintained through somatic divisions but erased and reset during gametogenesis, so all of a man's gametes carry a paternal imprint. A: Maintenance applies to somatic cells, not gametes. C: The imprint is reset, not lost. D: Gametes are 100% maternal or 100% paternal by the parent's sex. E: Imprints are set during gametogenesis, before fertilization.

lectures.title: Introduction to Epidemiology and Sources of Data

questions.stem: Which question is typical of epidemiology rather than clinical medicine?

options.A: What is the leading cause of death in this population?
options.C: What dose should this child receive?

questions.explanation: Epidemiology studies populations; clinical medicine focuses on individuals. B, C, D, E: These are individual clinical questions.
questions.source: Introduction to Epidemiology and Sources of Data, slide 8

questions.stem: Investigating 27 students with vomiting and diarrhea, you first chart cases by time of onset, the event attended, and age and sex. Which type of epidemiology is this?
questions.explanation: Describing frequency and pattern by time, place, and person (when, where, who) is descriptive epidemiology. A: Analytical epidemiology asks why: it tests determinants. B: Clinical epidemiology links epidemiology to patient care. C: Surveillance is ongoing, systematic collection of health data, not the description of one outbreak. D: Evaluation assesses interventions after they are implemented.
questions.source: Introduction to Epidemiology and Sources of Data, slides 3, 11–12

questions.stem: Influenza cases in a city rise well above the usual seasonal level for that time and place. This is best termed:
questions.explanation: An epidemic (outbreak) is an increase in cases above what is normally expected for that place and time. A: Endemic is the constant baseline presence. B: Sporadic means scattered, irregular cases. C: A pandemic crosses international boundaries. E: Epidemiologic transition is a long-term shift from infectious to chronic disease patterns.
questions.source: Introduction to Epidemiology and Sources of Data, slide 28

questions.stem: Which contribution belongs to John Snow?

options.A: Quantified patterns of birth and death in London's population
options.B: Linked cholera deaths to contaminated water by comparing water sources
options.C: Inoculated a boy with cowpox to protect against smallpox
options.D: Identified cardiovascular risk factors in a prospective cohort
options.E: Analyzed British mortality by marital status and occupation

questions.explanation: Snow (1854) compared cholera deaths by water company and linked cases to the Broad Street pump: father of field epidemiology. A: John Graunt (17th century). C: Edward Jenner (1796). D: Framingham Heart Study (1948). E: William Farr (19th century).
questions.source: Introduction to Epidemiology and Sources of Data, slides 18, 21–22, 24

questions.stem: Lebanon maintains a database that collects information on every person diagnosed with cancer. This source of health data is a:
questions.explanation: A registry is a database of cases diagnosed with a particular disease (e.g., Lebanon's cancer registry). A: A census enumerates the whole population with demographic data (Lebanon's last: 1932). B: Surveillance is ongoing collection, analysis and dissemination of data on health events to detect outbreaks and monitor burden. D: Death certificates record causes of death (ICD-11). E: Discharge summaries record hospitalizations.
questions.source: Introduction to Epidemiology and Sources of Data, slides 29–31

questions.stem: In the same outbreak, investigators compare how often students who ate the chicken salad became ill with how often those who didn't eat it became ill. This step is:
questions.explanation: Comparing groups to identify a determinant (why it happened) is analytical epidemiology. A: Descriptive epidemiology describes time, place and person without testing causes.
