B: Surveillance is ongoing routine data collection. C: Clinical medicine diagnoses and treats individuals. D: Epidemiologic transition is a long-term change in disease patterns.
questions.source: Introduction to Epidemiology and Sources of Data, slides 11–12, 15

questions.stem: In a city of 100,000 adults, 5,000 had diabetes on January 1 and 500 new cases occurred during the year. What is the incidence risk?
questions.explanation: Incidence risk = 500 / (100,000 − 5,000) ≈ 0.53%. A: Point prevalence. B: Period prevalence. C: Uses the whole population as the denominator. E: Ratio of new to existing cases.

questions.stem: 500 adults were enrolled; 5 had TB at baseline. Over 2 years, the 495 at-risk participants contributed 900 person-years, and 45 new cases occurred. What is the incidence rate?
questions.explanation: Incidence rate = new cases / person-time at risk = 45 / 900 PY = 0.05 = 5 per 100 person-years. A: 45/495 is the 2-year incidence risk. C: (5 + 45)/500 is the period prevalence. D: 5/500 is the baseline point prevalence. E: Divides again by 2 years; person-years already include time.

questions.stem: Why does diabetes have a much higher prevalence than the common cold despite a lower incidence?

options.A: Diabetes lasts far longer, so cases accumulate
options.B: Diabetes cases are more often diagnosed
options.C: The common cold has a higher case-fatality
options.D: Diabetes incidence is measured per person-time
options.E: Colds give lasting immunity after infection

questions.explanation: Prevalence ≈ incidence × duration; diabetes lasts for life, while a cold lasts days. B: Detection differences can't explain a gap this size; duration is the driver. C: Colds rarely kill, and fatality isn't what separates them here. D: The unit used for incidence doesn't change prevalence. E: Colds recur; lasting immunity would lower incidence, not explain prevalence.

questions.stem: Prevalence of a disease has been stable for years. A prevention program lowers its incidence. What happens to prevalence?
questions.explanation: Fewer new cases enter the pool, so prevalence falls (duration unchanged). A, B, D: Not expected. C: The direction is predictable.

questions.stem: Which change would increase prevalence without changing incidence?
questions.explanation: Longer duration raises prevalence. A, B: Shorten duration and lower prevalence. D, E: Lower incidence.

questions.stem: Which measure best estimates the number of dialysis units a region needs?
questions.explanation: Prevalence measures disease burden for planning services. A: Incidence reflects new cases only. B, C: Mortality measures. E: A denominator, not a measure.

questions.stem: A hospital reports '12 new central-line infections per 1,000 patient-days'. What kind of measure is this?
questions.explanation: New cases per unit of person-time at risk is an incidence rate (incidence density), a true rate. A: Incidence risk is new cases / people at risk at the start, a proportion without time units. B: Point prevalence counts existing cases at one moment. C: Period prevalence counts existing cases over a period. D: A ratio compares two separate quantities, not events over person-time.

questions.stem: Ten disease-free workers are followed. Six stay healthy for the full 2 years, 2 develop asthma at exactly 1 year, and 2 are lost to follow-up at 1 year. What is the incidence rate of asthma?
questions.explanation: Person-time = 6 × 2 + 2 × 1 + 2 × 1 = 16 PY; rate = 2 / 16 = 12.5 per 100 PY. B: 2/20 assumes everyone was at risk for 2 years. C: 2/10 is a risk, not a rate. D: 2/14 leaves out the lost workers' time at risk. E: 2/12 counts only the workers who completed follow-up.

lectures.title: Measures and Indicators of Health Status

questions.stem: In a town of 200,000, 40 people are diagnosed with disease X during a year, and 10 of them die of it. What is the case-fatality rate?
questions.explanation: CFR = deaths from the disease / diagnosed cases = 10 / 40 = 25%. A: 10/200,000 is the mortality rate. B: 40/200,000 is the proportion of the town with the disease. C: 30/40 is the proportion who survived. E: CFR is a proportion of diagnosed cases; no person-time is needed.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slides 8–9

questions.stem: Early in an outbreak only severe hospitalized cases are tested. Testing then expands to the community and finds many mild cases; the number of deaths is unchanged. What happens to the case-fatality rate (CFR) and the mortality rate?
questions.explanation: CFR = deaths / confirmed cases: the denominator grows while deaths stay constant, so CFR falls. Mortality rate = deaths / whole population: neither part changes. B: CFR changes because its denominator changes; the mortality rate doesn't. C: The mortality rate's denominator is the whole population, not confirmed cases. D: More confirmed cases lowers CFR. E: CFR's denominator has changed.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slides 10, 34

questions.stem: City 1 has a crude mortality rate of 296 per 100,000 and City 2 of 469 per 100,000. City 2's population is much older. What is the best conclusion?
questions.explanation: Crude rates are influenced by age structure; standardization removes this so populations can be compared fairly. A: The higher crude rate may simply reflect an older population. C: Only true after adjustment for age. D: CFR measures disease severity, not population mortality. E: Proportionate mortality is the fraction of deaths by cause and isn't a measure of risk.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slides 16–18, 35

questions.stem: A ministry wants to rank conditions by the total healthy life they cost the population, including low back pain, which rarely kills. Which measure fits best?
questions.explanation: DALYs = YLL + YLD, combining premature death and disability; low back pain's burden is almost all YLD. A: QALYs measure health gained by an intervention. B: Life expectancy summarizes a whole population, not the burden of one condition. D: Counts deaths only. E: Counts deaths only.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slides 28–30

questions.stem: Without treatment, a patient will live 4 years at a utility weight of 0.5. With a new treatment, the patient will live 6 years at a utility weight of 0.75. How many QALYs does the treatment gain?
questions.explanation: QALY = years × utility: without = 4 × 0.5 = 2; with = 6 × 0.75 = 4.5; gain = 2.5 QALYs. A: QALYs without treatment (also the extra life-years alone). B: QALYs with treatment. C: The change in utility weight alone. D: Applies the utility gain to the original 4 years only and ignores the 2 extra years.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slides 31–32

questions.stem: Which measure of mortality uses total births (live births plus stillbirths) as its denominator?
questions.explanation: Perinatal and stillbirth rates use total births because the numerator includes stillbirths. A, C, D, E: These use live births.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slide 14

questions.stem: A region records 2,000 live births and 20 stillbirths in one year. Twelve infants die before 28 days and 8 die between 28 days and 1 year. What is the infant mortality rate?
questions.explanation: Infant mortality = deaths < 1 year / live births × 1,000 = (12 + 8) / 2,000 × 1,000 = 10 (= neonatal + post-neonatal). A: 12/2,000 is the neonatal rate. B: 8/2,000 is the post-neonatal rate. D: Uses total births; the infant rate uses live births. E: Adds stillbirths and uses total births.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slides 13–14

questions.stem: A small village wants to compare its mortality with the national population, but its age-specific death rates are unstable because each age group has very few deaths. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.A: Direct standardization to a standard population

questions.explanation: Indirect standardization applies standard (national) rates to the study population; it is used when population-specific rates are unavailable or unstable and gives a standardized mortality ratio. A: Direct standardization needs reliable age-specific rates in each population. B: Crude rates ignore age structure. C: CFR measures disease severity. E: Proportionate mortality isn't a measure of risk.
questions.source: Measures and Indicators of Health Status, slides 16, 18

questions.stem: Muscle strength graded from 1 (no movement) to 5 (normal) is which type of variable?
questions.explanation: Ordered categories without equal measured intervals → ordinal. A: Nominal has no order. B, D: Grades aren't measured or counted quantities. E: Binary has two categories.

questions.stem: Number of migraine attacks per month is which type of variable?
questions.explanation: It results from counting whole numbers. A, B: Not categorical. C: Not measured on a continuous scale. D: Not two categories.

questions.stem: A study examines whether daily screen time predicts sleep-quality scores in adolescents, accounting for age. Which is the dependent variable?
questions.explanation: The dependent (outcome, y) variable is the one expected to change: sleep quality. B: Screen time is the independent (predictor, x) variable. C: Age is a control variable affecting the association. D: Sample size isn't a study variable. E: Sex isn't part of the stated question.

questions.stem: Researchers use the mean BMI in a random sample of 500 students to estimate the mean BMI of all university students. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Generalizing from sample to population is inference. A: Describing the sample alone would be descriptive. B: A census includes everyone. C, E: These are ways of organizing data.

questions.stem: Why is random sampling essential?
questions.explanation: If every individual has an equal chance of selection, the sample represents the population, so results can be generalized by inference. A: Sample size is set separately. C: Random sampling doesn't equalize groups. D: Significance isn't guaranteed. E: Measurement error depends on the tools, not on sampling.

questions.stem: In a survey, 117 participants are smokers: 66 men and 51 women. Overall there are 250 men, 239 women, and 489 participants. What percentage of smokers are men?
questions.explanation: Among smokers is a column percentage: male smokers / all smokers = 66/117 (≈ 56%). B: 66/250 is the row percentage: the proportion of men who smoke. C: 66/489 is the proportion of all participants who are male smokers. D: 117/489 is the proportion of all participants who smoke. E: 51/117 is the proportion of smokers who are women.

questions.stem: Age recorded in categories (0–4, 5–9, 10–14 years, …) is which type of variable?
questions.explanation: Grouping age into ordered categories makes it ordinal (qualitative, ranked). A: Age in months is continuous, but categories are not. B: Discrete variables come from counting. C: Nominal categories have no order. D: Dichotomous means only two categories.

questions.stem: A competent adult Jehovah's Witness refuses a life-saving transfusion after being fully informed. Which principle most directly requires the physician to respect this?
questions.explanation: A voluntary, informed, competent refusal must be respected, even for life-saving treatment (autonomy). A: Beneficence pulls toward transfusing. B: Overriding the refusal would be paternalism, which the lecture says is no longer the accepted norm. D: Justice concerns fair distribution. E: Utility is the consequentialist principle of the greatest good for the greatest number.

questions.stem: A resident believes she must disclose a colleague's missed lesion to the patient because lying is wrong regardless of consequences. Which theory is she applying?
questions.explanation: Deontology (Kant, duty-based): an act is right or wrong in itself under a rule, regardless of outcome; Kant's first formulation is to always tell patients the truth. B, D: These judge an act by its consequences. C: Virtue theory asks what a good person would do. E: Double effect concerns an act with an intended good effect and a foreseen, unintended harmful one.

questions.stem: Which Belmont Report principle is applied through fair selection of research subjects?
questions.explanation: Justice → fair subject selection. A: Respect for persons → informed consent. B: Beneficence → risk/benefit assessment. C, E: Not Belmont's three principles.

questions.stem: A hysterectomy for uterine cancer in a pregnant woman ends the pregnancy. Which reasoning justifies the surgery?
questions.explanation: The intended, good effect is saving her life; fetal death is foreseen but neither intended nor the means to the good effect. A: Weighing the greatest good for the greatest number is not the reasoning the lecture applies. C: She decides, so it isn't paternalism. D: Justice concerns fair distribution of resources. E: Virtue theory asks what a good person would do, not how to treat a harmful side effect.

questions.stem: Which set of criteria do standard (UNOS-style) organ-allocation ethics weigh?

options.A: Urgency, age, social role, time on the waiting list
options.B: Compatibility, social support, number of dependents, urgency
options.C: Likelihood of benefit, ability to pay, compatibility, waiting time
options.D: Lifestyle, urgency, compatibility, time on the waiting list
options.E: Urgency, compatibility, likelihood of benefit, time on the waiting list

questions.explanation: Medical urgency, compatibility, likelihood of benefit and waiting time are weighed; judgments of social worth, lifestyle or 'deservingness' are deliberately excluded. A: Social role is a social-worth judgment. B: Social support and dependents are social-worth judgments. C: Ability to pay is not a criterion. D: Lifestyle is excluded.

questions.stem: On the lecture's risk–benefit grid, how is an intervention with high risk and high benefit classified and handled?
questions.explanation: High risk with high benefit is 'hazardous', and the decision is the patient's. A: Futile is low risk, low benefit. B: Consented is low risk, high benefit. C: Unacceptable is high risk, low benefit. E: Letting the physician decide would be paternalism.

questions.stem: In which situation does the lecture describe paternalism as broadly accepted?

options.A: A competent Jehovah's Witness refusing a transfusion
options.B: An 88-year-old choosing watchful waiting for metastatic cancer
options.C: A patient who is an immediate danger to himself after a suicide attempt
options.D: A well-informed patient who disagrees with the physician's preferred option
options.E: A patient who asks that his HIV status be kept from his wife

questions.explanation: Justified paternalism: when a patient is a danger to themselves, beneficence requires intervening because the patient cannot, at that moment, act in their own best interest. A, B: Competent, informed refusals that autonomy requires respecting. D: The ideal physician respects the informed patient as a partner. E: A confidentiality question, not one of overriding the patient's own treatment choice.

questions.stem: A physician becomes angry at her 80-year-old patient for not following his diet; her own father died of heart failure after ignoring similar advice. What is happening?
questions.explanation: The physician's unconscious reaction stems from her own past. A, B: Transference is the patient's reaction to the physician. C: Denial is a patient defense. E: Paternalism is deciding for the patient.
questions.source: Relationship Between Physician and Patient, slides 37, 46

questions.stem: Which model has the physician explain options and help the patient clarify their own values before choosing?
questions.explanation: The interpretive model elucidates the patient's values and helps select matching interventions. B: The physician decides. C: The physician informs; the patient chooses alone. D: The physician guides toward the best health values as a teacher/friend. E: A practice style, not one of the four models.
questions.source: Relationship Between Physician and Patient, slides 15–16

questions.stem: Which factor does the lecture link to a patient not adhering to the treatment plan?
questions.explanation: Patients with negative transference feel excessive resentment or anger when their expectations aren't met and may not adhere to the treatment plan. A, B, D, E: The lecture states adherence is not related to gender, religion, socioeconomic or marital status, race, intelligence, or education.
questions.source: Relationship Between Physician and Patient, slides 36–37

questions.stem: A 7-year-old girl involved in an accident won't say her name. What should the physician do?

options.A: Repeat the question using direct closed questions
options.B: Ask her questions in the third person
options.C: Avoid speaking with her until a parent arrives
options.D: Tell her that nothing bad will happen to her
options.E: Ask open-ended questions about the accident

questions.explanation: For young children the lecture recommends questions in the third person and non-verbal means such as drawing together. A: Repeating direct questions doesn't help a child who won't answer. C: Waiting delays communication. D: Falsely reassuring statements are inappropriate. E: Open-ended questions suit adults who speak freely; the slide's child-specific techniques are third-person questions and drawing.
questions.source: Relationship Between Physician and Patient, slides 32, 45

questions.stem: In a two-person conversation, roughly how much of the social meaning is carried by non-verbal components?
questions.explanation: Non-verbal cues (eye contact, posture, voice, proximity) carry ≥65%; verbal content carries <35%. A, B, C, D: Too low.
questions.source: Relationship Between Physician and Patient, slide 29

questions.stem: A patient is overly talkative and keeps drifting to unrelated topics. Which interviewing technique does the lecture recommend?

options.D: Remaining silent until the patient stops

questions.explanation: Direct questions elicit information quickly in an emergency or when the patient is seductive or overly talkative. A: Open-ended questions encourage free speech, the opposite of what's needed here. C, E: Techniques for young children. D: Silence lets the digression continue.
questions.source: Relationship Between Physician and Patient, slides 31–32

questions.stem: A competent 60-year-old's biopsy shows cancer. His adult children ask the physician to tell them first and let them relay the news. What does the lecture say?

options.A: Tell the children, who know him best
options.B: Tell him only the diagnosis, not the prognosis
options.C: Reassure him that the result is probably nothing serious
options.D: Refer him to a psychiatrist to deliver the news
options.E: Tell him directly and completely about diagnosis and prognosis

questions.explanation: Adult patients are generally told the complete truth about diagnosis and prognosis, directly and not relayed through relatives. A: Information is not relayed through relatives. B: The truth should be complete. C: Falsely reassuring statements are inappropriate. D: The treating physician is responsible; referral is for medical problems outside his range.
questions.source: Relationship Between Physician and Patient, slide 30

questions.stem: A surgeon decides how much to disclose by asking what a typical surgeon would tell patients about this operation. Which disclosure standard is this, and what is its main weakness?

options.A: Reasonable patient standard; hardest to apply because it must be tailored to each patient
options.B: Subjective standard; it focuses on the physician rather than the patient
options.C: Reasonable patient standard; it focuses on the physician rather than the patient
options.D: Reasonable physician standard; it focuses on the physician rather than the patient
options.E: Reasonable physician standard; hardest to apply because it must be tailored to each patient

questions.explanation: The reasonable physician standard asks what a typical physician would say; it is considered inconsistent with the goals of informed consent because it centers on the physician, not on what the patient needs to know. A, E: Tailoring to each patient is the subjective standard, the most challenging to practice. B: The subjective standard centers on this particular patient. C: The reasonable patient standard asks what the average patient needs to know.

questions.stem: An unconscious 45-year-old man in shock is brought to the emergency department with an intestinal perforation. No relatives or surrogate can be reached, and the surgeon judges that delay will be fatal. What is the appropriate basis for operating?

options.A: Presumed (implied) consent for an emergency intervention that prevents death
options.B: A general consent form signed at admission covers the surgery
options.C: The patient's presence in the hospital implies consent to treatment
options.D: A court order must be obtained before any surgery
options.E: Surgery must wait until the patient regains consciousness

questions.explanation: Presumed/implied consent applies only in emergencies when the patient is unconscious or incompetent, no surrogate is available, and the intervention prevents death or disability; a surgeon who acts with due care in good faith is not held responsible for an unfavourable outcome. B: Surgery and anesthesia require their own specific signed consent. C: Presence in the ward, ICU or clinic is not implied consent to all treatment. D, E: Delay would harm the patient; neither is required in a life-threatening emergency.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis agrees in the morning to a feeding tube. That evening she is disoriented and refuses it. The next morning she is lucid again and agrees, but cannot recall the evening. What should the team do?

options.A: Honor the evening refusal, since it is her most recent decision
options.B: Ask the court to appoint a guardian before proceeding
options.C: Place the tube, honoring the consistent decision made while lucid
options.D: Let her family decide, since her capacity varies
options.E: Postpone the procedure until she never shows confusion

questions.explanation: Decision-making capacity can vary with disease and medications; capacity is assessed during lucid periods, and a decision made consistently and persistently over time is honored. A: The refusal was made while disoriented. B: A court-appointed guardian is a rare last resort when no surrogate exists. D: She has capacity when lucid, so she decides. E: Unnecessary delay; her lucid decision is consistent.

questions.stem: Which practice meets the lecture's requirements for documenting informed consent before surgery?

options.A: A standard hospital form, signed by the patient, used for every procedure
options.B: A form signed routinely by the patient after a staff member points to the signature line
options.C: Verbal agreement recorded by the surgeon in the operative note
options.D: A form signed by the patient only, kept in the surgeon's office
options.E: A form in duplicate, signed by patient, doctor and an independent witness

questions.explanation: Consent should be dated, prepared in duplicate (a copy goes to the patient), signed by the patient or guardian, the doctor and an independent witness, and kept in the medical record. A: Consent is person- and procedure-specific; there is no standard form. B: Consent cannot be a signature on a dotted line obtained routinely by staff. C: Surgery and anesthesia usually require a signed form. D: The doctor and a witness must also sign, and it belongs in the patient's medical record.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her school teacher after a serious injury. Her parents and guardians cannot be reached. According to the lecture, from whom is consent obtained?

options.B: The teacher who brought the child
options.C: A judge, through a court order
options.E: No one until the parents are reached

questions.explanation: For children in an emergency when parents or guardians are unavailable, consent is taken from the person who brought the child, such as a school teacher. A: Children lack decision-making capacity to give consent, though their assent is sought when possible. C: Courts are for unresolved disputes or when no surrogate can be found. D: Not a listed decision-maker. E: Waiting would harm the child in an emergency.

questions.stem: Which Lebanese law governs patients' rights and informed consent?
questions.explanation: Law No. 574 of 2004 is the Lebanese law on Patients' Rights and Informed Consent. A: Human tissue and organ transplantation. B: Genetic tests. D: Implements the 1983 organ transplantation decree-law. E: Established the Lebanese National Consultative Committee on Ethics.
questions.source: Informed Consent, slide 16; Laws in Bioethics, slides 9–10

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with early dementia refuses surgery. His son wants him declared incompetent. Who makes that determination?

options.A: The treating physician, through a capacity assessment
options.B: A psychiatrist, since dementia is a mental disorder
options.C: A judge, possibly after consulting physicians
options.E: The son, as next of kin

questions.explanation: Competence is a legal term, and only the judge determines it; physicians are often consulted about the patient's decision-making capacity. If found incompetent, the court appoints a legal guardian. A, B: Physicians assess capacity, a clinical term, not legal competence. D: Not the body that rules on competence. E: Relatives cannot declare competence; all adults are presumed competent.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old married woman who cares for her 1-year-old son comes alone to the clinic and requests treatment for herself. Her parents live in another city. Who can consent to her treatment?

options.A: Her parents, since she is younger than 18
options.B: Her husband, as her legal representative
options.D: No one; treatment must wait until she turns 18
options.E: She can consent herself as an emancipated minor

questions.explanation: Minors (<18) are not legally competent, but an emancipated minor (self-supporting or in the military, or married or caring for her own children) is considered an adult and consents to her own care. A: Parental consent is not needed once emancipated. B: Marriage makes her emancipated; it does not transfer decisions to her husband. C: Guardians are appointed for persons found incompetent. D: She can consent now.

questions.stem: While examining a 25-year-old woman, a Lebanese physician finds evidence that she was raped. According to Article 7 (professional secrecy) of the Lebanese code, what must the physician do?

options.A: Report to the appropriate authorities whatever the victim wishes
options.B: Report to the Public Prosecutor if the victim gives written consent
options.C: Notify the Ministry of Public Health
options.D: Keep it secret unless summoned by the court as an expert
options.E: Report only if the physician believes it will prevent further crimes

questions.explanation: Article 7, clause 13: cases of rape and offenses against honor are reported to the Public Prosecutor provided the victim gives written consent. A: Reporting without consent applies to minors or incapacitated persons (clause 14). C: Notification to the Ministry is for reportable venereal diseases (clause 9). D: The expert exemption (clause 7) is a different situation. E: That wording concerns crimes the physician discovers, not this clause.

questions.stem: During a routine visit, an adult patient confesses to his Lebanese physician that he committed a burglary last year. According to Article 7 of the Lebanese code, what should the physician do?

options.B: Report it to the public prosecution
options.C: Report it to the judicial police
options.D: Report it only if the patient gives written consent
options.E: Warn the victim directly, as in the Tarasoff decision

questions.explanation: Article 7, clause 5: a physician shall not report a crime that a patient confessed to; only a crime the physician discovers during examination must be reported to the public prosecution. B: Applies to crimes discovered on examination, not confessed ones. C: Even when summoned by the judicial police, the physician may keep some secrets (clause 4). D: Written consent is the condition for reporting rape (clause 13). E: Tarasoff concerns a credible threat to another person, not a past crime.

questions.stem: In a Lebanese hospital, a competent 40-year-old man whose beliefs forbid blood transfusion refuses blood. He then develops hemorrhage that puts his life in permanent danger. According to the Lebanese code, what should the physician do?

options.B: Respect the refusal in all circumstances
options.C: Obtain consent for transfusion from his family
options.D: Obtain judicial authorization, then act by professional conscience
options.E: Advise him of his responsibility and report to the health authorities

questions.explanation: Clause 9: the physician respects the refusal, except when there is permanent danger; then, after obtaining authorization from the appropriate judicial authorities, the physician acts according to professional conscience, bearing full responsibility. A: Judicial authorization is required first. B: The law makes an exception for permanent danger. C: Family consent is not the mechanism in the law. E: That is the rule for refusal of required vaccinations (clause 8).

questions.stem: One month after naming her neighbor in a durable power of attorney for health care, a 75-year-old woman has a stroke and is unlikely to regain consciousness. Her son, who lives with her, insists on continued life support; the neighbor asks that it be withdrawn. Whose decision should the physician follow?

options.A: The son's, as next of kin
options.B: The neighbor's, as her designated representative
options.C: The physician's own judgment of her best interest
options.E: Neither; keep her on life support until they agree

questions.explanation: A durable power of attorney is an advance directive in which a competent person designates someone as her legal representative for health care decisions when she can no longer make them, so the neighbor decides. A: Family members act as surrogates (substituted judgment) only when there is no advance directive, and their personal wishes are irrelevant. C: Best-interest decisions apply when no surrogate is available. D: A valid designated representative already exists. E: The designated representative's decision stands.

questions.stem: According to the lecture, the medical history reveals approximately what share of the information needed for an accurate diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The history reveals 60–80% of the information needed; the studies shown give history 60–76%, examination 12–20%, tests 11–20%. A: Roughly the share from examination or tests. B, C: Too low. E: Too high; examination and tests still add information.

questions.stem: In Beckman's 1984 study, how long did patients usually need to finish their opening statement if not interrupted?
questions.explanation: Most patients who weren't interrupted finished in under 60 seconds and none took longer than 150 seconds, so interrupting saves little time and costs information. A: 18 seconds is when doctors interrupted. C: Longer than most needed. D: 150 seconds was the maximum, not the usual. E: No patient took this long.

questions.stem: A doctor types on the computer while asking questions. The patient pauses before answering and shifts in her chair to catch the doctor's attention. Which non-verbal element is missing?
questions.explanation: Without eye contact, patients give less information, withhold their initial reply until eye contact is given, and use body movement to catch the doctor's gaze. A: Handshake or physical contact. B: Physical distance between communicators. C: Rate, volume, rhythm, intonation. D: Punctuality, being hurried or slow to respond.

questions.stem: Which is an appropriate way to open the interview after introductions?

options.C: "What would you like to discuss today?"

questions.explanation: An open question identifies the patient's reasons for coming. A: Leading. B, D: Closed questions too early. E: Doctor's agenda first.

questions.stem: Which property belongs to non-verbal rather than verbal communication?

options.A: It is discrete, with clear endpoints
options.B: It occurs in a single mode at a time
options.C: It is mostly under voluntary control
options.D: It continues as long as both are present
options.E: It carries less weight than verbal cues

questions.explanation: Non-verbal communication is continuous, occurs in several modes at once, and operates at or beyond conscious awareness. A, B, C: Properties of verbal communication. E: Non-verbal wins out over verbal cues.

questions.stem: Diagnostic errors occur in 10–15% of diagnoses. According to the lecture, about 80% of these errors stem from:
questions.explanation: 80% of diagnostic errors are based on information missed in the history or physical examination. A, B: Tests contribute only a minority of diagnostic information. D, E: Not cited as the source of diagnostic error.

questions.stem: "Anyone would find this very difficult." Which empathic technique is this?
questions.explanation: Legitimation validates the patient's feelings as understandable. B: Reflection names the emotion ("I can see this upsets you"). C: Partnership is "Let's work together." D: Support is "I want to help." E: Summarizing restates content.

questions.stem: Which question is a leading question that should be avoided?

options.C: "Do you have chest pain, cough, or fever?"
options.D: "How would you rate the pain from 1 to 10?"
options.E: "You haven't had any urine problems, have you?"

questions.explanation: A leading question suggests the expected answer. A: An open question. B, D: Appropriate focused questions. C: A multiple question, also to be avoided, but it doesn't suggest an answer.

questions.stem: While taking a pain history, the student asks, "Does the pain interfere with your daily activities or with your sleep?" Which SOCRATES component is this?
questions.explanation: In the lecture's SOCRATES, Severity asks whether the pain interferes with daily activities or sleep. A: Timing is variation in intensity during the day. C: Associations are other accompanying features. D: Character describes the pain (sharp, burning, crushing). E: What makes it better or worse.

questions.stem: After obtaining the HPI, the student asks how the illness affects daily life, what the patient thinks is causing it, how they feel, and what they hope for. Which approach is this?
questions.explanation: FIFE: Function, Ideas, Feelings, Expectations. A, B: Characterize symptoms. D: A note format. E: A head-to-toe screen.

questions.stem: Which is a correctly written chief complaint?

options.A: JN, 45-year-old male truck driver, with three weeks of "bad back pains."
options.B: JN, 45-year-old man with three weeks of acute lumbar radiculopathy.
options.D: JN, 45, sharp back pain since lifting, worse in the morning, 6/10.
options.E: JN, 45-year-old smoker with hypertension and back pain.

questions.explanation: The chief complaint is a one-liner in the patient's own words with age, sex, occupation, problem and duration. B: Uses medical jargon. C: Missing age, sex and occupation. D: Characterizing the pain belongs in the HPI. E: Habits and chronic problems belong in social and past medical history; no duration.

questions.stem: During the review of systems, a patient with abdominal pain reports nausea, which is relevant to the present illness. Where should it be recorded?

options.A: In the review of systems only
options.B: In both the HPI and the review of systems
options.C: In the HPI, not repeated in the review of systems

questions.explanation: Symptoms relevant to the HPI go in the HPI and are not repeated in the review of systems. A: The ROS screens for symptoms not otherwise elicited. B: The slide says not to repeat HPI information. D: For major past health events. E: A one-line reason for the visit.

questions.stem: Using the lecture's definitions, how is a woman with 3 pregnancies and 2 live births recorded?
questions.explanation: G (gravida) = number of pregnancies = 3; P (para) = live births = 2. A: Reverses G and P. C: P counts live births, not pregnancies. D: G counts all pregnancies. E: G is not pregnancies plus births.

questions.stem: Which statement is one of Virchow's principles for reforming medicine?

options.A: Health is primarily the responsibility of the individual patient
options.B: Social conditions affect health but lie outside scientific study
options.C: Disease prevention belongs to the state, not to physicians
options.D: Measures to promote health and combat disease must be social as well as medical
options.E: Epidemics are best controlled by medical measures such as quarantine

questions.explanation: Virchow's three principles: the people's health is a matter of direct social concern; social and economic conditions affect health and must be scientifically investigated; and measures must be social as well as medical. A: He made health a social concern. B: He insisted these relations be studied scientifically. C: He saw the physician as the natural advocate for the poor. E: He called for social, not only medical, measures.

questions.stem: What did Virchow conclude caused the 1848 typhus epidemic in Upper Silesia?
questions.explanation: He traced it to poverty and underdevelopment, recommending education, freedom, and welfare. B, C, D, E: Not his conclusions.

questions.stem: Higher HIV rates among low-income women who exchange sex for food are best described as:

options.B: A health disparity without a social cause

questions.explanation: A disparity is any difference in health outcomes; an inequity is the type closely linked with social or economic disadvantage, here poverty driving transactional sex. A, C: The cause is social, not biological. B: The difference has a clear socioeconomic cause. D: Too narrow; the driver is limited economic opportunity.

questions.stem: Which public-health achievement is credited to Virchow?

options.B: Legislation creating the Chilean National Health Service
options.C: Berlin city sewage systems and mandatory meat inspection
options.D: Founding the Latin American Social Medicine Association
options.E: Training physicians in 'revolutionary medicine' in Cuba

questions.explanation: Virchow's accomplishments: city sewage systems, mandatory meat inspection, ventilation and heating of public buildings, school health services, and better working conditions for nurses. A, B: Allende. D: Reformers from Juan Cesar Garcia's seminar group (1984). E: Che Guevara.

questions.stem: Unemployment among people living with HIV/AIDS ranges from 45% to 65%. Which relationship between SES and HIV does this illustrate?

options.D: Rural residence affects access to HIV care

questions.explanation: HIV status can lower SES by constraining the ability to work and earn income. A: Limited economic opportunity leading to risky sex. C: Low SES delaying treatment and lowering adherence. D: Distance, few HIV-expert providers, stigma. E: A cause of infection, not an effect on SES.

questions.stem: Which feature made smallpox a good candidate for eradication?

options.B: An animal reservoir allowed targeted culling
options.E: Patients were most contagious before symptoms appeared

questions.explanation: Smallpox features: direct person-to-person spread with no vector or reservoir, a distinctive rash that made diagnosis easy, lifelong immunity in survivors, and severe symptoms that kept infectious patients in bed. B, C: There was no reservoir or vector. D: The distinctive rash made cases obvious. E: Once infectious, patients were bedridden and infected few others.

questions.stem: USAID funding a vaccination program in one partner country is an example of which kind of global-health player?
questions.explanation: Bilateral organizations involve one donor and one recipient. A: Banks are owned by many member states. B: UN agencies are multilateral. C: Movements are networks of activists. D: USAID is governmental.

questions.stem: Which global-health challenge does the lecture link specifically to large private foundations such as the Gates Foundation?
questions.explanation: The growing influence of philanthropic organizations in setting priorities raises questions about accountability, transparency and priority-setting. A: Linked to multiple institutions, donors and actors. B: Linked to WHO's limited, unevenly distributed funding. D: Infectious disease, NCDs, emergencies and climate change at once. E: Linked to differences in national resources.

questions.stem: Which risk factor is linked to the top ten causes of death worldwide?
questions.explanation: Tobacco is related to all top ten causes of mortality. A: Linked mainly to HIV and STIs. B: Linked to diarrheal disease. C: Linked to infection susceptibility. E: Not listed.

questions.stem: Which global-health player is owned and governed by member states and provides long-term loans and grants to low- and middle-income countries?

options.C: Multilateral development bank such as the World Bank

questions.explanation: Multilateral development banks (World Bank, African, Asian and Inter-American Development Banks) are owned by member states and mobilize development financing through loans, grants and technical assistance. A: WHO gives technical assistance, standards and coordination. B: One donor country, one recipient. D: Fosters public-health collaboration among member states. E: Loose activist networks that shape the agenda.

questions.stem: Although a smallpox vaccine existed since 1796, what made eradication a practical goal in the 1950s?

options.B: The vaccine could be mass-produced and stored without refrigeration
options.C: Creation of the WHO Smallpox Eradication Unit
options.D: Mandatory case reporting by all WHO member states
options.E: Discovery that smallpox had no animal reservoir

questions.explanation: Eradication became practical once the vaccine could be mass-produced and stored without refrigeration. A: The bifurcated needle (1960s) was a later breakthrough that cut costs. C, D: Parts of the later WHO campaign, not what made the goal practical. E: A disease feature that made smallpox a good candidate, not the 1950s development.

questions.stem: Under-5 mortality falls steadily from the poorest to the richest household quintile within a country. What does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Health improves step by step with socioeconomic position. A: A threshold would affect only the poorest. B: Not genetic. D: The pattern is systematic. E: Too narrow.
questions.source: The Social Determinants of Health, slide 11

questions.stem: The WHO defines social determinants of health as the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work and age. What does the WHO say shapes these conditions?

options.C: Availability and quality of health care services
options.E: Distribution of money, power and resources

questions.explanation: The WHO definition states these conditions are shaped by the distribution of money, power and resources at global and local levels. A, B, D: Layers of the Dahlgren–Whitehead model, not what the WHO definition names as the shaping force. C: Health care services are one determinant among many.
questions.source: The Social Determinants of Health, slides 4–5

questions.stem: Road traffic deaths fell in highly motorized countries between 1987 and 1995 mainly because of:

options.A: Policies such as compulsory seat belts and drunk-driving penalties
options.D: Lower speed of vehicles due to congestion

questions.explanation: The lecture cites seat-belt laws and penalties for driving under the influence. B, C, D, E: Not the cited cause.
questions.source: The Social Determinants of Health, slide 20

questions.stem: According to the lecture, which sectors should health policy addressing the social determinants of health involve?

options.A: The health ministry alone, since health is its mandate
options.B: Health and finance ministries, which fund care
options.C: All sectors, since policy in each one shapes health
options.D: The private sector, through insurance coverage

questions.explanation: Policy relevance of SDH: health concerns should involve all sectors (transport, economy, employment, education, agriculture, environment, security), not just health policy. A, B, D, E: Too narrow; each leaves out sectors that shape health.
questions.source: The Social Determinants of Health, slide 6

questions.stem: Two unemployed men receive identical income support and housing. The one who feels ashamed of being jobless and is shunned by his neighbours has worse health. What does this illustrate?
questions.explanation: Beyond material conditions, the social meaning of being poor, unemployed or excluded, including stigma, affects health. A: Their material circumstances are identical. C: The gradient compares socioeconomic levels; both men are at the same level. D: Access is not mentioned as different. E: Nothing suggests a genetic cause.
questions.source: The Social Determinants of Health, slides 11, 14

questions.stem: A government passes a law to stop private companies from polluting a town's water supply. Which state obligation does this fulfill?
questions.explanation: Protect = preventing third parties from interfering with the right. B: Respect = the state itself not interfering. C: Fulfil = adopting measures to realize the right (e.g., building water systems). D, E: Not obligation levels.

questions.stem: Which international treaty article contains the most detailed provision on the right to health?
questions.explanation: ICESCR includes the most detailed provision: Article 12.1, the right to the highest attainable standard of physical and mental health. A: UDHR 25.1 is the right to a standard of living adequate for health (food, clothing, housing, medical care). B, C, E: Right-to-health provisions limited to specific populations (persons with disabilities, children, women).

questions.stem: A state signed a human-rights treaty but hasn't ratified it. What is its legal position?

options.A: Fully bound by every provision, as if ratified
options.B: Not bound, but must not undermine the treaty's purpose
options.C: Not bound, and free to act against its aims
options.D: Bound only to the treaty's minimum core obligations
options.E: A full party, as with accession

questions.explanation: Signature is a preliminary endorsement: no binding legal obligation, but the State must refrain from acts that undermine the treaty's object and purpose. A, D: Only ratification or accession creates binding obligations. C: Signature still carries the duty not to undermine the treaty. E: Accession makes a State a full party (same effect as ratification); signature alone does not.

questions.stem: According to the lecture, what distinguishes harm reduction for people who use drugs?

options.A: It requires abstinence before services are offered
options.B: It relies on criminal penalties to deter use
options.C: It serves only people already in drug treatment
options.D: It puts legal outcomes ahead of health outcomes
options.E: It does not necessarily require abstinence

questions.explanation: Harm reduction is evidence-based policy and practice that minimizes the health, social and legal harms of drug use and protects rights, without necessarily requiring abstinence, meeting people 'where they are'. A, C: It doesn't require abstinence or prior treatment. B: Criminalization drives unsafe injecting. D: It focuses on improving health outcomes.

questions.stem: A country cannot build a national primary-care network immediately because of limited resources, but it expands coverage every year toward measurable targets. Which ICESCR concept allows this?
questions.explanation: Progressive realization recognizes resource constraints and that the right to health can't be achieved immediately, but requires States to move as expeditiously and effectively as possible, tracked with indicators and benchmarks. A: The minimum core is what all States are obligated to implement, not a time allowance. B: Specific essential services (e.g., immunization, maternal care), not a timeline. D: A way of joining a treaty. E: Refraining from interfering with the right.

questions.stem: Which item is part of the minimum core obligations of the right to health, rather than the ICESCR priority obligations?

options.B: Provision of essential drugs as defined by the WHO
options.C: Reproductive, maternal and child health care
options.E: Education on the main health problems

questions.explanation: Minimum core: non-discriminatory access, minimum safe food, basic shelter, sanitation and water, essential drugs (WHO), equitable distribution, and a national public health strategy. A, C, D, E: Priority obligations listed by the ICESCR in addition to the core.

questions.stem: A State that took no part in negotiating or signing a treaty later becomes a party after the treaty has entered into force. What is this called, and what is its effect?

options.C: Accession; same legal effect as ratification
options.E: Reservation; binding only for chosen articles

questions.explanation: Accession is accepting the opportunity to join a treaty already negotiated and signed by others, usually after it enters into force; it has the same legal effect as ratification. A: Signature is only a preliminary endorsement. B: Ratification follows the State's own prior signature. D: Accession is not weaker. E: Reservations are not covered in the lecture.
